# Emergency Wound and Trauma Care — A Practical Manual for First Responders and Health Professionals

This manual is for the person who arrives first and has to act: the lay first aider at a road crash, the trained first responder, the emergency medical technician or paramedic on an ambulance, the nurse in a district hospital, and the physician or surgeon who receives what they send. It follows the injured patient from the moment of the injury to the operating theatre, covering wounds and bleeding, penetrating and firearm trauma, injuries of the chest, fractures of every limb, burns, amputations, head, neck and spinal injury, and the complications that kill after the injury itself: shock, compartment syndrome, crush syndrome and infection.

The manual keeps three levels of practice apart, and says which one it is speaking to at every step. There is what the lay first aider may do with bare hands and whatever is in the car, what the trained responder may do with a kit, a protocol and authorization, and what belongs to definitive hospital and surgical care. The same wound asks something different of each pair of hands, and knowing what one must not attempt is as much a part of competence as knowing what to do.

The principle that governs every chapter is that the first responder's job is not to make the injury look normal. The priorities, in the order they must be met, are to keep the patient alive, to control life-threatening bleeding, to keep the airway open and the breathing working, to prevent further injury, to protect wounds and exposed tissue, to immobilize what must be immobilized, to recognize shock and the other lethal complications, to keep the patient warm, to watch continuously, and to reach definitive care as quickly and safely as possible.

The manual has forty-nine chapters in seventeen parts, followed by four appendices: the emergency algorithms spoken as sequences of actions, the practical skills laboratory with its simulation scenarios, a quick-reference card for the problems met most often, and the closing statement of the core principle and the limits of each scope of practice.

This is educational material. It does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol or the law of the country in which you work. It teaches decisions rather than prescriptions, and it gives no dose of any drug. Procedures such as the extraction of a bullet, the surgical exploration of a wound, the reduction of a fracture, internal or external fixation, the repair of a vessel, tendon or nerve, fasciotomy and deep debridement belong to definitive surgical care: they are described here so that a responder recognizes when they are needed, never as first-aid measures.

# Chapter 1 — Principles of Emergency Trauma Care

The person who arrives first at a scene of injury holds the whole course of the patient's survival in a few unglamorous acts, and almost none of them look like the emergency that people imagine. The goals of first aid are not to make the injury look normal, to name the damage, or to finish a treatment, because none of those things saves a life in the field. They are to keep the airway open, to stop the bleeding that can be stopped by hand, to keep the patient warm, and to move the patient toward definitive care as quickly and as safely as the scene allows. A list of that kind is easy to remember and easy to dismiss, because it is boring, and the boredom is precisely why it works, since a frightened person in the rain can repeat it without hesitation. What kills patients in the first hours is rarely a lack of sophistication; it is a failure to do one of those simple things, or to do them in the wrong order. This chapter sets out the principles that govern every other chapter of this manual, and it is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The list is boring because each item asks the responder to do less than instinct demands rather than more. Instinct says to lift the dressing and see whether the bleeding has stopped, to move the patient to a place that looks tidier, and to straighten the limb that looks wrong, and each of those instincts can undo work that has already been done. The discipline of first aid is therefore a discipline of holding still: pressure is held without lifting an edge, the patient is kept in the position found, wet clothing is replaced with covering rather than with exposure, and the journey begins as soon as it is safe rather than as soon as the patient looks comfortable. The uncomfortable truth is that such restraint feels like doing nothing, and a bystander may judge the responder as inactive while the responder is in fact keeping the patient alive. Restraint also protects the patient from the second injury, which is the injury caused by the rescue itself.

No clinical act may begin before the scene has been made safe, because a responder who is injured adds a patient to a scene that already has more than it can manage. The hazards that kill rescuers form a short and repeating list, and every one of them can be recognized before it is entered. Moving traffic on a road, fire and its smoke, live electrical cables and the current in a wire believed to be dead, deep or fast water, structures that may collapse, an animal that is still loose, and a person who is still violent are the dangers of the scene itself, and each is a lethal possibility rather than a nuisance. Contaminated material is the quieter hazard, because blood, vomit, and tissue carry infection that enters through a break in the skin or a splash into the eye. The finding that reveals the hazard is often simply looking before moving: the smell of fuel, the hum of a generator, a wire lying across the water, and a crowd that has not yet stopped shouting. The lay first aider who cannot make the scene safe does not enter it, and the willingness to stop at the edge is one of the most valuable skills taught in this manual.

Making a scene safe is a sequence, and it begins with removing the threat rather than reaching the patient. Traffic is answered by warning approaching drivers, by placing a vehicle to protect the space, and by waiting until the road is held before stepping into it. Fire is answered by moving upwind and by refusing to enter a burning vehicle, because a fuel tank can burst and a structure can fall without warning. Electricity is answered by having the supply isolated by a person authorized to do it, and until that isolation is confirmed the wire is treated as live and the patient touching it is not touched. Water is answered by reaching with an object from the bank rather than entering the current, and violence is answered by withdrawing to a position that can be defended and by waiting for those trained and authorized to control it. The trained responder or paramedic works within the same order but has the equipment and the authority to hold the road, to cut the power, and to enter a structure that has been declared stable.

Protection of the rescuer's own body belongs before the first hand is laid on a patient, and it is measured by what is actually available rather than by what is ideal. The trained responder carries personal protective equipment that is issued and replenished, which includes gloves, eye protection, a gown or apron, and a barrier for the mouth if resuscitation is needed, and it is used for every patient rather than only for the ones who look infectious. The lay first aider has whatever is in the car or the house, and ordinary gloves, a plastic bag over the hands, glasses or a scarf over the eyes, and a folded cloth over the mouth are each better than bare hands. The purpose is not a sterile field, which the roadside cannot provide, but a barrier between the patient's blood and the responder's skin and eyes. A responder with a cut on the hand covers it before the glove goes on, and a responder who is splashed washes the area with soap and water as soon as another person has taken over the patient. The finding that tells the responder to replace the barrier is a glove that has torn, a barrier that has become soaked, or bleeding heavy enough to strike the face.

Once the scene is safe, the first piece of clinical evidence is not the wound but the mechanism of injury, which is the story of the energy that acted on the body. A mechanism is a prediction about damage that no eye can see from the outside. A fall from a height greater than 3 meters, a figure offered only as a teaching illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, predicts compression of the spine and of the heels, damage inside the abdomen, and fractures of the pelvis and the long bones. A vehicle collision predicts deceleration injuries in which organs move within the body and tear where they are attached, and the direction of the impact decides which organs are at risk. A blast predicts a pressure wave that injures the lungs and the eardrums, and fragments that travel far beyond the place where the device exploded. A knife or a bullet predicts a track whose depth cannot be judged from its opening, and a crushing weight predicts muscle damage that may poison the patient hours later.

The reason mechanism predicts hidden damage is that injury is a transfer of energy, and the body absorbs that energy according to the tissue it meets. Skin may close over a cavity that has been torn inside, a bone may break without piercing the skin while the vessels beside it are torn, and a blow that leaves no mark on the head may still have shaken the brain within the skull. The responder who understands this stops searching for a wound that explains the patient's condition and begins searching for the injury that the mechanism makes likely. A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient or a real incident, is the rider thrown over the handlebars who stands up with a grazed knee, where the knee explains nothing about the pain in the abdomen, the tenderness over the spleen, or the blood collecting where no one can see it. The same reasoning applies to the patient who fell down a short flight of stairs, whose alcohol and whose age may distract the responder from the injury the fall produced. Mechanism is not a diagnosis, but it is the question that makes the examination purposeful instead of random.

The examination is divided into two surveys, and the difference between them is the difference between saving a life and missing an injury. The primary survey is the search for the conditions that will kill the patient within minutes, and it is performed in a fixed order remembered as ABCDE: airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure. Each letter is a question, and the answer to each decides whether the responder moves to the next or stops to treat what has just been found. The secondary survey is the full head-to-toe examination that follows, and it looks for every injury not yet found, together with the history of what happened and the patient's own account where the patient can give one. The primary survey is repeated whenever the patient's condition changes, because a patient who was stable when first seen may not be stable after a move, a dressing, or part of a journey. The order of the primary survey is not a preference but a rule, and the reason is that treating a broken limb before opening an airway will not help a patient who is not breathing.

The order is not negotiable because each step protects the one that follows, and because a later step performed first can make an earlier one impossible. Airway comes first because no work on the chest or on a bleeding limb can revive a patient whose passage for air is closed, and breathing comes next because oxygen that cannot enter the lungs cannot reach the brain. Circulation comes after that because a patient who has lost the blood to carry the oxygen is dying for a different reason, and in many services the control of catastrophic external hemorrhage is placed ahead of everything else, so that a limb pouring blood is controlled before the airway is examined. Disability follows, which means the level of consciousness together with the pupils and the movement of the limbs, because a patient who was talking and has become silent is telling the responder that the brain is losing its supply. Exposure comes last, in which the patient is undressed enough to be examined and then covered at once, because the search for injuries must not become a cause of cooling. The finding that returns the responder to the beginning of the sequence is any change for the worse, at any point, in any patient.

The principle of life before limb decides the order when two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands. It means that an action which preserves the patient's survival is chosen before one that preserves a limb, even when the limb is the more urgent-looking problem and even when it could still be saved by prompt care. The situations where it decides are specific and repeated: a patient with a mangled leg and a closed airway, a patient with an amputated hand and a chest filling with air, and a patient with a deformed limb and a circulation failing from bleeding somewhere else. In each of those pairs both actions are correct, and the principle chooses the one performed first rather than the one performed instead. The reason is that a limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot, and that the attempt to save a limb while the patient is dying of something else usually loses both. The finding that settles the order is not the size of the wound but whether the patient is currently able to breathe and to circulate.

The first of the two failures that most often undo a rescue is the hemorrhage that is not seen, and it is missed because the responder is looking at the injury that is visible. Blood can collect in the chest until the lung is compressed, in the abdomen until the belly is distended and rigid, in the pelvis behind the peritoneum, and in the thigh around a broken femur, and none of those collections is obvious at the roadside. The findings that reveal concealed bleeding are a patient who is pale, cool, restless, thirsty, or increasingly confused while the visible wound is small, and a pulse that is climbing while the pressure is falling. The lay first aider cannot measure these and must not press into a tender belly or spring the pelvis to test it, because both acts may worsen the bleeding, so what the lay first aider does is call emergency medical services early, keep the patient still and warm, and report every change observed. The trained responder repeats the observations, watches the abdomen for distension and the chest for dullness, and supports the circulation while moving toward the place where the bleeding can be stopped. Definitive hospital care opens the cavity, finds the bleeding vessel or organ, and controls it, and no field measure takes the place of that operation.

Emergency medical services are activated as soon as the scene has been made safe and the patient has been assessed, and they are activated early rather than at the moment the responder runs out of ideas. The call carries the same information in the same order every time, so that the dispatcher can send the right resource without asking twice. The location is given first, with a landmark, a road name, and a direction of travel, because a team that cannot find the patient is no help at all. The number of patients is given next, with a brief statement of what is wrong with each, so that the response is scaled to the scene rather than to the first patient found. The mechanism of injury is reported, because it tells the receiving team what to expect and what equipment to bring, and the hazards that remain are named so that nobody else is injured on arrival. What has already been done is stated plainly, including pressure applied, a tourniquet placed and the time it was placed, and whether the patient has been moved.

When there are more patients than there are hands, the responder stops treating the nearest patient and begins to sort them, and that act has a name, which is triage. Triage is the deliberate decision about who is treated first, and it is made by the trained responder or by a clinician under the authority of the local protocol, because it involves withholding care from some patients in order to give it to others. The sorting asks a small number of questions in a fixed order: who can walk, who is breathing, who is breathing after the airway is opened, who has a pulse that can be felt, and who responds to voice or to pain. Those questions are answered with the eyes and the hands within seconds, and the answers place each patient into a group that carries a priority rather than a diagnosis. A patient who can walk is moved to a safe place and given a task, because that patient is not the most urgent and may be able to help. A patient who is not breathing after the airway has been opened is placed in the group treated last when the scene is overwhelmed, and this is the counterintuitive part of triage that must be stated plainly.

The decision to leave a patient who is already dying, in order to reach patients who can still be saved, is the hardest decision in this chapter and the one most likely to be called inhuman. It is taken because a rescue that spends all its hands on one patient who cannot be saved may lose several who could have been saved, and because the number of survivors is the measure the scene must answer to. The responder who makes that decision does not make it alone where a medical controller or a senior clinician can be reached, and the local protocol decides how such patients are identified and how they are kept as comfortable as the scene allows. Comfort in this setting means warmth, shelter from the weather, a position that eases breathing where that is possible, and the presence of a person who stays with the patient if one can be spared. Nobody in this manual is authorized to end a life or to hasten a death, and nothing in triage is a substitute for the ethical and legal framework of the country in which the responder works. The lay first aider does not perform triage and is not asked to choose between patients, because that decision belongs to the trained responder and to the system that supports them.

The secondary survey begins only when the primary survey has been completed and the patient has been stabilized enough to tolerate it, and it belongs to the trained responder and to definitive hospital care rather than to the lay first aider. It is a head-to-toe examination performed in a fixed order, beginning at the scalp and the face and moving to the neck, the chest, the abdomen, the pelvis, the back, and then each limb, with the front and the back of the patient both examined. The history that accompanies it includes the mechanism of injury, the time of the injury, the patient's illnesses and medicines, the last time the patient ate, and the patient's allergies and tetanus status where those are known. The secondary survey is where the injury that the primary survey did not need to find is discovered, which is the fractured wrist, the dislocated shoulder, the bruise over the kidney, and the small wound that will need cleaning and protection against tetanus. The finding that ends the secondary survey and returns the responder to the beginning is any deterioration in the patient, because a patient who is worsening needs the primary survey again before the examination continues. The lay first aider's part in this survey is to keep the patient warm, to keep the patient still, and to answer the questions of the receiving team as accurately as possible.

Cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and protecting the patient against it is part of the same work as stopping the bleeding. A patient who is bleeding, burned, undressed for examination, lying on cold ground, or receiving fluids at room temperature loses heat quickly, and cold makes blood clot poorly, deepens shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is the figure often used to describe the point at which those effects become serious, and that figure, like every other in this chapter, is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line differs between services and between editions. The lay first aider removes wet clothing, covers the patient with whatever is at hand, including blankets, coats, and foil, and insulates the patient from the ground, because much of the heat is lost downward. The trained responder continues that protection during transport and limits the time the patient is exposed during repeated examinations. The finding that warns the responder that cooling has already begun is a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold, because shivering is the body's attempt to make heat.

Every action in this manual belongs to a named level of provider, and the level is decided by training, equipment, authorization, and protocol rather than by the urgency of the moment. The lay first aider may press on a wound, open an airway with the hands, keep a patient warm, and send for help, and may not perform any act that requires a kit or a decision about a substance. The trained responder and the paramedic may use the equipment they carry and the procedures their service authorizes, which may include a tourniquet, a dressing that controls bleeding, splinting, airway adjuncts, and oxygen, with the decision about whether oxygen is given belonging to the protocol and the prescriber rather than to this book. The decisions about pain relief, about antibiotics, about protection against tetanus, and about fluids are clinical decisions, and the substance, the amount, the route, and the timing are set by the local protocol and the prescriber, so a listener cannot take a prescription from these pages. Definitive hospital care owns the removal of an embedded object, the exploration of a wound, the reduction of a fracture, the repair of a vessel or a tendon or a nerve, the opening of a cavity, and the operation that controls internal bleeding, and none of those is a field procedure. Knowing what one must not attempt is as much a part of competence as knowing what to do, because an unauthorized attempt often converts a survivable injury into a fatal one.

The two causes of a rescue that fails are the scene hazard that was not recognized and the hemorrhage that was not seen, and both are failures of attention rather than failures of skill. The first is prevented by looking before moving, by naming the hazard aloud, and by refusing to enter a scene that has not been made safe by someone with the authority to make it safe. The second is prevented by treating the mechanism of injury as a prediction, by examining the patient rather than the wound, and by repeating the observations until the patient reaches a place where the bleeding can be controlled. A third and quieter failure belongs with them, which is the failure to record what was done, whether it is a tourniquet whose time was not written where the receiving team will see it or a change in the patient that was never passed on. The record is part of the treatment, because the receiving team continues a story that the field began, and a story with a gap in it forces them to start again. The finding that should prompt a written note is any intervention, any change, and the time at which either occurred.

The patient is watched continuously from the first contact until the handover, because the condition of a trauma patient can change within a single journey. Watching means repeating the same observations in the same order and comparing them with what was found before, rather than trusting the impression of the moment. The findings that should send the responder back to the beginning are a falling level of consciousness, a breathing pattern that has become faster or slower or noisier, a pulse that has become weak or rapid, skin that has become colder or paler, and bleeding that has restarted beneath a dressing. The destination is chosen before the patient is moved, and it is the nearest facility that can provide the care the patient needs, which may be a trauma center with imaging, an operating room, and an intensive care unit, or a district hospital that can stabilize the patient and arrange a transfer. Transport is both urgent and gentle, because speed that throws the patient around adds injuries and pain, and because a patient who arrives in worse condition has gained nothing from the hurry.

A manual can describe principles, but it cannot stand in the place of training, and the difference matters most at the moment when a reader becomes a responder. The skills in this book are learned with a teacher, practiced on models and on each other, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without supervision. Local protocol decides what equipment is carried, what procedures are authorized, whom the responder may call for advice, and which hospital receives the patient, and that protocol takes precedence over anything written here. Where this manual describes a figure or a threshold, it does so to explain the reasoning and never to set a rule, because such numbers differ between services, countries, and editions of the same guideline. The reader is asked to bring the principles to the training, to keep the training current, and to work within the system that supervises the care.

To summarize, the first responder's task is not to make the injury look normal but to keep the patient alive, and the acts that accomplish this are few and unglamorous. Scene safety comes before the patient, so traffic, fire, electricity, water, unstable structures, violence, animals, and contaminated material are dealt with before any hand is laid on a wound, and personal protective equipment is whatever barrier is actually available. The mechanism of injury is the first clinical evidence, because it predicts damage that no eye can see, and the primary survey is performed in the fixed order of ABCDE before the secondary survey begins. Life comes before limb when two correct actions compete, concealed hemorrhage is sought in every patient whose circulation is failing without a wound to explain it, emergency medical services are activated early with a report that is complete and calm, and triage decides who is treated first when there are more patients than hands. Cold is treated as a complication, the provider level is named for every intervention, the record is written as carefully as the treatment is given, and the patient is watched from the first contact until the handover. The two failures to guard against are the scene hazard that was not recognized and the hemorrhage that was not seen, and both are defeated by looking, by repeating the examination, and by refusing to be reassured too early. Every number in this chapter, whether a time, a pressure, a temperature, a depth, or a distance, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries, and editions. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 2 — The Primary Survey

The primary survey is a single habit performed the same way every time by everyone who touches an injured patient, so that what kills first is found first. It is called ABCDE, and each letter is a station that must be cleared before the next is entered. The survey is not a complete examination of the injury; it is a search for the conditions that will end the patient's life in the next few moments, and it is blind to everything that can wait. A lay first aider performs it with bare hands, a trained first responder or paramedic performs the same sequence with a kit and an authorization, and the physician or trauma surgeon repeats it in definitive hospital care with tools the field does not carry. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol or the law of the country in which you work.

Before any letter is spoken, the scene must be made safe, because a rescuer struck by traffic, burned by fire, electrocuted, attacked by an assailant or exposed to contaminated body fluids becomes a second patient and takes away the help the first one needed. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, is used as far as it is available, and the emergency medical services are called before the patient is touched whenever there are hands enough to do both. A patient who is silent, snoring or gurgling may have an airway that is already closing. A patient who is pale, restless and lying in a pool of blood may be losing blood faster than any hand can replace it. Cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, so the patient is covered, insulated from the ground and shielded from wind and rain from the first moment, whatever the injury.

The order of the letters is not negotiable, because an airway kills before breathing and breathing kills before circulation, and each station prevents the death that the next would reach too late. The rule that holds the survey together must be said aloud: any finding that stops the sequence restarts it at the beginning, from the airway, because an act at one station can undo the work of another. A patient who vomits while the chest is examined has an airway problem again, and a patient whose bleeding is controlled but who then becomes unresponsive has a breathing problem and a disability problem again. The sequence loops as many times as the patient demands, and each station answers one question that makes the next possible.

The airway is the first station because an unconscious patient cannot protect it, and the most common obstruction in trauma is the patient's own tongue, which falls back against the throat when the muscles of the jaw lose their tone. The finding is a patient who is not moving air quietly, who snores, who gurgles, or whose chest and abdomen move in opposite directions as the patient fights for a breath. The first action belongs to anyone present, including the lay first aider, and it is position: the head is tilted back gently and the chin is lifted, which raises the tongue away from the back of the throat. When an injury of the neck is possible, a trained first responder or paramedic holds the head steady in the position found while the jaw is lifted forward without tilting the neck, so the spine is protected and the airway is still opened. A cervical collar never takes priority over an airway and is never applied so tightly that it presses on the throat. Quiet air moving in and out with the chest rising on both sides is the finding that lets the responder move on.

Foreign material is the next question, asked in the same order every time: blood, vomit, loose teeth, broken dentures, and whatever the patient was carrying in the mouth when the injury happened. The lay first aider may remove material that is visible and within reach, using a hooked finger along the inside of the cheek, but never a blind sweep of the throat, because a finger that pushes material deeper turns a partial obstruction into a complete one. Suction, forceps and a laryngoscope belong to the trained responder or paramedic acting under a protocol, and the decision to use them rests on material that can be seen but not reached. The recovery position is the next tool and the one that most often saves an unconscious patient who is breathing but cannot protect the airway, and the lay first aider rolls the patient onto one side with the upper knee brought forward and the head resting slightly downward, so blood and vomit run out of the mouth instead of back into the lungs. A pregnant patient is turned onto the left side where possible, because the weight of the womb on the great vessels can reduce the blood returning to the heart, and a patient with a suspected injury of the spine is kept in the position found by the lay first aider while the trained responder or paramedic turns the body as one movement. Any sound of obstruction, any pause in breathing or any vomit appearing in the mouth forces a change of position and a return to the start of the survey.

Advanced airway management is not a first-aid measure at any level, and it belongs to the paramedic working under a protocol and to definitive hospital care. Placing a tube in the windpipe, cutting the front of the neck to create a passage, and using a mechanical device to push air into the lungs require training, equipment and authorization, and a manual that describes them as first aid teaches a dangerous habit. For the lay first aider the correct acts remain the head tilt, the chin lift, the jaw thrust and the recovery position, and the correct act when these fail is to call for help without delay. Children are not small adults at this station, because a child's airway is narrower, the tongue is proportionally larger and the head is proportionally heavier, so the neck is not tilted as far back.

Breathing is the second station because injuries of the chest kill here, and the two signs that carry the most information without equipment are the respiratory rate and the work of breathing. Effort is read by the responder from the shape of the patient: the muscles of the neck standing out, the spaces between the ribs drawing in, the nostrils flaring, the sentence that cannot be finished, the tripod position with the arms braced, and the grunt on each breath. A respiratory rate above 30 breaths per minute should be treated as an alarm, and the exact line that turns a rate into an emergency is fixed by the current guideline and the local protocol rather than by this page. A rate below 8 breaths per minute or above 30 in an adult warns that breathing may be failing, and both figures are illustrations whose values shift between services, countries and editions, so they must be confirmed against the guideline in force and against local protocol where you work. A quiet, effortless, symmetric breath at a rate the patient tolerates lets the responder move on, and that same breath is rechecked after every intervention and every move, because breathing changes fastest.

Oxygenation is judged at the bedside by the color of the lips, the tongue and the nail beds and by the level of consciousness, because a brain short of oxygen becomes restless before it becomes quiet. A probe placed on the finger to measure the oxygen saturation belongs to the trained responder or paramedic, and its reading is interpreted with the patient present, since cold hands, nail polish and poor circulation can mislead it. The decision to give oxygen belongs to the trained responder or paramedic acting under authorization and local protocol, and the substance, the amount and the way it is delivered are set by that protocol and that prescriber. The lay first aider does not administer oxygen but keeps the airway open, keeps the patient warm and keeps the patient still. A patient who is blue, confused, breathless at rest or unable to finish a sentence makes oxygen urgent, and a patient whose color and awareness have improved lets the responder move on.

Several injuries of the chest kill quickly, and each announces itself with a finding that can be sought before any equipment arrives. A patient whose chest does not move on one side, whose neck veins are swollen and whose pulse is fading may have air trapped under pressure around a lung, a tension pneumothorax, and that patient needs decompression by a paramedic under protocol or in definitive hospital care, never by a lay first aider. A patient with a wound of the chest that makes a sucking or bubbling sound may have an open chest wound, and the first action belongs to the trained responder, who covers the wound so that air cannot enter while the patient breathes in, without sealing it so tightly that trapped air cannot escape. A patient with a large collection of blood around a lung becomes pale and breathless, and that bleeding is internal and can only be treated in definitive hospital care. A patient whose chest moves in one part while the rest moves the opposite way has a flail chest, and a simple rib fracture is not a minor injury, because a broken rib may have injured what lies beneath it. Tight binding of the chest is never done at any provider level, because it reduces the depth of every breath and invites infection of the lung, and a chest moving on both sides with quiet air lets the responder continue.

Recognizing respiratory distress before failure is the skill that separates a responder who waits for the arrest from one who prevents it. The early signs are restlessness, anxiety, a rising rate, a rising effort, and a patient who wants to sit up and forward. The late signs are the opposite of noise: a rate that begins to fall, a chest that moves less, a patient who becomes drowsy and quiet, and a chest in which air is barely moving at all, and that quiet is the most dangerous moment in the survey because it looks like improvement and is in fact exhaustion. A needle or tube placed into the chest to release trapped air is a paramedic or hospital procedure performed under protocol, and a patient whose effort is falling while the rate and the color remain normal must travel toward definitive care without delay.

Circulation begins with the search for major external hemorrhage, because blood leaving the body is the fastest killer in trauma and the one most often missed. The findings are blood pooling under the patient, clothing dark and heavy with blood, a stump from an amputation, a limb spurting in time with the heart, or a wound that keeps filling no matter how many dressings are placed on it. The first action, owned by the lay first aider, is firm direct pressure with whatever clean material is at hand, held without lifting to look. A tourniquet belongs to the trained responder or paramedic, and it is used when pressure cannot control bleeding from a limb, when a limb is mangled, or when the patient must be moved before control can be achieved. Once a tourniquet has controlled the bleeding it is not loosened in the field, and the time it was applied is written on the patient where the receiving team will see it, because the length of time the limb has been without blood changes what the surgeon can do with it. Packing a deep wound with gauze and holding pressure inside it is a trained responder or paramedic act performed under protocol, and the lay first aider is not asked to reach into a wound. Bleeding that has stopped under the dressing lets the responder move on, and a dressing that keeps soaking through holds the responder at this station.

Shock is the state in which the circulation can no longer deliver enough blood to the organs, and it is recognized by a pattern of findings rather than by a single number. The patient becomes restless, anxious or confused before becoming drowsy, the skin turns pale, cool and clammy, and the patient feels thirsty and cold. The pulse is felt at the wrist for its rate and its strength, and a fast, thin pulse is the earliest sign the hand can detect; a pulse above 100 beats per minute in a calm patient is a teaching illustration that changes with age, fitness and pain, so it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The pressure is measured by the trained responder or paramedic, and a systolic pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury is a figure quoted only to show how a measurement becomes a decision, one that has to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol before it is relied on. The combination of a fast pulse, cool skin and a change in behavior makes shock urgent even when the measured pressure still looks acceptable, because the pressure falls late and a normal pressure is not reassurance. Children compensate for a long time before they collapse, and older patients who take medicines for the heart may not develop a fast pulse at all, so the pattern is read against the patient's own baseline. A warm patient with a strong pulse, clear skin color and calm behavior lets the responder move on, and any move away from that picture restarts the search from the airway.

Tissue perfusion can be assessed with the hand alone, and the lay first aider can be taught to do it in the first moments. The fingertips are pressed against the skin of the chest or the knee until the color leaves, and the time for the color to return is counted; refill that takes longer than 3 seconds is a warning, and that number is only an illustration of the reasoning, because the technique and the cut-off are described differently by different services, so it must be verified against the current guideline and the local protocol. The temperature of the hands and feet is compared with the temperature of the trunk, and a line of cold that climbs from the toes toward the knee shows that the body is closing down the outer circulation to protect the center. Warm, dry skin with a brisk return of color and a strong pulse lets the responder move on, and cold makes every one of these signs worse, because warmth is part of the treatment of shock, not a separate concern.

Bleeding that cannot be seen is suspected from the mechanism of injury, and the mechanism is the first piece of evidence the responder collects. A fall from a height, a strike by a vehicle, a crush, a blast or a penetrating wound of the trunk predicts damage inside the abdomen, the pelvis or the thigh, where blood can be lost in large quantity without a drop appearing on the ground. The abdomen is examined by the trained responder or paramedic for tenderness, swelling and guarding, the pelvis is tested once and only once, and a swollen, tense thigh after a fracture can hold a great volume of blood. Fluid given to a bleeding patient belongs to the paramedic or the physician acting under the local protocol, and the substance, the amount and the way it is given are decisions made by that protocol and that prescriber, while nothing is given by mouth to a patient who may need an operation. The lay first aider keeps the patient lying flat unless breathing demands otherwise, keeps the patient warm, does not raise the legs of a patient with a suspected injury of the spine or the pelvis, and treats worsening signs of shock despite control of the visible bleeding as a reason for immediate transport.

Disability is the fourth station, and it asks one question above all others: is the brain receiving enough blood and oxygen, and is the brain itself injured? The level of consciousness is the most useful single measure, and it is described in plain words at the bedside as alert, drowsy but rousable, responding only to voice, responding only to pain, or unresponsive. The Glasgow coma scale puts the same observation into a total, and a scale whose total runs from 3 to 15 is recorded by the trained responder or the physician to follow a patient over time, with the way that total decides urgency set by the current guideline and the local protocol. Any fall in the level of consciousness from the level first found makes this station urgent, because a patient who is becoming less awake is a patient whose airway is about to become the problem again, and every change in consciousness restarts the sequence from the airway. A patient who is fully alert and oriented to place, time and person lets the responder move on, and even that patient is rechecked, because consciousness can fall quickly after an injury of the head.

The pupils are examined with a light, one at a time, and what matters is the size of each pupil compared with the other, the shape, and whether the pupil narrows when light is shone into it. A pupil that is larger than its fellow and does not react to light suggests pressure inside the head, and that finding belongs in the report to the receiving team whether or not the patient looks unwell otherwise. The neurological examination that can be done in the first moments is a short pass for the trained responder: ask the patient to show the teeth and squeeze both hands, to lift each arm and each leg against resistance, and to say a sentence, then look for a side that moves less. A face that droops on one side, a grip that is weak on one side or a limb that does not move at all makes an injury of the head or the spine likely. A patient who is unresponsive is placed in the recovery position by whoever is present, with the neck kept in line, and a patient who is alert, moving every limb equally, speaking clearly and showing equal, reactive pupils lets the responder continue.

Exposure is the fifth station, and it means what it says: the patient is undressed enough to be examined completely, because injuries hide under clothing and the wound that was missed is the wound that kills. Clothing is cut away rather than pulled over a broken limb, and the whole surface of the body is looked at, including the back, the buttocks, the scalp, the armpits, the groin and the soles of the feet. A log roll, in which the patient is turned as a single unit with the head and the trunk kept in line, belongs to the trained responder or paramedic when an injury of the spine is possible, and the lay first aider does not roll a patient alone but keeps the patient still and warm until help arrives. Blood on the clothing that matches no wound already found, a limb that is deformed or shortened, or a wound in a place the patient did not mention makes this station urgent. A body fully examined with every wound found and every source of bleeding accounted for lets the responder move on, and any injury found during exposure restarts the sequence at the airway, because a wound that was hidden may be the one that changes the whole picture.

The moment the patient is exposed is the moment the patient begins to lose heat, and the prevention of hypothermia must follow exposure as closely as a dressing follows a wound. Wet clothing is removed, the patient is covered with blankets or whatever insulating material is at hand, the head and the back are insulated, and the patient is separated from the cold ground and from the wind. A patient who is bleeding, burned, immobilized or simply waiting is a patient who is losing heat, and cold makes blood clot poorly, makes the heart irritable and makes every sign of shock harder to read. Warm fluid belongs to the paramedic or the physician under the local protocol, and the decision to warm a patient actively is made by the trained responder or in definitive hospital care, with the method and the amount set by the current guideline and the local protocol. The aim is to keep the patient warm enough that cold is not adding to the injury, and 35 degrees Celsius is named only as an illustration of the line below which cold itself becomes dangerous, a figure that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The survey is not finished when the fifth letter has been spoken; it is finished when the patient has been handed over and the findings have been passed on in a form the next team can use. The sequence is repeated from the beginning after every intervention, after every move, and at intervals set by the current guideline and the local protocol, because a patient who was stable at the scene can be dying by the time the ambulance doors close. The handover names the mechanism of injury, the time the injury happened if it is known, the level of consciousness, the airway findings, the breathing rate and effort, the signs of circulation, the wounds found, the acts performed by each provider, and the time any tourniquet was applied. The receiving team includes the nurse, the physician and the trauma surgeon in definitive hospital care, and they repeat the same survey with imaging, including computed tomography, or CT, and ultrasound, and with the operating room when it is needed. A trauma center is a hospital organized to receive these patients at any hour, and the survey has done its work when the patient reaches it alive, with the airway open, the bleeding controlled, the breathing supported, the brain protected and the body warm.

Across all five stations, who does what is answered by the reach of the hands, not by the urgency of the moment. The lay first aider keeps the airway open, counts the breathing, applies direct pressure to bleeding, keeps the patient warm and calls for help, and that list saves more lives than any procedure in this book. The trained first responder, the emergency medical technician or the paramedic adds oxygen under protocol, suction, a tourniquet, wound packing, a pressure dressing, the measurement of the pressure, restriction of spinal movement and transport, within the authorization and equipment of the service. The nurse, the physician and the trauma surgeon in definitive hospital care add decompression of the chest, the tube in the windpipe, the surgical airway, blood and fluid given under protocol, the imaging, the operation and the intensive care unit, or ICU. None of those hospital acts becomes a first-aid measure because the patient is far from a hospital, and a procedure performed without training, equipment and authorization is a second injury waiting to happen. Restraint of a patient, extraction of a bullet, exploration of a wound, reduction of a fracture and repair of a vessel are never field procedures, and a problem that will not yield to the tools at hand tells any provider to stop and call for a higher level of care.

A constructed illustration may fix the sequence in the mind, and it is offered as a scene built for teaching rather than as a real patient or a real incident. A responder arrives at a crash in which a driver is still in the seat, the engine is running and fuel is on the ground; the scene is made safe by switching off the ignition and standing clear of traffic, and only then is the patient approached. The patient is unresponsive, breathing with a snore, pale and cool, with a swollen abdomen and blood on the clothing, and the airway is opened with a chin lift and a jaw thrust that keeps the neck in line until the snore stops. The breathing is fast and shallow with the muscles of the neck working, the chest moves less on one side, the pulse at the wrist is fast and thin and the skin is clammy, so the paramedic dresses a wound hidden under the clothing, measures the pressure and records a low reading. The patient is covered, insulated from the ground and kept warm while the ambulance moves toward a trauma center, the survey is repeated each time the patient is moved, and any figure in this illustration must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

To summarize, the primary survey is one habit performed in the same order every time, and the order is the treatment. The airway is opened by position and protected from foreign material before anything else is done, and the neck is kept in line without closing the passage. Breathing is judged by the rate and the work of breathing, and the injuries of the chest that kill quickly are named at the bedside with the finding that reveals them. Circulation is judged by the bleeding that can be seen and by the pulse, the skin and the perfusion that the hand can feel, and shock is treated as a pattern rather than as a number. Disability is judged by the level of consciousness and by a short neurological pass, and exposure completes the examination and is followed at once by warmth. At every level the provider stays inside the reach of the hands and the authorization of the service, and any finding that stops the sequence restarts it from the airway. Every figure in this chapter, whether a rate, a pressure, a time or a temperature, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between services, countries and editions, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, supervision or local protocol.

# Chapter 3 — Recognizing Life-Threatening Injuries

An injury that will kill a patient within minutes seldom announces itself with the noise of an emergency, and the responder who waits to be impressed has already waited too long. The lethal injuries of trauma are recognized by a small number of findings that can be sought with the eyes and the hands, and each of those findings takes less than a minute to look for once the responder knows what it is. Before any examination begins, the scene must be made safe, because traffic that is still moving, fire, live electricity, deep water, unstable structures, animals, and violence are lethal possibilities in their own right, and a rescuer who becomes a second patient has helped no one. The fluids of the patient's body are a hazard as well, so gloves, eye protection, and a barrier for the mouth belong in place before the first hand is laid on a wound. This chapter names the injuries that kill in the first minutes and hours, names the finding that reveals each of them, and says plainly what each level of responder may do about them. It is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The first discipline this chapter asks for is the difference between an injury that is dramatic and an injury that is lethal, because the two are not the same and the noisier one often takes the responder's attention. A patient with a broken forearm bent at an impossible angle will draw every eye on a scene and may be in no immediate danger at all, while a patient who is quietly pale, quiet, and slow to answer may be bleeding to death inside a body that shows no wound. A constructed illustration makes the trap clear, and it is offered only as a construction and never as a real patient or a real incident: at a road crash, one casualty cries out and holds a deformed arm while another sits silent and still against a wall, and the responder who runs first to the screaming patient has chosen the wrong order. The silent patient is the one to reach first when both can be reached, and the reason is not that the screaming patient does not matter but that the quiet one may have only minutes left. The responder who understands this keeps looking past the wound that is visible to the patient who is saying nothing, and asks what the mechanism of injury was and what forces the body met.

Massive external hemorrhage is the injury that can empty a patient in minutes, and the finding that reveals it is blood that is pouring, spurting, or pooling faster than a dressing can hold it. The lay first aider acts first and acts simply: firm direct pressure with both hands, or with a folded clean cloth if one is at hand, held without lifting an edge to see whether the bleeding has stopped. Lifting to look is the commonest way to lose the clot that has begun to form, so the pressure is held until a trained responder or the receiving team takes over. When bleeding from a limb continues despite correct direct pressure, the trained responder or paramedic may apply a tourniquet where protocol authorizes it, and once the bleeding has been controlled the tourniquet is not loosened in the field. The time it was applied is written on the patient in a place the receiving team will see, because the duration of limb ischemia decides what the hospital must do and how quickly. Where an object is embedded in the wound it is left exactly where it is and stabilized in place, since pulling it out may release hemorrhage that cannot be controlled and may tear vessels and nerves that are still intact. Blood loss also takes heat from the patient, so wet clothing is removed and the patient is covered while these actions are taken.

Not every lethal hemorrhage can be seen, and the finding that reveals concealed bleeding is a patient whose circulation is failing without a wound to explain it. Blood pooling in the abdomen produces a belly that becomes tender, then rigid, then visibly distended, and blood filling the chest produces a dullness on one side, breathlessness, and the same failing circulation. A fracture of the pelvis can bleed into the space behind the peritoneum, and a long bone can bleed into the thigh or the arm until the limb is tight and swollen. The lay first aider cannot see any of this and must not press hard into an injured belly, because pressing may increase the bleeding and may cause pain that hides the change. What the lay first aider can do is keep the patient still, keep the patient warm, call emergency medical services early, and report exactly what was seen: the pale skin, the confusion, the thirst, the restlessness. The trained responder watches the abdomen for distension and the chest for dullness, records repeated observations, and supports the failing circulation while the patient travels to a place where the bleeding can be stopped. Definitive hospital care opens the abdomen or the chest and controls the source, and no field measure substitutes for that operation.

Airway compromise is the first lethal possibility of the primary survey, and its findings are heard before they are seen: a snore, a gurgle, a whistle, a harsh rasping sound on inspiration, or a voice that has become hoarse. Blood, vomit, broken teeth, and swelling of the tongue or the throat can all close the passage, and a burn of the face, a blast injury, or a blow to the neck can narrow it over the following minutes without any wound at all. The lay first aider opens the mouth, removes only what is loose and visible, and if the patient is breathing and has no suspected spinal injury, turns the patient onto one side so that fluid drains rather than pools. Where a spinal injury is possible the head is kept in line with the trunk, and help is called before the patient is turned at all. The trained responder or paramedic may use suction, airway adjuncts, and oxygen according to protocol, and only a provider authorized by protocol performs the definitive airway that bypasses the obstruction. That definitive airway is never a first-aid measure, and a responder who attempts it without training and equipment can convert a partial obstruction into a complete one.

Tension pneumothorax is the chest injury that kills fastest, and it develops when air enters the space around the lung and cannot escape. The finding that reveals it is a patient who is increasingly breathless and distressed, with breath sounds that are absent on one side, a chest that sounds hollow when tapped, and neck veins that become distended as the pressure inside the chest rises. As the pressure continues to build, the heart is compressed, the pulse becomes weak and rapid, and the pressure falls, and a shift of the windpipe away from the injured side is a late sign that must not be waited for. The lay first aider cannot relieve this injury but can still save time by calling emergency medical services at once, keeping the patient sitting if that is more comfortable, and reporting that the breathing is one-sided and getting worse. Needle decompression and the chest drain that follows belong to definitive care, performed by a physician or by a paramedic where the local protocol explicitly authorizes it. The same signs appearing after such a procedure are a reason to look again, since the pressure can return.

An open chest wound, sometimes described as a sucking wound, declares itself by the sound of air moving through the opening with each breath and by bubbles appearing at the wound. The immediate danger is that air is drawn into the chest with every inspiration and cannot leave, so the wound can produce the same rising pressure as a tension pneumothorax. The trained responder covers the wound with a dressing sealed on most of its border but left free on one edge, so that air trapped inside can escape while air from outside is kept out, and the patient is watched closely for the return of breathlessness and the distension of the neck veins. A chest is never bound tightly, because tight binding prevents the chest from expanding and turns a survivable injury into a fatal one, and this is true even when the wound is small. The lay first aider covers the wound with a clean hand or cloth and does not tape it down on every side unless a trained responder directs it. Definitive hospital care places a chest drain and repairs the injured lung or chest wall, and that work belongs to the hospital and the surgeon.

Traumatic brain injury is dangerous less because of the blow than because of what happens inside the closed box of the skull afterward, where a small volume of blood can raise the pressure until the brain is pushed through the openings at its base. The findings that must be sought are a change in the level of consciousness, a headache that worsens, repeated vomiting, a seizure, weakness of one side of the body, an unequal pupil, and a period of apparent recovery that is then followed by deterioration. That interval of seeming recovery is a trap of its own, because the patient who speaks clearly and then becomes drowsy has not improved but has entered a more dangerous phase. The trained responder records the level of consciousness in a repeatable form using the Glasgow coma scale, writes the time beside each recording, and repeats it, because the direction of change carries more meaning than any single value. The lay first aider keeps the airway clear, keeps the patient still and warm, gives nothing by mouth, and reports every change in behavior to the arriving team. Computed tomography, or CT, of the head and any operation to remove blood or to relieve pressure belong to definitive hospital care, where the surgeon and the imaging suite take over.

Spinal injury does not always announce itself with paralysis, and the reason it must be assumed is that movement of an unstable spine can convert a recoverable injury into a permanent one. The mechanism of injury is the first clue: a fall from a height, a dive into shallow water, a collision at speed, a heavy object striking the head or the back, or any patient found unconscious after trauma. The findings that support it are pain or tenderness along the midline of the neck or the back, weakness or numbness in the limbs, a loss of sensation in a band around the trunk, and an inability to control the bladder or the bowel. The lay first aider keeps the head, the neck, and the trunk in line, does not move the patient unless there is immediate danger such as fire, and never asks the patient to turn the head or to sit up in order to test the neck. The trained responder applies manual in-line stabilization, uses a collar and a board where protocol provides them, and moves the patient with enough trained hands to keep the spine from bending or twisting. Straightening a deformed spine, or pulling on the head to realign it, is not a field procedure, and imaging of the spine with CT or magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, belongs to the hospital.

Pelvic trauma is lethal in a way that is easy to underestimate, because the pelvis is a ring of bone with large vessels running against it, and a fracture that opens the ring can bleed into the space behind the abdomen without any swelling that a hand can feel. The mechanism is usually a high-energy one such as a collision between a vehicle and a pedestrian, a fall from a height, or a crush, and the findings include pain in the pelvis or the lower back, an inability to stand or to lift the legs, bruising over the perineum or the flanks, and blood at the opening of the urinary passage. The lay first aider does not spring the pelvis to test it, because repeated compression can make the bleeding worse, and instead keeps the patient flat, still, and warm. The trained responder may place a pelvic binder around the pelvis at the level the local protocol specifies, and once it is in place it is left there until the receiving team assesses it. Definitive hospital care includes early transfusion, imaging of the vessels, and stabilization of the ring in the operating theater, and none of that can be reproduced in the field.

Major fractures of the long bones are dangerous for two reasons that arrive together, because the bone itself can injure the vessels and nerves beside it, and the bleeding inside the limb can be enough to produce shock on its own. The findings of a fractured thigh are a swollen, tense thigh, shortening of the limb, and the foot turned outward, and the limb may look almost normal in the first minutes before the swelling grows. A fractured thigh can hold an amount of blood large enough to endanger the circulation, and a fractured pelvis can hold more, so a patient with either injury is treated as a patient in shock until the opposite is proven. The lay first aider does not straighten the limb to make it look normal, because forcing the ends of the bone into line may tear a vessel or a nerve that is still intact, and the limb is supported in the position in which it was found. The trained responder checks the pulse, the movement, and the feeling in the limb before and after splinting, splints the joint above and the joint below the fracture, and binds the limb to the body when no splint is available. Reduction of the fracture and the fixation that holds it belong to definitive care in the operating theater.

Traumatic shock is not a diagnosis but a state in which the delivery of oxygen to the tissues has fallen below what they need, and it begins long before the patient looks unwell. In its early phase the body defends itself: the pulse rises, the vessels of the skin and the gut narrow to preserve the brain and the heart, and the pressure is held near normal while the tissues that have lost their supply begin to suffer. The findings of this phase are a pulse that has climbed, skin that is cool and pale, a hand that feels clammy, a delay in the return of color after a fingernail or the forehead is pressed, and a patient who is anxious or unusually quiet. As the state worsens the pressure falls, the pulse becomes weak and fast, the breathing becomes rapid and shallow, and the level of consciousness declines. A pulse of 110 beats per minute, a pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury, or a capillary refill longer than 2 seconds are the sort of figures used to teach that change, but each of them must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold that matters depends on the patient, on the patient's age, and on the service. The lay first aider cannot measure most of this and does not need to, since pale, cold, clammy, restless, and confused together are enough to act on: keep the patient flat and warm, control any bleeding that can be seen, and call emergency medical services without delay.

The patient who looks well and is not is one of the central traps of trauma, and it is produced by the body's own defense of the circulation. A young, fit patient can lose a large share of the blood volume and still hold a normal pressure while the pulse quietly climbs, so a reassuring pressure taken once is not evidence of safety. Children compensate in the same way and then deteriorate very suddenly, an athlete with a slow resting pulse may never show the expected increase, and a patient who takes medicine that slows the heart may not develop the rapid pulse that would otherwise give the injury away. A pregnant patient has more circulating volume than before the pregnancy, which hides loss for longer, and an older patient may have less reserve and may be taking medicine that changes the response to bleeding. The trend taken over time, with the same findings looked for in the same order and written down with the time of each set, is what reveals the patient who is compensating and beginning to fail.

The trend matters more than the single observation, and the reason is that a change over time belongs to the patient while any one figure may belong only to the moment. A pressure that was comfortable and is now lower, a pulse that was steady and is now quick and thready, a patient who was answering questions and now only nods: these movements say what the body is doing, and they say it before the final collapse. The trained responder therefore repeats the primary survey at intervals that the local protocol sets, records each set with the time, and compares rather than merely collecting. The lay first aider can contribute to this by staying with the patient and noticing what has changed, because the person who has watched from the beginning often sees the difference before anyone arriving can. Records written on paper or on the hand, with the time beside each finding, travel with the patient and shape the decisions of the receiving team.

Between the moment of injury and the arrival of help, the lay first aider holds the patient's chances in a small number of actions that require no equipment. The first is safety, for the rescuer and for the patient, because a second casualty makes the situation worse for everyone. The second is a call to emergency medical services that gives the location, the number of patients, the mechanism of injury, and the findings that worry the caller, since that information decides what help is sent and how quickly. The third is control of any bleeding that can be seen, by firm direct pressure that is not lifted to check, and the fourth is an airway kept clear and a patient kept still and warm. Nothing is given by mouth, nothing is removed from a wound, and no limb is straightened, because each of those acts has harmed patients who were otherwise surviving. The first aider who does these things, and who then watches without stopping, has done the work that this level of care owns.

The trained responder and the paramedic bring equipment, a protocol, and authorization to acts that the lay first aider must not attempt. Oxygen is given according to the protocol of the service, with the amount and the method set there and not in this book, and the decision to give it is made on findings such as breathlessness, a blue tinge of the lips, or a level of consciousness that is falling. A breathing rate that has risen above 30 breaths per minute, or a pulse that has become difficult to feel, is the kind of observation that changes the plan, though the exact figure that should trigger a given action must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol. The trained responder may apply a tourniquet, place a pelvic binder, splint a fracture, insert an airway adjunct, and suction the mouth and the throat, and each of those acts carries a finding that tells the responder whether it has worked. Analgesia is a decision rather than an instruction: the responder may recognize that pain is severe enough to threaten breathing and movement, but the substance, the amount, the route, and the interval belong to the prescriber and the local protocol, and the same is true of antibiotics and of tetanus protection. No amount, no regimen, and no route is given in this manual, because a listener must not be able to take a prescription from it.

Definitive hospital care begins where the field ends, and its first actions are a continuation of the same primary survey rather than a different subject. A patient with a suspected chest injury is assessed with ultrasound and a chest radiograph, a chest drain is placed if air or blood is compressing the lung, and a patient whose circulation is failing without an obvious cause may go directly to the operating theater. Computed tomography, or CT, answers questions about the head, the chest, the abdomen, and the pelvis, and magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, is used for the spine and the spinal cord when the patient is stable enough to be in the scanner. The intensive care unit, or ICU, receives the patient who needs support of breathing or of circulation, and the trauma center that holds all of these resources is the destination the field team is trying to reach. Transfusion, the control of a bleeding vessel, the removal of a blood clot from the skull, the reduction of a fracture, and the repair of a torn organ all belong to this level. The first responder's task is not to perform them but to recognize the injury, do what the field permits, and deliver the patient to them in the best condition possible.

Each of these injuries has its own clock, and knowing the clock is what turns recognition into action. Airway obstruction and massive external hemorrhage act within minutes, tension pneumothorax within minutes after that, and a patient with a torn major vessel may be lost before any vehicle arrives. Internal bleeding, an expanding blood clot inside the skull, and the leakage of fluid into the tissues of a crushed limb act over a period of hours, which is why the quietly worsening patient is as dangerous as the dramatic one. The first 6 hours after a major injury are often described as decisive for the patient who needs an operation, and that interval is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the meaningful window depends on the injury, the distance to care, and the resources of the receiving service. The practical consequence is that recognition must be fast, and that transport must not be delayed by procedures which can wait.

Hypothermia is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and it begins on the ground in the first minutes. A patient who is bleeding, burned, undressed for examination, lying on a cold surface, or receiving fluids at room temperature loses heat quickly, and cold makes blood clot poorly, worsens the state of shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is the figure commonly used to describe the point at which these effects become serious, and that figure, like every other in this chapter, must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line varies between services and between editions. The lay first aider removes wet clothing, covers the patient with whatever is available, including blankets, coats, and foil, and insulates the patient from the ground. The trained responder continues that protection during transport and limits unnecessary exposure during the examination. Warmth is maintained for every patient who is bleeding, burned, or waiting, and it is not withdrawn when the patient begins to look better.

The errors that cost lives in this chapter are mostly errors of doing too much or of doing it in the wrong order. Removing a knife or a piece of glass from a wound, pulling a bullet out of the skin, pressing hard into an injured belly, springing the pelvis to see whether it is stable, straightening a deformed limb, binding the chest tightly, and loosening a tourniquet that has stopped the bleeding are each acts that can turn a survivable injury into a fatal one. Each of those acts belongs either to definitive hospital care or to no one at all, and the reason is always the same: the field cannot control what the act releases. The other family of errors is the error of attention, in which the responder treats the wound that is visible and misses the patient who is bleeding internally or the airway that is quietly closing. A third is the error of the single observation, in which a comfortable first reading is allowed to close the assessment. The antidote to all three is a fixed order of looking, a repeated examination, and a refusal to be reassured by a patient who is only briefly better.

To summarize, the injuries that kill in trauma are a short list, and each is recognized by a finding rather than by a name: hemorrhage that pours or hides, an airway that is narrowing, a chest under rising pressure, a brain whose level of consciousness is falling, a spine that must not be moved, a pelvis that can bleed without swelling, long bones that bleed enough to cause shock, and the state of shock itself, which begins quietly and ends quickly. The dramatic injury is not always the lethal one, the patient who looks well may be compensating, and the trend over repeated observations matters more than any single value. Every responder acts within a level of practice: the lay first aider gives pressure, position, warmth, and an early call; the trained responder and the paramedic add equipment and protocol; and the definitive procedures belong to the hospital and the surgeon. Every number in this chapter, whether a rate, a pressure, a temperature, or a duration, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries, and editions. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 4 — Understanding Wounds

The wound is a mechanical event before it is anything a responder can see, and the surface of the skin is the least reliable guide to what lies beneath it. Energy delivered to the body cuts, stretches, crushes, or tears whatever tissue lies in its path, and the mark on the skin is only the place where that energy entered or left. A blade divides structures in a line, a blow spreads force across a wide area, and a projectile carries energy far beyond the track it makes. Reading a wound therefore begins with the mechanism of injury, because the mechanism describes the forces that acted and the structures they may have reached. This chapter describes the categories of wounds, the assessment that follows them, and the level of care that owns each act, and it is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

Before any wound is examined, the scene must be made safe, because a responder who becomes a second patient helps no one. Traffic, unstable vehicles, fire, electricity, water, animals, violence, structural collapse, and the hazards of the patient's own body fluids all take precedence, and personal protective equipment, or PPE, with gloves at the least, protects both the responder and the patient. The lethal possibility that must be named first is hemorrhage that cannot be controlled by direct pressure, and the finding that reveals it is blood that spurts with each beat of the heart, blood that soaks through dressing after dressing, or a swelling that grows while the responder watches. The second lethal possibility is a wound that has taken the airway, and the finding is a patient who coughs blood, whose voice has changed, or who struggles to breathe after an injury to the face or the neck. The third is a penetrating wound of the chest that has opened the pleural space, and the finding is air that moves in and out of the wound with each breath. A patient who is bleeding, burned, or lying exposed also loses heat, so protection against hypothermia begins with hemorrhage control and is not delayed until the journey.

With the scene safe and catastrophic bleeding addressed, the wound can be assessed without being probed, and probing is the first temptation to resist. Beneath the skin lie fat, then a tough sheet of fascia, then muscle, and within and between those layers run the vessels that carry blood, the nerves that carry feeling and movement, and the tendons that transmit the pull of muscle to bone.
