A wound that reaches only skin and fat damages little that cannot heal, while a wound of the same length that passes through fascia may have divided a tendon, a nerve, or an artery. The lay first aider covers the wound and does not probe it, because a finger or an instrument introduced into a wound can push contamination deeper, dislodge the clot that is holding back hemorrhage, and injure a structure that was intact. The trained responder may inspect and clean within the limits of training, equipment, and protocol, and exploration and repair belong to definitive hospital care.

An abrasion is a wound of friction, in which the surface of the skin is scraped away while the deeper layers stay intact. It is the wound of the road and of the sliding fall, and its importance lies less in the tissue lost than in what has been ground into the raw surface. Dirt, grit, glass, and the material of the road are driven into the skin, so a wound that looks shallow can carry a heavy load of contamination. An abrasion that covers a large area weeps fluid and loses heat, and a patient with extensive abrasions from a road crash is at risk of hypothermia as well as infection. Cleaning belongs to the trained responder or to hospital care according to the protocol in force, protection against tetanus is decided at the first contact, and the lay first aider covers the wound, keeps the patient warm, and does not scrub it.

A laceration is a wound produced by blunt force that splits the skin, and its edges are irregular because the tissue has been torn rather than cut. The force that opens the skin also bruises and crushes the tissue around the tear, so the visible wound sits inside a zone of injury that may not survive. A laceration over a bone may be the only sign of a fracture beneath it, and a laceration over a joint may communicate with the joint space, which turns a skin wound into an orthopedic emergency. Scalp lacerations bleed heavily because the scalp is richly supplied with blood, so closure of a possibly contaminated wound is not a field decision but one made by the trained responder under protocol and by definitive hospital care.

An incision is a wound made by a sharp edge that divides tissue cleanly, and its innocent appearance is its danger. The edges are neat, the tissue around them is undamaged, and the wound may close on its own if nothing important has been cut, which is why an incision is the wound most easily underestimated. The same sharp edge that produces a clean skin wound passes without resistance through a tendon, a nerve, or a vessel, and a patient may have lost the use of a hand while the skin wound looks trivial. The depth of an incision cannot be judged from the surface, and the finding that reveals a deep injury is a loss of movement, a loss of sensation, or a pulse that cannot be felt beyond the wound. The lay first aider controls bleeding with direct pressure, covers the wound, and keeps the limb still, while definitive hospital care explores the wound and repairs what has been divided.

A puncture wound is produced by a narrow object that passes through the skin and leaves a small opening, and the small opening is exactly what makes it deceptive. The surface may be 4 millimeters across, and any figure for such a size is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the importance of a wound lies in its depth and its track rather than its width. The object may have carried clothing, dirt, or metal into the depths, and it may have passed through a vessel, a nerve, the bowel, or the lung while leaving almost no external mark. A puncture over the abdomen may have perforated bowel, and the finding that raises suspicion is pain out of proportion to the wound, tenderness away from the wound, or a rigid abdomen, while a puncture over the chest may have entered the pleural space and produced breathlessness, chest pain, or a pulse that rises while the pressure falls. A puncture of a limb may have divided an artery that has sealed itself temporarily, and the wound may bleed again when the clot is disturbed, which is one reason a puncture is never probed in the field.

A crush injury is produced when a heavy force squeezes tissue between two surfaces, and the damage extends far beyond the skin. The skin may be intact while the muscle beneath has been compressed beyond the point where it can survive, so the visible wound is only one part of a much larger zone of injury. Crushed muscle releases its contents into the circulation, and the consequences include a dangerous rise in the substances the kidney must clear and swelling that can increase for hours after the patient is freed. Compartment syndrome is the complication to fear in a crushed limb, and the finding that reveals it is pain that is severe, out of proportion to the injury, and worse when the fingers or the toes are moved. Crush syndrome is the complication to fear in the patient as a whole, and the finding is a patient who was trapped, who may look stable at first, and whose pulse and pressure change as the effects of the crushed muscle appear. The lay first aider keeps the patient warm and does not attempt to release a long-trapped limb alone, while the trained responder follows the protocol and definitive hospital care manages the fluids and the surgical decisions.

An avulsion is a wound in which tissue is torn away or left hanging as a flap, and a degloving injury is the extreme form in which skin and fat are stripped from the fascia beneath them. The avulsed skin loses its blood supply even when it remains attached, because the vessels that fed it have been torn, and a flap that looks pink at the edges may be dead over most of its surface. A degloving injury of a limb or a hand is a severely contaminated wound with a large area of dead tissue, and it belongs to definitive hospital care from the first contact. The lay first aider controls bleeding with pressure that does not further tear the flap, covers the wound, keeps the patient warm, and sends any detached piece of tissue with the patient in the manner the local service directs. The trained responder does not cut, trim, or replace the flap, because the decision about which tissue can survive belongs to the surgeon who can see it. The finding that demands immediate transport is a limb or a hand stripped over a wide area, with bleeding that continues and a patient who is becoming cold and pale.

Every wound is contaminated to some degree, and the risk of infection is decided by what entered it, how much entered, and what the tissue has left to defend itself with. The organisms that matter most come from soil, manure, saliva, stagnant water, and the skin and clothing of the patient, and each source carries a different set of threats. The wound with the greatest risk combines heavy contamination with dead tissue and a poor blood supply, because antibiotics and the body's own defenses reach living, well-perfused tissue and not the dead tissue at the center of a wound. A wound left untreated for 6 hours or more has accumulated organisms and has lost the chance of clean closure, and that interval is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the safe period differs between services. A bite carries the organisms of the mouth that made it, and a human bite is especially aggressive, while a bite over a joint or the hand is the most dangerous of all because the joint space and the tendon sheaths lie close to the surface. The assessment therefore records the source of contamination, the time that has passed, and the state of the tissue at the base and the edges of the wound, and the decision about protection against infection is made by the prescriber under the local protocol.

An open fracture is a broken bone that communicates with the outside through a wound, and it is a surgical emergency rather than a wound to be dressed and forgotten. The bone end may be visible, or the wound may be small and the fracture discovered only when the limb is examined, so a fracture with a skin wound anywhere near it is treated as open until definitive care decides otherwise. The exposed bone and deep tissues are contaminated at the moment of injury, and the risk of infection is far greater than in a closed fracture because the organisms have direct access to the bone. The lay first aider covers the wound with a clean dressing, controls bleeding with pressure around the wound rather than on the bone end, and immobilizes the limb in the position found. The trained responder splints the limb, records the pulses and the feeling beyond the fracture, and does not push the bone end back into the wound. A severely deformed limb is never straightened to make it look normal, because of the risk of further damage to vessels and nerves, and the cleaning, the removal of dead tissue, and the stabilization of the bone all belong to definitive hospital care.

The assessment begins with the history that the scene provides, and the mechanism of injury is the most important single piece of information. The responder asks what object produced the wound, in what direction the force traveled, how much energy was involved, and how far the patient fell or was thrown. The answers describe the forces that acted on the body and therefore the structures that may have been injured, and they are more reliable than the appearance of the wound. The patient's own history matters, and the responder asks about diabetes, about medicines that suppress the immune system, and about protection against tetanus in the past.

The examination of a wound follows the same order every time, so that nothing is omitted when the scene is loud and the patient is frightened. The patient is first assessed by the primary survey, and only when the airway, the breathing, the circulation, the level of consciousness, and the exposure have been addressed does the wound itself receive attention. The wound is then exposed fully, which may require cutting away clothing rather than pulling it over the wound, and it is examined in good light with the limb in the position found. The responder looks at the size, the shape, the edges, the color of the tissue, the presence of foreign material, and the direction of the wound, and notes whether blood is flowing, oozing, or absent. The responder feels the limb beyond the wound for warmth, swelling, tenderness, and deformity, compares it with the uninjured side, records the pulse beyond the wound, tests the feeling in the skin, and asks the patient to move the part if movement is safe. The finding that a pulse is absent, that feeling is lost, or that movement is impossible sends the patient to definitive hospital care without delay.

The contrast between the small wound and the dramatic one is the lesson this chapter exists to teach. A small puncture can hide a deep injury because the surface closes behind the object, because the track is narrow, and because the structures that were divided may bleed slowly or not at all until the clot that sealed them is disturbed. A spectacular laceration can be superficial because the skin and the fat beneath it are the only tissues the force reached, and the bleeding from a richly supplied area makes the wound look worse than it is. The responder therefore judges a wound by the mechanism and by what lies beneath it, and never by its size or by the amount of blood on the dressing alone. A wound of 3 millimeters over the abdomen, the chest, the neck, or a major vessel is as serious as a large open wound, and the number itself is a teaching illustration whose value must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Certain findings mark a wound as one that needs surgical evaluation rather than a dressing, and the responder who holds them in the order of the examination will not miss them. The first is bleeding that continues despite sustained direct pressure, and the second is a swelling that expands while the responder watches, which suggests a vessel is bleeding into the tissue. The third is a wound in which bone, tendon, muscle, or bowel is visible, because those structures must not be handled in the field. The fourth is a wound with an embedded object, which is stabilized in place and never removed in the field, because removal may release hemorrhage that cannot be controlled or cause further damage to the tissue around it. The fifth is a wound that crosses a joint, a wound over the palm or the sole, a wound of the face, and a wound of the genital area, and the sixth is any wound with a pulse, feeling, or movement lost beyond it. The seventh is gross contamination with dead tissue at the edges or the base, and a wound present for many hours, a wound in a patient whose immune defenses are impaired, and a wound with a foul discharge or crackling in the tissues all belong on the same list.

Location decides the meaning of a wound as much as its size, and some regions tolerate no delay. A wound of the neck may have divided the great vessels, the airway, or the esophagus, and the finding that reveals danger is a swelling that enlarges, a voice that changes, or air that moves in the tissues of the neck. A wound of the chest may have entered the pleural space or the heart, and the finding is breathlessness, a rising pulse, a falling pressure, or a wound that bubbles with each breath, while a wound of the abdomen may have entered the peritoneal cavity and produced tenderness, rigidity, or pain that spreads away from the wound. A wound of the back may have entered the spine, and the finding is a loss of feeling or movement below the level of the wound. A wound of a limb may have injured a vessel or a nerve, and the findings beyond it are the pulse, the feeling, and the movement that the responder must record before and after any splinting.

The tetanus question must be raised at the first contact, because the decision is most effective when it is made early and the patient may not be seen again. Tetanus is a disease caused by a toxin produced by organisms that live in soil and manure, and it follows contamination of a wound, especially a wound with dead tissue, a deep puncture, or a wound that was not cleaned. The responder asks whether the patient has been protected against tetanus in the past and when the last protection was given, and asks in the same breath about the nature of the wound and the material that contaminated it. The finding that makes the decision urgent is a wound that is deep, that contains dead tissue, or that was contaminated with soil or manure, while a clean superficial wound in a patient with documented past protection makes it less urgent. The decision about whether protection is needed, and with what, belongs to the trained responder or the prescriber acting under the local protocol, and the lay first aider asks the question and passes it on without giving any medicine.

Antibiotics are a decision and never a dose in this book, and the decision belongs to the prescriber who knows the wound, the patient, and the local resistance of organisms. The finding that makes the decision urgent is a wound with heavy contamination, dead tissue, a deep track, or a delay in treatment, together with a patient whose defenses are impaired. The finding that makes it less clear is a clean wound of recent onset in a healthy patient, and the prescriber weighs the benefit of protection against the harm of unnecessary medicine. The lay first aider never gives an antibiotic and never carries one, and the trained responder gives one only where the protocol and the authority to do so exist. The whole decision is governed by the local protocol and the judgment of the clinician responsible for the patient.

Pain is a wound in its own right, and its relief is part of care rather than an afterthought. The finding that makes relief urgent is pain that is severe, pain that prevents the patient from moving or breathing deeply, and pain accompanied by fear and a rising pulse. The decision about pain relief belongs to the trained responder or the physician acting under the local protocol, and the substance, the amount, the route, and the interval are the business of the prescriber and are never learned from a manual. The lay first aider reduces pain by splinting, by positioning, by covering the wound, by keeping the patient warm, and by speaking calmly, while the patient in shock, with a head injury, or a child requires particular caution and the most senior clinician available. A patient whose pain is out of proportion to the wound, or whose pain increases after an initial improvement, must be re-examined, because that change may be the first sign of a compartment syndrome or of a developing infection.

The three levels of care run through this chapter because the same wound asks a different act from each pair of hands. The lay first aider makes the scene safe, calls for help, controls bleeding with direct pressure, covers the wound with a clean dressing, keeps the patient warm, does not probe, does not remove an embedded object, does not straighten a deformed limb, and does not give any medicine. The trained responder or paramedic adds the recording of the pulse, the feeling, and the movement beyond the wound, the splinting of the limb, the control of hemorrhage with the devices the service authorizes, and the decision to move the patient rapidly toward definitive care. The nurse and the physician in a district hospital add the cleaning of the wound, the assessment of the deep structures, the decision about tetanus protection and about antibiotics, and the referral of the patient who needs more than the hospital can provide. Definitive hospital care, with the operating theater, the imaging, and the surgeon, owns exploration, the removal of dead tissue, the repair of vessels, tendons, and nerves, the stabilization of fractures, and the removal of a retained foreign body when that removal is clinically indicated. No manual can transfer those acts to the field, and a responder who attempts them does harm that the patient did not have before.

Documentation is part of treatment, because the receiving team acts on what the responder has recorded and cannot act on what has been forgotten. The record carries the mechanism of injury, the time of the injury, the time any tourniquet was applied, the wounds that were found, the contamination that was seen, the pulses and the feeling and the movement that were present, and the protection against tetanus that was discussed. The time a tourniquet is applied is written on the patient, in a place the receiving team will see, because the duration of its use changes the decisions made in the hospital and because the tourniquet itself is not loosened in the field once it has controlled the bleeding. The record also carries what was not done, including the dressing applied and the object left in place, and the handover is spoken in the same order as the primary survey. A constructed illustration may help here: a responder who writes the time of a tourniquet on the skin of the patient's forehead, where no dressing will cover it, has given the hospital a fact it could not otherwise recover, and that example is invented for teaching and describes no real patient or incident.

Warmth and continuous watching are the duties that continue after the wound is covered and before the patient reaches care. A patient who is bleeding loses heat with the blood, a patient who is exposed loses heat to the air, and a patient who is immobilized on a cold surface loses heat to the ground, and cold makes bleeding worse because it interferes with the clotting the body is trying to achieve. The responder removes wet clothing where that is possible, covers the patient with blankets or whatever is available, insulates the patient from the ground, and keeps the head covered, all without delaying transport. The observations are repeated rather than taken once, because the trend of the pulse, the pressure, the breathing, and the level of consciousness is more informative than any single measurement. A temperature of 38 degrees Celsius, or a pulse of 110 beats per minute, is a change to report, and both figures are illustrations that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A wound that becomes more painful, that begins to smell, that discharges, or that shows darkening tissue around its edges has changed, and the responder who looks again and says out loud what has changed is doing the most valuable thing that can be done at the roadside.

To summarize, a wound is a mechanical event whose surface appearance is the least reliable guide to the injury beneath it, and the responder reads it by the mechanism of injury, by the structures at risk, and by the findings beyond the wound. Scene safety and hemorrhage control come before every other act, an embedded object is left in place, a deformed limb is not straightened, and no wound is probed in the field. Abrasions, lacerations, incisions, punctures, crush injuries, avulsions, degloving injuries, open fractures, and bites each destroy a different tissue and each carry a different risk of contamination, and the small puncture may hide more than the spectacular laceration. The findings that demand surgical evaluation rather than a dressing are bleeding that will not stop, an expanding swelling, exposed deep structures, a wound that crosses a joint, a lost pulse, lost feeling, lost movement, and gross contamination with dead tissue. The tetanus question is asked at the first contact, and the decisions about protection against tetanus, about antibiotics, about pain relief, about fluids, and about oxygen belong to the trained responder or the prescriber under the local protocol. Every number in this chapter is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries, and editions. The lay first aider covers, warms, and sends, the trained responder assesses, splints, and records, and definitive hospital care explores, repairs, and removes, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 5 — External Bleeding

External bleeding is the injury a responder sees before any other, and it kills faster than any other, so the scene is made safe before the wound is touched. Traffic, fire, electricity, water, animals, violence, structural collapse, and the hazards of the patient's own body fluids must be made safe before hands are laid on anyone, and personal protective equipment, or PPE, with gloves at the least, protects the responder and the patient at once. The lethal possibility to be named first is hemorrhage that cannot be controlled, and the finding that reveals it is blood that spurts with each beat of the heart, blood that soaks through dressing after dressing, or a swelling that grows while the responder watches, while a patient who is anxious, pale, and restless with a rapid pulse shows the same warning in the body rather than in the wound. This chapter follows bleeding from its source, through the ladder of control, to the point where definitive hospital care takes over, and it is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work. Every intervention is named with the provider level that owns it, because the same wound demands a different act from a lay first aider and from a trauma team.

Bleeding is classified by the vessel it comes from, and the classification guides behavior rather than naming a label. Capillary bleeding comes from the smallest vessels in the skin and the tissue just beneath it, and it oozes rather than flows, seeping from a raw area that may be large but shallow. Its pressure is low, so it usually stops when the surface is covered and pressed, and this is the one source that a lay first aider can control with a clean dressing and the flat of the hand. Capillary bleeding becomes serious when the area is vast, as in a large abrasion from a road crash, because a continuously weeping surface loses fluid and heat and can exhaust a child or an older patient. The physics is simple, in that a hand laid flat over the whole surface exceeds the pressure inside the smallest vessels, and the flow stops without any need for a tourniquet or a hemostatic agent.

Venous bleeding comes from the vessels that carry blood back to the heart, and it appears as a steady, low-pressure flow of dark blood that does not spurt and does not stop on its own as readily as the capillary ooze. The pressure within a vein is only a little above the pressure of the surrounding tissue, so a firm dressing is often enough, but the size of the vessel decides the danger, and a torn vein in the neck, the groin, or the thigh can empty the circulation in minutes without ever spurting. A wound of the neck or the upper chest near a large vein carries a second hazard, because air can be drawn into the open vessel with each breath, and the finding is a wound that bubbles or sucks at the moment of inspiration. The lay first aider covers the wound and presses firmly without probing and without removing a dressing that has become soaked, adding further layers on top instead. The trained responder may pack an appropriate deep wound and must move the patient toward definitive care without delay when a large vein is torn, because the volume lost rather than the appearance of the wound is what kills.

Arterial bleeding comes from the vessels that carry blood away from the heart under the highest pressure in the circulation, and its behavior is the opposite of the venous flow. The blood is bright, it leaves the wound in jets that keep time with the heartbeat, and it can travel some distance from the patient, while a wound in a limb may bleed into the tissues so that the limb swells and feels tight while the surface looks almost dry. The finding that marks an arterial injury is the pulsatile jet, but the absence of a jet proves nothing, because a torn artery can retract and spasm and bleed into a closed space, and a deep wound with an expanding swelling is an arterial injury until proved otherwise. An artery divided cleanly may clot and stop for a time, then bleed again when the pressure of the circulation rises or when a dressing is lifted, and that pause is one of the traps of early assessment. Control of arterial bleeding is the most urgent task in this chapter, and the ladder of pressure begins with a hand and ends with a tourniquet for the limb and with hospital care for the wound that pressure cannot reach.

The mixed bleeding of a crushed wound follows a heavy blow, a vehicle wheel, a machinery injury, or a fall under a heavy object, and it combines all three sources at once. The vessels are torn rather than cut, the tissue around them is bruised and swollen, and the bleeding may stop quickly because the swelling itself presses on the torn vessels from within. That calm is deceptive, because the pressure that stops the surface flow also raises the pressure inside the limb, and the finding that should worry the responder is a limb that is tense, cool, and painful out of proportion to the wound, with numbness or weakness below the injury. A crush wound may also hide a fracture and a divided vessel at the same time, and the responder must not straighten a deformed limb to make it look better, because movement can release a clot and turn a contained injury into a free hemorrhage. The lay first aider keeps the limb in the position found, covers the wound, keeps the patient warm, and does not try to reduce a swelling by binding the limb tightly. Definitive hospital care is where the pressure inside the limb is measured, the fracture is assessed, and the vessels are examined, and no field technique substitutes for that assessment.

Recognition of life-threatening hemorrhage depends on the behavior of the blood and on the behavior of the patient rather than on the color of what is on the ground. The wound that matters is the one that keeps bleeding through every dressing, the one that pools under the patient so that a hand placed beneath the back comes away wet, and the one whose surrounding swelling grows while the responder watches, and these findings speak of a rate of loss that the eye cannot measure. The patient tells the same story in a different language, with a level of consciousness that is becoming dull, a pulse that is fast and thin, a breathing rate that is rising, skin that is pale and cool, and a restlessness or a thirst that appears before the collapse. The teaching that arterial blood is bright and venous blood is dark is useful in the classroom and unreliable at the roadside, because lighting, contamination, and the depth of the wound all change the color, and a wound can bleed from more than one source at once. The responder therefore asks whether bleeding continues despite control and whether shock is appearing, because either answer moves the patient toward definitive hospital care at once. A measured pressure such as 90 millimeters of mercury may be quoted as a threshold, but it is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the line that matters shifts with age, with pregnancy, and with the patient's usual state.

The ladder of control rests on one physical idea, that bleeding stops when the pressure applied at the bleeding point exceeds the pressure inside the torn vessel, and every step brings more pressure to bear on a smaller area or holds that pressure without human hands. A flat hand over a broad dressing spreads the force and is the first move for surface bleeding, while fingertips or a fist concentrated over the exact point of a spurt produce a far higher local pressure and are the correct move when a jet continues despite the first attempt. The mistake that costs the most is the repeated lifting of the dressing to see whether the bleeding has stopped, because each look breaks the forming clot and returns the wound to the beginning, so the dressing is left in place and further layers are added if blood shows through. The second mistake is to press on a foreign body embedded in the wound, because a knife, a fragment of glass, or a piece of metal may be plugging the vessel beneath it, and the correct act is to build padding around the object and stabilize it while the patient is moved with it in place. Pressure works best when it is directed along the track of the wound rather than across the surface, which is why packing a deep wound can succeed where a dressing over the skin fails. Each step is held until a finding tells the responder to move on, since bleeding controlled and the patient stable means the step is right, while continued soaking, a rising pulse, or a shrinking level of consciousness means the next step is required now.

Direct pressure is the first step and the one most patients need, and it belongs to the lay first aider as much as to the paramedic. The bare hand, protected by gloves or by any barrier that keeps blood from broken skin, is placed over a clean cloth or a dressing on the wound, and the pressure is applied firmly and without interruption while help is called and the patient is kept warm. If blood soaks through, the pad is not removed, and a second pad is laid over the first while the hand returns to the same place with the same force. Pain is expected and does not mean the pressure is wrong, but a patient who becomes unresponsive or whose pulse becomes impalpable means the step has failed and that the next rung of the ladder and the fastest journey to definitive care are now required. A period such as 10 minutes of uninterrupted pressure is often described as enough time to judge whether a wound will stop with direct pressure, and that figure is an illustration which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the time differs with the size of the vessel and with the patient's clotting.

A pressure dressing is the second step, and it is the trained responder's way of handing the work of the hand over to a bandage so that the patient can be moved without losing the pressure achieved. The principle is unchanged, in that the dressing is applied directly over the wound and the bandage is wound over it tightly enough to keep pressure on the bleeding point and loosely enough that the tissue beyond it is not starved. After the dressing is secured, the responder checks what lies beyond it, looking at the color and the warmth of the skin, feeling the pulse at the wrist or the foot, and asking the patient to move the fingers or the toes if the injury allows. A finger that has turned pale or blue and a pulse that can no longer be felt below the dressing are findings that the bandage has become a tourniquet by accident, and the correct response is to release it and reapply with less tension rather than to wait and watch. A limb that continues to swell inside a pressure dressing, or a patient whose pain becomes severe and out of proportion, points toward compartment syndrome, and the responder must escalate and move the patient rather than tighten the bandage further.

Wound packing is the third step, and it belongs to the trained responder or to the paramedic working within a protocol, because it requires the wound to be appropriate, the technique to be learned, and the pressure to be delivered to the exact source. Packing is used for deep wounds in the groin, the armpit, and the neck, where a tourniquet cannot reach and a dressing across the surface cannot press on the vessel; these junctional wounds are among the most lethal of external bleeding sites. The gauze is pushed to the bleeding point and packed firmly back along the track until the cavity is filled, and then pressure is held over the packed wound with the flat of the hand. Packing is not a technique for a chest wound, it is not a technique for a wound of the abdomen with bowel exposed, and it is not a technique for the lay first aider, who covers and presses from the outside and waits for trained help. The finding that packing has worked is blood that stops rising through the gauze while pressure is held, together with a patient whose level of consciousness and pulse remain steady; the finding that it has failed is gauze that keeps filling with blood, and that finding means the tourniquet or the operating room, not another attempt. A foreign body embedded in the wound is stabilized in place and packed around, and it is never removed in the field, because removal may release hemorrhage that cannot be controlled and may injure a structure that is still intact.

A hemostatic dressing is a gauze or a sponge carrying an agent that helps blood to clot where it is pressed, and it is a tool for the trained responder or the paramedic, not for the lay first aider with bare hands. These dressings exist in some services and not in others, they are carried under a protocol, and their use requires training, because the agent works only when it touches the bleeding vessel and only when pressure is still applied over it. The most important thing to say is what they do not replace, since they do not replace direct pressure, they do not replace packing technique, they do not replace the tourniquet when a limb is bleeding beyond control, and they do not replace the operating room where a vessel is torn beyond the reach of any dressing. A hemostatic dressing is therefore not a reason to delay transport or to stop watching the wound, and the responder who has used one records what was used, because the receiving team must know what is in the wound. The choice of agent and the decision to carry it belong to the local protocol and to the service, and no amount or duration of use should be taken from a manual rather than from that protocol.

The tourniquet is the fourth step and the one most often misused, and its place is narrow and owned by the trained responder or the paramedic under a protocol. The indication is life-threatening bleeding from a limb that has not been controlled by direct pressure and by packing, and a further indication is a scene with many casualties in which a responder must free both hands for the next patient. The contraindication is bleeding that does not come from a limb, because a tourniquet cannot be placed around the neck, the chest, the abdomen, or the groin, and attempting to do so causes harm without controlling the source; bleeding from those places belongs to packing and to immediate surgery. A tourniquet is placed between the wound and the heart, as close to the wound as the anatomy allows and never over a joint if a length of limb above the joint is available, and it is tightened until the bleeding stops rather than until some particular number of turns has been made. The lay first aider does not apply a manufactured tourniquet unless instructed to do so by emergency medical services and trained to use it, and a makeshift band used as a tourniquet can tighten a limb without stopping the flow, which adds pain and tissue damage while the patient continues to bleed. Once a tourniquet has controlled the bleeding, it is not loosened in the field, and that rule is stated again below because it is the rule most often broken.

The time a tourniquet was applied is as important as the tourniquet itself, and it must be recorded on the patient in a way the receiving team cannot miss. The reason is that a limb deprived of blood begins to suffer, and the receiving team must know how long the limb has been without flow in order to judge the risks of releasing the tourniquet and the urgency of restoring the circulation. The record is written on the skin near the tourniquet, on a tape fixed to the limb, or in a place agreed by the local protocol, and it is spoken aloud at handover, because a time not written down is a time that will be lost. A tourniquet is not loosened in the field once it has controlled bleeding, because the clot that has formed behind it may not hold and the patient may hemorrhage again where no one can restore control; release is a decision for definitive hospital care, made with preparation for what may follow. A period such as 2 hours is often quoted as the point at which the risk to the limb becomes serious, and that interval is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the tolerance of muscle and nerve differs with temperature, with the patient, and with the injury. Reassessment after a tourniquet means checking that bleeding has truly stopped, watching for the signs of shock, checking the limb beyond the tourniquet, and looking for a second wound missed while attention was fixed on the first.

Reassessment is not a single act performed once but a rhythm that continues from the scene to the handover, and it follows the same order as the primary survey. The responder returns to the airway, the breathing, and the circulation, and then to the level of consciousness, the pupils, and the limbs, because a patient who was talking a minute ago and is silent now has told the responder more than any wound can. The findings that mark a patient who is still bleeding are a dressing soaked through, a swelling that has grown, a pulse that has risen and softened, a breathing rate that has climbed, skin that has become cold and clammy, and a level of consciousness that is dulling, and these are recorded and compared with the previous set rather than judged alone. The Glasgow coma scale is used where the responder is trained in it, and it turns the impression of drowsiness into something two people can compare, while the trend over time carries more meaning than any single score. A blood pressure that falls and a pulse that rises are the language of concealed blood loss, and the responder must suspect a wound that has stopped bleeding into a cavity, because a limb and a chest can hold a large volume before anything is seen outside.

Hypothermia is a companion of hemorrhage rather than a detail of comfort, and it begins the moment a patient bleeds, lies on cold ground, or has clothing cut away. Blood loss reduces the volume that carries heat, exposure removes heat from the surface, and the cold that follows makes the clotting system work less well, so a patient who is cold bleeds more and a patient who bleeds more becomes colder, and that circle can become impossible to break outside a hospital. The responder breaks it by covering the patient before the journey rather than after, by insulating the patient from the ground, by removing wet clothing and replacing it with dry coverings where that can be done without exposing the wound, and by keeping the ambulance or the vehicle warm on the way. A patient who is bleeding, burned, or exposed is protected against hypothermia at the same moment as the bleeding is controlled, and warming is not delayed until the bleeding stops, because the two tasks run together. A temperature such as 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the line at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold shifts with age and with the way the measurement is taken.

Shock is the state in which the circulation can no longer deliver enough oxygen to the tissues, and hemorrhage is its most common cause in trauma, so every patient who is bleeding is watched for it from the first minute. The early patient compensates, with a fast pulse, a narrowing pulse pressure, cool hands, and a blood pressure that is normal or slightly raised, and that stability is the most dangerous moment, because the loss is already large while the numbers still look acceptable. The patient who can no longer compensate becomes confused, then restless, then drowsy, with rapid shallow breathing and a pressure that falls, and by that stage the loss is severe and the remaining time is short. Fluid replacement, the choice of what is given into a vein, and the decision to give blood products belong to the paramedic under a protocol and to definitive hospital care, and they are decisions about a patient and a local system rather than instructions that can be carried away from a manual, so nothing here names a substance, an amount, a route, or a frequency. Analgesia for the patient with a severe wound is decided in the same way, by the provider authorized to prescribe it and by the protocol in force, because pain is real and poorly treated pain worsens the circulation, while the wrong choice in a bleeding patient can worsen the injury. The responder's own contribution to shock is to stop the bleeding, keep the patient warm, keep the patient flat and still unless a head or chest injury forbids it, and shorten the time to the surgeon.

Definitive hospital care owns everything that repairs rather than contains, and knowing where that line lies is part of competence for every responder. Exploration of a wound, repair of a torn vessel, removal of a bullet or a fragment, deep cleaning of dead tissue, release of pressure inside a swollen limb, and closure of a wound that may be contaminated all belong to the surgeon and to the operating room, and none is a field procedure no matter how urgent the patient appears. The tetanus question is raised at the first contact and answered by the provider authorized to make that decision under the local protocol, because the patient's vaccination history and the nature of the wound both change the answer, and no reader should take the choice from a chapter rather than from the protocol and the prescriber. Antibiotics follow the same rule, in that the finding which makes the decision urgent is a wound that is deep, contaminated, or caused by a bite, while the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber and to the local guideline. Every patient who has bled must also be watched for the complications that follow, including infection, compartment syndrome, and the delayed effects of a large transfusion, and the handover must carry the wound history, the bleeding history, and the times at which each intervention was performed.

Some sites deserve a word of their own because their anatomy changes the technique. A scalp wound bleeds heavily and frightens everyone, and its control is the same direct pressure as anywhere else, but the responder must not mistake a dramatic flow for a deep head injury and must watch the level of consciousness at the same time, because a patient who is bleeding from the scalp may also be bleeding inside the skull. A wound of the face or the neck may bleed into the airway, so the first question is whether the patient can breathe and speak, and pressure is applied around the wound rather than over a structure that is keeping the airway open. A nosebleed that does not stop is controlled by pinching the soft part of the nose and leaning the patient forward, which belongs to the lay first aider, while bleeding that continues belongs to the trained responder and to hospital care, and the patient who is swallowing blood must be watched for vomiting. A traumatic amputation has a stump that bleeds, and the stump is controlled with direct pressure, packing, and a tourniquet where the protocol allows, while the severed part is wrapped in clean material, kept cool, and sent with the patient, because reattachment is a decision for a trauma center and the part must not be placed directly on ice.

To summarize, external bleeding is read by its source and by its behavior, and the responder treats the patient rather than the wound. Capillary bleeding oozes and yields to a covered, pressing hand; venous bleeding flows steadily and becomes deadly when the vein is large; arterial bleeding jets with the heartbeat and may hide inside a swollen limb; and a crushed wound mixes all three while the swelling itself conceals the loss. The ladder of control runs from direct pressure, through a pressure dressing, through packing of an appropriate deep wound, through a hemostatic dressing where the service carries one, to the tourniquet for a limb that will not stop, and each rung is held until the finding that tells the responder to move on, while every step is named with the provider level that owns it and no definitive procedure is presented as first aid. The tourniquet is not loosened in the field, its time is written on the patient, and reassessment continues in a rhythm until handover. Hypothermia and shock travel with hemorrhage, so warmth, monitoring, and the shortest safe journey to definitive care are part of bleeding control and not additions to it. Every time, pressure, temperature, depth, and figure in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 6 — Wound Dressing

A dressing is a covering placed on a wound, and it is the most common act in trauma care and the most easily misunderstood. Its purposes are four and must be held together: to help control bleeding, to protect exposed tissue, to keep the wound clean, and to allow the patient to be moved. A dressing does none of these things permanently, and it does not clean a wound, close a wound, remove contamination, or repair anything that has been divided. It is a temporary shelter that buys time for the acts that do belong to treatment, and it is never a substitute for definitive hospital care. A dressing lies against the wound and is chosen for what it does there, while a bandage only holds it in place and may also exert pressure. The lay first aider covers the wound with whatever clean material is at hand and without probing it, the trained responder or paramedic opens the sealed dressing and applies it within training and protocol, and definitive hospital care decides what lies beneath the dressing and what must be repaired or removed. This chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

Before any dressing is opened, the scene must be made safe, because a responder who kneels in traffic or beside a fire becomes a second patient and helps no one. Traffic, unstable vehicles, fire, electricity, water, animals, violence, structural collapse, and the hazards of the patient's own body fluids all take precedence over the wound, and personal protective equipment, or PPE, with gloves at the least, protects both the responder and the patient. The lethal possibility that must be named first is hemorrhage that cannot be controlled, and the finding that reveals it is blood that spurts with each beat of the heart, blood that soaks through one dressing and then another, or a swelling that grows while the responder watches. A dressing applied to such a wound without a plan is a gesture rather than a treatment, and the trained responder or paramedic must move to the methods the protocol authorizes for catastrophic bleeding. The second lethal possibility is a wound that has taken the airway, and the finding is a patient coughing blood whose voice has changed or who is struggling to breathe after an injury to the face or the neck. The third is a wound that has opened the chest, and the finding is air that moves in and out of the opening with each breath. A patient who is bleeding, burned, or lying exposed also loses heat, so protection against hypothermia begins at the same moment as the dressing and is not postponed until transport.

A sterile dressing is one that has been prepared and packaged so that it carries no living organisms when it is opened, and it is the right choice for any wound whose surface is open to the air. An abrasion, a laceration, a burn, a puncture, or a wound with exposed deep tissue all qualify, because every one of them has lost the barrier that keeps contamination out. Sterility is a method as much as a supply, and it is preserved only by handling, so the responder touches the edges of the wrapper and never the surface that will lie on the wound. A dressing that touches the floor, the clothing, or the skin around the wound is no longer sterile, and a dressing that has been dropped or removed is never returned to a wound. The lay first aider may use the cleanest material available when no sterile dressing exists, because a clean covering is better than an exposed wound, and must not delay care while searching for a perfect package. The trained responder carries sealed dressings in a kit and follows the protocol for the size and the number to be applied. A sterile dressing placed on a heavily contaminated wound does not sterilize it, because contamination already in the tissue stays there until it is removed, and that removal belongs to the trained responder or to definitive hospital care rather than to the roadside.

A pressure dressing is built on top of direct pressure, and it is the dressing that is asked to stop bleeding rather than merely to cover. The material is placed over the bleeding point, a pad is stacked on it, and the bandage is wrapped firmly enough to press the pad into the wound while the circulation beyond remains. The situation that calls for it is bleeding that continues under a simple covering, and the finding that says it is working is that the flow stops and the dressing stays dry at its edges. The lay first aider may hold direct pressure with a gloved hand or a clean cloth and may add layers without removing the first one, because lifting the dressing to look can pull away the clot. The trained responder or paramedic applies a formal pressure dressing, checks the pulse, the feeling, and the movement beyond it, and reinforces rather than removes when blood appears at the margin. A pressure dressing that is too tight can shut off the circulation, and the findings are a limb that becomes pale, cold, and numb with pain that grows worse. The distinction between pressure that controls bleeding and pressure that strangles a limb is a clinical judgment the trained responder reviews repeatedly while moving toward definitive hospital care.

An occlusive dressing is one that does not allow air or fluid to pass, and its place is narrow and must be stated as a decision rather than as a habit. The wound that calls for it is an open wound of the chest, where air entering the pleural space with each breath can collapse a lung, and the finding that reveals the problem is the sound or the feel of air moving through the opening. It is also used to cover exposed bowel or other abdominal contents and to protect a wound that must not dry, such as an open joint or a burn surface that is being moved a short distance. The trained responder or paramedic places it within the protocol, and the lay first aider covers a chest wound with the cleanest available material and lets the arriving emergency medical services decide. An occlusive dressing applied to a wound that is already infected, or to a wound with dead tissue and heavy contamination, traps organisms and fluid and can turn a dirty wound into a worse one, so it is not a default covering. A plastic sheet pressed flat over a chest wound may seal the opening completely, and the finding that this has become a problem is a patient who becomes more breathless as the dressing is applied. The decision about how the occlusive dressing is made, how it is secured, and whether it is vented belongs to the trained responder and to the protocol, never to improvisation.

Packing is the act of placing material deep into a wound to press on a bleeding surface that cannot be reached from the outside, and it belongs in a short list of places. The wounds that should be packed are those in the junctional zones, the groin, the armpit, the base of the neck, and the stump of an amputation, where a surface dressing cannot press on the artery that is bleeding. Packing is not first aid with bare hands, and it belongs to the trained responder or paramedic who works under a protocol, or to a lay first aider only where a dispatcher or a training course has explicitly authorized the technique. The material is introduced firmly and continuously until the wound is filled and the bleeding is controlled, and the finding that packing has succeeded is that blood stops welling from the wound and the patient's pulse begins to steady. The wound is then covered with a pressure dressing so that the packing is held in place, and the patient is moved without delay toward definitive hospital care. Just as some wounds should be packed, others must never be, because packing a space that communicates with a body cavity pushes contamination inward and hides bleeding that the hospital needs to see. A wound of the chest, a wound of the abdomen with exposed bowel, and a wound of the eye are not packed, and an embedded object is never pushed deeper or removed in the field, because removal may cause hemorrhage that cannot be controlled. A wound whose depth is unknown, and a wound of the neck near the airway, are also not packed blindly, because the material may enter a vessel or the airway.

Contamination control is the part of dressing that is invisible when it is done well, and its logic is simple enough to state. Every wound carries organisms in its depths, and the dressing must keep new contamination out while not driving the contamination already there further in. The finding that makes contamination control urgent is visible dirt, grit, clothing fibers, or dead tissue, because each carries organisms and gives them a place to grow. The lay first aider covers the wound and does not clean it, does not scrub it, does not pour anything into it, and does not touch the wound surface with ungloved fingers. The trained responder may clean around a wound within training and protocol, and definitive hospital care performs the irrigation and the removal of dead tissue, and the decisions about antibiotics belong to the physician. A dressing that has been used once is never returned to a wound, and a dressing that has become soaked is reinforced from outside rather than lifted away. The responder who changes a dressing simply to see the wound has contaminated it again and has also disturbed whatever clot was forming.

Exposed tissue is the situation that most often frightens a responder into doing too much, and the correct response is restraint plus protection. Exposed bone looks pale or white and may be the end of a fractured bone that has come through the skin, and the finding that accompanies an open fracture is a wound that communicates with the bone and often a limb that is deformed. Exposed tendon appears as a white or silvery cord that may be under tension within the wound, and its presence means that the wound has crossed a structure whose repair belongs to the surgeon. Exposed bowel appears as loops of pink or dusky bowel that have left the abdomen through a wound, and the finding that demands immediate action is a wound that keeps the bowel outside and prevents its return. The protection of exposed tissue begins with covering it, and a moist dressing is used for exposed bowel and for other surfaces that must not dry, held with a clean outer layer that does not press on the tissue. Nothing is pushed back into the body, and no organ or bone is straightened, because forcing tissue back can strangulate it or introduce contamination the body had kept out. The trained responder or paramedic may apply a moist sterile covering and an occlusive layer within the protocol, and the patient is moved to definitive hospital care where the wound can be explored and repaired.

Certain materials must never be placed in a wound, and the reason is not cleanliness alone but the harm that the material itself does to tissue. Loose cotton, tissue paper, and any fabric that sheds fibers leave strands in the wound that act as a foreign body, keep organisms in place, and provoke inflammation that delays healing. Soil, sand, gravel, animal dung, and the ash of a fire are never used to pack or to cover a wound, because they carry organisms and particles that cannot be removed by the responder who put them there. Household remedies such as toothpaste, engine oil, butter, or a poultice of leaves have no place in a wound, because they injure the tissue, hide the appearance of the wound, and mislead the clinician. Adhesive tape is not laid directly on broken skin, because removing it tears the wound surface, and a dressing is never secured with a band so narrow that it cuts into the limb like a cord. A dressing is also never taken from another patient, never reused after it has been removed, and never applied from a package that is torn, damp, or already open. The material that belongs on a wound is a sterile or clean dressing of a kind the protocol recognizes, and the decision about what a particular wound needs belongs to the trained responder, the nurse, or the physician.

A dressing is a temporary act, and the moment it is in place the attention of the lay first aider, the trained responder or paramedic shifts from applying it to checking it. The first check is whether the bleeding has stopped, and the finding is a dressing that stays dry at its margins rather than one that is quietly filling underneath. The second check is the circulation beyond the dressing, which is judged by the pulse, the color, the warmth, the feeling, and the movement of the limb, and the finding that the dressing is too tight is a limb that is pale, cold, or numb with pain that increases. The third check is the position and the security of the dressing, and the finding that it has failed is a dressing that has slipped, that has been displaced by movement, or that no longer covers the wound. The fourth check is the patient as a whole, because a dressing that looks adequate on a limb means little if the patient is becoming restless, confused, or drowsy, and those findings belong to the assessment of the level of consciousness and to the search for shock. The signs that a dressing has failed include blood striking through the material, an expanding swelling around the wound, a limb that grows tense and hard, and air that is felt escaping near a chest dressing. A dressing soaked with fluid that lies cold and wet against the patient also steals heat, and cold worsens bleeding because it interferes with clotting.

The temptation to make a wound look normal is the error this chapter exists to prevent. A dressing that is neat and dry is satisfying to the eye, and it can persuade a responder that a patient who is still bleeding internally is stable, which is why the patient and not the dressing is the object of the assessment. A dressing is never lifted to look at a wound that is not bleeding through it, because every lifting disturbs the clot and introduces organisms, and the information gained is rarely worth the harm. An embedded object is stabilized in place by the trained responder or paramedic and the patient is moved with it, because the object may be tamponading a vessel whose bleeding cannot be controlled once the object is gone. A deformed limb is not straightened to make it look normal, because the movement can injure the vessels and the nerves that survived the original injury, and the limb is splinted in the position found. A burn is not dressed with a material that will have to be peeled from the surface, and a wound is not closed in the field when the protocol places closure in definitive hospital care. The responder who leaves a wound looking imperfect but keeps the patient alive has done the work, and the responder who makes it look tidy at the cost of a clot or a pulse has done harm.

Burns ask for dressings that do not stick, because the surface of a burn is tissue that will be lost and an adhering dressing will remove it when it is taken away. A burn is covered with a clean, non-adherent sheet, and in the field a clean plastic film may serve for a short time to keep the surface moist and reduce pain from the air. The finding that changes the plan is a burn that circles a limb or the chest, because such a burn can tighten as it swells and can interfere with the circulation or with breathing, and that patient belongs to definitive hospital care urgently. The stump of an amputation may bleed heavily, and the trained responder or paramedic controls the bleeding with the methods the protocol authorizes and applies a sterile pressure dressing. An open fracture is covered with a sterile dressing by the trained responder or paramedic, the limb is splinted in the position found, and the bone is not pushed back through the wound, because the wound is contaminated and the movement is a surgical decision. A wound that crosses a joint may have opened the joint space, and the finding is a wound that gapes with movement or that leaks a clear or blood-stained fluid, so it belongs to definitive hospital care because an open joint becomes an infected joint. A scalp wound bleeds heavily because the scalp is richly supplied with blood, and the finding that matters is not the blood on the outside but a change in the level of consciousness or a pupil that differs between the two eyes.

The dressing is also a message, and how it is described to the next clinician determines what that clinician does first. The handover carries the time the injury happened, the time the patient was first seen, the time the dressing or the tourniquet was applied, what was placed on the wound, and whether the bleeding has stopped. The tourniquet is not loosened in the field once it has controlled the bleeding, and the trained responder or paramedic writes the time it was applied on the patient where the receiving team will see it, because the duration of its use changes the decisions made in the hospital. The handover also carries what was not done, including the object that was left in place and the wound that was not packed, so that the next team does not have to guess what happened before arrival. The findings of the last check, including the pulse, the feeling, the movement, the color, and the warmth beyond the dressing, are more useful than a summary of how the wound looked.

Warmth is not a comfort but a treatment, because a bleeding patient loses heat with the blood, a burned patient loses it through the wound surface, and an immobilized patient loses it to cold ground. Wet clothing and soaked dressings conduct heat away far faster than dry ones, so a soaked dressing that has served its purpose is covered with dry layers where the protocol allows. A temperature of 35 degrees Celsius is sometimes named as a line for hypothermia, and that figure is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line differs with the patient and with the way the temperature is taken. Cold interferes with clotting and worsens shock, so a warm patient is easier to keep alive, and the lay first aider insulates the patient from the ground and covers the head without delaying transport. A patient who has lost blood loses the ability to keep warm as well as the blood itself, and that is why warmth is part of every dressing and not an afterthought.

Protection against tetanus and the decision about antibiotics are clinical decisions, and the dressing is the moment at which they are first considered. The finding that makes the tetanus question urgent is a wound that is deep, that is contaminated with soil or with animal or human material, that contains dead tissue, or that was produced by a puncture, and the question is asked at the first contact rather than at the next visit. The decision about whether protection is needed, and about what is given, belongs to the trained responder or paramedic under the local protocol, to the nurse, or to the physician, and this manual names the decision and never the amount. The same rule applies to antibiotics, which are considered when a wound is heavily contaminated, when it involves a joint or a body cavity, when tissue is dead, or when the patient has a condition that makes infection more dangerous. A patient with a fever, a wound that is becoming more painful, spreading redness, or a discharge after a dressing has been in place needs reassessment rather than a new dressing alone. Pain is information as well as suffering, and the decision about pain relief belongs to the trained responder or paramedic under the local protocol and to the prescribing clinician, so the choice of substance, the amount, and the way it is given are theirs and not this manual's. The lay first aider does not give any medicine, does not apply any substance to the wound, and reports what was seen and when the injury happened so that the clinician can make the decision.

Observation after the dressing is continuous rather than a single act, and it is the trend of the observations that guides the next decision. The trained responder records the pulse, the blood pressure, the breathing rate, the temperature, the level of consciousness, and the findings of the Glasgow coma scale where it is used, and repeats them so the direction of travel is visible. A pulse of 110 beats per minute in a bleeding patient is a finding to report and to follow, and that figure is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the rate that signals danger depends on the patient's age, fitness, and usual state. A blood pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury is the same kind of illustration, and the number alone never replaces the examination of the patient, because a young patient may hold a pressure until the loss of blood is severe. A patient whose pulse rises while the pressure falls, whose breathing becomes faster, whose skin becomes pale and clammy, and whose level of consciousness declines is a patient who is bleeding or in shock, and the dressing is only one part of that picture. The trained responder or paramedic acts on that pattern at once and moves the patient toward definitive hospital care, while the lay first aider reports the change in plain words rather than waiting for a measurement. Nothing in this chapter can be learned from listening alone, because the skills it describes are learned in a practical course with supervision and repetition, and when stores are short the substitute must imitate the dressing rather than the treatment. The finding that a responder has reached the limits of the role is a wound that cannot be controlled by pressure, an exposed structure that cannot be protected with what is at hand, or a patient whose condition is changing in a way the responder does not understand.

A constructed illustration may make the sequence easier to hold, and it is invented for teaching and describes no real patient and no real incident. Two trained responders reach a driver who is sitting in a car after a collision, and one of them makes the scene safe while the other puts on gloves and looks at the patient. The first finding is blood soaking through the clothing over the thigh, and the responder holds direct pressure while the second checks the pulse, the feeling, and the movement in the foot below. The bleeding continues under the first covering, so the responder packs the wound as the protocol allows and adds a pressure dressing above the packing, and the flow slows. The patient is covered with a blanket, insulated from the metal floor, and moved toward a trauma center with the time of the packing written where the receiving team will see it. At the hospital the dressing is removed by the surgical team, the wound is explored under proper conditions, and the decisions about repair, antibiotics, and protection against tetanus are made by those who are trained and authorized to make them.

To summarize, a dressing exists for four purposes, which are to help control bleeding, to protect exposed tissue, to keep the wound clean, and to allow a patient to be moved, and it is a temporary act rather than a treatment. The sterile dressing covers an open wound, the pressure dressing presses on a bleeding point, and the occlusive dressing excludes air or keeps a surface moist, and each is chosen for a situation rather than applied by habit. Packing belongs in the junctional zones when the protocol authorizes it, and it never belongs in a wound of the chest, the abdomen, or the eye, around an embedded object, or in a depth that cannot be seen. Exposed bone, tendon, and bowel are covered and protected and never pushed back, and no material that sheds fibers, carries contamination, or injures tissue is ever placed in a wound. After the dressing is applied the responder asks whether the bleeding has stopped, whether the circulation beyond it is intact, whether the dressing is secure, and whether the patient as a whole is changing, and then repeats those checks because the trend is what matters. The signs of failure are blood striking through, an expanding swelling, a limb that is pale, cold, or numb, air escaping near a chest wound, and a patient who becomes restless or drowsy, and any of them sends the patient faster toward definitive hospital care. Warmth, continuous observation, an honest record, and a clear handover are part of the dressing, and the lay first aider, the trained responder or paramedic, and definitive hospital care each own a different part of the act. Every figure mentioned in this chapter is an illustration whose value must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 7 — Wound Cleaning and Infection Prevention

Before any wound is examined the scene is made safe, because a responder struck by traffic, shocked by current, burned by fire, or bitten while kneeling becomes a second patient and removes the only help the first patient had. Moving vehicles, unstable structures, spilled fuel, water that carries current, animals, and the violence that caused the injury are settled first, and violence may still be present when help arrives, so the emergency medical services are called early and the responder does not enter until the scene is safe. The patient's own blood and body fluids are a hazard too, so gloves, eye protection, and a barrier over the mouth and nose go on before contact. The lethal possibility to name early is an infection already spreading through tissue, revealed by pain far greater than the wound appears to explain with skin that is tense, dusky, or discolored. Skin that fails to blanch, a crackling sensation in the tissues, and a falling level of consciousness mean a surgical emergency rather than a dirty wound. Hypothermia is prevented from this first moment, because a patient who is bleeding, burned, wet, or lying on a cold surface loses heat quickly, and cold worsens bleeding and infection alike.

A wound is cleaned to reduce the number of organisms and the load of dead tissue and foreign material that would otherwise feed them, and the aim is not a wound that looks clean but a wound that heals. Cleaning does not sterilize a wound and no field method can, so the honest goal is to remove what can safely be removed and to leave the remaining tissue able to defend itself. Contamination means organisms are present, colonization means they multiply without injuring tissue, and infection means they invade and the patient shows the signs of that invasion. The movement from one state to the next is not always visible from outside, so a laboratory result is read together with the wound, the patient, and the clock. Infection begins where organisms find dead tissue, a pool of blood, or a closed cavity in which to multiply, which is why every careful step of cleaning is also a step of prevention.

The first action in cleaning a wound is irrigation, which washes loose contamination and organisms out of the wound instead of driving them deeper. The fluid is delivered as a gentle stream directed across and into the wound, not as a jet aimed straight into the depths, because force can push contamination into tissue planes where it cannot escape. The volume of fluid matters more than the name of the fluid, and clean water that is safe to drink is better than an ideal solution that is not there. The lay first aider may pour clean water over a wound and let it run, the trained responder or paramedic may irrigate with the device the service provides, and irrigation under controlled pressure belongs to definitive hospital care. The pressure at which irrigation should be delivered is described differently by different services, so the figure for the equipment in use must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Cleaning means lifting contamination away from a wound, and scrubbing means rubbing the surface to detach material that has stuck to it, and confusing the two turns a helpful act into a harmful one. Scrubbing belongs to the intact skin around a wound, where it removes dirt and grease without injuring tissue that must heal, and it does not belong to the wound bed, where it tears the surface and opens raw areas. Some tissue must not be disturbed at all, among it the fine layer over a healing surface, the cut ends of tendons, the sheath of a nerve, the wall of a vessel, the surface of bone, the lining of a joint, and any exposed bowel or organ. Those structures are protected with a clean, moist cover and left for definitive hospital care, because a responder who cleans them can turn a survivable wound into a damaged limb or a contaminated abdomen. The finding that tells the responder to cover rather than continue is the sight of a structure that looks like tendon, nerve, vessel, bone, joint surface, or bowel. Dead tissue and firmly embedded material also stay in place in the field, because their removal is a surgical decision made where bleeding can be controlled.

Sterile technique is a method rather than a supply, and it can be practiced well with modest materials when the method is understood. It begins with hand hygiene, continues with single-use gloves changed when soiled or torn, and depends on never touching the part of a dressing or instrument that will enter the wound. The field is kept as clean as the setting allows, packaging is opened without contaminating its contents, and an item that has touched the ground or the patient's skin is treated as dirty and discarded. Where personal protective equipment, or PPE, is available it is worn for every wound and every body fluid, and where it is scarce the responder protects the eyes, the mouth, and the hands in that order. Needles, blades, and broken glass are handled with a device rather than with fingers, a used sharp goes into a rigid container and is never recapped by hand, and any exposure through a needlestick, a splash, or a bite is reported at once.

The removal of superficial contamination begins with the skin around the wound, which is cleaned outward from the wound edge so that dirt is not carried into it. Visible grit, grass, clothing fragments, and dried blood at the margin are lifted away with clean forceps or clean gloved fingers, and the trained responder or paramedic may do this with the instruments the service provides. The lay first aider who has only hands and water washes the surrounding skin and pours water over the wound, and does not probe inside it. A foreign body that is embedded, that resists gentle traction, or that lies in the depths is stabilized in place and never pulled, because removal in the field may start a hemorrhage that cannot be controlled. Hair around a wound is not shaved, because shaving creates small cuts that become new sites of infection, and hair that obstructs the view is parted or clipped only where a trained provider judges it necessary.

Certain substances must never be poured into a wound, because they injure the tissue that has to heal while leaving the organisms that matter untouched. Strong antiseptic solutions, alcohol, hydrogen peroxide, and concentrated cleaning agents damage the cells of the wound surface, and the choice of any solution belongs to the trained provider and the local protocol. Powders, ointments, leaves, soil, ash, coffee grounds, engine oil, and traditional preparations placed in a wound become foreign material that provokes inflammation and traps organisms, and petroleum jelly or an oily dressing packed into a cavity seals the surface while the depths collect fluid. A wound heals best in a clean, moist environment, so a dressing that keeps the surface moist without soaking the skin supports healing, while a wound left to dry forms a crust under which organisms collect. A cavity closed over a pool of blood gives organisms a protected place to multiply, which is why a wound that becomes tense, swollen, and dark beneath the skin needs surgical assessment rather than a tighter dressing.

Field cleaning reaches only what water can reach, and everything deeper belongs to definitive hospital care. Surgical exploration, extension of a wound, excision of dead tissue, removal of deeply embedded material, and irrigation of the depths under controlled conditions are surgical procedures, and they are not field procedures however contaminated the wound appears.
