The trained responder or paramedic may clean, irrigate, cover, and immobilize, and may not explore a wound with a finger or an instrument beyond what the protocol permits. The finding that tells the responder the operating room is needed is tissue that is dead, gray, or insensate, a wound that extends into a cavity, a wound over a joint, or a wound whose depth cannot be judged. A wound that reached care many hours after the injury, with the safe interval confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because services define it differently, needs surgical judgment rather than field cleaning alone, and the patient is taken to the facility able to provide it, which may be a trauma center.

Tetanus is a disease of muscle rigidity and lockjaw caused by a toxin from organisms that live in soil, dust, and manure, and it is prevented rather than treated, because once the spasms begin it is severe and often fatal. Tetanus begins with stiffness of the jaw and neck, difficulty in swallowing, and rigidity of the muscles of the back and abdomen, and it can follow a wound that appeared to heal. The time between injury and the first symptom varies with the wound and the patient, so no interval is offered here, and any figure used for it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The decision about protection rests on the wound and on the patient's history, and the history is what the first responder can gather at no cost. The questions are whether the patient has completed a course of vaccination, when the last protection was received, and whether the wound is of the kind that favors the organism, such as a deep puncture, a wound contaminated with soil or manure, a burn, or a bite. The finding that changes the answer is an incomplete or unknown history together with such a wound, and the substance and the timing are chosen by the authorized prescriber or by the protocol that governs the service. A patient whose vaccination status cannot be established is treated as unprotected, and that judgment is stated clearly at handover rather than left in the margin of a note.

Antibiotics given before infection is established are prophylaxis, antibiotics given to treat an established infection are treatment, and the two decisions differ even when the same substance is used. The finding that makes prophylaxis the right answer is usually a wound at high risk, such as a bite from an animal or a human, a wound contaminated with soil, feces, or saliva, a deep puncture, a wound with dead tissue, a wound crossing a joint or a bone, or a wound in a patient whose immune defense is weakened. The finding that makes prophylaxis the wrong answer is a clean, superficial wound in a healthy, vaccinated patient that has been properly cleaned, because antibiotics there add risk without benefit and encourage resistance. Who is authorized to decide is set by law and by the service, so the trained responder or paramedic may follow a standing protocol where one exists, and the prescriber at definitive hospital care decides where no protocol applies. The substance, the amount, and how long it continues are decisions for the prescriber and the local protocol, deliberately not stated here so that no listener can take a prescription from this book. The responder's contribution is to describe the wound, the contamination, the delay, the patient's reported allergies, and the patient's other illnesses, because those facts change the answer, and a patient who already has the signs of infection is a candidate for treatment and surgical assessment rather than for prophylaxis.

Infection announces itself first at the wound, and the earliest signs are easy to dismiss as the ordinary soreness that follows any injury. The wound becomes more painful rather than less, the pain spreads beyond the original margin, the surrounding skin becomes red, warm, and swollen, and the discharge changes from clear fluid to cloudy or foul fluid. The margins may separate, the tissue inside may turn gray or black, and the wound may smell offensive, a finding the patient often reports before anyone inspects it. A wound that was dry and now weeps, a dressing that is soaked sooner than expected, and a dressing that must be changed more often are all signs that the wound is not following the expected course. The lay first aider can see redness, swelling, discharge, and a change in color and can report them, the trained responder or paramedic can clean and inspect the wound and record the findings, and the physician at definitive hospital care decides whether it must be opened, sampled, or taken to the operating room.

The timeline on which infection appears depends on the organism, the wound, and the patient, and it is a guide to watchfulness rather than a schedule to trust. The earliest infections become visible on the first day or the second, when a wound that was quiet becomes painful and red, and that interval is an illustration which must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol because it varies with the organism and the setting. Other infections appear over several days, and some appear after the first week, so a wound that looked well at the first inspection is not finished with being watched. A wound is checked at a fixed interval after closure, examining the same signs each time, and the interval chosen belongs to the protocol of the service and must be confirmed there rather than taken from a book. The patient who leaves care is given clear instructions about which changes must bring a return, among them spreading redness, increasing pain, fever, discharge, and a wound that opens, because a patient told only to watch for infection has not been told anything actionable.

Infection that has moved beyond the wound produces general signs, and those signs are the ones that kill. Fever, shaking chills, a rapid heart rate, rapid breathing, nausea, and rising confusion are the findings of a body fighting a spreading infection, and a temperature such as 38 degrees Celsius is a common illustration of that fever, though the threshold that should raise alarm must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because it differs with age and with the way the temperature is taken. A patient who is unusually confused, drowsy, difficult to rouse, or whose level of consciousness falls is assessed with the Glasgow coma scale by the trained provider and treated as seriously ill. Cold, clammy skin, a weak and rapid pulse, and a falling pressure are the signs of shock from infection, and that patient needs definitive hospital care at once and possibly the intensive care unit, or ICU. The lay first aider who sees shivering with fever, confusion, or a change in behavior reports it immediately, because such findings are easily attributed to fear or to the injury itself. Warmth, cover, and continuous observation accompany every transfer, since a patient who is losing blood, cold from exposure, or immobilized deteriorates faster when infection is added.

Some wound infections destroy tissue at a speed that field care cannot follow, and they are recognized by their behavior rather than by their appearance at the first look. Pain out of proportion to the wound, skin that is tense and discolored, a bronze or dusky color that advances along a limb, blisters filled with dark fluid, and a crackling sensation under the skin are the findings of an infection spreading through deeper tissue. When muscle is involved the limb may become swollen, firm, and painful, the patient may be agitated or withdrawn, and the general signs of severe illness appear alongside the local ones. This condition and the gas-producing infection of muscle that follows deep contamination are surgical emergencies, and their treatment is surgical removal of dead tissue at definitive hospital care together with the medicines chosen by the treating team. No field cleaning, dressing, or medicine outside the hospital changes this course, and the exact interval within which such a limb must reach surgery must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it differs between services.

The decision to send a wound for surgical evaluation is made on features the responder can see and describe, and it does not require a diagnosis. A wound that extends into a cavity, over a joint, across the line of a tendon or a nerve, or one that contains a retained foreign body, dead tissue, or continued bleeding is an indication for definitive hospital care. A wound of the hand, the foot, the face, the genital area, or the eye deserves surgical review even when it looks small, because structures there are packed closely and the consequences of loss are great. A wound whose depth cannot be judged, whose contamination cannot be seen, or that comes with a fracture, a dislocation, or lost sensation also belongs to surgical care. Imaging such as a plain radiograph, an ultrasound, a computed tomography, or CT, or a magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, may be used at the hospital to find a foreign body or to define the path of a wound, and each of those decisions belongs to the treating team. The finding that suggests a wound may wait is a clean, superficial wound in a healthy patient with intact sensation, intact movement, and no foreign material, and even then the wound is documented and reviewed.

Certain wounds are dangerous precisely because they look minor, and a responder who judges by size will be misled. A small puncture from a nail, a thorn, a splinter, or a tooth may carry organisms into a joint, a tendon sheath, or the deep tissue of the foot while the surface closes over the contamination. A bite from a human being carries the organisms of the mouth into a crushed wound, and it is treated more seriously than its size suggests. A wound in a patient with diabetes, poor circulation, a weakened immune defense, or an implanted joint or heart valve may become severe while the patient feels little, because the warning pain and redness are muted. The finding that turns a minor wound into a serious one is anything that delays care, such as a patient who lives far away, who is alone, who is confused, or who cannot return, and each of those findings argues for treatment now rather than advice to watch.

When a patient arrives with a wound that is already infected, the task changes from prevention to recognition and referral. The wound may be swollen, red, hot, and discharging pus, the patient may have a fever and feel generally unwell, and the limb may be painful to move. The finding that makes the situation urgent is skin that is advancing, tissue that is gray or black, or discharge that is foul and thin, because those features suggest infection in the deeper tissue rather than on the surface. The first responder covers the wound with a clean dressing, does not squeeze it, does not open it, applies no heat and no poultice, and moves the patient to definitive hospital care. Definitive care decides whether the wound is opened, sampled, or taken to the operating room, and the medicines used there belong to the treating team and the local protocol.

The patient's own condition decides much of the outcome, and it is part of the assessment rather than a background detail. Poor blood supply, diabetes, a weakened immune defense, malnutrition, smoking, and medicines that suppress inflammation all slow healing and raise the risk of infection, and an older patient, an infant, or a pregnant patient deserves early review because each has less reserve. A patient who is anemic, who has lost blood, or who is in shock carries less oxygen to the wound, so warmth, rest, and the relief of pain improve the flow of blood while cold and agitation work against it. Pain control is a decision for the trained responder or paramedic under protocol and for the prescriber at definitive care, and no substance, amount, or timing is given here, so the lay first aider keeps the patient warm, still, and reassured and gives no medicine at all. The finding that makes the wound urgent in any of these patients is a wound that would be minor in a healthy adult, and the safe interval for review in each group must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A patient who is shivering or whose skin is cold is warmed before and during transport, because a cold patient bleeds more, resists infection less, and suffers more pain.

What is written and what is said at handover decides how the wound is followed, and the record is part of the treatment. The record names the time of injury, the time of first care, the mechanism of injury, the environment of the injury, what the wound looked like when first seen, what was removed, what was left in place, what was used to clean and cover it, and whether tetanus protection was discussed. It also names the patient's reported allergies, other illnesses, medicines, and vaccination history, because each of those changes the decisions made later. The finding that must never be omitted is a wound left with an embedded object, dead tissue, or a covered structure such as tendon, nerve, vessel, or bone, because the next team must know before the dressing is removed. A dressing that is soaked, shifted, loose, foul, or painful under its edges has failed and is replaced by the trained responder or paramedic using the same clean method, while bleeding that restarts, swelling that increases, a limb that becomes tight or numb, or a patient who becomes more confused calls for immediate reassessment and faster transport.

At definitive hospital care the wound is assessed where the light is good, the instruments are sterile, and the patient can be kept warm and monitored. The surgeon or clinician in charge may extend the wound to see its depths, remove dead tissue and foreign material, irrigate the whole wound, sample tissue or fluid for the laboratory, and decide whether the wound is left open or closed. The care of an established infection may include surgical removal of dead tissue, drainage of a collection, and medicines chosen by the treating team according to the organism and the patient. Nothing in this chapter authorizes a field provider to perform surgical exploration, to remove an embedded object, to open a joint, or to give a medicine, and those boundaries are stated so that a listener knows what competence forbids as well as what it permits. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, the local protocol, or the law of the country in which the responder works, and any wound described here is a constructed illustration rather than a real patient or a real incident.

To summarize, a wound is cleaned to reduce organisms and dead material so that the tissue can defend itself, and cleaning is never the same as sterilizing. Scene safety, protection from body fluids, and the early naming of a spreading infection come before any wound is touched, and the finding that reveals that lethal infection is pain out of proportion to the wound with tense, discolored skin and a falling level of consciousness. Irrigation with clean fluid is the first cleaning action, the wound bed is never scrubbed, and tendon, nerve, vessel, bone, joint, and bowel are covered and left undisturbed. Sterile technique is a method of clean hands, clean gloves, clean fields, and untouched wound surfaces, and its value lies in how it is performed rather than in what it is called. Tetanus protection and antibiotic prophylaxis are decisions made by the authorized prescriber under the local protocol, and the responder's part is to gather the history, describe the wound, and name the findings that change the answer. Infection is watched for at the wound and in the patient on a timeline that varies, and the wounds that look minor, such as punctures, bites, and wounds in patients with diabetes or poor circulation, most often surprise the unwary. The patient is kept warm, moved to definitive hospital care when the wound needs surgery, and given a plan for review in words that can be repeated, while every number in this chapter remains an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

# Chapter 8 — Special Wounds

Some wounds are special not because they are larger than others but because the way they were made adds risks that a simple cut does not carry. An animal bite drives living organisms deep into tissue, a puncture wound conceals how far it has traveled, and an embedded object may be the only thing holding a torn vessel closed. This chapter covers bites from animals and from people, puncture wounds, foreign bodies, and objects left in place, at the three levels of care this manual keeps separate. It is educational material, it does not replace training, certification, supervision, or local protocol, and every example is constructed rather than drawn from a real patient or incident.

Scene safety is a sequence rather than a slogan, and it begins with the hazard that is still active. An attacking dog must be controlled or contained, and where an animal cannot be secured the responders wait at a distance and let the animal control service work, because a rescuer who is bitten becomes a second casualty and reduces the help available to the first. Where the bite happened in a conflict between people, the police must be present or the scene left until it is calm, and a responder does not step between two people who are still fighting. Where the wound was made by a needle, a blade, or broken glass, every surface is treated as contaminated, and personal protective equipment, after which PPE is the short form, is worn before the first glove touches the patient. A sharps container, never a pocket or a bare hand, receives anything sharp that is recovered. Only when the scene is safe does the assessment begin, and it begins with the lethal possibilities rather than with the wound.

Three lethal possibilities stand behind these wounds, and each announces itself with a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. The first is hemorrhage that will not stop, shown by blood that keeps coming through every dressing, a fast and thready pulse, pale and cool skin, and a level of consciousness that is drifting. A systolic pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury is often quoted as the line at which such bleeding is critical, but that figure is only an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The second is injury to a deep structure beneath a small wound, shown by a limb that cannot move as it should, a hand or foot that is cold or blue, or a pulse that has disappeared beyond the wound. The third is infection, which may be established already or may follow, and the finding may be absent at first, so the history of a bite or a puncture through a shoe matters more than the skin. Rabies and tetanus belong in the same opening thought, because a bite from an animal carrying the virus is a lethal exposure rather than a wound, and a small puncture with dead tissue and no bleeding is where the tetanus organism thrives.

An animal bite is a crush injury and a contaminated wound at once, and the teeth act as a delivery system rather than as a blade. The jaw crushes muscle and drives oral organisms along the track of the tooth, so the injury extends farther than the visible puncture. Dogs produce ragged lacerations and avulsion, while cats produce fine punctures that seal over and trap organisms beneath the skin. The organisms include Pasteurella species and anaerobic organisms, which flourish where the blood supply has been crushed. Capnocytophaga canimorsus, carried by dogs and cats, can cause severe infection in a person whose spleen has been removed, whose liver is diseased, or whose immune defense is weakened, and that history must be asked out loud. The bite is not cleaned by scrubbing it, because scrubbing drives organisms deeper and tears crushed tissue.

A human bite is treated more seriously than its size suggests, because the human mouth carries aggressive organisms and because the way the injury is made hides its depth. A bite on the hand made when one person strikes another in the mouth is the classic example, and the skin wound may look tiny while the tendon, the joint capsule, or the bone beneath has been opened. The injury often lies over the knuckle, so a wound that looks superficial while the hand is relaxed may slide over a joint and a tendon when the fist is closed. Eikenella corrodens and other organisms of the mouth, with anaerobic organisms, produce infection quickly, and that infection can destroy a tendon sheath or a joint. A human bite therefore belongs to definitive hospital care and surgical assessment, not to a dressing and reassurance at the roadside. The lay first aider controls bleeding and covers the wound without probing it, the trained responder or paramedic documents it and arranges transport, and the surgeon decides whether it must be explored in an operating theatre.

A puncture wound is defined by what it hides, because the surface opening says almost nothing about the depth of the track or the structures along it. A nail driven through a shoe reaches the fat pad, the tendon, the joint, or the bone, and a needle may break and leave its tip inside. The deep structures a puncture can reach include a tendon sheath, a joint space, a bone, a nerve, a blood vessel, the peritoneum, the pleura, and the globe of the eye. A puncture over the chest or the abdomen is a penetrating wound in this manual until proven otherwise, because the track can enter a cavity while the skin closes behind it. The findings that demand definitive hospital care are a joint that will not move fully, a tendon that does not pull when its muscle is used, a bone tender over a point, and a foreign body that can be felt but not seen. A puncture through the sole is the wound most often underestimated, because the patient walks on it, the bleeding is small, and a nail that passed through rubber carries a fragment of the sole into the tissue. The lay first aider does not probe the wound, squeeze it, or open it to search for a fragment, because a blind search in an unclean field turns a closed wound into an open one.

A foreign body is any object inside the wound that did not belong to the patient, and the assessment asks what it is, where it lies, and what it is touching. The material matters because wood and thorns are soft, they break further on removal, and they are poorly seen on a plain radiograph, while metal and glass are usually visible. The location matters because an object in the skin can be removed in a controlled setting, while one near a vessel, a nerve, a tendon, or an organ must be left to the surgeon. The relationship matters most, because an object against a major vessel may be sealing it, and its removal may open a hemorrhage that cannot be controlled in the field. The lay first aider therefore does not remove a foreign body larger than a splinter at the surface, and never one that is embedded, over the eye, in the neck, or in the chest or the abdomen. Where an image is available, the choice among a plain radiograph, an ultrasound, a computed tomography, after which CT is allowed, and a magnetic resonance imaging, after which MRI is allowed, belongs to the clinician who knows the material and the tissue near it. A retained object is often diagnosed late, because the wound closes over it, and the findings are tenderness that persists after healing, a swelling that appears long afterward, a discharge from a small opening, and a limb that will not move normally. Removal is a decision for definitive hospital care, where the tissue can be explored under vision, and some objects are deliberately left in place because removal is more dangerous than keeping them, which is a judgment for the surgeon.

An embedded object is the most dangerous of these wounds because it may be the only barrier between the patient and fatal hemorrhage. A knife, a piece of metal, a wooden stake, a shard of glass, or a broken bone in a limb or the trunk is stabilized in the position found, and it is not withdrawn by anyone in the field. The reason is mechanical, because the object may be pressing on a torn vessel, and pulling it out removes the plug and releases bleeding that no dressing can reach. A second reason is that the object may be tangled in tissue, so dragging it out tears nerves, tendons, and vessels that it had cut cleanly. A third is that the track is contaminated, and moving the object spreads that contamination along structures that were not yet involved. The rule holds at every level below the operating theatre, where the object is finally removed with hemorrhage control and surgical repair immediately available.

The technique of stabilization changes nothing about the object except how safely it can travel. The lay first aider controls bleeding beside the object with direct pressure on the skin around it and never on the object, then builds a ring of padding so that it cannot move. Rolled bandages, cloth, or clean dressings are packed on every side and held with further bandage, so the object is cradled rather than gripped. The object is not shortened, cut, bent, or straightened, because each act moves it inside the tissue and can convert a controlled wound into an uncontrolled one. Where it passes through a limb, both ends are padded and the limb is immobilized as a whole, and the trained responder or paramedic may splint the joints above and below. Where an object projects about 10 centimeters from the skin, that figure is an estimate by eye and is only an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the description in words matters more. Transport is a plan rather than a lift, so the airway and breathing are checked, the level of consciousness is recorded with the Glasgow coma scale where it is available, and the patient is kept still. An object in the eye is protected with a rigid shield resting on the bones around the eye and never on the eye, and an object in the neck is left alone with the airway watched continuously.

The local care of a bite is a sequence that begins with the safety of the responder and ends with a decision rather than with a dressing. Bleeding that is not life-threatening is allowed to flow briefly, because flow helps to carry organisms out, and then pressure is applied with a clean dressing. The wound is washed with clean water or saline and the surrounding skin is cleaned, while the inside of the wound is not scrubbed, not rubbed with a brush, and not packed with an antiseptic that the local protocol does not authorize. High-pressure irrigation that forces fluid into the tissue is avoided in the field, because it can drive organisms and fragments deeper and injure the tissue further. A bite wound is generally not closed by a first responder, and primary closure is a decision for definitive hospital care, made after cleaning, after assessment of the deep structures, and after the risk of infection has been weighed. The lay first aider does not attempt to close the wound with tape, glue, or a suture, and does not apply a tight band that would hide the wound from the team that receives it.

Tetanus is a disease of a wound that has been forgotten, and it is prevented by a decision made at the time of the wound rather than by a dressing. The organism lives in soil, in dust, and in the intestine of animals and people, and it produces its poison in tissue that has no oxygen, which is why a deep puncture, a crush injury, a bite, a wound with dead tissue, and a wound containing soil or a foreign body carry the greatest risk. The lay first aider cannot make the tetanus decision alone and must pass the question to the trained responder, the paramedic, the nurse, or the physician who holds the protocol. The finding that changes the answer is the patient's vaccination history and its documentation, with the nature of the wound and the time since the injury, and where the history is unknown the question is treated as unanswered rather than as reassuring. The substance given, the amount, and the route belong to the local protocol and to the prescriber, and this manual names the decision rather than the dose. Antibiotic prophylaxis after a bite or a puncture is also a clinical decision and never a routine, and the finding that makes it urgent is a wound closed over contaminated tissue, a wound that involves a joint, a tendon, or a bone, a wound with crushed and devitalized tissue, or a patient whose immune defense is weakened. The choice of substance, amount, route, and interval belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol, and no listener should be able to take a prescription from this chapter, so the field team records the animal, the circumstances, the time, the allergies, and the patient's other illnesses for the decision made later.

Rabies is the most feared consequence of a special wound because it is almost always fatal once symptoms begin, and because the wound that transmits it may be trivial. The virus travels in the saliva of an infected animal and enters through a bite, a scratch, or contact of saliva with a break in the skin or with the moist surface of an eye, a nose, or a mouth. The animals that matter most are dogs, bats, monkeys, raccoons, skunks, and foxes, and a bite from a bat may be so small that the patient does not remember being bitten at all. The immediate care is thorough washing of the wound with soap and water and the application of a substance that the local protocol specifies for the virus, done as soon as possible because washing removes virus from the tissue. The decision about vaccination and about the treatment given after exposure belongs to the physician and to the local public health protocol, and the substance, the number of visits, and the route are set there rather than here. The animal must not be killed if it can be observed safely, because observation of a healthy dog or cat over a defined period can change the whole plan, and where that period is given as 10 days the figure is only an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since public health authorities differ.

Infection in a special wound announces itself in a defined way, and the responder who knows the sequence recognizes it before it becomes an abscess or a spreading infection. The early findings are pain that increases rather than settles, redness that spreads beyond the wound edge, warmth of the surrounding skin, swelling, and a discharge that becomes thick or foul. The later findings are a fever, a fast pulse, a rising breathing rate, a level of consciousness that changes, and streaks of redness running along a limb toward the body. A fever may for teaching purposes be described as a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius, but that figure is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line differs with the site of measurement and with the patient. A wound that becomes painful and red within 24 hours of a bite suggests a fast organism, and that interval is also only an illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, while a wound that becomes painful long afterward suggests a retained foreign body or a deep infection of bone. The specific deep infections that must be named are infection of a tendon sheath, infection of a joint, infection of bone, and a spreading infection of the deep tissues that kills muscle and skin. An infection of a tendon sheath makes the finger swell evenly, holds it in a bent position, and makes it painful along the whole length of the sheath, and a spreading deep infection produces pain out of proportion to the wound, tense or discolored skin, and sometimes air beneath the skin that can be felt as crackling, so both are surgical emergencies rather than a course of medicine.

Some wounds appear minor and are not, and the responder who can name them prevents the delay that costs a hand or a life. A small puncture over a joint, a bite over the knuckle, a wound made by a needle that may have broken, a puncture through a shoe, a wound with a retained fragment, and any wound over the eye are all in that group. The wounds that require operative care include a wound that has opened a joint, a wound that has divided a tendon, a nerve, or a major vessel, a wound with an open fracture, a wound with dead tissue that must be removed, and a wound with an object that must be extracted under vision. Surgical exploration, removal of a bullet, deep cleaning of a wound, repair of a tendon, a nerve, or a vessel, and removal of an embedded object all belong to definitive hospital care and are never field procedures. The lay first aider may control bleeding, cover the wound, immobilize the part, keep the patient warm, and arrange transport, and that is the whole of the field task. The trained responder or paramedic may add wound cleaning that the protocol allows, splinting, pain relief under authorization, and a report that names the structures that may be involved. Where a limb has lost its pulse, where movement has been lost, where the skin beyond the wound is pale or blue, or where pain is severe and growing, the transfer to a trauma center is urgent rather than routine.

Pain in these wounds is treated as a finding rather than as a complaint, because pain out of proportion to the wound may be the first sign of a deep infection or of a compartment syndrome. The lay first aider offers comfort, position, quiet, and warmth, and does not give any medicine. The trained responder or paramedic may give analgesia only where the protocol authorizes it and only after the assessment has recorded what was found, because pain relief that hides a worsening limb delays the operation that saves it. The substance, the amount, the route, and the interval belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol, and this chapter names the decision rather than the dose. Bleeding from these wounds follows the same rules as any other bleeding: direct pressure is applied to the skin around an embedded object and never to the object, and a tourniquet is used only where the protocol authorizes it and only with the time of application written on the patient where the receiving team will see it. A tourniquet is not loosened once it has controlled the bleeding, because loosening releases the clot and the pressure holding the vessel closed, and every patient with a bite, a puncture, an embedded object, or blood loss is kept warm, since cold impairs clotting, worsens shock, and makes the injured heart work harder.

The handover for these wounds is short and it decides much of what happens next, so it is prepared while the patient is being moved rather than at the door of the receiving unit. The report names the mechanism of injury, the animal or the object where it is known, the time of the injury, the time the dressing or the tourniquet was applied, and the treatment already given. It names the findings that point to deep injury, which are the loss of movement, the loss of sensation, the loss of a pulse, the pain that is growing, and any bleeding that continues despite pressure. It names the patient's vaccination history where that is known, the allergies, the illnesses that weaken the immune defense, and whether the patient is pregnant, because each of those changes the decisions made in the hospital. It names the object still in the wound, its material, its visible size, and the direction it entered, and it says plainly that the object was stabilized rather than removed, so every measured figure in that report is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Definitive hospital care then begins with the same priorities as the field, which are the airway, the breathing, and the circulation, and the surgeon examines the wound for damage beneath it, tests movement, sensation, and pulses, and decides whether it must be explored in an operating theatre.

Where a foreign body is suspected, an image is chosen for the material, with a plain radiograph for metal and glass, an ultrasound for the soft tissue, a computed tomography, after which CT is allowed, for the deeper planes, and a magnetic resonance imaging, after which MRI is allowed, where soft tissue detail is needed and the object is safe in a magnetic field. Where the wound has entered a cavity, imaging of the chest or the abdomen and consultation with the appropriate surgeon follow, and the patient is watched for the hemorrhage, the air, or the infection that the track may have created. Operative care includes exploration under vision, control of bleeding that the field could not reach, removal of dead tissue, removal of the embedded object, repair of the structures that were divided, and closure only when the wound is clean enough that closure will not trap infection, and all of it is performed under anesthesia. Antibiotics, tetanus protection, and analgesia are decided here by the clinician who holds the protocol, and a patient who remains unstable after the first operation is cared for in an intensive care unit, after which ICU is the short form. A pediatric patient is smaller, so the same bite covers a larger part of the body and carries a greater risk of blood loss, an older patient may have thin skin and a reduced immune defense, a patient whose spleen has been removed or whose immune defense is weakened faces a higher risk of overwhelming infection, and a pregnant patient is assessed with attention to the circulation and to the fetus, while a patient who cannot give a history is treated on the findings rather than on the silence.

Several errors recur in the care of these wounds and each has a reason that makes it worth remembering. The first is probing a puncture to see how deep it goes, which introduces organisms and can open a track that was closed. The second is pulling out an embedded object because it looks loose, which can release bleeding that cannot be stopped in the field. The third is closing a bite, which traps organisms beneath the skin and turns a contaminated wound into an abscess. The fourth is judging a wound by its size, which fails for the human bite, the puncture through a shoe, and the bite in a patient whose immune defense is weak. The fifth is forgetting tetanus and rabies until the patient has left, which loses the time in which the decisions must be made. The responder must also consider the exposure the responder may have suffered, because a bite that broke the skin, a needle that pierced a glove, or blood that reached the eyes or the mouth must be reported at once and the wound washed with soap and water.

A constructed illustration may make the sequence concrete, and it is a teaching example rather than a report of a real patient or a real incident. Imagine a patient who steps on a nail that passes through a rubber sole, walks on it, bleeds very little, and seems to need only a dressing, so the trained responder cleans and covers the wound, records that the nail came through the shoe, and sends the patient to be seen where the deep structures can be examined. At the hospital the surgeon finds that the track reaches the flexor tendon sheath, and the early recognition of the mechanism, rather than the size of the wound, is what made the patient arrive in time. No detail in that illustration belongs to any real person, and no outcome described here may be expected to repeat itself.

To summarize, the special wounds are special because of what they hide and what they carry, not because of how they look. Scene safety comes first, the lethal possibilities are hemorrhage, deep structure injury, and infection, and the biting animal or the violent person may still be present when the responder arrives. Animal bites and human bites are contaminated and often deeper than they appear, puncture wounds must be judged by the structures they can reach rather than by their opening, and foreign bodies must be assessed by material, location, and what they touch. An embedded object is stabilized in the position found and is never removed in the field, because removal may release hemorrhage that cannot be controlled or damage tissue further, and the object travels with the patient. Tetanus, rabies, and antibiotic decisions belong to the trained responder, the paramedic, the nurse, the physician, or the surgeon who holds the protocol, and this chapter names the decision while the substance and the amount belong to the local protocol and the prescriber. Every figure in this chapter, whether a time, a temperature, a distance, a depth, or a rate, is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this material is educational and does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 9 — Knife and Stabbing Injuries

A knife is the most deceptive of the objects that penetrate the body, because a blade is judged by what it has crossed rather than by what can be seen. A blade divides tissue along a narrow line, and the skin closes over that line almost at once. A wound a few millimeters across can lie above a track that has opened the heart, the aorta, the liver, or the great vein behind the collarbone. The responder who arrives first must therefore treat the visible injury as the least reliable clue on the scene. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of your country.

Before anything is done for the patient, the scene must be made safe, because a stabbing is an act of violence. The person who held the knife may still be present, so the first action is to look at the whole scene rather than at the bleeding. Where the assailant may still be near, the responder stays behind cover, calls emergency medical services, and waits for the police to secure the area. Personal protective equipment is worn before contact, and the blade is never picked up with bare hands. Only when the scene is calm does the patient become the object of care.

Several lethal possibilities must be named early, because each announces itself with a finding that can be sought in the first minutes. A patient who becomes breathless, whose breath sounds are absent on one side, and whose neck veins are distended may have a tension pneumothorax. A patient whose heart sounds are muffled and whose pulse weakens with each breath may have blood collecting in the sac around the heart. A patient who is pale, restless, and sweating with a rapid, thin pulse may be bleeding from a major vessel or a solid organ, even when the wound is tiny. A patient who cannot be roused is treated as having an airway injury until hospital care proves otherwise.

The central lesson of penetrating trauma is the mismatch between the size of the wound and the depth of the track. A blade that is 15 centimeters long can cross a whole cavity and reach the spine while the entry remains a slit a dressing covers completely. That length is only an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since services describe blades and wounds differently. The track is not always straight, because a patient who twists or falls with the blade inside can deepen a shallow wound. The search for a second wound matters as much as the first, because a knife used more than once leaves wounds the patient cannot show, and a blade that passes completely through a limb or the neck leaves an exit wound that is often smaller and more ragged than the entry. A stab wound is classified by where it goes and not by how it looks, and any wound whose track can enter the chest, the abdomen, the pelvis, the neck, or a limb is treated as having entered it until hospital care says otherwise.

The mechanism of injury turns a wound into a prediction, and the responder should ask about it while the patient can still answer. Was the blade long or short, held overhand or underhand, and was the patient standing, sitting, or lying down. A blade driven downward into the upper abdomen can reach the heart through the diaphragm, and the same blade driven upward can reach it by another path. A knife that broke, a blade left in the wound, and blows struck afterward all change the picture. The account of the patient is valuable but never a substitute for examination, since a stabbed person may not have felt the wound at the time.

A wound to the chest threatens more structures than a wound anywhere else, and the structures at risk are the heart, the great vessels, the lungs, and the diaphragm. The heart lies behind the lower breastbone and the left ribs, but a blade entering the upper abdomen or the right chest can reach it when the track crosses the midline. The diaphragm is a thin sheet that is crossed easily, so a wound below the nipple line may also have entered the abdomen. The findings to seek are breathlessness, pain on breathing, a bubbling wound, reduced breath sounds on one side, and a fast, weak pulse. The trap is the patient who talks comfortably and complains only of soreness at the wound.

Air in the pleural space, or pneumothorax, and blood in the pleural space, or hemothorax, are the two complications of chest stabbing that must be recognized without imaging. A pneumothorax turns lethal when air can enter but cannot escape, so the pressure rises, the lung collapses, and the heart and windpipe are pushed to the other side. The findings of that tension are worsening breathlessness, a silent side of the chest, distended neck veins, and a windpipe no longer in the middle of the neck. A hemothorax is quieter and may be large before signs appear. Tight binding of the chest is forbidden, because it stops the chest from expanding and hides the deterioration. Covering a bubbling chest wound is first aid, but relieving tension by needle or finger and inserting a chest drain belong to trained hospital staff.

A wound to the abdomen is dangerous because the cavity tolerates injury silently and then declares it without warning. The liver on the right and the spleen on the left are solid organs that bleed heavily, and both can bleed while the patient still looks well. The stomach and the bowel leak their contents, producing a chemical peritonitis that begins as a deep ache and becomes a board-like rigidity. The findings to seek are pain, tenderness, guarding, a rigid abdomen, distension, and a rising pulse, and the absence of pain early proves nothing. The wound is never probed, because probing introduces infection, opens a clot that was holding, and tells the responder nothing the hospital cannot learn better.

The pelvis and the back are regions of large vessels and deep organs, and a wound there combines hemorrhage with contamination. The iliac arteries and veins, the bladder, the rectum, the prostate, the uterus, and the vagina lie within or behind the pelvic ring. The retroperitoneal space holds the kidneys, the pancreas, the duodenum, the great vessels, and the colon, and it is not protected by the abdominal wall. The findings to seek are bleeding from the wound, blood at the meatus, blood in the rectum or urine, lower abdominal pain, and a fast, weak pulse. A broken pelvis can bleed behind the peritoneum until the patient is close to death, and a wound reaching the spinal cord can cause weakness, numbness, or loss of bladder control.

The neck is the most crowded and least forgiving region of the body, holding the airway, the esophagus, the carotid arteries, the jugular veins, and the spinal cord within the width of a hand. A wound there can bleed into the tissues rather than out of them, so an expanding hematoma may compress the airway while the external wound stays small. The findings to seek are a bubbling wound, a hoarse or absent voice, blood in the mouth, a growing swelling, and any change in the level of consciousness. The head and neck are held in the position found while the airway is managed. No responder probes or explores a neck wound, and none removes a blade sitting in it, because a clot may be the only thing closing a torn vessel. Pressure in the neck is gentle, since firm pressure on both sides can stop the blood to the brain, and repair of a torn vessel belongs to the vascular surgeon.

A wound to an arm or a leg is often treated as the least frightening kind of stabbing, and that judgment is wrong. The brachial artery in the upper arm, the femoral artery in the groin and thigh, and the popliteal artery behind the knee are all within reach of a short blade. The nerves to the hand and the foot lie beside those vessels, and tendons crossing the wrist and the ankle are divided by wounds that look trivial. The findings of a vascular injury are bleeding that pressure cannot stop, a pulsating or expanding swelling, a pale and cold limb, a pulse absent beyond the wound, and lost sensation or movement below it. A tourniquet that has controlled bleeding is not loosened in the field, and the time it was applied is recorded on the patient where the receiving team will see it.

Some patients carry a higher risk from the same wound, and the responder who recognizes them moves faster. A child has a smaller blood volume and a greater surface area, so a wound that appears minor can produce shock more quickly than in an adult. A pregnant patient has a uterus that rises out of the pelvis after the early months, so a wound to the lower abdomen may injure the uterus and the fetus. An older patient may take a medicine that prevents clotting, so a wound that would seal in another patient may bleed for a long time. A patient whose level of consciousness is reduced by alcohol, drugs, or a head injury may not report pain, so the examination must be complete rather than guided by complaint.

Hemorrhage is the complication that kills most stabbed patients who die before reaching hospital, and it kills by taking away the volume the heart needs to fill. Blood may leave through the wound, which can be seen and treated, or it may collect in the chest, the abdomen, the pelvis, or the tissues of a limb, which is missed because the skin is intact. The body compensates by narrowing the vessels of the skin and gut, then by raising the heart rate, and only then by failing. The transition is marked by a rapid, thin pulse, cold clammy skin, delayed return of color to a pressed fingernail, restlessness that turns into drowsiness, and a thirst the patient cannot satisfy. The responder treats those findings as hemorrhage until proven otherwise, stops what can be stopped, keeps the patient warm, and reaches definitive care without delay.

The measurement of the pulse and the pressure is part of every assessment, and the figures taught as the line between stability and shock are illustrations rather than rules. A pulse above 110 beats per minute in an adult who is not frightened and not in pain may be the first sign of blood loss, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A systolic pressure below 90 millimeters of mercury is often described as the threshold of shock, and that threshold must be checked against the guideline and the protocol that govern your service. A temperature below 36 degrees Celsius and a falling level of consciousness point the same way, and each of those figures must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol before it drives a decision.

Injury to a major vessel is the complication that turns a limb or neck wound into a fatal one, and it is recognized by findings rather than by imaging in the field. The hard findings are blood that spits or pulses from the wound, a swelling that expands while it is watched, a wound over the path of a named vessel, a pulse absent beyond the wound, and a limb that is pale, cold, and without sensation. Bleeding from a major vessel in a limb is controlled first by direct pressure, and where pressure fails, a tourniquet applied by a trained responder or paramedic under protocol is the next step. A tourniquet is not loosened in the field once it has worked, and the time of application is written on the patient and spoken in the handover. The repair of a divided vessel belongs to the vascular surgeon in the operating room.

The responder does not try to decide which abdominal organ has been injured, but records the position of the wound, notes the pain and the tenderness, and passes the patient to hospital care quickly. An abdomen that becomes rigid and that is tender when pressed and released has peritonitis, and tenderness on release turns a soft abdomen into a surgical emergency. Where bowel has come out through the wound, a condition called evisceration, the bowel is not pushed back, because pushing it back drives contamination into the cavity. The eviscerated bowel is covered with a dressing moistened as the local protocol directs, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is transported with the knees slightly bent. The definitive care of an injured organ belongs to the operating room and never to the roadside.

Hemorrhage control at the scene follows an order that must not be rearranged, and the first action is always the simplest. The lay first aider applies firm direct pressure over a dressing, adds further dressings without removing the first, and keeps the pressure on while help travels. The trained responder may pack a wound bleeding from a deep track, pushing gauze firmly into the wound to its full depth, and may apply a tourniquet to a limb when pressure and packing have failed. The paramedic may use a hemostatic dressing where the local protocol authorizes it, and may consider a junctional tourniquet for bleeding at the groin, the armpit, or the base of the neck. No lay first aider applies a tourniquet, packs a deep wound, or uses a hemostatic agent without training and authorization. The finding that tells the responder to move on is that the bleeding has stopped and the dressing is holding.

An object that remains in the wound, whether a blade, a fragment of it, or a piece of clothing, is never removed in the field, and this rule has a reason that must be spoken aloud. The object may be pressing on a torn vessel and acting as the only plug holding the bleeding back, so removing it may release a hemorrhage that no pressure can control. The object may also be the only thing showing the direction of the track, and the surgeon learns more from it in place than from a wound emptied at the roadside. The object is stabilized where it was found, with dressings packed around it and secured so that it cannot move, and the patient is moved with it still in place. An object in the chest, the neck, or the abdomen is stabilized and left entirely alone.

Protecting the wound is the next task after bleeding is controlled, and it begins with clean hands and clean dressings. The wound is covered with a sterile or clean dressing, and the dressing is left in place rather than changed at the scene, because every change disturbs the clot and adds contamination. A dressing that becomes soaked is covered with another rather than removed, and the number of dressings used is recorded. A wound that bubbles at the chest is covered in a way that lets air leave but not enter, and a responder not trained to do this covers it simply and watches closely for the signs of a tension pneumothorax. The responder does not wash out a deep stab wound, does not pour antiseptic into it, and does not close it with tape or clips, since closing a wound that may have injured deep structures belongs to hospital care.

After hemorrhage control, the responder returns to the beginning of the primary survey, which is the ABCDE approach, and assesses the airway, the breathing, the circulation, the level of consciousness, and the exposure of the whole body. The airway is assessed by listening for air movement and by looking into the mouth for blood or vomit, and a patient who answers clearly has a patent airway for the moment. The breathing is assessed by looking for equal chest movement, by listening for breath sounds on both sides, and by feeling for air at the mouth and nose. The circulation is assessed by feeling the pulse and by watching the color of the skin. The level of consciousness is recorded with the Glasgow coma scale, a score that runs from 3 to 15, and that range must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol where you work. A patient who stops breathing and has no pulse needs cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR, at once, and the exposure step is what finds the second wound.

Cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, and a patient who is bleeding or exposed loses heat faster than a healthy person can replace it. The patient is placed on a barrier against the ground, wet clothing is removed only when it can be replaced with dry covering, and blankets are placed over and under the patient. Warm coverings are applied to the head and neck, and the patient is shielded from wind and rain. A low body temperature impairs the clotting of blood and makes shock deeper. Pain is also real, and the lay first aider answers it with position, reassurance, quiet, warmth, and the presence of someone calm. The trained responder or paramedic may give an analgesic when the local protocol authorizes it, and the physician in hospital makes the further decisions, none of which is reproduced here.

Every stab wound carries the risk of tetanus and of infection, and the questions are the same for every patient even though the answers are local. Tetanus is caused by a bacterium that lives in soil and in manure and enters through a wound, and the wound at greatest risk is deep, contains dead tissue or soil, or was made by an object that was not clean. The first task for the responder is to ask about the immunization history and record the answer, because a patient who cannot remember is treated as a patient who is not protected. The decision to provide protection against tetanus is made by a clinician who knows the history and the local protocol. Antibiotics are likewise not a first-aid measure, and the decision to use them belongs to a prescriber who has examined the wound, so the responder describes the wound, says what contaminated it, and reports any fever or spreading redness. The deep cleaning of a wound, the removal of dead tissue, and the drainage of pus belong to definitive hospital care.

Movement of a stabbed patient is a clinical decision and not a matter of convenience, and the destination is the nearest facility that can provide definitive care. The responder calls emergency medical services early, states that the patient has a penetrating wound, names the regions of the body involved, and gives the number of patients so that the receiving team can prepare. A patient with a wound to the chest, the abdomen, the pelvis, or the neck is transported to a trauma center where a surgeon and imaging are available, and the local protocol defines which facility that is and how far it lies. The target time from injury to definitive care is a figure that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The search for other wounds continues during transport and again at the hospital, because the clothing is cut away, the patient is examined from the scalp to the soles, and the back is examined by rolling the patient as a unit. The mouth, the ears, the nose, the armpits, the groin, the buttocks, and the spaces between the fingers and toes are all examined, because these are the places where a wound hides. Any wound found is described by its position in relation to a fixed landmark and by whether it is bleeding, bubbling, or discharging anything. In hospital, the assessment continues with imaging chosen to answer a specific question that the examination has already raised. A plain radiograph shows air outside the lung, the level of blood in the chest, the position of a retained fragment, and sometimes the track of a blade that has marked bone. An ultrasound at the bedside answers the question of fluid in the chest, the abdomen, or around the heart, and it is repeated because a negative first look does not exclude an injury that is still bleeding.

A computed tomography, or CT, scan answers the question of which structures lie along the track, and it is used in stable patients whose wound has entered a dangerous region. A magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, scan has a limited role in the acute phase because it takes time and because metallic fragments may make it unsafe, and it is used later for nerves and the spinal cord. Every one of these tests is ordered by the clinician who can act on the result. Surgical consultation is requested as soon as a stab wound has entered a dangerous region, and it is requested before the imaging is complete rather than after. The decision to explore a wound is a surgical decision, made on the combination of the track, the findings, and the stability of the patient. The abdomen may be explored when there is peritonitis, when there is evisceration, or when imaging shows free fluid or free air, and that exploration is the definitive treatment of an injured organ.

The chest may be explored when there is continuing hemorrhage, when a great vessel is injured, or when the heart is bleeding into its sac, and that repair is performed by the thoracic or trauma surgeon. The neck may be explored when there is an expanding hematoma, when a vessel is bleeding, or when the airway or the esophagus has been injured. None of these procedures belongs to the field, and a patient who survives the operation may still need the intensive care unit, or ICU, for support of breathing and circulation. The assessment of the blood supply to a limb is performed by a clinician and it decides whether the limb can wait. The pulses beyond the wound are felt and compared with the other side, the color and temperature of the limb are recorded, and movement and sensation below the wound are tested.

The repair of an injured artery by suture, by patch, or by graft is performed by the vascular surgeon in the operating room, and the pressures that decide whether the fascia must be opened are measured in hospital. A divided tendon is repaired by the hand or orthopedic surgeon under anesthesia in an operating room, with the wound cleaned and explored first. A divided nerve is repaired in the same setting or is left for a later procedure, and the decision depends on the contamination of the wound and on the condition of the patient. A wound that has injured the bowel is repaired or resected and joined again, and a wound that has injured the liver or spleen may require packing, repair, or removal. The closure of the skin is sometimes deliberately delayed, because a contaminated wound closed too early becomes an abscess.

Not every stab wound requires an operation, and the patients who do not are the ones who require the closest watching. A patient whose wound has not entered a cavity, whose pulses are intact, whose abdomen is soft, and whose observations are stable may be observed with repeated examination rather than taken to the operating room. The observation is performed by nursing staff and medical staff at intervals set by the local protocol, and each examination is compared with the one before. The findings that end the period of observation are a rising pulse, a falling pressure, increasing pain, a rigid abdomen, a falling urine output, a new breathlessness, or a change in the level of consciousness. The interval of observation is a figure that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

A constructed illustration may make the reasoning clearer, and it is explicitly a construction rather than the record of any real patient or incident. Consider a person who arrives at a clinic with a small slit below the left nipple, walking without help, speaking normally, and complaining only of soreness when breathing deeply. The pulse is a little fast, the breath sounds are equal, and the pressure is normal, so the temptation is to dress the wound and send the patient home. The reasoning of this chapter says otherwise, because the wound lies in a region whose track can reach the heart, the lung, and the diaphragm, and the absence of a dramatic finding proves nothing. The correct decision, made by the clinician who examines the patient, is to keep the patient under observation with repeated examination and imaging if it is available, and to transfer the patient if the condition changes.

To summarize, a knife wound is judged by the track it may have made and not by the size of the opening in the skin, and the regions that make a stabbing lethal are the chest, the abdomen, the pelvis, the neck, the back and flank, and the limbs. The lethal possibilities are named early with the finding that reveals each one, including a silent side of the chest, muffled heart sounds with distended neck veins, a rigid abdomen, and a cold clammy patient with a racing pulse. The first responder makes the scene safe, controls bleeding within the limits of that responder's training, stabilizes any embedded object, protects the wound, assesses the airway and the breathing, protects the patient from cold, and moves the patient to definitive care without delay. Exploration, vessel repair, tendon and nerve repair, fasciotomy, and the removal of an embedded object belong to hospital care and never to the field. Every figure in this chapter is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 10 — Gunshot Wounds

A firearm wound is never only a hole, and the responder who treats it as one will miss the injury that kills. Before the patient is touched, the scene must be made safe, because a weapon that has already fired may fire again and the person who fired it may still be present, so the possibility of a second shot is the first lethal possibility to name, together with traffic, broken glass, and the patient's own blood as a hazard to the rescuer. The finding that tells the responder to hold back, to call the emergency medical services, and to wait rather than to move in is a scene that has not been secured, a crowd that is hostile, or a weapon still within reach of anyone. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, with gloves at the least, is put on before there is any contact with blood or tissue. The lethal possibility inside the patient is hemorrhage that cannot be controlled, and the finding that reveals it is blood that soaks through dressing after dressing, a swelling that grows while the responder watches, or a level of consciousness that is becoming dull while the pulse turns fast and thin. Because a patient who is bleeding and exposed loses heat quickly, protection against hypothermia begins in the first minute, with the patient covered and the surface beneath insulated, since cold worsens bleeding and shock rather than causing only discomfort. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

What a projectile does inside a body is decided less by the projectile than by the energy it carries and by the tissue it crosses, and that single idea explains most of what a responder sees. A firearm turns the chemical energy of a propellant into the motion of a small mass, and the wound is made when that moving mass gives its energy to the tissue in its path. The energy of a moving projectile rises with its mass and rises far more steeply with its speed, so a light projectile that travels fast can transfer more energy than a heavy one that travels slowly, and the shape of the projectile decides how much of that energy is given up and how quickly. A stable, pointed projectile passes through with less transfer, while one that tumbles, flattens, or breaks apart gives more of its energy to the tissue and produces a wider and more irregular injury. Distance changes the speed at which the projectile arrives, because it slows as it travels through air, so a wound from a distant shot and a wound from a shot at contact can differ greatly even when the same weapon was used. The responder therefore treats the visible wound as the opening of a question about energy and about the structures beneath, and reconstructs the mechanism of injury from the scene, from the weapon if it is known, and from the pattern of the wounds, rather than from the wound alone.

A slow projectile produces a track rather than a cavity, and its injury is close to what a blade of the same width would cause. Because the projectile is moving slowly, the tissue ahead of it is pushed aside and cut rather than stretched, and the damage is largely confined to the narrow path the projectile has traveled. Such a wound can still be lethal when the track crosses the heart, a great vessel, or a major nerve, and its quiet external appearance is exactly what makes it dangerous. A projectile that has passed through an intermediate object, or that has traveled a long distance, may arrive with little energy left and produce a wound that a responder is tempted to dismiss. The teaching is that speed decides the pattern and not the seriousness, because a slow projectile that crosses a vital structure kills as surely as a fast one. The responder reads the track as an unknown corridor through the body and asks what lies along it.

A fast projectile stretches the tissue around its path and creates a temporary cavity that opens and closes in a fraction of a second. That cavity is far wider than the projectile itself, and the structures at its wall are pulled, torn, and bruised even though the projectile never touched them. The finding that reveals this remote injury is damage that does not line up with the visible wound, such as a fracture of a bone the projectile did not strike or a nerve that has stopped working far from the track. Tissue that is elastic, such as lung, muscle, and skin, tolerates the stretch reasonably well, while tissue that is dense and inelastic, such as liver, spleen, kidney, brain, and fat, tears under the same force. A cavity described as spanning 10 to 15 centimeters is offered only to make the mechanism imaginable, and any such measurement is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the size depends on the projectile, the tissue, and the distance fired. The responder who understands the temporary cavity stops expecting the wound to explain the patient and starts examining the patient to explain the wound.

Entry wounds are the most reliable part of the picture and the easiest to misread. A typical entry wound is a small, circular or oval defect whose edge is bruised and slightly abraded, and it may carry a ring of dirt or a rim of dried tissue where the projectile rubbed the skin as it entered. When the shot was fired at close range, the skin around the wound may show soot, unburned powder, or a fine speckling that cannot be wiped away, and a contact shot may leave a star-shaped tear or a mark of the muzzle pressed against the skin. These findings speak to the distance of the shot, and the distance is worth recording for the team that receives the patient, although it never replaces the assessment of the patient. The finding that matters more than the appearance is the location of the entry, because the location names the structures that may lie in the path. A small, neat entry wound in the upper abdomen or the chest can sit above an injury that will kill within minutes.

Exit wounds are more variable than entry wounds and are not a measure of the damage done. An exit wound is often larger, more ragged, and more irregular than the entry, with edges that are turned outward and without soot or powder, because the projectile has already given up part of its energy and often carries fragments of tissue with it. Some projectiles do not leave the body at all, and the absence of an exit wound is a normal finding rather than a sign that the injury is minor. When a projectile has crossed the body and left, the responder should not assume that the track was straight, because a projectile can be deflected by bone and can arrive somewhere far from the line between the two wounds. The trap is to treat the number of holes as a count of injuries, when two wounds may belong to one track and several tracks may be hidden entirely. The responder marks and describes each wound, records its position in words, and leaves the interpretation of the track to the team with imaging and an operating theater available to it.

Counting holes is the most common error at the scene, because an even number of wounds suggests one track and an odd number suggests that a projectile is still inside, and neither inference can be trusted. A projectile can leave by a route that seems impossible, can be swallowed or lost in clothing, or can remain in the body after entering and leaving the tissues in a way that produces wounds which look unrelated. More important, a single small entry wound can hide a wound channel through several organs, so the number of holes says very little about the number of injuries. The responder therefore searches the whole patient rather than the visible wound, including the scalp under the hair, the armpits, the groin, the perineum, the mouth, and the back, and rolls the patient to look at what has been lying against the ground. Clothing is cut away rather than pulled over the wound, because pulling can move a projectile, dislodge a clot, or hide a wound that was not yet seen. The search continues until the responder is satisfied that every wound has been found, and any wound discovered later is reported to the receiving team as a new finding.

The principle that organizes this chapter is that the wound is the visible part of an unknown internal injury, and the structures in the path matter more than the number of wounds. A wound of a few millimeters on the surface can sit above a torn artery, a perforated intestine, or a divided spinal cord, and no examination at the scene can exclude any of them. What the responder can do is reason from the location, from the direction the projectile seems to have traveled, and from the patient's behavior, and then act on the worst plausible injury rather than on the most comfortable one. A wound that crosses the midline of the trunk, a wound above the collarbone, and a wound in the groin or the armpit all deserve special concern, because these regions contain vessels and organs that cannot be compressed from outside. The finding that changes the plan is never the size of the wound but a change in the patient, such as a falling level of consciousness, a rising pulse, or a breathing pattern that is becoming labored. The responder who keeps this principle in view will treat the patient rather than the photograph of the injury.

Bone struck by a projectile becomes a source of secondary projectiles, and the fragments travel outward from the fracture with their own energy. A long bone that is shattered in this way sends pieces through the surrounding muscle, and each fragment can cut a vessel or a nerve that the projectile itself had passed by. The finding that suggests this mechanism is a limb that is deformed, that is swelling rapidly, or that has lost its pulse or its movement after a wound near a major bone. A joint crossed by the track is a special concern, because the fragments and the projectile can carry contamination deep into a space that is difficult to clean, and the injury then threatens the limb long after the bleeding has stopped. The trained responder splints the limb in the position found, without attempting to straighten it, because movement of the fragments can turn a contained injury into a free hemorrhage or can divide a vessel that was only bruised. Definitive hospital care is where the bone is examined by radiograph, where the joint is assessed, and where the decision is made about cleaning and repair.

Neurovascular injury is the complication that decides whether a limb survives and whether a patient keeps the use of a hand or a foot. The findings that must be sought below every wound of a limb are the pulse, the color and warmth of the skin, the ability to move the part, and the ability to feel light touch, and each is compared with the same part on the other side. An expanding swelling, blood that continues to spurt despite pressure, a pulse that cannot be felt, a part that is pale or cool, and a loss of feeling or movement are all findings that demand immediate movement toward definitive care. A pulse that is present does not exclude a serious arterial injury, because a torn artery can spasm or can be partly blocked while still transmitting a weak pulse. The trained responder repeats the examination after every intervention, because a pulse that disappears after splinting or after a dressing is applied reports a new problem rather than a stable one. The responder records what was found and when, so that the receiving team can tell whether the deficit is old or new.

The region of the body that the track crosses determines which lethal possibility is named first. A wound of the chest may have crossed the lung, the heart, or a great vessel, and the findings that reveal these are a breathing pattern that is becoming labored, breath sounds that are absent on one side, distended neck veins, a falling blood pressure, or a wound that sucks air. A wound of the abdomen or the pelvis may have crossed the liver, the spleen, the kidney, the intestine, or the large vessels, and the abdomen may look almost normal while the patient is losing blood inside it. A wound of the neck may have crossed the airway, the esophagus, or the vessels that carry blood to the brain, and a wound of the head may have crossed the brain even when consciousness is still intact. A wound of a limb may have crossed a major vessel, a nerve, or a bone, and a wound of the groin, the armpit, or the buttock is a junctional wound that sits where a tourniquet cannot reach. Naming the region and the structures at risk is the first act of reasoning, and it is done before any dressing is placed.

Hemorrhage control follows the ladder of pressure, and each step belongs to a named provider level. The lay first aider presses firmly on the wound with a clean dressing and does not lift the dressing to look beneath it, adding further layers if blood shows through, because each look breaks the forming clot. When bleeding continues from a wound of a limb despite firm pressure, a trained responder or paramedic may apply a tourniquet under a protocol that authorizes it, placing it above the wound and tightening it until the bleeding stops. Once a tourniquet has controlled the bleeding it is not loosened in the field, and the time it was applied is written on the patient where the receiving team will see it, because the duration of application changes what the hospital team must do first. A trained responder may pack a deep wound that pressure cannot control, and may use a hemostatic dressing where the local protocol provides one, while a lay first aider is not asked to pack a wound that requires instruments to reach the bleeding point.
