The finding that tells the responder to move to the next step is bleeding that continues despite the step just taken, and the finding that tells the responder the step is working is a dressing that stays dry and a patient who is becoming calmer and warmer. Definitive hospital care is where the vessel is found, repaired, or bypassed, and no field measure replaces that.

An embedded object, and a projectile that can be seen or felt, are left exactly where they are and are stabilized in place. The reason is not caution but mechanics, because the object may be pressing on a torn vessel and removal can release a hemorrhage that cannot be controlled at the scene, and because a projectile lodged near a nerve or a vessel can cause further damage as it is pulled. The responder builds padding around the object so that it cannot move, secures the padding without pressing the object deeper, and transports the patient with the object in place. The lay first aider never pulls a projectile from a wound and never probes the wound with a finger or an instrument to find out how deep it goes. First responders do not extract projectiles, because removal is a surgical decision made when it is clinically indicated, and the section of this manual that deals with retained projectiles says the same. The finding that changes this rule is an object in the airway or one that is obstructing the breathing, and even then the maneuver belongs to a trained responder or paramedic working to a protocol, never to a lay first aider.

Breathing and the airway come before the wound once hemorrhage that is immediately lethal has been controlled, and the sequence is the same primary survey that governs every injury in this manual. The responder follows the ABCDE order, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure, and each letter is completed before the next is given full attention. The airway is opened and kept open, the chest is examined for a wound that sucks air or for breath sounds that are absent on one side, and the circulation is judged from the pulse, the skin, and the level of consciousness. Exposure means that the whole patient is uncovered long enough to find every wound, and it is done while protecting the patient from cold with blankets and a warm surface. The Glasgow coma scale is recorded at first contact and repeated, because the trend in the level of consciousness is more useful than a single figure, and any value taken from this manual must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The finding that moves the responder onward is a patient who is breathing, has a pulse, and has been examined from head to foot, and the finding that stops the sequence is a patient who needs cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR, at once.

Cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, and a patient who is bleeding, exposed, or waiting for transport loses heat in every part of the body. The responder covers the patient with whatever is available, insulates the surface beneath from the ground, removes wet clothing in a way that does not expose the patient for longer than necessary, and keeps the vehicle or the room warm. A core temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is a teaching illustration of the point at which cold becomes dangerous, and the exact figure at which a service acts must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because cold impairs clotting, worsens shock, and changes the heart's rhythm. A patient who is shivering is using energy that the body needs for other purposes, and a patient who has stopped shivering while remaining cold is a greater concern rather than a lesser one. The trained responder moves the patient with attention to the neck and the back when spinal injury is possible, using a coordinated roll rather than pulling on the arms or the head. Definitive hospital care includes active warming, and the receiving team is told how long the patient has been cold and how the patient was covered.

Pain relief is a decision rather than a routine, and it belongs to the provider whose authorization covers it. A lay first aider offers comfort, calm speech, a warm cover, and careful handling, and does not give any substance for pain. A trained responder or paramedic may give a medicine for pain only under a protocol that names the substance, the amount, and the route, and none of those details belongs in this manual, because a listener must never be able to take a prescription from these pages. The finding that makes pain relief urgent is pain that is severe, that is worsening, or that is preventing the patient from being moved or examined, and the decision is then made by the clinician responsible for the patient under the local protocol. The same reasoning applies to antibiotics, to protection against tetanus, to fluids, and to oxygen, each of which is a clinical decision whose urgency is set by the patient's condition and whose details belong to the prescriber and the local protocol. The responder records what was given and when, so that the receiving team can continue the plan, and the responder never gives a substance that the protocol does not authorize.

Definitive hospital care is where the unknown becomes visible, and the pathway starts with the questions the assessment has already framed. A computed tomography, or CT, examination answers questions about the track and about structures that the examination could not reach, a plain radiograph answers questions about bones and about retained projectiles, and ultrasound answers questions about fluid in the abdomen or around the heart. Surgical exploration of a wound, repair of a vessel, repair of a tendon or a nerve, removal of a projectile, debridement of deep tissue, and fasciotomy for compartment syndrome all belong to the operating theater and never to the field, and a listener who is tempted to perform them at the scene should hear this plainly. A trauma surgeon and an anesthetist lead this phase, with imaging, blood products, and an intensive care unit, or ICU, available for the patient who needs them. The receiving team needs the time of the injury, the time any tourniquet was applied, the wounds that were found and those that were searched for, the treatment given, and the trend in the patient's condition. The most valuable single message at handover is that the patient has changed in a particular way, because a change is what turns a stable patient into one who needs the operating theater now.

A constructed illustration may make the reasoning concrete without describing any real patient or incident. Imagine a person wounded by a single shot in the upper thigh, with a small entry wound, no exit wound, and a thigh that is swelling while the pulse at the ankle becomes difficult to feel. The wound itself looks modest, and a responder who counted holes would count one wound and move on, yet the structures in the path include the large artery and the vein of the thigh and the bone beneath them. The correct acts are to control the bleeding with firm pressure, to move to a tourniquet only if a trained provider is present and the protocol allows it, to splint the limb in the position found, to keep the patient warm, and to travel toward a trauma center without delay. The illustration is constructed for teaching, and the numbers, distances, and times that would be attached to it in a real case must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The point of the example is that the visible wound and the actual injury are two different things, and the responder who treats the second rather than the first gives the patient the only real chance.

Children and pregnant patients deserve a specific word, because the same wound behaves differently in each. A child has a smaller body, so a track that would cross one structure in an adult may cross several, and a child's blood volume is small, so a loss that looks moderate can be a large fraction of the circulation. A pregnant patient may have the womb wounded, and the findings that matter include abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, a uterus that is tense or tender, and any change in the baby's movement, all of which demand immediate transport to a center with obstetric and surgical capability. In both patients the responder protects against hypothermia with the same care as in any other patient, and the responder keeps the patient flat and still when spinal injury is possible. The provider level does not change with the age of the patient, because a lay first aider still controls what can be controlled with hands and dressings, and definitive hospital care still owns the surgery. The decisions about medicine, about fluids, and about oxygen remain with the clinician and the local protocol, and the details of those decisions are not taught here.

To summarize, a firearm wound is the visible part of an unknown internal injury, and the responder reasons from the energy of the projectile and from the structures in its path rather than from the number of holes. A slow projectile cuts a track and a fast one stretches a temporary cavity that injures tissue it never touched, bone struck by a projectile becomes a source of secondary projectiles, and a pulse that is present never excludes a serious vascular injury. Scene safety and the possibility of a second shot come before the patient, hemorrhage control follows the ladder of pressure with each step owned by a named provider level, and an embedded object or a projectile is stabilized in place and never removed in the field. The whole patient is searched for wounds that have not yet been found, hypothermia is prevented from the first minute, and the patient is moved toward definitive hospital care where the imaging, the surgical exploration, and the repair belong. Pain relief, antibiotics, protection against tetanus, fluids, and oxygen are clinical decisions whose substance and amount belong to the prescriber and the local protocol, and no such detail can be taken from this chapter. Every figure in this chapter, whether a speed, a distance, a cavity size, a temperature, or a time, is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such values differ between services, countries, and editions. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 11 — Immediate Management of Gunshot Wounds

A gunshot wound is the injury in which the first minutes decide the most, and in which the strongest instinct, which is to run straight to the patient, is the instinct that must be resisted. The scene is made safe before anything else, and the hazard particular to a firearm is a second shot, because the person who fired may still be present, may still be armed, and may not have finished. The lethal possibility is named before any wound is examined, and it is hemorrhage that will not stop, whose finding is blood that soaks through dressing after dressing, blood that spurts with each beat of the heart, or a swelling in a limb or a buttock that grows while the responder watches. The lay first aider who arrives first can control that bleeding with a gloved hand, a clean cloth, and steady pressure, while the trained responder and the paramedic bring wound packing, a tourniquet, oxygen, and a protocol that authorizes them. Definitive hospital care brings the surgeon, the imaging, and the operating theater, and it is the destination of every action taken at the scene. Nothing in this chapter replaces training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work, and calling emergency medical services early is itself a clinical act.

Safety at a shooting is not a formality, and the responder who kneels beside the patient while the threat is unresolved may become the next patient. Cover is taken before contact, the patient is approached only after the threat has been controlled by those whose task that is, and a patient moved out of the line of fire is moved under direction rather than on personal initiative. When the shooting happened on a road, as happens in a drive-by incident or after a pursuit, traffic becomes the second hazard, and reflective clothing, a warning triangle, and a vehicle placed to shield the working area protect more lives than any dressing. The patient's own blood and body fluids are a hazard as well, so personal protective equipment, or PPE, with gloves, eye protection, and a barrier for the mouth and nose where it is available, goes on before hands are laid on anyone. Bystanders are given a useful task or moved away, because a crowd hides the scene, blocks the ambulance, and may contain the assailant. The scene is declared safe by the person responsible for it, and only then does the sequence of care begin.

Attention at the scene goes to the wounds that bleed, not to the wounds that look worst, and that reversal of natural sympathy is the central skill of this chapter. A small puncture in the groin or the thigh may have divided an artery and may be filling the leg with blood, while a shattered jaw or a torn scalp can look appalling and lose almost nothing. The first action is direct pressure, applied with the flat of the hand over a dressing or any clean cloth, held firmly and without interruption, and the reason is that pressure from outside the limb exceeds the pressure inside the vessel. If blood strikes through the pad, the pad is not lifted to see what is beneath it, because lifting removes the clot that has begun to form, and a second pad is laid over the first while the hand returns to the same place with the same force. Packing a deep wound belongs to the trained responder for sites where a hand cannot compress the vessel, such as the groin, the armpit, the buttock, or the root of the limb, and the packing is held with continuous pressure rather than released to check whether it has worked. A tourniquet belongs to the trained responder within the protocol of the service, it is applied when pressure and packing have failed or cannot be performed, and once it has controlled the bleeding it is not loosened in the field.

The moment a tourniquet is applied is recorded on the patient where the receiving team cannot miss it, and the reason is that the team must know how long the limb has been without flow in order to judge the risk of release and the urgency of restoring circulation. A period such as 2 hours is often quoted as the point at which the risk to nerve and muscle becomes serious, and that interval must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because tolerance changes with temperature, with the patient, and with the injury. Reassessment follows every attempt at control, and it asks whether bleeding has truly stopped, whether the dressings are still doing their work, whether a limb beyond a tourniquet is changing, and whether a wound was missed while attention was fixed on the first one. A patient who is pale, restless, thirsty, and breathing quickly is telling the responder that the bleeding is not controlled, however dry the dressing looks. A tourniquet is painful, and pain is expected, but pain is never a reason to loosen it in the field, because the bleeding it has stopped may return where no field measure can restore control. The tourniquet is released only in definitive hospital care, where preparation for renewed hemorrhage exists, and a field release is never justified by the appearance of a limb.

The number of wounds is a poor guide to the danger, and the search is not finished until the whole body has been examined. A bullet that entered the chest may have left through the back, a wound in the flank may have crossed the abdomen, and a single projectile may have made several openings as bone fragments were driven outward as secondary projectiles. Every surface is therefore looked at, including the back, the buttocks, the armpits, the scalp, the mouth, and the perineum, because a wound hidden under clothing or hair will be found later by the hospital only if the responder looked first. Turning a patient to see the back belongs to the trained responder and is done with movement precautions for the spine when the mechanism of injury suggests it, with the head and the trunk kept in line as a unit. The wound that is visible is only the visible part of an injury whose depth is unknown, and the structures in its path matter far more than the size of the opening. A calm patient with a small hole and no bleeding to show is not a reassuring patient, and the finding that should worry the responder is any change in the level of consciousness, in the breathing, or in the pulse over the minutes of the assessment.

The airway is the next question once hemorrhage is controlled, and in gunshot wounds it is threatened by blood, vomit, broken teeth, and a swollen tongue rather than by the injury alone. A wound of the face, the mouth, or the neck can fill the throat with blood, and a wound of the neck can produce a swelling that closes the airway from outside as it expands, with a hoarse voice, a difficulty in swallowing, or air that bubbles from the wound as the findings that announce it. The lay first aider keeps the airway open by positioning, by turning the patient onto the side when breathing is adequate and no spinal injury is suspected, and by clearing loose debris from the mouth with a finger only when it can be seen and reached safely. The trained responder, the emergency medical technician or paramedic, may use suction, an airway adjunct, and a jaw thrust, and each of those acts requires equipment, training, and authorization that the lay first aider does not have. A cervical spine precaution must never be allowed to prevent the opening of an airway, because a patient who cannot breathe has no use for an intact neck, and the airway is always the first priority. A patient who is talking has an airway for the moment, and the responder who hears the voice change must treat that change as an emergency and move faster.

Breathing is assessed by looking at the chest, listening at the mouth, and feeling the movement of air, and the most sensitive sign available without equipment is the breathing rate and the effort it costs. A rate that climbs, a patient who can speak only a few words at a time, a chest that does not move on one side, or a wound that sucks and bubbles with each breath are findings that must change the plan at once. The injury that kills fastest in the chest is a tension pneumothorax, and the findings that reveal it are severe breathlessness, absent breath sounds on the affected side, a neck whose veins are distended, and a blood pressure that is falling, with a shift of the windpipe as a late sign that must not be waited for. An open chest wound is covered by the trained responder with an occlusive dressing that is monitored closely, because such a dressing can itself trap air and create the tension it was meant to prevent. A breathing rate above 30 breaths per minute is the sort of figure that is taught as a warning, and that number must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the line that matters shifts with age, with pain, and with the patient's usual state. The chest is never bound tightly by anyone, because a bound chest cannot expand and the patient suffocates inside the bandage.

Circulation is judged by the pulse, the color and the temperature of the skin, the return of color after pressure on a fingernail, and the level of consciousness, and none of those signs excludes hidden bleeding. A patient who has no visible wound of consequence may still be dying into the chest, the abdomen, the pelvis, the thighs, or the space behind the peritoneum, so the search for bleeding never depends on what can be seen. The findings that suggest internal hemorrhage are a pulse that is fast and thin, skin that is pale and cool, restlessness or unusual quietness, thirst, and a level of consciousness that is slipping, and the trend over several minutes carries more information than any single observation. A measured pressure such as 90 millimeters of mercury may be quoted as a threshold, but it is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line that matters depends on the age of the patient, on pregnancy, and on the patient's usual pressure. The pelvis is treated as a bleeding space rather than as a bone, and a pelvic binder belongs to the trained responder within the protocol of the service, applied at the level of the greater trochanters with the position and the monitoring that the protocol requires. The responder who suspects bleeding into a cavity does not wait to prove it, because proof belongs to imaging in the hospital and the patient belongs in an operating theater.

The neurological assessment is short, and it is repeated more often than any other part of the sequence, because a change in the level of consciousness is the earliest sign of a brain injury that is expanding or of a circulation that is failing. The level of consciousness is recorded in a consistent way, the Glasgow coma scale is the standard spoken scale for that record, and the pupil size and reaction, the movement of each limb, and the symmetry of the face are written down at the same time. The finding that must be taught and remembered is the lucid interval, in which a patient who was speaking and oriented becomes drowsy and then unresponsive, and that interval is the signature of bleeding inside the skull rather than a reason for reassurance. A gunshot wound of the head, the neck, or the back raises the question of spinal injury, and the movement precautions for the spine are maintained without ever preventing the airway from being opened. The record is made on the patient where the receiving team will find it, because a neurological observation spoken once and never written is an observation that will be lost. Every movement, every dressing, and every splint is followed by the same neurological check, and a patient whose examination has changed is a patient whose journey must accelerate.

The sequence of care is one habit performed in the same order every time, and that order is scene safety, catastrophic hemorrhage control, airway, breathing, circulation, neurological assessment, exposure with protection from cold, and transport. Its letters are taught as the ABCDE sequence, and its value lies in the fact that a finding which stops the sequence restarts it, so that a patient who vomits during the examination returns to the airway before anything else continues. Exposure means that the whole patient is looked at, with clothing cut away rather than pulled over a wounded limb, and it ends with the patient covered and warm because the examination itself creates the cold that harms. The sequence is performed by the lay first aider in the parts that belong to bare hands, by the trained responder with equipment and authorization, and again on arrival at the hospital as the definitive team takes over. A patient who looks well is the patient who must be watched hardest, because the body compensates for blood loss for a time and then fails quickly, and the observation that matters is the direction of travel rather than the single reading.

Shock is a state of failing tissue perfusion rather than a number, and it is recognized by the same signs that reveal hidden bleeding, which are a fast and thin pulse, cool and pale skin, a rising breathing rate, and a level of consciousness that is dulling. The lay first aider treats it by keeping the patient flat, keeping the patient warm, controlling any bleeding that can be reached, and withholding food and drink, because either may be vomited into an airway and may complicate the operation that follows. The trained responder brings oxygen according to the protocol of the service, with the amount and the method set by that protocol and never by this manual, and continues the warmth and the monitoring while the vehicle moves. Fluids and blood are decisions of definitive hospital care, made by a physician who can measure what the patient has lost and can watch what the patient does with what is given, and no amount, no route, and no rate belongs in a field manual.

Cold is a complication of gunshot trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and it begins on the ground in the first minutes while the patient is bleeding and undressed for examination. A patient who is bleeding, exposed, or receiving fluid at room temperature loses heat quickly, and cold makes the clotting system work poorly, deepens shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often used to describe the point at which those effects become serious, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line differs between services and between editions. The lay first aider cuts away wet clothing rather than pulling it over a wound, covers the patient with blankets, coats, or foil, and insulates the patient from the ground, because much of the heat is lost downward. The trained responder continues that protection inside the vehicle, warms the cabin, limits the time the patient is uncovered for each examination, and reports the protection given at handover. Warming runs alongside hemorrhage control rather than after it, and it is continued in the hospital, because a cold patient remains a bleeding patient.

No embedded object is removed in the field, and the rule includes a knife, a fragment of glass, a piece of metal, and a bullet that can be seen sitting in the wound. Removal may release hemorrhage that no field measure can control, and it may cause further damage to vessels, nerves, and tissues that the object is currently tamponading, so the object is stabilized in place with bulky padding built up around it and the patient is moved with it. The wound is not probed with a finger or an instrument, because the depth of a track cannot be judged from its opening and because probing introduces contamination and may start the bleeding that everyone is trying to prevent. A bullet that has come to rest inside the body is not pulled out by a first responder, and the decision to remove it is a surgical decision made in the hospital when the bullet is causing harm where it lies. The information that a projectile is retained is passed to the receiving team, and every wound is described in relation to fixed landmarks, because a description travels and a gesture does not. The lay first aider's task ends with a clean cover and pressure kept off the object itself, and any attempt at extraction is a definitive procedure and never a first-aid measure.

Every wound that is not bleeding dangerously is covered to protect it, to keep it clean, and to allow the patient to be moved, and the covering is a temporary act rather than a treatment. Exposed tissue is protected, including exposed bone, exposed tendon, and exposed bowel, and the last of these is covered with a clean dressing that is kept moist by the trained responder according to the protocol and never pushed back inside the abdomen. A dressing that is soaked is reinforced rather than removed, and a circumferential bandage that tightens with swelling is avoided, because a bandage that becomes a tourniquet without a tourniquet's purpose can cost the limb. The dressing is checked for bleeding through it and for its effect on the circulation beyond it, and the check is repeated often enough that a change is noticed while there is still time to act. Materials that must never be placed in a wound include soil, ashes, powders, and any remedy brought by a bystander, because each adds contamination and none controls bleeding. The lay first aider covers, the trained responder packs and seals within protocol, and the definitive team explores, cleans, and closes, and the three levels are never blended.

Limbs are immobilized to prevent further injury and to control pain, and a gunshot wound of a limb is treated as a fractured limb until the hospital proves otherwise. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found, and it is never straightened to make it look normal, because the ends of a broken bone lie near vessels and nerves and moving them may convert a limb that could be saved into one that cannot. The neurovascular examination, which is the pulse, the color, the warmth, the sensation, and the movement beyond the injury, is recorded before and after every splint, every dressing, and every move, and the second examination is compared with the first rather than with the memory of it. The trained responder splints with the joints above and below the injury supported and every bony prominence padded, and the lay first aider supports the limb in the position found without attempting any realignment. The spine is treated with movement precautions when the mechanism of injury suggests it, which means that the head and the trunk are kept in line and that immobilization follows the protocol of the service. Immobilization is never allowed to delay the transport of a patient who is bleeding internally, because a limb that is protected has no value to a patient who dies of a wound in the abdomen.

Three decisions belong to someone other than the responder at the roadside, and each is described here only as a decision, because a listener must never be able to take a prescription from this manual. The first is analgesia, whose urgency is decided by pain that threatens breathing, by pain that prevents splinting or transport, and by pain that is out of proportion to the wound, while the substance, the amount, the route, and the interval belong to the prescriber and the local protocol. The second is tetanus protection, whose urgency is decided by the wound itself, since a deep, contaminated, devitalized wound from a projectile carries a risk that a simple graze does not, and the decision is made by a clinician who knows the patient's immunization history. The third is antibiotic prophylaxis, whose urgency is decided by contamination, by the cavity of the wound, and by the delay before surgical care, and which is again the decision of the prescriber and the local protocol. The trained responder may recognize all three needs and must report them at handover, and the hospital decides what is given and when. The rule is absolute, in that no dose, no regimen, no route, and no frequency appears anywhere in this manual, and the provider who needs them consults the current guideline and the local protocol.

The hardest decision at the scene is the balance between staying to stabilize and leaving to operate, and the balance is decided by the mechanism of injury, by the distance to the trauma center, by the number of patients, and by the scope of practice of the provider who is present. Where the distance is short and the patient is bleeding internally, the correct action is a fast dressing, a warm blanket, and immediate movement, because the only treatment for that bleeding is an operation that cannot be performed at the roadside. Where the distance is long, the trained responder may gain by doing what the protocol authorizes, and by calling for a faster form of transport where one exists. The time spent on scene is time removed from the operating theater, and a responder who performs a procedure that changes nothing while an artery continues to bleed has spent the patient's reserve rather than saved it. The destination is a trauma center rather than the nearest building, because a hospital without a surgeon, without an operating theater, and without blood is a place where the patient will be stabilized and then transferred again. A transport interval such as 30 minutes is sometimes quoted as the point at which the choice of destination changes, and any such figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because systems differ in what they can reach and how quickly.

The receiving hospital is notified before the patient arrives, and the notification is short, specific, and given in the order the receiving team needs it. That same information is what must travel with the patient, so it is written on the patient and spoken aloud at handover rather than trusted to memory. The message names the mechanism of injury, the number and the location of every wound, the observations of breathing, pulse, and level of consciousness together with their trend, the treatment already given and the time each act was performed, and the estimated time of arrival. The time a tourniquet was applied, the warmth and the covering already provided, and any retained projectile are part of that message, because each changes what the receiving team does in the first minutes. A pediatric patient is taken to a center with pediatric capability where the distance allows it, because a child compensates differently and the equipment and the expertise are not the same.

An illustration helps here, and it is constructed for teaching rather than drawn from any real patient or incident. In a training hall, a mannequin is laid beside a wall with a single small wound in the left thigh, painted blood on the trousers, and no other visible injury, and the learners are told only that a shot was heard and that the scene has been declared safe. The first group goes straight to the wound and applies a dressing, and the mannequin's simulated pulse rises and its simulated pressure falls, while the second group turns the mannequin, finds a second wound in the back, controls it, keeps the patient warm, and calls for transport while the first group is still dressing the thigh. The debrief names the traps, which are the search that stopped at the first hole, the reassurance taken from a small opening, the pressure that was released to look, and the time spent on a wound that was not the one killing the patient. The case is invented, and no real patient, family, or service is represented by it.

To summarize, a gunshot wound is managed in a fixed order that begins with scene safety against a second shot and against traffic, moves to the control of catastrophic hemorrhage, and then follows the ABCDE sequence through airway, breathing, circulation, and neurological assessment to exposure, warmth, and rapid transport to a trauma center. The wounds that receive attention first are the ones that bleed rather than the ones that look worst, because the size of an opening says nothing about the structures inside. Every act is named with the provider level that owns it, and no bullet is extracted, no wound is probed, and no fracture is straightened outside definitive hospital care. The balance between staying to stabilize and leaving to operate is decided by the mechanism of injury, the distance to the trauma center, and the scope of practice of the provider, and the time spent on scene is time taken from the operating theater. Every figure in this chapter, whether a pressure, a rate, a temperature, or an interval, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between services, countries, and editions. The information that travels with the patient is part of the treatment, since a tourniquet time and a trend in the level of consciousness can change what the receiving team does in the first minutes. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 12 — Gunshot Wounds to the Chest

A gunshot wound to the chest begins, for the responder, before the patient is touched, because the scene decides whether anyone can be helped at all. The first question is whether the shooter is gone, whether a second shot is possible, and whether the police have made the area safe, since a responder who becomes a casualty removes two people from help. Traffic, fire, a crowd that may contain the person who fired, and the hazards of the patient's own blood all belong to the same assessment, and gloves and personal protective equipment, or PPE, go on before contact. Only when the scene is safe does the responder approach, count the breathing, and search for the wound on the chest, the back, the armpits, and the flanks. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the protocol of the service in which the patient is treated.

Four lethal possibilities must be named before any comfortable explanation is accepted, because each announces itself with a finding that can be sought in the opening assessment. A tension pneumothorax is air trapped in the chest under pressure, and it reveals itself by desperate breathing, distended neck veins, and absent breath sounds on one side. A pericardial tamponade is blood around the heart that prevents it from filling, and it reveals itself as shock with quiet breath sounds and a falling pressure while the neck veins stay full. A massive hemothorax is a large volume of blood in the chest, and it shows as shock, dullness on tapping, and diminished breath sounds on the injured side. Injury to a major vessel may show nothing outside at all, so a patient who fades with no wound to explain it is treated as though such an injury is present.

The chest is a cage of ribs and muscle containing two lungs, each separated from the chest wall by a space that normally holds no air, while between them sit the heart, the great vessels, the esophagus, and the trachea. A wound near that crowded corridor is more dangerous than one at the edge, and a bullet entering the upper abdomen can pass upward through the diaphragm and injure the chest without leaving a wound on the chest. The path of a bullet is never predictable, and a wound that looks small on the skin may conceal a large cavity within, so the responder must never judge the injury by the entrance alone. A wound on the back may be missed if the patient lies on it, so the patient is rolled with the spine kept in line while the back, the armpits, and the flanks are examined. Where a figure such as 2 centimeters is used for an entrance wound in a teaching example, it is only an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The first aider's order of work begins with the bleeding that can kill in minutes, and the chest is covered and pressed where it bleeds but never bound tightly, because a tight band stops the chest from expanding and turns a survivable injury into a fatal one. The airway is checked by looking in the mouth, by listening for air movement, and by asking the patient to speak, since a patient who answers clearly has an open airway. Breathing is judged by four things that need no instrument, which are the rate, the effort, the symmetry, and the sound, and the two sides are compared from the armpits, where air movement is heard most cleanly. A patient breathing at 30 breaths per minute, a figure offered here as an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, is working hard, and one who can no longer speak a full sentence is working harder still. While this is done, another person calls the emergency medical services, and the patient is kept still, warm, and covered, because cold worsens bleeding and shock.

A pneumothorax is air in the space between the lung and the chest wall, and it is the most common chest injury a bullet produces. The lung on that side collapses partly or completely, because the air outside it removes the pressure difference that holds it open, and breathlessness grows with the amount of lung lost. The findings are a fast breathing rate, diminished breath sounds on the injured side, and sometimes pain that worsens with a deep breath. A small pneumothorax may cause almost no symptoms, and that quiet appearance is exactly why it is dangerous, since a small leak can enlarge with every breath. The first aider's task is not to treat it but to recognize it, to keep the patient warm, and to reach a place where a chest radiograph and a trained team can decide what it means.

A tension pneumothorax is the same air under a rising pressure, and it kills quickly because it pushes the heart and the great veins aside rather than merely collapsing one lung. Air enters the chest with each breath and cannot leave, so the pressure grows until the vena cava is compressed and no blood can return to the heart. When the heart receives no blood, it has nothing to pump, and the pressure falls until the brain and the heart itself are no longer supplied. The sequence may take only a few minutes, and it can follow an open wound, a closed wound, or a wound already covered with a dressing. This is why the responder must keep watching every chest wound, and why a patient who was talking a moment ago and is now drowsy and gasping has a new and lethal problem. A pressure such as 90 millimeters of mercury is used in some teaching as the point at which shock becomes obvious, but that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line depends on the patient and on the way it is measured.

Tension pneumothorax is separated from a simple pneumothorax by the direction of the patient's condition rather than by any single sign. In a simple pneumothorax the patient is breathless but stable, the neck veins are flat, and the pressure holds, while in a tension pneumothorax the breathlessness worsens steadily, the neck veins become visibly full, and the pressure falls. The trachea, felt at the notch above the breastbone, may be pushed away from the injured side, but that finding appears late and never excludes the diagnosis. The injured side is quiet to the ear and dull or drum-like to the tapping finger depending on whether blood or air predominates, and the responder records what was found and when, because comparison over time is the most useful information the hospital will receive. Any table that sets these signs side by side is of no use in the ear, so the responder carries the single question that matters, which is whether this patient is getting worse.

There is a hard line between what may be done for a tension pneumothorax outside a hospital and what may not. The lay first aider may recognize the pattern, keep the patient sitting up if that helps and the pressure allows, keep the patient warm, and call for help without delay, and that is all. The first aider must not insert a needle, a pen, a tube, or any object into the chest, because the structures beneath cannot be identified by touch, and an untrained puncture can injure the lung, a vessel, or the heart. The trained responder or paramedic may relieve the pressure with a needle only when the service authorizes that act, the equipment is carried for it, and the protocol sets the site and the decision. Definitive hospital care owns the chest drain, the surgery, and the repair, and even a needle placed in the field is a bridge to that care rather than a treatment that finishes the job.

A hemothorax is blood in the space between the lung and the chest wall, and a bullet produces it by tearing the lung, an intercostal vessel along the inside of the ribs, or a vessel of the mediastinum. A small hemothorax behaves much like a small pneumothorax, with breathlessness and diminished breath sounds on one side, and it may be found only when the chest is imaged. A large hemothorax is a different disease, because the chest can hold several liters of blood and a patient can bleed to death into it while the outside of the body shows almost nothing. The findings are shock with a fast, thin pulse, breathlessness, dullness when the chest is tapped on the injured side, and diminished breath sounds, while the neck veins may be flat because the problem is lost volume rather than trapped pressure. The responder who finds shock with a quiet, dull chest and no external bleeding must think of bleeding into the chest, not of bleeding that has stopped.

An open pneumothorax is a wound of the chest wall that stays open, so that air moves in and out of the chest through the hole instead of through the trachea, and the classic finding is a wound that sucks and bubbles with each breath. The danger is not only the collapsed lung but the loss of every breath, because the air the patient draws follows the path of least resistance and moves through the wound rather than into the lungs, so the patient suffocates while the chest is moving. Heat and moisture are lost through the same opening, and a patient with a large open chest wound becomes cold quickly, which worsens shock and makes the blood less able to clot. A wound of 2 centimeters in a teaching example may look modest, yet the same figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the effect depends on the site and the tissue around the wound as much as on its size. The responder covers the wound and then watches the patient, since the cover can create the very pressure that follows.

The occlusive dressing is the central field act for an open chest wound, and it belongs to the trained responder, while the lay first aider uses whatever clean, airtight material is at hand. The aim is to stop air entering through the wound while allowing air that is already trapped to escape, which is why a commercial seal or a dressing taped on three sides has been the traditional teaching. The dressing must cover the wound completely and extend well beyond its edges, and it must be fixed so that it does not shift during transport, because a seal that slides off leaves the wound open again. The lay first aider who has plastic sheeting and tape may place it and must then say clearly what was placed and when. The responder records the time of the dressing, the condition before and after, and any change in the breathing, because those comparisons are what the receiving team uses. No dressing and no seal is a substitute for moving the patient to a hospital where the chest can be examined and drained.

Once an occlusive dressing is in place, the patient must be monitored for the build-up of pressure behind it, because a seal that works too well can produce a tension pneumothorax. The signs to watch are worsening breathlessness, a rising breathing rate, a falling level of consciousness, distended neck veins, and a pressure that cannot be maintained. If a trained responder finds those signs, the protocol may direct that a corner of the dressing be lifted briefly to let the trapped air escape and then resealed, and that decision belongs to the service protocol and not to improvisation. The lay first aider does not lift the dressing on a hunch but reports the change to the emergency medical services and keeps the patient warm and still. The final judgment about whether the seal should stay, be changed, or be removed belongs to the team that can see the chest and image it.

A bullet that passes near the heart can injure it in several ways, and not all of them involve a hole in the muscle. The heart may be bruised by the passage of a projectile nearby, which weakens the pumping and can produce an abnormal rhythm hours later. A chamber may be perforated so that blood leaks into the pericardial sac or into the chest, and a valve, the septum between the chambers, or a coronary artery on the surface of the heart may be torn. The patient may present with chest pain, a fast or irregular pulse, breathlessness, or a falling pressure, and in the worst case the patient collapses and needs cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR, at once. A wound between the nipple line and the lower end of the breastbone, sometimes called the cardiac box in teaching, raises the probability of cardiac injury, but a bullet can reach the heart from the abdomen or the back as well. Because the surface wound cannot settle the question, any patient with a gunshot wound near the heart is treated as though the heart is injured.

Pericardial tamponade is the consequence that makes cardiac injury so deceptive, and it presents as shock with quiet breath sounds. The pericardial sac is a tough envelope that cannot stretch quickly, so a small amount of blood inside it can raise the pressure around the heart until the chambers can no longer fill. The result is a heart that beats but moves almost no blood, and the patient slides into shock while the chest looks and sounds deceptively calm. The findings are a falling pressure, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, a fast and weak pulse, and a level of consciousness that drifts, and breath sounds may be quiet simply because the patient is not moving enough air. The lay first aider cannot separate this from other causes of shock on scene and does not need to, because the action is the same, which is to treat the shock, keep the patient warm, and transport without delay. The needle that drains the sac and the surgery that repairs the heart belong to definitive hospital care.

Tamponade and tension pneumothorax can look alike at the roadside, and separating them is worth the effort because the two demand different help. Both produce shock, distended neck veins, and a struggling patient, and both can follow a wound to the chest. In tension pneumothorax the breath sounds are absent on one side, that side does not move, and the tapping finger finds drum-like air or dull blood, while in tamponade the breath sounds may be quiet but equal on both sides and the chest moves more evenly. The trachea may be pushed away from the injured side in tension and stays central in tamponade, though this sign is late and unreliable. The pressure in tamponade often falls in a way that does not respond to the measures used for other shocks, and the neck veins do not empty when the patient sits up. When the two cannot be separated, the responder reports both possibilities and moves, because the receiving team can settle the question with an ultrasound of the heart and a chest radiograph.

Injury to a major vessel inside the chest is the injury that most often leaves no sign at all, and it must stay in mind. The aorta, the pulmonary artery and its branches, the vena cava, and the vessels beneath the collarbone all lie within reach of a bullet, and each can bleed into the chest or into the tissues of the neck and shoulder. A patient with such an injury may have a small wound, may be awake and talking, and may then lose consciousness and die within minutes as the blood volume falls. The findings that suggest it are shock with no external bleeding, a difference in the pulses or the pressures between the two arms, a swelling at the base of the neck, and a wound whose track points toward the center of the chest. The responder's role is to recognize the possibility, to control what external bleeding can be controlled, to keep the patient flat and warm, and to move quickly to a trauma center. Nothing outside a hospital repairs a torn vessel, and the attempt belongs to the surgeon and the surgical team.

Support of the airway and the breathing follows the patient's condition rather than a fixed script, and each act has an owner. The lay first aider opens the airway by the method taught in training, clears what can be seen, and places the patient in the position that keeps the airway open while protecting the spine. The trained responder or paramedic may use a bag and mask, an airway device, and oxygen according to the protocol of the service, and the decision to give oxygen is a clinical one that the protocol and the prescriber govern rather than this manual. A patient who stops breathing needs cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR, started at once by whoever is present, with compressions and breaths given as the training and the protocol direct. A patient who is breathing but tiring needs help before the breathing stops, so the responder watches the effort, the rate, and the level of consciousness and calls for advanced help early. Positive pressure given by an untrained hand can drive air into the stomach and worsen the injury.

Circulation in a chest wound is managed by controlling what can be seen and by restoring what has been lost, and the second belongs to hospital care. A bleeding wound of the chest wall is pressed with a dressing, and a wound of the armpit, the shoulder, or the base of the neck may need a pressure dressing applied by a trained responder, because those junctional areas cannot be compressed against a bone. A patient in shock is kept flat and warm, and the legs may be raised, though this measure buys time and does not replace lost blood. Fluid and blood replacement belong to the hospital and to the prescriber, and the choice of what to give, how much, and by which route is made by the receiving team under the current guideline and the local protocol. The responder's true contribution to circulation is the fastest safe journey, because the only definitive treatment for hemorrhage inside the chest is surgical.

Hypothermia is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and a patient with a chest wound is at high risk of it. The patient is often lying on cold ground, undressed for examination, losing blood, and losing heat and moisture through an open chest wound, and each of those paths adds to the cooling. A temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is the teaching figure for significant hypothermia, and that value must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold at which harm begins differs with the patient and the measurement. Cold makes the blood clot poorly, makes the heart irritable, worsens shock, and blurs the level of consciousness, so warmth is part of the resuscitation and not an afterthought. The patient is covered with blankets or any insulating material, the back is protected from the ground, and the ambulance is warmed before the patient is placed in it. Every movement is kept gentle, because cold and rough handling together can precipitate a rhythm that stops the heart.

The decision whether to stay and stabilize or to leave for the hospital is made on the mechanism of injury, the distance, the patient's condition, and the responder's scope of practice. A patient with a chest wound who is short of breath, whose pressure is falling, or whose level of consciousness is changing needs a trauma center quickly, and time spent on scene is time lost before surgery. The trained responder may perform the few field acts that the protocol permits, such as covering an open wound and supporting the breathing, and then travels, because a dressing is not a substitute for a surgeon. Where the distance is long, the decision may be to meet an air service or to move toward the nearest facility that can place a chest drain, and that judgment is made with medical direction. A period such as 10 to 15 minutes on scene is sometimes quoted as a goal for the fastest patients, but any such interval is an illustration and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services differ in what they expect.

The information that travels with the patient is as important as the treatment given, and it must be spoken and written in a form the receiving team can use at once. The mechanism of injury, the time of the shooting, the number and site of the wounds, and whether an exit wound was found belong at the top of the account. The observations recorded on scene, with their times, must be handed over, including the breathing rate, the level of consciousness, the pulse character, and any pressure that was measured. Every intervention is named with its time, including the occlusive dressing, the position the patient was kept in, the warmth provided, and any tourniquet or pressure dressing placed elsewhere, and the time a tourniquet was applied must be written on the patient where the next team will see it. The account also names what was not done and why, because a decision not to attempt a procedure is part of the record and protects the patient from a repeated and useless attempt.

Hospital assessment begins with the same primary survey that was begun in the field, now with equipment, and it follows the ABCDE order until each problem is found and addressed. The airway is secured by the team that owns that skill, breathing is assessed with the chest exposed and both sides examined, and circulation is judged by the pulse, the pressure, the skin, and the level of consciousness, with the pelvic and abdominal examination done at the same time. A chest radiograph is taken early, and an ultrasound of the chest and the heart answers the questions of blood around the heart, air or blood in the pleural space, and the movement of the heart muscle. A computed tomography, or CT, scan gives the detailed picture of the track, the vessels, the mediastinum, and the retained fragments, and it is used when the patient is stable enough to travel to the scanner. The examination is repeated, because a chest that was quiet on arrival can become a tension pneumothorax as the observation continues, and the trend of the observations is the most sensitive test in the building.

The interventions that belong to definitive hospital care are named plainly here so that no listener mistakes them for field procedures. A chest drain placed through the chest wall lets air and blood out of the pleural space and allows the lung to re-expand, and it belongs to the physician, the surgeon, or the trained team working under protocol. Blood and fluid replacement, the correction of the clotting, and the warming of the patient are managed by the hospital team, and the substances, the amounts, and the routes are decisions of the prescriber under the current guideline and the local protocol. Pericardial drainage and the repair of a wounded heart belong to the surgeon and the surgical team, and so does the repair of a torn vessel or the control of bleeding that cannot be reached by a drain. A large hemothorax that keeps bleeding may need an operation through the chest wall, and that decision is made on the imaging, the drain output, and the patient's response. A trauma surgeon decides which of these is needed, and the earlier that decision is made, the better the patient's chance.

Not every chest wound needs an operation, and the choice between watching and operating is one of the central judgments of hospital care. A patient with a small pneumothorax, stable observations, and no ongoing bleeding may be watched with repeated examination and imaging, and a drain may still be placed to be safe. A patient whose drain returns a large volume of blood, whose pressure will not hold, or whose imaging shows a vessel injury goes to surgery, and that decision is made by the surgical team and not by the responder. A retained bullet is not removed for its own sake, because removal is a surgical decision made when it is clinically indicated, such as when it presses on a structure, lies in a joint, or causes infection that can be traced to it. A bullet that sits quietly in the chest of a stable patient may be watched for years, and no responder may attempt to extract it, because the attempt risks bleeding and tissue damage that cannot be controlled outside a surgical setting.

To summarize, a gunshot wound to the chest is managed by naming the lethal possibilities early, by making the scene safe before the patient is touched, and by following the ABCDE order with the chest examined on both sides and the back never forgotten. Pneumothorax, tension pneumothorax, hemothorax, open pneumothorax, cardiac injury, and major-vessel injury each announce themselves through the breathing, the neck veins, the tapping finger, and the breath sounds. Tension pneumothorax kills by pressure that prevents the heart from filling, open pneumothorax suffocates the patient through the wound itself, and tamponade presents as shock with quiet breath sounds, so all three must be kept in mind together. Only needle decompression within protocol, an occlusive dressing with monitoring, and warmth, oxygen or positioning within protocol belong to the field, while chest drainage, pericardial drainage, blood replacement, and the repair of the heart or a vessel belong to definitive hospital care. Every pressure, rate, temperature, depth, and interval named in this chapter is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between countries, between services, and between editions. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, supervision, clinical judgment, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 13 — Gunshot Wounds to the Abdomen and Pelvis

A gunshot wound to the abdomen or the pelvis is a scene before it is a patient, and the scene must be made safe before anyone kneels down. The first questions are whether the person who fired is gone, whether the police or another authority has control of the area, whether a second shot or a moving vehicle is possible, and whether broken glass, fire, or a crowd threatens the responders. Gloves and personal protective equipment, or PPE, are worn before contact, because blood and body fluids from a firearm wound carry infection, and a responder who becomes a casualty doubles the number of people who need help. Only when the area is secure does the responder approach, and even then the approach is planned, with the patient moved as little as possible and the mind already fixed on the lethal possibility that dominates this chapter. That possibility is pelvic hemorrhage, the bleeding from torn vessels behind and within the pelvis, which can fill the space it creates and kill a patient whose skin shows almost nothing. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The abdomen is the part of the body that hides its catastrophes best, and the reason lies in what it is, a cavity with room to spare. A wound of entry may be a small hole in the skin, sometimes no larger than a fingertip, while the track inside crosses several organs and opens a space that can hold a large volume of blood without pushing the wall outward enough to be seen. A bullet that enters the chest may pass downward through the diaphragm, and one that enters the abdomen may travel upward into the chest, so the visible wound is a poor guide to the organs at risk. A wound on the back, the flank, the buttock, or the groin may be hidden by the position of the patient or by clothing, and it will be missed by anyone who examines only the front. The abdomen also shares its neighborhood with the pelvis, where the bones, the bladder, the rectum, and the great vessels lie close together, and an injury to one of them rarely respects the boundary a textbook draws. The listener should therefore hold one rule above all others, that a gunshot wound anywhere between the nipple line and the groin is a torso wound until a hospital has proved otherwise.

To reason about the abdomen, the listener needs a simple picture of what lies inside it. A thin membrane called the peritoneum lines the cavity and wraps most of the organs, and the space it encloses is normally empty of everything but a little fluid. Behind the peritoneum lies the retroperitoneal space, where the kidneys, the pancreas, the great vessels, and part of the duodenum sit, and bleeding there is even quieter than bleeding in the open cavity because the peritoneum hides it. Above and in front are the solid organs, the liver on the right and the spleen on the left, which are rich in blood and bleed steadily when torn. The hollow organs, the stomach, the small intestine, the colon, the rectum, and the bladder, hold contents that are not meant to be free, and their injury spills those contents into spaces where infection begins at once. The pelvis is a ring of bone with vessels running along its inner surface, and the space inside it is not empty, because it contains the bladder, the rectum, and in the female patient the reproductive organs.

Several lethal possibilities should be named in the first minutes, each with the finding that reveals it. The first is intra-abdominal hemorrhage, which shows as shock that is out of proportion to the blood visible on the ground, with a rising pulse, a falling pressure, pale cool skin, thirst, anxiety, and a patient who cannot settle. The second is injury to a solid organ, the liver, the spleen, or a kidney, which may bleed slowly enough to allow a brief improvement before the bleeding resumes, so a patient who seems to steady is not a patient who is safe. The third is hollow-organ injury, which declares itself later with pain that spreads, tenderness that becomes guarding, and a quiet fever that speaks of contamination and peritonitis. The fourth is pelvic vascular injury, and this is the one to name aloud as the lethal possibility, because bleeding from the vessels beside the pelvic bones can fill the pelvis and the retroperitoneum with blood while the abdomen stays soft and the external wound stays small.

The most dangerous abdomen is the one that cannot be diagnosed by pressing on it, and the responder must understand why. Blood irritates the peritoneum far less than the contents of a torn bowel, so a patient with a cavity full of blood may have no rigidity at all and may tolerate examination without flinching. A distracted patient with a broken limb, a head injury, or a reduced level of consciousness may not report pain, and a patient whose awareness is fading may answer questions with a delay that hides the truth. The findings that should raise suspicion are therefore general rather than local, and they include a pulse that climbs while the pressure falls, breathing that becomes faster and shallower, skin that turns pale and clammy, a patient who is restless or unusually thirsty, and a belly that slowly distends or that feels dull when tapped in the flanks. Pain at the tip of the shoulder, caused by blood under the diaphragm, and pain referred to the back or the groin, are further clues that the cavity is not innocent. Any one of these findings, and especially a combination of them, is enough to treat the patient as bleeding internally and to move without delay.

A single reading can be misleading, so the responder records the observations that can be taken without instruments and watches their direction rather than their absolute value. The pulse is counted carefully, the breathing rate is counted without telling the patient, and the skin is felt for its warmth and moisture. A pulse of 110 beats per minute in a young adult at rest is a warning, and a pressure measured at 90 millimeters of mercury systolic is a warning of a different order, but both figures are teaching illustrations that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because normal values shift with age, fitness, pregnancy, and the medicines a patient already takes. The trend matters more than the snapshot, which is why the same observations are repeated and written down with the time beside them. Where no instrument exists to measure pressure, the signs of shock must carry the whole assessment, and a patient who is pale, cool, anxious, and thirsty is treated as shocked even when the pressure cannot be numbered. A patient whose measured values look acceptable but whose appearance is poor is judged by the appearance.

The pelvis deserves its own passage of reasoning because a fracture there bleeds into a space that the bone itself creates. When the ring is broken in more than one place and springs open, the volume inside it grows, and the vessels that run along the bone, the veins especially, are torn or stretched until they bleed into that enlarged space. A pelvic fracture can therefore produce a large loss of blood with no wound on the abdomen at all, and the only external sign may be a small wound of entry near the hip, the buttock, or the groin. The finding that should make the responder think of the pelvis is pain or instability when the bones are moved, though the pelvis must not be rocked or sprung repeatedly to test it, because that movement can restart or worsen bleeding that is already under way. Blood at the urinary opening, inability to pass urine, or a wound near the perineum supports the suspicion, and so does a leg that appears shortened or rotated. A patient with a gunshot wound near the pelvis and any sign of shock is a patient whose pelvis is treated as broken until imaging proves otherwise.

The first aider's work begins with the bleeding that can be seen, because that is the bleeding that can be touched. Gloved hands press directly on any wound that is pouring blood, using a dressing or the cleanest cloth available, and the pressure is held without lifting the cloth to look underneath. A wound that continues to bleed through the first layer of dressing is covered with more material and pressed harder rather than unpacked, and a limb wound that cannot be controlled by pressure may be treated with a tourniquet by a trained responder or paramedic acting under protocol. An embedded object, a blade, a fragment of glass, or a piece of metal, is never removed in the field, because pulling it free may open a vessel that nothing can then close, and it is stabilized in place with padding built up around it while the patient is moved with it. Bullets are not extracted by first responders, since removal is a surgical decision made later and only when it is clinically indicated, and it is not a field procedure. Nothing is pushed back into the abdomen, and exposed bowel or omentum is covered with a clean, moist dressing and left alone.

While the bleeding is controlled, the rest of the first aid is deliberately simple and deliberately disciplined. The airway is checked by looking, listening, and asking the patient to speak, and a patient who answers clearly has an airway that is open for the moment. The patient is kept flat, still, and warm, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a matter of comfort, since blood loss makes the body lose heat quickly and a cold patient bleeds more and tolerates the loss less well. Blankets, foil sheeting, and whatever else is at hand are placed under and over the patient, and the patient is kept off cold ground or a cold metal surface wherever that is possible. Nothing is given by mouth, no food and no drink, because the patient may need an operation and because vomiting after a belly injury can fill the airway. The emergency medical services are called early, the wound and the mechanism are described plainly, and the patient is moved only when the move carries the patient toward a hospital that can operate.

The responder watches for shock while the patient travels, and the watch is continuous rather than occasional. Shock is the state in which the circulation can no longer deliver enough oxygen to the tissues, and after an abdominal gunshot wound it is usually the result of blood loss, though contamination and later infection can deepen it. The signs are a rising pulse, a falling pressure, fast and shallow breathing, pale and clammy skin, thirst, restlessness, and a level of awareness that drifts, and the Glasgow coma scale is the tool the trained responder uses to record that drift in a way the receiving team can follow. A core temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is a threshold that adds its own harm, but the exact line used to define hypothermia differs between services and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than remembered as a fixed value. Warming and hemorrhage control are therefore the same task and not two tasks, and they are carried out together from the first minute to the last. A patient who was talking and then stops talking, or who was restless and then becomes quiet in a way that is not calm, is a patient who is deteriorating.

The decision that saves the most lives in this chapter is not a procedure but a destination. A patient with a gunshot wound to the abdomen or the pelvis belongs in a trauma center where a surgeon, an operating room, blood for transfusion, and imaging are all under the same roof, and the responder who recognizes this early gives the patient the only real treatment available in the field, which is rapid and gentle transport. The receiving team is warned before arrival, with the mechanism, the number of wounds, the observations, and the trend over time passed on in plain words, because that warning lets the hospital prepare blood, a room, and a team before the patient arrives. A delay on scene for actions that do not control bleeding or open an airway costs the patient the time that surgery needs, and the responder who is tempted to do more should remember that the abdomen is not a place for improvisation. If the patient must be carried, the carrying is done with the spine kept in line and the pelvis supported, and the patient is not made to walk even when the patient insists. The shortest safe route is chosen, and the patient is not taken to a place that cannot operate unless that place is the only one within reach and can stabilize the patient and transfer.

The trained responder or paramedic builds a fuller assessment within the protocol of the service, and the purpose of each step is to decide how fast the patient must move. The primary survey follows the ABCDE order, in which airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure are addressed in turn, and the exposure step is the one that finds the wound on the back, the flank, or the buttock that was hidden. The abdomen is inspected, gently felt, and listened to, but it is not pressed repeatedly, because repeated examination both hurts the patient and tells the responder little that the trend has not already told. The pelvis is assessed once, gently, with the hands on the hip bones and the knees kept together, and a pelvic binder is applied by the responder or paramedic under protocol when the mechanism and the findings support it, since the binder is not a first-aid measure for an untrained hand to improvise. The patient is kept warm, the observations are recorded with times, and the findings are handed to the receiving team in the order in which they were found.

In the hospital, the same reasoning continues but the tools change. The receiving team repeats the primary survey, secures the airway if it is threatened, supports breathing, obtains access to the circulation, and takes blood for the tests that will guide transfusion and operation. The abdomen is examined again, the rectum and the vagina may be examined where the wound pattern calls for it, and a urinary catheter may be placed after the team has confirmed that no injury makes that unsafe. The history is taken from the patient if the patient can give it and from the responders if the patient cannot, and the exact time of the injury and the time of the last observation are written down. A patient who is unstable is not sent for a long study before the team has decided what the instability means, because a patient who is bleeding to death is treated before the bleeding is mapped in detail. The physician or trauma surgeon decides the order of the tests, and that order is a clinical judgment rather than a fixed rule.

Imaging answers specific questions, and each study is chosen because its answer would change what happens next. Plain radiographs of the chest and the pelvis show the position of a bullet, the presence of free air, and the shape of a pelvic ring that may be broken and sprung. An ultrasound examination of the abdomen performed at the bedside answers whether there is free fluid, which in this setting usually means blood, and it can be repeated at the bedside as the patient changes. Computed tomography, or CT, gives the most complete picture of the track, the solid organs, the retroperitoneum, and the pelvic bones, and it is used when the patient is stable enough to travel to the scanner and when its result will direct the operation. A patient who is too unstable for CT goes to the operating room or to an intervention that stops bleeding, and the imaging is done afterward or not at all. The choice between these studies belongs to the physician or trauma surgeon, and the responder's task is to give the team the information that makes the choice possible.

Blood replacement is a hospital decision that begins with the recognition that the patient is bleeding, and it is guided by the patient's condition, the observed loss, and the results of testing rather than by any single figure. A trauma center keeps blood available, and a patient with major hemorrhage may be treated through a massive transfusion protocol that the local service defines and that the physician activates. The substances given, the amounts, the order in which they are given, and the tests that follow belong to the treating team and to the protocol of that hospital, and no amount or schedule can be taken from a manual such as this one. A patient who is still bleeding may need an operation or a procedure to stop the bleeding before transfusion can succeed, because replacing blood that continues to pour out is a losing race. The decision to give blood is therefore tied to the decision to control the source, and the two are made together by the physician or trauma surgeon.

Operation is the definitive treatment for most of the injuries in this chapter, and it belongs entirely to the hospital and the surgical team. A laparotomy opens the abdomen so that the surgeon can find and control the bleeding, repair or remove a damaged organ, close or divert a torn bowel, and wash out the contamination that has spilled. In a patient who is too unstable for a long repair, the surgeon may choose damage control, in which bleeding and contamination are controlled quickly, the abdomen is packed or left open with a temporary cover, and the patient is warmed and stabilized in the intensive care unit, or ICU, before returning to the operating room. A torn spleen may be repaired or removed, a torn liver may be packed or repaired, a kidney may be preserved or removed, and a torn vessel may be repaired or bypassed, and each of those choices is made on the findings at operation. Pelvic bleeding may be controlled by packing the pelvis, by stabilizing the ring with an external frame, or by a radiological procedure that blocks the bleeding vessel, and all of these are definitive interventions rather than field measures.

Three decisions deserve to be named even though none of them can be reduced to a prescription in this book. The first is the decision about antibiotics, which becomes urgent when a hollow organ has been torn and its contents have spilled, because contamination of the peritoneal cavity is the beginning of an infection that can kill days later, and the choice of substance belongs to the prescriber and to the local protocol while the responder's contribution is to report the contamination and the delay. The second is the decision about tetanus protection, which the treating clinician makes after considering the wound, the patient's history, and the local schedule, and which is not a decision for the roadside. The third is the decision about pain, which should be made early rather than late, because pain itself worsens breathing, raises the pulse, and adds to the work of an already strained body.
