Analgesia may be given by a paramedic under protocol or by the hospital team, and the substance, the amount, and the method of giving it are the business of the prescriber and the local protocol, while a lay first aider gives no medicine at all. Oxygen and fluids given into a vein follow the same rule, in that the trained responder, paramedic, or hospital team gives them when the protocol allows, and the amount and the device belong to that protocol.

Two groups of patients need a word of their own because their injury hides even better than the usual abdomen. A child has a smaller cavity and organs that sit closer together, so a single bullet can injure more of them, and a child may keep a normal pulse and pressure for longer before the circulation fails, which makes the eventual collapse more sudden. A pregnant patient has a uterus that rises out of the pelvis and pushes the bowel upward, so a wound low in the abdomen may injure the uterus and the fetus while the bowel above is spared, and a wound higher up may injure the bowel while the uterus escapes. The finding that decides the urgency is often the state of the mother, because the best treatment for the fetus is a mother whose circulation works. Both groups belong in a center with pediatric or obstetric and surgical capability, and the local protocol decides where the patient is taken.

Consider a constructed illustration, not a real patient and not a real incident, to see how the reasoning runs. A young man is found beside a road after a shooting, awake and talking, with a single small wound below the ribs on the left and no blood on the ground. His pulse is fast, his skin is cool and damp, he asks for water, and he says the pain is not bad, and a responder who judged only by the pain would call him stable. The responder instead counts the breathing, records the pulse and the pressure, inspects the back and the flank, and finds a second wound near the spine, and the picture becomes clear, that this is a torso wound with internal bleeding and a hidden exit. The scene is made safe, the wound is covered, the patient is kept warm and flat, nothing is given by mouth, and the emergency medical services are asked to take him to a trauma center with a warning that the abdomen and the pelvis are involved. The illustration is constructed to teach the order of the actions, and every figure in it would have to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol in any real service.

Several traps recur often enough to be named plainly. The first is the patient who looks well at first, sometimes called the honeymoon period, when a young person with a strong circulation keeps a normal pulse and pressure while the abdomen fills, and then deteriorates quickly, so the responder who was reassured by the first set of observations has been misled by compensation rather than by any lie. The second is the small wound, which says nothing about the size of the cavity within it, because the skin closes behind a bullet and a tiny entrance can hide a track through several organs. The third is the distracting injury, the broken leg or the scalp wound that draws the eye and takes the attention while the abdomen bleeds quietly. The fourth is the assumption that a bullet which passed through has done no harm, when a through-and-through track can cross the liver, the bowel, or the vessels just as easily as a retained one.

Some things must be said again because the temptation to do them is strong. First responders do not explore a wound with a finger or an instrument, because probing neither finds the bleeding nor stops it, and it can dislodge a clot that was holding a vessel closed. First responders do not remove a bullet, and they do not remove a blade or any other embedded object, because removal in the field may cause hemorrhage that cannot be controlled and further damage to tissue, so the object is stabilized and the patient is moved with it. First responders do not push bowel or omentum back into the abdomen, do not tie off vessels they cannot see, and do not straighten a deformed limb to make the patient look better, because the position found is the position that protects the vessels and nerves. First responders do not give food or drink, and they do not give medicines unless their scope of practice and their protocol authorize it. A pelvic binder, a splint, or a traction device is applied only by a responder trained and authorized to use it, and a lay first aider who has no such training keeps the patient still and warm and waits for help to arrive.

To summarize, a gunshot wound to the abdomen or the pelvis is dangerous mainly because it is quiet, and the responder must treat the wound and the scene before trusting the appearance of either. The abdomen holds its blood without showing it, a solid organ may bleed steadily and then pause before bleeding again, a hollow organ spills its contents and starts an infection, and a broken pelvis can fill with blood from the vessels beside the bone, so pelvic hemorrhage is the lethal possibility that must be named early. The findings that matter are general rather than local, and a rising pulse, a falling pressure, pale clammy skin, thirst, restlessness, a changing level of awareness, and a slowly distending belly are enough to act upon even when the belly is soft. First aid is hemorrhage control, warmth, and transport, the trained responder assesses within protocol, applies a pelvic binder when authorized, records the trend, and warns the receiving team, and hospital imaging, transfusion, and operation are the definitive care. Every figure in this chapter, whether a pressure, a pulse, a temperature, a time, or a depth, is an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between services, countries, and editions. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the protocol of the service in which you work, and any example here is constructed rather than drawn from a real patient. A patient whose story and appearance do not match the wound deserves another set of observations, a clearer plan, and a faster journey, and the discipline of that judgment is the skill this chapter teaches.

# Chapter 14 — Gunshot Wounds to the Limbs

A gunshot wound to a limb is the most common and the most survivable firearm injury. Its ordinary appearance is why it is underestimated, because the wound is small while the injury that kills is a torn vessel deep inside. The lethal possibility is hemorrhage from a major artery of the limb, and its finding is blood that spurts with the heartbeat. The same warning is a swelling that grows while the responder watches, or blood that soaks through dressing after dressing. The scene is made safe first, because a firearm scene may hold a weapon, a person who may fire again, traffic, or broken glass. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, with gloves at the least, is worn before contact, and protection against hypothermia begins at once, because a bleeding patient on cold ground loses heat quickly. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

Making a shooting scene safe is a sequence, and it begins before the patient is approached. The first question is whether the person who fired is still present and whether any authority controls the area. The trained responder or the paramedic waits for that control, and the lay first aider waits with them, because a rescuer who is shot adds a second patient to a scene with too few hands. The other hazards are traffic, unstable glass, fire, and a structure that may fall. The finding that tells the responder to hold back is a hostile crowd, an unsecured weapon, or a scene no authority has declared safe.

The injury inside a limb threatens the limb first and the life second, and the order is not fixed. A torn artery in the thigh can threaten both at once, because the thigh holds a large volume of tissue and blood. The structures at risk are the artery, the vein beside it, the nerve that runs with them, the muscle, and the bone. Muscle tolerates lost blood flow far less well than skin, and nerve tolerates it least of all. The principle of life before limb decides the order when the two compete, because a patient who is breathing and circulating can be given a limb later. The finding that settles the order is not the size of the wound but whether the patient can breathe and circulate.

The mechanism of injury is the first prediction the responder makes. With a bullet, the prediction is that the track is longer and wider than the openings suggest. A projectile deposits energy in the tissue it crosses, so muscle some distance from the wound may be dead. The entrance and the exit, if there is one, show direction of travel and never depth, so one small opening may hide a shattered bone and a torn vessel. A wound that crosses a joint is especially dangerous, because the joint may be contaminated and the vessels behind the knee are tethered. A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and not as a real patient or a real incident, is a person struck in the calf who later feels the leg tighten and swell.

Arterial injury announces itself in a small number of ways, and each is taught in the examination. The clearest finding is blood that leaves the wound in jets that keep time with the heartbeat. The next is a swelling beneath the skin that grows while the responder's hand rests on it. A limb beyond the wound that has become pale, cool, and numb, or a pulse at the wrist or foot that cannot be felt, points to a vessel no longer carrying flow. A wound that stopped bleeding may resume when the circulation rises or a dressing is lifted, because a divided artery can retract and clot for a time. The trap is a wound that looks dry while the limb is still warm, because a torn artery may bleed into deep tissue.

Venous injury is quieter and can be just as dangerous, because the large veins of the thigh, the groin, and the armpit return blood to the heart. The bleeding is a steady flow of dark blood rather than a jet, and it may stop with firm pressure and restart when pressure is released. A torn vein in the groin or the armpit lies where no tourniquet can be placed, so pressure must reach the exact bleeding point. A wound near a large vein in the upper chest may draw air into the open vessel with each breath, and the finding is a wound that sucks at the moment of inspiration. Arterial and venous injury often occur together, and blood escaping into a closed compartment has nowhere to go but into the tissue. The finding is a limb that is tense, larger than its partner, and painful beyond what the wound explains, while the pulse may still be present.

Nerve injury is the part of a limb wound most easily missed, because it makes no blood and no swelling. A nerve that runs beside a major vessel is often injured with it, so numbness, weakness, and an inability to move the fingers or the toes belong to the examination. The responder asks the patient to move each part of the limb and to say what can be felt along the skin. A nerve deficit appearing after an examination that was first normal is a finding of the greatest importance. It suggests that swelling or a dressing is now pressing on the nerve rather than that the nerve was cut by the bullet. Repair of a divided nerve is a surgical decision made later, and it is never a field procedure. The lay first aider does not test sensation with a needle or a pin, because the test itself can injure tissue that is already at risk.

An open fracture is present when bone is exposed in the wound or when the wound connects with a broken bone that cannot be seen. A gunshot wound to a limb is treated as an open fracture until imaging shows otherwise. The bone is not straightened and the limb is not pulled into a better shape, because that movement can tear a vessel or a nerve and can release a clot holding back hemorrhage. The limb is splinted in the position found, with the wound covered and the joints above and below supported, and that work belongs to the trained responder or the paramedic. Distal circulation is then assessed by looking, feeling, and asking, on the injured limb and on the uninjured limb for comparison. The responder checks the color and warmth of the skin, seeks the pulse at the wrist or the foot, and asks about movement and feeling. A pulse that is present does not exclude an arterial injury, so each element is recorded separately.

The neurovascular examination is not performed once and then trusted, because a limb can deteriorate quietly between the first normal examination and the handover. It is repeated at the points the local protocol defines, which may be at the scene and again at the receiving facility, and each result is written with the time it was taken. A patient whose first examination was normal can develop an absent pulse, a new numbness, or a limb that has become tense and painful. The recorded trend is the gift the field gives the hospital, because a normal examination followed by a worsening one says more than a single reassuring note. The trained responder and the paramedic own this repeated examination. The lay first aider reports what the patient says about pain, movement, and feeling and does not remove a dressing to look underneath it.

Compartment syndrome is the delayed complication that follows a limb which was saved. The limb is divided by tough sheets of tissue into compartments holding muscle, vessels, and nerves. When bleeding or swelling raises the pressure in one of those closed spaces, the smallest vessels are compressed and the muscle begins to die. The earliest and most reliable finding is pain far greater than the wound appears to justify, together with pain when the muscles are gently stretched. The compartment becomes tense and firm, and numbness appears in the territory of the nerve passing through it, while the pulse is often still present. Weakness and an absent pulse are late findings, so the responder escalates on pain and tension rather than on the pulse. Release of the pressure is a surgical procedure called fasciotomy, and it is never attempted in the field. The pressure inside a compartment is measured in the hospital, and any figure quoted for it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold differs with the patient and with the way the measurement is taken.

Restoring flow to a limb that has been without blood can itself cause harm, a paradox the responder must understand without managing it in the field. When the surgeon reopens a vessel, the starved muscle receives blood again and swells, and compartment syndrome can appear in a limb whose pulse has just returned. The finding that should raise the alarm is new and severe pain together with a limb that has become tense and hard. A limb without flow for a long period may also release substances into the circulation that affect the heart and the kidneys. The responder's part is to keep the limb in the position found, leave every dressing and splint as it was applied, record the times, and move the patient quickly.

What the lay first aider may do for a bleeding limb is narrow, effective, and worth doing well. The first action is direct pressure on the wound through a clean cloth or dressing, applied with gloved hands and held without interruption while help is called. If blood shows through, a further layer is placed on top and the hand returns to the same place, because lifting the dressing breaks the clot that is forming. A foreign body such as a fragment of metal or glass is not removed, and it is stabilized in place with padding built around it. The patient is covered and insulated from the ground at the same time, because cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort. The lay first aider does not probe the wound, pour anything into it, or straighten a deformity, and hands over when the trained responder arrives.

The tourniquet is the next rung of the ladder and is owned by the trained responder or the paramedic working under a protocol. The indication is life-threatening bleeding from a limb that direct pressure and packing have not controlled. The place is between the wound and the heart, as close to the wound as the anatomy allows and away from a joint when a length of limb above it is available. The tourniquet is tightened until the bleeding stops rather than until a particular number of turns has been made, and it is not loosened in the field. The time it was applied is written on the patient where the receiving team cannot miss it and spoken aloud at handover. A duration such as 2 hours is often quoted as the point at which the risk to muscle and nerve becomes serious, and that interval is an illustration which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The reason it is not loosened is that the clot behind it may not hold and the patient may hemorrhage again where control cannot be restored.

A wound in the groin, the armpit, the shoulder, or the base of the neck lies where no tourniquet can be placed, and bleeding there is among the most lethal of limb wounds. The trained responder answers it with wound packing, pushing gauze to the bleeding point and packing it firmly back along the track until the cavity is filled. Pressure is then held over the packed wound with the flat of the hand while the patient is moved toward definitive care. This is a technique for the trained responder or the paramedic under a protocol, and it is not taught to the lay first aider. A foreign body embedded in a junctional wound is stabilized in place and packed around, and it is never removed in the field. The finding that packing has worked is gauze that stops filling with blood while pressure is held.

Splinting is the trained responder's work, and its one purpose is to hold the limb still so that movement does not tear what the bullet left intact. The limb is splinted in the position found, and a severely deformed fracture is not straightened to make it look normal. The movement that improves the shape can injure a vessel or a nerve and can release a clot that was holding back hemorrhage. A splint supports the joints above and below the wound and is applied over a dressing that is already controlling the bleeding. The neurovascular examination is performed before the splint is applied and repeated after it is secured, because a splint that is too tight can starve the limb beyond it. The finding that the splint must be adjusted is a limb that has become pale, cold, or numb, and the answer is to loosen and reapply rather than to wait.

The destination of a patient with a limb wound is chosen with the injuries in mind rather than the distance. It is the nearest facility that can assess the vessels, image the bone, and provide an operating room. A trauma center is preferred for a limb with an absent pulse, an expanding swelling, an open fracture, or a worsening examination, because the time to restore flow decides whether the limb survives. Transport is urgent and gentle at once, because speed that throws the patient around adds pain and can move a fracture whose ends lie near a vessel. Emergency medical services are activated early with a report naming the wound, the bleeding, what has been done, and the times. The finding that changes the destination is a patient whose condition is worsening, because a patient in shock needs the closest facility that can begin resuscitation.

Pain after a limb wound is severe and must be acknowledged rather than endured. The provider authorized to prescribe decides which substance is given, by which route, and how often, and those decisions belong to the local protocol and the prescriber rather than to this manual. The finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that is severe, worsening, or out of proportion to the wound, because that finding may also point to compartment syndrome. The scope of practice forbids the lay first aider from giving any medicine and forbids any responder from acting outside the local protocol. The decision about whether a nerve block is appropriate belongs to a physician or a trauma surgeon in definitive care.

Protection against tetanus is raised at the first contact with a limb wound, because the projectile carries cloth, soil, and metal into deep tissue. The question of whether the patient is protected is answered by the immunization history and the nature of the wound, and the decision belongs to the provider authorized to make it under the local protocol. Antibiotics are considered in the same way, as a decision made by a prescriber rather than as a field treatment. The finding that makes it urgent is a wound that is deep, heavily contaminated, or associated with an open fracture or dead muscle. Nothing about the substance, the amount, the route, the timing, or the interval may be taken from this chapter. The responder's part is to describe the wound accurately, to record what was done and when, and to keep the patient warm and moving toward the place where that decision can be made well.

Fluids and blood products are decisions about a patient and a local system, and they belong to the paramedic under a protocol and to definitive hospital care. The finding that makes them urgent is a patient whose pulse is climbing while the pressure is falling and whose skin is pale and cool. The choice of what is given into a vein, the amount, and the rate are set by the protocol and the prescriber, and none may be taken from these pages. Oxygen is a decision about a patient rather than a routine act, and whether it is given, how, and to what target belong to the local protocol. The lay first aider does not administer oxygen, and the responder's own task is to stop the bleeding, keep the patient warm and still, and shorten the time to the surgeon.

Hypothermia is a companion of limb trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and it begins when the patient bleeds, lies on cold ground, or is exposed. Blood loss reduces the volume that carries heat, and cold makes the clotting system work less well, so a cold patient bleeds more. The responder breaks that circle by covering the patient before the journey, insulating the patient from the ground, and keeping the vehicle warm. The limb itself is covered with the rest of the patient, because tissue short of blood tolerates cold poorly. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which cold becomes dangerous, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold differs with age and with the way the measurement is taken. The finding that warns the responder that cooling has begun is a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold.

Definitive hospital care begins with imaging, and the choice of study is made by the physician or the trauma surgeon. A plain radiograph shows the fracture and the position of any retained projectile, and it is the first study for most limb wounds. Ultrasound can look for blood around a vessel, and computed tomography, or CT, with dye in the circulation can show whether an artery is torn or blocked. Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, is used later and more selectively, chiefly when a nerve injury must be defined after the patient is stable. The finding that decides which study is needed is the neurovascular examination itself, so the record of that examination travels with the patient. None of these studies is a field procedure, and a responder who delays transport to obtain one has reversed the order of care.

Restoring the flow to a limb is surgical work, and it includes the repair of the artery and the vein, the release of the compartments, the cleaning away of dead muscle, and the stabilization of the bone. Some limbs are held open with a temporary tube that carries blood across the injured segment until the patient is stable, and that is a decision made in the operating room. A limb that cannot be saved is amputated in definitive care, and the decision rests on the injury, the time without flow, and the state of the patient. The handover is part of the treatment, and it must carry the mechanism of injury, the times of the injury and of every dressing and tourniquet, and the trend of the examinations. The responder states plainly what was not done and why, because an omission that is known is safer than one that is discovered. The finding that should prompt a written note at the scene is any intervention, any change in the patient, and the moment at which either occurred.

Certain limb sites deserve their own warning because their anatomy changes the danger. The thigh holds the largest bone in the body and the large vessels beside it, and bleeding there can dull the patient's level of consciousness while the wound looks small. A wound near the knee threatens the artery behind it, which is tethered and easily torn, so the pulse at the foot and the movement of the toes are examined. The shoulder and the armpit lie in the junctional zone discussed above, and a wound there may injure the vessels and the nerves of the whole arm. The forearm and the lower leg each contain a pair of bones and tight compartments, so a fracture there can raise the pressure inside a compartment. The finding that must be carried to the receiving team is the site of the wound with the examination of the limb beyond it.

A constructed illustration may help to fix the sequence, and it is offered as a construction and never as a real patient or a real incident. A person is struck in the outer thigh by a single projectile, and at first the wound is small and the pulse at the ankle is easy to feel. The responder controls the bleeding, covers the wound, splints the limb in the position found, keeps the person warm, and repeats the examination. On the second assessment the thigh is larger and firmer, and the person reports pain that the wound does not explain. That change, rather than the wound itself, must be reported at handover, because it suggests bleeding into the tissue or pressure building inside a compartment.

The mistakes that cost a limb or a life in this kind of wound are few and they repeat. The first is to straighten a deformed limb so that it looks better, and the second is to lift a dressing to see whether the bleeding has stopped. The third is to loosen a tourniquet in the field, which can release hemorrhage that no one can control again. The fourth is to wait for the pulse to disappear before taking compartment syndrome seriously, because by then the muscle may already be dying. The fifth is to treat the wound rather than the patient, which means missing shock and missing a second wound on the same limb. The patient is watched continuously until the handover, with the observations repeated in the same order, and the findings that should send the responder back to the beginning are a falling level of consciousness, a pulse that has become weak or rapid, skin that has become colder or paler, and bleeding that has restarted beneath a dressing.

To summarize, a gunshot wound to a limb is the most common and the most survivable of firearm injuries, and it threatens the limb first while still being capable of killing through hemorrhage. The scene is made safe before the patient is touched, personal protective equipment is worn, and protection against hypothermia begins in the first minute. The lethal possibility is hemorrhage from a major vessel of the limb, whose finding is blood that spurts with the heartbeat, a swelling that grows while the responder watches, or blood that soaks through dressing after dressing. The first aid for it is direct pressure, while the trained responder may pack a junctional wound and apply a tourniquet that is not loosened in the field. Arterial, venous, and nerve injuries often travel together, an open fracture is treated as contaminated, and the distal circulation, movement, and sensation are recorded and repeated because a first normal examination can be followed by a worsening one. Compartment syndrome is the delayed complication that follows a limb that was saved, it is suspected on pain and tension rather than on an absent pulse, and its release is a surgical procedure. Definitive care owns imaging, the repair of vessels and nerves, and the cleaning and stabilization of bone, the provider level is named for every intervention, and every time, pressure, temperature, and figure in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. This chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 15 — Retained Bullets and Foreign Bodies

The retained projectile is the injury that most often tempts a responder to act, and it is the one where acting is most likely to kill the patient. Scene safety comes before the patient here as in every other chapter, because a place where shots were fired may still hold a shooter, a weapon nearby may still be loaded, and the patient's own blood carries infection that enters through a break in the responder's skin, so the area is made safe by those authorized to hold it and personal protective equipment, or PPE, is worn before a dressing is opened. The lethal possibility to be named first is hemorrhage that is being held back by the object itself, and the finding that reveals it is a wound that has stopped bleeding around a projectile with a pulse beside it or a swelling that grows while the responder watches. The rule that governs everything that follows can be spoken in one sentence, which is that a first responder never pulls a bullet or an embedded object out of a wound. This chapter explains why that is so, how to tell a retained fragment that can safely be left from one that must come out, how the hospital decides, and what surgical removal costs. It is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

The reason a bullet is not routinely removed is not that surgeons are timid but that the wound left by removal is a second injury, often worse than the wound the projectile made. A bullet that has come to rest has already spent its energy, and the tissue around it has closed down and sealed the track, so the object may be plugging the very vessel that would pour blood the moment it is drawn out. Removing it also means passing instruments along a track whose course is known only from imaging, and the structures beside that track, which include nerves, tendons, and named vessels, can be divided by the instrument hunting for the metal. A further reason belongs to the operating room itself, because an operation has its own risks of infection, of anesthesia, and of bleeding, and a fragment causing no harm does not earn those risks. The principle is the same one that governs an embedded knife at the roadside, in that what can be contained is contained and what must be repaired is repaired, and the two acts are separated by the finding that the object is already causing harm. This is the distinction the listener must carry away, because the popular picture of a bullet that must be chased through the body is a picture that costs lives.

The retained fragment that can be left is the one at rest in a place where it does nothing, and the hospital recognizes it by a set of findings rather than by a single test. It lies in muscle or in the soft tissue beneath the skin, it is away from a joint, away from a major vessel, and away from a nerve, and it is producing no symptom the patient can describe and no sign the examiner can find. The wound around it has stopped bleeding, the limb beyond it has normal color and warmth and a pulse that can be felt, and the movement and the feeling of the limb are intact. A patient with such a fragment is watched rather than operated on, and the watch continues after discharge, because a piece of metal that is quiet today can announce itself months later. A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient or a real incident, is the fragment that comes to rest in the outer muscle of the thigh, where the patient has full strength, full feeling, and no pain, and where the surgical decision is to leave it and record exactly where it sits. The finding that tells the receiving team which fragment this is, is the combination of its location, of an intact examination of the vessels and nerves, and of the absence of any symptom the fragment explains.

The fragment that must come out is the one already producing harm or positioned where harm is expected, and the brief names the three situations that decide it. The first is a fragment near a joint, because a joint is a closed space with a delicate lining and a surface that must glide, and metal inside or beside it grinds, inflames, and releases lead into the fluid that bathes the cartilage. The second is a fragment near a major vessel, because a vessel wall pressed on or nicked by metal can give way days or weeks later, and the hemorrhage that follows may be the first symptom the patient has. The third is a fragment producing neurological symptoms, because an object touching the spinal cord or a nerve is telling the examiner that the tissue it touches is already losing function, and delay may make that loss permanent. Each of those three is a reason for the hospital to plan an operation rather than a reason for a responder to touch the wound, and that distinction is the whole of the field rule. Other fragments are also removed when they lie in the eye, the airway, the heart, or a vessel they have entered, but these are the three that a listener must be able to repeat.

A joint deserves its own explanation because the harm a fragment does there is mechanical and chemical at the same time. The lining of a joint produces fluid that lubricates the surfaces, and a piece of metal sitting in that fluid is bathed continuously rather than fixed in place, so it can migrate within the joint and be carried into the space where the bones meet. Every movement then becomes a grinding movement against the fragment, and the cartilage wears at a rate no healthy joint would see, while the patient reports a click, a catch, or a pain that appears only at the end of a movement. Lead that dissolves from the fragment into the joint fluid is absorbed by the lining and can produce a delayed inflammation that looks like an arthritis rather than an injury. The finding that should raise the question is a wound near a joint with a painful arc of movement, a joint that swells after use, or metal seen on imaging within the capsule, and that question belongs to the orthopedic surgeon rather than to the responder. Removal in that setting is a planned operation performed with imaging available in the operating room, because the fragment must be found precisely and the joint protected while it is retrieved, and a fragment deep in a joint is never a target for a hand in the field.

A fragment near a major vessel is a delayed emergency, and the delay is what makes it dangerous, because the patient may be discharged well and return in collapse. The wall of an artery or a large vein is elastic and can be pressed on by metal for a long time without tearing, and the pressure of the fragment against that wall can thin it until a false aneurysm forms, which is a sac of blood held together by the tissue around the vessel. That sac can enlarge quietly and then rupture, and the finding that announces it is a pulsatile swelling near the wound, a new sound the examiner can hear with a stethoscope, or a limb that becomes cool and pulseless without any new injury. A fragment that has entered the wall of a vein can also be carried by the bloodstream, so the imaging that follows must look along the whole vessel and not only at the place where the projectile entered. The decision to operate is made with the vascular team and with preparation for the blood loss removal may release, and the operation is planned with the ability to control the vessel above and below the fragment. Nothing in that plan is available at the roadside, and a responder who pulls the fragment out to see what happens has taken the decision away from the people who could have controlled it.

A fragment that produces neurological symptoms is the third situation, and the symptoms may be as loud as a paralyzed limb or as quiet as a numbness the patient mentions in passing. An object lying in the spinal canal can press on the cord, and the finding that reveals it is a change in the strength, the feeling, or the control of the bowel and the bladder below the level of the wound, together with a level of consciousness that is otherwise normal. An object lying against a peripheral nerve can produce a shooting pain along the limb, a weakness of a single muscle group, or a patch of skin that has lost its feeling, and the pattern of that loss tells the examiner which nerve the fragment is touching. Movement of the patient can push a fragment that was merely touching a nerve into the nerve, so the patient with a suspected fragment near the spine is kept still and moved with the spine protected. The neurological examination is repeated and recorded, because a deficit present on arrival and a deficit that appears after a journey mean different things to the receiving team. Imaging and the decision about removal both belong to definitive hospital care, and the finding that makes the decision urgent is a deficit that is getting worse rather than one that is stable.

Lead toxicity is the late consequence that makes a retained fragment a long term problem, and it appears after an interval that may be measured in months or in years. Lead dissolves slowly from metal, and the rate rises when the fragment sits in joint fluid or in the acidic environment of the stomach after it has been swallowed, so the findings are vague and easily attributed to other causes, including abdominal pain, constipation, a headache, a general weakness, and a blood picture that shows anemia. Children are the group at greatest risk, because a growing nervous system is more sensitive and a small body carries a smaller margin, and the pediatric patient with a retained fragment is watched more closely for that reason. A shotgun wound is a special case, because the pellets spread as they travel and the removal of every one is neither possible nor desirable, so imaging maps the spread and the surgical team chooses the few pellets near a joint, a vessel, or a nerve and leaves the rest. The wadding and the clothing carried into such a wound are often a greater threat than the metal, because organic material feeds infection, and the finding that reveals that threat is a wound that becomes hot, swollen, and painful over the following days. The measurement at which concern about lead begins differs between guidelines and laboratories, so it must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

A fragment is not always still, and migration is the reason a retained projectile is documented precisely and watched over time. Metal lying in a joint can move within the joint, a fragment in the soft tissue can be pushed along a tissue plane by the movement of a muscle, and a fragment that has entered the lumen of a vessel can be carried by the flow of blood to a place far from the wound. The most feared migration is into the heart or into the lung, where the fragment can produce a rhythm disturbance, a cough of blood, or a sudden collapse, and the finding that reveals it may be a new symptom in a patient whose wound was considered closed. A fragment that travels in a vein moves toward the heart and the lungs, while a fragment that travels in an artery moves downstream toward the limb, and the direction of travel follows the direction of the flow. Gravity also acts on a fragment in a large vein, so the position of the patient during transport can change where the fragment is later found, which is one more reason the receiving team must be told what position the patient was kept in. The response to migration is not a field maneuver but repeated imaging and a surgical plan, and the finding that triggers the imaging is any new symptom the old wound cannot explain.

Imaging is the hospital's method of deciding, and it is also the reason a field responder does not need to know where the fragment sits. The first examination is usually a plain radiograph of the region, taken from more than one direction, because a fragment seen from a single direction only can be drawn as sitting anywhere along the line of the beam. Computed tomography, after which CT is allowed, shows the fragment in relation to the organs and the bones around it and is the examination of choice when the fragment lies near the spine, the abdomen, or a major vessel, while ultrasound can be used at the bedside to look for fluid, for a swelling, or for a fragment close to the skin. Magnetic resonance imaging, after which MRI is allowed, is used with care, because a fragment containing iron can be moved or heated by the magnetic field, and the decision to perform it belongs to the radiologist who knows the composition of the fragment. The number of views and the choice of examination follow the local protocol, and any figure quoted for the smallest fragment the equipment can show must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because machines and techniques differ between hospitals. Localization during the operation is a further step, using imaging in the operating room so that the surgeon can find the fragment with the smallest possible dissection, and none of these steps belongs to the field.

Surgical extraction is a definitive procedure with its own risks, and the listener must hear that clearly because a fragment invisible from the outside looks easy to take. The operation requires an incision through tissue that has already been injured, and the track must be followed without dividing the structures beside it, so a fragment close to a nerve may be reached only by passing instruments immediately beside that nerve. Every operation carries the risk of infection, of bleeding, and of anesthesia, and a fragment deep in the abdomen or the chest may require the opening of a cavity, a far larger act than the wound itself. Removal can also be incomplete, because a projectile may have fragmented into pieces too small to find, and the surgeon must then decide whether further searching does more harm than the pieces that remain. The operation can worsen a neurological deficit when a fragment is embedded in the spinal cord, and in that setting the surgeon may deliberately leave the fragment in place rather than risk converting a partial deficit into a complete one. The decision is therefore a balance of the harm the fragment is doing against the harm of the operation, and it is made by the trauma surgeon together with the orthopedic, vascular, or neurosurgical team that owns the tissue involved.

The field rule is short and absolute, in that a lay first aider and a trained responder never attempt to extract a bullet or any other embedded object. The object is stabilized in place, the patient is transported with it, and the receiving team is told what it is, where it is, and how long it has been there. The reason is not tidiness but hemorrhage, because the object may be the only thing pressing on a torn vessel, and the moment it is drawn out the bleeding may become impossible to control with the equipment that is present. A second reason is that pulling an object drags with it the tissue that has closed around it, and a hooked fragment or a piece of glass with a sharp edge can cut a structure that was intact. The strongest temptation is the urge to find out what the object is doing, and probing with a finger, with forceps, or with any instrument pushes bacteria into the track, breaks the clot that has sealed it, and can push the object into a structure it was only touching. The finding that tells the responder the rule has been broken is bleeding that restarts from a wound that had stopped, or a new deficit in the limb after an object was moved, and in either case the patient needs definitive care immediately.

Foreign bodies other than bullets arrive in the same wounds and behave in ways that change the plan, so the responder should be able to name them without holding a list in the hand. Glass and metal are dense and are usually seen on a radiograph, while wood, thorns, and clothing are often invisible on a plain radiograph and may be found only by ultrasound or by examination of the wound. A fragment of wood or a piece of cloth that remains in a wound is a persistent source of infection, and the finding that reveals it may be a wound that keeps discharging weeks after it appeared to heal. Tetanus is the specific concern that follows any wound contaminated by soil, by clothing, or by an object that carried dirt into the tissue, and the decision about protection against tetanus belongs to the provider authorized to make it under the local protocol. The finding that makes that decision urgent is a wound that is deep, contaminated, or caused by an object that traveled through the environment before entering the body, while the substance, the amount, the route, and the timing belong to the prescriber and to the local guideline rather than to this book. Antibiotics follow the same rule, in that the decision belongs to the clinician who has examined the wound, and a listener cannot take a prescription from these pages.

An impaled object is the extreme case of the same rule, and it demands a deliberate calm because the object is large, visible, and frightening to everyone at the scene. The object is left exactly where it is, the patient is positioned so that it is supported rather than levered by the ground or the stretcher, and the padding around it is built up until the object can no longer move independently of the body. Stabilization is a skill a lay first aider can perform with the materials at hand, and it begins with a clean dressing placed around the base of the object without pressing on it, followed by padding built up on both sides until the object is held in the middle of a firm ring. A cup, a rolled bandage, or a folded cloth can serve as the ring when nothing better is available, and the ring is fixed to the skin rather than to the object, because a bandage tied to the object transmits every movement of the body directly to the tissue it has entered. The responder does not cut the object, does not push it back, and does not use it as a handle to turn the patient, and the object is cut only when a clinician authorizes it and when the cut is needed to free the patient for transport, well away from the skin so that the inner end does not shift. The finding that tells the responder the stabilization has failed is a change in the patient's pain, a new bleeding, or a new deficit that appears when the object shifts, and any of those findings turns the transport into an emergency within an emergency.

Some sites make the object dangerous in a way that is specific to the anatomy, and the responder should know them because they change the urgency rather than the rule. A foreign body in the eye is protected with a rigid shield that rests on the bone around the eye and touches neither the lid nor the object, and the lay first aider does not attempt to remove a fragment from the eye, does not press on the eye, and does not patch the eye tightly. An object in the neck may lie beside the airway or beside a large vessel, so the first question is whether the patient can breathe and speak, and pressure is applied around the object rather than over it. An object in the chest may have entered the heart or a great vessel, and the finding that reveals that possibility is a wound near the heart with a rising pulse, a falling pressure, or distended neck veins, and that patient belongs to immediate surgical care. A projectile retained in a body cavity raises the same question differently, because the hospital does not open an abdomen merely because a bullet is inside it, but because the track has opened the bowel, the liver, or a vessel, and the finding may be a rigid and tender abdomen or a rising pulse. In every one of those sites the rule is unchanged, which is that the object stays where it is and the patient moves, and the difference is only the speed with which the patient must reach the surgical team.

The lay first aider's part in this chapter is small, specific, and more valuable than the dramatic act it replaces, and the first aider makes the scene safe or stays out of it, protects the hands and the eyes, sends for emergency medical services, covers the wound, stabilizes the object, keeps the patient still and warm, and reports everything observed. The first aider does not probe the wound with a finger, does not use a magnet, does not cut the object free, and does not let a bystander do any of those things, because the only fragment safe to remove is one that is not embedded in anyone. The trained responder and the paramedic add assessment, documentation, and transport, and they examine the limb beyond the wound for color, warmth, pulse, movement, and feeling, recording what they find so that the receiving team can compare it with what follows. They repeat that examination after every move, because a fragment can shift with the patient and a deficit that appears during transport is a finding the surgeon must have. They do not remove the object, do not explore the wound with an instrument, and do not enlarge the wound to see the track, because all three belong to definitive hospital care. They may cover the wound, stabilize the object, splint the limb where required, protect the patient against hypothermia, and begin the journey toward the trauma center that can provide imaging and an operating room, while the decision about pain relief belongs to the provider authorized under the protocol, and the substance, the amount, the route, and the timing are set by that protocol and the prescriber rather than by this book.

Documentation is part of the treatment, because the receiving team inherits a track they cannot see and a decision already made to leave it alone, so the record names the number of wounds, the site of each, whether an entry wound has a matching exit wound, and the position of every object left in place. It states that the object was not removed, that it was stabilized, at what time that was done, and in what position the patient was carried, because a change in position can change where the fragment now sits. It states what the responder observed at each examination of the limb beyond the wound, and the time of it, together with any change that followed, because a trend tells the surgeon more than a single measurement, and it carries the mechanism of injury and the patient's account where one can be given. Hypothermia accompanies every patient in this chapter who is bleeding, exposed, immobilized, or simply waiting, and it is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort. A patient who has been undressed to be examined, who lies on cold ground while an object is stabilized, or who is losing blood loses heat from the surface and from the circulation at once, and the responder breaks that circle by covering the patient before the journey, by insulating from the ground, by replacing wet clothing with dry covering that does not disturb the object, and by keeping the vehicle warm. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the line at which cold itself becomes serious, and that figure, like every other in this chapter, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services and editions differ.

To summarize, a retained bullet is usually left where it is, and the reason is that removal can release hemorrhage that no field measure can control and can injure structures the projectile is not touching. The distinction the listener must carry is between the fragment at rest in muscle with an intact limb beyond it, which is watched, and the fragment near a joint, near a major vessel, or producing neurological symptoms, which is planned for removal by the surgical team. Lead toxicity and migration are the late complications that keep a retained fragment a living problem, and both are found by follow up and by imaging rather than by the examination at the roadside. Imaging, which includes plain radiographs, computed tomography, ultrasound, and in selected cases magnetic resonance imaging, is the hospital's method of localization and of deciding, and extraction is a definitive operation with its own risks of infection, of bleeding, of nerve injury, and of an incomplete result. The field rule is absolute, in that a first responder never extracts a bullet or any other embedded object, and the patient is transported with the object stabilized and the wound covered. Every time, temperature, depth, size, and number named in this chapter is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries, and editions, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of your country.

# Chapter 16 — Rib Fractures

A fractured rib is common and underestimated, because the bone that breaks is rarely what endangers the patient. The scene is made safe first, because a patient with a chest injury usually lies on a road, at a worksite, or beside a fire. The lethal possibility is a chest that no longer moves air, revealed by fast shallow breathing, speech that cannot be finished, or a level of consciousness that is dulling. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, is whatever barrier is available, and it is used for every patient rather than only the ones who look infectious. The fracture is not the danger; the breathing and the lung beneath it are, and this material does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

The ribs are paired curved bones joining the spine behind and the sternum in front, forming a cage that serves both protection and movement. The upper ribs shield the great vessels entering and leaving the heart, while the lower ribs shield the liver, the spleen, and the kidneys. The cage is also the mechanism of breathing, because the ribs are levers that rise and fall with every breath. The lower ribs are the most mobile and the most exposed to a blow from the side, so a break there can injure an organ beneath the bone. A constructed illustration, never a real patient or incident, is the driver whose chest met the steering wheel and whose only mark was a bruise over the lower left ribs, with the spleen beneath taking the force.

The mechanism of injury is the first clinical evidence, because it predicts what the bone and the tissue beneath have already suffered. A direct blow concentrates force at a single place, while a crush squeezes the whole cage and may break several ribs at more than a single point. A fall from a height or a deceleration tears structures where they are attached, so a torn vessel and a bruised lung can exist with no fracture visible. The responder therefore asks what happened before asking where it hurts, and uses the answer to decide how closely the patient is watched. An impact strong enough to break a rib was strong enough to bruise the lung beneath it, and that bruise can worsen over the following hours.

The simple rib fracture, a break of a single rib or a few ribs with an intact chest wall, is the most common pattern. Its findings are pain at a single point that worsens with a deep breath, a cough, or any movement of the trunk, with tenderness over the bone. The patient then breathes shallowly to avoid pain, and that shallow breathing begins the trouble, because air that does not move lets secretions collect and small areas of lung collapse. That collapse, called atelectasis, is the first step toward pneumonia in a patient who is otherwise not seriously injured. The lay first aider keeps the patient still, warm, and in the position that eases breathing, calls emergency medical services, and never straps the chest or presses the tender rib.

When several ribs are broken, the cage stops behaving as a unit and the ability to move air begins to fail. The finding is fast shallow breathing, with visible effort of the neck and shoulder muscles, speech in short phrases, and less movement on the injured side. Pain is a reason for that failure, because every movement costs the patient, and the loss of mechanical integrity is the other. A count of 3 or more broken ribs is often used as a warning line, and that number must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because age and lung disease change what any count means. The responder does not need to count ribs, because a patient working hard to breathe has already shown the danger.

A flail chest is the extreme form, in which a segment of the chest wall is broken at more than a single point on several ribs. The revealing finding is paradoxical movement, where the injured segment sinks inward as the patient breathes in and rises outward as the patient breathes out. That movement is easiest to see during spontaneous breathing and hardest when the patient breathes rapidly or the chest is covered, so the responder looks again once the patient is exposed. The lung beneath a flail segment is usually bruised as well, which is why breathing fails more than the mechanics alone would suggest. Definitive hospital care owns the decisions about supporting ventilation, about pain control that lets the chest move, and about any operation to stabilize the wall, and none of those is a field procedure. The lay first aider covers the patient, keeps the patient still and warm, and calls for help without pressing on the segment.

A pulmonary contusion is a bruise of the lung itself, and it often decides whether a patient with broken ribs recovers without complication. Blood and fluid leak into the air spaces, so a region that was exchanging oxygen stops doing so, and the breathing becomes fast and labored while the chest wall looks almost unmarked. Its timing is cruel, because it can be small when the patient is first seen and can grow over the following hours. That is why a patient with a significant mechanism is watched and re-examined rather than reassured by a first set of acceptable observations. A measured oxygen level below a number such as 90 per cent is often named as a warning, and that number is an illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol. Definitive hospital care follows a contusion with imaging, support of breathing, and an intensive care unit, or ICU, when the injury demands it.

A pneumothorax is air that escapes into the space between the lung and the chest wall, where it compresses the lung. It can follow a broken rib that has torn the lung surface, and it can occur without any fracture when a deceleration tears the tissue, so a normal image does not rule it out. The findings are sudden worsening of breathlessness, sharp pain on a single side, reduced movement on the injured side, and a hollow sound when the chest is tapped by a trained responder. A tension pneumothorax is the lethal form, in which air enters with each breath and cannot leave, so the pressure rises, the lung collapses, and the heart is compressed. Rapid deterioration, a rising breathing rate, a falling level of consciousness, distended neck veins, and a windpipe shifted away from the injured side demand immediate movement rather than more examination. Relief of that pressure belongs to the paramedic under a protocol or to definitive hospital care, and chest tube insertion, the definitive drainage of air or blood, is a hospital procedure and never a field measure.

A hemothorax is blood in the same space, and it is dangerous because it compresses the lung and removes blood from the circulation. A fractured rib can tear a vessel between the ribs, and a torn vessel can bleed steadily into a space that holds a large volume before anything is seen outside. The finding that reveals concealed bleeding is the language this manual uses for hemorrhage: pallor, cool clammy skin, restlessness or thirst, a fast soft pulse, and a level of consciousness that dulls while the visible injury looks modest. A dull sound when the chest is tapped on the injured side is the sign that blood rather than air has collected, and it is a finding for the trained responder. A measured pressure such as 90 millimeters of mercury is quoted only as an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line differs with age and with the patient's usual state. The responder recognizes the pattern, keeps the patient warm and still, and reaches definitive care quickly, because draining the blood and controlling the torn vessel are hospital work.

The first examination of a rib fracture can be reassuring while the patient is still in the early stage of a serious injury. A patient with a bruised lung, an undrained collection of blood, or a slowly enlarging pneumothorax may walk, talk, and give a clear history. The responder must therefore treat the mechanism and the trend rather than the moment, repeating the same observations in the same order and comparing them with the earlier set. The findings that should send the responder back to the beginning of the primary survey are a rising breathing rate, increasing effort, a falling level of consciousness, a fast thin pulse, and cold pale skin. A patient who was comfortable and is now quiet is not necessarily resting, because quietness in a trauma patient can be the sound of a patient losing the ability to respond.

Assessment of breathing is the center of this chapter, and it comes before the ribs are examined. The responder looks at the rate, the depth, the symmetry, and the effort of the chest, and listens for speech that has become short and a voice that has become weak. The hands are used gently, because pressing hard on a fractured rib causes pain and discourages the very breathing that must be encouraged. A breathing rate above 20 breaths per minute in an adult is a commonly taught warning sign, and that number must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because normal rates differ with age. A child is watched with particular care, because a child's chest wall is flexible and can absorb force without breaking, so severe bruising of the lung can occur with no fracture to explain it. The sequence of the primary survey is remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure.

The lay first aider's work in a rib fracture is small, and each part of it protects the breathing. The scene is made safe before the patient is approached, and emergency medical services are called early with a report of what happened, how many patients there are, and whether breathing is difficult. The patient is kept in the position that is easiest for breathing, usually sitting up or leaning slightly forward, and is not forced to lie flat. Loose clothing is opened so the chest can be seen, the patient is covered to stay warm, and wet clothing is replaced with dry covering. The lay first aider does not bind the chest, does not press on the tender ribs, and does not give anything by mouth to a patient who may need an operation. What the lay first aider gives is calm presence and an accurate description of what is seen, because a responder who reports a change has already helped.

The trained responder and the paramedic add measured observations, and those numbers make a trend visible. Breathing is counted over a full minute rather than estimated, the color and warmth of the skin are recorded, and the level of consciousness is compared with the earlier finding where the responder is trained in the Glasgow coma scale. Where the service carries the equipment, oxygen saturation is measured and the chest is listened to with a stethoscope, and the findings on both sides are compared. Oxygen is given when the patient's breathing or measured oxygen level indicates it, and the decision, the amount, and the way it is delivered belong to the provider authorized by the local protocol and to the prescriber rather than to this book. The trained responder may support breathing with the equipment the service authorizes, and none of that replaces the fastest safe journey to a facility that can image the chest and drain it if needed. Every pressure, rate, and oxygen number is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Pain control in a patient with broken ribs is a treatment of breathing, because a patient who cannot take a deep breath cannot clear the lung. The decision to treat pain belongs to the provider authorized to make it, which means the paramedic under a protocol and the clinician in definitive hospital care. The substance, the amount, the route, and the timing are set by the local protocol and the prescriber, so no listener may take a prescription from this chapter. The lay first aider may offer position, quiet, warmth, and reassurance, and may not offer any medicine. The finding that makes the decision urgent is a patient who is splinting so strongly that breathing is shallow, whose cough is suppressed, or who is exhausted by pain, because that patient is on the way to retained secretions and pneumonia. In definitive care the options are wider and include methods that block the pain of several ribs at once, and those are hospital procedures rather than field techniques.

Position is a treatment in a patient with a chest injury, because it changes the work of breathing without any equipment at all. A conscious patient who is short of breath is usually most comfortable sitting up, sometimes leaning forward with the arms supported. A patient who is drowsy, who is in shock, or who has a suspected injury of the spine is not sat up, because the airway must be protected and the spine kept in the position found. The responding team decides position by watching the patient rather than by applying a rule, and it moves the patient gently because a twisted trunk adds pain and can worsen a fracture. A patient who becomes more breathless after being laid flat is returned to the position that helped, and a patient who cannot be made comfortable in any position is treated as a patient who is deteriorating.

Monitoring is a rhythm rather than a single act, and it begins at the first contact and continues through the handover. The responder repeats the sequence of airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure, compares each set with the one before, and writes down what changed and when. The findings that mark a patient who is worsening are a rising breathing rate, increasing effort, shortening speech, a fast weak pulse, cold clammy skin, and pain no longer controlled by the measures in use. The responder also watches the injured side for swelling, for movement that is not symmetrical, and for a wound that begins to bubble or suck. A patient who has been drinking alcohol or who has taken a substance is watched more closely rather than less, because drowsiness has more than a single possible cause. Every interval and measured value used to judge the trend is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The first thing never to do is to bind the chest tightly, because the bandage treats the appearance of the injury while it worsens the injury itself. A tight binding limits the movement of the whole cage, so the patient breathes with a smaller volume, secretions collect, areas of lung collapse, and pneumonia follows. It also hides the chest from the examiner, so a swelling on a single side, a segment moving the wrong way, or a wound that has begun to suck may go unseen. Every service that once taught strapping has abandoned it, and any request to bind a chest should be refused and explained. The correct alternative is position, warmth, calm, pain control by the provider authorized to give it, and the shortest safe journey to definitive care.

The second thing never to do is to dismiss an apparently uncomplicated rib fracture in an older patient, because age changes what a broken rib means. An older patient has less reserve in the lung, a weaker cough, and a chest wall that breaks more easily because the bone is thinner. An age of 65 years or more is often used as a warning line in chest injury, and that threshold is an illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, since services and editions differ on where the line is drawn. The danger is not the bone but the pneumonia that follows, because a patient who cannot cough clears nothing, and an older patient who cannot clear the lung can die of an infection that began as a small break. An older patient may also report less pain than the injury deserves, or may be unable to describe it because of confusion, so the responder trusts the mechanism and the examination. The finding that should keep the responder concerned is a breathing rate faster than expected, a cough that has become weak, or a new confusion.

Children and other vulnerable patients need the same suspicion for the opposite reason. A child's chest wall bends rather than breaks, so a child may have a bruised lung, a pneumothorax, or bleeding inside the chest with no fracture visible on an image, and the child is judged by the work of breathing and by the mechanism. A child also loses heat quickly and compensates for blood loss until the compensation fails suddenly, so observations are repeated more often and the journey to a trauma center is planned earlier. A pregnant patient is watched with the same care, because the delivery of oxygen to the fetus depends on the mother's breathing and circulation. A patient with a long-standing lung disease, a chest deformity, or frailty from another illness has less room to absorb a chest injury than a healthy adult of the same age. What these groups share is that a small fracture and a large consequence can arrive together.

The criteria for transport are written in the patient's breathing rather than in the appearance of the fracture, and the destination is chosen before the patient is moved. A patient with difficulty in breathing, a breathing rate outside the accepted range, a falling level of consciousness, more than a small number of broken ribs, or an injury to both sides of the chest goes to a facility that can provide imaging, monitoring, and a chest drain, usually a trauma center. A patient whose pain cannot be controlled, whose oxygen level remains low despite treatment, or who is older or frail is transported on the same reasoning. A patient who appears comfortable but has a violent mechanism, a break of the first rib near the great vessels, or a fracture of the lower ribs over the liver or the spleen is watched during the journey. Where the nearest facility cannot provide the needed care, the patient is stabilized there and transferred, and the receiving team is told what has been observed. A count of ribs, a pressure, a rate, or an age used in these decisions is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Protection against hypothermia belongs to every patient with a chest injury, because a chest being examined is a chest being exposed. A patient who is undressed, who is lying on cold ground, or who is bleeding inside the chest loses heat quickly, and cold makes blood clot poorly, deepens shock, and makes a dangerous heart rhythm more likely. The responder uncovers only the part being examined, covers it again at once, insulates the patient from the ground, replaces wet clothing with dry covering, and keeps the vehicle warm. A temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that number must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold shifts with age and with the way the measurement is taken. The finding that warns the responder that cooling has begun is a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold, because shivering is the body's attempt to make heat.

Some complications of a rib fracture arrive hours or days later, which is why the patient sent home or admitted is given clear instructions about what to watch for. Pneumonia and the collapse of small areas of lung are the most common, and they begin with the shallow breathing that pain encourages. A pneumothorax can appear late, after a rib has moved or after a patient has been walking and talking comfortably, and a collection of blood can organize and cause infection if it is not drained. A fracture of the lower ribs may be followed by pain and tenderness in the abdomen, which raises the question of injury to the liver or the spleen. The patient and the family are told to seek care again for worsening breathlessness, fever, a cough that brings up blood, increasing pain, or a change in the level of consciousness. The finding that should never be explained away is a patient who was improving and has begun to worsen.

Definitive hospital care owns the diagnosis and the repair, and it begins with imaging that shows the bones, the lung, and the space around it. A chest radiograph is usually the first study, and computed tomography, after which CT is allowed, gives a fuller picture of the lung, the ribs, and any collection of air or blood. Ultrasound at the bedside is used in many centers to look for fluid around the lung, and magnetic resonance imaging, after which MRI is allowed, is not usually needed for this injury. The clinician controls pain by methods a paramedic cannot use in the field, drains air or blood from the chest, supports the breathing when the effort becomes too great, and operates when a torn vessel continues to bleed or the chest wall must be stabilized. An operation to fix the ribs with plates and screws belongs to the trauma surgeon in an operating room and is never a field procedure, while a patient who needs support of breathing is cared for in an ICU.

A constructed illustration, described as a construction and never as a real patient or incident, shows how these pieces fit together. A middle-aged driver is pulled from a car after a low-speed collision and complains of pain over the lower left ribs, and at first the breathing rate is normal and the patient talks in full sentences. Then the breathing becomes faster and shallower, the skin becomes pale, and the patient stops finishing sentences, while the chest shows only a bruise. The responder does not press the ribs, does not bind the chest, and does not wait for the patient to complain more, but calls early, keeps the patient sitting up and warm, and reports the trend. In hospital the imaging shows a small pneumothorax and a bruised lung, and the patient is monitored and treated for pain before being admitted for observation.

The record and the handover are part of the treatment, because the receiving team continues a story that the field began. What is reported includes the mechanism of injury and its time, the number of patients, the breathing rate and effort, the level of consciousness and any change in it, the color and warmth of the skin, and the treatment given with the patient's response. The times matter as much as the acts, and a change that was observed is reported even when it has resolved, because a patient who improved and then worsened is not the same patient as one who never changed. The responder states plainly what was not done and why, so the receiving team does not assume a measure was attempted or omit one the field could not give. A handover that names the mechanism, the trend, and the provider level of each act allows the hospital to plan rather than to start the assessment from nothing.

A chapter can explain the reasoning, but it cannot certify a reader, and the difference matters when a listener becomes a responder. The skills described here are learned with a teacher, practiced on models, and authorized by a service that defines what may be done without supervision. Where this chapter names a number or a threshold, it does so to explain a decision and not to set a rule, because such numbers differ between services, countries, and editions of the same guideline. No one should take from these pages a substance, an amount, a route, or a frequency, and no one should read a hospital procedure as something a first aider may attempt. This is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

To summarize, a rib fracture is judged by the breathing and by the lung beneath it rather than by the bone. The scene is made safe and the lethal possibility is named early, and the finding that reveals it is a patient who is breathing fast and shallow, who cannot finish a sentence, or whose level of consciousness is dulling. The anatomy explains the risk, since the upper ribs lie over the great vessels and the lower ribs over the liver, the spleen, and the kidneys, while the whole cage is the mechanism of breathing itself. Simple fractures, multiple fractures, flail chest, pulmonary contusion, pneumothorax, and hemothorax arrive in that order of severity, and any of them can worsen over the hours after the injury, so the trend is watched rather than the moment. Management follows the primary survey, so breathing is assessed in the order of ABCDE, pain and oxygen are decided by the provider authorized to decide them, position is chosen by what eases the patient's breathing, monitoring continues to the handover, and transport goes to a facility that can image, drain, and support the chest. The chest is never bound tightly, and an apparently simple fracture in an older patient is never dismissed, because age removes the reserve that hides the complication. Hypothermia is prevented whenever the chest is exposed, the provider level is named for every act, and no dose, route, or frequency is taken from this book. Every number and threshold here is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 17 — Flail Chest

A chest that has lost the ability to move as one piece is among the quietest catastrophes in trauma, because the patient may speak, sit upright, and look almost well while the breathing is already failing from within. Before any hand is laid on that patient the scene must be made safe, since the same energy that broke the ribs may have left traffic moving, fuel escaping, a structure unstable, a wire live, or a person still violent, and the patient's own blood and body fluids are a hazard that a barrier of gloves and eye protection is meant to answer.
