The lethal possibility to name first is respiratory failure, and the finding that reveals it is a section of the chest wall that sinks as the patient breathes in and rises as the patient breathes out, moving against the rest of the rib cage instead of with it. This chapter describes what that movement means, why the bruised lung beneath it matters more than the broken bones, what each level of provider may do, and where definitive hospital care begins, and it is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

Flail chest is the condition in which a portion of the chest wall loses its bony continuity with the rest of the rib cage and can no longer carry the pull of the muscles that normally lift and spread the ribs. The usual description speaks of several adjacent ribs, each broken in more than one place, so that the piece between the breaks is attached to the spine and to nothing else, and the exact count of ribs and of breaks that defines the segment is a teaching figure to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services and editions do not all draw that line in the same spot. The loose piece is sometimes called a floating segment, although the name misleads, because the piece does not move freely; it moves with the pressure inside the chest rather than with the muscles outside it. That distinction is the whole of the injury, because the chest wall is a pump, and a pump whose wall no longer follows the muscle cannot move air with the same efficiency.

The mechanism that produces this injury transfers a great deal of energy into a broad area of the chest, and the mechanism of injury is therefore the first clue available before any examination begins. A vehicle collision in which the chest strikes the steering wheel or the door, a fall from a height onto the side, a heavy object that crushes the trunk, a blast wave, and a blow delivered by a horse or a machine are the familiar stories, and each predicts injury to the lung beneath the break as surely as to the bone. A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient or a real incident, is the restrained driver whose chest met the wheel, who climbed out of the vehicle with a bruised side, and who before long was breathing quickly and could not finish a sentence, because the ribs were not the part of the injury that was worsening. The responder who hears such a story should stop searching for a wound that explains the patient and start listening to the breathing, because the account has already named the organ at risk.

The reason the loose segment travels the wrong way lies in the pressure that surrounds it on both sides of the chest wall. During inspiration the muscles enlarge the chest and the pressure inside falls below the pressure of the air outside, so the loose piece is pushed inward while the intact rib cage moves outward, and during expiration the pressure inside rises and the piece is pushed outward while the rest of the chest falls. The result is the paradoxical movement that gives the injury its name, a section of wall that travels in the opposite direction to its neighbors with every breath. That sign is easy to miss, because it can be hidden by clothing, by a blanket, or by the position in which the patient is sitting, so the chest must be exposed for the examination while the patient is kept warm. The movement may also be delayed, since in the first minutes the patient splints the chest by tensing the muscles around it, and the paradox becomes plain only when those muscles tire. The finding that tells the responder the injury is present is that opposition of movement, seen with the chest exposed and in good light, and the finding that tells the responder it is worsening is a breathing pattern that becomes faster, shallower, and more effortful.

Beneath the broken ribs, and sometimes beneath a chest wall that still moves almost normally, lies the injury that actually kills, which is the bruise of the lung itself. A pulmonary contusion is bleeding and fluid collecting in the tissue of the lung, and it does not respect the borders of the broken bones, because the energy that fractured the ribs passed through the lung and tore the small vessels and the air sacs within it. The bruised area becomes stiff and filled with fluid, so it cannot expand, cannot clear its secretions, and cannot pass oxygen into the blood even though air may be reaching it. The injury is progressive rather than static, which means the lung is usually less damaged at the first examination than it will be hours later, and a patient who seems comfortable at the roadside may be approaching respiratory failure by the time the ambulance reaches the hospital. The conclusion is that the ribs are the visible part of the injury and the lung is the dangerous part, and treatment aimed only at the ribs will not save the patient.

Respiratory failure is the destination toward which all of this travels, and it arrives by a path that the responder can recognize in stages. Pain limits the depth of every breath, the bruised lung cannot take part in the exchange, and the small airways begin to close where secretions collect, so the patient compensates by breathing faster and faster. That compensation is exhausting, and a patient who has been breathing at a rapid rate for hours begins to tire, at which point the rate may fall and the breathing becomes shallow and ineffective. Carbon dioxide then accumulates while oxygen falls, and the patient becomes restless, then drowsy, then confused, and the color of the lips and the skin may change toward blue. The finding that should frighten the responder is not a single measurement but a trend, because a patient who is breathing faster than before, working harder than before, and answering more slowly than before is moving toward failure whatever the first impression suggested. The endpoint is a patient who cannot maintain the work of breathing at all, and that patient needs a hospital team and a ventilator rather than a dressing and a longer wait.

Recognition at the scene rests on the mechanism, the breathing, and the whole appearance of the patient rather than on any instrument. A breathing rate above 30 breaths per minute in an adult is often quoted as a warning figure, and that number, like every other in this chapter, is an illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold differs with age and with the patient's usual state. The findings that accompany it are visible use of the neck and shoulder muscles, a patient who cannot speak a full sentence without stopping for air, a chest that does not rise equally on both sides, tenderness over several ribs, and a crackling sensation under the fingers where air has escaped into the tissue. The patient may also be anxious, restless, or difficult to keep still, and that behavior is a sign of oxygen shortage rather than of poor cooperation. The responder who finds these signs should not wait for the paradox to become obvious, because the judgment is made from the whole picture and not from one sign alone, and that picture includes the head, the abdomen, the pelvis, and the limbs, since a patient with a flail chest has usually been subjected to enough energy to injure more than the chest.

Flail chest seldom travels alone, and the reason is the amount of energy required to produce it. The same blow that breaks a series of ribs may tear the pleura and allow air into the space around the lung, may fill that space with blood, may bruise the heart, may tear the diaphragm, and may injure the liver or the spleen beneath the lower rib cage. A patient who becomes suddenly worse, with a rising breathing rate, a falling level of consciousness, distended neck veins, and an absent breath sound on one side, may have a tension pneumothorax, which is air trapped under pressure around a lung and is a lethal state that a trained responder may relieve under a protocol while a surgeon treats its cause. A hemothorax is blood collecting in that same space, and it is suspected when the chest is dull to percussion and the circulation is failing without an external wound to explain the loss. A needle introduced into the chest, a tube left in the chest, and the opening of the chest in an operating room are all definitive procedures and not field measures, and this manual names them so that a listener recognizes the urgency without being tempted to imitate it. The finding that must prompt immediate escalation is any deterioration the responder cannot explain by the ribs alone.

The lay first aider's part in this injury is small, specific, and more valuable than any improvised procedure. The scene is made safe first, and then emergency medical services are called at once and told that a patient has been struck in the chest, is breathing quickly, and cannot speak without pausing, because that description moves the right resources toward the scene. The patient is kept in the position that eases the breathing, which is usually sitting up and leaning slightly forward with the arms supported, and the patient is not made to lie flat, because lying flat worsens the work of breathing in most chest injuries. A conscious patient usually finds that position without instruction, and the responder should let the patient choose it while protecting the neck and the spine if the mechanism makes spinal injury possible. Nothing is bound around the chest, nothing is pressed onto the broken ribs to test them, and nothing is given by mouth, because a patient who may need an operation should arrive with an empty stomach. The patient is covered and insulated from the ground, because a chest exposed for examination and a patient who lies still for a long time both lose heat quickly, and the lay first aider then stays with the patient and reports any change in the breathing or the level of consciousness to the team on arrival, because that continuous observation is itself a treatment.

Oxygen is one of the measures that can change the course of this injury before the hospital, and its use is a decision that belongs to the trained responder and the paramedic under a protocol, never to the lay first aider with bare hands. The trained responder carries oxygen, a mask or a cannula, and an authorization that names when and how it is given, so the amount, the flow, and the delivery method are set by the local protocol and the prescriber rather than by any figure in this book. The finding that makes the decision urgent is a patient who is short of breath, confused, restless, or blue about the lips, together with a breathing pattern that is failing to keep up with the demand. Oxygen does not repair the bruised lung, and it must never become a reason to delay transport, because the definitive treatment for a contused lung is hospital care, monitoring, and often a ventilator. The patient receiving oxygen is watched continuously, because the appearance of the patient matters more than the device, and a patient who becomes drowsy while receiving oxygen is a patient whose breathing is failing. Nothing in this paragraph is a prescription, and no reader should carry away a flow, a concentration, or a duration from this manual rather than from the protocol that governs their practice.

The trap that has killed more patients with this injury than any other error in first aid is the tightly bound chest. For much of the last century the treatment taught for broken ribs was to strap the chest, to bind it with wide tape, or to hold it still between sandbags, and the reasoning seemed sensible because the patient was in pain and movement hurt. The result was the opposite of help, because a chest that cannot expand cannot clear its secretions and cannot keep the small airways open, so the lung beneath the fracture collapsed, infection followed, and the patient died of the treatment rather than of the injury. No provider at any level in this manual binds a chest tightly, straps a chest, or places weight upon it, and that rule holds for the lay first aider, for the trained responder, and for the paramedic alike. Splinting the chest is not the same as supporting a limb, because the chest wall is a moving pump and must be allowed to move, and the pain it causes is treated by other means and by professional decisions. The finding that should make the responder stop any binding at once is a patient who is breathing less deeply and making less noise after the chest has been wrapped, because a quiet chest in an injured patient is not a comfort but a warning.

Once the patient is positioned, covered, and moving toward care, the work becomes a rhythm of watching rather than a series of new acts. The trained responder repeats the observations of the primary survey in the same order, because a breathing rate that has climbed or fallen, a breathing pattern that has become noisy, a pulse that has become rapid and weak, skin that has become pale and cool, or a level of consciousness that has dulled all mean the patient is moving in the wrong direction. The record carries the position that helped, the oxygen that was given where the protocol allowed it, and the time of every change, because the receiving team continues a story that began in the field. The finding that ends the watching is the handover, and even then the account of the trend is the most useful thing the responder can pass on.

Cold is a complication of chest trauma rather than a matter of comfort, and a patient with a flail chest is unusually easy to cool. The chest is often undressed for examination, the patient lies still because movement hurts, and the work of breathing already consumes a great deal of energy, so heat is lost from an exposed surface by a body that cannot spare it. Cold makes the blood clot poorly, deepens shock, and makes the heart prone to dangerous rhythms, and in a patient whose oxygen supply is already fragile those effects can be decisive. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line shifts with age, with the site of measurement, and with the way the temperature is taken. The lay first aider covers the patient with whatever is available, insulates the patient from the ground, and removes wet clothing without exposing the chest longer than the examination requires. The trained responder keeps the vehicle or the room warm during transport, limits the number of times the patient is uncovered, and remembers that a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold has already lost the ability to make heat.

Pain is not a side issue in this injury, because pain is the reason the patient cannot breathe deeply enough to keep the lung open. A patient who is hurting guards the chest, takes small quick breaths, and cannot cough, and that pattern is what allows secretions to collect and the lung to collapse, so the relief of pain is part of the treatment of the breathing and not a kindness added afterward. The decision about pain relief belongs to the provider authorized to make it under the local protocol, which in most systems means the paramedic and the physician, and the substance, the amount, the route, and the frequency are set by that protocol and that prescriber rather than by this manual. The lay first aider gives no medicine for this injury, offers nothing by mouth, and does not move the patient to a more comfortable place if movement makes the breathing worse. The finding that makes the decision urgent is a patient whose breathing is shallow and whose coughing is absent because of pain, and the finding that must be reported before any medicine is considered is a falling level of consciousness or a breathing pattern that is already failing. Definitive hospital care may use methods that block the sensation from a group of ribs, and those methods require a trained operator and monitoring that the field does not have.

Movement is a treatment decision in a patient with a flail chest, and it must be as gentle as the urgency allows, because a patient with broken ribs who is rolled roughly or carried in an awkward position splints the chest further and arrives worse than they left. If the mechanism makes a spinal injury possible, the head and the neck are held and the patient is moved as a unit, and the chest injury is not used as a reason to abandon that precaution. The destination is chosen before the patient is lifted, and it is the nearest facility that can provide imaging, breathing support, and surgical care, which is usually a trauma center rather than the closest building with a bed. A patient with a failing breathing pattern should not wait for a distant specialist if a nearer hospital can stabilize the breathing and arrange the transfer. The finding that decides the destination is not the size of the injury but the stability of the breathing, and a patient who is tiring needs the shortest safe route to a team that can support ventilation.

In the hospital, the diagnosis is confirmed by examination and by imaging, and the imaging serves the whole patient rather than the ribs alone. A chest radiograph may show the fractures, the blood or air around the lung, and the separation of the ribs, while computed tomography, or CT, shows the contused lung far more clearly and reveals injuries that a plain film can miss. Ultrasound performed by a trained clinician can find blood or air around the lung at the bedside, and it is used where the service has the equipment and the training. The examination also weighs the patient's age, the state of the lungs before the injury, and the presence of other injuries, because those factors decide the course more than the count of broken ribs does. A contused volume of about one fifth of the lung is sometimes used in teaching to describe the extent of the bruise, and any such figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the measure differs with the method and with the observer. The diagnosis is therefore not a count of fractures but a judgment about a patient whose breathing is at risk.

Much of the hospital treatment of a flail chest is devoted to the lung rather than to the bones, and it begins with the same priorities with which the field began. Pain control is provided in a way that allows deep breathing and coughing, and the team watches the level of consciousness and the breathing while that is achieved. Breathing exercises, devices that encourage a deep breath, clearance of secretions, and movement out of bed are used to keep the small airways open and to prevent pneumonia, because infection in a lung that is already bruised is a common cause of a poor outcome. The patient is monitored with repeated examination and with measurements of oxygen and carbon dioxide, and the trend of those measurements decides whether the breathing is being supported adequately. When the work of breathing cannot be sustained, the patient is supported with a ventilator in an intensive care unit, where the machine takes over the work of the muscles, holds the lung open, and allows the contused areas time to heal. Ventilation is a clinical decision made on the trend of the breathing and the blood gases rather than on a single reading, and no figure in this paragraph should be taken as a rule, because every threshold must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The finding that tells the team a patient is ready to breathe alone is a stable breathing pattern with adequate gas exchange while the support is reduced, and that trial is conducted by the intensive care team with continuous observation.

Surgical fixation of the broken ribs is a definitive procedure that belongs to the trauma surgeon and the operating room, and it is not a field measure under any circumstance. Plates, screws, and pins may be used to rebuild the chest wall in selected patients, usually when the wall is so unstable that the patient cannot be separated from the ventilator, when a deformity threatens the lung, or when the chest is already open for another reason. The purpose is to restore a wall that can move with the muscles and to reduce pain enough that the patient can breathe and cough, and the decision rests on the whole patient rather than on the appearance of the ribs on an image. Even a skilled paramedic does not reduce, stabilize, or reposition the ribs of a flail chest in the field, and no responder should press on the loose segment to test it or attempt to push it back into place. A chest tube placed to drain blood or air, and an operation on the heart or the great vessels, are further definitive procedures under the same rule, and the field responder's task is to recognize the need and to deliver the patient quickly. The listener should hear in this paragraph the boundary of practice, because an unauthorized attempt at the roadside may turn an injury that could be repaired into one that cannot.

Flail chest is best understood as a diagnosis of the whole patient rather than of the ribs, because the ribs will heal whether or not anyone touches them and the patient may not survive to see it. The outcome is decided by the extent of the pulmonary contusion, by the patient's reserve of lung and heart, by the presence of other injuries, and by the speed with which breathing support and pain control are provided. An older patient with chronic lung disease and a modest fracture may fare worse than a young patient with a more dramatic injury, because reserve matters more than the visible damage, and a patient older than 65 years is often described as being at higher risk, a figure to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A child's chest wall is soft and yielding, so a great deal of energy can pass into the lung with few or no ribs broken, and a pregnant patient adds further considerations because the growing uterus changes the position of the diaphragm. Certain failures recur, and each is preventable, beginning with the dismissal of a patient who looks well at first contact, continuing with the bound or strapped chest that an older teaching still encourages, and ending with the missed companion injury such as air trapped under pressure around the lung. The defense against all of them is the same, which is to treat the mechanism as a prediction, to repeat the examination in the same order, and to move the patient toward definitive care without waiting for certainty.

To summarize, a flail chest is a segment of the chest wall that has lost its continuity and moves with the pressure of breathing rather than with the muscles, and paradoxical movement is the sign that reveals it. The bruise of the lung beneath the break is the injury that kills, and respiratory failure is the destination toward which pain, collapse, and infection all lead, so the patient is treated as a whole person and not as a set of broken ribs. The scene is made safe first, emergency medical services are called early, the patient is positioned upright and supported and kept warm, and the lay first aider binds nothing, presses nothing, and gives nothing by mouth. Oxygen and pain relief are decisions owned by the trained responder, the paramedic, and the prescriber under the local protocol, and no dose, route, or frequency may be taken from these pages. Definitive hospital care owns analgesia, ventilation, drainage of the chest, and surgical fixation of the chest wall, and none of those is a field procedure, while the field contribution is recognition, support, warmth, continuous observation, and the shortest safe journey to a trauma center. Every figure in this chapter, whether a breathing rate, a temperature, an age, or an extent of contusion, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between services, countries, and editions. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 18 — Open Chest Wounds

An open chest wound is a wound of the chest wall that opens a path into the pleural space, the thin sealed gap between the lung and the inside of the rib cage. When that path opens, the slight negative pressure that holds the lung against the ribs is lost, and the lung on that side begins to collapse while the patient breathes with the other lung alone. The scene is made safe before the patient is touched, since traffic, fire, electricity, water, animals, violence, structural collapse, and the patient's own blood are hazards that turn one casualty into two. The lethal possibility to name at once is air trapped under pressure inside the chest, and the finding that announces the wound is the movement of air at the opening, heard as a hiss and seen as froth with each breath. The lay first aider, the trained responder, and the paramedic each have a different part here, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The pleural space is a potential gap, a film of fluid between two membranes that slide on each other, and its slight negative pressure keeps the elastic lung stretched against the chest wall. A wound that stays open lets air move in and out with each breath, so the lung cannot expand, while a wound that closes, whether by its own edges, a clot, a flap of tissue, or a dressing laid over it, lets air in during inspiration and traps it during expiration. That trapping is the mechanism of the emergency that follows, and it is why this chapter treats the dressing both as a treatment and as a hazard. The finding that tells the responder which situation is present is whether air can still escape, and that question must be asked again each time the wound is checked, because the answer can change within minutes.

Recognition begins with the mechanism of injury, because the story predicts where the wound is likely to be and what lies beneath it. A knife, a bullet, a blast fragment, a rib broken inward, a fall onto a sharp object, and a collision with a fence post can each open the chest, and the opening may hide in the armpit, the back, the flank, or a fold of skin the patient is holding. Because the track cannot be judged from its opening, no responder may probe it with a finger or an instrument, and no responder may assume that a wound low on the chest has spared the cavity, since the diaphragm moves with every breath. A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient or incident, is a young person who fell against a metal stake, whose small wound below the shoulder blade whistled quietly each time he breathed in. The finding that settles the question is the behavior of the wound at the moment of breathing rather than its size.

The sound and the movement of air are the signature of this injury, and a responder who listens at the wound before covering it learns more than one who only looks. Air may leave with a soft hiss that keeps time with the breath, with a bubbling like liquid through a straw, or with a suck loud enough to be heard across a quiet room. Froth may gather at the opening, blood may bubble pink where it mixes with air, and a loose dressing may flutter against the skin with inspiration. The sound is not always present, and its absence proves nothing, because a wound may be sealed by clot or by the patient's position and may open again when the patient is moved. The patient's condition carries the same message, with rapid shallow breathing, a forward lean, and a level of consciousness that stays clear at first and then dulls as the circulation fails. Air that has escaped into the tissues may be felt as a crackling under the skin of the neck, the chest wall, or the armpit, which must be reported even when the wound looks small. A pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury measured in the arm is sometimes taught as a warning level, and any such figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line differs with age, with pregnancy, and with the way the measurement is taken.

Bleeding travels with this injury and must be named beside the air, because the track may also have torn a vessel between the ribs, the lung, or the heart. Blood collecting in the space compresses the lung and the heart much as air does, and the wound whose own edges act as a flap may let air out and then fall shut, so a dressing applied too completely can turn a wound that was venting into a wound that traps. The findings that point to blood rather than air are a patient who is pale and restless with a rising pulse and a falling pressure, a side of the chest that is dull where it was resonant, and a wound that keeps draining dark blood beneath the dressing. The finding that ends this assessment is any sign of shock in a patient with a chest wound, and that finding moves the patient immediately toward definitive hospital care, because the treatment for bleeding into the chest is an operation and not a dressing. Fluids and blood belong to a decision that only the paramedic under a protocol and the prescriber may make, and the choice of what is given, the amount, the route, and the timing cannot be carried away from a manual.

The immediate action for the lay first aider is small and specific, and it is the only chest procedure this manual permits without equipment, authorization, and training. The lay first aider covers the wound, presses a gloved or otherwise protected hand over it, calls emergency medical services, keeps the patient warm, and stays until help arrives. If a dressing is at hand it is laid over the opening, and if nothing is at hand the flat of the hand is enough, and the hand is not lifted to look beneath it, since covering the wound and leaving for help is the whole of the task. The patient is left in the position that makes breathing easiest, usually sitting up and leaning slightly forward, unless the patient is unresponsive or another injury forbids it. The lay first aider does not cut, probe, pack, remove an embedded object, or try to release air from the chest with any instrument, and if the patient stops breathing, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, after which CPR is allowed, must begin while help is summoned again.

An occlusive dressing is a covering that does not allow air to pass, and it is placed by the trained responder or the paramedic under a protocol rather than by the lay first aider, who has only a hand. It works by sealing the opening against the outside atmosphere, so the patient's own breathing no longer pumps room air into the chest. The classic instruction is to tape the dressing on most of its edges and leave one edge free, so that the free edge lifts when pressure inside rises and lets air out while the taped edges keep air from entering. A dressing that seals the wound completely on every side becomes a one-way valve that lets air in during inspiration and keeps it in during expiration, and it can create the very emergency it was meant to prevent. The finding that says the dressing is doing its work is a quiet wound and a patient who is not struggling more, while any deterioration after it is applied is a signal to reassess the dressing before anything else.

Occlusive dressings fail in a small number of predictable ways, and each failure has a finding that announces it. A dressing may fail to seal at all, lifting at one edge with every breath so that air keeps moving in and out and the lung keeps collapsing. It may fail in the opposite direction, sealing too well and turning the wound into a valve, which is the most dangerous failure and the reason monitoring is inseparable from the dressing. It may fail because the wound is not the only opening, since a second wound in the back or the armpit that no one has seen keeps admitting air, or because the dressing becomes soaked with blood and lifts. The finding that requires the responder to replace or readjust it is any new difficulty in breathing, any change in the sound at the wound, and any change in the patient's color.

The emergency that must be watched for after every chest dressing is air trapped under pressure in one side of the chest, and it develops because air enters the space and cannot leave. As the pressure rises, the lung on that side is compressed, the mediastinum, the central partition that holds the heart and the great vessels, is pushed toward the other side, and the return of blood to the heart is obstructed, so the patient dies of a circulation problem caused by a breathing injury. The warning findings are a patient who becomes more breathless and more distressed, a breathing rate that climbs, a pulse that becomes rapid and weak, neck veins that become visibly distended, and a level of consciousness that dulls. The finding that demands the fastest possible response is a patient who deteriorates after a chest wound has been covered, because the dressing is now part of the problem. Any figure quoted for the time in which this emergency can develop, whether 15 minutes or another interval, is an illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the pace differs with the size of the leak and with the patient.

Monitoring is a rhythm rather than a single check, and it begins the moment the dressing is placed and continues until the receiving team takes over. The trained responder repeats the observations of the primary survey in the same order, returning to the airway, then breathing, then the circulation, then the level of consciousness, and compares each set with the one before. The Glasgow coma scale, used where the responder is trained in it, turns the impression of drowsiness into something two people can compare, and the trend over time carries more meaning than any single score. The lay first aider monitors with the eyes and the voice, noticing whether breathing has become harder, whether the patient speaks less, and whether the skin has become pale, cool, or damp, and reports every change to emergency medical services. The finding that returns the responder to the beginning of the sequence is any worsening at any point, and each such return is recorded with the time it was observed.

Positioning is a treatment here because it changes the work of breathing and the movement of air. A patient who is awake and breathing should be allowed to sit up and lean forward, since that lets the diaphragm descend and the muscles of the chest and neck work more efficiently. A patient who is unresponsive must be managed with the airway protected, and the responder rolls the patient as a unit where a roll is needed and looks at the back as well as the front, because a wound in the back can be the only opening. The lay first aider does not force a position on a patient who fights it, and does not leave an unresponsive patient on the back without help, because the tongue and the stomach contents can close the airway of a patient who cannot protect it.

Oxygen is a clinical decision rather than a first-aid routine, and the decision to give it belongs to the trained responder or the paramedic under a protocol and to the prescriber, while the substance, the amount, the means of delivery, and the frequency are set by the local protocol and never by this book. The finding that makes the decision urgent is a patient who is working to breathe, who is confused or restless, or whose color and level of consciousness are worsening. The lay first aider cannot give oxygen and is not asked to, and the lay first aider's contribution is to keep the airway open, to keep the patient in the position that eases breathing, and to shorten the time until trained help arrives. The trained responder who is authorized to assist the patient's breathing must do so with attention to the chest, because air pushed into a chest that cannot vent can raise the pressure and worsen the emergency, and any target or threshold mentioned here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Pain in an open chest wound is severe, it worsens with every breath, and it restricts the breathing the patient most needs to do, so the relief of pain is part of the treatment rather than a courtesy added at the end. The decision to treat pain belongs to the provider authorized to prescribe, and the substance, the amount, the route, and the frequency belong to the local protocol and to that prescriber, so no reader may take a prescription from this manual. The finding that makes the decision urgent is a patient who guards the chest, breathes in short shallow breaths, and becomes exhausted, because that pattern leads to a collapse of the lung and a worsening of the circulation. The tetanus question and the question of antibiotics are raised at the first contact and answered by the provider authorized to decide, and the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber and the local guideline, with the finding that makes the answer urgent being a wound that is deep, contaminated, or caused by a bite.

Hypothermia is a companion of chest trauma and not a detail of comfort, because a patient who is bleeding, exposed for examination, lying on cold ground, or receiving cool fluids loses heat quickly. Cold makes clotting work poorly, deepens shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm, and the patient with an open chest wound is especially vulnerable. The lay first aider covers the patient before the journey rather than after it, removes wet clothing and replaces it with dry covering where that can be done without exposing the wound, and insulates the patient from the ground. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the line at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that figure is an illustration which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold shifts with age and with the way the measurement is taken. The finding that warns the responder that cooling has already begun is a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold, because shivering is the body's attempt to make heat.

Emergency evacuation is the definitive field treatment for this injury, and the reasons not to delay are specific and must be spoken plainly. The first reason is that only an operating room can repair the track, stop the bleeding inside the chest, and place a drain that lets air and blood leave the space under control. The second is that the pressure emergency can develop within minutes and can kill a patient who was talking, and no dressing can be guaranteed to prevent it. The third is that the patient's own breathing drives the injury while the wound remains in contact with the outside air, so no minute on the scene improves the wound. The lay first aider covers the wound, keeps the patient warm, and hands the patient to a moving team as quickly as the scene allows, and the finding that ends the argument about whether to move is any deterioration at all.

The destination is chosen before the patient is moved, and it is the nearest facility that can provide the care the patient needs, which for a penetrating chest wound usually means a trauma center with imaging, an operating room, and an intensive care unit. Where such a center is far away, the local protocol decides whether the patient goes first to a nearer hospital for stabilization and a drain or travels directly to the trauma center, and that decision belongs to the paramedic and to the medical control that supports them. The receiving team is given a report in a fixed order, with the location, the number of patients, the mechanism of injury, the wound and its behavior, what has been done, and every change observed. A delay of more than 6 hours before definitive care is often described as a point at which infection and other complications become more likely, and that interval is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the risk depends on the wound, the patient, and the system. The finding that must be written without fail is any deterioration after the dressing, with the time of that deterioration, because the receiving team reads the trend rather than a single value.

Some interventions here belong to the trained responder, to the paramedic, or to definitive hospital care, and each is named with the level of training and authorization it requires. Needle decompression, in which air under pressure is released from the chest through a needle passed through the chest wall, may be performed by a trained responder or a paramedic only where the service protocol authorizes it, only after training, and only when the findings of a pressure emergency are present. It is not a first-aid measure, it is not a lay skill, and it is not a substitute for the operation that follows, because the release is temporary. The finding that tells the responder it has worked is an improvement in breathing and in the circulation together, while a patient who keeps deteriorating points toward a further attempt by an authorized provider or toward immediate surgery. The lay first aider must never attempt this, because a needle placed blindly into a chest can injure the lung, the heart, and the vessels, and because the act without the operation behind it buys very little time.

Placement of a chest drain, a tube passed into the pleural space and connected to a system that lets air and blood out while keeping air from returning, is a definitive procedure that belongs to a physician or a surgeon in a hospital or to a trained provider under a specific protocol in a service that authorizes it. It is not a field procedure for a lay first aider, it is not the same act as covering a wound, and it must be described as what it is so that no listener mistakes the dressing for the drain. The drain lets trapped air escape and lets blood out so that the lung can re-expand and the source can be assessed, and surgical exploration, repair of a torn vessel or lung, and control of bleeding from the heart or the great vessels belong to the operating room. Definitive hospital care also owns the imaging that confirms the diagnosis, including the chest radiograph, ultrasound, and computed tomography, which is called CT. Each of those studies and operations is chosen by the hospital team rather than by the field responder, and no field measure takes their place.

A short set of acts must never be performed on an open chest wound, and each is forbidden for a reason the listener can carry away. No object embedded in the chest wall is removed in the field, because it may be plugging a torn vessel or sealing the opening, and its removal may release a hemorrhage that cannot be controlled. No wound of the chest is packed with gauze in the field, because packing does not seal the pleural space and may push contamination deeper, and packing the chest is a different matter from packing a bleeding groin or armpit. No wound of the chest is tightly bound, because binding restricts the movement of the chest wall and hides the very breathing the responder must watch. No chest wound is explored with a finger or an instrument, because probing can convert a sealed wound into a venting one, and no chest wound is left uncovered while the responder searches for equipment, because a hand is a better cover than nothing.

Certain patients deserve a word of their own, because the same wound behaves differently in each. A child has a smaller chest and a more mobile central partition, so the pressure emergency can develop faster and the signs can be harder to read, and children compensate for blood loss until they suddenly do not. A pregnant patient has a diaphragm pushed upward by the uterus, so a wound that appears to lie below the chest may still open the pleural space, and two patients are being moved at once, since the fetus depends entirely on the mother's breathing and circulation. An older patient may have less reserve in the heart and the lungs and may be taking medicines that change the response to bleeding, and a patient with long-standing lung disease may already be short of breath, so the responder compares the patient with the patient rather than with a textbook.

A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient or a real incident, may show how the decisions fit together. A factory worker is struck in the side of the chest by a piece of metal thrown from a machine, and the wound is small and partly hidden under his shirt, but the responders hear a soft hiss each time he breathes and see a few bubbles of blood at the opening. The lay first aider who arrives first presses a clean dressing over the wound with a protected hand, keeps the worker sitting up and warm, and calls emergency medical services with the location and the mechanism of injury. The paramedic arrives, confirms the behavior of the wound, applies a chest seal according to the local protocol, watches the breathing and the circulation while the patient is carried, and reports the dressing and the time to the receiving team. When the worker becomes restless and his neck veins become prominent, the paramedic reassesses the seal at once, considers the authorized intervention for trapped air, and brings the patient to a trauma center where imaging confirms the diagnosis and a surgeon places a drain that controls what the injury has hidden.

To summarize, an open chest wound is a wound of the chest wall that communicates with the pleural space, and it is recognized by the sound and the movement of air at the opening rather than by the size of the wound. The lethal possibility to name first is air trapped under pressure in the chest, and the dressing that stops air from entering can itself create that emergency, so monitoring for worsening breathing, a rising pulse, distended neck veins, and a dulling level of consciousness must follow every dressing as closely as the dressing itself. The lay first aider covers the wound with a protected hand or a clean dressing, calls emergency medical services, keeps the patient warm and in the position that eases breathing, and leaves the advanced interventions to the trained responder, the paramedic, or the hospital team trained and authorized to perform them. Needle decompression, placement of a chest drain, imaging, and surgical repair are named with the level of training and authorization they require, and none of them is a first-aid measure. Emergency evacuation is part of the treatment, because only definitive hospital care can control the bleeding and let the trapped air out under observation. Every time, pressure, temperature, depth, and figure in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 19 — General Principles of Fractures

A fracture is a break in the continuity of a bone, and the person who first reaches a patient with one faces a decision that has nothing to do with the broken bone itself. Before any hand is laid on the patient, the scene must be made safe, because moving traffic, a live electrical wire, a fire, unstable ground, an animal still loose, or a person still violent can create a second casualty in the seconds it takes to kneel down. The lethal possibility to be named first is not the fracture but the bleeding and the damaged vessels that a broken bone can produce, and the finding that reveals it is a limb that is swelling inside its skin while the patient becomes pale, restless, and cool, or a wound that pours blood where the bone has torn through the surface. The responder also protects against hypothermia from the first minute, because a patient who is bleeding, exposed for examination, or lying on cold ground loses heat quickly, and cold worsens clotting, deepens shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm. This chapter sets out the vocabulary of fractures, the examination that finds them, and the levels of care that own each response, and it is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

The vocabulary of fractures begins with the skin, because the state of the skin decides the urgency of everything that follows. A closed fracture is one in which the bone is broken and the skin over it remains intact, so the break has not been opened to the outside world, but closed does not mean harmless, since the bone ends can still have torn a vessel or a nerve and the limb can still be bleeding into its own tissues. An open fracture is one in which the broken bone communicates with a wound in the skin, whether the bone is visible in the wound or the wound is small enough to be missed, and the opening may have been made from the inside by a bone end that pushed out and then withdrew. The distinction matters to the patient because an open fracture carries contamination into the depth of the limb, where bacteria find warm, dead, and poorly supplied tissue, and because the wound and the fracture must be treated together rather than as two separate problems. The finding that makes a fracture open is any break in the skin near the break in the bone, including a puncture, a laceration, or a raw graze, and a responder who cannot tell whether a wound reaches the bone treats the fracture as open until definitive hospital care decides otherwise.

The next pair of terms describes where the broken ends have come to rest, and it is the pair that most changes what the first responder must do. A nondisplaced fracture is one in which the ends remain in their normal alignment, so the limb looks straight and the injury may be mistaken for a bad bruise, while a displaced fracture is one in which the ends have shifted, angulated, or shortened, so the limb is deformed and the normal line of the bone is lost. Displacement is dangerous not because of its appearance but because of what lies beside the bone, since the same movement that shifted the ends can have stretched, torn, or trapped the artery, the vein, and the nerve that run close to it. A severely deformed limb therefore tells the responder that the blood supply and the sensation beyond the injury are at risk, and the rule that follows is absolute, in that a severely deformed fracture is never straightened in the field to make it look normal. The reason is that the position in which the limb was found may be the position in which the vessels and the nerves are least damaged, and an attempt to restore a normal shape can convert a limb with a marginal blood supply into a limb with none.

The shape of the break adds a second layer of meaning, and each pattern predicts a different behavior in the patient. A complete fracture is one in which the bone is broken across its full width, so the two parts can move independently, while an incomplete fracture is one in which part of the circumference remains intact, so the bone is cracked rather than divided and may bend instead of separating. A comminuted fracture is one in which the bone has broken into several fragments, and it speaks of a large transfer of energy, so the responder should expect damage to the soft tissue around it and should look for other injuries produced by the same force. A spiral fracture is one in which the break runs around the shaft in a curve, and it is produced by a twisting force, which is a pattern that should raise the question of how the force was applied, particularly in a child or in a patient who cannot explain the injury. A greenstick fracture is an incomplete break in a child, whose bone is softer and bends before it snaps, so the limb may be bent without a clear break and the injury may be underestimated. A stress fracture is a fine crack produced by repeated loading rather than by one event, and it may cause pain with activity and no deformity at all, so it belongs to the slower assessment of a clinic rather than to the roadside.

An open fracture is the emergency that this chapter returns to again and again, because the wound turns a mechanical injury into an infective one. The wound admits dirt, clothing, road surface, and fragments of the environment into the same space as the broken bone, and the tissue around the break is often bruised and deprived of blood, which is exactly the ground on which infection grows. The finding that should raise the alarm is a wound over or near a fracture, a wound that continues to ooze, a wound with visible bone or marrow, or a wound that the patient received when a limb was crushed or dragged. The lay first aider does not push a protruding bone end back into the limb, does not probe the wound with a finger or an instrument, and does not pour anything into it, because each of those acts pushes contamination deeper and may injure a vessel or a nerve that is still intact. Instead the wound is covered with a clean dressing, the limb is supported in the position found, the patient is kept warm, and the patient is moved quickly toward a facility where the wound can be cleaned and the fracture can be assessed. The decisions about protection against tetanus and about antibiotics belong to the provider authorized to make them under the local protocol, and the finding that makes the decision urgent is a wound that is deep, contaminated, or produced by a bite or by soil, while the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber and never to this book. Definitive hospital care opens the wound, removes dead and foreign material, washes the tissues, and stabilizes the bone, and none of those steps is a field procedure.

Assessment of a suspected fracture begins before the limb is touched, with the mechanism of injury and with a look at the patient as a whole. The mechanism of injury is the story of the energy that acted on the body, and it predicts damage that the eye cannot see, so a fall from a height greater than 3 meters, a figure offered only as a teaching illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, should raise the suspicion of fractures in the spine, the pelvis, the heels, and the long bones at the same time. A vehicle collision, a crushing weight, a blast, and a direct blow each produce their own pattern, and the responder who understands the pattern examines with a purpose instead of searching at random. Only when the scene is safe and the primary survey has been completed does the examiner turn to the limb, and the order of the limb examination is fixed because each finding changes the meaning of the next. The first questions are whether the patient is in pain and whether the limb looks different from its fellow, and only then does the hand come down to feel for warmth, swelling, tenderness, and the integrity of the skin.

The examination of the limb itself follows a fixed sequence, and the sequence is what keeps a responder from missing the finding that matters. Pain is asked about and observed, because pain that is severe, that worsens with the smallest movement, or that is out of proportion to the visible injury is a warning about the tissue inside the limb rather than a complaint to be soothed. Deformity is looked for next, and it means any departure from the normal line, length, or rotation of the limb, including a limb that is shortened, angulated, or turned so that the foot or the hand points in the wrong direction. Swelling is compared with the other side, and a limb that is swelling while the responder watches, or that feels tense and firm rather than soft, is telling the examiner that pressure is rising inside a closed space. Abnormal movement is the next question, and it means movement at a place where no joint exists, but the responder does not deliberately bend a limb to look for it, because the search itself can complete a partial break and can injure the vessels and nerves beside the bone. The skin is examined last in this part of the sequence, because a wound changes everything that came before it, and the finding of any break in the skin turns a closed fracture into an open one.

Swelling deserves its own warning because a fracture can kill a limb slowly while the patient's general condition still looks reassuring. Blood and fluid collect inside the limb, the tissues around the broken bone become tight, and the pressure inside the closed space of a fascial compartment can rise until it exceeds the pressure that fills the small vessels, so the muscle and the nerve within that space begin to die. The findings that reveal this emergency are pain that is severe and increasing, pain that is made worse by stretching the muscles of the compartment, a limb that feels tense and hard, numbness or tingling in the skin beyond the injury, and weakness of the muscles that the nerve supplies. A pulse that can still be felt does not exclude the problem, because the pressure that starves the muscle can be present while the main artery still carries blood, and waiting for a pulse to disappear is waiting too long. The lay first aider does not loosen, tighten, or remove a splint to test the limb, and does not massage the swelling, and instead keeps the limb in the position found, keeps the patient warm, and reports every change to the receiving team. The trained responder reassesses the limb, releases a bandage that has become too tight where the protocol allows, and moves the patient urgently toward definitive care, where the pressure can be measured and the compartment can be released by the surgeon. A pressure figure such as the reading taken inside the compartment in millimeters of mercury is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold used differs between services and between editions.

Skin integrity is examined with the eyes and with a gloved hand, and it is examined over the whole limb rather than only at the point of greatest pain. A wound may sit some distance from the break, a bone end may have pierced the skin and returned, and a small puncture may be the only evidence that the fracture is open, so the responder looks at the front, the back, the inner, and the outer surfaces of the limb. An embedded object in the wound, whether glass, metal, wood, or a fragment of the environment, is stabilized in place and never removed in the field, because removal may release a hemorrhage that cannot be controlled or may injure a structure that the object is currently holding apart. The correct act is to build padding around the object so that it cannot move, to cover the surrounding wound, and to move the patient with the object still in place and with the receiving team told what is there. Where an object is protruding from a limb and cannot be accommodated, the trained responder and the paramedic manage it within their protocol and their equipment, and the lay first aider improvises support rather than extraction. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, is worn for this examination, because the wound of a fracture can carry blood and tissue that transmit infection to the responder's skin and eyes.

The neurovascular examination is the part of the assessment that decides how fast the patient must travel, and it is performed in a fixed order at the far end of the limb. Circulation is checked by the color and the warmth of the skin beyond the injury, by the time it takes for the color to return after the skin is pressed and released, and by the pulse that can be felt at the wrist or at the foot when the responder is trained to find it. Sensation is checked by asking the patient what can be felt, by touching the skin lightly on each side of the limb, and by comparing the injured side with the uninjured one, since a patient who cannot feel a light touch may have a nerve injury that will not recover without prompt care. Movement is checked by asking the patient to move the fingers or the toes, and where the patient cannot, the responder notes whether the failure is caused by pain, by weakness, or by an obvious deformity. A limb that is pale, cool, pulseless, or numb below the fracture is a surgical emergency, and the finding must be passed to the receiving team at once, because the time between the injury and the restoration of blood flow decides whether the limb survives. The lay first aider reports what the patient says and what the skin looks like, and does not attempt to test the pulse or the sensation beyond what can be seen and heard.

The examination performed before the limb is immobilized and the examination performed after it are the same examination, and this is the single most important habit in the care of a fracture. Immobilization changes the patient, because a splint, a sling, a bandage, or a traction device can press on a vessel, a nerve, or a swelling, and because a limb that was straight and perfused may become bent and starved once it is secured. The purpose of repeating the same questions in the same order is that the responder is not looking for a new injury but for a change caused by the treatment, and a change that appears after immobilization is a signal to adjust the splint rather than to wait and watch. Immobilization is therefore never the end of the assessment, and the finding that the limb is now cooler, paler, more painful, or more numb than it was before the splint means the splint must be examined and the patient must move faster toward definitive care. The same rule applies after any movement of the patient, any change of position, any new dressing, and any part of the journey, because each of those events can alter the pressure inside the limb. The record of both examinations is written and passed on, since the receiving team needs to know what was found before and after, and a limb whose condition changed in transit is a different patient from the one described at the scene.

The three levels of care divide the response to a fracture, and the division follows training, equipment, authorization, and protocol rather than the urgency of the moment. The lay first aider may cover an open wound with a clean dressing, support the limb in the position found, keep the patient still and warm, and call emergency medical services early, and those acts are enough to protect the patient while help is coming. The lay first aider does not straighten a deformed limb, does not push a bone end back into the skin, does not pull on the limb to make it longer, does not remove an embedded object, and does not try to test the limb by bending it. Where a limb is bleeding heavily, the lay first aider applies firm direct pressure over a dressing and adds further layers rather than lifting the first, and the decision to place a manufactured tourniquet belongs to emergency medical services, to the trained responder, and to the protocol that authorizes it. Warmth is part of the lay first aider's work from the first minute, because a patient with a fracture is often exposed, immobile, and lying on cold ground, and cold deepens shock and worsens the outcome.

The trained responder and the paramedic may splint and immobilize within the procedures their service authorizes, and their work is defined by doing that one task well rather than by doing more. Immobilization of a fracture belongs to this level because it requires a device, a technique, and the judgment to know which position the limb should be held in, and because the device itself must be checked against the circulation and the nerves before and after it is applied. The paramedic may also decide about pain relief, and the finding that makes relief urgent is a patient whose pain is severe enough to prevent movement, to prevent sleep, or to worsen the circulation, while the choice of substance, the amount, the route, and the timing belong to the local protocol and to the prescriber. Reduction of a fracture, which means restoring the broken ends to their normal alignment, is not a field procedure for the trained responder either, and it is attempted outside the hospital only in the narrow circumstances that the service protocol defines and with the authorization that the protocol requires. Where a limb has lost its blood supply, the trained responder recognizes the emergency, protects the limb in the position found, and shortens the time to definitive care rather than attempting a reduction to restore a pulse.

Definitive hospital care owns everything that repairs, aligns, and fixes, and knowing where that line lies is as much a part of competence as knowing how to splint. A plain radiograph, a computed tomography scan, and where it is available an MRI are used to define the pattern of the break and the position of the fragments, and those images are read by the clinician who will decide the treatment. Reduction of a fracture, whether it is done by closed manipulation or through an open operation, and fixation, whether by a cast, by pins, by plates and screws, or by an external frame, belong to the physician and the surgeon in a place where imaging, anesthesia, and sterile conditions exist. The surgeon also cleans an open fracture, removes dead and contaminated tissue, stabilizes the bone, and closes or leaves open the wound according to the state of the tissues, and the release of a compartment under pressure is performed by the same hands. The decisions about antibiotics, about protection against tetanus, and about fluids and analgesia are made by the providers authorized to make them under the local protocol and with the patient in front of them, because a manual cannot carry a prescription. A patient with a suspected fracture of the hip, the pelvis, or the femur belongs in a trauma center where the operating room and the intensive care unit are available, and the field responder's task is to immobilize, to keep the patient warm, and to hand over a clear account of what was found and what was done.

A fracture is also a marker of the energy that produced it, and that is why the examination of the limb is never finished until the whole patient has been examined. The same force that broke a femur, a pelvis, or a rib can have injured the head, the chest, the abdomen, and the spine, and the finding that should send the responder back to the beginning of the primary survey is any change in the level of consciousness, the breathing, or the circulation. A patient with a fracture of the pelvis can lose a large volume of blood into the space behind the peritoneum, and a patient with a fracture of the femur can lose as much as 2 liters into the thigh, a teaching figure that must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol in force, so the limb that looks dramatic may be the quieter emergency of the two. Children need a special mention because their bones bend and crack in patterns that adults do not share, and because a child who is frightened may not report pain or may report it in a place that does not match the injury. The record that travels with the patient includes the mechanism of injury, the time it happened, the appearance and the neurovascular findings of the limb before and after splinting, the time of any intervention, and the changes observed along the way, because the receiving team needs the trend and not only the latest reading.

Two failures run through the care of fractures, and both are failures of attention rather than of skill. The first is the fracture that is missed because a more dramatic injury holds the eye, which is the wrist that is not examined in a patient with a bleeding thigh, the rib that is not counted in a patient with a head injury, and the second fracture of the same limb that is hidden above or below the one that is found. The second is the fracture that is treated as the emergency while the patient is dying of something else, because a limb can wait for minutes that an airway, a breathing, and a circulation cannot. Life comes before limb when two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands, and that principle decides the order rather than the importance of the limb, so the patient who is not breathing is treated before the patient's deformed leg. The finding that settles the order is not the appearance of the limb but whether the patient can currently breathe, circulate, and respond.

Everything in this chapter points toward one purpose, which is to prevent further harm while the patient is moved toward the care that can repair the break. Immobilization serves that purpose by holding the broken ends still, by controlling pain, by protecting the vessels and the nerves that run beside the bone, and by preventing the sharp ends from moving inside the skin, so the limb is splinted in the position found rather than in the position that looks best. Pain is treated as a clinical problem rather than as an unavoidable companion of injury, and the responder who is authorized to relieve it does so within the protocol, because pain that is severe enough to prevent movement or to disturb breathing adds to the patient's risk. The hypothermia that accompanies a fracture is prevented by covering the patient before the journey, by insulating the patient from the ground, and by removing wet clothing and replacing it with dry coverings without exposing the wound, and a body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is a threshold to be verified against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than taken from these pages. The patient is watched continuously from the first contact to the handover, and the observations that matter are repeated in the same order so that the trend can be compared rather than guessed. The handover carries the mechanism of injury, the state of the skin, the neurovascular findings before and after immobilization, the time of every intervention, and every change seen, because the receiving team must be able to continue without starting again.

To summarize, a fracture is defined first by the skin, since an open break is an emergency of contamination and infection while a closed break can still have torn a vessel or a nerve, and it is defined next by displacement, completeness, and pattern, because each of those terms predicts what the patient will do and what the responder must avoid. The severely deformed limb is never straightened in the field, a protruding bone end is never pushed back, an embedded object is never removed, and abnormal movement is a finding rather than a test. The examination of pain, deformity, swelling, abnormal movement, skin integrity, and neurovascular status follows a fixed order, the limb beyond the fracture is examined before and after immobilization with the same questions, and a limb that becomes cooler, paler, more painful, or more numb after splinting is a signal to adjust and to hurry. The lay first aider covers, supports, warms, and calls for help; the trained responder and the paramedic splint and immobilize within the protocols that authorize them; and reduction, fixation, cleaning of an open fracture, and release of a compartment belong to definitive hospital care. Scene safety comes before the patient, the lethal possibilities are named early, cold is treated as a complication, and life comes before limb when two correct actions compete. Every time, pressure, temperature, depth, and figure in this chapter is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 20 — Immobilization and Splinting

Immobilization holds an injured part still, and its purpose is not to make the limb look normal but to prevent further injury and to control pain while the patient is carried toward definitive care. The scene is made safe before any injured part is touched, because traffic, fire, electricity, water, an animal that is not yet secured, and a person who is still violent are each a lethal possibility, and the patient's own blood is treated as infectious, with personal protective equipment, or PPE, wherever it is available. The lethal finding to be named first is the damage that movement has already caused, revealed by a limb that is pale, cold, and pulseless with a swelling that grows while the responder watches, or by a neck or a back that is painful or deformed with numbness or weakness in the arms or the legs. Splinting is rarely the act that saves a life, but the wrong splint or movement can end one, because sharp bone ends lie beside vessels, nerves, and skin that are still intact. The lay first aider may support, pad, and steady an injured part, the trained responder or paramedic may apply the splints the service authorizes, and the reduction of a fracture, the fixation of a bone, the repair of a vessel or a nerve, and the release of pressure inside a swollen limb belong to definitive hospital care and the surgeon. This chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

The reason to hold a fractured part still is that movement of the broken ends causes harm that the fracture itself has not yet caused. A broken bone is no longer a column but a lever with a jagged end, and every jolt of a vehicle, every attempt to sit up, and every pull on the limb drags that end across the tissue beside it. The vessels that run close to the bone can be torn, a clot that has sealed a torn vessel can be dislodged, and a nerve that was only stretched can be cut, so an injury that was survivable becomes one that threatens the limb or the life. Pain is the second reason, and it is not a detail of comfort, because severe pain drives the pulse up, deepens shock, and makes the patient move in ways that add to the damage. A splint is therefore a container and a support rather than a treatment of the fracture, since it neither puts the bone back nor makes it heal, and the listener should hear that distinction plainly. What the splint does is keep the limb in the position found, take the weight off the broken part, and remove movement from the journey. Correction of the position, restoration of the length of the bone, and the holding of the pieces together with metal belong to definitive hospital care.

Recognizing that a part needs immobilization begins with the mechanism of injury rather than with the shape of the limb, because the energy that acted on the body predicts damage that the eye cannot see. A fall from a height, a vehicle collision, a falling object, a twisting injury, and a direct blow each produce patterns that a trained eye expects, and a fall from greater than 3 meters, offered as an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, should raise the question of injury to the spine, the pelvis, the heels, and the long bones. The findings that point to a fracture are sharp and well localized pain, swelling that appears quickly, a deformity or an unnatural angle, an inability to use the limb or to bear weight, a wound over a bone, and a snap the patient heard at the moment of injury. The lay first aider looks and asks rather than tests, and never moves the part deliberately to see whether it is broken, because such a test causes pain, may convert a closed fracture into an open one, and may injure a vessel that is still intact. A limb that is pale, cool, blue, pulseless, or numb below the injury, and a limb whose swelling is tight and growing, make the injury an emergency of its own and demand the fastest safe transport. Older patients and patients whose bones are weakened by illness may have a fracture with very little deformity, so a mechanism severe enough to break a bone justifies immobilization even when the limb looks almost normal.

The first principle of splinting is that the limb is splinted in the position in which it is found, and a severely deformed fracture is never straightened to make it look normal. The reason is anatomical, because the bone ends have come to rest where the vessels and nerves beside them may be compressed but not yet torn, and pulling the limb straight can drag a sharp end through a vessel that was still carrying blood or a nerve that was still working. A clot that has sealed a torn vessel is also fragile, and the movement of straightening can release it and turn a contained injury into a hemorrhage that no dressing will control. The exception is narrow and it belongs to a trained provider working under a protocol, who may apply gentle traction along the line of the limb in a specific situation, usually when the limb beyond the injury has no pulse and the protocol authorizes the attempt, and this is not a maneuver for the lay first aider or for a responder without that authorization. When such a decision is made, the limb is moved once, slowly, and held in the new position, and the circulation, the sensation, and the movement are checked again at once. The patient's pain and the appearance of the limb are not the measure of correct splinting, since the purpose is to prevent further harm rather than to satisfy the eye.

The second principle is that a splint must control the joint above the injury and the joint below it, because a broken bone is only one part of a chain that moves. An unsupported bone can rotate and angulate at the fracture even when the middle of the limb is bound, so a forearm splint holds the elbow and the wrist, a lower leg splint holds the knee and the ankle, and a thigh splint holds the hip and the knee. A bone that lies between two joints, such as the shaft of the thigh bone or of the upper arm bone, cannot be held still by a short splint, however firmly it is tied, and a splint that stops short of a joint allows the movement it was meant to prevent. A broken finger is comfortable when bound to the finger beside it with a small pad of cloth between them, a technique the lay first aider can learn and use. The finding that the joints are controlled is a limb that does not move at either end during a transfer or a turn, and the finding that the splint is inadequate is movement, a new angle, or a return of severe pain. Where a fracture of the thigh is suspected, the device that holds the limb in traction belongs to the trained responder or the paramedic and to the protocol of the service, and the lay first aider supports the limb where it lies and waits.

The third principle is that every bony prominence under the splint is padded, and the padding must be rigid enough, long enough, and secured without becoming a tourniquet. The prominences to protect are the elbow, the wrist, the knuckles, the hip, the knee, the ankle, and the heel, and each needs a layer of soft material between the skin and whatever holds the limb. Padding is made from what is at hand, including folded cloth, a spare shirt, a towel, a sanitary pad, foam from a vehicle seat, a rolled blanket, or a pillow, and it is placed so that the pressure of the ties is spread over a broad area rather than one point.
