The rigid part must be stiff enough not to bend when the limb is lifted, long enough to cross the joints above and below, and broad enough to spread the force, and the limb is secured at several points with triangular bandages, strips of cloth, tape, or a strap. A narrow cord, a wire, and a cloth rolled into a hard rope concentrate force and can injure the skin and the nerve beneath them even when the fracture is held well. The finding that the ties are too tight is a groove in the skin, a limb that tingles, or a tie that cannot be slid under with a finger, and because swelling grows for hours after an injury, a splint that is comfortable at the scene is checked after every move and loosened when the check has changed.

Commercial splints exist in many forms, and the choice among them belongs to the trained responder, to the paramedic, and to the service that carries them. A rigid padded splint is a stiff board or molded shell lined with foam and held with straps, useful for a forearm, a wrist, or a lower leg when the padding is adequate and the joints are crossed. A malleable splint can be bent to the shape of the limb and then holds that shape, a vacuum splint becomes rigid when the air is drawn out of it and molds itself around the limb, and an inflatable splint surrounds the limb with air pressure but must be watched closely because it can become too tight as the limb swells. A traction splint holds the thigh bone in gentle pull and belongs to the trained responder or paramedic taught and authorized to use it, and it is never improvised by a lay first aider. A cervical collar is a device for a trained provider and it supports the neck but does not immobilize it by itself, so it is used with manual support and with the movement restrictions the local protocol describes. A pelvic binder, a spine board, and a vacuum mattress are also devices of the trained responder and of definitive hospital care, and each has a place, a method, and a limit that training teaches and that no chapter can replace.

Where no manufactured splint is available, a serviceable one is built from the objects that a house, a vehicle, or a clinic already holds, and the listener should be able to picture a few of them in the ear. A wooden board, a rolled newspaper or magazine, stiff cardboard, a broom handle, a walking stick, an umbrella, and a tool handle can all serve as the rigid part of a splint once wrapped in cloth so that the edges do not cut the skin. A rolled blanket, a pillow, a folded jacket, and a stack of cloth can hold a limb in a comfortable position when the injury does not need rigid support, as in a simple sprain or a suspected fracture of a finger. In a clinic without supplies, tongue depressors taped together make a finger splint, plastic pipe padded with gauze makes a forearm splint, and a cardboard carton cut into a strip makes a splint for a lower leg. The uninjured leg is the finest splint for the injured leg, because it is the correct length, it is already padded with muscle, and it moves with the patient, and the chest wall serves the same purpose for an injured arm when the arm is supported against it. Whatever object is chosen, it is padded at every bony point, it crosses the joints above and below, and it is secured with ties that spread their force, because a hard object held against skin without padding causes an injury of its own.

The upper limb is immobilized with a sling that carries the weight of the arm and with a swathe that holds the arm against the body, and both belong to the lay first aider as much as to the trained responder. A triangular bandage, a scarf, or a strip of cloth is passed under the forearm and tied behind the neck so that the hand sits a little higher than the elbow, because an arm that hangs down swells and hurts more. The swathe is a broad band around the chest and the arm, placed low, tightened only until the arm is held, since a band that crosses the chest too high or too tightly restricts breathing, and the danger is greater when the ribs are also injured. The fingertips are left uncovered so that the circulation, the sensation, and the movement can be checked at every stage, and the patient is asked to open and close the hand, to spread the fingers, and to say whether the hand feels numb or cold. A deformed elbow or upper arm is not forced into a sling, and if the arm cannot be brought to the chest without moving the fracture, it is supported in the position found, padded and splinted, and the patient is carried that way. The finding that the sling must be adjusted is a hand that has become pale or blue, a hand that tingles, or a wrist pulse that cannot be felt, and the response is to lower the arm slightly, to loosen the swathe, and to check again.

The lower limb is immobilized with the same principles applied to greater weight, and the patient is not asked to stand or to bear weight on a suspected fracture. A suspected fracture of the thigh is supported in the position found, often with a pillow under the limb and the legs bound together, with binding around the ankles, the calves, and the thighs and padding between the knees. A suspected fracture of the lower leg is held with a rigid splint that crosses the knee and the ankle, or with the injured leg bound to the uninjured one, and the foot is kept at a right angle to the leg so that the ankle does not drop and stretch the tissue at the back of the leg. A suspected fracture of the knee is splinted as it lies, neither forced straight nor forced into a bend, because the deformity is the position in which the vessels behind the knee are least stretched. A suspected fracture of the ankle or foot is supported with a pillow or a soft splint and the shoe is left in place unless it must be cut away to check the circulation, because the shoe supports the foot and removal is difficult once the limb has swollen. The finding that the lower limb splint has failed is a foot that has become cold, white, or numb, a calf that is tight and increasingly painful, or a patient who describes pain far worse than the injury appears to explain.

The spine deserves its own paragraph because a broken neck or back can turn a walking patient into a paralyzed one through movement alone, and the suspicion is raised by the mechanism of injury and the findings rather than by a radiograph at the roadside. A fall from a height, a collision in which the patient was thrown, a dive into shallow water, and a heavy blow to the head are situations in which the spine is treated as injured until proved otherwise. The findings that support the suspicion are pain or tenderness in the neck or back, a step or deformity along the spine, numbness, tingling, or weakness in the arms or legs, and loss of bowel or bladder control, and any of these makes protection of the spine urgent. The lay first aider does not move such a patient at all unless there is immediate danger such as fire or traffic, and if a move is unavoidable, the head and the body are kept in one line and the patient is slid rather than lifted, with as many hands as the scene allows. The trained responder or paramedic may hold the head and neck by hand, apply a properly sized cervical collar, and roll the patient onto a board or vacuum mattress with a team, a skill taught and practiced rather than read. The board is a tool for the move, not a bed, and it is removed as early as definitive hospital care allows, because a hard surface under a patient who cannot feel it causes pressure injury, and the number of hours is a figure to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

An open fracture, in which bone has broken through the skin, combines the fracture with a contaminated wound and changes the priority of care. The wound is covered with a clean or sterile dressing, the bone end is not pushed back under the skin, and an object embedded in the wound is left exactly where it is and stabilized with padding around it, because removal may release hemorrhage that cannot be controlled and may tear a structure that is still intact. The limb is then splinted in the position found, with the dressing protected from the pressure of the splint, and the patient is moved toward definitive hospital care without an attempt to clean the wound beyond removing obvious gross dirt from the skin around it. The decision about protection against tetanus is made by the provider authorized to make it under the local protocol, because the wound, the contamination, and the patient's vaccination history all shape the answer, and the decision about antibiotics follows the same rule, so this chapter names the decisions and never the substance, the amount, the route, or the frequency. The findings that make the open fracture urgent are tissue that has lost its blood supply, dirt or clothing driven deep into the wound, and bleeding that continues despite pressure, and any of these means the fastest safe journey. Bleeding from an open fracture is controlled with direct pressure around the wound and, where the protocol authorizes it and the bleeding is from a limb and cannot be stopped, with a tourniquet whose time is written on the patient in a place the receiving team will see.

Reassessment after splinting is the same examination that was performed before it, repeated until the handover, and it checks the circulation, the sensation, and the movement of the part beyond the splint. The circulation is judged by the color and the warmth of the skin, by the pulse felt at the wrist or the top of the foot, and by the time it takes for the color to return after the nail bed is pressed and released, and a delay longer than 2 seconds is one figure used to describe poor flow, an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The sensation is judged by asking the patient whether the fingers or the toes feel normal, numb, or tingling, and by comparing the injured side with the uninjured side, because a change the patient reports is more reliable than the impression of the responder. The movement is judged by asking the patient to move the fingers or the toes gently, where pain allows, and by noting any movement that was possible before the splint and is no longer possible after it. The findings are written down and spoken aloud, together with the time of the splint and the material used, because a receiving team that knows what was found before can judge what has changed since. The findings that require immediate action are any loss of pulse, any new numbness or weakness, and pain out of proportion to the injury, and the response is to loosen the splint, reassess, and transport without delay.

A splint that is too tight, a circumferential bandage wound too firmly, and a limb that continues to swell can together produce compartment syndrome, in which the pressure inside a closed space of the limb rises until muscle and nerve lose their blood supply. The earliest and most reliable finding is pain out of proportion to the injury that becomes worse when the fingers or the toes are gently straightened, joined by a limb that feels tense and tight, by numbness, by weakness, and by a pulse that may still be present because the pressure can close the small vessels before it closes the large one. The responder must not wait for the pulse to disappear before acting, because a pulse that can still be felt does not mean that the tissue is receiving blood. The measurement of the pressure inside the limb and the operation that releases it belong to definitive hospital care, and the release is a surgical procedure that is never performed in the field. A limb that has been without adequate flow for a number of hours can suffer damage that cannot be repaired, and that number of hours is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the tolerance of muscle and nerve differs with the temperature and with the patient. The responder's part is to loosen anything that encircles the limb, to keep the limb at the level of the heart, to keep the patient warm, and to move toward the surgeon as quickly as is safe.

Hypothermia is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and an immobilized patient is especially exposed because the patient cannot move to keep warm and often lies on cold ground while clothing is cut away. Cold makes the blood clot less effectively, deepens shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm, so every bleeding, wounded, immobilized, or waiting patient is protected against heat loss. The responder covers the patient before the journey rather than at the end, insulates the patient from the ground, replaces wet clothing with dry covering where the wound allows, and keeps the vehicle warm, and the splint and its padding are part of the warmth because cloth and foam insulate as they support. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is one figure for the point at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that threshold must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because it differs with age, the site of measurement, and the patient's usual state. The finding that cooling has already begun is a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold, with confusion and a slow pulse, and that means warmth and transport without delay. Comfort is part of the treatment, because a patient in severe pain moves, breathes shallowly, and worsens shock, so the patient is kept comfortable without moving the fracture and is asked about pain, numbness, and tingling. The decision about pain relief belongs to the provider authorized to prescribe it and to the local protocol, and the substance, the amount, the route, and the frequency are set there rather than in a chapter, so the listener is given the decision and not a prescription.

The record includes what was immobilized, with which material, the position found, the circulation, sensation, and movement checks before and after the splint, and the time of each entry, because the receiving team continues a story the field began. The handover is spoken in the same order as the record and it names the provider level of every act that was performed, since a receiving team must know what was done and by whom in order to judge what is safe to do next. Emergency medical services are activated early where they exist, and the report states the location, the number of patients, the mechanism of injury, what has been splinted, and what remains hazardous at the scene. The receiving facility is chosen for the care the patient needs, which may be a trauma center with imaging and an operating room, or a hospital that can stabilize the patient and arrange a transfer, and the choice is made before the patient is moved. Transport is urgent and gentle at the same time, because speed that throws the patient around adds injuries and pain, and a patient who arrives in worse condition has gained nothing from the hurry. This material is educational and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law of the country in which you work, and no reader should attempt a technique that has not been taught, practiced, and authorized by the system that supervises the care.

To summarize, splinting holds an injured part still in order to prevent further injury and to control pain, and its purpose is never to make the limb look normal. Scene safety comes before the patient, the lethal findings of a pulseless limb or a moved spine are sought early, and every intervention is named with the provider level that owns it, so the lay first aider supports and pads while the trained responder or paramedic applies the authorized devices and definitive hospital care performs the reduction, the fixation, and the release of pressure. The joints above and below the injury are controlled, every bony prominence is padded, the limb is supported in the position found, and a severely deformed fracture is not straightened, because the bone ends may lie beside vessels and nerves that are still intact. The circulation, the sensation, and the movement are checked before and after the splint, repeated until the handover, and written down with the time and the material, since an unrecorded change is one the receiving team will not know about. The patient is protected against hypothermia from the first minute, the decision about pain relief belongs to the prescriber and the protocol, and the journey to definitive care is both urgent and gentle. Every time, temperature, distance, and figure in this chapter is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between services, countries, and editions. This chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 21 — Shoulder Injuries

No injury of the shoulder may be examined before the scene has been made safe, because a responder struck by traffic, burned, electrocuted, or attacked becomes a second casualty on a scene that already has too few hands. Traffic is held, power is isolated by a person authorized to do so, and a violent person is left to those trained to control violence before any hand is laid on the patient. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, is worn for every patient rather than only for the ones who look infectious, because blood and body fluids carry infection that enters through a break in the skin or a splash into the eye. The lethal possibility to be named first is not the deformed shoulder but the injury that arrived with it, since the force that dislocates a shoulder or breaks a collarbone can also tear the great vessels beneath it, collapse a lung, and fracture the neck. The findings that reveal neurovascular danger are an arm that is pale, cool, and pulseless or a hand that has gone numb or weak, while the hidden chest injury shows itself as breathing that has become fast, shallow, and painful. Warmth belongs to the treatment from this first minute, because a patient who is bleeding, exposed, or lying on cold ground loses heat quickly and cold makes bleeding, shock, and clotting worse. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

Why shoulder injuries behave so differently from one another begins with the anatomy of the shoulder girdle, which is a small set of bones and joints rather than a single structure. The collarbone is the only bony strut connecting the arm to the trunk, and it lies directly under the skin, so it breaks easily and shows its breaks easily. The shoulder blade is a broad plate of bone buried under heavy muscle, so it is protected from ordinary blows and shattered by extraordinary ones. The ball and socket between the head of the upper arm bone and the shallow cup of the shoulder blade gives the arm the greatest range of motion in the body and pays for that freedom with the least stability, which is why it dislocates more often than any other joint. The nerves and vessels that supply the whole arm pass through a narrow corridor beneath the collarbone and close to the socket, so an injury that moves bone can also stretch, bruise, or tear what lies beside it.

The mechanism of injury is the first evidence at the shoulder, and it predicts damage before the examination confirms it. A fall onto the outstretched hand drives force up the arm into the collarbone and the socket, and it is the classic way in which a collarbone breaks or a shoulder dislocates. A fall onto the point of the shoulder disrupts the joint between collarbone and shoulder blade, while a blow to the back of the shoulder can push the head of the arm bone out of the socket toward the back and produce a dislocation that is quiet and easily missed. A heavy direct blow, a fall from a height, a vehicle collision, or a crush carries the force required to break the shoulder blade, and that mechanism should raise the expectation of chest, neck, and head injury rather than of the shoulder alone. A seizure, an electric shock, and a violent wrench of the arm are also mechanisms of dislocation, and they deserve to be asked about directly rather than assumed away.

The shoulder never comes first, however dramatic it looks, because a shoulder cannot kill a patient while an airway, a breathing chest, or a torn vessel can. The primary survey is completed in its fixed order of airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure before the shoulder is examined in detail, and the arm is left in the position found while that survey is performed. Life comes before limb whenever two correct actions compete, so a patient with an open shoulder wound, a closed airway, and a fast weak pulse needs the airway secured and the hidden bleeding sought before any splint is considered. A patient who holds the shoulder protectively may be holding it still because the neck is injured, so the head is not allowed to roll, and any change in the level of consciousness, the breathing, or the pulse sends the responder back to the beginning. The lay first aider keeps the head still, supports the arm as found, keeps the patient warm, and calls emergency medical services early.

The neurovascular assessment is a short examination repeated before any handling of the shoulder and again after every handling, including after the sling has been tied, and it belongs to the trained responder, the paramedic, and definitive hospital care. The pulse is felt at the wrist on the thumb side and compared with the uninjured side, and the color and warmth of the hand are compared in the same way. Sensation is tested over the outer side of the shoulder, where the nerve that winds around the neck of the arm bone supplies the skin, and then over the thumb, the little finger, and the palm, because each area belongs to a different nerve. Movement is tested by asking the patient to lift the arm away from the side, bend the elbow, make a fist, and spread the fingers, and any movement the patient cannot perform is recorded rather than argued with. The finding that matters most is a difference between the two arms, since a limb that is pale, cool, pulseless, numb, or weak is a surgical emergency and must not be made worse by pulling on the arm.

A fracture of the collarbone is the most common injury of the shoulder girdle and one of the most forgiving, because the bone lies under the skin where it can be seen and felt without deep probing. The patient usually supports the injured arm with the other hand, keeps the shoulder still, and reports pain when the arm is moved or the bone is pressed, while swelling, tenderness over the bone, and an obvious step in the contour are the usual findings. Most of these fractures heal well with support of the arm and time, which is why the lay first aider may apply a simple sling for comfort while making no attempt to line the bone up. A small group is dangerous and is recognized by findings rather than by worry, namely bone pressing so hard that the skin is white or broken, a fracture near the inner end of the collarbone where the bone can press backward onto the great vessels, the windpipe, and the food pipe, and any fracture with numbness, weakness, or a lost pulse in the arm. A fracture with any of those findings belongs to definitive hospital care and demands immediate transport rather than a longer stay at the scene.

Support of the arm is the whole of field treatment for an uncomplicated fracture of the collarbone, and it is a lay first aid measure that requires nothing more than a triangular bandage, a strip of cloth, or a shirt used as a sling. The shoulder is never pulled, pushed, or rotated to make the bone look straight, because the bone ends lie beside vessels and nerves and because movement of a fragment can turn a closed fracture into an open one through the skin. A figure of eight bandage pulled tight around both shoulders is not the treatment of choice and can compress the armpit and the nerves within it, so where such a bandage is used at all it must be applied by a trained responder under a protocol and checked repeatedly. The fingers are examined after any binding is tied, because a bandage that crosses the wrist can interfere with the circulation even when it was meant only to hold the forearm. Pain relief is a decision made by the provider authorized to prescribe it under the local protocol, and the substance, the amount, and the way it is given are never taken from a manual such as this one.

A dislocation of the shoulder is the displacement of the head of the upper arm bone out of the socket of the shoulder blade, and the direction of that displacement decides both the appearance of the patient and the structures at risk. The most common direction is forward and downward, and the patient holds the arm slightly away from the body and rotated outward, refuses to bring the elbow to the chest, and cannot touch the opposite shoulder with the hand of the injured side. The outline of the shoulder is squared off rather than rounded, the head of the bone can sometimes be felt in front of the socket, and the muscles around the joint are in spasm. A dislocation toward the back is far less common and far more easily missed, because the arm is held close to the body and rotated inward, the front of the shoulder looks almost normal, and the patient cannot turn the palm outward. Because that appearance is subtle, a responder who does not test outward rotation will not find it, a radiograph in a single view can miss it, and the suspicion is stated at handover so that the imaging includes the view that reveals it. The finding that must always be sought is the neurovascular state of the arm, because a dislocated shoulder can injure the nerves and vessels before anyone touches it and can injure them further during any attempt to put it back.

The structures at risk in a shoulder dislocation are specific, and each announces itself through a finding that a trained responder can test without moving the joint. The nerve that winds around the neck of the arm bone supplies the skin over the outer shoulder and helps to lift the arm, so numbness in that patch or weakness when the arm is lifted away from the side points to it. The bundle of nerves that passes from the neck into the arm can be stretched by the displaced head, and the finding is numbness or weakness in the hand or the forearm rather than in the shoulder itself. The artery that runs through the armpit can be torn or blocked by the displaced head, and although this is uncommon it is catastrophic, with a hand that is pale, cold, and pulseless, and it is seen most often in older patients whose vessels are stiff. Because nerve and vessel injury may exist before the joint is put back, the examination is recorded before any handling and repeated afterwards, any worsening is reported in the same breath as the dislocation itself, and the lay first aider never attempts to put a shoulder back into its socket while the trained responder does so only where training, authorization, and a protocol allow.

Putting a dislocated shoulder back into its socket is a procedure with a defined owner, and in most circumstances that owner is definitive hospital care, where imaging can be performed before and after the reduction and where a clinician can decide whether the reduction is safe. The trained responder or paramedic may reduce a dislocation in the field only where the local protocol authorizes it, where the patient has no fracture and no neurovascular deficit, where monitoring is available, and where the attempt will not delay transport to a place that can manage failure. Pain relief and sedation for the procedure are decisions made by the provider authorized to prescribe them under the local protocol, and nothing in this chapter names a substance, an amount, a route, or a frequency, because a manual is not a prescription. The reduction is performed gently with the technique the provider has been trained and certified to use, it is abandoned at once if the pain becomes uncontrollable or the neurovascular examination worsens, and the joint that goes back into place is not proof of success until the pulse, the sensation, and the movement have been checked again.

A fracture of the shoulder blade is unusual in ordinary life and common in the patient who has been through enormous force, and its presence is a message about the rest of the body rather than about the shoulder. The shoulder blade is wrapped in heavy muscle and lies against the rib cage, so the energy required to break it is the energy of a vehicle collision, a fall from a height, a crush, or a blast. The findings are pain over the flat of the shoulder blade, swelling and bruising that may appear late and low on the back, a shoulder the patient holds rigidly still, and tenderness that can be localized to the bone rather than to the joint. Because the same force strikes the ribs, the lung, the spine, and the head, the responder who finds a fractured shoulder blade stops looking at the shoulder and begins a deliberate search that includes the breathing rate and the effort of breathing, the movement of the chest on each side, the tenderness of the ribs and the breastbone, the tenderness of the neck and the back, and the level of consciousness.

The chest injuries that accompany a fractured shoulder blade and a severe shoulder blow are the ones that kill, and they announce themselves through breathing rather than through the shoulder. Broken ribs are felt as tenderness or as a grinding sensation when the chest wall is pressed, and the patient guards the chest and breathes shallowly to avoid the pain. Air that leaks from a torn lung into the space around it collapses that lung, and the findings are increasing breathlessness, reduced breath sounds on the injured side, and a chest that moves less on that side than on the other. Blood that collects in the same space adds a loss of circulating volume, with the same breathlessness together with a pulse that is climbing and a patient becoming pale and restless, while bruising of the lung makes it stiff and shows itself as a patient who works harder for every breath. The responder does not bind the chest tightly to ease the pain of broken ribs, because a tightly bound chest prevents the deep breathing and coughing that keep the lung open, and that restriction can kill a patient whose ribs would have healed.

Because the force that injures the shoulder often passes through the neck, the cervical spine is treated as injured until it has been cleared by the appropriate examination and imaging. The findings that raise suspicion are pain or tenderness in the neck, an injury above the collarbone, an altered level of consciousness, an unreliable patient, and a mechanism of injury that included a fall from a height or a high-speed collision. The lay first aider supports the head in the position found and does not turn the head to look at the shoulder, while the trained responder applies manual stabilization and then the collar and the board or split stretcher that the local protocol requires. An unconscious patient is moved with the head, the neck, and the trunk kept in line, and any turn of the patient is a coordinated act performed by several trained hands rather than by one person rolling a patient alone, because a patient who walked away from a collision and then complains of neck pain is not cleared by having walked.

The joint between the collarbone and the shoulder blade is injured by a fall onto the point of the shoulder, and the patient reports pain at the top of the shoulder, tenderness directly over the joint, and a small step in the contour where the end of the collarbone has risen above the shoulder blade. That injury is painful and disabling but rarely threatens the limb, and its field treatment is support of the arm in a sling with the joint left as it lies and no attempt to push the collarbone down. The joint between the collarbone and the breastbone is injured far less often, usually by a heavy blow to the front of the chest or by a vehicle collision, and its danger depends on direction, because an inner end driven backward can press on the windpipe, the food pipe, and the great vessels at the top of the chest. The findings of such a backward displacement are difficulty in breathing or swallowing, a hoarse voice, swelling at the base of the neck, and a sense of pressure in the throat, and a suspected case is a hospital emergency requiring imaging and specialist care, so no one at the scene pushes on the inner end of a collarbone to test it.

Immobilization of the shoulder is performed for comfort, for protection of the injured structures, and for safe transport, and it follows a fixed order that can be carried out with simple materials. The first action is to leave the arm in the position in which it was found and to support it there with a hand or a knee so that it is not hanging by its own weight. The second action, only when the arm is supported, is to slide a triangular bandage, a wide strip of cloth, or a folded shirt beneath the forearm without lifting or rotating the shoulder. The third action is to bring the ends of the sling over the shoulder of the uninjured side and tie them so that the hand rests a little above the level of the elbow. The fourth action is to secure the arm against the body with a broad band passed around the chest and the arm, tied loosely enough that the patient can still take a full deep breath, since a band that restricts breathing is more dangerous than the injury it supports. The fifth action is to recheck the fingers and the wrist for color, warmth, pulse, and movement and to loosen anything that has changed them for the worse. A simple sling belongs to the lay first aider, while a splint that includes the chest and the arm together belongs to the trained responder or paramedic working within a protocol.

Certain positions and movements must never be forced on an injured shoulder, and the reason is always the same, that the bone ends and the displaced head lie beside structures that cannot be repaired at the roadside. The arm is never pulled lengthwise to compare its length with the other side, because traction can stretch a nerve that is already bruised and can pull a clot from a torn vessel, and it is never lifted to the horizontal or above the head to inspect the armpit, because that movement increases pain and can convert a stable fracture into a displaced one. The elbow is never forced toward the chest and the hand is never forced onto the opposite shoulder to prove that a joint is dislocated, because a test that hurts is a test that can harm. A sling is never tied so tightly that the wrist is compressed, and the patient is never lifted by the injured arm or moved with the arm used as a handle. Where a position cannot be achieved without force the correct response is to leave the limb as found and to move the patient toward definitive care.

Transport of the patient with a shoulder injury is arranged around the whole patient rather than around the arm, and the position is chosen to protect breathing and circulation first. A patient who is fully alert, breathing comfortably, and not in shock may travel sitting up with the arm supported in the sling, because the upright position eases the work of breathing and reduces the pull on the injured shoulder. A patient who is drowsy, pale, or short of breath travels lying flat or in whatever position best supports breathing, with the arm supported on a pillow beside the body rather than folded tightly across the chest, and a patient with a suspected spinal injury travels in the position and on the device that the local protocol requires. Cold is prevented by covering the patient before departure, insulating from the floor of the vehicle, and removing wet clothing, because a patient who is bleeding, exposed, or immobilized loses heat and cold worsens shock and clotting.

The findings that should stop a responder from being reassured are the ones that describe a limb losing its blood supply or a patient losing the ability to compensate. Pain that is severe, increasing, and out of proportion to the injury, a limb that feels tense and tight when it is touched, pain that becomes worse when the fingers are stretched, and numbness or weakness that was not there before all point to rising pressure inside the arm, which is compartment syndrome and belongs to immediate surgical assessment. A hand that has become pale or blue, cool to the touch, and pulseless points to the artery rather than to the compartment and is equally urgent, while a pulse that has become faster and thinner, breathing that has become rapid, skin that has become cold and clammy, and a level of consciousness that is dulling point to bleeding or to shock somewhere in the body beyond the shoulder. A record is written for every intervention and every change, including the time the sling was applied and the neurovascular findings before and after, and it is spoken aloud at handover together with the mechanism of injury and the treatments given, because the receiving team continues a story that the field began.

Definitive hospital care owns everything that restores the shoulder rather than merely supporting it, and the first of those acts is imaging. A radiograph confirms the fracture or the dislocation, shows the direction of the dislocation, and reveals fractures around the socket that change the plan, while computed tomography, after which CT is allowed, is used where the plain images leave a question about the socket or the shoulder blade. Reduction of the dislocation, internal fixation of a fracture, repair of a torn vessel, and release of a nerve under pressure are operations performed by a surgeon in an operating room with anesthesia, and none of them is a field procedure, so the lay first aider supports and transports while the trained responder works only within the protocol that authorizes a reduction. The decision about pain relief belongs to the provider authorized to prescribe it under the local protocol, and the decision about protection against tetanus and about antibiotics where they are indicated follows the same rule, with the finding that makes the decision urgent being a wound that is open, deep, or contaminated. The patient who needs surgery is moved to a trauma center where imaging, an operating room, and an intensive care unit are available, and after the acute treatment rehabilitation restores movement and strength over weeks and months, so the patient who leaves with a stiff shoulder is told that the stiffness is part of the injury and not a sign of failure.

A child with a broken collarbone may have a fracture that bends rather than breaks, and the bone may heal with remarkable speed, but the same finding in a child who cannot yet walk or whose mechanism of injury does not fit the injury should raise the question of how the injury happened at all, and that question belongs to the clinicians and to the authorities who protect children rather than to a manual. An older patient may fracture the upper end of the arm bone rather than dislocate the joint, so the arm may look deformed while the socket is intact, and the examination is recorded without forcing the joint while the imaging decides. A patient whose shoulder pain appears after a fall but whose abdomen is tender and swelling may be describing blood under the diaphragm, which irritates the nerve that refers pain to the shoulder tip, so the shoulder is examined and the abdomen is examined too. A constructed illustration, never a real patient or incident, is the young rider who lands on the point of the shoulder and is found with a painful step and no other complaint, in whom the responder supports the arm, checks the hand, checks the neck, and transports for imaging rather than pushing the collarbone flat.

To summarize, the shoulder is a girdle of small bones and shallow joints in which the position of the bone matters far less than the state of the nerves and vessels beside it. Scene safety comes first, the primary survey comes before the shoulder, and the lethal possibilities to be named are the chest injury, the spinal injury, and the neurovascular injury that accompanied the blow rather than the deformity itself. A fracture of the collarbone is common and usually forgiving, and it is treated by support of the arm in a sling with the limb left as found, while a fracture with skin pressed white or broken, a backward push of the inner end, or a lost pulse belongs to definitive hospital care at once. A dislocation is recognized by the position in which the patient holds the arm and by the inability to move it, and the nerves and vessels are examined before and after every handling because they may already be injured. A fracture of the shoulder blade is a marker of enormous force, so its discovery turns the examination toward the chest, the neck, and the head, and the same force may have injured the spine. Immobilization is performed gently in the order that supports rather than corrects, no position is ever forced, no lay first aider puts a joint back into place, and no drug, amount, route, or frequency is taken from these pages. Every number, time, pressure, temperature, and depth mentioned here is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 22 — Humerus Fractures

The responder who reaches a patient with a suspected broken upper arm arrives at a scene first and at a fracture second. Traffic is held, power is isolated by an authorized person, and fire, water, unstable structures, animals, and violence are left to those trained to control them. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, is worn for every patient, because blood carries infection through broken skin or an eye splash. The lethal possibility to name first is the injury that came with the break, since the same force can tear the artery, open the skin, and injure the chest and neck. Warmth belongs to the treatment from this first minute, and this chapter does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

Why the same bone behaves differently in each region begins with what lies beside it. The upper end carries the head in the shoulder socket, the tuberosities, and the narrow surgical neck, and it lies close to the axillary nerve and artery. The lower end widens into the condyles that form the elbow, where the brachial artery and the median nerve pass into the forearm. The provider level matters throughout, because the person who recognizes the pattern and the person who repairs it are not the same.

The mechanism of injury is the first evidence, and it is a prediction rather than a diagnosis. A fall onto the outstretched hand drives force through the wrist and elbow into the upper or lower end of the bone. A direct blow breaks the shaft where it strikes, and a twisting force produces a long spiral break, the pattern most often found with a nerve injury. A distance such as 3 meters is only a teaching illustration and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The injuries that travel with the break are what make the first minutes decisive. The neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis are examined as carefully as the arm, because the same force may have injured an organ that bleeds where no one can see. An open fracture carries heavy bleeding and deep infection, and a fragment that presses the skin white is an open fracture about to happen. A torn brachial artery may bleed into the tissues so that the arm swells and tightens while the surface wound looks small. The nerves may be bruised, stretched, or divided, and lost movement or feeling is often the only sign that the injury is more than a bone.

No examination of the arm begins until the primary survey is complete, because the airway, breathing, and circulation decide whether the patient lives long enough for the arm to matter. The survey follows the fixed order remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure. The principle of life before limb decides the order when two correct actions compete, and a deformed arm never precedes a closing airway or a filling chest. Exposure means undressing the patient enough to find every injury and then covering the patient at once, because the search for damage must not become a cause of cooling.

Once the patient is stable, the arm is assessed in a fixed order that begins with the story and ends with the nerves and vessels. The examiner looks before touching, noting the position in which the arm is held, because a patient supporting the forearm protects a break that hurts to move. The skin is inspected for a wound, a bruise, a pale area, or a place where a bone end presses the skin outward. The examiner feels gently along the bone rather than grinding it, because repeated testing of crepitation adds pain and may move a fragment against a vessel. The finding that ends the inspection is a deformity, an open wound, or skin pushed white from within, because each means the limb must be supported as it lies.

When the skin over the break is broken, the wound is covered with a clean dressing and the bone is not pushed back, because pressing a contaminated fragment inward drives infection deep and may release bleeding that was contained. A fragment that tents the skin without breaking it is treated as an open fracture about to happen, and the limb is supported as it lies. The lay first aider does not wash the wound, probe it, remove any fragment, or line the bone up, but covers it and keeps the patient warm while emergency medical services are called. A fragment or foreign object embedded in the wound is stabilized in place and the patient is moved with it, because removal may cause hemorrhage that cannot be controlled.

The wish to straighten the arm must be named plainly, because the deformity is frightening and correction looks like help. The arm is never straightened in the field, because a bone end lying against the brachial artery or a nerve may be pulled away or driven through it. A fracture is splinted in the position found, and a joint that will not move is not forced, since force can convert a closed injury into an open one or a simple break into a vascular emergency. The responder does not spring the shoulder, does not test crepitation again and again, and does not lift the arm by the hand to see how far it travels.

The neurovascular examination must not be skipped, and it asks what lies beyond the break rather than what the bone looks like. The color of the hand is compared with the other side, because a hand that has turned pale, white, or blue is a hand whose blood supply is failing. The pulse is felt at the wrist and the elbow, and capillary refill is tested by pressing the nail bed, with both recorded rather than assumed present. Sensation is tested in each territory of the hand and movement at the wrist and fingers, and the results are compared with the uninjured side and written down at once.

Each nerve that crosses the arm has a territory that can be tested with a simple request. The radial nerve straightens the wrist and fingers and supplies feeling over the back of the hand and the web between the thumb and the index finger. The median nerve turns the thumb across the palm and bends the index finger, and the ulnar nerve spreads the fingers apart and supplies feeling over the little finger. What matters is not the name of the nerve but whether a deficit exists, where it is, and the time it was found.

The radial nerve is the nerve most often injured with a break of the upper arm, and the sign it produces is unmistakable once it has been seen. It winds around the back of the shaft in a groove against the bone, so a fragment that displaces backward can bruise, stretch, or divide it without any wound. The hand that results hangs at the wrist and cannot be lifted, which is called wrist drop, and the fingers cannot be straightened at the knuckles. Feeling is lost or blunted over the back of the hand and in the web between the thumb and the index finger. A wrist drop is a finding and not a diagnosis, because it may also follow pressure of the arm against a hard edge during unconsciousness.

The nerve examination is performed and recorded before the arm is splinted, and the record protects the patient and the clinician at the same time. If a deficit is discovered only after a splint is applied, no one can tell whether the nerve was injured by the fracture or by the splint. If the deficit is written before the splint goes on, the receiving team knows the injury produced it, and the clinician who applied the splint is protected from a suspicion that is easy to raise. The examination is repeated after the splint is applied, and both findings are written on the patient, on the splint, or on tape fixed to the limb, with the time of each. Any new weakness or numbness after handling, splinting, or transport requires the examination at once, because a new deficit is a new emergency.

A break of the upper end is common in older patients after a fall from standing height, and it ranges from a crack to a head split and pushed out of place. The axillary nerve passes close to the surgical neck, so the examiner tests feeling over the outer shoulder and the power to lift the arm sideways. The blood supply to the rounded head runs through the bone just below it, so a badly displaced break may leave the head without a supply, and the surgeon may replace the head rather than fix it. Many of these breaks are treated without an operation, while a displaced break in a younger patient, an open break, or one that threatens the nerves and vessels belongs to definitive hospital care.

Because the shoulder and the upper arm share a small space, a break of the upper end is often accompanied by a dislocated shoulder or a broken collarbone. The axillary artery lies close to the surgical neck, and although it is torn less often than the nerves are injured, a tear is a limb-threatening event whose signs are a rapidly swelling shoulder, a pale cold hand, and a pulse that cannot be felt. The lay first aider supports the arm in the position found, covers any wound, keeps the patient warm, and does not pull on the arm to test the shoulder. The trained responder reassesses the hand before and after every move and reports the direction of the force.

A break of the shaft is the injury that most often produces a visible deformity, with the arm shortened, bent, and rotated. The radial nerve runs in its groove against the middle and lower shaft, and it is the structure most at risk, so the wrist and fingers are examined before anything else is done. The brachial artery runs along the inner side and is at greater risk in a break of the lower shaft, and its injury shows as a pale, cool, pulseless hand with a swelling that keeps enlarging. The shaft may also be broken by a gunshot wound, and the wounds of entry and exit tell nothing about the nerve and the artery. The trained responder immobilizes the arm as it lies, and the surgeon decides which breaks can be held in a brace.

Most radial nerve palsies that accompany a closed break of the shaft are bruises rather than divisions, and most of them recover, though the course must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. A wrist allowed to hang unsupported may become stiff and swollen, so the wrist is supported during transport by the trained responder under the local protocol. The surgeon decides whether the nerve is watched, studied with imaging, or explored during the operation that fixes the bone. The finding that makes the nerve question urgent is a pulse that has disappeared or a hand that is cold, because that combination suggests that the artery as well as the nerve is in danger.

A break of the lower end of the bone involves the elbow, and it is the pattern that most often threatens the hand, because the artery and the median nerve pass directly beside the joint. The signs that make this injury urgent are a pale, cool, pulseless hand, a hand that has lost feeling, and an elbow that grows tense while the responder watches. A break of the lower end may also be open, and the wound is covered without probing and without forcing the joint straight. The trained responder immobilizes the arm and elbow in the position found and moves the patient without delay, because a hand that is not perfused loses muscle and nerve within hours, and that interval is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

In children, the lower end of the bone is the site of a break that is common, difficult to see on a radiograph, and dangerous out of proportion to its size. The growing end of the bone is softer than the shaft, and the same force that would sprain an adult elbow may separate a fragment and injure the artery. The findings that demand immediate movement toward definitive care are a pale or cool hand, a pulse that cannot be felt, pain when the fingers are straightened, and a tense forearm. The decision about imaging, reduction, and fixation belongs to the pediatric orthopedic surgeon, and a lay first aider does not attempt to straighten a child's swollen elbow.

Compartment syndrome is the complication that turns a broken arm into a lost arm, and the responder is the person most likely to see it first. The earliest and most reliable finding is pain out of proportion to the injury and growing worse, with pain produced by gently stretching the fingers. The responder must not loosen a splint at random, must not massage the limb, and must not elevate the arm above the heart. The correct act is to remove any band that is clearly too tight, to keep the arm at heart level, to record the findings, and to move the patient to a place where the tissue can be released by fasciotomy. A pressure such as 30 millimeters of mercury is sometimes quoted as a threshold, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Immobilization is the field treatment that matters most for a broken upper arm, and its purpose is to stop movement rather than to correct the bone. The arm is supported in the position found, with the joints above and below the fracture held still, because every movement produces pain, bleeding, and risk to a nerve or vessel. The trained responder chooses the splint and applies it under the local protocol, while the lay first aider supports the arm with the body, a sling, or whatever is at hand. Padding is placed over the bony points and in the armpit before the bandage is applied, because pressure harmless over muscle can injure skin over bone. The hand is examined again after the splint is applied and at intervals during transport, and the record is updated each time.

A sling and a swathe are the usual way to hold a broken upper arm, and their two jobs are different. The sling supports the weight of the forearm and hand and takes the pull of gravity off the fracture, and it is placed so that the hand is higher than the elbow. The swathe is a broad band passed around the chest and over the injured arm, and its job is to stop the arm from swinging away and rotating. The chest band is applied without constricting the ribs, because a band tight enough to stop the arm can make breathing difficult, and a patient with a chest injury must never have the chest bound. The finding that the sling is too tight is a hand that becomes swollen, blue, or numb below the wrist, and the correction is to loosen it rather than hope.

When the break is in the shaft or near the elbow, a splint spans the shoulder and the elbow or the elbow and the wrist, so the joints above and below the break are controlled together. A rigid support, a padded board, or a folded magazine is placed along the outer side of the arm and secured with broad bands rather than narrow cord. A break near the elbow is immobilized with the elbow at the angle at which it was found, and the elbow is not forced open or closed to make the splint easier. The trained responder checks the hand after every band is tied, because each band is a chance to make the splint too tight. The finding that requires the splint to be released at once is a hand that has lost its warmth, its color, or its feeling.

The position for transport depends on the patient's other injuries, and comfort is a consideration rather than the rule. A patient who is awake, breathing well, and free of injury to the chest, abdomen, or spine may sit up, because sitting reduces the pull of the arm on the shoulder. A patient who is pale, restless, confused, or whose circulation is failing is laid flat with the legs raised where the protocol allows, and the arm is kept supported across the body. The hand is examined repeatedly during transport, and color, warmth, pulse, movement, and feeling are compared with the findings before the journey. The finding that requires the receiving team to be warned in advance is a hand that has lost its pulse or a falling level of consciousness.

A patient with a broken arm is a patient at risk of cold, and the risk is greater when the patient is bleeding, undressed, lying on the ground, or waiting in a vehicle. Cold makes the blood clot poorly, deepens shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm, so warming is part of the treatment of the fracture. The responder removes wet clothing, covers the patient with blankets, coats, or foil, and insulates the patient from the ground, because much of the heat is lost downward. A patient who has stopped shivering while still cold is a patient whose warming has already failed. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the line at which cold becomes dangerous, and that figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Pain from a broken upper arm is severe, and the responder's first and most effective treatment for it is immobilization, because a limb that does not move hurts far less. The decision to give a medicine for pain belongs to the provider authorized to make it and to the local protocol, and the substance, the amount, the route, and the timing are set there rather than here. The trained responder may give a medicine only where the service authorizes it, and the lay first aider offers comfort, position, warmth, and reassurance instead. The finding that makes relief urgent is a patient whose pain is increasing despite a splint that has not moved, because that pattern suggests that swelling inside the limb is rising. The record must carry what was given, when it was given, and by whom.

An open fracture of the upper arm raises two decisions that belong to the prescriber and to the protocol, and the responder's part is to recognize the wound and to move the patient. Protection against tetanus is considered for every open fracture, and the decision depends on the vaccination history and the nature of the wound, so the substance and the schedule belong to the local protocol. Antibiotics are considered in the same way, and the finding that makes the decision urgent is a wound that is deep, contaminated, or produced by a bite or a projectile. The responder does not irrigate the wound, does not apply a substance to it, and does not close it, because those acts belong to definitive care. The wound is covered with a clean dressing, the limb is splinted as it lies, and the patient is kept warm and moved without delay.

Bleeding from a wound near the shoulder or in the armpit is difficult to control, because the vessel lies where a tourniquet cannot reach and where a dressing cannot press evenly. The lay first aider presses directly on the wound with a clean dressing and the flat of the hand, adds layers rather than lifting the first one, and keeps the pressure on. The trained responder may pack the wound firmly to the bleeding point where the protocol teaches the technique, because packing along the track can succeed where a dressing over the surface fails. A tourniquet may be applied to the arm only where the local protocol authorizes it, because the upper arm is a short and muscular segment in which a tourniquet easily becomes ineffective. Once a tourniquet has controlled the bleeding it is not loosened in the field, and the time it was applied is written on the patient where the receiving team cannot miss it.

Definitive hospital care owns everything that repairs rather than contains, and knowing where that line lies is part of competence for every responder. Imaging with radiographs and, where it is needed, computed tomography shows the pattern of the break and the position of the fragments. Reduction, fixation with plates and screws or with a nail inside the bone, fixation with an external frame, replacement of the shoulder joint, repair of a torn artery, exploration of a nerve, debridement of dead tissue, and fasciotomy are all surgical acts. The field responder's contribution is the shortest safe journey, the warm patient, the controlled bleeding, the splinted limb, and the record of the nerve examination. The finding that should change the destination is a hand without a pulse or a wound that keeps bleeding, because those mean the patient needs a facility with a surgeon.

The fractures that require an operation are recognized by their behavior rather than by their name. An open fracture requires surgical cleaning and stabilization, and a fracture with a lost pulse or a cold hand requires an urgent examination of the artery. A break that cannot be held in line by a splint, a break with a fragment between the ends, and a break of the shaft with a break of the forearm on the same side all point toward fixation. A displaced break of the upper end in a younger patient, a break that has split the joint surface, and a break that has left the head without a blood supply may be fixed or replaced, and the choice belongs to the surgeon. A break that injures the radial nerve, that is accompanied by a torn artery, or that fails to unite after a period of observation also belongs to the operating room.

The complications that follow a broken upper arm are the reason the record matters as much as the first splint. A radial nerve palsy recorded before splinting can be followed honestly, because the receiving team knows where it began and can judge whether it is improving. The responder's part is to keep the limb still in the position found, keep the patient warm, protect the wound, record the nerve examination and the time, and hand over with a story that has no gaps. The handover names the mechanism of injury, the time of the injury, the position of the arm, the nerve and vessel findings before and after splinting, and every change observed. The finding that must never be omitted is any deterioration in the hand or in the patient, because the receiving team can act on a change that is spoken.

A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and not as a real patient, shows how the order of this chapter works. A rider is thrown from a bicycle onto the outstretched arm, and the scene is held against traffic before anyone kneels beside the patient. The pulse at the wrist is weak, the fingers are cool, and the responder writes on the tape that the wrist drop was present before any splint was applied and the time it was found. The arm is supported in the position found, a sling and a swathe are applied without binding the chest, and the receiving team is told the mechanism and the nerve finding. The point of the illustration is that the responder never made the arm look normal and never guessed at the nerve.

Nothing in this chapter authorizes a lay first aider to do more than support, cover, warm, and send, because every repair of this bone demands training, imaging, and an operating room. The trained responder and the paramedic act within a protocol that names the splints they may use, the medicines they may give, and the tourniquets they may apply. The nurse and the physician in a district hospital stabilize the patient, control the pain within their authority, protect the wound, and arrange the transfer to a trauma center. Every number in this chapter, whether a time, a pressure, a temperature, a depth, or a distance, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

To summarize, a fracture of the upper arm is treated by protecting the limb and the patient rather than by correcting the bone, and the scene is made safe before any hand is laid on either. The bone breaks at its upper end, along its shaft, and at its lower end, and each region carries its own risks, with the axillary nerve at the shoulder, the radial nerve along the shaft, and the artery and the median nerve beside the elbow. The lethal possibilities are the hemorrhage that will not stop, the open wound over the bone, the torn artery that leaves a cold and pulseless hand, and the chest, neck, and spinal injuries that arrived with the same force. The radial nerve is examined and the finding of wrist drop is written down before the splint is applied, because that record protects the patient from a missed injury and the clinician from a false accusation. The arm is splinted in the position found, never straightened and never forced, with the joints above and below the break supported and the hand examined after every band. Every number in this chapter, whether a time, a pressure, a temperature, a depth, or a distance, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 23 — Elbow Injuries

The elbow is a joint where a small injury can destroy the whole limb, because the bones, the artery, and the three nerves that cross it lie in a tight envelope with no room to swell. Scene safety comes before the patient, so traffic, fire, electricity, water, animals, violence, and the patient's own blood are dealt with before a hand is laid on the arm. The lethal possibility to name first is an injury that has interrupted the blood supply to the hand, and the finding that reveals it is a hand that is pale, cool, pulseless at the wrist, and painful while the fingers no longer move. This chapter names the provider level for every intervention: the sling of the lay first aider, the splint of the trained responder or the paramedic, and the surgery of definitive hospital care. It is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work. A small injury here can leave a stiff and useless arm, so the responder moves the joint less and the patient sooner.

The elbow is not one joint but a meeting of three bones, the humerus above and the radius and the ulna below, held in one tight capsule. The brachial artery passes in front of the joint and divides below it into the arteries of the forearm, while the median, the ulnar, and the radial nerves pass around the joint to supply the hand. The ulnar nerve lies in a shallow groove behind the inner side of the elbow, and the radial nerve winds around the bone above the joint, where a displaced fracture can stretch it. Because the capsule is tight and the space inside it is small, swelling after a fracture or a dislocation raises the pressure quickly, and that pressure squeezes the vessels and nerves within the same envelope. There is almost no muscle over the prominences of the elbow, only skin and a thin layer of fat, so a bone end can open the skin from inside and turn a closed fracture into an open one.

The mechanism of injury is the first evidence at the elbow, because the direction of the force predicts which structure has been damaged. A fall onto the outstretched hand drives force up the forearm into the joint and is the classic cause of a fracture of the radial head, of a break just above the joint, and of a dislocation. A direct blow to the point of the elbow breaks the olecranon, the bony tip that the triceps muscle pulls on, and that fracture may open the skin over it. A fall from a height or a vehicle collision delivers far more energy and produces fractures that are comminuted, meaning broken into several pieces, with damage to the artery and the nerves. A mechanism such as a fall from 3 meters is a teaching illustration whose height and meaning must be checked against the guideline in force and the local protocol, because the energy absorbed depends on the surface and on the body's position. The responder who hears the mechanism is already looking for a specific injury rather than examining at random.

The primary survey in its fixed order of airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure is not abandoned because the arm looks terrible. Life comes before limb when two correct actions compete, so a patient whose airway is obstructed or whose circulation is failing is treated before the elbow is examined, and the responder says this order aloud so that no helper pulls on the arm. Catastrophic bleeding from an open elbow wound is controlled by firm direct pressure with a clean dressing and, where the trained responder or the paramedic works under a protocol, by packing the wound or by a tourniquet above the injury. A foreign body embedded in the elbow is stabilized in place and never removed in the field, because removal may release hemorrhage that cannot be controlled and may cut a vessel or a nerve that is still intact. The finding that tells the responder that pressure has failed is blood that soaks through every layer, a swelling that grows while the hand is held in place, or a level of consciousness that is dulling. An open fracture of the elbow is a surgical emergency, and the field dressing protects the wound but does not clean it, does not reduce it, and does not close it.

The neurovascular examination of the elbow is performed before the arm is splinted and again after every intervention, because a record made after the splint cannot tell anyone what the splint changed. The pulse is felt at the wrist on the thumb side, which is the radial artery, and the responder compares it with the other arm. The color and warmth of the hand are compared with the other hand, and the time it takes for color to return after a fingertip is pressed and released is observed. Sensation is tested in the areas each nerve owns, on the thumb side of the palm for the median nerve, on the little finger for the ulnar nerve, and between the thumb and the index finger for the radial nerve. Movement is tested by asking the patient to bend the fingers, to spread them, to oppose the thumb to the little finger, and to bend the wrist upward. The classic signs of compromise are pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, and coldness, and pain out of proportion to the wound and increased by passively straightening the fingers is the earliest and most reliable. The finding that makes this an emergency is any loss of pulse, new numbness or weakness, or a hand that is colder and paler than its partner, and a pulse that can still be felt never proves that the limb is safe.

Fractures of the distal humerus, the part of the upper arm bone that forms the upper half of the joint, most often threaten the limb, because the bone splits between the two columns that support the joint. A fall on the elbow or on the outstretched hand in an older patient with thin bone commonly produces this fracture, and the arm is swollen, deformed, and painful, with movement refused. In a young child the fracture occurs just above the joint, where the bone is still growing, and it is called a supracondylar fracture; the child cries when the arm is moved, and the pulse at the wrist may be lost later as swelling increases. The brachial artery and the median nerve pass in front of this bone, so a displaced fracture can injure either, and the finding is a pale, cool hand with a weak or absent pulse and numbness on the palm side. A fracture that has opened the skin, or one whose pieces are far apart, cannot be treated with a splint alone, and definitive hospital care owns the decision about how it will be held. The responder does not reduce the fracture, does not pull on the forearm to make the arm straight, and does not test the joint through its range, because each act can convert a repairable injury into a lost limb.

Fractures of the radial head, the disc of bone at the top of the radius that turns when the palm is turned, are often the mildest-looking injuries at the elbow and the easiest to underestimate. They follow a fall onto the outstretched hand, and the patient reports pain on the outer side of the elbow that becomes sharp when the forearm is turned, with the joint held slightly bent. The swelling may be modest and the deformity absent, so a responder who looks only for a crooked arm will miss the fracture, and the tenderness is found by pressing gently over the outer side of the joint. Fractures of the olecranon, the bony point into which the triceps inserts, follow a direct blow, and the muscle pulls the broken piece upward so the patient cannot straighten the elbow against resistance, while the thin skin over the point is frequently torn. Definitive hospital care owns the imaging, which may include a computed tomography scan, or CT, and the decision about fixing or replacing the broken bone, because an untreated fracture that blocks the joint leaves a stiff elbow. The lay first aider covers an open wound with a clean dressing, supports the arm in the position found, and sends the patient for surgical care without exploring the wound.

A dislocation of the elbow means that the bones have lost their normal relationship, and the posterior dislocation, in which the forearm bones move behind the humerus, is by far the most common. It follows a fall onto the outstretched hand with the elbow slightly bent, and the arm is held in a fixed partial bend that the patient will not allow to be changed. The findings are a shortened forearm, a bony prominence that gives the elbow a squared-off shape, a hollow where the tip of the elbow normally sits, and severe pain with a refusal to move. The vessels and nerves are stretched across the displaced bones, so the pulse at the wrist may be weak or absent and the fingers may tingle or feel numb. Reduction, which is the act of putting the joint back into its place, belongs to definitive hospital care and is performed by a physician with sedation, analgesia, and preparation for what may be found. It is never a field procedure for a lay first aider, a trained responder, or a paramedic, because a dislocation may carry a fracture, a torn artery, or a trapped nerve, and an unskilled pull can lose the limb.

A dislocation with an associated fracture is the injury that most deserves the respect of every responder, because the combination is greater than the sum of its parts. The most familiar form is a posterior dislocation in which the head of the radius and a piece of the ulna are also broken, a pattern that leaves the joint unstable and the blood supply to the bone at risk. Another form is a dislocation with a fracture of the humerus at the joint, and another is the open dislocation in which the bone has torn the skin, and each requires imaging, anesthesia, and often an operation. The finding that suggests an associated fracture is a dislocation without the usual shape, a bony fragment that can be felt, a wound that communicates with the joint, or a deficit that does not improve when the arm is supported. Definitive hospital care owns the reduction and the repair, and images taken before and after the reduction decide the operation that follows. A first responder who tries to reduce such an elbow because the deformity looks like a simple dislocation may push a bone fragment into a vessel and may be the reason the limb is lost.

The position of comfort is the position in which the patient holds the injured arm when it is left alone. The lay first aider supports that position rather than changing it, with a folded blanket or a pillow beneath the arm, and then a sling to take the weight of the forearm. The position that must never be forced is any position the patient resists, and above all the fully straight arm that a responder might try to produce to make the limb look normal. Forcing the elbow straight may drive bone through the skin, tear the artery, and stretch a nerve beyond recovery, and pulling the forearm to reduce a dislocation does the same damage. A child who will not use the arm after being lifted by the hand may have a slipped radial head rather than a fracture, and no lay first aider may attempt to put it back, because that maneuver is a clinical act. Immobilization for transport is performed in the position found, with padding over the bony points and a rigid support from the upper arm to the wrist. The device is not placed over an open wound and is not tightened so much that the fingers become pale or numb, because a splint that stops the circulation has done the work of a tourniquet. The pulse, color, warmth, and sensation are rechecked after the splint is secured, and a pale or pulseless hand means the splint must be loosened at once.

The assessment of the elbow is not an act performed once at the roadside but a rhythm repeated from the first contact to the handover, because the injury can worsen while the responder watches. The examination is repeated in the same order every time, with the pulse, the color and warmth of the hand, the sensation in the three nerve areas, the movement of the fingers, and the pain reported by the patient. It is repeated after a dressing, a sling, a splint, a move onto a stretcher, and after any change in the patient's condition, because an intervention that helps one patient can harm another. The level of consciousness, the breathing, and the pulse of the patient are recorded with the same discipline, since a patient whose hand remains well but whose circulation is failing elsewhere has a new priority. The finding that returns the responder to the beginning of the primary survey is any deterioration at all, and the finding that marks a worsening limb is a weaker pulse, a colder hand, or sharper and more diffuse pain. A time such as 30 minutes between the first and the second examination is a teaching illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the interval suited to one service may not suit another.

Compartment syndrome turns a treatable elbow injury into a destroyed forearm, and it happens when pressure inside the closed envelopes of tissue around the muscles rises until blood can no longer enter. The forearm is divided into compartments by sheets of tough tissue, and swelling after a fracture, a dislocation, or a crush injury raises the pressure within them, so muscle and nerve begin to die while the skin remains intact and the pulse remains palpable.
