The earliest and most reliable finding is pain out of proportion to the injury, increased by passively straightening the fingers and not relieved by the support the responder has applied, with a forearm that feels tense and wood-like. Numbness, weakness, and a hand that becomes pale and cold follow, but they follow late, and a responder who waits for them has waited too long, while the presence of a pulse never rules the condition out. The responder removes any bandage or splint that constricts the limb, keeps the arm at the level of the heart rather than raised above it, keeps the patient warm, and moves the patient to definitive care with the history of the pain. Definitive hospital care owns the measurement of pressure within the compartments and the operation called a fasciotomy, in which the tight sheets are opened to let the muscle expand.

A wound over the elbow is treated with firm and uninterrupted pressure, a clean covering, and no probing of the track with a finger or an instrument. The trained responder may irrigate a contaminated wound where the local protocol authorizes it, using the technique and the volume the protocol sets. An open fracture is covered with a clean or sterile dressing and splinted in the position found, and the exposed bone is not pushed back beneath the skin, because pushing it in drives contamination deeper. The decision about protection against tetanus is made at the first contact by the provider authorized to make it, and it depends on the vaccination history of the patient and the nature of the wound, while the substance and amount belong to the prescriber. The decision about antibiotics is made in the same way, and the finding that makes it urgent is a wound that is deep, contaminated, or connected to a broken bone. The finding that marks the wound as a surgical problem is bone visible in the wound, a wound that communicates with the joint, or bleeding that continues despite correct pressure.

A torn artery at the elbow can kill the patient as well as lose the limb, and its findings are blood that spurts or soaks through every dressing, a swelling that expands while the responder watches, and a hand that is pale, cold, and insensate. A tourniquet above the elbow is the field answer to bleeding from the arm that cannot be controlled by direct pressure and packing, and it belongs to the trained responder or paramedic working under a protocol. Once a tourniquet has controlled the bleeding it is not loosened in the field, and the time it was applied is written on the patient where the receiving team cannot miss it, because that time decides how the circulation is restored. An interval such as 2 hours is often named as the point at which the risk to muscle and nerve becomes serious, and that interval must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because tolerance differs with temperature and with the patient. The finding that tells the responder a tourniquet is not enough is bleeding that continues below a correctly tightened device, and the finding that the patient is losing the battle is a level of consciousness that dulls while the pulse climbs. A tourniquet is never a reason to delay transport, and it is never relaxed to see whether the bleeding has stopped, because the clot behind it may not hold.

Damage to a nerve at the elbow may be present from the moment of injury and may be discovered only by an examination performed deliberately, and the record of that examination is as important as any treatment given in the field. Injury to the median nerve weakens the muscles that bend the thumb and fingers, so the patient may be unable to oppose the thumb to the little finger, while sensation is lost over the palm side of the thumb and index finger. Injury to the ulnar nerve weakens the small muscles of the hand, so the fingers cannot be spread with force, the little finger drifts away, and sensation is lost along the little finger and the edge of the hand. Injury to the radial nerve produces a wrist drop, in which the hand hangs at the wrist and cannot be lifted, with numbness between the thumb and the index finger on the back of the hand. The examination is recorded before the arm is splinted and repeated after, because a deficit that appears only after immobilization points to the splint, while a deficit present from the beginning must be known to the receiving team. Nothing done in the field restores a torn nerve, and the exploration and repair of a nerve belong to definitive hospital care, where the decision is made with the operating microscope.

A young child with a supracondylar fracture may hold the arm still and cry only when it is moved, and a child who refuses to use an arm after a fall must be treated as seriously injured until a clinician decides otherwise, because swelling can close the blood supply to the hand. A child who has been lifted or swung by the hand may have a slipped radial head rather than a fracture, and that child needs clinical assessment rather than a lay attempt at manipulation. An older patient with thin bone may sustain a distal humerus fracture broken into many pieces from a fall at standing height, and the same patient may have a dislocated elbow with little deformity and a great deal of pain. A patient who has been drinking alcohol, or whose level of consciousness is reduced, cannot be relied on to report pain or numbness, so the physical findings of pulse, color, warmth, and swelling carry the whole assessment. An injury at the elbow is rarely the only injury in a patient who has fallen from a height or been in a collision, so the patient is examined from head to toe when the primary survey allows. A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient or incident, is a worker who falls from a ladder onto an outstretched hand and complains only of the elbow, while tenderness over the wrist is found because the mechanism demanded the search.

Pain is real, and poorly treated pain worsens the patient's condition and makes every examination harder, so the relief of pain is a clinical objective rather than a courtesy. The decision to give analgesia, the choice of substance, the amount, the route, and the frequency belong to the provider authorized to prescribe under the local protocol, and this manual names only the decision. Protection against tetanus, the choice of antibiotics, the decision to give oxygen, and fluids given into a vein are decisions of the same kind, made by the clinician authorized to make them under the local protocol. Hypothermia travels with every serious limb injury and must be prevented from the first minute, because a cold patient bleeds more, feels more pain, and tolerates the journey less well. Protection begins by moving the patient onto a dry insulating layer, removing wet clothing without exposing the wound, and covering the patient, including the injured arm. A body temperature such as 35 degrees Celsius is often described as the point at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line differs with age and with the way the temperature is measured. A patient who has stopped shivering while still cold is a patient in whom the warming has failed, and that finding is reported rather than noted.

The record is part of the treatment, and at the elbow it carries information that no receiving team can reconstruct from the arm alone. The handover states the mechanism and the time of injury, the position in which the limb was found, the nerve and pulse findings before and after each dressing, sling, and splint, and every tourniquet with its time. Definitive hospital care owns everything that repairs rather than supports, and the physician orders the radiographs and, where the fracture is complex, a computed tomography scan, or CT, while magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, answers the remaining questions. In hospital a dislocation is reduced with analgesia, sedation, or anesthesia and with imaging before and after, and unstable pieces are fixed internally with plates and screws. A damaged artery or nerve is repaired by a surgeon with the appropriate training, a compartment syndrome is treated by fasciotomy, and the intensive care unit, or ICU, receives the patient whose injuries reach beyond the limb. The surgeon decides when the elbow may begin to move and what rehabilitation follows, because a joint kept still for too long becomes stiff and a joint moved too early loses the repair.

Urgent hospital evaluation is required for any deformity, any wound over the elbow, any inability to move the joint, any tense or increasing swelling, any loss of pulse, sensation, or strength in the hand, and any severe pain. It is required for every dislocation and every suspected fracture, because the joint cannot be examined properly without images and because a missed injury leaves a permanently stiff arm. It is required for the child who will not use the arm and for the older patient whose bone has broken with little force, because both injuries are more serious than they appear. The destination is chosen before the patient is moved, and it is the nearest facility that can image the joint and provide surgical care, which may be a trauma center or a district hospital that stabilizes and transfers. The mistakes that cost limbs are few and repeating: forcing the joint straight, pulling the forearm to reduce a dislocation, binding a splint so tightly that the fingers lose their color and pulse, probing a wound, and failing to repeat the examination. The finding that makes evaluation an emergency rather than an urgency is any neurovascular deficit, any open wound, or a growing swelling, because the interval in which the limb can still be saved is measured in hours.

To summarize, the elbow is a joint where a small injury can destroy the limb, because the artery, the nerves, and the bones that cross it lie within a tight envelope, and the first duty at the scene is safety and the control of hemorrhage. The mechanism of injury predicts the damage, and the fractures that matter are the distal humerus, the radial head, and the olecranon, together with dislocations and the dislocation with an associated fracture. The neurovascular examination is performed before and after every intervention, recorded with the time, and repeated until handover, because a pulse that is present does not prove that the limb is safe and the earliest sign of disaster is pain out of proportion. The position of comfort is supported and the position the patient resists is never forced, the arm is splinted in the position found, no dislocation or fracture is reduced in the field, and no exposed bone is pushed back into a wound. Pain relief, protection against tetanus, antibiotics, oxygen, and fluids are decisions of the provider authorized to prescribe under the local protocol, and no substance, amount, route, or frequency may be taken from this chapter. Hypothermia is prevented from the first minute, the record travels with the patient, and every figure named here must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Definitive hospital care owns the imaging, the reduction, the repair of vessels and nerves, the fixation of bones, and the operation for compartment syndrome, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law where you work.

# Chapter 24 — Forearm Fractures

A forearm fracture can look dramatic and still be the least of a patient's problems, and it can look almost innocent while a compartment inside the limb is filling with pressure that will kill muscle if nobody recognizes it. Before any of that is considered, the scene must be made safe, and the hazards are the ordinary ones of traffic, fire, live electricity, unstable structures, animals, violence, and the patient's own blood, which carries infection into any break in the responder's skin. The lethal possibility to be named first is an open forearm fracture that has torn the radial or the ulnar artery, and the finding that reveals it is blood that soaks dressing after dressing, a swelling that grows while the responder watches, or a hand that has become pale and cold beyond the wound. The other lethal possibility is bleeding inside the closed space of the forearm, whose early finding is pain far greater than the injury appears to explain, with a limb that feels tight and hard rather than merely swollen. The response begins with personal protective equipment, which means gloves at the least and eye protection where it is available, and it continues with the primary survey in the fixed order remembered as ABCDE, because a fracture of the forearm never outranks an airway that is closing or a chest that is not moving air. The provider level is named for every act in this chapter, since a lay first aider may cover, support, and keep a patient warm, while the trained responder, the emergency medical technician, or the paramedic may splint with equipment and carry the patient toward a hospital, and definitive hospital care owns the reduction, the fixation, and the release of a compartment under pressure. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

The mechanism of injury is the first piece of clinical evidence because it predicts what the eye cannot see, and the forearm has a short list of repeating mechanisms. A fall onto the outstretched hand drives force up through the wrist into the radius, and a direct blow across the raised forearm, the kind taken while shielding the head, breaks the ulna alone in what is often described as a nightstick fracture. A vehicle collision, a fall from a height greater than 2 meters, a machinery injury, or a gunshot wound produces the both-bone fracture and also predicts damage to the chest, the head, and the abdomen that must be sought in the same patient. A figure such as that height is offered only as a teaching illustration and must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services set their own thresholds for a dangerous fall. A twisting force applied while the hand is fixed, as happens when a sleeve is caught in a rotating machine, produces a fracture with a rotational component that no splint applied in the field can correct. An illustration constructed for teaching, and identified as a construction rather than a real patient or incident, is the cyclist who lands on an extended arm and holds the forearm across the chest, where the visible bend is only part of the story because the same fall may have broken a small wrist bone that will not show for weeks. The mechanism also decides the urgency, since a low-energy fall and a high-energy collision demand different degrees of suspicion.

The forearm is not a single bone but a pair that works as a unit, and understanding that unit separates a useful assessment from a guess. The radius lies on the thumb side and the ulna on the little-finger side, and between them runs the interosseous membrane, a sheet of tough tissue that binds the bones and carries part of the force traveling from the hand to the elbow. Together with the joints at the wrist and at the elbow, the pair of bones and the membrane form a ring, and a ring that breaks at a single point usually breaks somewhere else as well. That is why a fracture of the ulna may be accompanied by a dislocation of the head of the radius at the elbow, and why a fracture of the radius may be accompanied by a dislocation of the joint between the bones at the wrist. The same logic explains the shape of the limb, because the radius rotates around the ulna when the palm is turned up or down, and a fracture that alters the length or the rotation of either bone changes the way the whole forearm moves. The finding that should make the responder suspicious of a second injury is tenderness or deformity far from the visible break, at the elbow or at the wrist, and the responder reports it rather than testing it by moving the joint.

The distinction between a fracture of a single bone and a fracture of both bones is the distinction between an injury that a splint can hold and an injury that changes the shape of the limb. In an isolated fracture of the ulna or of the radius, the other bone acts as an internal splint, so the deformity is often modest and the limb may keep a nearly normal outline. In a both-bone fracture nothing remains to hold the length or the rotation, and the forearm shortens, bends, and twists, so the limb takes on a shape that everyone at the scene can see. The muscles that cross the fracture pull the fragments toward each other and rotate them, which is why a both-bone fracture that looks acceptable on the ground may look unacceptable once the patient relaxes or once the limb is lifted. The responder must never straighten a severely deformed fracture to make it look normal, and the reason is not tidiness but the risk to the vessels and the nerves that lie close to the bone and can be torn by a fragment moved without control. The correct act is to splint the limb in the position found and to let the reduction belong to definitive hospital care, where it is performed with imaging and with preparation for the anesthesia the procedure requires. An isolated fracture is not a minor injury either, because the same fall that breaks a single bone can dislocate the joint at the end of the other.

Assessment begins with the eyes and the hands and never with a probe, because the wound and the swelling are the only evidence the field will offer. The responder looks at the whole limb rather than at the point of pain, compares it with the other side, and notes the contour, the length, the rotation of the hand at rest, and any wound that communicates with the fracture. An open fracture is present when bone is visible or when a wound lies over the line of the bone, and it turns a closed fracture into an emergency of contamination as well as of structure. The responder does not push a protruding fragment back beneath the skin, because the act drives contamination deeper and can tear what is still intact, and instead covers the wound with a clean or sterile dressing and builds the splint around it. Bleeding is controlled with direct pressure over a dressing and never with a finger inside the wound, and an embedded object is stabilized in place and never removed in the field, because removal may release hemorrhage that cannot be controlled or divide a structure the object is currently splinting. Swelling is expected and is not itself the danger, but a swelling that is tight, tense, and growing, with skin that shines and does not pit when pressed, is the finding that changes the whole plan. Every one of these observations is repeated after the limb has been splinted, because a splint that is too tight can create the very problem the responder is trying to prevent.

The neurovascular examination is the part of the assessment that decides how fast the patient must travel, and it is performed before and after every intervention. The responder feels for the pulse at the wrist on the thumb side and on the little-finger side, because the arteries of the forearm supply the hand along separate routes and either can be lost while the other still beats. The color, the warmth, and the refill of the fingertips are compared with the uninjured hand, and the time taken for color to return after the nail is pressed is noted as a rough guide rather than a measurement. Sensation is tested in the territory of each nerve that crosses the forearm, which means the pad of the index finger, the pad of the little finger, and the web space between the thumb and the index finger, and the patient is asked whether feeling is normal, reduced, or absent. Movement is tested by asking the patient to bend and straighten the fingers, to spread them, and to touch the thumb to each fingertip, because a tendon divided at the wrist can leave the fingers limp. The finding that must be reported at once is a hand that has become pale, cold, numb, or weak after a splint was applied, because it means the splint, the swelling, or the fracture itself is compromising the blood supply or the nerves. A pulse that can still be felt does not exclude a compartment syndrome, and a hand without a pulse is a surgical emergency that belongs to definitive hospital care and not to a second attempt at splinting.

Several structures cross the forearm in close company with the bones, and each can be injured by the same force that broke the bone. The radial and the ulnar arteries run along the bones, and a fragment can tear or compress either, while the interosseous membrane between the bones can be torn and can allow either bone to ride over the other. The median, the ulnar, and the radial nerves travel through the forearm and supply the muscles of the fingers and the thumb, so a nerve injury may show itself first as a hand that cannot grip or as a patch of skin that has gone numb. Tendons pass through the same region on their way to the hand, and a laceration that reaches a tendon can disable a finger even when the bone is untouched and the wound looks small. A nerve or a tendon that has been divided cannot be repaired in the field, and a responder who believes that moving the fingers has restored function has learned nothing and risked much. The field contribution is to record what was found before the splint and after it, to immobilize the limb so that torn structures are not pulled further, and to carry the patient to a place where a surgeon can explore and repair. The finding that should raise the priority is a hand that never had normal feeling or movement from the moment of injury.

Compartment syndrome is the complication of a forearm fracture that must be anticipated rather than discovered, and it is a surgical emergency rather than a late observation. The muscles of the forearm are divided into compartments by sheets of tough tissue that do not stretch, and a fracture, a crush, or a tight dressing can raise the pressure inside a compartment until the small vessels feeding the muscle are closed. The earliest and most reliable sign is pain out of proportion to the injury that does not settle with the comfort measures a responder can offer, together with pain that appears when the fingers are gently straightened by someone else. The limb feels tense and hard, the skin may look shiny, and the patient often describes a deep ache different from the pain of the broken bone itself. Numbness in the territory of a nerve and weakness of the fingers come next, and pallor, coolness, and loss of the pulse come last, which means a hand with a good pulse can still be losing its muscle. The responder must never wait for the pulse to disappear before acting, because by then the muscle may already be dead and the patient may be developing the systemic illness that follows the breakdown of muscle. The finding that should trigger escalation is any pain increasing despite splinting and despite the measures the protocol allows, and the response is to remove anything encircling the limb, to keep the limb at the level of the heart, and to move the patient to a hospital without delay. The measurement of pressure inside a compartment, and its release by cutting the tight tissue, belong to definitive hospital care and are never a field procedure.

Elevation is a comfort measure with a narrow place in the care of a forearm fracture, and the rule changes as soon as a compartment is suspected. A closed fracture with swelling but no tense compartment may be supported on a pillow and raised a little to reduce edema, which belongs to the lay first aider as much as to the trained responder, provided the hand stays visible and the fingers keep their color and feeling. Once a compartment is suspected, the limb is kept at the level of the heart rather than raised above it, because raising the limb lowers the pressure that drives blood into the muscle and can make a struggling compartment worse. Nothing that encircles the limb is left in place, so rings are removed from the fingers before swelling makes that impossible, and any bandage tight enough to leave a mark is released by the provider who applied it. A ring that cannot be removed, a splint that has become tight, and a bandage cutting into the skin are findings to report, and each is a reason to look again at the hand. Cold applied to the limb may be used in some services as a comfort measure, but that decision belongs to the trained responder and to the local protocol. The decision about pressure inside a compartment and about the operation that releases it belongs to definitive hospital care, and no amount of elevation substitutes for that operation.

Pain relief for a forearm fracture is a clinical decision and not an instruction that can be carried away from a page. The finding that makes it urgent is a patient in severe pain, a patient whose pain is increasing inside a splint, or a patient whose age or condition makes distress dangerous, and the choice of substance, amount, route, and timing belong to the provider authorized to prescribe and to the local protocol in force. The lay first aider contributes by supporting the limb, keeping the patient still and warm, and asking the trained responder for help with pain rather than offering anything from a bag. Protection against tetanus is decided by the provider authorized to make that decision under the local protocol, because the answer depends on the wound, the contamination, and the patient's vaccination history, and no reader should take that decision from this chapter. Antibiotics are considered when a fracture is open or a wound is deep, contaminated, or caused by a bite, and again the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber and the guideline rather than to the field responder. Oxygen, where available, is given only under the protocol that authorizes it, because that decision rests on the patient's breathing and circulation and on the local rule. Splinting itself is among the most effective comfort measures in the field, because a limb held still hurts less, and that is a contribution the lay first aider can make with a pillow, a board, or a folded magazine.

Immobilization is the central field act for a forearm fracture, and it must hold the elbow, the forearm, and the wrist as a single unit because the bones rotate against each other when the hand turns. The lay first aider begins by leaving the limb in the position found and supporting it with both hands while emergency medical services are called, because a limb left unsupported pulls on the fracture with its own weight. Padding is placed under whatever rigid object is available, which may be a pillow, a rolled magazine, or a folded blanket, and it is placed so that the bony points of the elbow and the wrist are cushioned rather than pressed. The forearm is then bound to that support above and below the fracture, with the bindings firm enough to hold the limb and loose enough that the fingers keep their color and warmth. A sling is added afterward to carry the weight of the forearm from the shoulder, and the hand is left visible so the fingers can be watched for color, warmth, and movement during the journey. The lay first aider does not pull the limb straight, does not push a bone back into place, does not remove an embedded object, and does not give anything by mouth unless the local protocol directs otherwise, because those acts belong to other hands. The finding that tells the lay first aider the splint is too tight is a hand that has become pale, blue, cold, or numb, and the response is to loosen the binding at once and call for the trained responder.

The trained responder or paramedic applies the same principles with equipment the service authorizes, and the aim is a limb held securely enough to travel and lightly enough to keep the hand alive. A rigid splint, a molded splint, or a vacuum splint is padded and applied along the line of the forearm, and where the local protocol allows, the position of function is used so the hand is supported with the wrist slightly extended rather than left to hang. The splint extends from the upper arm to the hand so the elbow cannot bend and the wrist cannot rotate, because a splint that stops at the wrist allows the very movement that displaces the fracture. The bindings are checked by touch and by the appearance of the hand, and the hand is examined again for color, warmth, pulse, and feeling before the patient is moved. The responder records the time the splint was applied and the state of the hand at that moment, because the receiving team must compare what they find with what the field found. A fracture that cannot be held because of extreme deformity, or a limb whose circulation is failing, is a reason to move faster rather than to apply more force, and any adjustment belongs to the protocol and to the clinician who can be reached. Traction applied to the forearm in the field is not a technique of this manual, because pulling on a fractured forearm can damage nerves and vessels and turn a closed injury into an open one.

Definitive care begins with imaging and with the decision about how the fracture will be held while it heals. A radiograph of the forearm is taken from different directions and usually includes the elbow and the wrist, because the second injury at the end of a broken bone is easy to miss. Computed tomography may be used when a fracture reaches a joint, when the pattern is complex, or when the surgeon needs to plan the fixation, and it belongs entirely to the hospital and to the clinician who orders it. A fracture of both bones that is displaced, unstable, or rotated needs an operation to restore the length and alignment of the forearm, and this is usually done with plates and screws or with a rod passed inside the bone, which are techniques of the operating room and never of the field. An isolated fracture of a single bone may heal in a cast when it is stable and undisplaced, while an unstable one, an open one, or one accompanied by a dislocation at the other joint also needs operative fixation. A badly contaminated open fracture may be held first with an external frame that passes pins through the skin above and below the wound, and that frame, like the wound itself, is the responsibility of the surgical team. The decision to operate rests on the pattern of the fracture, the state of the soft tissue, the condition of the nerves and vessels, and the needs of the patient, and none of that can be judged from the roadside. The responder's part is to deliver a patient whose limb is splinted in the position found, whose hand has been examined and documented, and whose wound is covered with a clean dressing, because the cleaning, the removal of dead tissue, the irrigation, and the closure of an open fracture belong to the operating room and never to the field.

Hypothermia is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and a patient with a forearm fracture is at risk from the moment of injury. The patient may be lying on cold ground, may have had a sleeve cut away to expose the limb, may be losing blood from an open wound, and may be waiting in wet clothing, and each condition removes heat from a body already using its reserves to answer injury. Cold makes the blood clot less effectively, deepens shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm, so warming is part of the treatment of the fracture and begins before the journey rather than at the hospital door. The lay first aider covers the patient with whatever is available, insulates the patient from the ground, removes wet clothing where that can be done without exposing the wound, and keeps the vehicle warm during transport. The trained responder continues that protection during splinting and repeated examinations, and limits the time the limb and the patient are uncovered. A temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that figure is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line shifts with age, with illness, and with the way the measurement is taken. A patient who has stopped shivering while still cold is losing the ability to make heat, and that finding should be reported and treated as urgent.

From the first contact to the handover, the patient is watched in a rhythm that repeats the same observations in the same order, because the condition of a patient with a forearm fracture can change within a single journey. The responder returns to the airway, the breathing, and the circulation, then to the level of consciousness and the limbs, and then to the injured forearm, where the findings that matter are the color and warmth of the hand, the pulse at the wrist, the feeling in the fingers, the tightness of the swelling, and the amount of blood on the dressing. The Glasgow coma scale is used where the responder is trained in it, and its value lies in the trend over time rather than in a single score. The record carries the mechanism of injury, the time of the injury, the state of the hand before and after splinting, the time the splint was applied, whether a tourniquet was used and when, and every change observed, because the receiving team continues a story the field began and a gap in it forces them to start again. The destination is chosen before the patient is moved, and for a both-bone fracture, an open fracture, or a hand that has lost its circulation it is a trauma center with orthopedic and vascular surgery, and with an intensive care unit if the patient is unstable. Transport is urgent and gentle at the same time, because speed that throws the limb around adds pain and can displace the fracture further, and because a patient who arrives in worse condition has gained nothing from the hurry. The findings that should send the responder back to the beginning are a falling level of consciousness, breathing that has become faster or noisier, a pulse that has become weak or rapid, and a hand that has become pale, cold, or numb.

To summarize, a forearm fracture is an injury of a pair of bones that work as a ring, so a break at a single point should always raise the question of a second injury at the elbow or the wrist, and the responder treats the limb rather than the picture it makes. Scene safety and the primary survey come first, an open fracture with arterial bleeding is the lethal possibility to name early, and a compartment that is filling announces itself with pain out of proportion to the injury and with pain when the fingers are gently straightened. The limb is splinted in the position found and never straightened to look normal, the splint holds the elbow, the forearm, and the wrist together, an embedded object is stabilized and never removed, and the hand is examined for color, warmth, pulse, and feeling before and after every intervention. The lay first aider covers, supports, warms, and calls for help, the trained responder or paramedic splints with equipment under a protocol, and reduction, fixation, imaging, repair of vessels and nerves, and the release of a compartment belong to definitive hospital care. Analgesia, protection against tetanus, antibiotics, fluids, and oxygen are decisions of the authorized prescriber and the local protocol, and no substance, amount, route, or frequency can be taken from these pages. Hypothermia travels with every injured and exposed patient, so warming begins at the scene, the limb and the patient are watched continuously, and the time of every intervention is written on the patient in a way the receiving team will see. Every time, pressure, temperature, depth, and figure in this chapter is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such values differ between services and editions, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 25 — Wrist and Hand Injuries

The wrist and the hand carry the work of a whole life, so an injury there is as serious as a bleeding thigh. Scene safety comes before the patient, because the machine that caused the injury may still be running, the blade may still lie in the wound, and the traffic that caused the fall has not stopped. The lethal possibility to name first is a hand or a finger that has lost its blood supply, revealed by a digit that is pale, cool, and insensate beyond a wound. The second is hemorrhage that soaks through every dressing while the patient turns pale and restless. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, guards against the patient's blood, and the same moment guards the patient against hypothermia, because an injured hand on cold ground loses heat quickly. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

The mechanism of injury is the first clinical evidence, because it predicts structures that no eye can see. A fall onto an outstretched hand drives force through the wrist and can break the distal radius, dislocate a carpal bone, or fracture the scaphoid beneath intact skin. A punch against a wall loads the knuckles and may break a metacarpal neck or drive a tooth into a joint through a wound that looks like a scratch. A blade makes a wound whose depth cannot be judged from its length, and a crush beneath a wheel injures bone, tendon, nerve, and vessel together. These injuries are missed because attention goes to the larger wound elsewhere, so the trained responder examines both hands in the secondary survey and compares them.

Life comes before limb, and an injured hand does not change that order. A patient with a shattered wrist and a closed airway is treated for the airway, and a patient with an amputated finger and a chest filling with air is treated for the chest. The hand can wait for minutes that the brain and the heart cannot, and saving a fingertip while the patient dies saves nothing. The responder completes the primary survey in the fixed order of ABCDE before turning to the wrist, and returns to it whenever the patient changes. Only when the patient is breathing, circulating, and protected does the hand become the urgent problem, and then tendon, nerve, and vessel tolerate delay poorly.

Some anatomy must be held in the ear, because the examination depends on it. The radius on the thumb side and the ulna on the small-finger side meet the wrist, and the radius carries most of the load. The small bones of the wrist move as a unit, and the scaphoid lies at the base of the thumb with so fragile a blood supply that a break can starve it. Tendons that bend the fingers run through sheaths on the palm side and tendons that straighten them along the back, while the median, ulnar, and radial nerves cross the wrist to the hand and the radial and ulnar arteries meet in a loop within it. The position of function, with the wrist slightly extended and the fingers gently curled, is the posture in which the hand works best.

The examination begins with looking and compares the injured hand with the uninjured hand. The responder notes the position of the limb, any deformity, the color, the swelling, the wounds, and the posture of the fingers at rest. Feeling follows, with gentle touch along the bones and a question about where the pain is worst, because an injured hand does not need to be hurt further. Movement is tested last and in the smallest amount that answers the question, because a torn structure can be torn further by a vigorous test. The trained responder records the findings before any splint and repeats them afterwards, since a hand that was intact before a splint and numb after it tells a story about the splint.

The neurovascular examination decides the destination and is repeated before and after every intervention. Color and warmth are compared with the uninjured hand, and a finger that is pale, blue, or cooler than its neighbor must not wait. Capillary refill is judged by pressing the nail bed until it blanches and counting the seconds until color returns, and a refill time greater than 2 seconds is a warning that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted figure shifts with room temperature, age, and lighting. A single pulse felt at the wrist does not prove that the other artery is open, so both are sought. Sensation is tested in the territory of each nerve, and the distance at which separate points of touch can still be told apart is measured where training allows, with a distance such as 5 millimeters offered only to explain the reasoning and requiring confirmation against the current guideline and the local protocol. Movement is tested by asking the patient to bend and straighten each finger against light resistance, which asks whether the tendons remain connected.

A sprain and a severed structure can look alike from outside, and the examination separates them. A sprain hurts at the joint that is moved rather than along a tendon or in the territory of a nerve. A divided tendon changes what the finger can do, so a finger that cannot bend at its far joint when the nearer joint is held straight has lost the deep flexor tendon even if the wound is small. A divided extensor tendon leaves a finger that droops and cannot be lifted against gravity, and a divided nerve leaves skin that cannot feel and muscle that cannot act. The response is not to explore the wound, not to pass an instrument along it, and not to test the finger again and again, because each act may complete a partial division. The correct act is to cover the wound, splint the hand, record exactly what the patient could and could not do, and send the patient to a surgeon.

The distal radius fracture is the most common serious injury of the wrist and usually follows a fall on the outstretched hand. The finding is pain and tenderness just above the wrist on the thumb side, with swelling, bruising over hours, and sometimes a deformity in which the far fragment tilts backward so the wrist looks like a fork. The lay first aider does not straighten that deformity, because the bone ends may rest against a vessel or a nerve and movement can turn a closed injury into an open bleeding injury. The trained responder splints the wrist and forearm, supports the joint above and the hand below, checks the fingers before and after, and keeps the arm in a sling so its weight does not pull on the break. Definitive hospital care restores the length and angle of the bone and fixes it when the break is unstable or the joint surface is involved, and that reduction belongs to the surgeon and not to the field.

Among the small bones of the wrist, the scaphoid hides for weeks, and missing it is a classic error. It lies at the base of the thumb, and a break may cause only a dull ache, with tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb when the thumb is drawn back. Suspicion must rise when that hollow is tender and loading the thumb along its length hurts, even when the first radiograph shows nothing. A scaphoid fracture can take 10 to 14 days to appear on a repeat radiograph, a period offered only as an illustration and to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and the delay matters because the blood supply enters from a single direction and a break can cut it off. A missed scaphoid dies and leaves an arthritic wrist, a permanent loss for a patient who arrived with a sore thumb. The trained responder splints the wrist and thumb whenever that tenderness is present and asks for computed tomography, or CT, or magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, where available.

The bones of the palm break in patterns named by the finger they serve. A punch against a hard surface commonly breaks the neck of the metacarpal of the small finger, and the back of the hand looks bruised with a knuckle that has lost its height. The finding that most changes the plan is rotation, in which a finger turns and crosses its neighbor when the patient curls the hand into a fist, because a rotated finger that heals rotated will not close the hand again. The lay first aider supports the hand in the position of function, keeps the fingers apart with soft padding, and does not pull on a finger to straighten it. The trained responder splints with the knuckles bent and the fingers gently curled, checks sensation and pulses afterwards, and sends the patient for surgical assessment when rotation, an open wound, or several broken bones are present.

The fingers break in ways that decide whether a fingertip will ever straighten or bend again. A blow to the tip of an outstretched finger can tear the tendon that straightens the far joint and leave the tip drooping, an injury called a mallet finger. A forceful pull on a bent finger can tear the tendon that bends the far joint from its attachment and leave a finger that cannot curl at the tip. A break through the body of a phalanx causes swelling, tenderness, and sometimes a visible bend, and a break into a joint may leave a fragment that blocks movement. The lay first aider does not pull on the finger, because a fragment already pulled from the bone may be pulled further away, and a finger splinted as found is safer than a finger that has been manipulated. The trained responder splints the finger in the position found, pads between the fingers, and refers every injury involving a joint surface or an open wound.

A dislocation of a finger joint is unmistakable when the finger bends at an angle no joint allows, and the lay first aider must resist pulling it straight. A displaced joint may rest against a nerve or a vessel, and a blind reduction can injure what is still intact, while a joint reduced without assessing the tendons may hide a torn structure. A dislocation at the base of the thumb is a different matter, because the ligament holding the thumb to the palm may tear with a fragment of bone and leave the thumb weak and painful if it is treated as a sprain. The finding is tenderness over the inner side of that joint with pain when the thumb is bent away from the palm, often after a fall on a ski pole or onto the thumb. Definitive hospital care examines and images the joint and repairs the ligament, and no field test or field reduction takes its place.

Wounds of the wrist and the hand are deeper than they look, because tendons, nerves, and vessels lie immediately beneath thin skin. A cut across the front of the wrist may divide several tendons and the median nerve at once, and a cut across the back of a finger may divide the tendon that straightens it, while the skin wound closes over the damage and looks small. The lay first aider covers the wound, controls bleeding with direct pressure around rather than over the wound, and does not pour anything into it or pack it tightly. The trained responder examines the structures, records what the patient can move and feel, and dresses the wound without a constricting bandage, because a hand that swells inside a tight dressing loses its circulation. Every wound that might involve a tendon, a nerve, a vessel, or a joint belongs to a surgeon, and repair is definitive care. Protection against tetanus is a clinical decision made under the local protocol by the provider authorized to make it, and the substance and the timing belong to the prescriber.

Nerve injuries change what the patient will be able to do and are easily overlooked while a wound is dressed. Injury to the median nerve weakens the muscles at the base of the thumb so the patient cannot bring the thumb across the palm, and it removes sensation from the palm side of the index and middle fingers. Injury to the ulnar nerve weakens the small muscles of the hand and removes sensation from the small-finger side, and the hand takes on a clawed appearance with a weak grip. Injury to the radial nerve removes the ability to lift the wrist, so the hand hangs down when the arm is held out, and it removes sensation from the back of the hand between the thumb and the index finger. The exact area of numbness and the exact weak movement must be recorded before and after every splint and dressing, and repair of these nerves is a surgical act performed in an operating room and never at the roadside.

The blood supply of the hand runs through the radial and ulnar arteries at the wrist and then along each side of every finger, so an injury to any vessel can threaten a digit. A laceration at the base of a finger may divide the vessel on that side, and the finger beyond becomes pale, cool, painful, and then insensate. A crush or a closed fracture can tear a vessel with no external wound, so a hand that is tense, cool, and painful out of proportion deserves the same alarm as a bleeding hand. The findings that circulation is failing are a finger that has changed color beside its neighbor, a slow capillary refill, a pulse that cannot be felt, and numbness reported by the patient. The lay first aider supports the limb as found, keeps it warm, and does not massage it or warm it aggressively, because heat increases the oxygen demand of tissue that is starved of blood. Definitive hospital care examines the vessels and decides whether the finger can be saved, and that decision cannot be made in the field.

An amputation of a finger or of a hand is a vascular emergency, because the remaining tissue and the separated part both lose viability from the moment of injury. The stump is controlled first with direct pressure over a dressing, and the responder does not clamp or tie vessels, because blind clamping crushes nerves that might be repaired and does not reliably stop bleeding. A tourniquet on the arm is a measure for the trained responder or the paramedic under a protocol when the stump will not stop, and once it controls the bleeding it is not loosened in the field, with the time written on the patient where the receiving team will see it. The severed part is wrapped in clean dry material and sealed in a bag, and the bag is placed in a cool container rather than directly on ice, because ice damages tissue the surgeon hopes to replant. A period such as 6 hours of warm ischemia is often quoted as the limit for replantation, and that interval is offered only as an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since tolerance differs with the level of amputation and the storage of the part. The part travels with the patient and its label and time, and the lay first aider does not place it back on the stump.

Splinting protects what remains, and the position of function is the shape in which it is done. The wrist is supported in slight extension rather than allowed to drop, the knuckles are bent as though holding a small ball, and the thumb is held away from the palm so the web does not tighten. The splint supports the joint above and the joint below the injury and must not press on a bony point or circle the limb so tightly that circulation is lost, which is why the fingers are checked after it is secured. Rings and bracelets come off early where they come off without force, because swelling turns a ring into a tourniquet within hours, and a ring that will not come off is reported rather than cut from a swollen finger by an untrained hand. The trained responder chooses the splint and the padding, while the lay first aider may support the limb on a folded magazine, a piece of board, or a sling, provided the support does not press on the wound.

Covering the wound is done with clean material rather than with anything expected to disinfect. The dressing is held with a bandage firm enough to stay and loose enough that the fingers beyond do not change color, and the fingertips are left visible so circulation can be watched. The responder does not probe the wound, remove a foreign body, or press on an embedded object, because a shard of glass or a fragment of metal may be plugging a vessel or resting against a nerve, and it is stabilized in place while the patient is moved with it in place. A bite, whether human or animal, is treated with particular suspicion, because the mouth carries organisms into a joint or a tendon sheath and infection can destroy a hand quickly. Protection against tetanus and the decision about antibiotics belong to the provider authorized by the local protocol and to the prescriber, while the lay first aider cleans the surface gently, covers the wound, and records the time and the cause.

A wound over a knuckle from a fight is the most commonly underestimated injury of the hand. When a person strikes another person's teeth with a closed fist, a small wound appears over a knuckle and may look like a scrape that needs only a dressing. The teeth have driven organisms into the joint beneath the knuckle, and the wound closes over them, so the hand becomes swollen, hot, and painful while the surface injury is already healing. The finding that reveals the depth is pain and swelling over a knuckle that grow over the following day, and every such wound is a joint injury until a surgeon says otherwise. The lay first aider covers the wound, supports the hand in the position of function, and insists that the patient be seen, because the patient who is embarrassed about the fight is the patient most likely to leave before assessment, while definitive care opens the wound, examines the joint and the tendon sheath, and makes the decisions about infection under the local protocol.

Compartment syndrome must be anticipated in the hand and the forearm rather than discovered, and its earliest sign is pain out of proportion to the injury. The finding that matters most is pain on stretching the fingers or the wrist, which is pain produced by moving a part that is not itself injured, together with a limb that is tense and numbness that appears later. A measured pressure such as 30 millimeters of mercury is sometimes quoted as a threshold for concern, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the diagnosis rests on the whole picture and not on a single number. The lay first aider must not wait for a diagnosis, and must remove any bandage that has become tight, keep the limb as found, and send the patient to definitive care quickly. Release of the pressure, which is called fasciotomy, is a surgical procedure performed in an operating room and never a field act.

Some injuries of the wrist and the hand require surgical assessment, and the responder must recognize them without needing to name a diagnosis. An open wound over a joint, a wound that crosses a tendon, a wound that leaves part of the hand unable to feel or move, a deformity that does not improve with support, a finger that has lost its circulation, an unstable thumb base, a fracture that involves a joint surface, a fracture with rotation, an amputation, a bite, a crush with a tense swelling, and a tender hollow at the base of the thumb with a radiograph that shows nothing all belong in that group. The lay first aider does not decide which of these needs an operating room, and the lay first aider's duty is to keep the hand supported, keep the patient warm, and make certain that the patient reaches a place where the question can be answered. The trained responder chooses the destination under the local protocol, which may be a district hospital that can stabilize the limb and arrange a transfer or a trauma center with imaging, an operating room, and an intensive care unit. Every hand injury that might involve a tendon, a nerve, a vessel, or a joint is a patient for definitive care, and the field phase ends when that care begins.

Cold deserves a further word in a chapter about an exposed limb, because a hand on the ground while the responder works loses heat from a large surface. Wet clothing is replaced with dry covering where that can be done without disturbing the wound, the arm is wrapped along its whole length rather than only at the splint, and the patient is insulated from the ground and from the metal of a vehicle. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which cold becomes dangerous, and that figure is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the effects appear at different temperatures in different patients and the way the temperature is measured changes the reading. Cold makes blood clot poorly, deepens shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm, so warming and bleeding control run together rather than in sequence. The receiving team should be told how long the hand was exposed, because exposure time is part of the injury and not a detail of the journey.

It is worth saying plainly what the lay first aider may do with a wrist or a hand, because the temptation to do more is strong when the injury is visible and the patient is in pain. The lay first aider may cover the wound, apply direct pressure around but not on an embedded object, support the limb as found, keep the fingers visible and the hand warm, remove a ring that comes off easily, place the arm in a sling, and send for emergency medical services without delay. The lay first aider may not reduce a dislocation, straighten a deformed wrist, pull on a finger, explore a wound, remove a foreign body, cut a ring from a swollen finger, apply a tight bandage, or give any substance by any route. The trained responder may splint, dress, reassess, and use the equipment and the procedures the service authorizes, and the paramedic may consider a tourniquet for a stump that will not stop bleeding, with the time recorded and the device left in place. Everything that restores structure, whether it is a bone, a tendon, a nerve, or a vessel, belongs to a surgeon in an operating room. Knowing the line between support and repair is the competence this chapter most wants to teach.

To summarize, the wrist and the hand are treated with the seriousness of any other limb, and the injury that matters most has lost its blood supply or its connection to tendon, nerve, or bone. Scene safety comes first, the lethal possibilities are a hand without circulation and a hemorrhage that will not stop, and the patient is protected against hypothermia while the wound is protected from probing hands. The mechanism of injury predicts damage beneath intact skin, the examination looks, feels, and moves in that order, and the neurovascular examination is repeated before and after every intervention, because the capillary refill, the pulses, and the sensation decide the destination. Distal radius fractures are splinted as found and never straightened, the scaphoid is treated as broken whenever the hollow at the base of the thumb is tender, and metacarpal, phalangeal, tendon, nerve, and vessel injuries each change what the hand will be able to do. Amputation of a digit is a vascular emergency in which the stump is controlled, the severed part is wrapped, cooled, and sent with the patient, and any tourniquet applied by the trained responder or the paramedic is not loosened and is timed on the patient. Splinting in the position of function, covering the wound, removing a ring before swelling, and moving early to definitive care are the acts that save hands, while reduction, repair, fasciotomy, and the removal of a foreign body belong to the surgeon and never to the field. Every time, pressure, temperature, depth, and figure in this chapter is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 26 — Hip and Pelvis

An injury to the hip or the pelvis announces itself in a way that rarely matches the danger beneath it, and the first thing a responder must understand is that a broken pelvis is a hemorrhage before it is a fracture. The pelvis is a ring of bone wrapped around a network of veins and arteries that lie in a space the examining hand cannot reach, so a fracture of that ring can pour blood into the abdomen, the buttocks, and the thighs while the skin remains unbroken and the patient looks, for a moment, almost intact. The lethal possibility to be named first is pelvic hemorrhage, and the finding that reveals it is a patient who is pale, restless, and thirsty after a high-energy mechanism, with a pulse that is climbing while the pressure falls, in whom no external wound explains the loss. Blood loss of this kind can kill within minutes to a few hours, and a patient who reaches a hospital alive may still die of it, which is why every responder at every level must treat a suspected pelvic injury as a time-critical emergency. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work, and every intervention it describes is named with the provider level that owns it.

No clinical act may begin before the scene has been made safe, because a responder who is injured while approaching a patient with a pelvic injury has added a second casualty to a scene that is already short of hands. The hazards are the ones that accompany the mechanisms which break a pelvis: moving traffic at a road crash, a vehicle that may still be burning or may roll, a load that has shifted, a structure that has collapsed onto the patient, and the violence that may have caused the injury in the first place. The quieter hazard is the patient's own blood, which may be present in quantity beneath the body and around the hips, so gloves and eye protection, which is the personal protective equipment the responder actually has, are put on before the first hand is laid on anyone. The finding that tells the responder to stop and withdraw is a scene that has not yet been held: traffic that has not been warned, a wire that has not been isolated, a surface that has not been made stable, or a person who is still dangerous. Only when the scene is safe does the responder approach, and the approach itself is part of the treatment, because dragging or rolling a patient with an unstable pelvis can turn a contained bleed into a fatal one.

The reason the pelvis bleeds so badly is that it is not a solid block but a ring of bone with a rich and fragile vascular bed suspended inside it. The veins that drain the pelvic organs and the walls of the pelvis form a plexus that has little support from surrounding tissue, so a fracture that tears it does not seal itself with the pressure that a torn vessel in a limb would feel. Behind the peritoneum, in the space that lies against the back wall of the abdomen, there is room for a large volume of blood to collect without any visible swelling, and the bony surfaces of a fractured pelvis themselves bleed because the bone is spongy and rich in blood. The volume that can be lost into that space is measured in liters, and a figure such as 2 liters is often quoted as the capacity of the space before the swelling becomes obvious, a number that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because it differs with the size of the patient and with the way the loss is measured. The clinical consequence is simple, in that a patient can be exsanguinating into the pelvis while the abdomen is soft, the thighs look normal, and the only clue is the behavior of the circulation.

The mechanism of injury is the first predictor of pelvic damage, and it is read from the story rather than from the wound. A high-energy vehicle collision, a pedestrian struck by a vehicle, a fall from a height, a crush between two heavy objects, and a blast are the events that most often break the ring, and each of them delivers energy through the pelvis in a different direction. A lateral force compresses the ring from the side, an anteroposterior force opens it like a book, and a vertical force shears one half of the pelvis against the other, and the direction of the force decides which structures are torn. A fall from a height greater than 3 meters, a figure offered as a teaching illustration that must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, predicts pelvic injury together with injury to the spine, the heels, and the organs of the abdomen. The responder who knows the mechanism therefore examines the pelvis deliberately rather than waiting for the patient to complain about it, because a patient distracted by pain elsewhere may never mention the hip.

Instability of the pelvic ring is the finding that predicts major hemorrhage, and it is recognized by the position and the behavior of the patient rather than by any test the hands may perform. A patient whose pelvis is unstable often lies with one leg shorter than the other or rotated outward, with pain in the groin, the hip, or the lower back, and with an inability to lift the leg or to bear weight on it. Tenderness over the pubis, the sacrum, or the buttock, bruising over the perineum, and a visible deformity of the pelvic outline are further signs that the ring has been disrupted. The lay first aider and the trained responder must not spring the pelvis, that is, must not press the two halves of the ring together to see whether they move, because that act can tear a clot that is holding and start a hemorrhage that no field measure can stop. The examination is therefore performed with the eyes and with gentle pressure on the bony points, and any patient with a mechanism that could break the ring is treated as though the pelvis were unstable until definitive hospital care proves otherwise.

A fracture of the hip is a different injury from a fracture of the pelvic ring, and its danger lies in the days that follow rather than in the first minutes. The typical patient is older, often with thin bone, and the typical mechanism is a fall from standing rather than a high-energy crash, so the responder must not dismiss a hip fracture because the accident seemed minor. The findings are pain in the groin or the knee, an inability to bear weight, and a leg that lies shortened and rotated outward, and in some patients the only complaint is knee pain, which is why the knee must never be examined in isolation from the hip. The fracture may be in the neck of the femur, between the prominences at the upper end of the femur, or through the bone just below them, and each of those sites can bleed into the thigh and can injure the vessels that supply the head of the femur. The lay first aider keeps the patient still and warm, does not attempt to straighten the leg, and calls emergency medical services, while definitive hospital care decides whether the fracture needs an operation and how soon, because early surgery reduces the complications of immobility.

A dislocation of the hip is a true emergency of the joint, and it belongs to the same high-energy mechanisms that break the pelvis. The head of the femur is driven out of its socket, most often backward after a blow to the knee in a vehicle collision, and the limb then lies flexed, turned inward, and drawn toward the middle of the body. The danger is not the position of the bone but the structures trapped beside it, because the sciatic nerve and the vessels that supply the head of the femur can be stretched or torn, and a dislocation left unreduced threatens both the function of the leg and the survival of the bone. Reduction of a dislocated hip is a procedure of definitive hospital care performed with imaging and often with anesthesia, and it is not a field procedure, so no responder at any level should attempt to pull the joint back into place. The same rule applies to a severely deformed limb of any kind, in that it is splinted in the position found and never straightened to make it look normal, because the movement can injure a vessel or a nerve that is still intact.

Care of the patient with a suspected pelvic injury follows the same order as the care of every trauma patient, and that order is the primary survey remembered as ABCDE. The airway is opened and kept open, breathing is assessed and supported, and circulation is assessed with the hand on the pulse and the eyes on the skin, because a patient who is bleeding into the pelvis will show the failure of the circulation before any wound is found. The presence of catastrophic external bleeding is controlled where it is found, and the pelvic injury is treated as a source of concealed loss rather than as a limb to be splinted first. Disability is assessed through the level of consciousness and the movement of the limbs, and exposure means undressing the patient enough to see the pelvis and the perineum while covering the rest of the body at once to prevent cooling. The finding that returns the responder to the beginning of the sequence is any deterioration, and the pelvic injury is never allowed to hold attention so completely that the airway or the chest is neglected.

The neurovascular assessment of the limb is performed before and after every intervention, and it is the part of the pelvic examination that the responder can actually own. The trained responder feels the pulse at the groin and at the foot, compares the two sides, and notes the color and the temperature of the skin below the injury. Sensation is tested by asking the patient whether the leg feels normal and whether any part of it is numb, and movement is tested by asking the patient to move the toes and the ankle if the injury allows, because a loss of feeling or a loss of movement may be the first sign that a nerve or a vessel has been injured. The lay first aider performs the part that requires no equipment, which is to ask the patient about numbness, to look at the color of the foot, and to report any change at once, without moving the limb to test it. Any deterioration in the pulse, the sensation, or the movement is reported to the receiving team and recorded, because a change found late is a change that has already cost tissue.

The recognition of hemorrhage in the patient with a pelvic injury rests on the behavior of the circulation and on the trend of the observations rather than on a single measurement. A pulse that rises above 110 beats per minute, a figure given as an illustration which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and a blood pressure that falls below 90 millimeters of mercury, another figure that must be checked against the guideline and the protocol in force, together describe a patient whose loss is already serious. The earlier and more dangerous stage is the one in which the numbers still look acceptable while the patient is pale, cool, anxious, and thirsty, because the body is compensating and the loss is masked. The responder watches the level of consciousness, the breathing rate, the pulse, the skin, and the amount of urine where that can be observed, and compares each set of findings with the set before it. Fluid replacement and the decision to give blood belong to the paramedic under a protocol and to definitive hospital care, and nothing in this chapter names a substance, an amount, a route, or a frequency, because those decisions are made for a particular patient by an authorized provider under the local system.

Hypothermia is a complication of pelvic injury and not a detail of comfort, and it begins as soon as the patient is lying on cold ground with clothing cut away. A patient who is bleeding loses the volume that carries heat, and a patient who has been exposed loses heat from the surface, and cold then makes the clotting system work less well, so the bleeding worsens and the patient cools further in a circle that is difficult to break. The finding that warns the responder is a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold, because shivering is the body's attempt to make heat and its disappearance is a sign that the effort has failed. A temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the accepted line differs with age and with the way the temperature is taken. The lay first aider removes wet clothing, covers the patient including the pelvis and the legs, and insulates the patient from the ground, while the trained responder continues that protection in the vehicle and limits the time the patient is exposed for examination. Warming is never delayed until the bleeding is controlled, because the two tasks run together, and the patient is kept warm on the way to definitive care.

A pelvic binder is a device that encircles the pelvis and squeezes the two halves of the ring together, and it is the one field intervention that can reduce bleeding from an unstable pelvic fracture before the patient reaches hospital. It belongs to the trained responder or the paramedic working under a protocol, and in some services a trained first responder who has been taught and authorized to use it may apply one, so the level of training that owns the act is decided by the local system rather than by this chapter. The evidence on which the decision rests is a mechanism that could have broken the ring together with the findings of instability, and the binder is applied before the patient is moved rather than after bleeding has declared itself. A binder is not a treatment for a hip fracture or for a dislocated hip, and it is not a substitute for the operation that controls a torn vessel, so it is described here as a temporary measure that buys time rather than as a definitive repair. The lay first aider who has not been trained and authorized to apply a binder does not improvise one, and instead keeps the patient still, keeps the patient warm, and calls emergency medical services, because a binder applied wrongly can do harm without controlling the bleeding.

The position of a pelvic binder decides whether it helps or harms, and the correct level is across the greater trochanters at the widest part of the hips rather than across the waist or the upper thighs. A binder placed too high sits over the abdomen, where it compresses the belly, limits the movement of the diaphragm, and can worsen breathing while failing to close the pelvic ring, and a binder placed too low sits over the thighs and pulls the two halves of the pelvis apart at the top instead of bringing them together. A binder that is applied too tightly can injure the skin beneath it, can press on the nerves that cross the pelvis, and can cause pressure damage that is discovered only after hours, so the tension is set by the design of the device and by the training rather than by the strength of the responder. The device is checked for folds and for twisting, because a crease concentrates pressure on a small area of skin, and the patient's clothing is smoothed beneath it where that can be done without moving the pelvis. The finding that the binder has been placed correctly is a patient whose pain and instability appear reduced while the circulation is stable, and the finding that it is wrong is a patient whose breathing has worsened or whose skin is being damaged at the edge of the device.

Once a pelvic binder is in place it is monitored rather than forgotten, because a device that is left unexamined can hide the deterioration it was meant to prevent. The trained responder reassesses the breathing, the abdomen, the circulation, and the neurovascular state of both legs at regular intervals, checks the skin at the edges of the binder, and records the time the device was applied in a place the receiving team will see. The binder is not removed in the field once it has been placed, even when the patient improves, because the improvement may depend on the compression and because releasing it can restart a hemorrhage that field measures cannot control. Removal is a decision for definitive hospital care, made with imaging and with preparation for what may follow, and the receiving team must be told that a binder is present and when it was applied. The finding that requires the responder to escalate immediately is a patient whose circulation continues to fail despite the binder, because that patient needs blood and an operating room rather than a tighter device.

Immobilization for transport has one purpose, which is to prevent movement of the pelvis between the scene and the place where the bleeding can be controlled. The patient is kept lying flat on a firm surface, the legs are kept still, and the knees and the ankles may be bound together with a padded band or a folded sheet so that the limbs move as a single unit, which is a measure that belongs to the trained responder and to the paramedic. A scoop stretcher or a firm board is used to lift the patient without rolling the pelvis, and where a log roll is required to examine the back it is performed by a team that moves the patient as one piece, keeping the pelvis and the spine in line. The lay first aider keeps the patient in the position found, does not lift the legs, does not straighten a shortened leg, and does not pull on the limb, because each of those acts can move the fracture and restart the bleeding. The destination is chosen before the patient is moved, and it is the nearest trauma center or the nearest facility that can provide imaging, blood, and an operating room, with the receiving team warned in advance that a pelvic injury is coming.

An open pelvic fracture is the most dangerous form of the injury, and it is recognized by a wound that communicates with the broken bone or by bleeding from the perineum, the rectum, or the vagina. Blood at the opening of the urethra, an inability to pass urine, a bruise over the perineum, and a wound near the buttock are all findings that raise the possibility of injury to the bladder, the urethra, or the bowel, and each of them changes the care the patient will need. A fracture that has torn the skin of the perineum or the rectum carries contamination directly into the pelvis, so the tetanus question and the antibiotic decision are raised early, with the substance and the amount belonging to the prescriber and to the local protocol rather than to this manual. A fragment of bone or a foreign object embedded in the wound is stabilized in place and never removed in the field, because removal may release hemorrhage that cannot be controlled or damage a structure that is still intact. The lay first aider covers the wound with a clean dressing and does not pack it, and the trained responder protects the area, keeps the patient warm, and moves the patient toward definitive care without delay.

Two groups of patients deserve a separate word because their anatomy changes the risk. A child has a pelvis that is more elastic than an adult's, so the ring can absorb energy and spring back without breaking, while the vessels inside it are torn, and the child may therefore have a serious pelvic injury with an apparently normal radiograph and a normal examination. A pregnant patient carries two lives, and a pelvic fracture threatens the uterus, the placenta, and the fetus at the same time, so the responder treats the mother first because the best treatment for the fetus is a mother whose circulation is supported, and the receiving team is told that the patient is pregnant.
