An older patient may break the pelvis in a fall from standing, and the fracture may be a single break in one of the pubic bones rather than a disrupted ring, yet even that injury can bleed and can leave the patient unable to walk. In each of these patients the same principles apply, which are to keep the patient still, warm, and monitored, and to reach definitive care as quickly as is safe.

Definitive hospital care owns everything that repairs rather than contains, and the line between the field and the hospital must be clear to every responder. The hospital confirms the injury with imaging, which may include a computed tomography scan, called CT after the first mention, and it restores the circulating volume with blood and blood products given by the team that is authorized to prescribe them. Bleeding from a torn pelvic vessel may be controlled by external fixation of the ring, by packing of the pelvis in the operating room, or by a procedure that blocks the bleeding vessel from inside using imaging, and each of those is a decision of the trauma surgeon rather than a field procedure. Internal fixation, the repair of a torn vessel, the repair of the bladder or the urethra, and the removal of a fragment are operations performed in an operating room with anesthesia, and no responder should attempt any of them outside it. The patient who has lost a large volume of blood is watched in an intensive care unit, called ICU after the first mention, for the complications that follow, which include continued bleeding, infection, and the effects of a large transfusion.

Reassessment is not a single act but a rhythm that continues from the first contact to the handover, and it follows the same order as the primary survey. The trained responder repeats the airway, the breathing, the circulation, the level of consciousness, and the neurovascular state of the limbs, and compares each set of findings with the one before, because the trend carries more meaning than any single observation. The findings that mark a patient who is still bleeding are a pulse that has risen and softened, a breathing rate that has climbed, skin that has become cold and clammy, a level of consciousness that is dulling, and a binder or a dressing that has become soaked. What was done is recorded as carefully as the treatment is given, and the time at which a binder was applied, the time at which a tourniquet was placed, and every change in the patient are written where the receiving team will see them. The handover carries the mechanism of injury, the injuries found, the interventions performed with their times, and the observations that have changed, because a story with a gap forces the receiving team to begin again.

A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient or a real incident, may make the sequence concrete. A driver is struck on the side by another vehicle and is found awake and anxious at the wheel, with pain in the hip, a pulse that is fast and thin, and no blood on the ground. The responder makes the road safe, protects the hands and the eyes, opens the airway, and assesses the breathing, and then treats the mechanism as a prediction of a pelvic injury rather than waiting for a deformity that may never appear. The patient is kept flat, kept warm, and moved as one piece onto a firm surface, and a binder is applied by a trained responder only where the protocol authorizes it, at the level of the greater trochanters, with the time recorded. The patient's circulation continues to fail on the way, and the receiving team is warned before arrival so that blood and an operating room are ready when the vehicle doors open, which is the only definitive answer to a bleeding pelvis.

To summarize, a fracture of the hip or the pelvis is a hemorrhage before it is a fracture, and the pelvis is a bleeding space because its ring of bone surrounds a fragile vascular bed and a cavity that can hold liters of blood without a visible wound. The lethal possibility is pelvic hemorrhage, which can kill within minutes to a few hours, and the finding that reveals it is a patient whose circulation is failing after a high-energy mechanism with no external injury to explain the loss. Scene safety comes before the patient, the primary survey is performed in the order of ABCDE, the pelvis is never sprung, a deformed limb is never straightened, and an embedded object is never removed in the field. Immobilization, warmth, and the shortest safe journey to a trauma center are the field tasks, a pelvic binder belongs to the trained responder or paramedic working under a protocol and is placed at the level of the greater trochanters and monitored once in place, and transfusion, fixation, and the control of a torn vessel belong to definitive hospital care. Every time, pressure, temperature, depth, distance, and figure in this chapter, including every threshold and every interval, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between services, countries, and editions. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 27 — Femur Fractures

A fracture of the femur is dangerous well beyond the limb, because the thigh can conceal a large hemorrhage while the skin above it stays almost unbroken. The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body, so the energy required to break it in a healthy adult is usually enough to injure the head, the chest, and the abdomen as well. The lethal possibility is bleeding into the thigh followed by shock, and the findings that reveal it are a patient who is pale, restless, thirsty, or drowsy, with a pulse that climbs while the pressure falls. No care begins before the scene is safe, and the hazards to be cleared first are moving traffic, machinery that may still be running, fire, live electricity, water, a structure that can collapse, an animal that is loose, a violent person, and the patient's own blood. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

The mechanism of injury is the first prediction a responder makes, and it decides how suspicious to be about everything else. A vehicle collision, a fall from a height, a motorcycle crash, a pedestrian struck by a vehicle, and a crush beneath a heavy weight are the mechanisms that most often break a femur, and each predicts damage elsewhere. The direction of the force matters as much as its size, because a blow to the side of the thigh bends the bone where the force meets it, while a force along the line of the leg drives the shaft toward the hip or the knee. In an older patient with thin bone, a fall from standing is enough to break the hip or the shaft, so a gentle story does not exclude a serious fracture.

The thigh is not a solid column of muscle but a compartment that can hold a large volume before it changes shape, and that is why a femur fracture can bleed without a wound. A closed fracture of the shaft may lose a volume measured in liters into the soft tissue, and a value such as 1 to 2 liters is offered only as an illustration of that capacity, because the real amount depends on the bone, the vessels torn, and the patient, and every such number must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. An open fracture bleeds outward as well as inward, so the visible loss and the hidden loss are added together. The thigh can also swell until the limb is tight and cool, and this hidden loss is why a patient with a broken femur is treated as a bleeding patient from the first minute.

The femur is described in three parts, and the part that is broken changes both the danger and the treatment. A fracture of the neck or the region just below the hip is a proximal fracture, common in older patients after a simple fall, with the leg shortened and turned outward. A fracture of the middle of the bone is a shaft fracture, the one that most often follows high energy and the one a traction splint is designed for. A fracture near the knee is a distal fracture, and it may injure the vessels and nerves that pass close to the joint. Any of these may be open, meaning the bone has pierced the skin and the wound communicates with the fracture, and an open fracture is a different emergency from a closed one.

An open femur fracture is contaminated at the moment it occurs, so the patient needs a facility where the wound can be cleaned and debrided in an operating room. When bone is visible in the wound, or when a wound lies over the fracture line and blood oozes from it, the responder treats the injury as open even if no bone is seen. The responder covers the wound with a clean dressing, controls what external bleeding can be controlled, and never pushes a bone end back under the skin. Pushing the bone back is a form of reduction, it is not a field procedure, and it drives contamination deeper while risking a vessel or a nerve that is still intact.

Shock is the complication a femur fracture most often produces, and it must be sought in every patient with a broken thigh. In the early stage the patient compensates, with a rapid pulse, cool hands, a narrowed pulse pressure, and a measured pressure that still looks acceptable, and that apparent stability is the most dangerous moment. As compensation fails, the patient becomes restless and then drowsy, the breathing becomes rapid and shallow, the skin becomes cold and clammy, and the pressure falls. The responder cannot correct this by pressing on the wound, because the bleeding is inside the thigh, so the work is to keep the patient still and warm, to control external bleeding, and to shorten the time to definitive care. A pressure of 90 millimeters of mercury is sometimes named as a threshold in this reasoning, and it is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line shifts with age, with pregnancy, and with the patient's usual state.

The deformity of a fractured femur reflects the force involved and tells the responder how much tissue has been injured. The limb may be shortened, because the muscles of the thigh pull the fragments past one another, and it may be rotated or bent at an angle no joint could produce. A severely deformed limb is splinted in the position in which it is found, and it is not straightened to make it look normal, because the movement can tear a vessel or a nerve that had escaped and can release a clot holding back hemorrhage. Reduction belongs to definitive hospital care, where it is performed with anesthesia, imaging, and preparation for what may follow.

The first actions after the scene is safe follow the primary survey, and the broken thigh must not distract from them. The primary survey is performed in the fixed order of ABCDE, which means airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure, and catastrophic external bleeding is controlled first where the protocol places it. External bleeding from the fracture is controlled with direct pressure from a protected hand over a clean dressing, adding further layers if blood soaks through. A tourniquet may be needed when bleeding from the limb cannot be controlled and the service authorizes it, and once it has controlled the bleeding it is not loosened in the field, because the clot behind it may not hold. The time the tourniquet was applied is written on the patient where the receiving team cannot miss it, and a period such as 2 hours is often quoted as the point at which the risk to the limb becomes serious, an interval to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

The neurovascular assessment decides how urgently the limb must be treated, and it is performed before and after every intervention. The word carries both halves of the question, since the nerves below the fracture tell whether sensation and movement are intact, and the vessels tell whether blood is still reaching the foot. The examination is repeated after splinting, after any movement, and at intervals during transport, because a pulse that was present can disappear and a limb that was warm can cool. Everything found is recorded with the time it was found, because the hospital team compares the record with what they find on arrival. The finding that makes the injury a vascular emergency is a foot that is pale, cool, and pulseless, or a patient whose pain and numbness worsen in a limb that is tightly swollen.

The circulation below the fracture is checked in a fixed order that the responder can repeat aloud. The color of the skin is compared with the other foot, and a pale or mottled foot is abnormal, while the warmth is felt with the back of the hand. The pulses at the top of the foot and behind the inner ankle are felt and compared with the uninjured side. The time it takes for the color to return after the skin or the nail bed is pressed is noted, and a delay beyond 2 seconds is a warning that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the value changes with room temperature, with the patient's age, and with the examiner. The finding that matters most is a difference between the two limbs, because a limb that was never normal may mislead the responder.

Sensation and movement are tested gently, and the result is written down rather than remembered. The patient is asked whether the foot and toes feel normal, and whether tingling or numbness has appeared or changed. The patient is then asked to move the toes and the ankle, and the movement is compared with the other side, while the responder watches for pain that limits it. A nerve injured by the fracture may leave a patch of numbness on the top of the foot, between the toes, or along the outer side of the leg, and any such finding raises the urgency of the transfer. The responder does not test sensation by prodding the fracture itself, because that causes pain and adds nothing.

Reassessment is a rhythm rather than a single act, and it follows the same order as the primary survey. The responder returns to the airway, the breathing, and the circulation, then to the level of consciousness and to the limb, comparing each finding with the one before. The findings that mark a patient who is still bleeding are a dressing soaked through, a thigh that has swollen further, a pulse that has risen and softened, and skin that has become cold and clammy. The findings that mark a limb in danger are increasing pain, new numbness, a foot that has cooled, and a pulse that can no longer be felt. Either set of findings means that the next step is the fastest safe journey to definitive care, not another attempt at the same measure.

A traction splint is a device that pulls the lower leg away from the body along the line of the thigh while an anchor presses against the pelvis or the upper thigh, and its purpose is to hold the fracture out to its length. The steady pull opposes the spasm of the thigh muscles, which is what causes the shortening, the overlapping of the fragments, and much of the pain. By holding the fragments apart it can reduce further bleeding and protect the vessels and nerves from being crushed between the bone ends. It also makes the limb easier to secure for transport, and it is the reason a trained responder may choose it when the conditions are right. It is not a treatment that heals the fracture, and it never replaces the operation that fixes the bone.

A traction splint is indicated for a closed fracture of the shaft of the femur in a patient whose circulation and sensation below the injury are intact or can be restored by gentle traction, and it is applied by a trained responder or paramedic working under a protocol. It may also be considered for an open shaft fracture when the wound has been covered and the limb is grossly deformed, provided the local protocol allows it and the application does not delay transport. It is not indicated for a fracture of the hip or the neck of the femur, because the pull is applied below the injury and cannot correct a fracture above it. It is never a task for the lay first aider working alone with improvised material, because a device applied without training can tighten a limb and worsen the fracture.

The contraindications to a traction splint are as important as the indications, and a responder who cannot name them should not apply one. A suspected fracture of the pelvis is the first, because the counter-traction presses against a ring that may already be broken and bleeding. A suspected injury of the knee, including a dislocation or a fracture around the joint, is the second, because the pull passes through the knee and can worsen damage to the vessels behind it. A fracture of the ankle or the foot is the third, because the ankle hitch must grip a part that is itself injured, and a partial or complete amputation of the leg is the fourth, because the remaining stump cannot take the tension. A device that is not sized for a small child is a further reason to choose another method, as is any situation in which applying the splint would take longer than the journey to the hospital.

A fractured pelvis makes the traction splint the wrong choice because the pelvis is the anchor the device must pull against. When the ring of the pelvis is broken, the counter-traction can separate the fragments further, reopen bleeding that had been contained, and add to the internal hemorrhage that already threatens the patient. A pelvis that is painful, unstable, or bruised should be treated as broken until imaging proves otherwise, and the trained responder supports it with the measures the protocol provides rather than loading it. If a traction splint has already been applied and a pelvic injury is then suspected, the responder does not simply remove it in a hurry but reports the suspicion and follows the local protocol for the change. The safest rule for the listener is that a traction splint and an unstable pelvis do not belong together.

An injured knee makes the traction splint the wrong choice because the pull passes through the joint and along the vessels behind it. A dislocated knee is a limb-threatening injury rather than a sporting accident, since the artery behind the knee can be torn or stretched and the foot can lose its supply within a short time. Applying traction to such a knee can complete the injury to that vessel, and the pain and the deformity can be made worse. The limb is therefore splinted in the position in which it was found, the circulation below it is checked and recorded, and the patient is moved to a facility where the vessels can be assessed and the joint realigned under proper conditions. Any knee that cannot be straightened without force, and any knee with a cool or pulseless foot, belongs to that pathway.

When a traction splint is contraindicated or unavailable, the limb is still immobilized, and there are several ways to do it. A rigid splint long enough to span from the hip to beyond the foot, padded and secured without extreme pressure, holds the limb in the position found. The uninjured leg may serve as a natural splint when the patient must be moved and no other device is at hand, with padding between the limbs and broad bands above and below the fracture, though this requires care and is not a substitute for a proper device. A vacuum splint or a padded board, where the service carries one, gives similar support. Whatever is used, the rule is unchanged: the severely deformed limb is splinted as it lies, and it is never straightened to make it look normal.

Padding and gentle handling decide whether a splint protects the limb or injures it. The bony points, including the hip, the knee, the ankle, and the heel, are padded before the splint is secured, because pressure there can cause skin damage within a short time. The bands that hold the splint are tight enough to prevent movement and loose enough that the circulation beyond them is not impaired, and the limb is never bound so tightly that the toes change color or swell. After the splint is in place, the responder checks the pulses, the warmth, the color, and the sensation again, because a splint applied correctly should not change any of them for the worse. A finding that has changed means the splint is released, adjusted, and the examination repeated.

Positioning for transport is chosen to protect the fracture and the patient at the same time. The patient is kept flat and still on the stretcher unless a chest or head injury requires another position, and the fractured limb is supported along its whole length so that its weight does not pull on the fracture. The limb is not propped on an object that leaves the middle of the thigh unsupported, because a sagging fracture angulates and can injure what lies beside it. The patient is secured to the stretcher so that a sudden stop or a rough road cannot throw the body against the injury, and the straps are placed to avoid pressing on the fracture itself. The journey is made as smooth as the urgency allows, because speed that throws the patient about adds pain and can add injury.

Pain relief is a clinical decision rather than a field instruction, and this manual deliberately names no substance, no amount, no route, and no frequency. The lay first aider may keep the limb still, keep the patient warm, speak calmly, and reduce the jolting of the journey, and those acts genuinely reduce pain without any drug. The trained responder and the paramedic may give analgesia only when their service authorizes it and their protocol provides it, and the decision belongs to them and to the medical direction that supervises them. The finding that makes the decision urgent is severe pain that is not relieved by immobilization, or pain that is worsening despite a splint that appears correct, because that finding may mean the circulation is failing. Whatever is given is recorded with the time, so the receiving team knows what the patient has already had.

Hypothermia travels with a femur fracture, because the patient is bleeding, undressed for examination, lying on cold ground, and waiting for transport, and cold makes bleeding worse. The responder removes wet clothing, covers the patient before the journey rather than after it, insulates the patient from the ground, and keeps the vehicle warm. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that value is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold shifts with age and with the way the temperature is measured. A patient who has stopped shivering while still cold is a patient in whom the body has given up making heat, and that finding makes warming urgent rather than optional.

An open femur fracture is a surgical emergency, and the definitive care belongs to the operating room. The surgeon cleans the wound, removes dead and contaminated tissue, and stabilizes the bone, and the timing of that operation is decided by the receiving team with the patient's condition in view. The decision about antibiotics is made by the prescriber under the local guideline, and the decision about protection against tetanus belongs to the provider authorized to make it, with the wound's nature and the patient's vaccination history both taken into account. Nothing in a manual can tell a listener which substance to use or how much, because those choices belong to the protocol and to the clinician who knows the patient. The responder's part is to cover the wound, immobilize the limb, record what was seen and done, and reach the surgeon without delay.

Compartment syndrome is the complication of a broken thigh that is most often missed, and it can develop inside the thigh or in the leg below it. The pressure inside a closed compartment rises as blood and swelling accumulate, and when it rises far enough the muscle and the nerve within it begin to die. The findings are pain that is severe and out of proportion to the injury, pain that worsens when the muscle is stretched, a limb that feels tight and hard, and numbness or weakness below the injury. A pressure of 30 millimeters of mercury is often quoted in this reasoning, and that value must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the decision depends on the whole picture rather than on one number. The field response is to remove anything that is binding, to keep the limb at the level of the heart rather than above it, and to move the patient to definitive care at once.

A femur fracture in a child is not simply a smaller version of the adult injury, and an older patient is a different problem again. The bone of a child bends and springs before it breaks, so the same force may cause a fracture that is incomplete, and the child may walk on a limb an adult could not use. Because a child has less blood to lose, a smaller volume of hemorrhage can produce shock, and a device designed for an adult may be the wrong size for a small limb, so the responder uses the method the local protocol provides for children. In an older patient the bone is thinner, the fall was often gentle, and medicines that make bleeding easier may be in use, so a fracture that looks contained can bleed more than expected.

Definitive hospital care begins with imaging and ends in the operating room, and it is the surgeon who decides which route the patient takes. A radiograph shows the level and the pattern of the fracture, and a computed tomography scan, known as CT, may be used when the fracture reaches the hip or the knee or when other injuries are suspected. The surgeon may apply traction as a temporary measure to hold the bone while the patient is prepared, and the definitive repair is usually internal fixation, in which a nail or a plate holds the fragments until the bone heals. Where the wound is heavily contaminated or the patient is too unstable for a long operation, an external frame may be placed first. The destination is chosen before the patient is moved, and it is the nearest facility that can provide the care the fracture actually needs, with the handover naming the mechanism, the neurovascular findings before and after splinting, what was applied to the limb, and whether a tourniquet was placed and when.

Consider a constructed illustration, offered as a teaching construction and not as a real patient. A young rider is thrown from a motorcycle and is found lying on the road with the left leg shortened and turned outward and a swelling that grows while the responder watches. The responder makes the road safe, sends for emergency medical services, checks the airway, the breathing, and the circulation, and finds a pulse that is fast and a patient who is pale and thirsty. The limb is splinted in the position found, the foot is checked before and after the splint, and the patient is covered and insulated from the cold road. The lesson of the illustration is that the leg was never the only problem, and that the swelling in the thigh was the hemorrhage that mattered most.

Every act in this chapter belongs to a named level of provider, and the level is set by training, equipment, authorization, and protocol rather than by urgency. The lay first aider may make the scene safe, call for help, keep the patient still and warm, cover an open wound with a clean dressing, and support the limb in the position found. The trained responder and the paramedic may assess and record the neurovascular state, apply a splint or a traction splint where the protocol allows, control external bleeding, apply a tourniquet and record its time, and give analgesia under medical direction. Definitive hospital care owns the reduction of the fracture, the cleaning and repair of an open wound, the fixation of the bone, the release of a compartment under pressure, and the removal of an embedded object, and none of those is a field procedure. Knowing where that line lies is as much a part of competence as knowing what to do, because an act performed beyond one's training can turn a survivable injury into a fatal one.

To summarize, a fracture of the femur is a whole-body emergency because the thigh can conceal a large hemorrhage and because the force that broke the bone often injured something else. The lethal possibility is concealed bleeding into the thigh with shock, recognized by a patient who is pale, restless, thirsty, or drowsy, with a rising pulse and a falling pressure, so the patient is treated as a bleeding patient from the first minute. The limb is examined for color, warmth, pulses, sensation, and movement below the fracture, and those findings are recorded with their times and repeated before and after every intervention. A severely deformed limb is splinted in the position found and never straightened, an embedded object is never removed in the field, and a tourniquet that has controlled bleeding is not loosened, with its time written where the receiving team cannot miss it. A traction splint is a tool for the trained responder or paramedic under a protocol, indicated for a closed shaft fracture with intact or recoverable circulation, and contraindicated when the pelvis or the knee is injured, when the ankle or the foot cannot take the hitch, and when the device does not fit the patient. Hypothermia is prevented, pain relief belongs to the authorized prescriber under the local protocol and never to a prescription taken from this book, and the open fracture belongs to the operating room. Every value in this chapter, whether a volume, a distance, a time, a pressure, or a temperature, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such values differ between services, countries, and editions. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 28 — Knee Injuries

The knee is the joint where a weekend sports injury and a limb-threatening emergency can look almost the same, and the difference is often decided by findings that take less than a minute to obtain. A twisted knee that the patient can stand on is usually a ligament injury that will be assessed later, while a knee driven out of place by a dashboard, by a fall from a height, or by the front wheel of a motorcycle may have torn the artery behind it, and that injury can cost the limb and sometimes the life. This chapter treats the kneecap, the ligaments, and the joint itself, and it keeps one question at the front of every paragraph, which is whether the blood supply to the foot is still intact. The provider level is named for every act, because the lay first aider, the trained responder or paramedic, and the trauma team each own a different part of the care, and the acts that belong to the hospital are described as hospital acts so that nobody attempts them in the field. This is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

No hand is laid on a patient with a knee injury before the scene has been made safe, and the knee itself is rarely the hazard that matters. Moving traffic around a crashed vehicle, a vehicle that may still roll or burn, spilled fuel, broken glass and torn metal, a live electrical cable, an animal that is loose, and a person who is still violent are the dangers that injure rescuers, and each is dealt with before the patient is approached. Body fluids are the quiet hazard, because blood and tissue from an open knee wound can carry infection into a break in the responder's skin or a splash into the eye, so gloves and eye protection are used for every patient rather than only for those who look infectious. The lay first aider uses whatever barrier is at hand, including ordinary gloves, a plastic bag over the hands, and glasses or a scarf over the eyes, while the trained responder uses the personal protective equipment issued by the service. A responder who cannot make the scene safe does not enter it, and waiting at the edge for those with the authority to hold the road or isolate the current is a competent act rather than a failure.

Knowing what lies behind the knee explains why the injury is feared, and the anatomy can be spoken in a few sentences that a listener can carry. The knee joins the thigh bone to the shin bone, and the kneecap rides in front of the joint within the tendon of the muscle that straightens the leg, so the kneecap is part of the mechanism of movement rather than a separate bone. Stability comes from the ligaments, with the collateral ligaments on each side resisting a bending force and the cruciate ligaments in the center resisting the shin bone sliding forward or backward, and from the menisci, which are pads of cartilage that spread the load between the bone ends. The popliteal artery passes behind the knee, tethered above by the opening in the tendon of the adductor muscle and below by the fibrous arch of the calf muscle, so a joint driven out of place tears or stretches the artery rather than pushing it aside. The tibial nerve and the common peroneal nerve travel through the same region, and the peroneal nerve wraps around the neck of the fibula where it lies close to the surface, which is why a knee injury can take away the ability to lift the foot.

The mechanism of injury is the first clinical evidence at the knee, because it predicts damage that the surface does not show. A dashboard impact drives the shin bone backward against the thigh bone, a fall onto a bent knee compresses the kneecap against the bone beneath it, a twist with the foot planted tears ligaments and menisci, and a motorcycle crash combines a direct blow with a twisting force and with the patient being thrown. A low-energy twist in a sport and a high-energy collision can produce the same swelling, so the responder should not let a familiar story of sport lower the concern, because the mechanism that matters is the energy and the direction rather than the name of the activity. The findings that demand immediate attention are a knee that is visibly out of place, a knee that is already grossly swollen and tense, an open wound over the joint, a foot that has changed color or temperature, and a patient who cannot feel or move the foot. A constructed illustration, offered as a teaching construction rather than as a real patient, is the rider who stands after a crash, reports a sore knee, and walks a few steps while the pulse at the foot is never checked.

A fractured kneecap is the injury a responder is most likely to see and least likely to over-treat, and its danger lies in the mechanism of the leg rather than in the bone. A direct blow cracks the bone where it lies and usually leaves the surrounding tendon intact, while a sudden powerful contraction of the thigh muscle can pull the kneecap apart and tear the mechanism that straightens the knee. The findings are swelling over the front of the joint, tenderness directly on the bone, a gap that can sometimes be felt between the fragments, and, in the more serious pattern, an inability to straighten the knee against gravity or against gentle resistance. A break in the skin over the kneecap makes the injury an open fracture even when the wound is small, and an open wound that communicates with the joint turns it into a surgical problem for the hospital rather than a dressing problem for the roadside. The lay first aider covers the wound, presses gently around it rather than over the exposed bone, immobilizes the limb in the position found, and calls for help, while the trained responder splints the leg without testing how far the knee will straighten. The kneecap can also slip out of its groove, and when it does the limb is immobilized as it lies while the lay first aider refuses to push it back, because the attempt is painful and can injure the cartilage.

A dislocated knee is the injury in this chapter that threatens the limb and occasionally the life, and it is the one most easily missed because it may have corrected itself before the responder arrives. The thigh bone and the shin bone lose their normal relationship, and the joint may be driven forward, backward, or to the side, depending on the direction of the force, with the backward pattern most often associated with damage to the artery behind the knee. In some patients the joint returns to a normal position on its own or during the movement of the leg, and the knee can then look almost ordinary while the artery behind it is torn or blocked. The dangerous sequence is that the inner lining of the artery is injured and a clot forms over the following hours, so a pulse that was present at the scene can disappear later and a limb that was pink can become pale and cold. Every knee that has been grossly deformed, even briefly, is therefore treated as a vascular emergency until a hospital has proved otherwise.

The reason a dislocated knee is a vascular emergency is that the artery behind the knee is the only main supply to the leg below it, and the small branches around the joint are not reliably enough to keep the foot alive. The hard findings of a failing circulation are a foot that is pale or mottled, a foot that is cold compared with the other side, an absent pulse at the top of the foot or behind the inner ankle bone, and a patient who cannot feel the toes or move the ankle. The softer findings matter just as much, and they include a pulse that is present but weaker than on the other side, pain that is severe and out of proportion to the look of the knee, numbness in the web space between the first two toes, and a swelling behind the knee or in the calf that grows while the responder watches. A pulse that is felt once proves only that the artery was open at that moment, and it does not remove the need for reassessment, because the clot that closes the artery may form while the patient is being moved. The finding that settles the question in hospital is imaging of the blood vessels, which may be an ultrasound study or a computed tomography examination, followed by a repair in the operating room, and none of that can be replaced by a field test.

The time pressure in a knee dislocation is measured against the tolerance of muscle and nerve, and it is the reason the patient is moved rather than observed. Muscle and nerve can survive a period without blood flow that is often quoted as 6 hours, and that figure is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the true limit changes with the temperature of the limb, with the completeness of the blockage, and with the patient. The urgency is not reduced by a pulse that is still present, because the injury to the artery may be a tear in its inner layer that closes gradually rather than a clean division that stops the flow at once. The lay first aider shortens the time by calling for help immediately, by not moving the knee unnecessarily, and by keeping the patient still, while the trained responder reports the time of the injury, the condition of the foot, and every change in the pulse.

The criteria for immediate referral are simple enough to be remembered under pressure, and they begin with the mechanism rather than with the examination. Any knee that was dislocated and has returned to position, any knee that is still deformed, any knee with an absent or diminished pulse at the foot, any limb that is pale, cold, or numb, any knee with an expanding swelling behind the joint or in the calf, and any open wound that reaches the joint all require the fastest possible transfer to a hospital with orthopedic and vascular surgical capability. A patient who can walk does not cancel the referral, because a reduced dislocation can be walked on for a short distance before it declares itself, and a patient whose pain is blunted may look calmer than the injury deserves. The responder should say aloud what has been found and what has changed, including the side that is injured and the state of the pulses, so that the receiving team can prepare the right examination before the patient arrives. The finding that always justifies the transfer is a limb whose circulation is in doubt, because the cost of an unnecessary journey is far smaller than the cost of a limb lost while the patient waits.

Ligament injuries of the knee are common, and their importance in this chapter is that they can be the visible part of a much larger injury. A ligament is torn when the joint is forced beyond its normal range, and the patient often describes a twist, a pop, immediate swelling, and a knee that feels as though it will not hold the weight. An injury of one ligament usually leaves the knee sore but stable enough to bear weight, while an injury of several ligaments leaves a joint that moves in directions it should not, and that pattern of multiple ligaments torn is the signature of a knee that was dislocated and then returned to position. The finding that should raise the concern is a knee that is grossly loose, a knee that locks, or a knee with a numb or pulseless foot, and the lay first aider's part is to immobilize the limb and to avoid any test that moves the joint.

Assessment of the knee follows the same order as every other injury in this manual, and it begins with the eyes and the hands rather than with movement. The responder looks first at the position of the limb, at the swelling, at the color of the skin below the knee, at the wounds and the bleeding, and at whether the patient is holding the knee still or guarding it. The hands then compare the two limbs, feeling the temperature of the skin, the pulses at the top of the foot and behind the inner ankle bone, and the sensation over the top of the foot and between the first two toes, because the nerves that cross the knee supply those areas. The responder asks the patient what happened, whether the knee was ever out of place, whether the foot feels numb or cold, and whether the patient can move the toes. What the responder does not do is test the ligaments by pulling and pushing the joint, because a knee that is already injured can be made worse by the test, and the stability examination belongs to the clinician in the hospital. A comparison with the uninjured side is the most useful single act, because the patient's own normal pulse and normal sensation are the standard against which the injured side is judged.

Reassessment of the pulses and the sensation is not a single act but a rhythm that continues from the first contact to the handover, and it is repeated after every intervention. The two pulses are checked at the top of the foot and behind the inner ankle bone, and the responder writes on the limb or in the record where each pulse was felt, because a mark that two people can find makes the next comparison honest. Sensation is checked by asking the patient whether the touch on the top of the foot and between the first two toes feels the same as on the other side, and movement is checked by asking the patient to bend and straighten the toes and to lift the foot. The pulse and the sensation are checked before a splint is applied and again afterwards, and any change is treated as a reason to loosen the splint and to reassess rather than as a reason to wait. A reasonable interval for repeating the observations when the circulation is in doubt is 15 minutes, and that number is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because a limb with a threatened artery deserves a rhythm set by the receiving team. The finding that must be passed on at once is a pulse that has disappeared or weakened, or a patient who can no longer feel the toes.

Immobilization of the injured knee is done in the position found, and the rule that a deformed joint is never straightened to make it look normal applies here more than anywhere else in the limb. The reason is that the artery and the nerves lie within a short distance of the bone ends, and forcing the joint back into line can tear the vessel that is still intact or release a clot that is holding the bleeding. The lay first aider can immobilize the limb with a board, a folded blanket, a rigid object such as a rolled magazine, or by binding the injured leg to the uninjured one, with padding between the knees and the ankles so that the skin is not pressed against bone. The trained responder uses a padded long splint that extends from the groin to the ankle, applies it without traction, and checks the pulse and the sensation before and after, because a splint that is too tight can itself stop the circulation. A traction splint is not used on a knee injury, because pulling on the leg may worsen a dislocation and a vascular injury, and the knee is named among the injuries that make that device the wrong choice. The finding that tells the responder to loosen the splint is a foot that has become pale, cold, or numb, or pain that has increased rather than settled.

An open wound at the knee changes the problem from a closed injury to a contaminated one, and the responder's task is to protect the wound rather than to inspect it. A wound that communicates with the joint allows bacteria to enter the space between the bones, and that space has little defense against infection, so the injury becomes an urgent surgical problem that needs washing out in an operating room rather than a dressing at the roadside. An object embedded in the wound, whether a fragment of glass, a piece of metal, or a splinter of wood, is stabilized in place and never removed in the field, because removal may cause hemorrhage that cannot be controlled and may injure a structure that is still intact. The correct act is to build padding around the object, to keep it from moving, and to move the patient with it in place, while the trained responder controls any bleeding around it without pressing on the object itself. The decisions about protection against tetanus and about antibiotics belong to the clinician and to the local protocol, and the finding that makes the decision urgent is a wound that is deep, contaminated, or caused by a bite or by soil. Every such wound is described at handover, including the object that is still in place, the time of the injury, and the dressing that has been applied.

Swelling is expected after a knee injury, and a swelling that is tense or that keeps growing is a warning rather than a detail. Blood and fluid collect inside the joint and in the tissues of the thigh and the calf, and the pressure that builds can compress the vessels and the nerves of the leg, which is the beginning of compartment syndrome. The findings that should worry the responder are pain that is severe and out of proportion to the wound, pain that increases when the toes or the ankle are gently stretched, a calf or a thigh that feels hard and tight, numbness or weakness in the foot, and a pulse that is becoming difficult to find. The lay first aider does not bind the limb tightly to reduce the swelling and does not press repeatedly into the swollen tissue, because both acts raise the pressure further. The trained responder removes or loosens anything that encircles the limb, keeps the limb in the position found, and moves the patient toward definitive care, while the measurement of the pressure inside the limb, which is often described at a level of 30 millimeters of mercury, belongs to the hospital and to a clinician who can act on it. That figure, like every other in this chapter, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line at which the pressure becomes dangerous depends on the patient and on the injury.

External bleeding from a knee injury is usually modest, and the bleeding that kills is the bleeding that is not seen. A torn artery behind the knee can pour blood into the thigh and the calf, so the limb swells while the skin remains almost dry, and the patient shows shock before anyone sees a wound. The findings of shock are a patient who is anxious, restless, or thirsty, a pulse that is fast and thin, skin that is pale and cool, breathing that has become rapid, and a level of consciousness that is dulling. The lay first aider covers and presses any external wound, keeps the patient flat and still unless another injury forbids it, keeps the patient warm, and sends for help, while the trained responder watches the swelling and shortens the journey. A tourniquet is used only for a limb that is bleeding beyond control and only by a responder authorized and trained to apply it, and once it has controlled the bleeding it is not loosened in the field, and the time it was placed is written on the patient where the receiving team will see it. The reason the time matters is that the receiving team must know how long the limb has been without blood flow in order to judge the risk of releasing the tourniquet, and a time that was never written is a time that is lost.

Cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and a patient with a knee injury is at risk from the moment of the injury. The patient lies on cold ground, the clothing is often cut away to examine the limb, the injured leg is exposed while a splint is applied, and a patient who is bleeding from a torn vessel loses the volume that carries heat, so the body temperature falls while the responders work. Cold makes the clotting system work less well, deepens shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm, which is why the protection of warmth begins before the journey rather than after it. The responder removes wet clothing and replaces it with dry covering, insulates the patient from the ground, covers the patient including the uninjured limb and the head, and keeps the vehicle or the room warm on the way. A temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often quoted as the point at which cold becomes dangerous in itself, and that figure must be verified against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold differs with age and with the way the temperature is measured. The finding that warns the responder is a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold, because shivering is the body's attempt to make heat.

Moving a patient with a knee injury is a task of support rather than of speed, because the limb must travel in the position found and the whole patient must be considered. The injured leg is supported above and below the joint, the knee is not allowed to bend or twist during the lift, and the patient is moved as a unit, with the spine protected when the mechanism suggests that the spine may also be injured. The destination is chosen before the patient is moved, and it is the nearest facility that can examine the circulation of the limb and, if necessary, repair the vessels, which may mean a trauma center rather than the closest hospital with an emergency room, and that choice follows the local protocol for the region. The handover carries the time of the injury, the mechanism, whether the knee was ever out of place, the findings of the pulse and the sensation at each check, the swelling, the wounds, the splint, and every change that was observed.

Pain from a knee injury can be severe, and it is real, but the treatment of pain is a decision about a patient rather than a rule that can be carried away from a page. The lay first aider may comfort the patient, support the limb, protect the patient from cold and from unnecessary movement, and explain what is happening, and may not give any substance, because the choice of a medicine and the amount and the route belong to a prescriber. The trained responder and the paramedic may give pain relief only within the protocol of the service, and the finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that is severe, a joint that is deformed, or a limb whose circulation is in doubt, because pain of that kind worsens the circulation and makes the patient harder to assess. The choice of substance, the amount, the way it is given, and how often it is repeated are set by the local protocol and by the clinician, and no amount or interval may be taken from this manual. Definitive hospital care owns everything at the knee that repairs rather than contains, including the reduction of the dislocated joint under controlled conditions, the repair or bypass of a torn artery, the repair of ligaments, the washing out of an opened joint, and the fixation of a broken kneecap, and none of those is a field procedure.

To summarize, the knee is a joint where a common injury and a limb-threatening emergency look alike, and the responder decides between them by the mechanism, the position of the limb, and the condition of the foot. A fractured kneecap, a kneecap out of its groove, and a torn ligament are each painful and each needs immobilization in the position found, while a knee that has been dislocated, even if it has returned to place, is a vascular emergency because the artery behind the joint is the main supply to the leg below. The signs of a failing circulation are a pale or cold foot, an absent or weakened pulse at the top of the foot or behind the inner ankle bone, numbness between the first two toes, and a swelling behind the knee that keeps growing, and a single normal pulse does not cancel the emergency, because the artery can close over the hours that follow. The limb is splinted as it lies, never straightened, with the pulse and the sensation checked before and after and repeated in a rhythm until the handover, and the patient is covered and kept warm because cold is a complication of trauma. Every intervention is named with the provider level that owns it, no definitive procedure is presented as first aid, and the immediate referral criteria are a suspected or reduced dislocation, a doubtful pulse, an open wound into the joint, or a limb that is pale, cold, or numb. Every time, pressure, temperature, and number in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol before it is acted on, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 29 — Tibia and Fibula Fractures

Two bones share the lower leg, and only one of them carries the weight of the body, so the pair can be broken in ways that look alike and behave very differently. The tibia is the thick inner bone that runs from the knee to the ankle and bears the load, while the fibula is the slender bone on the outer side that steadies the ankle. Before either is examined the scene is made safe, because traffic, fire, electricity, water, an unrestrained animal, a violent person, and a structure that may collapse are each a lethal possibility, and the patient's own blood is treated as infectious, with personal protective equipment, or PPE, worn wherever it is available. The lethal possibilities in a broken lower leg are named at the first look: an open wound that carries contamination into the bone, a leg swelling inside its skin until the pressure starves the muscle, and bleeding from a torn vessel that can fill the limb while the surface looks almost dry. The lay first aider may steady the limb, cover a wound, and keep the patient warm; the trained responder or paramedic may splint, control bleeding within a protocol, and monitor; and the cleaning of an open fracture, the reduction and fixation of the bone, and the release of a compartment belong to definitive hospital care. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The tibia demands more caution than its size suggests because it lies directly beneath the skin along its front and inner border. In most of the body a broken bone is cushioned by a thick sleeve of muscle, but over the shin the covering is only skin, a thin layer of tissue, and bone, so a bone end that shifts can threaten the skin from the inside. A wound that seems small, a graze, or a puncture that a hurried responder might dismiss can therefore be the mouth of a track that reaches the fracture, and the break becomes open even when the bone is not visible. The fibula has more muscle around it and does not carry weight, so an isolated fracture of the fibula is usually a lesser injury, but the nerve that winds around its upper end can be injured by the same force or by a splint that presses there. The finding to seek on the outer side of the upper calf is a foot that cannot be lifted and a patch of skin on the top of the foot that has gone numb, because either one points to that nerve and changes the urgency of the journey.

The mechanism of injury is the first clinical evidence, and it predicts damage that no eye can see from the shape of the leg. A direct blow from a vehicle bumper, a motorcycle, a falling object, or a piece of machinery breaks the bone across its width and bruises the soft tissue at the same time, while a twist of the body against a planted foot produces a spiral break that may come with a torn ligament at the ankle. A fall from a height greater than 3 meters, offered only as a teaching illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, predicts compression of the spine and of the heels and should prompt an examination of the back, the pelvis, and the feet before attention settles on the leg. A crushing weight hides the most, because muscle beneath an intact skin can be damaged without an obvious fracture, and the same force that broke the tibia may have broken the thigh, the pelvis, or the ribs. The responder who reads the mechanism examines with a purpose, looking for the injury the force makes likely rather than the one that is most visible, and remembers that a patient who cannot breathe or circulate is treated before a leg is splinted.

A closed fracture of the tibia is one in which the skin over the break is intact, and closed must never be heard as harmless. The broken ends can have torn the vessels that run beside the bone or the nerves that cross it, and blood can collect inside the leg until the limb is tense and the circulation beyond the break is failing. The closed fracture is also the classic setting for compartment syndrome, because the fascia that wraps the muscle does not stretch and a swelling that has nowhere to go raises the pressure within. The findings that mark a closed fracture as serious are pain that is severe and increasing, a leg that feels hard and tight to the hand, numbness or tingling in the foot, and a foot that is pale or cool although the skin is unbroken. The lay first aider does not squeeze the leg to test it, tighten a bandage around it, or lift the patient to standing, and leaves the leg as it lies, covered, supported, and warm, while help is called.

Deformity is the sign that tells the responder most about the soft tissue, and it means any departure from the normal line of the leg, whether the bone is angled, the leg is shortened, or the foot is turned outward where it should point forward. The bone ends have come to rest in a position that may be pressing on an artery or a nerve without having torn it, and the tissue around the break is stretched or kinked in a way that straightening can reverse only by dragging the sharp end across what is still intact. The rule is therefore absolute and belongs to every level of provider: a deformed lower leg is splinted as it lies, and its shape is not corrected to make it look normal. The reason is survival of the limb rather than appearance, because a clot that has sealed a torn vessel can be released by the movement and a nerve that was only bruised can be cut, so an injury that was survivable becomes one that threatens the leg or the life. If the foot beyond the deformity is cold, pale, or pulseless, the responder says so plainly and shortens the journey rather than attempting a correction, because reduction is a decision for definitive hospital care and never a field procedure.

An open fracture of the lower leg turns a mechanical break into an infective one, and it is a surgical emergency from the moment it is recognized. The wound may be dramatic with bone visible in it, or it may be a small puncture over the shin that a responder almost misses, because a spike of bone can pierce the skin, withdraw, and leave a tiny mark above a widely contaminated track. The wound admits soil, road grit, fragments of clothing, and the material of whatever struck the leg into the same space as the broken bone, and the tissue around the break is often bruised and deprived of its blood supply, which is exactly the ground on which infection grows. The finding that establishes the fracture as open is any break in the skin of the leg near the break in the bone, and a responder who cannot tell whether the wound reaches the bone treats it as open until definitive care decides otherwise. No one pushes a protruding bone end back under the skin, puts a finger or an instrument into the wound, or pours anything into it, because each of those acts drives contamination deeper and may injure a structure that is still intact. The wound is covered with a clean or sterile dressing, the limb is supported where it lies, and the patient is moved toward a facility where the wound can be cleaned in an operating room.

Bleeding from an open fracture is controlled with firm direct pressure over a clean dressing placed around the wound rather than over the bone end, and if blood soaks through, further layers are added without lifting the first. A dressing pressed directly onto a protruding bone end achieves nothing and adds pain, so the padding is built up on either side of the bone and the force is directed at the soft tissue that is bleeding. An object embedded in the wound, whether glass, a splinter of metal, or a piece of the machinery that caused the injury, is stabilized in place with padding around it and is never removed in the field, because removal may release a hemorrhage that no dressing can control. A tourniquet on the lower leg belongs to the trained responder or the paramedic under a protocol, it is placed above the wound and never over the knee if a length of thigh is available, and once it has controlled the bleeding it is not loosened in the field. Its time of application is written on the patient where the receiving team will see it and spoken aloud at handover, because a limb deprived of blood has a limited tolerance and the receiving team must know how long the interval has been. A lay first aider without a manufactured tourniquet keeps firm pressure on the wound with both hands and does not improvise a narrow band, because such a band can tighten the limb without stopping the flow.

Care of the wound in the field is deliberately small, because the acts that clean and repair an open fracture belong to definitive hospital care. The responder covers the wound, protects the dressing from the pressure of the splint, and removes only obvious gross dirt from the skin around the wound without disturbing what lies within it. Nothing is poured into the wound, no antiseptic, no water under pressure, and no powder, because irrigation that is not performed with the right fluid, volume, and technique can push contamination deeper and damage tissue that is already fragile. The wound is not closed in the field by tape, by a suture, or by pulling the skin together, because a closed contaminated wound traps infection inside the leg and hides the tissue that the surgeon needs to see. The dressing is checked for strike-through as the patient is moved, a soaked dressing is covered rather than replaced, and the limb beneath it is examined for a swelling that is growing. The finding that should make the responder state the wound's age and contamination at handover is a wound produced by soil, by a farm machine, or by a delay of hours before help arrived, because those details shape the decisions about protection against tetanus and about antibiotics, and those decisions belong to the provider authorized to make them under the local protocol.

The decisions about protection against tetanus and about antibiotics in an open fracture are clinical decisions that belong to a prescriber working under a local protocol. The finding that makes the decision urgent is a wound that is deep, heavily contaminated, produced by soil or machinery, or seen many hours after the injury, and the responder's part is to describe those features accurately rather than to suggest a substance. The substance, the amount, the route, and the frequency are set by the local protocol and the prescriber in front of the patient, so no reader should take a prescription from these pages. The same rule governs pain relief, because a patient with a broken leg is in genuine pain, and untreated pain worsens the circulation and makes the patient move.

The neurovascular examination is performed in a fixed order at the foot, and it is the examination that decides how quickly the patient must travel. Circulation is judged by the color and the warmth of the skin of the foot, by the time it takes for color to return after the nail bed is pressed and released, and by the pulses that can be felt at the top of the foot and behind the inner ankle when the responder is trained to find them. A return of color that takes longer than 2 seconds is one figure used to describe poor flow, and that figure, like every other in this chapter, is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the acceptable time differs with the patient and with the temperature of the limb. Sensation is checked by asking the patient what can be felt, by touching the skin lightly on the top of the foot, between the first two toes, on the sole, and on each side of the leg, and by comparing the injured foot with the other one. Movement is checked by asking the patient to pull the toes up and to push them down, and where the patient cannot, the responder notes whether the failure comes from pain, from weakness, or from an obvious deformity. The lay first aider reports what the patient says and what the skin looks like, while the trained responder performs the full check and repeats it at every stage of the care.

Compartment syndrome is the complication of the lower leg that is most often missed, and it is missed because the leg can look almost undamaged from the outside while the tissue within is dying. The muscles of the lower leg are divided into four compartments by sheets of fascia, one at the front, one at the outer side, and two at the back, and each compartment is a closed space that cannot expand. When blood and fluid collect after a fracture, after a crush, or after a tight bandage, the pressure inside that space rises until it exceeds the pressure that fills the small vessels, and the muscle and the nerve within lose their blood supply. A fracture of the shaft of the tibia is the classic cause, and a splint applied too tightly, a circumferential bandage, and a limb that continues to swell can each produce the same result. The earliest and most reliable finding is pain that is severe and out of proportion to the injury, pain that is made worse when the toes are gently pulled upward or pushed downward, and a leg that feels tense and hard to the hand. The responder must not wait for the pulse to disappear, because the pressure that starves the muscle can be present while the main artery still carries blood, and waiting for a pulseless foot is waiting far too long.

The findings that follow the pain are numbness and tingling in the foot, weakness of the muscles that move the ankle and the toes, and a limb that is shiny and taut rather than soft. A patient who has been given strong pain relief, a patient who is unconscious, and a patient whose nerves are already damaged by illness may not report the pain at all, so the responder looks at the whole picture, including the swelling, the tightness, and the movement the patient can no longer make. The care that the field allows is narrow: loosen or remove anything that encircles the limb, release a bandage or splint that has become too tight where the protocol permits, keep the limb at the level of the heart rather than raised above it, keep the patient warm, and move toward the surgeon without delay. Elevation above the level of the heart is avoided when compartment syndrome is suspected, because it lowers the pressure that drives blood into the muscle and can deepen the injury even as it makes the swelling look less. The measurement of the pressure inside the compartment and the operation that opens the fascia belong to definitive hospital care, and a fasciotomy is never performed in the field by any responder, however urgent the leg appears. The lay first aider's part is to report the pain, the swelling, and the numbness honestly and to keep the leg still, since a leg that is moved and squeezed by many hands has been handled enough.

Reassessment is not one examination but a rhythm that begins at the scene and continues to the handover, and the same questions are asked in the same order each time. The circulation, the sensation, and the movement of the foot are checked before the splint is applied, immediately after it is applied, after every move of the patient, and at intervals during the journey. The purpose is not to find a new injury but to detect a change caused by the treatment, because a splint or a position that has made the foot colder, paler, more painful, or more numb than it was has become part of the problem. The findings are written down with the time of each entry and spoken aloud at handover, since the trend over time tells the receiving team more than any single reading. The findings that should send the responder back to the beginning of the primary survey are a falling level of consciousness, a changed breathing pattern, a pulse that has become fast and weak, and skin that has become cold and clammy, because those signs speak of bleeding or shock rather than of the leg alone.

Splinting the lower leg means holding both the knee and the ankle, because a bone that lies between two joints cannot be kept still by a support that stops short of either. A rigid support is placed along the back or the sides of the leg from above the knee to below the ankle, padded so that the force of the ties is spread, and secured at several points with broad strips rather than a narrow cord or a wire that concentrates pressure on one line of skin. A second support alongside the first, or the uninjured leg bound to the injured one with padding between the knees and the ankles, gives the same result when no manufactured splint is at hand, and the uninjured leg is a good splint because it is the right length and it moves with the patient. The foot is held at a right angle to the leg, neither dropped nor forced, so that the ankle does not fall forward and stretch the tissue at the back of the calf, and the heel and the tendon above it are supported rather than left hanging. The bony points that must be padded are the head of the fibula on the outer side of the upper calf, because the nerve passes there, the shin, the ankle bones on both sides, and the heel. The splint is checked as soon as it is in place, and the finding that it must be adjusted is a foot that has changed in color, warmth, or feeling.

Elevation and padding are the two details that make a lower leg splint safe to carry, and each has a limit the responder must understand. Padding under the whole length of the limb, including under the calf and the heel, spreads the weight and prevents the skin from breaking down over a bony point. Elevation of the leg above the level of the heart reduces swelling and eases pain in a closed fracture with an intact circulation, and it is a reasonable comfort measure while the patient waits or travels. The same elevation becomes harmful when compartment syndrome is suspected or when the foot is already pale and pulseless, because raising the limb lowers the pressure that pushes blood into the muscle and can worsen the very injury that is feared. For that reason the leg is kept at the level of the heart when the responder is worried about the compartment, and the decision is written down and passed on so that the next person does not raise it out of habit. The padding also protects against cold, because a patient lying still on the ground with a broken leg loses heat from the exposed limb, and warmth is a treatment rather than a comfort.

An open fracture of the tibia is a surgical emergency, and the operation it needs is called debridement, which means the removal of dead, contaminated, and foreign material from the wound together with washing of the tissues. The surgeon opens the wound fully, examines the muscle for tissue that has lost its blood supply, removes what cannot survive, and washes the wound under controlled conditions, and only then does the surgeon stabilize the bone and decide whether the wound can be closed or must be left open. A period such as 6 hours from the injury to the debridement is a common teaching figure for the window in which the risk of infection is lowest, and that figure is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the interval differs with the contamination, the state of the tissue, and the resources of the receiving hospital. The responder's contribution to that operation is made at the roadside, and it consists of covering the wound, keeping it still, controlling the bleeding, and delivering the patient quickly, because every hour of delay and every unnecessary handling adds to the work the surgeon must undo. Bleeding that continues despite pressure, tissue that has lost its color, and dirt or clothing driven deep into the wound are findings that make the journey urgent.

Definitive hospital care owns everything that aligns, repairs, and fixes a fracture of the lower leg, and knowing where that line lies is part of competence for every responder. A plain radiograph taken from the front and the side defines the pattern of the break, a computed tomography scan is used when the joint at the knee or the ankle is involved, and the images are read by the clinician who will decide the treatment. Reduction, which means bringing the broken ends back into alignment, may be performed by closed manipulation or through an operation, and fixation may be achieved with a rod placed inside the bone, with plates and screws along its surface, or with an external frame when the soft tissue will not tolerate an internal device. The surgeon also repairs a torn vessel, releases a compartment under pressure, covers exposed bone with a flap of tissue where that is needed, and closes the wound only when the tissue is clean enough to accept closure. The decisions about antibiotics, tetanus protection, fluids, and pain relief belong to the providers authorized to make them with the patient in front of them. The complications watched for over the following weeks are infection of the bone, failure of the break to unite, and union in a poor position.

The record and the handover carry the mechanism of injury, the time it happened, the state of every wound, the neurovascular findings before and after splinting, the material used, the time of every intervention, and every change observed along the way. The receiving facility is chosen for the care the patient needs, which may be a trauma center with imaging, an operating room, and an intensive care unit, and that choice is made before the patient is moved rather than after the journey has begun. Transport is urgent and gentle at once, because a jolting journey moves the broken ends, adds pain, and can convert a closed injury into an open one, so the patient is secured, the limb is supported, and the speed is the fastest that is safe. Life comes before limb when two correct actions compete for the same hands, so a patient whose airway is closed or whose circulation is failing is treated before the leg is splinted, even when the leg is the more frightening injury to look at. The two failures that run through the care of a broken lower leg are the compartment syndrome that was not suspected because the pulse could still be felt and the open fracture that was treated as a wound while the patient was bleeding somewhere else. Both are defeated by the same habits, which are to examine the leg rather than to look at it, to repeat the examination until the handover, and to say aloud what has changed.

To summarize, the tibia carries the weight and lies just beneath the skin, so its fractures are easily opened to contamination and easily hidden in their depth, while the fibula is a lesser bone whose upper end can still injure the nerve that lifts the foot. The mechanism of injury is the first evidence, a closed fracture is never a minor one, and a deformed lower leg is splinted exactly as it lies because straightening it can tear the vessels and the nerves that the position has spared. An open fracture is a surgical emergency, its wound is covered and never pushed, probed, poured into, or closed in the field, and the decisions about tetanus protection and antibiotics belong to the prescriber and the local protocol. Compartment syndrome is the complication most often missed, its earliest finding is pain out of proportion that worsens when the toes are stretched, and a pulse that can still be felt proves nothing, so anything that encircles the limb is loosened, the leg is kept at the level of the heart, and the patient moves quickly to the surgeon. Splinting holds the knee and the ankle, pads every bony point, keeps the foot at a right angle, and is checked before and after every move, and the neurovascular examination of the foot is repeated on the same rhythm until handover. Every number, time, pressure, temperature, and depth in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries, and editions, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 30 — Ankle Injuries

The ankle is a small joint asked to carry the whole weight of the body, and it fails in ordinary moments as well as violent ones. No hand is laid on such a patient until the scene is safe, so traffic is held, an unstable vehicle is left alone or made stable, spilled fuel is kept from any source of ignition, and a live wire, deep water, a loose animal, a violent person, or a wall that may still fall is handled by someone with authority to handle it. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, with gloves at the least, shields the responder from the patient's blood at the same moment that it shields the patient from the responder's hands. Three possibilities here can kill or cripple if they are missed: an open fracture that bleeds and becomes contaminated, a dislocated ankle that has shut off the blood supply to the foot, and an injury elsewhere that the swollen joint has hidden.
