The ankle is rarely the wound that kills, and that is why it is dangerous, because attention is limited and a dramatic joint can spend all of it; this chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Knowing what can break begins with knowing what the joint is made of. The shin bone, the tibia, carries the weight and ends in the inner knob of the ankle, the slender fibula runs down the outer side and ends in the outer knob, and these knobs are the malleoli that can be felt on either side of the joint. Between them sits the talus, the bone of the foot that fits into the arch the other two form, and ligaments hold the whole arrangement together. On the outer side a complex of ligaments resists the foot rolling inward, on the inner side a broad and powerful ligament resists the foot rolling outward, and above the joint a ligament binds the tibia and the fibula so the arch does not spread under weight. The same force produces different damage at different ages, because a young ligament tears while an older bone gives way first, so tenderness over bone is never assumed to be a sprain.

The mechanism of injury is read as a prediction rather than as a story. A foot rolling inward drives the talus against the outer malleolus, so the outer ligaments tear, or the outer bone breaks, or both happen together, and this is the commonest mechanism of all. A foot rolling outward presses the talus against the inner malleolus and opens the space between the tibia and the fibula, so the inner bone may break while the ligament above the joint tears as well, and a joint that loses that binding is unstable even when the bones look almost intact. A foot planted while the leg rotates produces a long crack that may climb the fibula far above the ankle, which is why tenderness high on the outer calf changes the whole assessment. A fall from a height drives the talus up into the lower tibia and can shatter the bone above the joint, while a wheel or a heavy weight tears skin from within and contaminates everything it opens; a wound over the joint makes the injury an open injury until a surgeon has looked at it.

A malleolar fracture is a break of one or both of the bony knobs, and the number broken predicts how stable the joint will remain. One broken malleolus with the ligaments on the other side intact is often a joint that still holds, while two broken malleoli, or a break that includes the back lip of the tibia where the talus rests, usually means a joint that can shift under the least load. What matters at the roadside is not the label but whether movement will drive the bones apart and stretch the thin skin over them. The findings of an unstable joint are deformity, an ankle that feels loose when a trained responder compares it gently with the other side, and an inability to bear any weight. The skin over the malleoli lies directly on bone, so a fracture that displaces even a little can tear it from within, and a wound over a broken ankle may have been made by the bone end; a puncture no larger than a fingertip over a malleolus is therefore treated as an open fracture, and its care begins with covering it and not with inspecting it.

An ankle dislocation is the displacement of the talus from under the tibia, and it is one of the few limb injuries in which minutes decide whether the foot survives. The joint looks wrong in a way that is hard to mistake: the foot is turned or shifted, the skin over one malleolus is stretched tight and pale or shiny, and the patient is in severe pain. The vessels that feed the foot run close to the bones behind the inner ankle and across the front of the joint, so a displaced joint can kink or compress them, and the finding that reveals this is a pale, cool foot with no pulse that can be felt, together with numbness or an inability to move the toes. The lay first aider must not pull the joint back into place, because the attempt may drive a bone end through skin or through a vessel and turn a threatened foot into a dead one, so the limb is left exactly as it lies, any wound is covered, the patient is kept warm, and help is sent for at once. The trained responder or paramedic may reduce the joint only where the local protocol authorizes it and only with the training and monitoring that make the attempt safe, and definitive hospital care confirms the position with radiography, checks the vessels and nerves again, and holds the joint with the fixation the injury requires.

A sprain is a torn ligament, and most ankle sprains are painful but forgiving, which is precisely why the serious variant is missed. The ordinary injury is a tear of the outer ligament complex after the foot rolls inward, and it produces swelling, bruising, and pain that settles over days with protection and gradual use. The dangerous variant is the high sprain in which the ligament binding the tibia and the fibula is torn, because that injury changes the width of the arch the talus sits in, and the joint behaves like a fracture even when the image shows no break; its signs are tenderness above the joint between the two bones, pain when the lower leg is gently squeezed so the bones press together, and an inability to bear weight. A sprain and a fracture can coexist, and a sprain never protects the bones from a second injury, so every ankle swollen enough to distrust is treated as broken until someone with imaging has said otherwise.

The difference between a joint that is swollen and a joint whose blood supply is failing is the most important judgment in this chapter, and it is made with the eyes and the hands. A swollen ankle is expected after any injury: the skin is soft, the foot beyond it stays warm and keeps its color, the pulses can be felt, the toes can be moved, and the pain is in proportion to what happened. A joint in trouble behaves differently, because the swelling becomes tense and shiny and keeps growing while the responder watches, and the pain becomes far greater than the injury would explain, often a deep ache or a burning that does not ease. The toes may go pale or blue, the skin may feel cool compared with the other limb, and a pulse that was easy to find earlier may become faint or disappear. This is not a reason to wait and watch, because these findings are the language of a foot being starved of blood, so whatever compresses it is removed, the limb is kept in the position found, and the patient is moved toward definitive care without delay; a swollen ankle inside a tight boot or a tightly wound bandage is the classic setting for this.

The neurovascular assessment is a short examination performed in the same order every time so that two people can compare what they find, and its parts that need only eyes and hands belong to the lay first aider while the whole of it belongs to the trained responder and the clinician. The first comparison is with the other limb, because what is normal for one patient is not a fixed standard and the uninjured side is the best reference available in the field. Color and warmth are looked at and felt, and the time taken for color to return after the tip of a toe is pressed is noted, since a slow or absent return warns that the smallest vessels are not filling; a delay of about 2 seconds is often taught as the line between normal and worrying, and that figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The pulse is felt behind the inner ankle and on the top of the foot, and the responder notes not only whether it is present but how easily it is found. Sensation is tested by asking whether the toes feel normal, whether there is tingling, and whether light touch is felt on both sides of the foot, while movement is tested by asking the patient to spread the toes and bend the foot, and any deterioration in these findings is an emergency.

One assessment is a photograph and a series of assessments is a film, and it is the film that tells the receiving team what is happening to the foot. The first check is made on contact, the second after any movement of the limb, the third after the splint or dressing is applied, and then at the intervals the local protocol sets until handover. The reason for checking after splinting is that a splint applied correctly can still become too tight as the limb swells inside it, and a bandage comfortable a few minutes ago can become a tourniquet without anyone intending it. The findings are written down with the time they were found, on the patient or on the record that travels with the patient, because a finding that is only remembered will be lost in the noise of a handover; a pulse that was present and has gone demands an immediate review of everything wrapped around the limb and the fastest safe journey onward.

Whether a painful ankle needs a radiograph is decided by criteria written to spare patients from images that cannot show what is feared, and the criteria are simple enough to hold in the ear. The assessment begins with where it hurts: if there is pain near either malleolus, the examiner looks for tenderness over bone along the back edge or the tip of that malleolus, or along the lower part of the bone just above it, which is where the tenderness of a break most often sits. If such tenderness is found, or if the patient cannot walk four steps, radiography is indicated, and those two tests are described here as they are commonly taught, to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because the accepted form of the rule differs between services. When the pain is in the middle of the foot, the examiner looks for tenderness over the base of the fifth metatarsal bone or over the navicular bone, because those points mark fractures that are easily missed. The criteria belong to the trained responder and the clinician who have been taught them and are used with the examination rather than instead of it, while the lay first aider treats every painful ankle as though a bone were broken, keeps it still, and lets the hospital decide with an image and a hands-on examination.

The most common failure with an ankle is not a technical error but an early surrender of suspicion. A patient who can stand, who has no deformity, and whose swelling is modest can still have a fracture, a tear of the ligament above the joint, or a dislocation that has already returned to place on its own. A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient or a real incident, is the cyclist who stands after a fall, walks a few steps to prove that nothing is broken, declines an ambulance, and is found hours later with an ankle swollen inside a boot and a foot that has lost its pulse. The lesson is not that every ankle must be treated as catastrophic, but that a few steps are weak evidence and a repeated examination is stronger; the responder who hears a patient refuse help records the refusal, keeps the patient warm and still, and reports what happened and when, because the decision to decline belongs to the patient.

The field sequence for an injured ankle begins not at the ankle but at the start of the primary survey, because a swollen joint is never a reason to skip the search for the injuries that kill. The airway, the breathing, and the circulation are checked first, catastrophic bleeding anywhere on the body is controlled, and only then is the ankle examined, which is the principle of life before limb applied to a patient who is usually stable. Bleeding from an open ankle wound is controlled with direct pressure over a clean dressing, with further layers added if blood soaks through and the first dressing left undisturbed, while a foreign body is stabilized in place and packed around rather than pulled out, because it may plug a torn vessel and its removal may release bleeding that cannot be controlled in the field. The wound is covered with the cleanest material available, and it is not scrubbed, not filled with anything the responder happens to carry, and not closed, since closure over contamination traps infection inside a joint and turns a treatable injury into a destructive one. The patient is kept flat, still, and warm, the ankle is left in the position found until the splint is ready, and the trained responder repeats the neurovascular check and decides whether the limb can be moved before transport begins.

Footwear must be a deliberate decision, because a boot can be a splint and a boot can also be a vise. A firm boot already on the foot and not compressing it holds the ankle better than most field splints and may be left in place while the patient is moved, which spares pain and spares the joint movement. A boot that is tight because the foot is swelling inside it is a different problem, because a foot can lose its blood supply inside a boot without any wound being present, and the sign that calls for action is a foot becoming numb, pale, or painful beyond what the injury explains. The safe way to remove such footwear is to cut the laces and open the boot along its length, working from the top downward while the other hand supports the ankle, and never to pull the boot off by the heel, because that movement levers the foot and can displace a fracture; the decision belongs to the trained responder, and the lay first aider removes only what clearly compresses the foot and can be taken away without moving the joint.

Immobilization of the ankle has one goal that governs every detail, which is to hold the joint in the position in which it will function best while preventing any movement that could worsen the injury. That position is the functional one, with the foot at approximately a right angle to the leg, neither pointed down as it hangs nor pulled up toward the shin, because this is the position in which the foot can later bear weight and in which tendons and skin are under the least tension. A severely deformed ankle is the exception, and the rule for it is absolute: it is splinted exactly as it lies, with padding built up around the deformity, and it is never straightened to make it look normal, because the force needed to straighten it can crush a vessel or stretch a nerve that is still intact. The splint is padded along its whole length, placed so that it supports the foot and the lower leg together, and secured with straps that hold without pinching, and a pillow, a folded blanket, or a commercial splint can serve if each is shaped and padded properly. The foot is supported as well as the leg because the ankle cannot be held still if the foot swings, and the padding is generous because every strap transfers its pressure to the skin beneath it; the splint is right when the joint does not move as the patient is lifted and the neurovascular check is unchanged after it is on.

Pressure injury is the quiet complication of splinting, and it happens where a hard surface meets skin over bone. The heel, the malleoli, the head of the fibula below the knee, and the outer edge of the foot have the least padding, and these are the places where a careless strap or an unpadded splint edge will cause damage over the hours of transport. A bandage wound in circles around the ankle is a particular danger, because as the limb swells the circles tighten together and behave like a tourniquet, so the trained responder prefers a wrap that crosses the joint rather than encircles it, applied evenly and checked at once by looking at the toes. The check that follows every application is the same neurovascular assessment performed before it, and any change in color, warmth, sensation, movement, or pulse means the wrap is released and reapplied more loosely; a splint that is comfortable when applied is not proof that it will be comfortable an hour later, since swelling inside it continues.

Pain relief is part of the care of an ankle injury, and it is also a clinical decision this manual deliberately does not make. The finding that makes relief urgent is severe pain that immobilization has not eased, and the finding that makes it more than a comfort problem is pain growing out of proportion to the injury, because that kind of pain may be the first voice of a compartment syndrome or of a foot losing its supply. The choice of substance, the amount, the route, and the interval belong to the prescriber and the local protocol, so the trained responder gives only what the protocol authorizes, the lay first aider gives nothing by mouth except what a clinician has directed, and nobody leaves a patient to wait in silence, because untreated pain worsens the circulation and deepens shock. Cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, and the patient with an ankle injury is unusually exposed to it. The limb is often bare while it is examined and splinted, the patient lies on the ground, clothing may have been cut away to reach the injury, and the journey may be long; a patient losing heat in those conditions clots poorly, tolerates shock badly, and is more likely to develop a dangerous heart rhythm. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which these effects become serious, and that figure is an illustration which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line differs between services, between countries, and between editions of the same guidance. The response is to cover the patient before the journey rather than after, to insulate the patient from the ground, to replace wet clothing with dry covering, and to keep the injured limb under the same blanket as the rest of the body, checking it briefly and covering it again; a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold is telling the responder that the body has given up trying to make heat.

The ankle does not exist on its own, and the mechanism that injured it often injured other parts of the body at the same time. A fall from a height that broke an ankle may also have fractured the heel, the pelvis, or the spine, a crash may also have produced a chest injury or a fracture of the thigh, and the swollen joint announces none of them; tenderness high on the outer calf, well above the ankle, suggests that the crack in the fibula climbs far up the leg. The trained responder therefore examines both limbs, the pelvis, the chest, and the spine before deciding where the patient should be taken, and any injury more dangerous than the ankle changes the destination, because the patient belongs at the facility that can treat the most serious problem. Definitive hospital care begins with imaging and continues with decisions no responder can make in the field. Radiography shows the bones and the position of the joint, computed tomography, after which CT is allowed, shows the complex fractures of the lower tibia where the plain image leaves doubt, and magnetic resonance imaging, after which MRI is allowed, shows the ligaments and tendons where the question is soft tissue rather than bone. Reduction of a dislocated joint belongs to the clinician who can monitor the patient and act at once if the circulation changes, and holding the reduction may require a splint, an external frame, or an operation, while fixation of a malleolus with plates and screws and repair of the ligament between the tibia and the fibula are operations performed in an operating room by a surgeon. An open ankle fracture is taken to the operating room for irrigation and debridement of every contaminated and dead fragment, and the wound may be left open where the surgeon judges that closing it would trap infection, which is exactly why the field responder must never close it first.

Certain patients break the ordinary rules of reassurance, and naming them keeps the responder from being misled by a calm appearance. A child whose bones are still growing has a growth plate near the lower end of the tibia and the fibula, and an injury through that plate may look like a sprain while it threatens the future length and shape of the leg, so a child with a painful ankle who cannot bear weight deserves the same gravity as an adult with a deformity. An older patient whose bones are thin may fracture a malleolus with a force that would only bruise a younger limb, a patient whose blood is thinned by medicine may bleed far more than the injury suggests, and a patient who cannot feel the feet may not feel a splint that is too tight and must be checked by eye; each of these patients lowers the threshold for calling emergency medical services. The handover carries the story of the ankle in a fixed order so that nothing important is lost, and it begins with the mechanism and the time of the injury. The position in which the limb was found, whether the skin was broken, whether a foreign body remains in the wound, whether footwear was removed or left in place, and what was applied to the limb are reported with the neurovascular findings and the times they were found; a pulse present shortly before arrival is different information from a pulse found on first contact much earlier. Any tourniquet or tight bandage is named with the time of its application, the receiving team is told whether pain has been increasing, because that observation may be the reason for a rapid move to the operating room, and what was given for pain is reported with the provider authorized to give it, which is a statement about the system and not a prescription.

To summarize, the ankle is a small joint that carries a large load and hides several serious injuries behind an ordinary appearance. The scene is made safe before the patient is touched, and the primary survey precedes the limb, because the ankle is rarely the injury that kills but often the one that distracts. Malleolar fractures, a dislocated ankle, a severe sprain, and an open injury are distinguished by the mechanism and by the examination rather than by the patient's ability to walk, and the difference between a swollen joint and a foot losing its blood supply is read in the color, the warmth, the pulses, the sensation, and the movement of the toes. The neurovascular assessment is repeated on contact, after movement, after splinting, and at every interval until handover, and any change in it is an emergency. The ankle is immobilized in the functional position with the foot at a right angle to the leg, a deformity is splinted as it lies and never straightened, the padding protects the heel and the malleoli, and no bandage is allowed to become a tourniquet. An open ankle wound is covered and never closed in the field, an embedded object is stabilized and never removed, footwear is cut away when it compresses the foot, and the patient is kept warm and moved toward definitive care at the pace the whole body demands. Radiography and the criteria that call for it belong to the trained responder and the clinician, while reduction, fixation, repair of ligaments, and debridement of an open joint belong to the surgeon, and every distance, count, temperature, and interval named here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries, and editions.

# Chapter 31 — Foot Injuries

A crushed foot, a broken heel, or a puncture through the sole of a shoe is easy to underestimate and hard to repair, so the scene is made safe before the foot is touched. The hazards named here are the machine still powered, the vehicle still in the roadway, the load still shifting above the patient, the cable dragged into water, and the animal or the person still dangerous. Blood, dirty water, and manure on the skin are the quieter hazards, and personal protective equipment, or PPE, with gloves and eye protection at the least is used for every foot wound. The lethal possibilities are hemorrhage from a mangled foot, the compartment syndrome that a swollen foot can hide, and the crush syndrome that may follow a limb released after a long compression. The foot rarely kills by itself, but the mechanism that broke it can, because a fall that shattered a heel may also have broken the spine. Every act below is named with the provider level that owns it, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

The foot is a platform of small bones bound by ligaments and moved by tendons that turn the corner at the ankle, and its shape can be described in words without a picture. The heel is the calcaneus, the large bone that receives the body's weight at landing, and above it sits the talus, which carries the load of the leg down into the foot. In front of these lies the midfoot, a cluster of small bones that builds the arches, and beyond it run the metatarsals, the long bones of the forefoot, ending in the phalanges of the toes. Two arches give the foot its spring, one along the inner border and one crossing the foot, and the soft tissue over the bones is thin, so swelling has little room to spread. The foot carries the whole weight of the body and it is wrapped in footwear, and those two features explain why a serious foot injury is so often called minor. A shoe hides swelling, holds a wound against dirt, and can become a band that strangles a foot whose circulation is failing, so the responder examines the bare foot and compares it with its neighbor.

A fall from a height lands the patient on the heels, and the force travels upward through the calcaneus into the ankle, the leg, the pelvis, and the spine. The finding is a heel that is swollen and bruised on the sole and around the ankle, widened and shortened, and painful beyond anything the skin suggests. A patient who cannot bear weight on either heel is describing a fracture rather than a sprain, and when both heels are injured the likelihood of a spinal and pelvic injury rises sharply. A fall from a height greater than 3 meters is often quoted as the point at which those secondary injuries become likely, and that distance must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The injury depends on the surface, the position of landing, and the patient as much as on the height, so the figure guides suspicion rather than proving damage. Compression of the spine can exist without pain at first, because the patient is distracted by the heel and the rescue, so the spine is protected from the first minute.

Machinery and vehicles produce the other great family of foot injuries, and they behave differently from a fall. A roller, a press, a conveyor, an agricultural machine, or the wheel of a car can crush the foot between two surfaces, and the skin may be intact while the bone and soft tissue beneath are destroyed. The finding that matters is a foot that is swollen, tense, and deformed even when the skin is whole, because a closed crush can tear vessels and muscle inside a compartment that does not stretch. A run-over injury often strips the skin from the sole, and those wounds are heavily contaminated by road surface, grit, and shoe material before the patient reaches help. A heavy object dropped onto the toes, a motorcycle that falls on the foot, and a bicycle chain that catches the ankle cause the same categories of damage on a smaller scale. A twisted foot may pull a fragment from the base of the fifth metatarsal, and a puncture, a bite, or a small wound from a nail or glass can become a deep infection in a foot with poor blood supply.

Scene safety in this chapter has features peculiar to machinery and industry. A machine that has caught a foot is isolated by a person authorized to isolate it, and until that isolation is confirmed the machine is treated as able to start. A guard removed and a switch left on have killed responders who trusted them, so the machine is not handled until it is locked out by someone with the authority and the key. A vehicle that has run over a patient is held by warning other drivers and positioning a vehicle to protect the space, and the patient is not moved from beneath a load until the load is stable. Water, whether a fast stream, a flooded ditch, or a wet floor beneath an electrical machine, is treated as a conductor and as a drowning hazard at once, and an animal or a violent person is met by withdrawal to a defensible position. A patient lying on cold, wet ground loses heat while the rescue is arranged, so warmth is part of the scene work and not an afterthought.

The foot injury is placed within the primary survey rather than treated on its own, because the mechanism that damaged the foot may have damaged the patient. Airway and breathing come first, then the control of life-threatening bleeding, then the level of consciousness and the movement of the limbs. The principle of life before limb decides the order, and a mangled foot beside a closed airway or a chest filling with air waits while the airway and chest are treated. The findings that send the responder back to the beginning are a falling level of consciousness, a changed breathing pattern, a pulse that is fast and thin, and skin that is pale and cool. A patient whose foot is crushed but whose circulation is otherwise intact is moved toward definitive care with the foot protected, and the journey is shortened rather than delayed by tidying the injury.

Exposure of the foot is the first diagnostic act, and it is done on both feet at once so that the injured one has a comparison. The shoe and sock are removed or cut away, the sole is inspected as carefully as the top, and the skin between the toes is examined because a wound there is easily missed. The size, shape, and color of the feet are compared, and a foot that is swollen, turned, shortened, or sitting at an angle is described before it is touched. Footwear is removed or opened when it threatens the circulation, and the decision is made by what the foot is doing rather than by a rule about every boot. The signs are a foot swelling while the responder watches, a boot tight across the instep, a toe that is pale, blue, or cold, and pain described as pressure rather than soreness. The trained responder cuts the laces and opens the boot along its seams and lifts it away without pulling or twisting, while the lay first aider may cut the laces and steady the limb. A foot trapped in a machine keeps its boot until the machine is released, and the foot is then supported exactly as it lies.

The neurovascular examination compares the injured foot with the uninjured one and asks four questions in a fixed order. Color and warmth are compared, and a foot that is pale, blue, mottled, or cooler than its neighbor is a foot whose blood is not arriving. The pulse on the top of the foot and the pulse behind the inner ankle bone are both sought, and a pulse that was present and has disappeared must be reported at once. Capillary refill is judged by pressing the skin or nail until it blanches and counting the seconds until color returns. A refill time greater than 2 seconds is a warning that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted figure shifts with room temperature, age, and lighting. Sensation is tested over the top of the foot, the sole, and both borders, and movement is tested by asking the patient to bend and straighten the toes against light resistance. A foot that is dusky or white, cold, numb in the sole, or unable to move its toes requires immediate definitive care, and the responder does not massage it, apply heat to it, or elevate it above the heart when the arterial supply is uncertain.

Bleeding from a foot wound is controlled in the same ladder as bleeding anywhere else, but the anatomy changes the technique. Direct pressure with a gloved hand over a clean dressing is the first act, and pressure is held without lifting the dressing, with further layers added on top if blood shows through. The trained responder may pack a deep wound of the foot or ankle firmly down to the bleeding point, and may use a hemostatic dressing where the service carries one, because the sole and heel can conceal a torn vessel. A tourniquet is a measure for the trained responder or paramedic under a protocol, and it is placed above the ankle on the leg rather than around the foot, because a band around the foot cannot compress the vessels between the small bones. Once a tourniquet has controlled the bleeding it is not loosened in the field, and the time it was applied is written on the patient where the receiving team will see it. A partly amputated foot is managed as it lies, and the amputation is never completed by pulling on the tissue, because that pull may release hemorrhage and tear what is still intact. A separated toe is wrapped in clean dry material, sealed in a bag, placed in a cool container rather than on ice, and sent with the patient, because reattachment is a decision for a trauma center.

Open wounds of the foot are among the most contaminated wounds in trauma, because of the environment in which the foot lives. The sole of a shoe carries soil, grit, fragments of glass, and the residue of whatever the patient has walked through, and a wound that passes through that layer carries all of it into the tissue. A puncture from a nail, a splinter, a thorn, or a bite leaves a narrow track that closes at the surface and traps organisms where there is little blood supply and no drainage. A crush or degloving injury presses dirt into a wide surface, and a wound from an agricultural machine adds manure and water to the mixture. Infection in the foot is more dangerous than the same infection elsewhere, because its blood supply is at the end of a long chain of vessels, the tissue over the bone is thin, and the foot sits below the heart. A patient with diabetes, narrowed arteries, or a neuropathy that has removed the feeling from the feet may not notice a wound until the infection is deep, and the decisions about tetanus protection and antibiotics belong to the authorized provider and the prescriber under the local protocol.

The field care of a contaminated foot wound is deliberately limited, and the limit is what keeps the patient safe. Gross dirt and pieces of shoe material on the surface may be lifted away by the trained responder with clean hands, but the wound is not probed, squeezed, or explored, because probing pushes contamination deeper. The trained responder may irrigate a dirty wound with clean water or saline under a protocol, and the lay first aider keeps the surface covered, because irrigation without training can drive fluid into a track that should have been left alone. The wound is covered with a clean dressing that does not constrict the foot, and a wound that is deep, gaping, or contaminated is not closed in the field, because closing it traps infection inside. An object embedded in the foot is stabilized in place and never removed, because a nail, a piece of glass, or a fragment of metal may be plugging the vessel beneath it, and pulling it out can release hemorrhage that no dressing will control. The responder builds padding around the object so pressure falls on the skin beside it, splints the foot with the object in place, and checks the toes after every layer for tightness.

Metatarsal fractures are common in the forefoot and follow a direct blow, a dropped object, a vehicle wheel, or a twisting injury to the front of the foot. The finding is swelling over the top of the foot, tenderness along the bone, bruising under the toes or across the sole, and pain when the patient tries to bear weight. A displaced fracture may show a step in the contour of the foot or an unnatural angle of a toe, and the responder describes that shape without attempting to correct it. The lay first aider supports the foot on a pillow or rolled clothing and keeps the patient from walking on it, and the trained responder applies a padded splint and records the neurovascular findings before and after. The fifth metatarsal deserves its own word, because a break at its base on the outer border heals slowly when the blood supply enters from one direction. Tenderness in the hollow at that base is treated as a fracture even when the patient can still walk, and definitive care decides from a radiograph whether the injury needs support, rest, or an operation.

Fractures of the toes usually follow a stubbed foot, a dropped object, or a crush, and they matter most when the great toe or the joint at its base is involved. The findings are swelling, bruising, pain on movement, and a toe that is bent or overlaps its neighbor. The great toe carries a large part of the push-off in walking, so a break at its base is more disabling than a break in a small toe and may be part of a larger midfoot injury. The trained responder may support an injured toe against its neighbor with soft padding between them, and the padding must be loose enough that the toes beyond it keep their color and warmth. The responder does not pull on the toe to straighten it, because the shape is set by the fracture and the pull can tear the soft tissue around it.

A calcaneal fracture is one of the most serious injuries in this chapter, and it begins with a fall onto the heel. The talus is driven down into the calcaneus and splits it, and the finding is a heel that is swollen, bruised on the sole and around the ankle, widened and shortened, and painful beyond the appearance of the skin. The patient cannot bear weight on the heel, and the responder must not press the heel to test it, because the pressure adds pain and can move the fragments. Because the same force travels into the spine and pelvis, the injury is treated as part of a whole-body injury until the spine is cleared, and the patient is kept flat and still with the head and neck supported. The trained responder immobilizes the foot and leg in the position found, keeps the patient warm, and moves the patient to a trauma center rather than a clinic. Definitive care uses computed tomography, or CT, to show the shape of the break, and an operation may be needed to rebuild the heel, because a calcaneus that heals badly leaves a patient who cannot walk without pain.

A crush injury of the foot is the mechanism in this chapter that most often hides a compartment syndrome, because the foot contains several tight compartments between its bones. A machine, a wheel, a heavy load, or a prolonged entrapment squeezes the muscle and small vessels inside those compartments, and when the pressure inside rises above the pressure that fills the vessels, the tissue is starved even though the skin is intact. The findings are a foot that is tense and swollen, pain that is severe and out of proportion, pain that increases when the toes are bent or straightened, and numbness that begins in the toes and moves inward. The responder removes anything that constricts the foot, including a boot, a sock, a bandage, or a splint that has become tight, and keeps the foot in the position found. The limb is not massaged, not warmed, and not elevated above the heart when the arterial supply is uncertain, and the patient is moved to a hospital where the pressure can be assessed. The diagnosis is clinical and is made from the story and the examination rather than from a single number, so a measured pressure such as 30 millimeters of mercury is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and the responder who waits for that number has waited too long. The act that relieves the pressure is called a fasciotomy, and it is a surgical procedure performed in an operating room and never a field procedure, so the field responder simply removes every constricting layer and states at handover that a compartment syndrome is suspected and why. The finding that demands the fastest possible transfer is pain on stretching the toes together with a foot that is becoming numb, because the window for saving the muscle is closing.

When a foot has been compressed for a long time, the danger is not only inside the foot but in the whole patient, and that is the crush syndrome described in its own chapter of this manual. Muscle without blood for a long period breaks down, and when the load is released the products of that breakdown enter the circulation and can poison the kidneys, disturb the rhythm of the heart, and deepen shock. The findings are a patient trapped for a long time, a limb that is swollen and tense when uncovered, urine that is dark, brown, or the color of cola, and a pulse that becomes fast and weak as the patient is freed. The release of a prolonged crush is therefore a rescue for a trained team with medical direction, and the lay first aider does not lift the load or pull the patient free, because the release itself can cause a sudden deterioration. The responder keeps the patient warm and still, watches the level of consciousness and the pulse, and reports the length of the entrapment and the weight involved to the receiving team. Definitive care gives the treatment this condition requires, and the substance, amount, and route of that treatment belong to the protocol and the clinician rather than to this chapter.

Splinting of the injured foot holds it in the position found, and the position found is never corrected to make the foot look normal. A deformed foot is splinted as it lies, because straightening it can move a fractured bone into a vessel or a nerve and turn a survivable injury into a lost foot. The trained responder uses a padded splint that supports the foot and ankle and extends up the leg, with the ankle held as close to a right angle as the injury allows. Padding is placed over the heel, the bumps on either side of the ankle, the top of the foot, and the toes, because pressure on those points can injure skin already short of blood. The toes are left uncovered so their color, warmth, and movement can be watched, and the splint is secured firmly enough to keep the foot still and loosely enough that the toes do not swell. A dressing on the foot must protect the wound and must not become a band, so the wound is covered with a clean dressing held with a bandage wound without stretching the skin, and blood that soaks through is answered by adding layers rather than by lifting the dressing. The lay first aider supports the foot on a pillow or rolled clothing and waits for trained help rather than applying a splint.

Hypothermia is a complication of a foot injury rather than a detail of comfort, because a patient lying on cold ground, a patient whose wet boot and sock are removed, and a patient waiting for a rescue in the rain all lose heat quickly. Cold makes blood clot poorly, deepens shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm, so the patient is covered before the journey rather than after it. The responder removes wet clothing and replaces it with dry coverings where the wound allows, insulates the patient from the ground, and keeps the vehicle or the room warm on the way. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold differs with age and with the way the temperature is measured. Heat is never applied directly to the injured foot, because a foot that has lost its feeling can be burned by a hot pack or a hot water bottle that the patient cannot feel. The finding that warns the responder that cooling has already begun is a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold, and that finding makes warmth an urgent treatment.

Definitive hospital care owns everything that repairs the foot rather than protects it, and the boundary is worth stating clearly. A radiograph is taken of the foot, and computed tomography, or CT, is used where the shape of a fracture or an injury of the midfoot needs to be seen in more detail. An operation may be needed to put the bones back into place and hold them with metal, which is called open reduction and internal fixation, and that procedure belongs to the surgeon and the operating room. An open wound is cleaned and dead tissue is removed in a procedure called debridement, and a heavily contaminated wound is often left open and closed later when the infection risk has fallen. A compartment syndrome is treated with a fasciotomy, a foot beyond saving may be amputated, and protection against tetanus and the use of antibiotics are decisions of the prescriber and the local protocol. The responder's part ends with an accurate handover, and that handover is what allows the surgeon to begin with the right question.

Reassessment continues from the scene to the handover and follows the same four questions in the same order, which are color and warmth, pulses, sensation, and movement. The comparison that matters is not a single set of findings but the difference between one set and the next, because a foot that is losing its blood supply tells the responder through change. The findings that send the responder back to the beginning are toes that have become pale or blue, a pulse that has disappeared, a foot that is more painful or more numb, a swelling inside a splint, and a patient whose pulse has risen. The receiving team is told the mechanism, the time, whether the patient was trapped and for how long, what was removed from the foot, what was left in it, and the time of every intervention. Two mistakes recur, which are the injury called a sprain while the skin is whole and the bandage or splint that becomes a tourniquet by accident, and both are prevented by comparing the feet, testing what the patient can do, and checking the toes after every layer. A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient, is a worker whose foot is caught between the rollers of a machine and whose boot is left in place until the machine is isolated, and the lesson is that the rescue itself can be the second injury.

To summarize, the foot is a weight-bearing platform of small bones with thin coverings, and the two mechanisms that dominate its injuries are the fall that drives the body's weight through the heel and the machine or vehicle that crushes it between hard surfaces. The scene is made safe before the patient is touched, with machinery isolated, traffic held, water and electricity treated as hazards, and PPE used for every wound, and the foot is then placed within the primary survey rather than examined on its own. The bare foot is compared with its neighbor, the footwear is removed or opened whenever it threatens the circulation, and the neurovascular examination asks in order about color and warmth, the two pulses, sensation, and the movement of the toes. Bleeding is controlled by direct pressure, by packing where the trained responder is authorized, and by a tourniquet above the ankle under a protocol, and the tourniquet is not loosened in the field and its time is written on the patient. A swollen foot inside a boot, a foot that is tense and painful out of proportion, and a foot that is numb all point toward a compartment syndrome, while a foot released after a long compression may produce the crush syndrome in the whole patient, and both require immediate definitive care. Fractures of the metatarsals, the toes, the fifth metatarsal, and the calcaneus are splinted in the position found, a deformed foot is never straightened, an embedded object is never removed, and an open or contaminated wound is covered and left for surgical cleaning. Hypothermia is treated as a complication, the special feet of children, older patients, and patients with diabetes are examined with the same suspicion as any other, and every time, pressure, temperature, distance, and threshold in this chapter is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 32 — Shock

Shock is not a number but the state in which the circulation can no longer deliver enough oxygen to the tissues, and it can be present while every measurement available to the responder still looks acceptable. Before anything is assessed, the scene is made safe, because traffic, fire, electricity, water, violence, animals, structural collapse, and the patient's own body fluids can injure a rescuer who has not looked first. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, with gloves at the least, protects the responder and the patient together, and a patient who is confused from a shortage of oxygen is a hazard as well as a casualty. The lethal possibility is named early, and the finding that reveals it is skin that is pale, cool, and damp, a pulse that is fast and thin, and attention that is drifting from the conversation. This chapter explains what shock is, how four mechanisms produce it, how it is recognized with the hands and the eyes alone, and what each level of provider may do, and it is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

Perfusion is the delivery of oxygen and fuel to every cell and the removal of the waste the cell produces, and it depends on a volume of blood, a working pump, vessels with enough tone, and a passage for air. Shock begins at the level of the cell, where delivery falls below what the tissue needs, so the cell turns to a wasteful metabolism, produces acid, and dies if the shortage continues. The body defends itself by narrowing the vessels of the skin and the gut to keep the brain and the heart supplied, by speeding the heart, and by holding fluid inside the circulation. The pressure is therefore the last measurement to fall and the least useful one to wait for, because a patient can be short of oxygen while the pressure is still held up by a body spending its reserve. What the responder reads instead is the direction in which the patient is moving, and the finding that matters is the same observation made again and found worse.

The four mechanisms that produce shock are named hypovolemic, obstructive, cardiogenic, and distributive, and the value of naming them is that the treatment of one can harm a patient with another. Hypovolemic shock is the loss of circulating volume, and in trauma it is almost always the loss of blood. Obstructive shock is a physical block to the flow of blood into or out of the heart, so the pump is sound but cannot fill. Cardiogenic shock is the failure of the pump itself, from an injury or a disease of the heart muscle or its rhythm. Distributive shock is the loss of vessel tone, or a circulation poisoned by infection or by an allergic reaction, so the container becomes too large for the volume inside it. No responder can measure the mechanism at the roadside, but the injury, the skin, and the pulse suggest it, and the substance and the amount of any treatment belong to the local protocol and the prescriber.

Hypovolemic shock in trauma is hemorrhage until proved otherwise, and the bleeding is often concealed where no dressing can reach it. Blood can collect in the chest until the lung is compressed, in the abdomen until the belly is firm and distended, in the pelvis behind the peritoneum, in the thigh around a broken femur, and in the tissues around any fracture. The findings that reveal concealed bleeding are a patient who is pale, cool, thirsty, and restless while the visible injury is minor, a pulse that climbs while the pressure falls, and a breathing rate that rises without a wound of the chest. The lay first aider calls emergency medical services early, controls visible bleeding with direct pressure, keeps the patient flat and warm, and does not press into a tender belly or spring the pelvis to test it. The trained responder repeats the observations, splints a deformed limb in the position found rather than straightening it, applies a pelvic binder where the protocol authorizes one, and shortens the journey, and definitive hospital care opens the cavity and controls the source.

Obstructive shock is produced by a block that a trained provider or a surgeon can sometimes relieve, and the two injuries to suspect in trauma are a chest filled with air under pressure and a heart compressed by blood in the sac around it. A tension pneumothorax occurs when air enters the chest and cannot escape, so the lung collapses, the vessels in the chest are kinked, and the return of blood to the heart fails. The findings are a patient who worsens quickly after a chest injury, a windpipe pushed to one side, absent breath sounds on the injured side, distended neck veins, and a pulse that weakens as the patient breathes in. Cardiac tamponade produces a similar collapse, with muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins, and a falling pressure, and it may follow a chest wound that looked small. Needle decompression of the chest belongs to the trained responder or paramedic who carries the equipment and works under a protocol and an authorization, and the definitive treatment of both conditions is an operation, while the chest is never bound tightly at any stage.

Cardiogenic shock is the failure of the pump, and in trauma it follows a blunt blow to the chest that bruises or tears the heart, while outside trauma it follows a heart attack or a dangerous rhythm. The patient may complain of chest pain, may be unable to lie flat because breathing becomes hard, may have a slow or irregular pulse, and may show cool skin together with congestion in the lungs. The distinction matters because the treatment that helps a patient who has lost blood can worsen a patient whose heart is failing, so the decision about fluid in this patient belongs to the clinician and not to the responder. The lay first aider keeps the patient still, warm, and in the position that breathing allows, calls emergency medical services, and stays with the patient. The trained responder supports the airway and the breathing within the protocol and moves the patient to a hospital where the heart can be examined and supported.

Distributive shock is the loss of vessel tone, and it appears in three forms that a responder may meet. A spinal cord injury removes the signals that keep the vessels narrowed, so the container widens, and the findings are warm dry skin, a pulse that is slow rather than fast, and a pressure that falls without the usual compensation. An allergic reaction to a sting, a food, or a medicine produces swelling of the airway, wheezing, hives, and a sudden collapse, and the decision about the substance that reverses it belongs to the protocol and to the provider authorized to give it. An infection that has entered the blood produces a patient who is feverish and confused, with warm skin at the beginning and cold skin later, and this form develops over hours rather than minutes. The finding that traps a responder is warm skin in a patient who otherwise looks desperately ill, because warmth is wrongly taken for safety, and the trained responder treats the airway, supports the breathing, and moves the patient without delay.

Recognition follows the primary survey in the fixed order of airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure, and the skin is the largest surface a responder can read, because its color, its temperature, and its moisture tell more about the circulation than any single number. A patient in shock is pale, then gray, and later mottled, with cool hands and feet, and the coolness climbs the limb toward the knee and the thigh as the body shuts down the periphery to protect the center. The skin may be damp with a cold sweat, and the lips, the gums, the inner eyelid, and the palms are the places to look in a patient whose skin is dark, because a change in color is easier to see there than on the forearm. Capillary refill, which is the return of color to the nailbed after it is pressed and released, is delayed when the periphery is shut down, and that delay is a finding that the circulation is already compensating.

The pulse is felt at the neck, in the groin, at the wrist, and on the top of the foot, and the character of the pulse matters more than its presence alone. A pulse that is fast and thin is one of the earliest signs of a falling circulation, because the heart is trying to move a smaller volume faster, and a pulse that is slow may belong to a patient with a spinal injury, a patient whose medicines slow the heart, or a patient whose heart is failing. The loss of the pulse at the wrist while a pulse can still be felt at the neck is a grave finding, because the body has closed the periphery completely, and it means that the remaining time is short. A rate above 100 beats per minute in an adult is a figure often taught as a warning, and that figure, like every threshold in this chapter, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line shifts with age, with pregnancy, with fitness, and with the patient's usual state.

The brain is the organ most sensitive to a fall in perfusion, so the level of consciousness is the most honest witness the responder has. The patient who is anxious, restless, argumentative, or thirsty is often at an earlier stage than the patient who has become quiet, because restlessness is the brain asking for oxygen while it can still speak. Confusion, drowsiness, and a failure to answer the same question twice in the same way are later findings, and a patient who has become silent after talking is deteriorating rather than settling. The responder asks the patient's name, the place, and the time, and repeats the questions later so that two answers can be compared, and the Glasgow coma scale is used where the responder has been trained in it because it turns an impression into something two people can compare. Alcohol, drugs, a head injury, and fear can each change the level of consciousness, and none of them may be allowed to explain a deterioration that could be shock.

The breathing rate is a quiet and early messenger, and it is counted while the patient is unaware of being watched. A patient in shock breathes faster and more shallowly as the body tries to take in more oxygen, and the patient may sigh, yawn, or be unable to finish a sentence without stopping for air. A breathing rate that climbs while the chest shows no wound suggests that oxygen is not reaching the tissues, and it belongs with the pulse and the skin as signs that move together. Monitoring without equipment is a skill of repetition, and it needs nothing more than a watch, a light, a pen, and the responder's own hands.

The most dangerous moment in shock is the moment when the patient still looks stable, because the body is defending the pressure by narrowing the vessels, speeding the heart, and holding fluid inside the circulation. A pressure that remains normal in a patient with a fast pulse, cool hands, delayed capillary refill, and thirst is not reassurance, and a narrowing pulse pressure is one of the earliest changes. The young patient and the fit patient compensate well and then deteriorate within a short time, and the finding that marks the turn is a pressure that begins to fall while the pulse continues to climb. The responder who waits for a low pressure before calling for help has waited too long, and the correct response is to treat the cause, keep the patient warm, and reduce the time to definitive care.

Positioning is a treatment, and its purpose is to help what volume remains reach the heart and the brain without making the breathing harder. The patient who has lost blood is laid flat and kept still, and the legs are raised only when there is no injury to the head, the chest, or the spine, no difficulty in breathing, and no pregnancy, because a raised leg in a patient who cannot breathe causes harm. A patient who is struggling for air is allowed to sit up, because breathing comes before the return of blood in that patient, and a patient who is unconscious but breathing is turned onto the side unless a spinal injury forbids it. Every movement is made slowly and with the neck and the trunk held in line, because movement costs pressure and pain, and the responder explains each movement before it is made. The finding that requires a change of position is any worsening of breathing or of the level of consciousness, and that change is reported at once.

Cold is a complication of trauma and not a detail of comfort, and a patient in shock becomes cold quickly because the volume that carried heat has been lost. A cold patient clots poorly, so the bleeding continues, and the continued bleeding removes more heat, so the two problems make each other worse, and a low body temperature also makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm. A temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which those effects become serious, and that figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line differs between services and editions. The lay first aider removes wet clothing by cutting it away, covers the patient with blankets, coats, or foil, insulates the patient from the ground, and keeps the vehicle or the room warm. The finding that warns the responder that cooling has already begun is a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold, because shivering is the body's attempt to make heat.

A patient in shock is usually thirsty, and thirst is a sign of the loss rather than a request that must be granted. Food and drink are withheld because an operation may be needed soon and a full stomach can be vomited into the airway when consciousness fades, and because the bowel tolerates little when the circulation is failing. The lips and the mouth may be moistened, and a note of the last time the patient ate or drank is carried to the receiving team, because that detail changes what the anesthesia team may do. The responder explains each act before it is performed, tells the patient what will happen next, answers questions honestly, and keeps talking to a patient whose eyes are closing.

The lay first aider has a defined and sufficient part in the care of a patient in shock, and it needs no equipment beyond the hands and whatever covering is at hand. The lay first aider calls emergency medical services early, describes the mechanism of injury and the condition of the patient, controls visible bleeding with firm uninterrupted pressure, and keeps that pressure in place without lifting the dressing to look. The patient is kept flat and warm, wet clothing is removed or covered, the patient is insulated from the ground, and the patient is given nothing to eat or drink. The lay first aider watches the skin, the pulse, the breathing, and the level of consciousness, and reports every change to the arriving team. The lay first aider does not press into a painful belly, does not straighten a deformed limb, does not remove an object embedded in a wound, does not loosen a tourniquet that has stopped the bleeding, and does not leave the patient alone.

The trained responder, the emergency medical technician, and the paramedic work within a protocol, a set of equipment, and an authorization that the lay first aider does not have. They repeat the primary survey, control bleeding by packing a wound that is suitable for packing, by a hemostatic dressing where the service carries one, and by a tourniquet where a limb continues to bleed, and each act is performed only as the protocol allows. They splint fractures in the position found, apply a pelvic binder where that device and that authorization exist, protect the spine, and give oxygen only as the protocol and the prescriber decide, because oxygen is a treatment with a decision behind it. They obtain access into a vein and make decisions about fluid and blood within the same protocol, and they monitor the patient continuously on the journey rather than at a single moment. Every one of those interventions is named with the provider level that owns it, and none becomes a lay skill because the patient looks desperate.

Fluid and blood resuscitation are advanced and hospital care, and the decisions are what a manual may describe while the amounts belong elsewhere. The substance that is given, the amount, the route, and the timing are set by the local protocol and by the prescriber, and the reason a book must not carry them is that the right answer changes with the mechanism, with the patient's age and illness, and with the distance to the hospital. Too little fluid leaves the tissues without oxygen, and too much dilutes the clotting factors, cools the patient, and may raise the pressure enough to restart bleeding that had stopped. The choice between a crystalloid solution and blood products, the use of blood that has been matched and blood that has not, and the decision to activate a massive transfusion belong to the hospital and to the trauma team. The finding that tells the team the bleeding is still active is a patient who responds to the first fluid and then deteriorates again, and that finding sends the patient to the operating room rather than to more fluid.

Definitive hospital care owns everything that repairs rather than contains, and the only true treatment of shock is the treatment of its cause. Stopping the bleeding inside the chest or the abdomen, repairing a torn vessel, relieving the pressure around the heart, decompressing a chest filled with air under pressure, supporting a failing heart, and treating an infection all belong to the hospital, and none is a field procedure no matter how urgent the patient appears. The surgeon may open the abdomen, open the chest, repair a vessel, remove a damaged organ, or place a drain, and the team watches the pressure, the pulse, the breathing, the urine output, the temperature, and the level of consciousness while those decisions are made. Needle decompression of the chest, an airway adjunct, oxygen, access into a vein, a pelvic binder, a traction splint, wound packing, a hemostatic dressing, a tourniquet, and spinal immobilization are advanced procedures decided by the protocol and the provider's training, while exploration of a wound, debridement, repair of a vessel or a tendon or a nerve, reduction of a fracture, fixation, fasciotomy, and transfusion are definitive procedures that no responder performs in the field.

A tourniquet that has controlled the bleeding of a limb is not loosened in the field, and the time it was applied is written on the patient where the receiving team will see it. The reason for the rule is that the clot that formed behind the tourniquet may not hold, so releasing it may produce hemorrhage that no one at the roadside can control, and the reason for the time is that the receiving team must know how long the limb has been without blood. A period such as 2 hours is often quoted as the point at which the risk to muscle and nerve becomes serious, and that interval is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because tolerance differs with temperature, with the patient, and with the injury. The record is written on the skin near the tourniquet, on a tape fixed to the limb, or in the place the local protocol agrees, and it is spoken aloud at handover. Reassessment after a tourniquet means confirming that the bleeding has stopped, watching for the signs of shock, checking the limb beyond the device, and searching for a second wound that was missed.

Some patients break the usual rules of recognition, and the responder who knows them is harder to mislead. A child compensates for a long time and then deteriorates within minutes, the child's usual pulse and breathing are faster than an adult's, and the caregiver who knows the child is often the first to see that something is wrong. An older patient may take medicines that slow the heart, so the pulse does not rise as expected, and may live with a pressure that is high at baseline, so a pressure that looks normal may already be too low for that patient. A pregnant patient can lose a large volume before the mother looks ill, the fetus is at risk before the mother is, and the pregnant patient who must lie down is tilted so that the weight of the womb does not press on the vessels that return blood to the heart. A patient with a spinal injury may have a slow pulse and warm skin rather than the fast pulse and cold skin of blood loss, so the pulse and the skin must be read together.

Shock may hide inside another injury, and the responder who fixes attention on the visible wound will miss it. A patient with a head injury may be confused from the brain injury, from alcohol, or from shock, and the three may exist together, so the level of consciousness cannot be used to dismiss the circulation. A patient with a burn loses plasma from the burned surface over the hours that follow, and a patient who has been crushed loses fluid into the muscle that was compressed, so both may be stable at the first contact and deteriorating later. A patient with an injury to the chest may be losing blood into the chest or developing a block to the return of blood to the heart while the outside of the chest looks untouched. A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient, is the rider who stands up after a collision with a grazed arm, whose pulse is fast and whose skin is cool while the arm explains none of it.

The traps that undo the care of a patient in shock are few and they repeat, and each has a finding that warns the responder in time. The first is to treat pain or fear as the whole explanation, when restlessness and a fast pulse in an injured patient belong to shock until proved otherwise. The second is to give fluid as though it were the treatment, when the treatment is to stop the bleeding and to reach the place where it can be stopped, and the third is to wait for a low pressure before calling for help. The fourth is to warm the patient after the journey rather than before it, and the fifth is to attribute a dulling level of consciousness to alcohol or to age rather than to the circulation. The sixth is to stop watching once the patient looks better, because a patient who improves after the first treatment can deteriorate again, and the seventh is to forget the record, since a tourniquet time that was never written is a time that was never made.

The record that travels with the patient carries the mechanism of injury, the time of the injury, the observations in the order they were made, the bleeding that was controlled, the tourniquet and its time, the warmth that was provided, and every change that was seen. A value written without a time cannot be compared with the next one, so the time belongs beside every number, and the trend across several sets of observations carries more meaning than any single set. Pain relief is a clinical decision, and the finding that makes it urgent is severe pain together with a circulation that is failing, while the substance, the amount, the route, and the timing belong to the provider authorized to prescribe and to the local protocol. The handover is spoken aloud in the same order, and the receiving team continues a story that the field began, so a gap in that story forces them to start again while the patient waits.

To summarize, shock is the failure of the circulation to deliver enough oxygen to the tissues, and it is recognized by the patient rather than by a number, because the pressure is defended until the reserve is spent. The four mechanisms are hypovolemic, obstructive, cardiogenic, and distributive, and naming the mechanism matters because the treatment of one can harm a patient with another. The skin, the pulse, the level of consciousness, and the breathing are read with the hands and the eyes, repeated in the same order, and compared so that the trend becomes the diagnosis. The lay first aider calls for help early, controls visible bleeding, keeps the patient flat and warm, withholds food and drink, and watches without stopping, while the trained responder works within a protocol and a defined authorization, and the surgeon owns everything that repairs. Fluids and blood are decisions of advanced and hospital care whose substance, amount, route, and timing belong to the local protocol and the prescriber, a tourniquet is never loosened in the field and its time is written on the patient, and every figure in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 33 — Compartment Syndrome

A compartment syndrome is the strangling of muscle and nerve inside a limb whose outer wrapping cannot stretch, and it decides within hours whether a patient keeps an arm or a leg. The limb is divided by sheets of tough tissue called fascia into closed spaces, and each space holds muscle, nerve, and the vessels that feed them. When blood or fluid collects in a space, or when injured tissue swells within it, the fascia holds the volume fixed while the pressure climbs and the tissue that depends on that pressure begins to starve. The danger is not always a wound that can be seen, because a patient may have no break in the skin and still lose the limb. The first responder's task is to suspect the condition early, to remove what constricts, to keep the limb in the position found, to keep the patient warm, and to reach surgical care without delay. This chapter explains the mechanism, the findings, the causes, the referral, and the operation, and it is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

No hand is laid on the patient until the scene has been made safe, because a responder struck while reaching a struck patient turns one casualty into two. Traffic, fire and smoke, live electrical cables, machinery that may restart, deep water, collapsing structures, loose animals, violence, and the patient's own blood and tissue are the hazards that kill rescuers. A limb pinned under a vehicle, a wall, or a machine is not freed by a bystander, because lifting the weight may crush the rescuer, may release a clot, and may let the trapped limb bleed or swell when the pressure comes off. The weight is lifted by a team with the training, the equipment, and the authority to do it, and the machine is isolated and locked before anyone reaches beneath it. Only when the scene is held does clinical work begin, the lay first aider who cannot make it safe stays at its edge and calls for those who can, and gloves or whatever barrier is available are worn before the first contact.

Fascia is the strong sheet of fibrous tissue that wraps the muscles of a limb and divides them into compartments, keeping the muscles in place and making their pull efficient. The lower leg contains several compartments, the forearm contains several, and the thigh, the upper arm, the hand, and the foot each have their own, separated by walls of the same unyielding tissue. Each compartment is a closed box whose only openings are the small passages for the vessels and nerves that enter and leave it. A normal compartment stretches a little for the swelling of exercise, but not enough for the blood and edema that follow a fracture, a crush, or a torn vessel. When the contents increase and the walls cannot give, the pressure inside must rise, and the finding that explains the rest of this chapter is the compartment that has become tense, swollen, and tender.

Blood reaches the muscle of a compartment because the pressure inside the small arteries is higher than the pressure of the tissue around them, so flow depends on that difference rather than on arterial pressure alone. As tissue pressure rises, the difference narrows, the small vessels are compressed, and the muscle receives less blood even though the heart is beating normally. The veins that drain the compartment are soft and are compressed first, so blood enters more easily than it leaves, which adds to the swelling and raises the pressure further. The artery that enters is tougher than the vein and resists compression longer, which is why a pulse can still be felt at the wrist or the ankle while the muscle inside is already dying. The teaching that follows is the most important sentence in this chapter, which is that a pulse that is present does not exclude a compartment syndrome, so the responder who waits for the pulse to disappear is waiting for the limb to be lost.

Nerve tissue is the most sensitive to the loss of blood supply and fails before the muscle around it, which is why a change in sensation often appears while the limb still looks almost normal. Muscle follows, and the time it can survive without flow is measured in hours rather than days, with an interval such as 4 to 6 hours sometimes quoted for the beginning of irreversible damage, offered here only as an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because tolerance differs with temperature, with age, and with the injury. When the pressure is finally relieved, blood returns to tissue that may already be dead and carries into the circulation the contents of the dying muscle cells. That washout can poison the patient even as it appears to rescue the limb, because the substances released may injure the kidneys, disturb the rhythm of the heart, and deepen shock, which is the territory of crush syndrome. Definitive hospital care watches for those effects with blood tests, with the color and volume of the urine, and with attention to the heart, while recognition in the field remains the first link in that chain.

The causes are the events that add volume to a closed space or squeeze it from outside, and the first of them is a fracture. A break of the tibia, of the forearm bones, or of any long bone can bleed into the compartment and swell enough to raise the pressure, and the fracture does not have to be open or dramatic. A crush injury, a wheel that has passed over a limb, a heavy object that has rested on it, or a machine that has caught it produces the same effect through torn muscle and torn vessels. A cast, a circumferential bandage, a splint strap, or a tight dressing can become the constricting layer itself, especially when it was applied before the swelling reached its full size. Prolonged positioning is the cause most easily forgotten, because an unconscious patient lying on an arm or a patient pinned in a vehicle compresses the limb for hours. A burn that hardens into a tight eschar, a torn vessel that bleeds into a compartment, and fluid that has leaked from a vein into the tissue during hospital care complete the list, and each is a reason to look at the limb rather than at the wound.

The patients in whom the diagnosis is most often missed are the ones who cannot describe pain, so the responder carries the suspicion into every examination. A patient with a head injury, a patient who has been drinking, a patient who has received sedation or anesthesia, a frightened child, and a patient whose attention is fixed on a more obvious injury may all fail to report the pain that would give the condition away. A regional nerve block given in hospital for the relief of a fracture can remove the pain while leaving the swelling untouched, so the examination must be made through the other findings rather than through the complaint.
