A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient or incident, is the person found on a cold floor hours after a fall, confused, with one calf swollen and firm and no wound anywhere on the skin, whose only chance lies in a responder who examines the limb. The finding that should raise the suspicion is any limb that is tense, swollen, or painful when its muscles are stretched, even when the patient says nothing.

The cardinal early symptom is pain that is out of proportion to the injury, and it is heard precisely in the moment when action still changes the outcome. The pain is deep and boring rather than sharp and superficial, it is felt within the limb rather than at the wound, and it often burns or throbs in a way that is hard for the patient to place. It does not settle when the limb is rested, it is not relieved by the splint that has just been applied, and it may be worse with any movement, so the patient cannot find a comfortable position. The pain may be the first complaint and the only one, which is why a patient who reports severe pain after an injury that looks minor must be examined rather than reassured. The absence of severe pain proves nothing in a patient whose sensation has already begun to fail, or in a patient who is unconscious or sedated. The finding that should move the responder from observation to action is pain that is increasing on repeated questioning, because a trend is more informative than any single report.

The most useful bedside test is pain on passive stretch, and the other early finding is the compartment that is tense, swollen, and tender along its whole length. The trained responder moves the muscles of the compartment gently in the direction that lengthens them, moving the foot and toes of a leg, or the wrist and fingers of a forearm, while asking where the pain is felt. The finding that matters is pain reported within the compartment and not in the joint that was just moved, because a painful joint points to the injury while a painful muscle belly points to the pressure. The test is performed gently, an unstable fracture is supported during the movement, and the injured limb is compared with the other side. The responder feels for tension with a flat hand rather than probing fingertips, because force on a compartment under pressure adds injury and teaches nothing. The finding that settles the matter is the combination of a tense compartment with pain on stretch, since either sign alone is common and the pair together is the syndrome.

The earliest objective sign of a failing compartment is often a change in sensation, and it appears before weakness and long before the loss of a pulse. The patient may describe tingling, pins and needles, or a numbness that spreads over the area supplied by the nerve passing through the affected compartment, and the responder maps that area with a light touch and compares it with the other side. Weakness of the muscles inside the compartment follows, tested by asking the patient to perform a movement those muscles produce, so that a foot that cannot be lifted or fingers that cannot be straightened are findings rather than impressions. Weakness may at first be blamed on pain, since a patient who hurts will move less, so the two limbs are compared and the patient is asked to try the movement gently. Sensation and movement are recorded with the area, the movement, and the time, and both are tested before and after every dressing, every splint, every cast, and every move. The finding that demands escalation is any deterioration between two examinations, however small it appears.

The late findings are the signs of a limb that has already been lost, and they are taught not so that the responder may wait for them but so that the responder may recognize how far the condition has gone. A limb that has become pale or mottled, that is cold and pulseless below the injury, that is paralyzed, and that no longer hurts is describing dead tissue rather than an injury that is merely severe. The painless limb is the most deceptive of these findings, because the patient who stops complaining appears to be improving while the nerve and muscle within are dying. Paralysis and numbness together mean the nerve has failed, and a pulse that has disappeared means even the tough artery has at last been compressed, and neither finding can be relied upon to appear in time. The responder who has been taught to look for pallor and pulselessness has been taught to arrive too late, and the purpose of the early findings is to make the late ones unnecessary.

The diagnosis of an acute compartment syndrome is clinical, made from the history and the examination, and it must never wait for a number to confirm it. A device may be used by a physician to measure the pressure inside a compartment, and a value in the range of 30 millimeters of mercury, or a difference between the tissue pressure and the diastolic pressure, is sometimes quoted as a threshold, but such figures must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because accepted values differ between services and editions. The measurement supports a decision that has usually already been made by the hands and the ears, and it cannot make the diagnosis on its own, because the pressure in a compartment changes from minute to minute. A normal measurement does not exclude the syndrome when the patient has the pain, the tension, and the sensory change, and a high measurement without those findings does not by itself send the patient to the operating theatre. The rule that must survive every detail of local practice is that a patient with the clinical findings is treated as having the condition, and that no test, no image, and no number is allowed to delay the referral.

Each provider level has its own part in the recognition of this condition, and the boundary between them is decided by training, equipment, authorization, and protocol rather than by the urgency of the moment. The lay first aider cannot measure pressure and cannot make the diagnosis, but may notice a limb that is swollen and tight, may hear the patient describe severe pain, may see that a foot or hand has changed color, and must pass those observations to the professionals with the time they were made. The lay first aider may also remove a ring, a watch, or a tight bracelet before the swelling makes removal impossible, and may loosen a garment that circles the limb, because those acts require no diagnosis and prevent harm. The trained responder and the paramedic examine the limb in a fixed order, compare it with the other side, record the findings with a time, repeat the examination after every intervention, and are authorized by protocol to release a bandage or splint strap that has become a tourniquet by accident. The decisions about a cast, about the release of a tourniquet, and about the operation belong to definitive hospital care and to the surgeon, and crossing that boundary without authority can convert a limb that was savable into one that is not.

The immediate measures in the field follow an order, and the first is to remove anything that circles the injured limb. Rings, watches, bangles, and tight clothing are taken off before the swelling arrives, and a ring that will not move is never forced over a swollen finger, because the finger may need to be cut free in hospital. The next measure is to examine every bandage, splint strap, and cast for tightness and to release whatever the protocol permits, since the finding that a dressing has become a tourniquet is a limb that is pale or cool beyond it, a pulse that can no longer be felt, and pain that is increasing. The limb is then positioned at the level of the heart rather than raised above it, because elevation lowers the arterial pressure that feeds the compartment, and this is one of the few places in trauma where the instinct to elevate is wrong. The limb is not massaged, pressed hard, or packed with ice, and it is covered lightly rather than bound, because none of those acts lowers the pressure inside the fascia. The patient is kept warm, kept still, and prepared for a possible operation, with the decision about food and drink left to the receiving surgical team.

Cold is a complication of trauma in its own right, and it travels with compartment syndrome because the patient is often trapped, exposed, and undressed for examination. A cold patient clots poorly, tolerates blood loss badly, and is more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm of the heart, and a limb that is already short of blood suffers sooner when the whole body is cold. The responder covers the patient, insulates the patient from the ground, removes wet clothing and replaces it with dry covering without disturbing the limb, and keeps the vehicle warm during transport. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which these effects become serious, and that figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line differs with age and with the way the temperature is measured. The patient is watched at the same time for shock, since the swelling of a crushed limb can hold a large volume of blood and dying muscle releases substances that disturb the circulation. The findings that send the responder back to the beginning are a falling level of consciousness, a pulse that has become fast and weak, skin that has become cold and clammy, and breathing that has become rapid and shallow.

Pain relief can make this condition easier to endure, and it can also hide it, so the decision belongs to the provider authorized to prescribe and to the local protocol. The finding that makes relief urgent is severe pain not controlled by splinting and positioning, and the finding that makes the decision delicate is the same severe pain that is the earliest sign of the syndrome. The responder records the examination before any relief is given, including the pain, the tension, the sensation, and the movement, so that the effect of the treatment on the findings can be judged rather than guessed. The substance, the amount, the route, and the timing are decisions of the prescriber under the protocol in force, and nothing in this manual names them, because a listener must not be able to take a prescription from these pages. Analgesia must never be used to make a patient quiet enough to be transported without an examination, because a quiet patient is not the same as a safe one.

A cast or a circumferential dressing applied before the limb finished swelling is a common cause of a compartment syndrome, and the patient who reports increasing pain, numbness, or a limb that feels too tight must be seen again at once. Splitting or bivalving a cast, and cutting a bandage down to the skin, belong to a provider authorized by the local protocol or to definitive hospital care, because releasing a constriction in the wrong way can destabilize a fracture and open a wound. Four rules of trauma care matter unusually much in this chapter, and each exists because breaking it can create the very pressure the responder is trying to relieve. A severely deformed fracture is never straightened in the field to make the limb look normal, because the movement can tear a vessel and force blood into a compartment that was intact. A tourniquet that has controlled bleeding from a limb is not loosened in the field, and the time it was applied is written on the patient where the receiving team will see it. An object embedded in a limb is never removed, because it may be plugging the vessel it has torn, so it is stabilized in place and packed around while the patient is moved with it.

The referral is an emergency referral, and it begins as soon as the clinical findings are recognized rather than when the diagnosis is confirmed. The receiving facility is called ahead so that the surgeon and the operating theatre are ready on arrival, and the call names the limb, the time of the injury, the time any cast or tourniquet was applied, and the findings on the examination. The destination is the nearest facility that can open a compartment, which usually means a hospital with an orthopedic or general surgeon and an operating theatre, and if it cannot provide that care, the local system arranges stabilization and transfer. Transport is urgent and gentle at the same time, because speed that throws the patient around adds injury, and because the limb must be examined again before the journey, during it where possible, and at the handover. No image, no laboratory result, and no measurement of pressure is allowed to delay the journey, because the diagnosis is clinical and the treatment is time-dependent. The handover passes on the pain, the tension, the sensation, the movement, the pulses, the warmth, and the times of every intervention, and it is spoken as well as written.

Definitive hospital care takes over on arrival, and its first act is to examine the limb again, because the findings may have changed during the journey. The physician may measure the pressure within the compartments with a device and may order blood tests that reveal the breakdown of muscle and the condition of the kidneys, but those investigations support a decision rather than replace the examination. The treatment of shock, the choice of fluids, the correction of the blood chemistry, and the monitoring of the heart belong to the treating clinician under the local protocol and to the intensive care unit, and the amounts and substances are decisions of that setting rather than instructions carried away from a manual. Fasciotomy is the definitive treatment, an operation performed in an operating theatre by a surgeon, never a procedure for the field and never a task for a first responder. The surgeon cuts through the skin and through the fascia that does not stretch, opening every compartment involved so that the muscle can swell outward, and the wound is left open and covered, to be closed later when the swelling has settled, sometimes with a skin graft. The operation does not repair the fracture and does not restore muscle that has already died, and it cannot bring back a limb in which the tissue has been lost.

Fasciotomy performed outside an operating theatre, by someone without the training and the instruments, risks infection, bleeding, injury to nerves and vessels, and an incomplete release that leaves the pressure in place. A circumferential burn can produce the same emergency through a different layer, because an eschar that has hardened can constrict a limb even when the fascia beneath it is not the cause, and the operation that releases that constriction is an escharotomy rather than a fasciotomy, performed by a burn surgeon. Compartment syndrome can also follow an electrical injury or a prolonged crush in which muscle has been damaged without a break in the skin, and those patients must be watched for the same findings. The consequence of a compartment syndrome recognized too late is measured in limbs and in lives, because muscle that has died is replaced by scar that contracts over the weeks that follow, so that a forearm may stiffen into a fixed deformity and a hand may lose the ability to open. Nerve tissue that has been starved may recover slowly and partially or not at all, and in the most severe cases the limb is amputated, or the patient develops kidney failure, a dangerous rhythm of the heart, or shock, and may die even after the limb has been lost.

Prevention is part of treatment for every responder who applies a dressing, a splint, or a cast, and it rests on a few habits repeated at every stage of care. A bandage is applied firmly enough to control bleeding and loosely enough that the tissue beyond it is not starved, a splint is padded rather than pressed against the skin, and the limb is left at the level of the heart rather than raised on a pillow above it. The patient is asked about pain and sensation after every intervention rather than only at the beginning, and the examiner writes down what was found and when and hands the record to the receiving team in speech as well as in writing. A patient who leaves with a cast is warned in words the patient can repeat to return without delay if the pain increases, if the fingers or toes change color, or if sensation alters.

To summarize, a compartment syndrome is the rise of pressure inside a closed fascial space until the muscle and the nerve within it lose their blood supply, and the fascia that cannot stretch is the reason the pressure has nowhere to go. The early findings are pain out of proportion to the injury, pain when the muscles of the compartment are gently stretched, a compartment that is tense and tender, and a change in sensation, while pallor, pulselessness, paralysis, and a limb that has stopped hurting are the findings of a limb that may already be lost, and a pulse that is still present proves nothing. The diagnosis is clinical and must not wait for a number, and a measurement of pressure supports the decision rather than making it. The causes include fractures, crush injuries, tight casts and dressings, prolonged positioning on a limb, burns, and bleeding within a compartment, and the patients most easily missed are those who cannot report pain. The first response is to remove what circles the limb, to release what the protocol allows to be released, to keep the limb at the level of the heart, to avoid massage, ice, and tight binding, to keep the patient warm, and to move the patient to a surgeon without delay, while a severely deformed fracture is splinted in the position found, a tourniquet is not loosened in the field, and an embedded object is left in place. Fasciotomy is the definitive treatment, performed in an operating theatre by a surgeon, opening every involved compartment and leaving the wound open for later closure, and it is never a field procedure. Every time, pressure, temperature, and interval named in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 34 — Neurovascular Injuries

When a limb is injured, the vessels that carry its blood and the nerves that give it feeling and movement are hurt together far more often than the surface of the wound suggests, and the responder's work is to suspect that damage early and to reach the care that can repair it. The scene is made safe before the patient is touched, because traffic, machinery that is still running, live electricity, fire, deep water, a loose animal, a violent person, and the patient's own blood are the hazards that kill rescuers and patients alike. The lethal possibility named first is an artery that has been torn where no dressing can press on it, and the harm that follows close behind is a limb whose blood supply or nerve supply has been lost while the wound itself looks modest. This chapter follows arterial injury, venous injury, and nerve injury in the limbs and at the places where the limb joins the body, and it gives the four observations that must be recorded before and after every dressing, every splint, and every move. Every act is named with the provider level that owns it, because the lay first aider, the trained responder or paramedic, and definitive hospital care do different things with the same wound, and a manual that blurs them teaches dangerous habits. This is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

The reason vessels and nerves are injured together is that they travel together. In an arm the main artery and the nerves of the hand run through the armpit and then along the inner side of the upper arm in one bundle beside the bone, and they divide near the elbow into the branches that reach the wrist and the fingers. In a leg the great artery and the great nerve run down the back of the thigh and pass behind the knee, where the vessel lies tethered against the bone and is stretched rather than cut when the joint is displaced, and below the knee they divide again toward the ankle and the foot. Because the bundle is anchored where it passes a joint, a dislocation can tear a vessel while the bone stays whole, and the knee is the joint where this is most feared. A sharp edge may divide a vessel and a nerve cleanly while the skin shows only a small wound, and a blunt blow may burst the same vessel while the skin stays closed, so the size of the opening is a poor guide to the damage beneath it. The responder therefore treats the mechanism, the position of the wound, and the state of the limb as a single question rather than three separate ones.

Arterial injury announces itself in several ways, and the first is bleeding that keeps time with the heartbeat. Bright blood may leave the wound in jets, or it may travel into the tissues so that the limb swells while the skin looks almost dry, and a swelling that grows while the responder watches is as serious as a wound that pours. When an artery and a vein are torn beside each other the two may connect, and the finding is a humming sensation under the fingers and a sound heard through a stethoscope over the wound, which speaks of blood moving where it should not. The artery of a limb may also be torn with no bleeding visible at all when a clot seals the opening for a time, and that pause is one of the traps of early assessment, because the vessel can open again when the pressure rises or when a dressing is lifted. Bleeding from the armpit, the groin, or the base of the neck cannot be controlled by a tourniquet, so it is packed where the provider is trained and the protocol allows, held under pressure, and carried to a surgeon. A jet of arterial blood from a limb that direct pressure does not stop is the clearest indication for a tourniquet, and the tourniquet belongs to the trained responder or paramedic acting under a protocol, not to the lay first aider.

The findings that demand immediate hospital care are grouped as hard signs, and any one of them is enough. They are bleeding that pulses from the wound, a swelling that enlarges while it is watched, a pulse that can no longer be felt beyond the injury, a limb that has turned pale or cold, pain that is severe and out of proportion to what is seen, numbness or tingling that was not there before, a part of the body that can no longer be moved, and a humming or a sound over the wound. A deep wound that lies over the track of a major vessel, a fracture beside the same track, and a joint that has been displaced are not hard signs by themselves, but they place the patient in the group that must be examined where imaging and a surgeon exist. The field response to a hard sign is to stop the external bleeding with direct pressure, to add a pressure dressing or to pack an appropriate deep wound where the provider is trained and the protocol allows, and to apply a tourniquet when the limb continues to bleed despite those measures. The patient is then splinted in the position found, kept warm, and carried to a facility that can repair a vessel, because no field act restores an artery that has been divided. A figure such as a journey of 1 hour is sometimes described as the window in which a warm limb can still be saved, and that figure is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the tolerance of muscle and nerve differs with temperature, with age, and with the injury.

Between the obvious arterial wound and the untouched limb lies a group of findings that prove nothing and are still important. A wound whose track passes close to a major vessel or nerve, a hematoma that is small but present, a history of brisk bleeding that stopped before the responder arrived, and a fracture of a long bone are each called a proximity finding, and the word exists because the vessel may be bruised, stretched, or partly torn without the signs of a complete rupture. The responder records these findings and passes them on at handover, because the receiving team decides what examination and what imaging the region needs, and that decision is not made at the roadside. A distance quoted as a proximity threshold, such as a wound within 2 centimeters of the vessel, is a teaching illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since services define the zone differently. The correct behavior is to treat the patient rather than the number, to complete the four observations, and to arrange a destination where the vessels can be assessed rather than to wait and watch at the scene.

Venous injury behaves differently from arterial injury and is no less dangerous. The blood is darker and leaves the wound in a steady flow that does not spurt, and the pressure inside the vessel is low enough that a firm dressing often holds it. The size of the vein decides the danger, because a torn vein in the groin, the armpit, or the neck can empty the circulation in minutes without ever spurting, and the wound may appear far less dramatic than the loss it is causing. A vein in the neck or the upper chest that is open to the air carries a second hazard, because air can be drawn into it with each breath, and the finding is a wound that bubbles or sucks at the moment the chest expands. The lay first aider covers the wound and presses firmly around it without probing and without lifting a dressing to look, adding layers when blood shows through, while the trained responder may pack an appropriate deep wound under a protocol and moves the patient without delay. Venous congestion in a limb, with swelling, duskiness, and a limb that feels tense, is another sign that the return of blood has been obstructed, and it belongs to the same urgent pathway as an arterial wound.

Nerve injury may be hidden by the bleeding that commands attention, and it is often found only when the responder tests the limb. A nerve that has been bruised and stunned stops working for a time but may recover on its own; a nerve whose fibers are torn while its outer sheath stays whole may regrow slowly over months; and a nerve divided across will not recover without an operation. The signs are a patch of skin that has lost its feeling, tingling or pins and needles in a territory that follows the nerve rather than the wound, weakness of a movement, and a limb that feels heavy or useless to the patient. Sensation and movement are tested in the four observations that follow, and the test is done on both sides so that the patient's own normal hand or foot becomes the reference. A nerve injury that appears after a splint, a bandage, or a move is the most serious version of the finding, because it means that the intervention itself has caused the harm, and the response is to relieve the pressure at once under the local protocol and to send the patient onward. Repair of a nerve, whether by joining it, by grafting a piece, or by transferring a tendon, is a surgical decision and never a field procedure, and its timing depends on the wound and on the patient.

The four observations that must be recorded before and after every immobilization, dressing, and movement are the distal pulses, the capillary refill, the sensation, and the motor function, and they are performed in that order on both limbs. The pulses are felt where the vessel lies near the surface, which for the arm means the thumb side and the little finger side of the wrist and for the leg means the top of the foot and behind the inner ankle, and the responder compares their strength with the other side rather than judging them alone. The capillary refill is tested by pressing the nail bed or the pad of a finger or toe until the skin blanches, releasing it, and watching how quickly the color returns, and a slow return speaks of a limb that is not being perfused. The sensation is tested with a light touch on the skin of each territory with the patient's eyes closed, and the motor function is tested by asking the patient to spread the fingers, to make a fist, to bend the wrist upward and downward, to lift the toes, and to push the foot down against the responder's hand. The responder records the four findings with the time at which they were made, because a finding without a time cannot be compared with the next one. Where the patient cannot cooperate, as with a drowsy patient, a child, or a patient whose language the responder does not share, the observations are made by watching for movement, by testing the response to a gentle pinch, and by asking a companion to interpret.

For the four observations to mean anything, they must be comparable from one examination to the next, so the same hand, the same site, and the same questions are used each time, and the uninjured limb is examined first so that the responder learns what is normal for this patient. Cold, shock, pain, fear, and the pressure of a tight bandage all change the way a limb behaves, so the responder notes the conditions along with the findings and does not blame the limb for the weather. An older patient with narrowing of the arteries may have a weak pulse in the foot before any injury, and a patient whose limb has been cold for hours may show a slow refill caused by cold rather than by a torn vessel, and both possibilities are reasons to record the state of the other side. A pulse that is present does not exclude a vascular injury, because a partly torn artery, an artery in spasm, an artery whose inner lining has lifted and is collecting clot, and an artery whose flow is maintained by smaller vessels around a block can each produce a pulse that the fingers can feel. The pulse also says nothing at all about the nerves, and a limb can have a strong pulse with a hand that cannot feel and cannot move.

This is why the deterioration between two examinations, rather than any single examination, is the finding that matters. A pulse that was strong and is now faint, a capillary refill that was brisk and is now slow, a numbness that has spread from one finger to the whole hand, a limb that was pink and is now pale or mottled, a pain that is climbing despite a splint, and a swelling that has grown by the width of a finger are each a change, and a change is evidence that something is still happening inside the limb. The responder does not answer such a change by looking under the dressing, by loosening a tourniquet that has controlled bleeding, or by tightening a bandage in the hope that pressure will help, because each of those acts can make the injury worse. The response is to stop the journey or the movement, to repeat the four observations and the general survey, to correct what can be corrected without harming the patient, and to reach the receiving team sooner with a clear account of what changed and when. Definitive hospital care is where the pressure inside the limb is measured, where the vessels are imaged, and where the decision to operate is made, and the field record of a falling examination is what tells the surgeon that the limb is losing its supply.

When the blood supply of a limb fails, the signs appear in a known order, and the order is the lesson. Pain comes first and is often severe, and it is followed by pallor as the skin loses its color, by coolness as the surface temperature falls, by numbness and tingling as the nerves feel the lack of blood, and by weakness or paralysis as the muscles follow. The loss of the pulse is one of the last signs and not the first, which is the reason that waiting for an absent pulse before acting is a way to lose a limb. The responder who finds pain, pallor, and a change in feeling below an injury has found an ischemic limb even while a pulse can still be felt, and that combination is a hard sign in practice whatever the pulse says. The limb is kept at the level of the heart or a little below it where the local protocol advises that position favors flow, it is protected from cold and from heat, and no dressing is wound tightly around it. A period such as 6 hours of warm ischemia is often quoted as the point past which a limb is unlikely to be saved, and that interval is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the tolerance of muscle and nerve changes with temperature, with the patient, and with the injury.

Every intervention that touches the limb is an opportunity to make the injury worse, which is why the four observations bracket each one. A bandage that is wound too tightly, a splint that presses over the inner side of the elbow or behind the knee, a traction device that pulls against a vessel, and a plaster that is applied while the limb is swelling can each convert a limb with a pulse into a limb without one, and the harm is found only if the observations are repeated. The rule is that the observations are taken before the dressing, before the splint, and before the move, and again after each of them, and that the two sets are compared and both are recorded. A severely deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened to make it look normal, because the movement can release a clot, stretch a vessel, or tear a nerve that was still intact, and the appearance of the limb is not the goal of first aid. Where a limb is pulseless and deformed, any attempt to bring it into line is a decision for a provider authorized by the local protocol and is not a technique taught by this manual, and even then it is done only with the observations recorded before and after. The lay first aider keeps the limb still, covers the wound, records what can be felt and seen, and hands those findings to the next provider.

A tourniquet may be the act that saves a life when a limb will not stop bleeding, and it carries its own cost to the nerves and the muscle beneath it. The nerve is among the tissues most sensitive to pressure and to the loss of blood, so a tourniquet is placed as close to the wound as the anatomy allows and never over a joint when a length of limb above the joint is free, and it is tightened until the bleeding stops rather than until a particular number of turns has been made. Once the tourniquet has controlled the bleeding it is not loosened in the field, because the clot behind it may not hold and the patient may bleed again where no one can restore control, and the time of application is written on the patient where the receiving team will see it. The reason the time matters is that the limb below the tourniquet is without flow, and the team that receives the patient must know how long that has been true in order to judge the risk of releasing it and the urgency of restoring the circulation. Because the tourniquet removes the distal pulse and changes the color of the limb, the observations during transport shift toward the tourniquet itself, the bleeding, the general circulation, and the level of consciousness, while the limb is checked for swelling and for the appearance of the skin. A limb that has been without flow for a long period and is then released can also set free substances that harm the whole patient, and that possibility is one more reason why release is a hospital decision made with preparation.

Certain injuries deserve to be named because their anatomy makes neurovascular damage likely, and the responder who recognizes them can act before the signs become obvious. A dislocated knee is the most feared, because the artery behind the knee is tethered and the foot may lose its supply, and the finding is a deformed knee with a foot that is cold or pulseless. A break of the upper arm bone may injure the nerve that lifts the wrist, and the finding is a wrist that drops when the patient tries to raise the hand, while a dislocated shoulder may leave a patch of numbness over the outer shoulder. A break of the smaller bone of the lower leg near the knee may injure the nerve that lifts the foot, and the finding is a foot that drags, while a broken thigh bone may bleed heavily into the thigh and also lie near the great vessel that runs behind it. A displaced elbow, and the break above the elbow that is common in children, can injure the vessel at the elbow and the nerves that serve the hand, and the swelling that follows may compress them further. Wounds of the palm, the armpit, the groin, and the back of the knee each cross a bundle that lies close to the skin, and they are treated with pressure, protection, and the shortest safe journey rather than with exploration.

Definitive hospital care owns everything that repairs rather than contains, and the line between the two is part of what a responder must know. Examination with ultrasound, a computed tomography scan after which the short form CT is used, an X-ray study of the vessels with contrast, and the operating room are the tools that decide whether a vessel can be repaired, whether a graft or a patch is needed, and whether the limb can be saved. Repair of an artery or a vein, repair or grafting of a nerve, transfer of a tendon, release of the pressure inside a swollen compartment, and the decision to amputate all belong to the surgeon, and none of them is a field procedure no matter how urgent the patient appears. A nerve injury may be watched for a time before it is repaired while a vessel injury is treated as an emergency, and that difference in timing is a decision made with the whole patient in view rather than from a single wound. Pain relief, protection against tetanus, and antibiotics for a contaminated wound are clinical decisions whose substance, amount, route, and timing belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol, and no reader should take them from a manual. The receiving team also needs the field record, the times of the four observations, the time any tourniquet was placed, and the changes that were seen, because a story with a gap in it forces the team to start again.

Cold travels with every serious limb injury, because the patient is exposed, often lying on the ground, and sometimes bleeding, and cold makes clotting poor and shock deeper. The responder covers the patient before the journey rather than after it, insulates the patient from the ground, replaces wet clothing with dry coverings where that can be done without disturbing the wound, and keeps the vehicle warm, while the injured limb is protected from both cold and heat. A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and not as a real patient, is a rider thrown from a motorcycle who arrives with a deformed knee and a foot that is pale and numb, where the visible injury is the knee and the emergency is the artery behind it, and where the observations taken at the scene and repeated in the ambulance are what tell the surgeon that the foot is losing its supply. The lesson of that construction is that the most dangerous finding is often the quietest one, that a pulse felt at the ankle at the first examination proves nothing about the next one, and that the record of both examinations is the most useful thing the responder carries into the hospital. Warmth, gentleness in handling, and the shortest safe journey are part of the treatment of a neurovascular injury and not additions to it.

Transport is the last field act, and it is done with the observations repeated rather than with the injury assumed to be unchanged. Before the patient is moved the destination is chosen, which is the nearest facility able to examine and repair vessels and nerves, and the receiving team is told what has been found, what has been done, and what is still changing. During the journey the responder watches the limb, the bleeding, the level of consciousness, the breathing, and the warmth of the patient, and repeats the four observations at the interval the local protocol sets, which may be more often when a finding is abnormal. A period such as every 15 minutes is often used for a stable patient and a shorter interval for one whose limb is threatened, and those intervals are illustrations that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services and patient ages differ. Any deterioration during the journey is reported ahead of arrival where the service can do so, because the surgeon who knows that a limb is failing can prepare while the patient is still moving. The record is finished at handover with the times, the findings, and the interventions, and the patient is handed over in person rather than left with the paperwork alone.

To summarize, neurovascular injury means damage to the arteries, the veins, and the nerves of a limb, and it must be suspected from the mechanism and the position of the wound long before the signs are severe. Arterial injury may jet, may swell the limb, may hum or make a sound, or may hide behind a clot for a time; venous injury may flow quietly and still empty the circulation, and may draw air into an open vein in the neck or the chest; nerve injury may leave numbness, tingling, or weakness that no bleeding reveals. The four observations are the distal pulses, the capillary refill, the sensation, and the motor function, and they are recorded on both limbs before and after every dressing, every splint, and every move, with the time at which each set was taken. A pulse that is present does not exclude a vascular injury, because a partly torn or narrowed vessel, a vessel in spasm, and a limb supplied by smaller vessels around a block can each keep a pulse while the tissue beyond it is starving, and the pulse says nothing about the nerves. The finding that matters is the deterioration between two examinations, and the hard signs of pulsatile bleeding, a growing swelling, an absent pulse, a pale or cold limb, spreading numbness, new weakness, and a hum over the wound each demand immediate hospital care. A deformed limb is splinted in the position found and is never straightened to make it look normal, a tourniquet that has controlled bleeding is not loosened in the field and its time is written on the patient, and the observations continue during transport until handover. Warmth, gentleness, and the shortest safe journey to a facility that can repair a vessel or a nerve are part of the treatment, and every time, distance, and interval named here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 35 — Crush Injuries

A patient pinned beneath a fallen wall, a vehicle, or a collapsed floor is living through two emergencies at once, and only one of them can be seen. The local injury is the crushed muscle, the broken bone, and the torn vessel held under the weight, and the systemic injury is the syndrome that begins when the weight is removed and the contents of dead muscle enter the blood. The lethal possibility that must be named first is cardiac arrest after extrication, because a patient who is talking and conscious under the load may lose the heartbeat within minutes of being freed. The scene is made safe before any hand reaches the patient, since the structure, the machinery, the traffic, and the live current that caused the crushing can easily produce another casualty. This chapter follows the crushed patient from entrapment to the hospital and names the provider level that owns each act. It is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

The hazards of a crush scene repeat, and each of them has killed rescuers who entered without looking. A slab that has already fallen may rest on unstable debris and may shift when the debris is disturbed, so the pile is treated as a structure and not as a heap. A vehicle resting on a patient may be held by a jack, a winch, or a second vehicle that can fail, and the ground beneath it may be soft enough to settle. Machinery may still be powered and a press may still hold pressure in a line that nobody has isolated, so the supply is shut down by a person authorized to do it and the shutdown is confirmed rather than assumed. Electricity, fuel, dust, and the gases of a confined space add their own dangers, and where a trench has collapsed its walls remain a threat to everyone at the edge. Contaminated blood and tissue are the quieter hazard, so personal protective equipment, meaning gloves and eye protection at the least, is worn before the first hand is laid on anyone. The lay first aider who cannot make the scene safe does not enter it, and calling for those who can is the correct first act rather than a delay.

The severity of a crush is written in the weight, the surface, and the time, and none of the three can be judged from the wound that shows. A heavy load over a broad area does more damage than a sharp load over a small one, a hard edge concentrates the force while a soft surface spreads it, and the duration decides how much muscle has been deprived of its blood. A patient pinned for a few minutes may have a bruise and a fracture, while a patient pinned for hours may have a limb in which the muscle has died in place, and the outside of that limb can look almost unremarkable at first. The responder therefore asks how long the patient has been trapped, what is pressing, and whether the pressure was continuous or released and reapplied, because that history changes what the receiving team expects. A teaching illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient or a real incident, is the driver trapped by a collapsed seat for a long period who is alert when found and whose only visible injury is a swollen thigh.

Crushed muscle has been squeezed until its blood supply can no longer reach it, and the tissue at the center of the compression dies while the tissue at the edge is merely bruised. Dead muscle does not stay inert, because its cells break open and release what they contain into the fluid around them, and that material sits within the limb until the pressure is removed. When the weight is lifted, the blood returning to the limb carries those contents into the general circulation in a single load, and the patient who was stable under the weight may become unstable within minutes. This is the distinction that governs the chapter, because a crush injury is the local damage to the limb, while crush syndrome is the systemic illness produced when the products of that damage reach the heart, the kidneys, and the rest of the body. The breakdown of muscle fibers with the escape of their contents into the blood has a name, which is rhabdomyolysis, and the most familiar of those contents is myoglobin, the protein that stores oxygen within muscle and gives it its color. Myoglobin is joined by potassium, phosphate, and uric acid, while fluid and calcium are drawn into the injured tissue so that the circulating volume falls. The finding that raises the suspicion is a limb that is swollen, firm, and painful in a patient who was trapped for a long period and whose pulse and awareness change after the release.

Of all the substances released by dead muscle, the one that kills soonest is potassium, and the disturbance it produces is hyperkalemia. Potassium governs the electrical behavior of the heart, and when its concentration in the blood rises, the rhythm becomes unstable, first slowing and weakening and then losing its coordination altogether. The finding is a pulse that becomes slow, irregular, or difficult to feel, often in a patient who is still conscious and still talking, and the change can be abrupt rather than gradual. This is why cardiac arrest after extrication is named as the lethal possibility of a crush, because the load of potassium that enters the circulation at the moment of release arrives at the heart within minutes. The trained responder watches the pulse and the level of consciousness without interruption after a release and is ready to begin cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR, at once if the patient stops breathing and loses a pulse.

The second organ to suffer is the kidney, and the injury it sustains is acute kidney injury, which may appear hours or days after the crush rather than at the moment of release. Myoglobin passes into the tubules of the kidney, and in the presence of a low circulating volume and acid conditions it can block and injure them, so the kidney that was healthy before the injury begins to produce less urine and to clear less waste. The finding in the field is a patient who is not passing urine, or whose urine is scanty and dark, and this is an observation that the trained responder records and passes on rather than treats. Low blood pressure from the loss of fluid into the crushed tissue makes the kidney injury worse, which is why restoring the circulation and protecting the kidney are managed together in hospital rather than separately. The treatment that clears the muscle products and supports the kidney belongs to definitive hospital care, and where the kidney does not recover it may need a machine to take over its work while the patient heals. The field task is to reach that care sooner rather than later.

Compartment syndrome is the companion of the crushed limb, and it is the injury that continues to develop after the patient is free. Muscle lies within compartments bounded by fascia that does not stretch, and when the tissue inside swells after a crush, the pressure within the compartment rises until it exceeds the pressure that drives blood through the capillaries. The findings that mark it are pain that is severe and out of proportion to the visible wound, pain that increases when the fingers or toes are straightened, a limb that feels tense and firm to the touch, numbness or tingling in the territory of the nerve that runs through the compartment, and weakness of the muscles the compartment contains. A pulse that is still present below the injured area does not exclude compartment syndrome, because the pressure that starves the muscle can be high while the main artery remains open. The definitive treatment is surgical release of the fascia, which is a hospital procedure and never a field procedure, and the field task is to remove anything constricting the limb and to move the patient toward the surgeon. A patient whose pain is escalating while a bandage is in place has told the responder that the bandage, and not the injury alone, may be part of the problem, so the dressing is reassessed rather than tightened further.

Extrication is a medical intervention rather than a rescue of pure muscle, because the manner and the timing of the release change the patient's survival. Rapid release without preparation can kill, and the mechanism is by now familiar, in that the moment the weight is lifted the trapped contents of dead muscle enter the circulation, while the blood that had been held in the compressed limb returns to a circulation that is already short of volume. The patient can also deteriorate because the pressure of the weight was the only thing closing a torn vessel, and its removal restores a hemorrhage that no one is prepared to control. A further hazard is the rescue itself, because a load shifted carelessly can fall on the patient or on the rescuers. The decision about when and how to release the weight therefore belongs to advanced providers and to the incident commander, who weigh the danger of the scene against the danger of the release. The lay first aider does not attempt to move the weight alone, does not pull the patient free, and does not dig into an unstable pile, but calls for a rescue team and stays with the patient.

The preparation before a release is where the outcome of a crush is often decided, and it follows a fixed order. The patient is assessed where they lie, with the airway, the breathing, and the circulation examined before any weight is moved, because a patient who cannot breathe will not benefit from being freed. The mechanism, the duration of entrapment, the part of the body that is compressed, and any bleeding the responder can see are reported to the receiving team and to the medical controller while the rescue is still being organized. Equipment and personnel are gathered for what may follow, including the means to control bleeding, to immobilize the limb, to keep the patient warm, and to begin resuscitation at the moment it is needed. The plan for lifting the weight is agreed in advance, including who will lift, in what direction the load will move, and where the patient will be placed once free, so that the release is a controlled act rather than a sudden one. The finding that tells the team to proceed is a scene made stable and a patient examined and prepared, and until both are true the weight is left where it is unless it is the immediate cause of death.

Monitoring during the release and after it is continuous, because the danger of a crush is concentrated in the minutes that follow the lifting of the weight. The trained responder watches the airway and the breathing, feels the pulse for rate and strength, looks at the level of consciousness and the pupils, observes the color and warmth of the skin, and repeats those observations at short intervals rather than once. The crushed limb is examined for swelling, for tension, for bleeding that has restarted, and for the pulse and movement beyond the injury, and anything constricting it is removed if that can be done without disturbing the wound. The patient is covered and insulated from the ground before the journey begins, because a patient trapped in cold debris is already losing heat and the release adds exposure to that loss. A sudden change for the worse, whether a pulse that slows, a consciousness that dulls, or a breathing that becomes shallow, is treated as the cardiac emergency it may be and is reported at once. The finding that should reassure nobody is a single normal set of observations, because the trend and not the single value tells the responder whether the patient is holding.

Cardiac arrest after extrication is the specific catastrophe this chapter exists to prevent, and it deserves to be described plainly so that no responder is surprised by it. The heart can stop within a short time of the release, driven by the potassium that has entered the blood, by the loss of circulating volume, by the cold, and by the sudden return of acid blood from the crushed tissue. The patient may arrest in front of the rescuers, sometimes while being carried, which is why the pulse and the breathing are watched without interruption from the moment the weight begins to move. If the patient stops breathing and has no pulse, CPR is begun at once by whoever is trained, compressions are continued without pause, and the patient is moved toward a hospital that can continue resuscitation while treating the cause. A duration such as 4 hours of continuous compression is often described in teaching as the point at which the risk of a serious crush syndrome becomes high, and that figure is an illustration which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the timing differs with the size of the crushed mass, with the duration of entrapment, and with the patient. The responder who expects the arrest is the responder who is ready to treat it.

The lay first aider has a defined and valuable part in a crush, and it is built on restraint as much as on action. The lay first aider calls for emergency medical services and for a technical rescue team, reports the location, the number of patients, the nature of the entrapment, and the time the patient has been trapped, and stays with the patient until help arrives. While waiting, the lay first aider keeps the airway open with the hands if it is obstructed, covers the patient and insulates them from the ground, and speaks to the patient in a calm and continuous way, because a trapped patient who is being talked to is a patient who is being observed. Bleeding that can be reached is controlled with direct pressure through a clean cloth or a dressing, and a foreign body or a piece of debris that is embedded is stabilized in place and never pulled out, because removal may release a hemorrhage that cannot be controlled. The lay first aider does not lift the weight, does not give anything by mouth, does not attempt to straighten a deformed limb, and does not attempt to free the patient by pulling. The finding that tells the lay first aider to stop and wait is any uncertainty about the stability of the scene or the weight, because a second casualty made by a premature rescue helps nobody.

The trained responder and the paramedic work within a protocol, and their contribution is monitoring, preparation, and safe transport rather than definitive repair. They assess the patient with the primary survey, control external bleeding with the measures their service authorizes, immobilize the injured limb in the position found, and protect the patient against hypothermia with blankets and insulation from the ground. They may give oxygen where the protocol and the prescriber authorize it, and they may begin the fluids or the medicines that the local protocol provides for a crushed patient, but the substance, the amount, the route, and the timing are decisions of that protocol and that prescriber and are not taken from a manual. They record the time of entrapment and the time of release as carefully as they record the time a tourniquet is placed, because the receiving team treats a patient whose history includes those times differently from one whose history does not. They make contact with a receiving hospital early, describe the mechanism and the expected complications, and follow the advice they are given about destination and about preparation. The finding that changes their plan is any deterioration after the release, and their response to it is to escalate, to resuscitate if they are trained and authorized, and to shorten the journey.

Definitive hospital care owns every act in this chapter that repairs, corrects, or replaces, and naming that boundary protects both the patient and the responder. The hospital measures the chemistry of the blood, including the potassium and the products of muscle breakdown, monitors the rhythm of the heart, and treats the electrolyte disturbance with the medicines and the amounts that the local guideline and the treating physician decide. It supports the circulation with fluids and blood products chosen for that patient, protects the kidney by restoring the circulation and by other measures within its protocol, and uses a machine to replace kidney function when the injury is severe enough to require it. It measures the pressure within the compartments of the crushed limb and performs the surgical release of the fascia, the removal of dead muscle, and the repair of vessels and bones in the operating room, with the patient under anesthesia. It treats the wound, decides about protection against tetanus and about antibiotics, and provides the pain relief that a crush demands. None of those things is a field procedure, and no responder should delay transport in order to attempt any part of them.

Cold is a complication of crush injury rather than a detail of comfort, and the crushed patient is unusually vulnerable to it. A patient who has been trapped under debris has often been lying on cold ground for a long time, may be wet from rain or from water used in the rescue, and will be exposed again when the weight is removed and the clothing is cut away. Cold impairs clotting, deepens the circulatory failure, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm, which is precisely the outcome a crushed patient is already at risk of. The responder removes wet clothing where that can be done safely, covers the patient with blankets, coats, or foil, insulates the patient from the ground beneath, and keeps the vehicle or the ambulance warm during transport. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which the effects of cold become serious, and that figure, like every other in this chapter, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line differs between services and between editions. The finding that warns the responder that cooling has already begun is a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold.

A patient who is trapped for a long time is frightened, in pain, and often alone in a space that the responder cannot easily enter, and the care of that patient begins long before the release. Someone should be assigned to stay with the patient, to speak in a steady voice, to explain what is being done, and to keep the patient oriented to time and to place. The patient is encouraged not to struggle against the weight, because struggling consumes muscle that is already short of blood and increases the load of muscle products that will later be released. Sips of fluid are not offered by the lay first aider, because the decision about anything taken by mouth in a patient who may need surgery belongs to the clinician, and because a patient who vomits while trapped is in danger of inhaling what is brought up. Pain is acknowledged and reported, and the decision about how it is treated belongs to the provider authorized to prescribe it under the local protocol, since the substance and the amount are not taken from a manual. The finding that is passed to the rescue team is any change in the patient's speech, awareness, or breathing, because those changes help decide how quickly the release must be made.

The crushed wound itself demands the ordinary care of any wound together with a heightened suspicion of infection. The surface may be deeply contaminated with soil, with clothing, and with fragments driven in by the weight, and the tissue beneath it may be dead, which is a combination that favors infection. The responder covers the wound with a clean dressing, keeps it protected during the journey, and does not attempt to clean or explore it in the field, because deep cleaning and the removal of dead tissue belong to the surgeon. The question of protection against tetanus is raised at the first contact and answered by the provider authorized to decide it under the local protocol, because the vaccination history of the patient and the nature of the wound both change the answer. Antibiotics follow the same rule, in that the finding which makes the decision urgent is a wound that is deep, contaminated, or accompanied by dead muscle, while the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber and to the local guideline. The finding that should be reported at handover is any wound that is spreading, foul smelling, or accompanied by fever, because infection in a crushed limb can progress rapidly.

Crush injuries arrive from a small number of recurring settings, and knowing them helps the responder anticipate the syndrome. A structure that collapses in an earthquake, a blast, or a demolition traps people beneath slabs and can produce many crushed patients at once. An industrial accident traps a hand, an arm, or a whole body in machinery, a press, or a roller, and the machine may have to be taken apart rather than reversed, because reversing it can pull the patient further in. An agricultural accident traps a limb under a tractor, a bale, or a falling implement on a farm far from a hospital, and a road crash traps a patient between a vehicle and the ground or beneath a wheel. A patient who lies unconscious on a hard surface for hours after a fall, a seizure, or an overdose suffers the same muscle injury without any external weight, and the responder who knows the pattern will suspect it. In every one of those settings the two problems of this chapter are present together, and the local injury is treated while the systemic one is anticipated.

Some patients tolerate a crush far less well than others, and the difference changes how quickly care must be delivered. A child has less muscle mass and less circulating volume than an adult, so the same weight over the same time releases a proportionally larger load of muscle contents and produces a larger fall in circulating volume. An older patient may have less reserve in the heart and the kidney before the injury begins, and may be taking medicines that affect the heart rhythm and the blood pressure, which the receiving team must know about. A pregnant patient has a circulation that is already altered, and the concerns of the fetus are added to those of the mother, so the care of the mother remains the care of the fetus and the receiving hospital is told that the patient is pregnant. A patient trapped with a head injury, with a chest injury, or with heavy bleeding has a second lethal problem that may kill before the crush syndrome does. The finding that must be reported in every one of these patients is the duration of entrapment, because time is the measure that most changes what the receiving team will do.

The handover is part of the treatment of a crushed patient, and a complete handover changes what the hospital does in the first minutes. The receiving team needs the mechanism, the time of entrapment, the time of release, and the part of the body that was compressed, because those four facts predict the complications and the speed with which they may appear. It needs to know what bleeding was found and how it was controlled, whether a tourniquet was placed and when, whether the limb was splinted, and whether the patient has been moved or turned. It needs the observations that were recorded over time, including the trend of the pulse, the breathing, and the level of consciousness, and it needs to know whether the patient has passed urine and what it looked like. It needs to know what the patient has been given, by whom, and under what protocol, and it needs to know what has not been given. The finding that must never be omitted is any deterioration that occurred during the journey, because a patient who changed on the way to hospital is a patient who is changing still.

To summarize, the crushed patient carries a local injury and a systemic syndrome at the same time, and the systemic one begins when the weight is released. Crushed muscle dies in place and releases potassium, myoglobin, and other contents into the blood, so the heart may stop from hyperkalemia within minutes of extrication, the kidney may fail from acute kidney injury over the following hours, and the crushed limb may develop compartment syndrome even while the patient is being rescued. The scene is made safe first, rapid release without preparation is a cause of death, and the decision about how and when to release the weight belongs to advanced providers and to the incident commander. The lay first aider calls for help, stays with the patient, keeps the airway open, controls what bleeding can be reached, covers the patient, and never pulls an embedded object free. The trained responder monitors the pulse, the breathing, and the level of consciousness continuously, protects the patient against hypothermia, records the times of entrapment and release, and reaches definitive care as quickly as is safe. Hospital care owns the correction of the electrolyte disturbance, the support of the kidney, the surgical release of the fascia, the removal of dead tissue, and the treatment of the wound. Every number, time, and temperature in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 36 — Head Injuries

A head injury is the injury that most often kills a patient who is still talking, and the responder who understands that sentence will act differently from the one who does not. The lethal possibility to be named first is bleeding inside the skull, and the finding that reveals it may be nothing more alarming than a patient who is drowsy, who repeats a question, or who vomits once and then seems to recover. No care begins before the scene has been made safe, and the hazards of a head injury scene are the ones that produced it, which are moving traffic on a road, a fall from a height above a surface that may still be unstable, fire, a live electrical cable, deep water, an animal that is still loose, a violent person who may strike again, and a structure that may collapse. The patient's own blood and vomit are hazards as well, so gloves and eye protection, or whatever barrier is actually at hand, come before the first touch. This chapter is educational material and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work, and every act described here is named with the provider level that owns it.

The skull is a closed box that holds the brain, the vessels that feed it, and the fluid that cushions it, and the box cannot stretch when something inside it grows. Blood that collects inside that space has nowhere to go, so the pressure within the skull rises and is passed on to the brain, which suffers first at the place where the blood lies and then everywhere as the pressure spreads. The structures that are compressed most easily are the ones that control the level of consciousness and the size of the pupils, which is why those two observations carry so much meaning after a blow to the head. The same pressure can force part of the brain downward through the narrow openings at the base of the skull, and that movement is the final and most lethal step of a hemorrhage that was small when it began. The injury outside the skull is therefore never the whole story, because a scalp wound may be trivial while the bleeding that will kill the patient is entirely hidden.

The mechanism of injury is the first clinical evidence, and it predicts damage that the eye cannot see. A fall from a height of 3 meters, a figure offered only as a teaching illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, predicts a deceleration injury in which the brain moves within the skull and tears where it is tethered. A vehicle collision predicts the same, and the direction of the impact decides where the brain strikes the bone, while an assault with a fist or a weapon predicts a blow that may leave no mark on the scalp. A blast predicts a pressure wave and fragments, and a fall from standing in an older patient, or any blow in a patient who takes a medicine that thins the blood, can produce a hemorrhage that nobody expects from the size of the event. The energy that reached the head is what matters rather than the size of the wound, and the responder who asks how the patient was injured is already thinking about what may be bleeding inside.

Scalp wounds bleed in a way that frightens everyone who sees them and that is rarely dangerous in itself, and the reason lies in the anatomy of the scalp. The scalp carries an unusually rich supply of blood vessels, and those vessels are held open by the firm layer beneath the skin, so a small cut can pour a startling volume over the face and the clothing while the total loss stays modest. The lay first aider controls such bleeding with firm direct pressure over a clean pad, exactly as for bleeding anywhere else, and does not lift the pad to see whether the flow has stopped, adding further layers on top instead if blood shows through. The opposite mistake is to dismiss the scalp wound as a nuisance and to stop watching the patient, because a wound on the scalp is a marker of energy that reached the skull and a fracture may lie beneath it. The trained responder examines the wound gently, without probing it with a finger or an instrument, and records what was seen while continuing to observe the patient.

A fracture of the skull may be open, with a break in the skin over it, or closed, and it may be a simple crack or a depressed segment that has been pushed inward against the brain. The findings that raise the suspicion are a wound or a swelling over the bone, a step or a soft depression felt through the scalp, and bruising that appears behind the ear or around both eyes some hours after the injury. Clear fluid, or blood mixed with clear fluid, escaping from the nose or an ear points to a fracture at the base of the skull, and that fluid is cerebrospinal fluid, which surrounds the brain and has leaked through the covering that should contain it. A fracture at the base of the skull may also produce bleeding from the ear, and the responder must not pack the ear or the nose to stop it, because the blood and the fluid need a way out and packing may push infection inward. When the bone is exposed or the brain itself is visible, the wound is covered with a clean dressing that is laid over it rather than pressed into it, and no attempt is made to push bone fragments back into place. An embedded object is stabilized in place and the patient is moved with it, because removal may release a hemorrhage that cannot be controlled and may destroy tissue that is still intact, and the confirmation of a fracture belongs to definitive hospital care.

Concussion is the most common form of traumatic brain injury, and it is a disturbance of brain function rather than a visible wound, which is why it is described as a diagnosis of exclusion. It is suspected when a patient who has struck the head reports a headache, dizziness, nausea, blurred vision, or a feeling of being slowed down, and when the patient cannot recall the moments before or after the impact. Loss of consciousness is neither required nor a reliable measure of severity, because a patient who never lost consciousness may still be confused, while a patient who was briefly unconscious may recover fully. The trained responder or the physician makes the diagnosis only after the more dangerous causes of the same complaints, above all bleeding inside the skull, have been considered and excluded. A patient suspected of concussion is not returned to sport, to driving, or to work on the day of the injury, and the decision about when any of those may resume belongs to a clinician after the local protocol has been followed.

The level of consciousness is the most important observation the responder repeats, because it is the earliest and most sensitive sign that the brain is losing ground. The assessment begins with speech, asking the patient's name, the place, the day, and what happened, and the answer reveals whether the patient is fully awake and oriented or merely capable of words. If the patient does not answer, the responder calls the patient's name loudly and then applies a painful stimulus in the way the local protocol teaches, and the response to voice and to pain is graded and recorded rather than described vaguely. A change in the level of consciousness carries more meaning than any single measurement, so the responder writes the finding together with the time it was made and compares it with the previous entry. The Glasgow coma scale is the formal tool for this purpose where the responder has been trained in it, and it turns an impression into a number that two people can compare, while the trend across repeated examinations matters more than any one score. A patient who is becoming harder to rouse, or who is roused and then drifts away again, has given the responder the finding that changes the plan.

Bleeding inside the skull is the injury that kills while the patient is talking, and it takes several forms that behave differently and demand the same urgency. Blood may collect between the skull and the tough outer covering of the brain, which is called an epidural hematoma, and this is often the result of a torn artery and expands quickly. Blood may collect beneath that covering and over the surface of the brain, which is called a subdural hematoma, and this is more often venous and may develop over hours or days, especially in an older patient or in one who takes a medicine that thins the blood. Blood may also collect within the brain itself after a severe blow, or in the space filled with cerebrospinal fluid, and every one of these collections raises the pressure inside the closed box. The findings are the same in their meaning whatever the name, and they are a level of consciousness that is falling, a headache that is worsening, vomiting, a seizure, and pupils that have become unequal. The name is a matter for the hospital, and the responder's task is to recognize that the patient is deteriorating and to reach definitive care before the deterioration becomes irreversible.

The lucid interval is the trap that must be taught to every responder, and it is the period in which a patient who has bled inside the skull appears to recover before collapsing. A constructed illustration, offered as a construction rather than as a real patient, is the young person who is struck on the side of the head, is briefly stunned, then stands, speaks normally, and asks to go home while a torn artery continues to bleed beneath the bone. The patient may remain lucid for a period often described as lasting from minutes to several hours, and any such interval is only an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because its length varies with the vessel, the patient, and the injury. When the volume of blood finally exceeds what the skull can accommodate, the level of consciousness falls quickly, one pupil may widen, and the patient may stop breathing. The lesson is not that the responder should wait for the collapse, because waiting is exactly what loses the patient, but that an apparently recovered patient after a significant blow to the head belongs in a place where imaging and a surgeon are available.

A change in the level of consciousness alters the plan more than any other single finding, and it must never be explained away by alcohol, by fatigue, or by the emotion of the scene. A patient who was alert and is now drowsy, who was answering sensibly and is now repeating the same question, or who has become restless and combative without a reason, may be showing the first effect of a rising pressure inside the skull. The same finding may come from a lack of oxygen, from a fall in the circulation caused by bleeding elsewhere, from a low blood sugar, from a seizure that has passed, or from a substance the patient has taken, and the responder cannot tell these apart in the field. The correct act is therefore to treat the change as serious, to correct within the responder's scope only what can be corrected there, and to move the patient toward the assessment that can separate the causes. The lay first aider does not try to arouse a patient with food, drink, or a slap, and does not leave a patient who has become drowsy unattended for any reason.

The pupils are examined together and compared with each other, because a difference between them points to something pressing on the structures that control them. A pupil that has become wider and no longer narrows when a light is shone into it, on the same side as the injury, points to pressure on that side, and it is one of the last findings before the patient is lost.
