A difference between the pupils may also come from an injury to the eye itself, from a previous eye operation, or from a medicine the patient has used, so the finding is a reason to act and not a diagnosis. The lay first aider may look at the pupils and report what is seen, but the interpretation belongs to the trained responder and to the physician. The finding that changes the plan is a pupil that was equal and has become unequal, or one that was reactive and has stopped responding to light, and it means the patient must reach imaging and a surgeon as fast as is safe.

Vomiting after a head injury is common and it is also a warning, and the responder must decide which of the two it is in the particular patient. A single episode in a patient who is otherwise alert and improving may come from the shock of the injury, while repeated vomiting, or vomiting in a patient whose level of consciousness is falling, points to a rising pressure inside the skull. The immediate danger of vomiting is the airway, because a patient who is drowsy may breathe the stomach contents into the lungs, and that injury can be fatal on its own. The correct response is to turn the patient onto one side, or into the position that lets the vomit drain, while keeping the head and the neck in line with the body when a spinal injury is suspected. The lay first aider clears the mouth with a finger wrapped in cloth only when something is visible, does not put a finger blindly into the throat, and gives nothing by mouth to a patient who is drowsy or vomiting. The trained responder protects the airway with the equipment and the authority of the service, and both levels move the patient toward definitive care without delay.

A seizure after a head injury may occur within moments of the blow or much later, and the two carry different meanings. A seizure at the time of the injury is often the immediate effect of the impact, while a seizure that appears after an interval, in a patient who had seemed stable, suggests bleeding or swelling inside the skull and changes the plan at once. During the seizure the responder protects the patient from injury rather than trying to stop the movement, clears the space around the patient, cushions the head, and neither restrains the limbs nor places anything in the mouth. After the movement stops, the patient is turned into a position that protects the airway, kept warm, and watched closely, because a period of drowsiness and confusion normally follows and must not be mistaken for a new deterioration without comparing it with what came before. The time the seizure began and how long it lasted are recorded, because the receiving team needs both to understand the course of the injury. A seizure that continues, or that repeats without recovery between episodes, is a medical emergency, and the trained responder treats it within the service protocol while the patient is moved to definitive care.

Airway management in a patient with a head injury must assume that the neck is also injured, because the force that injured the head often passed through the neck, and because a patient who cannot protect the airway cannot be left with the tongue blocking it. The lay first aider opens the airway with a jaw thrust or by lifting the chin while keeping the head and the neck as still as the situation allows, and does not twist or extend the neck to make the airway open. The trained responder uses the adjuncts and the techniques the service authorizes, holds the head in a neutral line with the hands or with the equipment carried, and calls for a second responder when the airway and the neck must be managed at the same time. Vomit, blood, and loose teeth are cleared from the mouth, and a patient who is breathing noisily or not at all is treated first, because no injury to the brain can be helped by a patient who is not breathing. Breathing is then watched for its rate, its depth, and its pattern, since the brain controls breathing and an injured brain disturbs it, and a pattern that becomes irregular, with pauses, points to injury at the base of the brain. When the patient stops breathing, cardiopulmonary resuscitation is begun by the lay first aider and continued by the trained responder, and it is performed with the same care for the neck.

The circulation must be assessed in every patient with a head injury, because bleeding elsewhere can imitate and worsen the injury inside the skull, and a patient who has fallen from a height may have a broken pelvis or a torn vessel in the abdomen. The responder examines the skin for its color and warmth, feels the pulse for its rate and strength, and looks for the wound that is bleeding or the abdomen that is becoming rigid. In a patient with a head injury the pressure must be kept high enough to perfuse the brain, so the support of the circulation is decided by the trained responder under the local protocol. Cold is a complication of a head injury and not a detail of comfort, because a patient lying on the ground after a blow to the head loses heat quickly, and a patient who is undressed, wet, or still for a long time is at particular risk. The lay first aider removes wet clothing where that can be done without disturbing the head and the neck, covers the patient with blankets, coats, or foil, and puts insulation between the patient and the ground, because much of the heat is lost downward. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is a figure often used to mark the point at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the accepted line differs between services and editions. The position itself is a treatment, since a patient who is vomiting or cannot protect the airway is turned onto one side with the head and the neck kept in line, while a patient in shock is kept flat and warm.

The rhythm of observation continues from the first contact until the handover, and it is the trend across repeated examinations rather than any single examination that tells the receiving team what is happening inside the skull. The observations are repeated in the same order every time, which is the level of consciousness, the pupils, the breathing, the pulse, the color and the warmth of the skin, the movement of the limbs, and the pain in the head. Each set is written down with the time, and the times matter as much as the findings, because a hemorrhage that took 2 hours to produce a change is understood differently from one that produced it in 20 minutes, and those intervals are illustrations to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The handover states the mechanism and the time of the injury, the level of consciousness when the patient was first seen and at every change since, the number of times the patient vomited, whether there was a seizure, the pupils on each side, what bleeding was controlled, how warm the patient has been kept, and any medicine the patient takes. The lay first aider contributes the observations and the times, and the trained responder adds the measurements and the record of every intervention. A gap in that story forces the receiving team to begin again.

Definitive hospital care begins with a reassessment of the whole patient and with imaging of the head, and the decision about which patients need imaging is made by the physician according to the local guideline. Computed tomography is the examination that shows blood inside the skull, a fracture of the bone, and the swelling of the brain, and it is available in some hospitals at all hours and in others only after a transfer, which is one reason for the field report to be accurate and early. The criteria that decide who is scanned include the mechanism, the level of consciousness, the findings on examination, the age of the patient, and whether the patient takes a medicine that thins the blood, and those criteria must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because they differ between services. A patient with a head injury and a normal examination may still be observed in hospital for a period set by the local guideline, and the responder must not tell the family that observation is unnecessary. Definitive care owns the removal of a collection of blood, the placing of a monitor to follow the pressure inside the skull, the intensive care unit, and the operation that repairs the skull, and none of those is a field procedure.

Some patients hide a serious head injury better than others, and the responder must lower the threshold for concern in each group. A young child may be alert and playing after a fall and may still have a fracture, and a child who vomits repeatedly, who is sleepy at the wrong hour, or who is not feeding normally needs assessment. An older patient may develop a subdural hematoma after a fall that looked trivial, and the bleeding may declare itself days later, so the history of a fall matters even when the examination seems reassuring. A patient who takes a medicine that thins the blood, or who has a bleeding disorder, may bleed inside the skull after a very small impact, and the finding that makes the decision urgent is any head injury at all in such a patient. Alcohol and other substances confuse the picture because they produce the same drowsiness and unsteadiness as a brain injury, and the safe rule is to attribute the change to the injury until a clinician has shown otherwise. A further danger belongs to the days after the injury, because a brain that has not yet recovered tolerates a second impact poorly and a second blow during that period can produce swelling out of all proportion to the force, which is why a patient suspected of concussion is removed from sport, from driving, and from work until a clinician permits a return.

Certain acts are named here so that no responder attempts them, since knowing what must not be done is as much a part of competence as knowing what to do. A responder does not give a patient food or drink after a head injury, because vomiting and the risk of aspiration follow, and does not give a medicine to relieve pain or to wake the patient when the substance and the amount belong to a prescriber and to the local protocol. A responder does not press on an open fracture of the skull, does not pack an ear or a nose that is leaking blood or cerebrospinal fluid, does not remove a fragment of bone or a foreign body from a head wound, and does not straighten the neck to inspect the back of the head. A responder does not diagnose concussion from a distance, does not decide that a patient is safe to go home, and does not quiet a patient with a medicine that may hide a falling level of consciousness. Restraint of a combative patient belongs to the trained responder and to the local protocol. The lay first aider is asked to do the few things that help, which are to make the scene safe, to keep the airway open, to control bleeding by pressure, to protect the patient from cold, to watch the level of consciousness, and to send for help early.

To summarize, the head injury that kills is usually the one that is hidden, and the responder reads it in the patient's behavior rather than in the wound. Scene safety comes before care, the mechanism of injury predicts what cannot be seen, and a scalp wound that bleeds alarmingly is controlled by direct pressure while the skull beneath it is treated as possibly fractured. Concussion is a diagnosis of exclusion, made only after bleeding inside the skull has been considered, and no patient suspected of it returns to sport, to driving, or to work on the day of the injury. The level of consciousness is the most important observation and it is repeated with the time of every change, while the pupils, the vomiting, and the seizures are the findings that alter the plan, and the lucid interval is the trap in which a talking patient deteriorates after seeming to recover. The airway is protected with the neck kept in line, breathing and the circulation are watched, and cold is treated as a complication from the first minute. Definitive hospital care owns computed tomography, the monitoring of the pressure inside the skull, the intensive care unit, and the operation that removes the blood, and no field responder explores a head wound, presses on an open fracture, packs a leaking ear or nose, or removes an embedded object. The patient is watched continuously to the handover, the times and the findings are written where the receiving team will see them, and every figure in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 37 — Facial Trauma

The face is the first thing a rescuer sees and the last thing that should hold the attention, because the injuries that kill a patient with facial trauma hide behind the appearance of the face. A face can look destroyed and the patient can still be saved, while a face with one small wound can be closing an airway that nobody is watching. Two dangers run through this chapter, which are the airway that fills with blood or swells shut, and the eye that is blinded by a hand that meant to help. A third is bleeding from the rich vessels of the face, dangerous less for its volume at the roadside than for where the blood goes. No clinical act begins before the scene is made safe, so traffic, fire, electricity, water, animals, violence, structural collapse, and the patient's own body fluids are dealt with first. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, with gloves and eye protection, is worn before any hand is laid on a wound, because blood and saliva carry infection into a break in the skin or a splash into the eye. Every act is named with the provider level that owns it, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

The mechanism of injury is the first clinical evidence, and in the face it predicts damage that no eye can see from outside. A punch, a fall onto the face, a steering wheel, an animal kick, a bat, a windshield, a blast wave, and a bullet break the face in different patterns, each with its own likely companions. The force that breaks the face has traveled through the skull and the neck, so such a patient is treated as having a head injury and a cervical spine injury until those are excluded. The finding that keeps the spine protected is any injury above the shoulders, any fall, and any patient who cannot be relied on to hold the neck still. The mouth and the nose open directly into the throat, so a fracture of the facial bones is a fracture of the walls of the passage for air. A blow to the face in a vehicle collision should also raise the question of the chest, the abdomen, and the limbs, because the face explains nothing about the rest of the body. A mechanism that seems trivial, such as a single punch, can still produce swelling that will close the airway over the following hours.

The reason a broken face bleeds into the airway is anatomical, and it explains every rule that follows. The facial bones are not solid blocks but thin shells around air-filled spaces, lined inside by a membrane with an exceptionally rich blood supply. When a fracture tears that lining, blood runs along the fracture lines into the sinuses, the nose, the mouth, and the loose tissue of the throat, none of which can be seen from outside. The tongue lies in a floor of soft tissue that can swell within minutes, so a fracture can both bleed and swell into the exact passage the patient needs for air. A patient lying flat cannot spit, swallow, or cough, and the tongue falls backward when consciousness is dulled, so blood and saliva collect at the back of the throat. The finding that reveals this is not the wound but the sound of the breathing and the change in the voice, which is why position matters as much as any dressing. Blood is an irritant to the stomach, so a patient who has swallowed a large amount may vomit, and vomit in a damaged face is another obstruction.

The primary survey is performed in its fixed order, and in facial trauma the airway decides everything else. A patient speaking in a clear voice has an airway that is open at that moment, and that observation is worth more than any field instrument. The findings of a failing airway are the ones a listener can hear, which are gurgling, snoring, a hoarse or muffled voice, a voice changed since the injury, noisy breathing on inspiration, and drooling because the patient cannot swallow. Swelling growing under the tongue, in the floor of the mouth, or in the soft tissue of the neck turns a stable patient into an emergency within minutes and can continue to enlarge after the examination. Loose teeth, bone fragments, pieces of denture, chewing gum, and vomit can be cleared, and a conscious patient who can be asked to spit is the easiest to protect. The trained responder may use suction and airway adjuncts under a protocol, while the lay first aider keeps the head in a position that lets blood run out. A blind finger sweep is never performed in an unconscious patient, because a finger can push a loose tooth or a fragment deeper into the throat, and only an object that is visible is removed.

The positioning of a patient with facial trauma is a treatment in itself, and it belongs to whoever has hands on the patient. A conscious patient who is breathing and not in shock sits up and leans forward, so that gravity carries blood and saliva out of the mouth instead of back into the throat. A patient who must lie down, because of a spinal injury, a low level of consciousness, or the requirements of the journey, is turned onto one side with the mouth as the lowest part of the drainage path. Where a cervical spine injury is suspected, the turn is a log roll with the head and the neck held in a straight line by a second person, so that the airway and the spine are protected together. No pillow is placed under the head of a patient who is bleeding into the mouth, because a pillow lets the blood pool at the back of the throat. A patient who vomits is turned at once, and the mouth is cleared of what can be seen. The finding that the position has failed is noisier breathing, a worsened voice, or repeated swallowing and coughing, and the position is maintained for the whole journey.

Bleeding from the face is dramatic and rarely fatal by volume alone, and the responder treats it as an airway problem rather than a race against blood loss. A cut lip, a torn nose, and the raw surface of a fractured cheek can produce a frightening flow, but the vessels are small enough that firm pressure around the wound usually controls them. Pressure is applied around the wound and along the line of bleeding, never in a way that pushes the tongue back, blocks the nose, or compresses the neck. A facial dressing is held rather than bound, because a bandage around the head can tighten the airway it is meant to protect. The lay first aider presses with a clean cloth, adds another layer instead of lifting the first, and keeps the patient upright and leaning forward. An object embedded in the face is stabilized with padding around it and never removed in the field, because it may be plugging a vessel or lying against an intact structure, and removal can release hemorrhage that no field measure can control. The trained responder may pack an appropriate wound under a protocol, and definitive hospital care repairs what pressure cannot reach.

The nose deserves its own examination, because it is the most commonly broken bone in the face and two of its injuries are easy to miss. A nasal fracture causes swelling, bruising under the eyes, bleeding, and a change of shape, and the responder does not straighten it, because manipulation worsens the bleeding and cannot be judged without imaging. A traumatic nosebleed is controlled by pinching the soft part of the nose and leaning the patient forward, so that blood runs out instead of down the throat, and a patient who is swallowing blood is watched for vomiting. A dark, tense bulge on the wall between the nostrils is a collection of blood under the lining and not a bruise, and a nose blocked on one side by a smooth, painless swelling needs review, because it can destroy the cartilage if it is left. Clear fluid from the nose, or a salty taste in the mouth, warns of a fracture at the base of the skull, and it changes the plan at once, because nothing is then packed into the nose and nothing is passed through it. Bruising around both eyes without a direct blow, bruising behind the ear, and clear fluid from the ear belong to the same family of findings, and a loose clean dressing over a leaking ear is all that is needed, because packing it introduces infection. The trained responder avoids any tube through the nose and protects the cervical spine, while definitive care makes the diagnosis with computed tomography.

Fractures of the lower jaw are dangerous because the lower jaw carries the tongue, and the tongue carries the airway. A break in the body of the jaw causes pain on opening, a change in the way the teeth meet, bleeding, and swelling, and a break on both sides can let the front of the jaw fall backward with the tongue. The findings are a patient who cannot close the mouth properly, cannot open it at all, cannot bite, a step or a gap in the line of the teeth, drooling, and numbness of the lower lip or the chin. The responder does not test the jaw by forcing it, does not put a displaced fragment back into place, and does not ask the patient to demonstrate movement, because the examination itself can move the tongue into the airway. Definitive care stabilizes and repairs the bone, and the field never does. In an unconscious patient whose tongue has fallen backward, the trained responder may lift the front of the jaw forward under a protocol, and in the conscious patient the drainage position is the correct act. A patient with a broken jaw who is bleeding and drooling is never left lying on the back, even for a short examination.

Dental injuries are easy to dismiss as cosmetic, and they are among the few injuries in this book where a small, fast act in the field decides whether a structure is saved. A tooth knocked completely out of its socket can survive, but only if it is handled correctly and replaced within a short time, and the handling belongs to the lay first aider. The tooth is picked up by the crown, the white part that shows in the mouth, and never by the root, where the living surface that must be preserved sits. If it is dirty, it is rinsed briefly in clean water, saline, or the patient's own saliva, and it is not scrubbed, dried, or wrapped in a dry cloth. The best transport keeps it moist and beyond the patient's reach, which for a fully conscious patient is between the cheek and the gum, and otherwise is a clean container of milk, saline, or the patient's own saliva. A tooth allowed to dry has lost most of its chance, and the time since it left the mouth decides whether it can be saved, with figures such as 30 minutes being an illustration to confirm against the current guideline and the local protocol. A baby tooth is not reimplanted, because that can damage the permanent tooth beneath it, while a broken piece of a permanent tooth is kept and sent, because it may be used in the repair.

A tooth that is loose but still in place is left exactly where it is, and the patient is warned not to bite on it, test it with the tongue, or swallow it, because a free tooth becomes a foreign body that can be inhaled. The responder does not pull a loose tooth, tie it to a neighbor, or pack its socket, because the socket is a wound that definitive care will assess. Replacement of a tooth is performed by the clinician who owns that decision, and where the local protocol authorizes a trained responder to do it, that act is performed under the protocol and not from a manual. The trained responder records which tooth was lost, where it was placed, and the time it left the mouth, because the receiving team needs that history. Definitive hospital care owns the reimplantation, the splinting of a loose tooth, the repair of a fractured crown, and the treatment of the socket. Dental injury is also a marker of force, because a patient with several broken teeth has usually taken a blow that injured the jaw and the neck as well.

The eye is the structure in this chapter that can be destroyed by the most natural human gesture, which is a hand laid on it to see whether it is all right. The eyeball is a globe of fluid held at a pressure slightly above the air around it, and when its wall has been cut or burst, any pressure from outside pushes the contents out through the wound. What has been pushed out cannot be replaced, and the eye is lost. A patient who has been struck in the eye, or who has a wound near the eye, or who has blood in the front of the eye, must never be pressed, massaged, or have the lids forced open, and never has a pressure patch applied. The findings of a possibly burst globe are a pupil that is not round, a tear in the colored part of the eye, blood filling the front chamber, tissue at the edge of the eye, or an eye sitting lower or more prominent than its neighbor. Vision is tested before the lids swell and close and is tested again later, because failing vision is an emergency. The lay first aider shields the eye with something that rests on the bones of the face and does nothing else.

A fragment of metal, glass, a thorn, or a splinter on or in the eye is stabilized and never removed in the field, because it may be the only thing sealing a wound in the globe. The shield is a rigid object such as the base of a clean paper cup, taped to the brow and the cheek so that nothing rests on the eye, and the trained responder covers both eyes where the protocol allows, because that reduces the movement of the injured one. A chemical injury is the exception that demands immediate action, because when a substance has entered the eye the responder irrigates at once and keeps irrigating with clean water or saline, holding the lids open gently and removing a contact lens if it comes away easily. The lay first aider may irrigate a chemical eye injury, and it is one of the few acts in this chapter that begins before anyone asks whether it is allowed, because the harm continues every second the chemical remains. The irrigation is continued on the way to definitive care rather than stopped once the patient is in the vehicle. No attempt is made to neutralize one chemical with another, because the heat and injury of that reaction are worse than the exposure itself.

Fractures of the bones around the eye may leave the globe untouched and still threaten sight and appearance, and their findings are quiet. A patient who sees double in a particular direction, cannot look up or down on one side, whose cheek is numb, or whose eye has sunk compared with the other may have a broken orbit with muscle or fat caught in the fracture. The responder asks about double vision, numbness of the cheek and upper lip, and pain on looking, and records the answers, because those findings may fade once swelling takes over the face. Definitive hospital care uses CT to define the fracture and decides whether the eye must be repositioned and the bone repaired, and none of that belongs to the field. The finding that must be passed on at handover is any change in vision, because a patient who could see at the roadside and cannot see on arrival has had something happen in between.

The examination of the face belongs to the secondary survey, and it is performed in a fixed order so that nothing is missed while the eye is held by the worst part. The scalp and forehead are examined first, then the eyes, the nose, the cheekbones, the upper jaw and mouth, the lower jaw and chin, and finally the neck, with the front and the back of the patient both seen. The responder looks for swelling that is growing, bruising that has appeared since the last look, a shape that does not match the other side, and blood or clear fluid coming from an opening. The skin is felt gently with the flat of the fingers, comparing the two sides, without pressing into a wound and without springing the facial bones, because that adds pain and may worsen bleeding. The inside of the mouth is inspected where it is safe, because a torn lip, a broken tooth, a swelling in the floor of the mouth, and a piece of bone pointing into the tongue are found there and nowhere else. Function is tested by asking whether the patient can bite, open, swallow, see, feel the upper lip, and speak clearly, because each answer describes a bone, a muscle, or a nerve. The lay first aider keeps the patient in the drainage position, keeps the patient warm, and reports what has changed, and the examination is repeated, because the face at the scene is not the face that arrives at the hospital.

Protection of the injured face is mostly covering without compressing, and keeping the patient warm while the examination is done. A facial wound is covered with a clean, dry dressing held in place rather than bound around the head, an eye is shielded without being touched, and an embedded object is stabilized with padding on both sides. The face is the most exposed part of the body, and a patient sitting upright to protect an airway loses heat from the head and chest, so the trunk is covered, wet clothing is replaced, the patient is insulated from the ground, and the vehicle is kept warm. Cold makes blood clot poorly, deepens shock, and makes a dangerous heart rhythm more likely, and a body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is the figure often used for the point at which those effects become serious, an illustration to confirm against the current guideline and the local protocol. The wound is not scrubbed, painted, or closed in the field, because cleaning and closure are decisions made in hospital where the depth of the injury can be seen. Tetanus protection is raised at the first contact, because a facial wound from soil, an animal bite, or a dirty fragment carries a risk, while the decision belongs to the clinician and the local protocol, and the substance, the amount, the route, and the timing belong to the prescriber and never to this book. Pain is decided in the same way by the provider authorized to prescribe, and the responder's own contribution to comfort is position, warmth, calm speech, and the shortest possible time to care.

Burns of the face deserve a separate warning, because the airway can close after the patient has looked well. A fire, a flash, a steam injury, or a chemical splash can burn the lining of the mouth and throat as surely as the skin, and the swelling of that lining grows over the hours after the injury rather than at the moment of it. The findings are soot around the mouth and the nose, singed hairs inside the nose, a burned or blistered mouth, a hoarse or changed voice, a cough, and a history of being in a closed space with smoke. Each of these is a reason to move the patient to a place where the airway can be controlled rather than to watch and wait. The lay first aider cools a facial burn with clean running water where the protocol of the service advises it, covers the face with a clean dry sheet, and applies no ointment or grease that will have to be peeled away. Swelling in the first hours can make a patient with a facial burn difficult to intubate later, which is why the decision about the airway is made early by the clinician who owns it. The finding that changes the plan is any noise in the breathing, and it changes the plan immediately.

The most important sentence in this chapter is that the appearance of the face must never delay the transfer. A swollen, bloodied, distorted face draws every eye on the scene, and the temptation is to clean it, straighten it, and cover it neatly before leaving, and every one of those acts spends time that the airway and the eye do not have. A patient who needs an operating room for a facial fracture, a torn eye, or a wound that will not stop bleeding needs it as surely as a patient with a bleeding limb, and the journey is the treatment. The destination is chosen before the patient is moved, and it is the nearest facility that can provide the needed care, which for a severe facial injury with an eye injury or an airway concern may be a trauma center with imaging, an operating room, and an intensive care unit. The responder reports what was done and what changed, including the times, the position used, the tooth preserved, the eye shielded, and the object left in place, because the receiving team continues a story the field began. Definitive hospital care owns the repair of the bones, the repair of the eye, the removal of retained fragments, the closure of the wounds, and the decision about reconstruction, and none of those is a field procedure. Every time, distance, temperature, and figure in this chapter is an illustration to confirm against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between services, countries, and editions.

Reassessment continues from the first contact to the handover, because the face changes while the responder watches it. The same observations are repeated in the same order, asking whether the patient is speaking clearly, whether the breathing has become noisy, whether the swelling is larger, whether the eye can still see, and whether bleeding has restarted under the dressing. A patient who was talking and has become quiet, one who has begun to drool, one whose voice has become hoarse, and one who swallows repeatedly have all said that the airway is narrowing, and the response is to return to the beginning of the primary survey. The record is part of the treatment, so the time a dressing was placed, the position the patient was carried in, and the tooth that was sent are written where the receiving team will see them. The finding that ends the observation of a facial injury is the arrival of the team that can see inside the face.

Knowing what must not be done to a face is as much a part of competence as knowing what must be done. The lay first aider positions the patient to drain, presses around a wound without pressing on an eye, preserves a tooth, shields an eye, irrigates a chemical exposure, covers and keeps the patient warm, and sends for help. The trained responder and the paramedic add suction, airway adjuncts, packing under a protocol, cervical spine protection during a log roll, and the monitoring that recognizes a failing airway. Definitive hospital care owns the CT, the repair of the facial bones, the repair of the globe and the eyelids, the removal of retained fragments and embedded objects, the reimplantation of a tooth, the release of a swollen airway, and the reconstruction that follows. Definitive care also owns the decisions about pain relief, tetanus protection, and antibiotics, with the substance, the amount, the route, and the timing set by the prescriber and the local protocol. The line between those levels is a matter of training, authorization, and protocol, and a responder who crosses it with good intentions can convert a survivable injury into a fatal or a blinding one.

To summarize, facial trauma kills through the airway and blinds through the eye, and it almost never kills through the appearance that frightens the scene. A broken face bleeds and swells into the throat because the facial bones are hollow shells lined with a membrane of enormous blood supply, so the patient who cannot sit up and lean forward is placed on one side, with the head low enough that blood drains out of the mouth rather than pooling at the back of it, and the neck is protected during the turn where a spinal injury is possible. The airway is the first step of the primary survey, its failure is heard in gurgling, snoring, a hoarse or changed voice, drooling, and growing swelling, and the lay first aider removes only what is visible, never performs a blind finger sweep, and never binds the face in a way that presses on the airway. The nose, the jaw, the teeth, and the eyes are each examined in their turn, the tooth that has been knocked out is picked up by the crown and kept moist and sent with the patient, and the eye that may have burst is shielded and never pressed, while a chemical exposure is irrigated at once and continuously. Embedded objects are stabilized in place and never removed in the field, the procedures of repair and reimplantation belong to hospital care, and the provider level is named for every act. Every time and temperature in this chapter is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and the appearance of the face must never delay the transfer. This chapter is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 38 — Neck Trauma

The neck is the narrowest column in the body to carry so much that cannot be given up, and a wound there is measured in minutes. Within a space a hand can nearly encircle lie the airway, the great vessels that supply the brain, the spinal cord, the esophagus, and the nerves that move the shoulder, the tongue, and the vocal cords. A knife, a bullet, a shard of glass, or a fragment of metal may open several of those structures with a single track, and a track entering the base of the neck may continue into the chest, where its damage is invisible from outside. This chapter follows neck trauma from injury to the operating room and names at each step who may do what, and it is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

Penetrating injury is the form usually meant when the neck is called dangerous, and it arrives as a knife in an assault, a bullet or a fragment, a fall through glass, a machinery accident, a spike on a building site, or the wire that strikes a rider across the throat. Blunt injury is quieter and just as lethal, and it comes from a seat belt, a punch or a choke hold, a hanging or a strangulation, a blow from a bar, or a fall onto a handlebar. The mechanism of injury is therefore the first prediction the responder makes, because it tells the examiner where to look and what to expect. In the neck more than anywhere else, the size of the opening says almost nothing about the structures beneath it.

The first danger in neck trauma is the airway, the second is a major blood vessel, and the two can arrive together. Airway compromise may be direct, when the trachea or the larynx is cut or crushed, or indirect, when blood, vomit, or swelling fills the space around it and closes it from outside. A major vessel may bleed outward through the wound, inward into the tissues where it forms a swelling that finally presses the airway shut, or into the chest, where the loss is entirely hidden. The spinal cord lies behind the airway and between the vessels, so a wound across the middle of the neck may leave a patient talking while the cord below it has stopped working. A wound at the base of the neck may open vessels and the lung without any swelling appearing outside.

No care begins until the scene is safe, and a stabbing or a shooting carries hazards an ordinary road crash does not. The assailant may still be present, a crowd may still be fighting, a weapon may lie on the ground, and a responder who kneels without looking up may become the next casualty. Traffic, fire, live electricity, water, a collapsing structure, an animal, and machinery that has not been isolated are the other hazards of the scene, and each is a lethal possibility rather than a nuisance. The patient's own blood is the quieter hazard, because a neck wound can spurt some distance, so personal protective equipment, or PPE, with gloves, eye protection, and a barrier for the face is worn before the first hand is laid on the wound. The finding that ends the pause is a scene made safe by someone with the authority to make it safe, and until then the responder waits at the edge and calls for help.

The finding that announces an airway in danger is most often a change in the voice, because the structures that make sound lie in the path of any injury to the middle of the neck. Hoarseness, a muffled or lost voice, a barking cough, noisy breathing on inspiration, and a patient who speaks a few words before pausing for air are each an airway that is narrowing while the responder watches. Blood in the mouth, a wound that bubbles with each breath, and a crackling under the skin that feels like pressed snow are signs that air or blood has escaped into tissue where it does not belong, and that crackling is called subcutaneous emphysema. A swelling on one side of the neck that grows, a windpipe that has shifted from the midline, difficulty in swallowing, and increasing restlessness in a patient who was calm are the same warning spoken in another language. Any of those findings turns a small-looking wound into an emergency that requires an airway plan at once and transport without delay.

The vascular finding that must never be missed is bleeding that does not stop, whether it pours from the wound, pulses with the heartbeat, or collects in the neck as a hematoma that enlarges while the responder holds it. A hematoma that expands is an artery bleeding into a closed space, and the calm that follows the first minutes may mean only that the pressure inside the swelling has matched the pressure inside the vessel. A pulse that cannot be felt on one side of the neck, a cool and pale limb, or a loss of movement or feeling on one side of the body points to a vessel that supplies the brain or a limb, and such a finding demands a surgical center as fast as the journey allows. A vibration felt over the swelling, which clinicians call a thrill or a bruit, is another sign of an abnormal connection between an artery and a vein. The responder does not probe the wound, does not press into the swelling to test it, and does not lift a dressing to look, because each act can release bleeding that was contained.

The order of action at the scene is fixed by what kills first, and in the neck that order is difficult because the airway and the bleeding are neighbors. The lay first aider presses on the bleeding point with a clean pad while keeping the middle of the throat free, and the trained responder adds suction, an airway device, and packing where a protocol authorizes it. Definitive hospital care owns the control of a vessel that cannot be reached from outside, the repair of the airway and the esophagus, and the removal of a foreign body. The finding that tells the responder which danger is winning is the patient's ability to speak and to breathe, and it is repeated at every stage.

The primary survey is performed in the order remembered as ABCDE, which stands for airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure, and each letter is a question whose answer decides whether the responder moves on or stops to treat what has just been found. In most patients the airway is examined first, but in a patient with catastrophic bleeding from a limb or the neck the control of that bleeding may be placed ahead of everything else, with the two acts performed together by two pairs of hands where they exist. Breathing follows and asks whether air is moving on both sides of the chest, whether the chest is rising evenly, and whether a wound at the base of the neck has entered the chest. Circulation follows, asking about the pulse, the color and warmth of the skin, and any bleeding that is ongoing, while disability asks about the level of consciousness, the pupils, and the movement and feeling of all four limbs. Exposure comes last, because the neck cannot be assessed in isolation, and the whole body is examined for other wounds before the patient is covered again and kept warm.

Opening an airway in a patient with a suspected neck injury requires a technique that does not bend the neck, so the trained responder holds the head neutral with both hands while lifting the jaw forward. The lay first aider who has been taught the same maneuver may use it, and the habit of tilting the head back is avoided here because it moves a spine that may already be unstable. The cervical spine is at risk in these injuries, and those precautions must never become the reason an airway is left closed, because a patient who is not breathing has no use for an intact spine. Blood, vomit, and loose teeth are cleared from the mouth only when they can be seen and reached, and a patient is turned onto the side as a unit only when the turn can be done without twisting the neck. Movement is kept to what is necessary, the head stays in line with the body, and the turn onto a board or stretcher is performed as one movement by a team that has practiced it, with any change in breathing, voice, or limb function recorded at once.

The trained responder or paramedic has tools the lay first aider does not, and each is used within training, authorization, and a protocol. Suction removes blood and vomit, a curved or straight plastic airway holds the tongue from the back of the throat in an unconscious patient, and a mask with a bag lets two hands hold the mask and jaw while an assistant squeezes the bag. A device sitting above the opening of the larynx may be used by a trained provider, and placing a tube through the vocal cords belongs to a provider authorized for that skill, most often a physician trained in anesthesia or a paramedic under a protocol naming it. Where the airway cannot be opened from above, a surgical opening through the front of the neck is made only by a provider trained and authorized for that procedure. Oxygen and the decision to give it belong to the protocol and the prescriber, and this manual names neither an amount nor a device setting.

Control of bleeding from the neck changes the usual ladder of pressure, because the same hand that stops the bleeding can also stop the breathing. The lay first aider presses with the fingertips on the bleeding point at the edge of the wound, or presses the wound closed from both sides, keeping the middle of the throat free so the windpipe is not compressed. Nothing is ever wound completely around the neck, because a band that encircles it can close the airway, press on the veins that drain the brain, and hide a swelling growing beneath it. The dressing must not compress the airway: a flat pad is held by hand or fixed to the side of the neck and the shoulder with tape that does not cross the front of the throat, and if blood soaks through, further pads are laid on top without lifting the first. A dressing that has become tight, a voice that has changed since it was applied, or a patient struggling for air shows that it is doing harm, and it is loosened or removed and the airway reassessed at once.

Packing a wound of the neck is a skill for the trained responder or the paramedic working under a protocol, and it is used when pressure on the surface cannot reach a bleeding point deep in the tissue. The gauze is directed along the track of the wound toward the source and held firmly, while the responder watches the breathing and keeps the packing away from the windpipe. The neck is a junctional site, the name for places where a limb joins the body and a tourniquet cannot be placed, and junctional bleeding is controlled by packing and pressure rather than by any encircling device. A hemostatic dressing, a gauze carrying an agent that helps blood clot, is carried in some services and not others, and its use requires training, an appropriate wound, and continued pressure. Nothing here names an agent, an amount, or a duration, because those belong to the local protocol and the authorized provider, and no dressing is a reason to delay the operating room.

A wound of a large vein in the neck carries a hazard that no other wound in this book carries in quite the same way, which is the entry of air into the circulation. When such a vein is open and the pressure inside the chest falls during a breath, air can be drawn into the vessel, and the finding is a wound that sucks or bubbles at the moment of inspiration, or a sudden deterioration in a patient whose wound looked controlled. The first response is to cover the wound with a dressing that does not allow air to pass, to press on it, and to keep it covered while the patient is moved, and the position that lowers the wound relative to the heart is used where it can be achieved without closing the airway or twisting the neck. A patient who becomes suddenly breathless, restless, or unresponsive after a neck wound is treated as having air in the circulation until proven otherwise. That is a hospital emergency from its first moment, and the field contribution is the occlusive dressing, the pressure, and the shortest safe journey.

The neck contains the spinal cord and the nerves that leave it for the arms, the diaphragm, the tongue, and the shoulder, so a neurologic examination belongs to the first minutes and not to the hospital alone. The trained responder records the level of consciousness, the size and reaction of the pupils, and, for each limb in turn, whether it can be moved against resistance, whether it can be moved at all, and whether sensation is present. A patient with a stab wound of the neck and weakness of one arm, or with numbness in a band across the chest, has a neurologic injury that changes the destination and the urgency even when the wound itself is small and dry. The level at which feeling or movement is lost is written down with the time, because the receiving team uses that level and its trend to judge whether the cord is being compressed. The lay first aider does not perform this examination but contributes by noticing and reporting any change and by keeping the patient still until trained help takes over.

Behind the airway and beside the spine run the esophagus and the pharynx, and injury to them is the one most often missed at the first examination because it announces itself late. The findings that raise the suspicion are pain on swallowing, blood mixed with saliva, air in the tissue of the neck, a wound near the midline or tracking down behind the windpipe, and a fever that appears after a delay. Those are not findings a responder confirms or excludes in the field, and no test performed at the roadside can settle the question, so a wound whose track could have reached those structures is treated as though it had. A missed injury of the esophagus or the pharynx leads to infection in the deep spaces of the neck and the chest, and that infection can kill a patient days after a wound that seemed minor has closed. Such a patient is therefore referred for hospital assessment even when the bleeding has stopped and the airway is quiet.

Blunt injury to the neck deserves its own warning, because it leaves no wound to remind anyone that something inside may be broken. A blow from a bar or a fist, a choke hold or a strangulation, a seat belt across the throat, a wire across the road, and a fall onto a bicycle handlebar can fracture the larynx or tear the tissues around the airway, and the patient may walk and talk at first. The findings are hoarseness, a change in the pitch of the voice, pain when the neck is touched, a loss of the usual landmarks at the front of the neck, crackling under the skin, and difficulty in breathing or swallowing that worsens over the first hours. A patient who has been strangled may have a neck that looks entirely normal and still develop a closing airway, so a normal appearance is never used to leave such a patient unobserved. Where a patient is still suspended, the trained responder supports the body before the ligature is released so that the weight does not tear the neck further, and a changed voice after any such injury is treated as an emergency.

Cold is a complication of neck trauma and not a detail of the patient's comfort, and a patient with a neck wound is at risk from the first minute. The neck is often left uncovered because the wound must be watched, blood and water soak the clothing, and a patient who is kept flat and still on the ground loses heat into the earth beneath. Cold makes the blood clot poorly, deepens shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm, so a neck wound that is being watched cannot be an excuse for leaving the patient exposed. The lay first aider removes wet clothing where that can be done without disturbing the wound, covers the patient with whatever is at hand, and insulates the patient from the ground, while the trained responder continues that protection during transport. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that value is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Shock follows neck trauma for the same reasons it follows any other injury, and it is harder to recognize because much of the lost blood may be somewhere the responder cannot see. A wound at the base of the neck can open a vessel in the chest, and the blood then collects around the lung, compressing it and reducing the oxygen that reaches the blood still circulating. The findings are breathing that has become rapid and shallow, a chest that moves unevenly, a pulse rising and softening, pale cool skin, and a level of consciousness dulling while the neck wound appears quiet. A pressure such as 90 millimeters of mercury is sometimes quoted as a threshold for concern, and it is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol rather than a rule taken from these pages. Fluids, blood products, and medicines for pain are decisions that belong to the prescriber and the local protocol, and this manual names no substance, no amount, no route, and no frequency.

A constructed illustration, offered as an illustration and not as a description of any real patient, is the young man who walks into a clinic holding the side of his neck with a bloodstained cloth over a wound below the angle of the jaw. He is talking, his voice is slightly hoarse, and the wound is small and has almost stopped bleeding, which is exactly the picture that invites a responder to be reassured. While the wound is examined, the neck on that side becomes fuller than the other, the hoarseness deepens, and the patient says that swallowing is painful. Those findings are why he is sent immediately to a surgical center rather than asked to wait, and nothing was probed, nothing was packed blindly, and no dressing was tied around the neck. The case shows only how a quiet wound and a loud neck can belong to the same patient.

The neck cannot be examined in isolation, because the injury that made the neck wound may have made others, and an object still embedded in the neck is left exactly where it is while the patient is moved with it in place. Removal in the field can release bleeding that cannot be controlled and can injure a structure the object is holding apart, and in the neck the object may be plugging a torn artery, supporting a crushed airway, or lying against the spinal cord. The correct act is to build bulky padding around it, press on the bleeding points beside it rather than on the object, and send the patient to a surgical team. The trained responder examines the front and back of the neck, the mouth, and the base of the skull, and undresses the patient enough to find every wound, because a bullet may enter the neck and leave elsewhere. Each wound is described by its position, its size, whether it bleeds, and whether it bubbles or sucks, and that description is repeated at handover.

The destination for a patient with a serious neck wound is a facility with a surgeon, an operating room, and the imaging needed to plan the operation, and immediate surgical referral is the rule for every wound that could have crossed the deep structures. Computed tomography, called CT after its first mention, is the main way of judging which structures are injured when the patient is stable enough to pass through the scanner, and it may be combined with an injection that makes the vessels stand out on the image. Ultrasound at the bedside can show blood around the lung in a patient too unstable to leave the resuscitation area, and catheter angiography, in which a dye is placed within a vessel and followed on an image, examines vessels that are difficult to reach. Definitive hospital care owns the exploration of the neck, the repair of a divided artery or vein, the repair of the larynx or the trachea, the repair of the esophagus, and the removal of a foreign body. None of that is a field procedure, and the transfer is not delayed by the appearance of the wound or by the hope that a quiet neck stays quiet.

The handover is part of the treatment, and in neck trauma it carries facts that no arriving team can reconstruct for itself. It states the mechanism of injury and its time, what caused the wound, how many wounds were found, whether the voice changed or the swelling grew, and what the patient could move and feel before and after movement. Reassessment continues in a rhythm from the scene to the operating room, returning in order to the airway, breathing, circulation, level of consciousness, and limbs, and a patient who was talking and has become silent has given more information than any single look at the wound. The most dangerous patient is the one who looks well, because a small wound under the jaw and a hoarse voice can precede a closing airway before any other sign appears, so the concern is named aloud and a patient who must wait is placed where the airway can be watched.

The position in which the patient is carried weighs the airway, the spine, and the circulation against one another. A patient who breathes with difficulty may sit up where the spine and circulation permit it, a patient in shock is kept flat, and an unconscious or vomiting patient is turned to the side as a unit so that blood drains rather than being inhaled. A patient with an unstable cervical spine is kept in line with the body, and movement of the neck during transport is avoided because it can add a spinal injury to the wound. The patient is often terrified, and terror makes the breathing faster and the movement greater, so the responder speaks in short sentences, says what is being done, and asks the patient to keep the head and body still, without calling the wound minor or removing the dressing. The finding that changes the position is a patient who can no longer breathe in the position chosen, and the position is changed at once.

Protection against infection begins at the first contact and is completed in the hospital. The field contribution is to cover the wound with a clean dressing, avoid touching the inside of the wound, and keep the dressing in place until the receiving team examines it, while cleaning and the removal of dead tissue belong to definitive care under good light and with anesthesia. The tetanus question is raised at the first contact and answered by the provider authorized under the local protocol, and antibiotics follow the same rule, in that a deep, contaminated, or bite wound makes the decision urgent while the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber and the local guideline. The anatomy of the neck also forbids two techniques that work elsewhere, because a tourniquet cannot be placed around the neck and a pressure dressing that binds it tightly would compress the airway and both carotid arteries. The skills in this chapter are learned with a teacher and certified by an authority that defines what may be done without supervision, and local protocol decides what equipment is carried and which hospital receives the patient.

To summarize, the neck packs the airway, the great vessels, the spinal cord, the esophagus, and the nerves into a small space, so a wound there can injure several vital structures with one track and kill while the opening looks small. Airway compromise is the first danger and major-vessel injury the second, and the bleeding may hide inside the neck as a growing swelling or inside the chest as blood around the lung. The scene is made safe first, because violence, traffic, machinery, and the patient's own blood can claim the responder as well. The order of action is the primary survey remembered as ABCDE, with the airway opened in a way that keeps the neck in line, with the cervical spine protected but never at the expense of a closing airway, and with a changed voice, noisy breathing, crackling under the skin, or a growing swelling treated as an emergency. Bleeding is controlled by localized pressure that spares the windpipe, by packing where the provider is trained and authorized, and never by a band around the neck, because the dressing must not compress the airway or hide a hematoma. An embedded object is stabilized and never removed in the field, a patient who is bleeding, exposed, or waiting is kept warm, and every patient whose wound could have crossed the deep structures is referred for immediate surgical assessment. Every number, time, and threshold here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 39 — Spinal Trauma

A rider lying twisted beside a motorcycle, a diver pulled from shallow water, and a driver held by a belt in a car stopped against a wall may all carry the same injury, and none of them may show it. The spinal column is the bony case that protects the spinal cord, and a force that damages the case may bruise, stretch, or divide the cord inside it, so the responder behaves as though the column may be broken rather than trying to prove that it is not. Two dangers are named first: an injury high in the neck can take away the drive to breathe, and an unstable column can convert a partial injury into a complete one during a careless move. The scene is made safe before any hand touches the patient, and the hazards are traffic, fire, electricity, water, animals, violence, falling structures, and the patient's own blood. This chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

The column is a stack of vertebrae joined in a curve, and the cord runs inside a canal the vertebrae enclose, so the bone is a helmet the cord wears along its length. The cervical region moves most and has the least bone to spare, and the cord there is wide in proportion to its canal, which is why a small displacement in the neck can produce a large deficit. The thoracic region is stiffened by the ribs and is injured less often, but a fracture there follows a severe transfer of energy and should prompt a search for injury to the chest and the great vessels. The lumbar region carries the weight of the trunk and holds a leash of nerve roots rather than cord in its lower part, so injury there may damage roots and produce weakness less complete than a cord injury.

Cervical injury is predicted by mechanisms that bend, straighten, rotate, compress, or pull the head away from the trunk. A collision from behind throws the head backward and then forward, a head-on collision throws it forward into the restraint, and a side impact bends the neck sideways while the shoulder is held by the belt. A dive into shallow water loads the crown of the head and drives the neck into itself, and the same load happens in a fall onto the head, in a tackle, and when a heavy object strikes the crown. The finding that should fix the responder's attention is often the mechanism itself rather than any wound, together with pain in the neck, tenderness at the back of the neck, a change in the voice, and weakness or numbness in the arms or the legs.

Thoracic and lumbar injury is predicted by compression, by bending forward, and by the shearing a lap belt produces. A fall from a height lands the patient on the feet or the buttocks and drives force upward through the pelvis and the spine, so the heel, the pelvis, and the spine are injured together, and a painful heel in a patient who fell should raise the question of a fracture above it. A lap belt without a shoulder belt folds the patient over the belt while the upper body is thrown forward, which can tear the column at the thoracic and lumbar hinge and can also injure the bowel. The finding that suggests cord or root injury here is a band of pain around the trunk, weakness of the legs, or a loss of the sense of a full bladder.

No responder can exclude a spinal injury at the roadside, and the attempt is not part of the lay first aider's work. Certain findings make the probability high enough that the patient is treated as injured, and they include a high-energy mechanism, pain in the neck or the back, tenderness when the spine is pressed, a wound or deformity over the column, weakness or numbness in a limb, an altered level of consciousness, intoxication, a head injury, and any other injury severe enough to distract the patient from the neck. Where the examination cannot be trusted, because the patient is confused, intoxicated, or unresponsive, the precaution is kept until a clinician with imaging clears it. A patient who is talking normally, moving all four limbs, and denying pain may still have an unstable column, and that is the quietest trap in this chapter.

Spinal injury produces two distinct emergencies, and a responder who confuses them will treat neither well. The first is a column that can no longer hold the cord, which threatens a deficit not yet present and is prevented by handling rather than by any device. The second is a cord injury that has already occurred, which may worsen for reasons inside the patient rather than because of movement, and which is watched rather than repaired in the field. An injury above the middle of the neck can take the drive from the diaphragm, so a patient breathing now may stop when swelling or bleeding rises around the cord, and the warning is breathing that becomes shallow, a voice that weakens, and a cough that fails. A high cord injury also removes the vessel tone that keeps the circulation tight, so the patient may have low blood pressure with a slow pulse instead of the fast pulse of blood loss, which is called neurogenic shock and is a different problem from hemorrhage.

The finding that reveals a cord injury is a change in what the patient can feel or do, and it is sought before the patient is moved. Weakness or paralysis of the arms, the legs, or both, a loss of sensation below a line on the trunk, an inability to feel the bladder filling, and an inability to hold urine or stool are cord findings. The patient may describe tingling, burning, or a band of tightness around the chest or the abdomen, and may also describe nothing at all, because a cord injury can be painless while the column that caused it is broken. Breathing that uses the belly rather than the chest, a weak cough, and a quiet voice suggest that the muscles of respiration are already involved.

The neurological examination is recorded before movement because movement changes what the examination will find, and a baseline never written cannot be reconstructed. The record begins with the time, the patient's level of consciousness, and whether the patient is alert, drowsy, or unresponsive, because an examination performed on an unresponsive patient is a different examination from one performed on a patient who can cooperate. The responder then records what the patient can move on each side, what the patient can feel on each side, and where the change begins. The findings are written on the patient or in the record that travels with the patient, together with the time, because a deficit present at the first contact and one that appears later tell two different stories.

The level of a spinal cord injury is the lowest segment of the cord that still works normally, and everything below that level is described as what remains, which is the phrase the receiving team needs. A sensory level is the lowest place on the skin where the patient can still feel a light touch reliably, and a motor level is the lowest place where a muscle can still move, and the two need not be the same. The responder describes the level in words, such as movement present at the elbows and the wrists but absent at the fingers, rather than naming a vertebra that has not been imaged. What remains below the level is recorded in the same way, because a patient who can move the toes has a different injury from one who cannot, and that difference changes the urgency and the destination. Sensation around the anus and the ability to tighten the anal muscle are the last functions tested and the most important to note, because their preservation predicts a better outcome than a complete loss.

Motor and sensory testing follow a fixed order so that two responders describe the same thing. The patient is asked to shrug the shoulders against the examiner's hands, to bend the elbow, to extend the wrist, to grip two fingers, to lift the knee, to straighten the knee, to pull the foot upward, and to push it downward, and each movement is recorded as present, weak, or absent rather than as a number. Sensation is tested with a light touch on both sides at the same level, working from the top of the body downward, and the patient is asked to say when the feeling changes, because the patient's own report is the finding. The pattern of loss matters more than its depth, because a loss beginning at the chest and sparing the face points to an injury high in the column, while a loss beginning at the groin points lower. The examiner compares the two sides, records limits imposed by a splint or a dressing, and repeats the examination after every move.

Breathing is the function a cervical cord injury threatens first, and it is watched from the first minute rather than assessed once. The diaphragm is driven by nerves that leave the cord high in the neck, and an injury at or above that level can leave a patient using only the muscles between the ribs and the muscles of the abdomen, which is seen as the belly rising while the chest stays still. The airway is opened with the jaw and the chin while the head and the neck are held in line by another pair of hands, and the trained responder uses the adjuncts and the equipment the service carries. The lay first aider watches for noisy breathing, for a voice that fades, for a patient who cannot clear the mouth, and for a patient who is becoming drowsy, and calls emergency medical services at the first of those findings.

Movement precautions are the heart of this chapter, and they are a set of small refusals rather than one maneuver. The head is kept in line with the trunk and the trunk with the pelvis, so the column stays in the position in which it was found, and no responder lifts the head to look at the neck or turns the face to see a wound. The patient is not sat up to drink, is not allowed to twist to look at the responder, and is not rolled onto the side to remove clothing unless the plan requires it and enough hands are present. The neck is not pulled, not massaged, and not tested by asking the patient to look in every direction, because those are the movements an unstable column cannot tolerate. The reason for all of this is that a movement too small to see can be the difference between a bruise and a division.

Immobilization is a sequence that begins with hands and continues with a device, and the device is chosen by the local protocol rather than by preference. The first act is manual stabilization, in which one responder takes the head with both hands and holds it in line with the trunk while the rest of the team works, and that hold is kept until a device takes over the work. The second act is the application of the device, which may be a rigid collar, a head support, a padded board, a vacuum mattress, or a combination the service has adopted, and the collar alone is not immobilization, because it limits some movement and leaves the rest. The finding that tells the responder the device is working is a patient whose head, neck, and trunk move as one piece when the stretcher is lifted, and the finding that it is not working is a head that still turns or a trunk that slides. The device is applied by the trained responder or the paramedic under the protocol, while the lay first aider keeps the head supported and waits.

The device is a means of moving the patient safely and not a treatment, and it is taken away as soon as definitive care can take over. A patient strapped to a rigid board for a long time develops pain and pressure damage over the bones of the back and the hips, breathes less deeply because the chest is held, and grows cold from the hard surface beneath, so the protocol of every service sets a limit and a plan for removing the board. The straps are secured firmly enough that the patient cannot slide, and no strap is placed so tightly across the chest that breathing is restricted. A patient who vomits while immobilized is turned as a unit by a team, or the front of the device is opened where its design allows, because a filling airway must be cleared before any consideration of the column.

The rule that settles every conflict in this chapter is that a spinal precaution must never prevent the treatment of an airway that is closing, because a patient without an airway is dead before the spine matters. When the airway is blocked by the tongue, by blood, by vomit, or by a swelling in the neck, the responder opens it, and the opening is done with the head and neck held in line by a second pair of hands rather than by tilting the head back. A jaw thrust lifts the tongue away from the throat while the neck stays neutral, and the removal of visible material from the mouth clears what blocks it, and the trained responder may use an airway adjunct the protocol authorizes. A collar that blocks the opening of the mouth may be loosened or removed at the front by the trained responder while the head is held, and that decision favors the airway over the device. A patient who is not breathing is given rescue breaths and, where the responder is trained and the protocol allows, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and whether oxygen is given, in what concentration, and by what route is set by the local protocol and the clinician responsible rather than by this book.

Turning the patient as one unit, which is called a log roll, is a controlled maneuver for a trained team, and it exists to reach what the examination from the front cannot reach. It is used to examine the back and the spine, to place a board or a mattress under the patient, to remove a bulky object from beneath the body, and to clear an airway when vomiting cannot be managed from the front. The team agrees on the side to turn toward and on the number of hands, one responder holds the head and gives the count, and the turn begins and ends on that count so that no part of the trunk lags behind. The lay first aider does not perform this maneuver, because a poorly coordinated roll is worse than no roll at all.

Extrication from a vehicle balances the danger of the scene against the danger of movement, and it is decided by the trained responder or the paramedic under the local protocol. The scene is made safe first, which means holding the traffic, stabilizing the vehicle so that it cannot roll or shift, controlling fire and fuel, and protecting the patient from glass and sharp metal. Where the vehicle is burning, where it may fall, where the airway is blocked, or where a second collision is imminent, the patient is moved quickly with the best spinal hold the time allows, because a perfect precaution in a burning car is no precaution at all. A confined space, such as a wrecked car, a trench, or a collapsed structure, is entered only by those trained and equipped to do so, and inside it the same order holds, with the head held and the device applied where the shape of the space allows. A patient who is fully alert, free of pain in the neck and the back, free of any neurological finding, and free of a distracting injury may sometimes be allowed to walk under the protocol of the service, but that decision belongs to the trained responder and never to the lay first aider, and it is never made for a patient who is intoxicated, confused, or unable to give a clear account.

Handling is the part of the work that most often undoes the precaution, and it depends on hands, on a count, and on a plan spoken before the move. The team decides the route, names who holds the head, and moves on a single command, and the head holder keeps the head in line and does not let go until the device is secured. The patient is lifted rather than dragged and kept level rather than tipped, and is laid on the stretcher without being allowed to roll, and the straps are secured before the stretcher is raised. The transfer into the vehicle is the moment when a slide is most likely, so the patient is fixed to the stretcher and the stretcher is fixed to the vehicle, and the receiving end of the journey is told what has been done.

Children and older patients change the details of this chapter, and both are injured by forces that would leave a fit adult unharmed. A young child's head is large in proportion to the body and the neck muscles are weak, so the same blow bends the neck further and the same restraint may fit poorly. An older patient's column is weakened by osteoporosis and stiffened by arthritis, so a fall from standing height can break the neck or the upper back, and the same patient may describe the pain as a familiar ache. The finding that should raise suspicion in either age group is pain that the patient dismisses, and the responder treats that pain as real.

When the patient is already paralyzed, the work changes from prevention to protection of what remains, and the manner of the care changes with it. The patient who cannot move the legs, cannot feel the bladder, or cannot take a deep breath may know exactly what has happened, so the responder speaks directly to the patient and explains each act before it is performed. The paralyzed patient is moved with the same care as any other, because a partial injury can become complete, and the level of the injury is recorded again after every move so that any change is caught. The patient cannot feel pain below the level and may not report a fracture of a leg or a burn from a hot surface, so the whole body is looked at. The patient's temperature falls quickly because the vessels below the level no longer tighten, so warmth is a clinical need and not a courtesy, and the patient is covered from the first minute.

Hypothermia belongs to every patient in this chapter, because a patient lying still on cold ground, undressed for examination, or wet from water or spilled fuel loses heat faster than a moving person replaces it. The responder removes wet clothing where the plan of movement allows, insulates the patient from the ground, covers the head and the trunk, and keeps the vehicle warm on the way.
