When the patient is on a device, the covering is placed over the device as well, and the straps are not loosened to do it. A temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that figure is a teaching illustration which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the threshold differs with the patient and with the way the temperature is measured.

Transport is a continuation of the same care rather than a pause in it, and the observations made at the scene are repeated in the vehicle and compared with what came before. The responder rechecks the breathing, the pulse, the level of consciousness, the movement and the feeling of each limb, and the pain, and every change is written with its time. The destination is chosen before the patient is moved, and it is the nearest facility that can image the spine and provide the care the patient needs, which may be a trauma center with a surgeon and an intensive care unit. The receiving team is told the mechanism of injury, the time of the injury, the neurological findings at each point, what was done, and what the patient was lying on, because a short report that is accurate is worth more than a long report that is vague.

Definitive hospital care owns the diagnosis and the repair of a spinal injury, and it begins with the clinician's examination and with imaging. A plain radiograph shows the bones, computed tomography, called CT after its first mention, shows them in finer detail and is faster in a patient who cannot cooperate, and magnetic resonance imaging, called MRI after its first mention, shows the cord, the discs, and the ligaments that bone images cannot. The decision to remove a collar and to declare the spine clear belongs to the clinician who has examined the patient and seen the images, and no responder in the field makes that decision. Surgery for a broken column, the decompression of a cord that is compressed, and the stabilization of a spine that cannot hold itself are performed in an operating room by a surgeon with an anesthesia team, while traction and the reduction of a displaced vertebra are hospital acts that must never be attempted in the field.

Several acts a tempted responder might attempt are not field procedures, and knowing them is as much a part of competence as knowing the ones that are. No responder reduces a displaced vertebra, applies traction to the neck, manipulates the spine to test it, or tries to straighten a column that looks wrong, because each of those movements can turn a bruised cord into a divided one. No responder removes a fragment or a bullet from the spine, because that is a surgical decision made when it is indicated, and the object is stabilized in place. The decisions about pain relief, about the prevention of infection, and about protection against tetanus belong to the clinician and the local protocol, and the substance, the amount, the route, and the timing are set there rather than here, so a listener cannot take a prescription from these pages.

Some patients combine the spinal question with another emergency, and the combination changes the order of the work without changing the rule. A patient with a head injury may be unresponsive, may be vomiting, and may be unable to cooperate with any examination, and that patient is treated as having a spinal injury until a clinician decides otherwise. A patient with a penetrating wound of the neck may have a cord injury and a bleeding vessel at the same time, and the airway and the bleeding come before the column in the order of the primary survey. The injury that is missed is usually the one that looked harmless at the first contact, and the defender against that is suspicion and repetition, which is why a patient who walked from a car and then sat down with a numb hand is a constructed illustration of a spinal injury that announced itself late rather than a reassuring story.

No manual can teach the hands to hold a head in line while a team turns a body, so these skills are learned on models and on each other under a teacher, and they are certified by an authority that also defines what a responder may do without supervision. Local protocol decides which device is carried, which patient may be allowed to walk, when a helmet may be removed, and which hospital receives the patient, and that protocol takes precedence over anything written here. Every number in this chapter, whether a temperature, a time, a distance, or a depth, is an illustration of the reasoning and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries, and editions of the same guideline. The reader is asked to bring these principles to the training, to keep the training current, and to work inside the system that supervises the care.

To summarize, the spinal column is the case that protects the spinal cord, and the responder behaves as though it may be broken rather than trying to prove that it is not, because a movement too small to see can turn a bruise into a division. The scene is made safe before the patient is touched, the lethal possibilities of a high cervical injury and of an unstable column are named early, and the neurological examination is recorded before any movement, including the level of the injury and what remains below it. The head is kept in line with the trunk, the patient is not sat up, turned, or tested by movement, and immobilization begins with the hands and continues with a device chosen by the local protocol. The device is a means of transport and is removed as soon as definitive care can take over, and a strap is never placed so tightly across the chest that breathing is restricted. A spinal precaution must never prevent the treatment of an airway that is closing, so the airway is opened with the head and neck held in line, and that rule settles every conflict in this chapter. Hypothermia travels with every immobilized patient, the paralyzed patient is protected and spoken to, and the observations are repeated until handover. Every temperature, time, distance, and figure here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 40 — Traumatic Amputation

Traumatic amputation is the injury that removes a part of the body in an instant and, with it, a volume of blood that no wound of the same size would ever lose. The part may be completely severed and lying on the ground, or it may hang by a bridge of skin, muscle, tendon, or nerve, and the second form is often the more dangerous because the responder sees a limb that still looks attached and underestimates the hemorrhage beneath it. The threat that kills is not the loss of the limb but the loss of blood, and the loss of blood is the first thing controlled and the last thing forgotten. This chapter follows the patient from the moment of injury through the control of bleeding, the protection of the wound, the recognition of shock, the preservation of the amputated tissue, and the journey to the hospital where the decision about replantation is made. Every act is named with the provider level that owns it, because a lay first aider, a trained responder, and a trauma surgeon each have a different and limited part to play. This is educational material and does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

Scene safety comes before the patient, and the scene of an amputation is usually a scene of machinery, traffic, or violence rather than a quiet room. A machine that has taken a limb may still be running or may still be holding the patient, and it is stopped and made safe by a person authorized to control it before anyone reaches inside, because a rescuer who is pulled into the same machine becomes a second casualty. Traffic on a road is held before the patient is approached, live electrical equipment is isolated before it is touched, and a structure that has fallen on a limb is lifted only by those with the equipment and the authority to do it. The patient's own blood is a hazard as well, because it carries infection, so gloves, eye protection, and a barrier for the mouth are worn for every patient rather than only for the ones who look infectious. A responder who is splashed washes the skin at once, and a responder whose glove tears replaces it before continuing. The finding that tells the responder that the scene is not yet safe is any hazard that cannot be named, controlled, or handed over to someone who owns it, and until that moment the correct act is to wait at the edge and to keep others back.

The mechanism of injury shapes the bleeding, the contamination, and the chance that the amputated part can be rejoined, so it is gathered before the wound is judged. A clean cut, as from a sharp tool or a sheet of metal, divides the vessels and the nerves in one plane, and such a part has the best prospect of replantation because the tissue between the cut ends is intact. A crushing amputation, as from a heavy wheel, a press, or a closing door, tears the vessels and bruises a length of tissue above the cut, and the part may be so damaged that rejoining is impossible even though the bleeding is no less dangerous. An avulsion, in which the part is pulled away and hangs by a bridge of skin or tendon, is often accompanied by a stripping of vessels and nerves far above the visible injury, and this hidden damage is one reason the part must be handled gently. A blast may remove several parts at once, contaminate them with foreign material, and injure the chest, the abdomen, and the other limbs, so the amputation becomes one problem among many. The mechanism also predicts the injuries that accompany the amputation, and the responder who reads it looks for the fracture above the stump, the wound of the opposite limb, and the head injury that the patient cannot report. The name of the mechanism, the time it happened, and the way the part was handled are all part of the history that the receiving surgeon will need.

The lethal possibility of a traumatic amputation is exsanguinating hemorrhage, and the finding that reveals it is bleeding that continues despite a dressing, blood that soaks pad after pad, or a swelling of the stump that grows while the responder watches. A major amputation of an arm or a leg can empty the circulation in minutes, and the danger is greatest when the division is close to the trunk, because the vessels there are large and cannot be compressed against a single bone. A torn artery often retracts into the tissue and spasms, so the stump may bleed less than expected at first, and that pause is deceptive because the vessel can open again when the pressure of the circulation rises or when a dressing is lifted. Blood also collects inside the soft tissue of the stump and in the compartments above it, where the amount lost is invisible and the swelling is the only sign. The patient tells the same story in the language of the body, with a level of consciousness that is dulling, a pulse that is fast and thready, breathing that is rapid, skin that is pale and cool, and a restlessness or a thirst that appears before the collapse. The responder does not wait for the wound to declare itself, because a stump that is not bleeding at this moment may be bleeding inside the thigh or under the dressing, and the safest assumption is that an amputation is a hemorrhage until it is controlled and observed.

The first act after scene safety is the control of hemorrhage, and it follows an order that a lay first aider can begin without any equipment. A clean dressing, a folded cloth, or any clean fabric is placed over the bleeding point on the stump, and the flat of the hand presses firmly and without interruption while help is summoned. The pad is never lifted to see whether the bleeding has stopped, because each look breaks the clot that is forming, and soaked pads are left in place and covered with fresh layers. Pressure on a stump is directed at the bleeding point rather than spread across the whole end, and fingertips or the heel of the hand can be concentrated where the blood is coming from when a broad pad does not stop it. For an amputation at the groin, the shoulder, or the base of the neck, where a tourniquet cannot be placed, the trained responder packs the wound firmly to its depth and holds pressure over the packing, because a dressing across the surface cannot press on a vessel that lies deep. The lay first aider does not probe the wound, does not pour anything into it, and does not try to find the vessel, because those acts add contamination and may release a clot. A period such as 10 minutes of uninterrupted pressure is a common teaching for judging whether a wound will stop, but that figure is an illustration which must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since the time depends on the size of the vessel and on the patient's clotting.

When pressure and packing do not stop the bleeding from a limb, the tourniquet is the next step, and it is applied promptly rather than as a last resort after the patient has already lost the blood that a tourniquet could have saved. The tourniquet is a device of the trained responder or the paramedic, carried under a protocol and used within the training that authorizes it, and the lay first aider applies a manufactured tourniquet only when emergency medical services instruct it and the responder has been taught to use it. It is placed between the wound and the heart, as close to the wound as the remaining anatomy allows and away from a joint where a length of limb permits, and it is tightened until the bleeding stops rather than until a set number of turns has been made. A device tightened over a limb without stopping the flow adds pain and tissue damage while the patient continues to bleed, so the finding that decides the tightness is the cessation of bleeding and not the appearance of the band. Once the tourniquet has controlled the bleeding, it is not loosened in the field, because the clot that has formed behind it may not hold and hemorrhage may restart where no one is prepared to control it. The time of application is written on the patient near the tourniquet, on a tape fixed to the limb, or wherever the local protocol requires, and it is spoken aloud at handover, because the receiving team must know how long the limb has been without flow. An interval such as 2 hours is often quoted as the point at which the risk to the limb becomes serious, and that number is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, since tolerance differs with the temperature, the patient, and the injury.

A partial amputation, in which the part is held by a bridge of skin, muscle, tendon, or nerve, must never be completed in the field, and the reason is that the bridge may contain vessels and nerves that keep the part alive and that a surgeon may be able to repair. The instinct to pull the part free, to straighten it, or to tidy the wound is wrong, and it can convert a limb that might be saved into a limb that cannot. The bridge is supported in the position found, with padding beneath it and a bandage that holds it without tension, and the part is never used as a handle for moving the patient. A deformed segment above the amputation is not straightened to make the limb look better, because movement can release a clot, tear a vessel that is still intact, or injure a nerve, and the limb is splinted in the position found. An object embedded in the stump or in the remaining limb is left where it lies and is stabilized with padding built up around it, because removal may cause hemorrhage that cannot be controlled and may damage a structure that is still whole. The finding that matters after a partial amputation is whether the part is warm, has a color close to the rest of the limb, and has any feeling or movement, and that finding is recorded and passed on rather than acted upon in the field. Definitive hospital care owns the decision to complete the amputation, to repair the vessels, or to attempt replantation, and no field technique replaces that assessment.

The stump is a wound like any other and is protected from further contamination while bleeding is controlled, but the protection is simple and does not become a procedure. The cleanest material available is laid over the wound, and where the service carries it, a sterile dressing moistened with sterile saline is used for exposed bone, tendon, or nerve so that the tissue does not dry, and this choice follows the local protocol and the equipment actually present. The dressing is not packed with soil, leaves, or cloth that has been on the ground, and no antiseptic, alcohol, or powder is poured into the wound, because those agents damage tissue and belong to no field decision. The responder wears gloves and eye protection, avoids touching the wound with bare hands, and does not breathe or cough over it, since contamination at this moment is measured in organisms that no field cleaning will remove. A dressing that becomes soaked through is covered with a fresh layer rather than replaced, and a dressing that has been placed is left until bleeding is controlled and the patient is ready to move. The decision about cleaning the wound, about removing dead tissue, and about protection against tetanus belongs to definitive hospital care and to the provider authorized to make it under the local protocol, because the substance and the timing are not decisions that can be taken from a manual. The finding that makes the tetanus question urgent is a wound that is deep, contaminated, or caused by machinery or soil, and that finding is reported rather than acted upon by the first responder.

The preservation of the amputated part is a short sequence whose purpose is to slow the death of tissue without freezing or poisoning it, and the correct order is wrap, seal, cool, and label. The part is recovered as soon as the patient's bleeding is controlled and the scene is safe, and the search never delays the transport of a patient who is bleeding or in shock, because the life comes before the limb. It is first wrapped in clean or sterile gauze, and the gauze is slightly moistened with sterile saline where that is available, because a dry dressing draws moisture from the tissue while a soaking wet one softens it. The wrapped part is then placed inside a clean plastic bag or a sealed container, and that sealed package is placed inside a second container holding ice and water, so that the cold reaches the tissue through the bag and never touches it directly. The part is never placed directly on ice, never buried in ice water, never packed in dry ice, and never immersed in water alone, because direct freezing forms crystals that destroy cells, while plain water swells and softens the tissue until it cannot be used. It is never placed in alcohol, in formalin, in bleach, or in any fixative or disinfectant, because those substances destroy the very cells that a surgeon would need to rejoin, and a part preserved in them must be discarded. A temperature near 4 degrees Celsius is often described as suitable for transport, and that figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the aim is cool and not frozen and the safe range is set by the receiving service. The finding that tells the responder the cooling is right is a part that feels cold but is not hard, and a part that has frozen is reported to the receiving team rather than warmed by the responder.

Labeling is what keeps the part with its patient, and it matters because a part that loses its identity cannot be used however well it was preserved. The bag or container is marked with the patient's name or identifying number, the time of the injury, the time the part was wrapped and cooled, and any treatment that was applied to it, and the same details are written in the patient's record and spoken at handover. The part travels with the patient in the same vehicle whenever that is possible, and it is handed directly to the receiving team rather than left in the ambulance, placed in a locker, or given to a relative. It is never sent ahead on a separate journey unless the local protocol and the receiving facility have arranged it, because a part that arrives before the patient is easily separated from the patient's identity and a part that arrives after a delay loses the time that matters. When the part cannot accompany the patient, the reason is documented and the receiving team is told where it is and who has it. The written record is part of the treatment rather than an administrative afterthought, and the finding that makes it urgent is any part that has been cooled, because the clock on the tissue is running and the receiving team must know when it started.

Shock is the state in which the circulation can no longer deliver enough oxygen to the tissues, and after a major amputation it is the expected companion of the blood that has been lost rather than a complication that might happen. The early patient compensates with a fast pulse, cool hands, and a blood pressure that still looks acceptable, and that apparent stability is the most dangerous moment because the loss is already large. The patient who can no longer compensate becomes restless, then confused, then drowsy, with rapid shallow breathing and a pulse that becomes weak, and by that stage the remaining time is short. The responder's own contribution to shock is to stop the bleeding, to keep the patient warm, to keep the patient flat and still unless a head or chest injury forbids it, and to shorten the journey to the place where blood and surgery are available. Fluid replacement, the choice of what is given, and the decision to give blood products belong to the paramedic under a protocol and to definitive hospital care, and they are decisions about a patient and a system rather than instructions that can be carried away from a manual, so nothing here names a substance, an amount, a route, or a frequency. The tourniquet is not loosened to find out whether the bleeding has stopped or to let the limb breathe, because that act can restart a hemorrhage in a patient who is already short of blood. The findings that are recorded at every reassessment are the level of consciousness, the pulse, the breathing, the color and warmth of the skin, and the amount of blood on the dressings, and the trend over time is worth more than any single observation.

Hypothermia travels with amputation as it travels with every severe injury, because the patient has bled, has often been undressed to expose the wound, and is lying on the ground while the responder works. Cold makes the clotting system work less well, deepens shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm, so the patient who is cold bleeds more and the patient who bleeds more becomes colder. The protection begins at the same moment as the bleeding control rather than after it, and it means removing wet clothing, covering the patient with blankets, coats, or foil, insulating the patient from the cold ground, and keeping the vehicle or the room warm. The stump itself is covered and the rest of the patient is covered with it, and the amputated part is cooled while the patient is warmed, because the need of the part and the need of the patient are opposite, and each belongs to its own object. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is the figure often used to describe the point at which cold becomes dangerous, and that number is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line differs between services and editions. The finding that warns the responder that cooling has already begun is a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold, because shivering is the body's attempt to make heat. The patient who is warm on arrival at the hospital is a patient whose blood clots and whose heart is more stable, and that advantage is bought in the field with coverings and insulation.

Packaging and transport are decided together, because the destination must be chosen for the injury and the journey must be made without adding to it. The stump is covered with a secure dressing, the limb is supported and immobilized so that the unsupported weight does not pull on the wound, and the patient is moved in a way that keeps the stump still and does not worsen the bleeding or the breathing. The amputated part is packaged, cooled, labeled, and kept in reach of the person who will hand the patient over, because the part and the patient must arrive together, and a part left in the footwell is a part that has been lost. The receiving facility is chosen for its ability to assess replantation and to provide surgery, which may be a trauma center with microsurgery rather than the nearest hospital, and the choice follows the local protocol and the advice of the medical controller. Early notification lets the receiving team call in the surgical and nursing staff, prepare the operating room, and arrange the tests that the decision about replantation requires, and that notice costs nothing and changes the outcome. Transport is urgent and gentle at the same time, because a patient thrown about on the way adds injuries and pain, and because a patient who arrives worse has gained nothing from the speed. A part that is not found, a tourniquet whose time is uncertain, or a stump whose bleeding has restarted are all spoken aloud at the beginning of the handover rather than left for the receiving team to discover.

The decision about replantation, which is the rejoining of the amputated part, belongs to the hospital, to the surgeon, and to the microsurgical team, and it is made with information that the field can only gather and preserve. The factors that enter the decision include the level of the amputation, whether the division was sharp or crushing, the amount of warm time the part has spent without blood, the age and general condition of the patient, the presence of other injuries, and the contamination of the tissue. A sharply divided thumb or finger in a young and otherwise healthy patient is the classic candidate, while a crushed and contaminated limb in a patient who is in shock from other injuries may be better served by completion of the amputation, and only the surgical team can weigh those matters. The field provider's task is to keep every option open by controlling the bleeding, protecting the wound, preserving the part, labeling it, and recording the times, and not to decide which option will be chosen. Warm ischemia, which is the time the part spends at body temperature before cooling, matters as much as the cooling itself, and a period such as 6 hours of warm ischemia is often discussed, though that number is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because tolerance differs with the tissue and the patient. The responder must not promise the patient or the family that the part will be rejoined, because that promise is not the responder's to make and the disappointment of a broken promise falls on people who are already frightened. Definitive hospital care also owns the exploration of the stump, the removal of dead tissue, the repair of vessels and nerves, the management of the pressure inside the limb, and the operations that may follow, and none of those is a field procedure no matter how urgent the patient appears.

The scope of practice for this injury is unusually clear, and each level owns a different part of the work. The lay first aider may press firmly on the bleeding point, cover the stump with the cleanest material available, keep the patient warm and still, recover the amputated part when it is safe to do so, and send for help, and may not place a tourniquet without instruction and training, may not probe or clean the wound, and may not remove an embedded object. The trained responder and the paramedic may apply a tourniquet under a protocol, pack a junctional wound, dress the stump, splint and immobilize the limb, monitor the patient, and preserve and transport the part, all within the training and the authorization of the service. Definitive hospital care owns the control of bleeding that no field method can reach, the cleaning and exploration of the wound, the removal of dead tissue, the repair of vessels, tendons, and nerves, the relief of pressure inside a swollen limb, the completion of an amputation, and the attempt at replantation. No responder should attempt to reopen the wound to find a vessel, to straighten a deformed limb, to complete a partial amputation, or to warm a frozen part, because each of those acts can destroy the possibility that the patient was carried to the hospital to preserve. The rule about the tourniquet is repeated because it is the rule most often broken: once it has controlled the bleeding, it is not loosened in the field, and its time is recorded where the receiving team cannot miss it. The reader is asked to bring these principles to training and to work within the protocol that governs the service, because a manual can describe decisions but cannot certify competence.

To summarize, a traumatic amputation kills by hemorrhage before it disables by the loss of the part, so the first act after the scene is made safe is the control of bleeding, and the tourniquet is applied promptly, tightened until the bleeding stops, never loosened in the field, and recorded with its time where the receiving team will see it. The stump is covered and protected from contamination without probing, without pouring anything into it, and without removing an embedded object, and the wound belongs to definitive care for cleaning, exploration, and repair. Shock and hypothermia travel with the injury, so warmth, insulation, flat positioning, and continuous reassessment are part of hemorrhage control and not additions to it, while fluids, blood products, and pain relief are decisions of the authorized provider and the local protocol. The amputated part is recovered when it is safe, wrapped in clean or slightly moistened gauze, sealed, cooled indirectly in ice and water, never placed directly on ice and never put in water, alcohol, formalin, or any fixative, and it is labeled with the patient's identity and the times and kept with the patient. Partial amputations are never completed in the field, deformed limbs are never straightened to look normal, and the decision about replantation is made by the surgical team with the information the field preserved. Every number, time, temperature, and interval in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 41 — Mangled Extremity

A mangled extremity is a limb in which severe soft-tissue destruction, vascular injury, exposed bone, nerve damage, and the threat of compartment syndrome occur together. Machinery, a wheel or heavy weight passing over a limb, a blast, or a large animal can produce it, and the energy far exceeds that of a bone broken cleanly. The limb no longer has the shape of a limb, with skin stripped away, muscle torn, bone exposed, and bleeding that may be enormous or hidden inside the swelling. The lethal possibility spoken first is hemorrhage that cannot be controlled, because such a limb can hold enough blood to kill the patient while the wound looks merely terrible. The scene is made safe before any hand is laid on the patient, and the choice between rebuilding and removing the limb belongs to a surgical team in a hospital. Nothing here replaces training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

These injuries share one feature, which is that they deliver energy to a broad area rather than a single point. A limb caught in a rotating shaft is pulled in and crushed along its length, a limb run over by a vehicle is compressed between a tire and the road, and an explosion drives fragments and pressure through the tissue. Because the force is spread, the vessels, nerves, muscles, and skin may each be injured at different distances from the visible opening. Muscle that looks pink at one moment may be dead and unable to contract, and tissue that appears attached may have lost its supply. The bone may be broken into many pieces with an end open to the air, the vessels may be divided, torn, in spasm, or blocked by clot, and the swelling that follows raises the pressure inside closed compartments.

A mangled extremity threatens the patient's life first and the limb only afterwards, and that order must survive every other consideration. The torn vessels of a thigh, a groin, or an armpit can empty the circulation in minutes, and the same amount can vanish into the soft tissues while the skin stays almost dry. A patient who is pale, restless, thirsty, and confused with a fast thin pulse is losing blood whether or not the wound pours. Crushed muscle also releases its contents into the circulation, and that load can injure the kidneys, disturb the heart rhythm, and deepen shock after bleeding is controlled. A fully detached limb is a traumatic amputation and belongs to the previous chapter, while a mangled limb is still attached, sometimes by a bridge of skin or one vessel. The honest statement of this manual is that a mangled limb kills when the bleeding is not controlled, and the priority remains the life.

The scene is more dangerous than most, because the machine that caused the injury may still be running and the structure that fell may still be moving. Machinery is shut down and locked out by a person authorized to do it, and until that isolation is confirmed nobody reaches into it, because a jammed roller or a raised load can move without warning. A limb trapped under a vehicle or a heavy object is not freed by a bystander, since the weight can shift onto the rescuer, the release can restart bleeding, and the returning blood can poison the patient. Live cables, spilled fuel, fire, a loose animal, and a violent person are each answered by withdrawal and by waiting for those trained to control them. A responder who cannot make the scene safe does not enter it, and gloves and eye protection, or whatever barrier is available, go on before the first contact.

Once the scene is held, the first act at the limb is the control of hemorrhage, before any attempt to examine, clean, or straighten it. The lay first aider presses firmly with a clean cloth over the bleeding point, adds layers when blood shows through, and never lifts the dressing to look. The trained responder or paramedic packs an appropriate deep wound in the groin, the armpit, or the base of the neck where a tourniquet cannot reach, and uses a hemostatic dressing where the service carries one. Those junctional wounds kill fastest, because the vessel is large, the bone is deep, and no band can circle the shoulder or the hip to compress it. A limb that keeps bleeding through pressure and packing needs a tourniquet, and that decision belongs to the trained responder or paramedic under a protocol. The principle that orders these acts is life before limb, which chooses survival over the limb even when the limb is the more dramatic problem.

A tourniquet is placed between the wound and the heart, as close to the wound as anatomy allows, and never over a joint when a length of limb above the joint is free. It is tightened until the bleeding stops rather than until a set number of turns has been made, and the wound judges the tightening. Once it has controlled the bleeding it is not loosened in the field, because the clot behind it may not hold and the patient may bleed again with nobody able to restore control. The time of application is written on the patient where the receiving team cannot miss it, and it is spoken aloud at the handover. The time matters because everything below the tourniquet is without blood, and the surgeon who may release it must know how long that has been true. An interval such as 2 hours is often quoted as the point at which the danger to the limb becomes serious, and that figure must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

A mangled limb often remains attached by a narrow bridge of skin, tendon, or one vessel, and that bridge is the most valuable tissue in the wound. Nobody in the field completes an amputation or pulls on a partially detached part, because the bridge may carry the only blood still reaching the tissue and tearing it turns a contained injury into free hemorrhage. The part is supported in the position found, never left to hang by its own weight. A piece of tissue that has already come away is not discarded, because a surgeon may use skin, bone, nerve, or vessel from it to rebuild the limb, so it is wrapped, kept cool, and sent with the patient. That part is never placed directly on ice, because freezing destroys the tissue the surgeon is trying to save, and every fragment travels to the same hospital as the patient.

An object embedded in a mangled limb is stabilized in place and never removed in the field, whether it is metal, glass, a spike, a blade, or part of the machine. Removal may release hemorrhage that cannot be controlled at the scene, may tear a vessel, a nerve, or a tendon the object is holding together, and may open a wound that was sealed. The correct act is to build padding around the object, to hold it steady, and to travel with it still in place. The object is not shortened, cut, or twisted, because those movements travel into the tissue, and the surgeon decides when and how it is removed. The same rule applies to an exposed bone end, which is covered and protected rather than pushed back under the skin, since pushing it back carries contamination deep into the limb.

Protecting the wound means covering it with a clean dressing that keeps dirt out, does not press on exposed bone or torn muscle, and can be removed by the surgeon without a second injury. The wound of a mangled limb is not cleaned, not scrubbed, and not irrigated in the field, because that work belongs to the operating room, where dead tissue is cut away under anesthesia. A dressing that circles the limb is applied with care rather than force, since a bandage wound tightly around a swelling limb can become a tourniquet by accident. The finding that a bandage has become too tight is skin beyond it that has turned pale or blue, a pulse that can no longer be felt, and pain that climbs rather than settles. The response is to release the bandage and reapply it with less tension under the authority of the local protocol, and a limb that swells inside a dressing needs the surgeon sooner rather than a tighter band.

A severely deformed limb is splinted in the position found and never straightened in the field to make it look normal. Straightening can release a clot that sealed a torn vessel, stretch or tear an intact artery, divide a nerve that was only bruised, and force blood into a compartment whose pressure was already rising. The appearance of the limb is not the goal of first aid, and a limb left crooked but perfused is worth more than one that looks straight and has no pulse. The limb is supported where it lies, with a splint built to hold the position rather than to change it. An authorized provider may attempt alignment in a few situations, but only with the distal observations recorded before and after, and never as a task for the lay first aider.

Immobilization is built around the position found and around the rule that support is given above and below the injury rather than across it. A rigid support is placed along the limb on the side away from the wound where possible, padded so that no hard edge presses on skin, and secured with straps that are snug but do not circle the wound. Where the limb cannot rest on a board without pressing the wound, the padding is built up first and the limb rests on it, so the support touches only intact tissue. A fractured thigh is supported with the pelvis and the joint below it, and a mangled forearm is supported with the elbow and the wrist, because a splint ending at the fracture lets the broken ends move. The straps go above and below the wound rather than over it, and the wound is examined after each strap is tightened, because even a well meant splint can become a constricting band.

The state of a mangled limb is recorded through four observations, which are the pulses beyond the injury, the refill of the capillaries, the sensation on the skin, and the movement the patient can produce. They are taken on both limbs before and after every dressing, every splint, and every move, because a finding without a comparison is almost useless. The pulses are felt at the thumb side and the little finger side of the wrist and at the top of the foot and behind the inner ankle, and they are compared with the other side. The refill is tested by pressing the nail bed until it blanches, the sensation by a light touch with the eyes closed, and the movement by asking the patient to bend the wrist, spread the fingers, lift the toes, and push the foot down. A finding without a time cannot be compared with the next, so the observations are written with the hour, and where some cannot be obtained the responder records what was found and states what could not be tested.

What matters is the difference between two sets of observations, and a limb whose pulse was strong and is now faint, whose color was pink and is now pale, or whose pain climbs despite a splint is losing its supply. The signs of a failing limb appear as pain, then pallor, then coolness, then numbness, then weakness, and the loss of the pulse comes late, so waiting for it is a way to lose the limb. The response is not to lift the dressing, loosen a tourniquet, or tighten a bandage, but to repeat the general survey, to warn the receiving team, and to shorten the journey. A period such as 6 hours of warm ischemia is often quoted as the point past which a limb is unlikely to be saved, and that interval is an illustration whose exact value belongs to the current guideline and the local protocol.

Compartment syndrome is not a separate possibility in a mangled limb but one of its expected consequences, because the same force that tears tissue adds blood and edema to closed spaces that cannot stretch. The fascia that wraps the muscles holds each compartment at a fixed volume, and as the contents increase the pressure rises until the small vessels are compressed and the muscle starves. The early findings are pain out of proportion to the injury, pain when the muscles are gently stretched, a compartment that is tense and tender, and a change in sensation over the territory of the nerve. The pulse below the limb may still be strong and the limb may still look well, which is why a pulse that is present does not exclude the condition. The late findings of pallor, pulselessness, paralysis, and a limb that has stopped hurting describe tissue already dead, and the responder who waits for them has waited too long. The patient who cannot describe pain, because of a head injury, alcohol, sedation, or youth, is the one in whom the condition is most often missed.

The immediate measures in the field follow an order, and the first is to remove everything that circles the injured limb, including rings, watches, bangles, and tight clothing. A ring that will not come off a swollen finger is never forced over the knuckle, because the finger may later need to be cut free, and the receiving team is told. Every bandage, splint strap, and cast is then examined for tightness, and whatever the local protocol permits to be released is released, because a dressing that has become a tourniquet is a limb being lost. The limb is kept at the level of the heart rather than raised above it, since elevation lowers the arterial pressure that feeds the compartment, and this is one of the few places in trauma where the instinct to elevate is wrong. The limb is not massaged, not packed in ice, and not bound tightly, and the patient is kept warm, kept still, and moved toward the surgeon.

Every patient with a mangled limb is watched for shock from the first minute, because the wound may have taken blood the eye has not seen and crushed muscle adds its own insult to the circulation. The early patient compensates with a fast pulse, cool hands, and a pressure that still looks acceptable, and that stability is the most dangerous moment, because the loss is already large while the numbers reassure. The patient who can no longer compensate becomes restless, then confused, then drowsy, with rapid shallow breathing and a falling pressure, and by then the remaining time is short. Fluid replacement, the choice of what is given, and the decision to give blood products belong to the paramedic under a protocol and to definitive hospital care, and nothing in this chapter names a substance, an amount, a route, or a frequency. The responder's own contribution is to stop the bleeding, to keep the patient warm and still, and to shorten the time to the operating room.

Cold is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and it travels with a mangled limb because the patient is exposed, often on the ground, and losing heat through the wound. A cold patient clots poorly, tolerates blood loss badly, and is more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm of the heart, so cold deepens the shock the wound began. The responder removes wet clothing and replaces it with dry covering without exposing the wound, insulates the patient from the ground, covers the patient before the journey, and keeps the vehicle warm. The injured limb is protected from cold and from direct heat, because a limb that has lost its supply must not be warmed aggressively at the scene. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the line at which the effects of cold become serious, and that figure is an illustration that each service sets in its own guideline and protocol.

Pain from a mangled limb is severe, and treating it is part of treating the patient rather than a courtesy at the end. The finding that makes relief urgent is pain not controlled by splinting and positioning, together with a pulse and a breathing rate that climb because of it. The decision belongs to the provider authorized to prescribe under the local protocol, and the substance, the amount, the route, and the timing are decisions of that protocol and that prescriber. The examination is recorded before relief is given, including the tension of the limb, the sensation, and the movement, so the effect of the treatment can be judged. Relief must never be used to make a patient quiet enough to be transported without an examination, because a quiet patient is not a safe one and a limb that has stopped hurting may have stopped living.

The wound of a mangled limb is contaminated by definition, since it has met soil, machinery, clothing, and the patient's own skin, and protection against tetanus is part of its care. The question is raised at the first contact, and the answer depends on the vaccination history and the nature of the wound, which is why it belongs to the provider authorized under the local protocol. Antibiotics follow the same rule, and the finding that makes the decision urgent is a wound that is deep, devitalized, heavily contaminated, or joined to a fracture opened to the air. The substance and the amount belong to the prescriber and the local guideline, and nothing in this chapter names either. The field responder helps that decision by describing the wound, reporting the mechanism and the time, and giving the patient's account of previous protection where the patient can, and the record of those times allows the receiving team to decide properly.

The decision between salvaging a mangled limb and amputating it is one of the hardest in surgery, and it belongs to a surgical team in a hospital with the imaging, instruments, blood bank, and intensive care it requires. Scoring systems weigh the injury to skin, bone, vessels, and nerves against the patient's age and condition, and they aid judgment at the hospital rather than serve as a roadside rule. No first responder and no paramedic completes an amputation, pronounces a limb unsalvageable, or tells the patient the limb will be lost. The decision depends on the whole patient, and a patient already in shock, cold, or injured elsewhere may be better served by rapid amputation than by hours of reconstruction, while a stable patient with a single injury may be offered a staged attempt to rebuild. The team weighs the chance the limb will function, the risk of infection and kidney injury, the patient's wishes, and the resources available, and the field provider's task is not to decide but to keep the decision possible.

What the prehospital provider must preserve is easy to list and demanding to carry out. The first thing preserved is the patient's life, because the limb can wait for minutes that a brain and a heart cannot. The second is the tissue, which means no fragment is discarded, no bone end is pushed back, no tissue is pulled away, and no wound is explored in the field. The third is the circulation, which means the tourniquet is not loosened once it has controlled bleeding and its time is written where the receiving team will see it. The fourth is the position of the limb, splinted as found, and the fifth is the record, which carries the mechanism, the injury time, the times of every intervention, and the four observations with the hour each set was taken. The sixth is warmth, because a cold patient tolerates the long operation that salvage requires far worse than a warm one.

Transport is urgent and gentle at the same time, and the destination is chosen before the patient is moved. The receiving facility is the nearest one that can examine and repair vessels, open a compartment, and provide an operating room and a surgeon, which usually means a trauma center. Where the nearest hospital cannot provide that care, the local system decides whether the patient is stabilized there and transferred or carried further at once. A call ahead names the limb, the mechanism, the time of the injury, the tourniquet and its time, what has been done, and what is changing, so the team and the operating room can be ready. The journey avoids unnecessary speed that throws the patient around, because a patient who arrives with more injuries has gained nothing from the hurry. During the journey the limb, the bleeding, the level of consciousness, the breathing, and the warmth of the patient are watched continuously.

The handover is a treatment in itself, because the receiving team continues a story the field began, and a story with a gap forces them to start again. The report follows a fixed order, beginning with the mechanism and the time, then the patient's condition and level of consciousness, then the injuries found, then the interventions with their times, then the observations with the hour they were made, and finally the allergies, medicines, and protection against tetanus where known. The record is written as carefully as the treatment is given, because a tourniquet time never written is a time that will be lost, and a finding never recorded cannot be compared with the next. The limb and every separated fragment are handed over in person rather than left with the paperwork, and the responder says plainly what could not be tested and why. The receiving team is also told what the responder learned about the machine, animal, weapon, or weight involved, because that changes what the surgeon expects inside the wound.

Some patients deserve a word of their own because their mangled limb must be treated within a larger emergency. Children lose heat faster and become shocked on a smaller volume of blood, while an older patient with narrowed arteries or a medicine that thins the blood may lose a limb a younger patient would keep. A patient with a mangled limb and a head, chest, or abdominal injury has more than one threat, and the primary survey in the order of airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure is repeated whenever the condition changes. A patient with two mangled limbs, or with a mangled limb and a pelvic injury, is the patient in whom life before limb decides the whole sequence, because the number of hands is fixed and the bleeding points are several.

Definitive hospital care owns everything in this injury that repairs rather than contains, and the boundary is part of what every provider must know. On arrival the limb is examined again, because the findings may have changed, and the patient is assessed for shock and cold before the limb is addressed in detail. Plain radiographs, ultrasound, and computed tomography study the bone and the vessels, and the surgeon may explore the wound in the operating room to judge which tissue is alive. Repair of a torn vessel, joining or grafting of a nerve, transfer of a tendon, an external frame to hold the bone, the cutting away of dead tissue, the opening of a compartment, and the decision to amputate are all operations and none is a field procedure. Salvage is usually staged, since the first operation controls bleeding and stabilizes the bone, while later operations clean the wound and reconstruct what can be reconstructed. Amputation, when chosen, is a treatment and not a failure, and it is chosen when the limb cannot be made to function or when the attempt would endanger the patient's life.

From the first contact to the handover the patient is watched continuously, because the condition of a mangled limb and its owner can change within a single journey. Watching means repeating the same observations in the same order and comparing them with what was found before. The findings that send the responder back to the beginning are a falling level of consciousness, breathing that has become faster, slower, or noisier, a pulse that has become weak or rapid, skin that has become colder or paler, and a limb that has changed color or feeling. The principle of life before limb is not a slogan but the rule that decides the order of the acts when two correct actions compete for the same pair of hands. The honest statement of this chapter is that a mangled limb is a life-threatening injury whenever the bleeding is not controlled, and that the priority remains the life. The responder who holds to that order, protects the limb without making it the only goal, and moves the patient to a surgeon without delay has done everything the field can do.

To summarize, a mangled extremity is a limb with severe soft-tissue destruction, vascular injury, exposed bone, nerve injury, and the threat of compartment syndrome at once, and it threatens the life before it threatens the limb. The scene is made safe first, and hemorrhage is controlled by pressure, by packing where the provider is trained, and by a tourniquet for a limb that will not stop. The tourniquet is not loosened in the field once it has controlled the bleeding and its time is written on the patient, a deformed limb is splinted as found and never straightened, an embedded object is stabilized, and a partially detached part is never completed. The wound is covered without tight binding, exposed bone is protected rather than pushed back, the limb is immobilized above and below the injury, and the four observations are recorded with their times. The choice between salvage and amputation belongs to a surgical team, and the field provider keeps that choice possible by preserving the life, the tissue, the circulation, the position of the limb, the warmth, and the record. Transport is urgent and gentle to a facility that can repair vessels and open compartments, and every number here is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. Nothing here replaces training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work, and the priority remains the life.

# Chapter 42 — Thermal Burns

Fire is the only injury in this manual that may still be happening when the responder arrives, so the scene is made safe before anyone is touched. The patient may still be on fire, against a hot surface, or in smoke, and traffic, a fuel tank, a falling wall, and molten material are the other hazards to name. The lethal possibilities are the airway that narrows over the hours that follow and the burn that encircles the chest or a limb. They are revealed by a hoarse voice, singed nasal hair, and a burn running all the way around a part, and this chapter cannot replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of your country.

The burning is stopped before it is cooled, because water poured on skin that is still being heated accomplishes very little. A patient whose clothes are on fire is stopped, laid down, and rolled, and the flames are smothered with a blanket, a coat, or any heavy cloth. The lay first aider may remove loose clothing that is no longer burning, but must leave clothing fused to the skin in place, because pulling it away tears living tissue. The trained responder enters only after the fire service declares the structure stable, and the burning has stopped when there is no flame, glow, or heat near the skin.

A thermal burn is a transfer of heat into tissue, and its depth depends on how hot the source was, how long it touched the skin, and how thick the skin was there. Scalds, flame, contact with a hot object, a flash of heat, and hot gases are the ordinary causes, and each leaves a pattern that says something about the patient's position. A scald that runs in a line speaks of liquid flowing, a burn of the palm speaks of a hand that closed around the source, and a burn of the face and chest speaks of a flash. A constructed illustration, never a real patient, is the cook whose sleeve catches fire at the stove, where the visible forearm burn draws every eye while the smoke she breathed may close her airway.

The superficial burn, once called a first-degree burn, has injured only the epidermis, the thin outer layer of the skin, and it shows redness, dryness, and pain without any blister. The skin blanches when pressed and refills when the pressure is released, the surface is intact, and the deeper structures are unharmed, so it usually heals without a scar. Sunburn is the common example, and it shows how a burn that looks trivial can cover a great area and cost fluid and heat. A large superficial burn is not minor in a small child or an older person, and the finding that should end home care is a burn of the face, hands, feet, or genitals.

The partial-thickness burn has destroyed the epidermis and part of the dermis beneath it, and it is the burn that blisters. The surface is moist and weeping, the color is pink or mottled red, it blanches when pressed, and the pain is often severe because nerve endings in the surviving dermis are exposed. A blister is a sterile roof lifted by fluid, and while it stays intact it is the best dressing the body can make, so the lay first aider does not break it. Healing depends on how much dermis survives and may take one to three weeks, a period to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, while the danger is infection and fluid loss shown by spreading redness or fever.

A deep partial-thickness burn destroys most or all of the dermis, and it looks different because the surface may be pale, waxy, or mottled and may blanch sluggishly. Sensation is often reduced because many nerve endings have been destroyed, so the wound the patient feels least may be the one that will need an operation. A full-thickness burn destroys every layer of the skin and may reach fat, muscle, or bone, and it looks leathery, firm, and white, gray, brown, or charred. It is painless in its center, because no nerves are left, and it cannot heal from its own edges, so it belongs to definitive hospital care, where dead tissue is removed and the wound is grafted.

Depth is difficult to judge at the roadside and often changes in the first days, so the responder should not argue about a label that even the receiving team will revise. The purpose of the field assessment is not to name the burn correctly but to recognize the features that make it major and to move the patient toward the care they demand. A burn is major when it is deep or large, when it involves the face, hands, feet, genitals, perineum, or a joint, when it encircles a part, when it came from an enclosed fire, or when the patient is very young, very old, pregnant, or ill. The finding that should stop the debate is any one of those features, because a responder who cannot decide the depth can still decide the destination.

Extent is estimated with the eye and spoken in words, because no chart can be consulted on scene and a number remembered badly is worse than a proportion understood well. The most portable measure is the patient's own palm, held with the fingers together, taken as about one per cent of the body surface, and that convention must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The older spoken rule makes the head and neck about one tenth, each arm about one tenth, each leg about one fifth, the trunk about two fifths, and the perineum a small remainder. The proportions change with age, because a small child's head is a larger share of the body, and the estimate is used above all to decide whether the patient must go to a burn center.

A burn of large extent leaks plasma from the circulation into the wound and the tissue around it, and the patient can enter shock without losing blood to the ground. The patient becomes restless, thirsty, pale, and cool, with a pulse that quickens and breathing that rises, and the loss continues for hours after the burning stops. The lay first aider cannot replace that fluid and must not try, keeping the patient warm and still instead, covering the burn, and getting help moving. The trained responder may begin fluid replacement within the protocol of the service, and the choice of fluid, amount, and route belongs to that protocol and the prescribing authority rather than to this manual.

A circumferential burn runs all the way around a part of the body, and it is dangerous not because of its depth but because burned skin can no longer stretch. The eschar that forms is like a band of stiff leather, and beneath it the tissue swells with the fluid of inflammation, so pressure inside the part rises while the band refuses to give. The two emergencies that follow are the burn that encircles a limb and the burn that encircles the chest, and both declare themselves as the swelling grows rather than at the first look. A burn that closes a full circle around an arm or a leg points to the limb, and a burn of the torso that meets itself from front to back points to the chest.

When a limb is encircled, the rising pressure compresses the veins first, then the arteries, then the nerves and muscle beneath the skin, in the same process that produces compartment syndrome. The findings are pain out of proportion, a limb that feels tight and hard, numbness in the fingers or toes, weakness, pallor or a bluish color, coolness beyond the burn, and a pulse at the wrist or foot that becomes hard to feel. The lay first aider does not cut the burn, does not wrap it tightly, and does not try to relieve the pressure by any field method, because the only relief is an incision through the eschar made by a physician or surgeon. What the lay first aider does is remove rings and tight clothing before swelling makes that impossible, keep the limb in the position found, and report the findings as they change.

When the chest is encircled, the band of eschar limits the movement of the chest wall, so the patient cannot take a deep breath and must work harder for every breath. The findings are rapid shallow breathing, visible use of the neck and rib muscles, a chest that does not rise well, restlessness, and a patient who becomes tired and then drowsy. The lay first aider keeps the patient sitting up if that eases breathing, gives nothing by mouth, keeps the patient warm, and does not bind or press on the chest. The relief is an escharotomy, an incision through the burned skin of the chest wall, which is a hospital procedure for a physician or surgeon and never a field act.

Both constrictions develop over hours rather than minutes, because the swelling that drives them grows after the burn, so a burn that looks stable cannot be left unobserved. The period in which swelling is most likely to become dangerous is often given as the first 24 to 48 hours, and that interval must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The responder returns to the same observations in the same order, looking at breathing, color, warmth, pulse, and pain, rather than treating a first impression as a diagnosis. Any worsening in those observations should send the responder back to the beginning and move the patient on the fastest safe journey to a place where the constriction can be released.

Inhalation injury is suspected from the story of the fire before it is seen in the patient, and the story is as important as the wound. A fire in an enclosed space, an explosion, a volatile fuel, a steam release, or any fire in which the patient was trapped or unconscious should raise the question at once. Heat usually injures the upper airway above the vocal cords, while smoke injures the airway lower down and the lung itself, so a serious inhalation injury can exist with few signs in the mouth. The finding that changes the whole plan is a history of enclosed fire combined with any abnormality of the voice, the breathing, or the level of consciousness.

The findings that predict an airway burn are looked for on the face and listened for in the voice. Singed hairs in the nostrils, soot around the mouth or nose, soot on the lips or tongue, and burns of the face, mouth, or throat are the visible signs. A hoarse or changing voice, a barking cough, noisy breathing, drooling, and trouble swallowing are the signs that are heard, and black sputum or chest tightness points to injury lower down. These findings are progressive, so a clear voice now is no reassurance, and a changing voice or a new noise on breathing should command the fastest journey.

Because the airway narrows as the tissue swells, the definitive treatment is to secure the airway before it closes, and that act belongs to a clinician able to pass a tube into the windpipe. It may be done in hospital or by an advanced prehospital team under protocol, but it is not an act for the lay first aider or an untrained responder. Until then, the lay first aider keeps the patient sitting upright if that eases breathing, gives nothing by mouth, and places no object in the mouth. Oxygen and any drug that might make the patient comfortable belong to the protocol and the prescriber, and the state of the voice and breathing must be passed on at the call and again at the handover.

Smoke poisons as well as burns, and a patient can be dying of the gases of combustion while wearing a burn that looks minor. Carbon monoxide takes the place of oxygen on the red cells of the blood, so the tissues are starved of oxygen even while the patient breathes, and the skin may keep a misleading pink color. Headache, nausea, confusion, drowsiness, and a falling level of consciousness should make the responder suspect this poisoning, especially after an enclosed fire or the burning of fuel. The trained responder may give oxygen within the protocol, and definitive care measures the gases in the blood, while the lay first aider removes the patient from the smoke and keeps the patient warm and still.

Cooling is the field act that actually changes a burn, because it carries heat out of the tissue before that heat can deepen the wound, and it also eases pain and limits swelling. The lay first aider cools a small burn with clean, cool running water poured gently over the area, and does not use ice, ice water, frozen packs, or iced cloths, because cold of that intensity injures the skin further. The trained responder cools a larger burn within the protocol, and the water temperature, the duration, and the method belong to the current guideline and the local protocol. A figure such as 20 minutes of cooling is often named as a teaching illustration and must be confirmed where the responder works, and cooling is stopped when the burn is extensive or the patient is already cold, because hypothermia then becomes the immediate danger.

What is put on a burn matters less than what is kept off it, and the list of things that must not be applied is long and familiar. Butter, oil, toothpaste, herbs, mud, flour, powders, and ice have all been placed on burns, and each holds heat in the wound, introduces infection, or causes further injury. The lay first aider covers the burn with a clean, dry cloth and leaves it alone, and the trained responder applies a dressing intended for burns under the protocol. A blister is left intact where it can be, because its roof is a covering the body has made, and the decision about an antibacterial dressing, tetanus protection, and antibiotics belongs to the prescriber and the local protocol.

Covering keeps contamination out of the wound and keeps the patient's heat in, and both matter when the skin no longer performs those jobs. The covering is laid on loosely and is not wound tightly around a limb or the chest, because a tight band over a burn can become the constriction the burn was threatening. The material is clean and, where available, non-adherent, so it can be lifted later without tearing the wound, and the responder does not pack a burn as a bleeding wound is packed. The finding that the covering is too tight is a change in color, warmth, or pulse beyond it, or pain that grows after the dressing is applied.

Hypothermia is a complication of burns rather than a detail of comfort, and it begins when the skin loses its ability to hold heat and the wound weeps fluid. A patient who is burned, wet, undressed for examination, lying on cold ground, or carried through cold air loses heat quickly, and cold worsens the circulation and deepens shock. The responder removes wet clothing that is not stuck to the skin, replaces it with dry covering, insulates the patient from the ground, covers the head, and warms the vehicle or room. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which cold becomes dangerous, and that figure, like every figure here, is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Every act in this chapter belongs to a named level of provider, decided by training, equipment, authorization, and protocol rather than by the urgency of the moment. The lay first aider may stop the burning, cool a small burn, remove loose clothing and jewelry, cover the burn, keep the patient warm and still, send for emergency medical services, and give nothing by mouth. The trained responder may assess the airway, give oxygen within the protocol, treat pain within the authority to prescribe, dress the wound, monitor the patient, and choose the destination. The physician, the surgeon, and the burn team own the acts that repair rather than contain, which are securing a closing airway, cutting the eschar that strangles a limb or chest, removing dead tissue, grafting the wound, and treating infection, and none of those is a field procedure.

Pain after a burn is severe and continuous, and it deserves to be treated as a problem in its own right. The cooling of a fresh burn eases pain, and so does a clean covering that keeps air away from exposed nerves, and both are within reach of the lay first aider. Analgesia belongs to the provider authorized to prescribe it under the local protocol, and the substance, the amount, the route, and the interval between doses are decisions for that provider and that protocol. Untreated pain drives up the pulse and the work of breathing, so the responder reports pain in plain words and asks for what the protocol allows.

A burned patient is also a trauma patient, because the fire, the explosion, the fall, or the crash that caused the burn may have caused injuries the burn disguises. A patient pulled from a vehicle, thrown by a blast, or forced to jump from a window may have a broken spine, a head injury, a fractured pelvis, or bleeding inside the chest or abdomen. The primary survey is therefore performed in its fixed order in every burned patient, and the burn itself is examined only after the airway, breathing, and circulation are dealt with. Any difficulty with the airway, any abnormality of breathing, or any sign that the circulation is failing should pull attention away from the burn, because a burn can wait for minutes that a hidden injury cannot.

Children and older adults deserve their own words, because their burns behave differently and their bodies compensate differently. A child's skin is thinner, so the same hot liquid that causes a partial-thickness burn in an adult may cause a deep burn in a child, and a child's head is a larger proportion of the body. A child also loses heat and fluid faster, has less reserve, and can move from looking well to looking critically ill within a short time, so the responder watches a burned child more closely. An older patient has thin skin that heals slowly, a heart and lungs with less reserve, and illnesses that change what the burn will do, and a pregnant patient requires care for two patients at once. The finding that should make a burn more serious than its size suggests is the condition of the patient rather than the appearance of the wound.

The burn wound is warm, moist, and open, and it is one of the easiest places for infection to begin, because the barrier that keeps organisms out has been destroyed. The findings that suggest infection are pain that increases after the first days, redness spreading beyond the wound, swelling, pus, a foul smell, fever, and a patient who becomes unwell in a way the burn does not explain. Prevention begins with a clean covering in the field and continues in definitive care with the cleaning of the wound and the removal of dead tissue. The decision about tetanus protection and about antibiotics belongs to the provider authorized to make it, so nothing here names a substance, an amount, or an interval.

Some burns must go to a burn center even when they look small, and the reasons are grouped around the site, the depth, the extent, the cause, and the patient. A burn of the face, hands, feet, genitals, perineum, or across a joint goes there because those areas demand fine surgery and long rehabilitation to keep their function, and a circumferential burn goes there because it may need an escharotomy without warning. An inhalation injury, a full-thickness burn of any size, an electrical or chemical burn, a burn with another injury, and a burn in a patient who is very young or very old also belong in a center with the whole team. The figures often used for a large burn, such as more than 20 per cent of the body surface in an adult or more than 10 per cent in a child, are teaching illustrations to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

A constructed illustration, never a real patient, is the man carried from a house fire who is awake and speaking, with soot around his mouth, singed nasal hairs, a hoarse voice, and a burn of the chest that meets itself from front to back. He looks like a patient who can wait, and he is in fact a patient with two emergencies, because his airway is narrowing and his chest wall cannot expand against the encircling eschar. A second constructed illustration is the toddler who pulled a cup of hot tea onto the arm and chest, whose small burn covers a larger share of the body than the same wound would in an adult. A third is the older woman found beside a space heater with a burn she could not feel, because the nerves in the skin had been destroyed.

The handover must carry the history that the receiving team cannot reconstruct from the wound, beginning with the time of the injury and the agent that caused it. The responder reports whether the fire was in an enclosed space, whether the patient was unconscious, how long the burning lasted, what was applied, how the patient was kept warm, and what the voice and breathing have done since first contact. The extent is reported in words, with the sites named, and the airway findings are reported as findings rather than as a diagnosis. The time matters because the burn continues to evolve after the heat is removed and the swelling that produces the constrictions grows over the hours that follow.

The burned patient is watched continuously from the first contact to the handover, because such a patient can change within a single journey. Watching means repeating the same observations in the same order and comparing them with what was found before, rather than trusting the impression of the moment. The observations that matter are the level of consciousness, the work and sound of the breathing, the pulse, the color and warmth of the skin, the pain, and the state of the wound. A voice that has become hoarse, breathing that has become noisy, a dulling level of consciousness, or a limb that has become hard and cold should send the responder back to the beginning.

The journey to definitive care begins as soon as the patient is stable enough to move, and the destination is chosen before the patient is placed in the vehicle. The nearest hospital that can stabilize the patient is not always the right destination, because the burn center may be distant and the patient may need to pass through a local facility first, and that choice belongs to the trained responder or clinician under the local protocol. Transport is both urgent and gentle, because speed that throws the patient around adds pain and injury, and a patient who arrives colder and more shocked has gained nothing from the hurry. The responder keeps the patient warm throughout, protects the wound from contamination, keeps the burned part still, and continues the observations begun at the scene.

Certain sites deserve a word of their own because their anatomy changes what the burn means. A burn of the face is feared because it may involve the airway and because the scar that follows changes how a person is seen and how that person eats, speaks, and sees. A burn of the hand is feared because the hand must remain supple, and a scar across the palm or fingers can steal the grip forever, which is why a burned hand belongs to a specialist even when it is small. A burn of the foot matters because the patient must walk, a burn of the genitals and perineum is hard to keep clean, and a burn across a joint may tighten into a scar that prevents movement.

The lay first aider is most often met with a scald in a kitchen or a bathroom, and the same few actions serve in almost every case.
