The burning is stopped by removing the patient from the source or the source from the patient, and by removing hot liquid soaked clothing that is not stuck to the skin. The burn is cooled with clean, cool running water for as long as the local teaching advises, covered with a clean, dry cloth, and the patient is kept warm while help is called, and nothing is given by mouth. The finding that should make the lay first aider call emergency medical services is a burn of the face, hands, feet, or genitals, a white or charred burn, or a patient who is very young, very old, or unwell.

A burn is not a finished injury when the heat is removed, because the tissue continues to react and some skin that looked alive may die in the days that follow. This is why the depth is reassessed in hospital and why a wound that looked partial may prove full-thickness, so the responder's early estimate is a starting point rather than a verdict. The wound is also most vulnerable in those first days, when the surface is open and the patient's defenses are weakened, so the covering and the cleanliness with which it is applied both matter. Keeping the patient warm is part of the same work, because the burn has removed the skin that held the heat in, and cool skin, shivering, or new drowsiness means the patient is not warm enough.

The record that travels with the burned patient is as important as any dressing, and it should carry the time, the agent, the extent estimate, the sites involved, the airway findings, what was applied, and every observation that changed. The time is written and spoken because the burn and its swelling run on a clock that began at the injury, and the receiving team uses that clock to decide when the airway must be watched closely and when an escharotomy may become necessary. The responder writes the record on the patient in a way the receiving team will see, or on the form the local protocol provides, and repeats it aloud at handover. No field responder performs an escharotomy, removes dead tissue, grafts a burn, or gives a fluid or a drug by a schedule of their own invention, because those acts belong to definitive care and its protocol.

To summarize, the burned patient is treated first as a trauma patient and always by provider level, and the burning itself is stopped before anything else is done. Scene hazards of fire, smoke, traffic, electricity, falling structures, and hot material are made safe first, and the two lethal emergencies to name early are the airway that is narrowing and the circumferential burn that strangles a limb or the chest. Superficial, partial-thickness, and full-thickness burns are told apart by what remains of the skin, the deepest burn is often the least painful, and the extent is estimated in words with the patient's palm and the spoken proportions of the body rather than with a chart. Cooling with clean, cool running water is the field act that changes a burn, but it is not applied over a large area when the patient is already cold, and covering, warmth, and the prevention of hypothermia run beside it throughout. The lay first aider stops the burning, cools a small burn, covers it, keeps the patient warm, and calls for help, while the trained responder adds airway assessment, oxygen and pain relief within the protocol, dressings, monitoring, and the choice of destination, and definitive care owns the airway, the escharotomy, the excision, the graft, and the treatment of infection. Burns of the face, hands, feet, genitals, perineum, or a joint, circumferential and full-thickness burns, inhalation injuries, electrical and chemical burns, and burns in the very young, the very old, or the already ill must go to a specialist unit, and every figure in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The record of the time, the agent, the extent, the airway findings, and every change travels with the patient, and this chapter does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 43 — Chemical Burns

A chemical burn is the one burn that does not stop when the patient is carried away from its source, because the substance that caused it remains on the skin, in the wound, and often inside the tissue, and it continues to destroy cells until it is removed, diluted, or at last spent. This single fact governs the whole chapter, and it is why the first task at a chemical scene is not the dressing of a wound but the removal of the agent and the protection of everyone near it. The lethal possibilities to be named early are an agent that is still burning while the responder watches, an airway that is closing from fumes that were breathed in, and a poisoning that reaches the heart from a substance that was absorbed through the skin. A fourth possibility is quieter and just as real, which is the rescuer who becomes the next patient because the same agent touched unprotected skin or eyes. This chapter follows the chemical burn from the scene, through decontamination and irrigation, to the transfer of information and the surgical assessment that belong to definitive hospital care, and it names the provider level that owns each act. It is educational material, and it does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

A thermal burn ends its destruction when the source of heat is removed, so cooling is a limit as much as a comfort, but a chemical burn has no such moment unless the chemical is taken off the body. The agent can sit as a liquid in a skin fold, as a powder inside a boot, or as a residue on a glove, and every minute it stays in contact is another minute of tissue loss, so depth is not fixed at the moment of contact and a wound that looks shallow may become full thickness over the following hours. Acids tend to produce a coagulative injury in which dead protein forms a barrier that slows deeper penetration, while alkalis tend to produce a liquefying injury that dissolves tissue and carries the agent deeper, which is why an alkali burn is usually the more destructive of the two. Concentration, volume, duration of contact, and the nature of the tissue all change the outcome, and a dilute agent left in place for a long time can do more harm than a concentrated one that was washed off at once. For all these reasons the response is measured in how quickly the agent is removed rather than in how quickly a dressing is applied, and every figure offered in this chapter is an illustration rather than a rule, to be checked against the guideline that is current in the responder's service.

No care begins until the scene has been made safe, and a chemical scene is made safe in a different way from a road crash, because the hazard may be invisible, odorless, and heavier than air. The responder approaches from upwind and from higher ground where that is possible, stays out of enclosed spaces where vapor collects, and does not enter a spill or a shed to reach a patient who is lying in it. The substance may be a liquid, a vapor, a gas, a fine powder, or a mixture of several, and the label, the container, the placard on a vehicle, and the smell are the first evidence of what is present. The hazardous materials team is the resource that owns the identification and the removal of the agent, and the lay first aider who has found such a scene calls for that team and does not attempt a rescue into it. The trained responder works within the equipment and the authority the service provides, and nobody enters a contaminated space in ordinary clothing on the assumption that the exposure will be brief. The finding that tells a responder to stop and withdraw is any doubt about what the substance is, any smell that irritates the throat, and any patient who is lying in a pool of liquid, because those are the signs that the scene has not yet been made safe.

Protection of the rescuer is not a courtesy to the responder but a condition of the rescue, because a contaminated responder cannot help anyone and becomes a second patient who consumes the resources sent for the first. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, is chosen for the agent rather than for the patient, and a service that carries only gloves and eye protection must call for the team that carries more when the substance is unknown or is a vapor. Gloves, eye protection or a face shield, a gown or an apron, and boots or covers for the feet are the minimum for a liquid or a powder, and clothing that has absorbed the agent is treated as contaminated material and removed as soon as there is a safe place to do it. The lay first aider uses whatever barrier is at hand, including plastic bags over the hands and a scarf or glasses over the eyes, and never lays a bare hand on a patient who is wet with a chemical. The patient's own clothing is part of the hazard rather than part of the patient, since a soaked shirt, a boot full of powder, and a glove that holds liquid against the skin all continue the injury after the patient has left the source. A responder who is splashed washes the area at once with plenty of water, and a responder whose eyes are splashed begins irrigation without waiting to finish any other task, because the eye is the tissue that tolerates delay least.

Decontamination begins with the removal of the patient from the source and continues with the removal of everything that carries the agent, and the order within that act matters. Contaminated clothing is cut away rather than pulled over the head, because pulling a shirt over the face can drag the agent into the eyes and the mouth, and the scissors are used along the seams so that the fabric never crosses the face. Jewelry, watches, belts, shoes, and anything else that holds liquid against the skin are removed at the same time, because a ring can hold an agent against a finger and a watch can hold it against the wrist long after the arm has been washed. Dry powder is brushed off the skin before water is added, because water can turn a powder into a concentrated solution, can drive the particles into the skin, and can react with some powders to produce heat. An object embedded in the skin, whether a fragment of glass or a piece of metal, is left where it is and padded around, because pulling it out in the field may release bleeding that cannot be controlled outside an operating room. The finding that marks the end of this step is skin that no longer carries visible powder, fabric that is no longer in contact with the patient, and a responder whose own gloves and eyes are still protected. Nothing in this book authorizes the use of a neutralizing chemical on the skin, because neutralization generates heat and can add a thermal burn to a chemical one, and the correct fluid is water in large amounts.

Some agents must be handled in a way that differs from the ordinary rule of water first, and the responder must know the classes even when the exact substance is unknown. Dry lime, cement powder, and other dry alkalis are brushed away before irrigation, because adding water to quicklime produces heat and can burn the skin a second time. The elemental metals, including sodium, potassium, lithium, and magnesium, react with water and may ignite or burst on contact, so they are removed as dry particles and the skin is protected as the local protocol directs rather than washed. White phosphorus ignites when it meets the air and burns until the air is excluded, so the particles are kept under water or under a wet dressing while the patient is moved. Phenol is poorly soluble in water and can be spread by a careless wash, and the particular solvent that is used to remove it belongs to the protocol and to the provider trained in its use. Hydrofluoric acid is the agent that most deserves to be called different, because it passes through the skin, destroys the tissue beneath it, and binds the calcium and magnesium in the blood in a way that can disturb the rhythm of the heart even when the visible burn is small. None of this changes the rule that the responder protects the skin, the eyes, and the airway first, and every decision about a special agent, its removal, and its antidote belongs to the local protocol and to the clinician authorized to make it.

Irrigation is the central act of chemical burn care, and it is performed copiously, gently, and for longer than instinct suggests. Water is applied at low pressure from a clean area toward a contaminated one so that the flow carries the agent away from the eyes, the mouth, and the wound rather than across them, and the fluid is tepid rather than ice cold, because cold water constricts the vessels and can deepen the injury. Irrigation is prolonged, with a period of 20 to 30 minutes as a common teaching figure, and with alkalis, hydrofluoric acid, and concentrated agents often requiring much longer washing; the exact figure is set by the guideline and the local protocol that govern the responder's service. The patient's pain, the visible residue, and the measured acidity or alkalinity of the runoff are the findings that decide whether washing continues, and a trained responder who measures the runoff does so under the protocol that authorizes the measurement. Irrigation is interrupted only for an airway that must be opened, for a cardiac arrest that must be treated, and for the move to the vehicle, and it is resumed during transport rather than abandoned at the door. Ointments, oils, butter, toothpaste, and herbal preparations are never applied to a chemical burn in the field, because they trap the agent, hide the wound, and give the receiving team a surface that must be cleaned before it can be assessed. The working rule is that the wound is washed until the fluid runs clear and the pain has eased, and then washed again, because a burn that looks clean may still hold agent in a fold of skin.

The extent and the depth of a chemical burn are judged in spoken words, and they are judged with caution because the agent may still be spreading. The palm of the patient's own hand, including the fingers, is a rough guide to one per cent of the body surface, while the rule of nines describes the head and each arm as about 9 per cent, each leg as about 18 per cent, and the front and the back of the trunk as about 18 per cent each, and these proportions vary in a child and differ between services and editions, so the local guideline and not this page is the authority. Depth is written as a word rather than as a numeral, with a partial-thickness burn and a full-thickness burn as the two categories that matter. A superficial burn is red and painful and does not blister, a partial-thickness burn blisters or weeps and is intensely painful, and a full-thickness burn may be white, waxy, brown, or black, may look dry and leathery, and may be painless because the nerves within it are gone, so a patient whose pain is far greater than the appearance suggests may be carrying an agent still at work, and the responder describes what is seen rather than guessing at a number of degrees.

An eye that has been exposed to a chemical is an emergency of the first order, and its treatment begins at the scene and continues without pause. Irrigation starts at once with whatever clean water is available, because the damage continues while the responder looks for a better fluid, and a delay of minutes can decide whether the patient keeps the sight of that eye. The lids are held open with the fingers, the patient is asked to look in different directions while the water runs, and the flow is directed from the inner corner outward so that the agent is not washed into the other eye. A contact lens is removed if it can be seen and reached without force, because a lens can hold the agent against the surface of the eye, and the responder does not delay irrigation in order to search for it. If only one eye is affected, the other is protected by positioning the patient with the contaminated side lower, and if the agent was a powder or a vapor, both eyes are assumed to be involved until they are examined. Irrigation continues during the journey, with a period of at least 20 minutes as a common teaching figure whose exact value comes from the current guideline and the local protocol rather than from this page, and it continues until the receiving clinician says that it can stop. No neutralizing solution, no ointment, and no eye drop are placed in a chemically burned eye in the field, and the decision about what is placed in the eye belongs to the clinician and to the protocol. The finding that makes the eye case urgent even when the patient says the eye feels better is the delayed injury of an alkali, which can go on damaging the surface for hours after the pain has settled.

Chemical injury does not always arrive through the skin, and the airway is the route that kills most quickly. Gases and vapors such as ammonia, chlorine, and the products of burning plastic reach the throat and the lungs within a breath, and the finding that predicts trouble is a patient who is hoarse, who is coughing, who has a burning throat, or whose voice has changed since the exposure. Stridor, drooling, and a rising effort to breathe are the findings that mark an airway that is closing, and they may appear after a quiet interval during which the patient felt almost well. The lay first aider moves the patient into fresh air, keeps the patient sitting upright if that makes breathing easier, and calls emergency medical services at once, and the full name is used here because the abbreviation is not spoken in this book. The trained responder or paramedic supports the airway with the equipment and the protocol the service authorizes, and gives oxygen only as that protocol directs, while definitive hospital care owns the examination of the airway and the decision about an artificial airway. Smoke from a fire and fumes in an enclosed space carry the same warning, and any patient who was unconscious in such an atmosphere is treated as an airway emergency until proved otherwise. The finding that moves the responder from watching to acting is any noise in the breathing, any change in the voice, and any fall in the level of consciousness, because each of those says that the airway is losing its width.

The primary survey keeps its order of airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure even at a chemical scene, but decontamination runs alongside it rather than waiting at the end. If the patient is not breathing, the airway and the breathing are treated first, while another pair of hands continues to remove clothing and to wash the skin, so that the agent is not left burning during resuscitation. If the patient is breathing and the agent is still on the skin, decontamination becomes the immediate priority, because the injury continues while the substance remains in contact and because the patient must be clean enough to be touched by the receiving team. Circulation is assessed with the same eye and hand as in any other patient, since a chemical burn can conceal bleeding from a wound made by the same incident, and bleeding that a tourniquet has controlled is not released in the field while the time of its placement is written on the patient. Disability is recorded as the level of consciousness, the pupils, and the movement of the limbs, and a limb that is deformed is splinted in the position found and is never straightened to make it look normal, because movement endangers the vessels and nerves that are still intact. Exposure is where the chemical burn is seen whole, and the responder looks in the skin folds, the armpits, the groin, the scalp, the ears, and the perineum, because a liquid pools in those places and a burn missed there will be found later by someone else. The finding that returns the responder to the start of the survey is any change for the worse, at any point, in any patient.

A chemical burn can poison the patient as well as injure the skin, and the substances that do this are few but lethal. Hydrofluoric acid is absorbed and binds calcium and magnesium in the blood, and the findings that should raise the alarm are muscle twitching, numbness, cramping, an irregular pulse, and a patient who becomes faint or unresponsive, all of which can occur when the visible burn looks small. Phenol is absorbed through intact skin and can produce weakness, sweating, a falling level of consciousness, and a disturbance of the heart rhythm, and the smell of the agent on the patient is itself a piece of information for the receiving team. The elemental metals that react with water and the phosphorus that burns in air add their own systemic hazards, and a patient exposed to any of them is moved to definitive care without waiting for the skin to look worse. The responder's part in these cases is to recognize that the patient is more ill than the wound explains, to keep the patient warm and still, to watch the breathing, the pulse, and the level of consciousness, and to say clearly in the handover which agent was involved. The specific antidote, the blood test, and the decision to give a substance into a vein belong to the clinician, to the poison control center, and to the local protocol, and no reader should take a treatment from these pages. The finding that should make a responder suspect systemic poisoning is a patient whose general condition is worse than the burn can account for, because the skin is not always the whole of a chemical injury.

Cold is a complication of chemical burn care rather than a detail of comfort, and the act of washing a patient makes it worse. Prolonged irrigation wets the skin and the clothing, the patient lies on the ground while the responders work, and burned skin can no longer hold heat or water, so the patient who is being decontaminated is also losing temperature. The responder protects the patient by using tepid water rather than cold water, by placing insulation between the patient and the ground, by working in a sheltered place where that is possible, and by covering every part of the patient that is not being washed at that moment. Wet clothing is cut away and replaced with dry coverings, and the vehicle is warmed before the patient is placed in it, because a warm ambulance is part of the treatment and not a luxury. The patient's temperature is watched during transport, and a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold is a patient whose body has given up the attempt to make heat. A body temperature such as 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the line at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and the accepted threshold varies with age and with the way the temperature is taken, so the local guideline decides the figure that is used. The finding that tells the responder that warming must become active rather than passive is a patient who is cold to the touch, who has stopped shivering, and whose level of consciousness is dulling.

The information that travels with a chemically burned patient is part of the treatment, because the receiving team cannot undo an exposure it does not know about. The name of the agent is the first item, taken from the label, the container, the placard, or the safety data sheet if one is available, and the container itself is sent with the patient when the hazardous materials team says that it is safe to do so. The time of the exposure, the duration of contact, the concentration if it is known, and the parts of the body that were affected are stated next, together with the decontamination already performed and the time at which irrigation began. The patient's allergies, other illnesses and medicines, and tetanus status where it is known are added to the handover, because a chemical burn is a wound and carries the risk of infection. Emergency medical services are told what is coming before the patient arrives, and the poison control center may be consulted for advice about a particular agent. A record of what was done, when it was done, and who did it is written where the receiving team will see it, and anything applied to the skin is named. Reassessment is a rhythm rather than a single act, so the responder repeats the airway, the breathing, the circulation, the level of consciousness, and the look at the skin, and compares each set of findings with the one before. The finding that makes this step urgent rather than routine is a patient whose wound is enlarging, whose breathing is changing, or whose pulse is becoming irregular, because in each of those cases the receiving team needs the name of the agent before the patient reaches the door.

Definitive hospital care owns the assessment and the surgery of every chemical burn that will not heal by itself, and the responder's task is to recognize which patients belong there. A full-thickness burn, a burn that crosses a joint, a burn of the hands, the face, the eyes, or the genitalia, and a burn that encircles a limb or the chest all require surgical assessment, because the swelling that follows can compress vessels, nerves, and the chest wall. A burn that covers a large part of the body, a burn in a child or in an older patient, a burn with an inhalation injury, and a burn in a patient who has other injuries from the same incident are also referred to a center with the staff and the equipment to treat them, and the destination is chosen by the local protocol and the receiving system. The operations that follow belong entirely to the surgeon, and they include the release of a constricting eschar, the removal of dead tissue, the early excision of a deep burn, and the grafting of skin, none of which is a field procedure no matter how urgent the patient appears. The chest is never bound tightly in a patient with a circumferential burn, because the swelling inside the burn is the danger and a tight bandage adds to it rather than relieving it. A chemical burn may continue to deepen after arrival, so the surgeon often waits and reassesses before operating, and the responder who understood that the injury was still active has already served the patient. The patient must also be watched for the complications that follow any serious wound, including infection, fluid loss, hypothermia, and the effects of the agent on the organs, and the handover must carry the history that makes those complications likely. The finding that changes the destination is any burn that meets the criteria for a specialist unit, and the decision about that destination belongs to the local protocol and to the receiving system rather than to the responder's preference.

To summarize, a chemical burn is an injury that continues until the agent is removed, so decontamination comes before everything except scene safety and the protection of the rescuer. The scene is approached from upwind, the hazardous materials team owns the identification and the removal of the substance, and no responder enters a contaminated space without the equipment and the authority to do so. Contaminated clothing is cut away rather than pulled over the face, dry powder is brushed off before water is added, jewelry and anything else holding liquid against the skin is removed, and an embedded object is stabilized in place and never pulled out in the field. Irrigation is copious, tepid, low pressure, and prolonged, directed from a clean area toward a contaminated one, with a period of 20 to 30 minutes as a common teaching figure that the current guideline and the local protocol are the authority on, and an exposed eye is irrigated at once and continuously from the inner corner outward while the patient is moved, with both eyes treated as involved when the agent was a powder or a vapor. Some agents behave differently, and dry alkalis, elemental metals, white phosphorus, phenol, and hydrofluoric acid each require the special handling the local protocol defines, while acids and alkalis differ in the depth they reach and alkalis go on injuring longer. The primary survey keeps its order while decontamination runs beside it, hypothermia is prevented because washing cools the patient, and pain is treated by the provider authorized to prescribe and never by a dose taken from this book. The name of the agent, the time of exposure, the duration of contact, the decontamination performed, and the time irrigation began all travel with the patient, while full-thickness burns, burns across joints, burns of the hands, face, eyes, or genitalia, circumferential burns, large burns, and burns with inhalation injury belong to definitive hospital care, where the surgeon releases, removes, excises, and grafts, and none of that is a field procedure. Every number in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such figures differ between services, countries, and editions, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 44 — Electrical Injuries

Electrical injury is a systemic event that enters through a wound too small to explain it, and the responder who judges the damage by the skin will underestimate it every time. The current follows the tissues that conduct best, which are nerve, muscle, and blood vessel, so a small charred mark may sit above muscle that has been cooked and killed, and the path from the entry point to the exit point decides which organs are at risk. Scene safety is therefore the first clinical act of this chapter, because the wire, the rail, or the appliance that injured the patient may still be energized and may injure the next person who touches it. The lethal possibilities are named early, which are an ineffective rhythm of the heart, a breathing drive that has been paralyzed, deep muscle destruction that poisons the body hours later, and the injuries of a fall from height. Every act is named with the provider level that owns it, whether the lay first aider, the trained responder or paramedic, or definitive hospital care, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

The first act at any scene where electricity may be involved is to stop the current, and that act belongs to a person authorized by the utility or by the emergency service to operate the isolation point. Until the isolation is confirmed by the person who performed it, every wire, rail, puddle, and appliance is treated as live, and no hand is laid on a patient who is still in contact with the source. A downed conductor kills without being touched, because the ground near its broken end carries a difference in potential across each step, so the safe approach keeps the feet together and does not lift the soles. A separation such as 10 meters is a figure that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the safe distance grows with the voltage. A vehicle resting against a live wire is a trap in which the patient may be safest while seated inside, and the rescuer who pulls the patient out may complete a circuit that the tires had insulated. The trained responder or paramedic may hold the scene, request the isolation, and use insulated tools where the service authorizes them, while the lay first aider keeps others back, calls for help from a safe place, and covers the hands, the eyes, and the mouth with whatever barrier is at hand. The finding that permits the rescue to begin is a clear statement that the supply is isolated, and anything less leaves the scene unsafe.

Electricity injures by passing through the body, and what it damages depends on the path it takes, the current it carries, the time it lasts, and the resistance of the tissue it meets. Dry skin resists the current and may be burned where it enters, while wet skin conducts far more readily and can leave a smaller mark for a larger internal injury, which is why a patient found in water may be more damaged than the wound suggests. Alternating current at household frequency can hold a victim against the source with a sustained muscular contraction, so the exposure lasts longer than the patient intended and the hand cannot open. Direct current, as from a battery bank or a lightning strike, tends to throw the patient clear, and that separation is why a lightning victim may have no burn at all and still be in cardiac arrest. Nerve, muscle, and blood vessel carry current well and are heated by it, while bone and fat resist and may be spared while the structures beside them are destroyed, so the visible wound is a poor measure of the injury.

Electrical injuries differ in kind, and the kind decides the urgency. A low-voltage injury in the home, from a socket, a cord, or a small appliance, may cause only a tingling sensation and a small burn, and yet it can also produce a rhythm disturbance that appears later, so a minor wound does not make the patient safe. A high-voltage injury from an overhead line, a substation, a railway supply, or industrial equipment destroys tissue along the whole path of the current, and the destruction is often deep and progressive rather than confined to the skin. An arc injury occurs when current jumps an air gap without the patient becoming part of the circuit, and it delivers an intense flash of heat that burns exposed skin and ignites clothing, so the patient may suffer a flash burn, a flame burn, and the blunt injury of a blast at once. A lightning strike is a brief and enormous current that may stop the heart and the breathing at once, and the patient who is revived may remain confused, weak, or unable to move the limbs for a time, so every mechanism must be identified from the scene and reported to the receiving team.

The heart fails first and most quietly, and the rhythm it develops is the reason this chapter insists on monitoring rather than on the wound. Current through the chest can throw the heart into an ineffective rhythm in which it quivers instead of pumping, into beats that arise from the wrong part of the heart, or into a complete standstill, and any of these may occur at the moment of the shock or hours afterwards. The finding at the scene may be no more than a patient who felt faint and sat down, and the danger is that such a patient is allowed to walk, to drive, or to wait unobserved. A patient who is unresponsive and not breathing normally is treated as being in cardiac arrest, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR, begins as soon as the scene is safe and the patient is separated from the source. The trained responder or paramedic applies a cardiac monitor and keeps it attached during transport, because a rhythm that is normal on arrival may deteriorate later and a monitored patient can be treated before the deterioration becomes irreversible. Definitive hospital care decides how long the patient must be observed and whether an intensive care unit is required, and that decision rests on the rhythm, on the path of the current, and on the patient's history rather than on the size of the burn.

Breathing fails for two immediate reasons, and both are answered by the primary survey. The current can paralyze the muscles of respiration so that the chest does not move, and it can also cause a sustained contraction of the hand or the arm that holds the patient on the source, so the exposure continues until the current is stopped or a muscle tears. A patient who is not breathing but whose heart is still beating will suffer a cardiac arrest within minutes unless the breathing is supported, so the airway and the breathing hold their place at the front of the primary survey. The trained responder opens the airway, gives oxygen where the protocol provides it, and assists the breathing with the equipment the service authorizes, while the lay first aider supports the head, checks that the chest is rising, and calls for help without delay. A patient who has been thrown clear may have injured the neck and the spine, so the head and the neck are held in the position found and the patient is not sat up to make breathing easier, while the finding that tells the responder the breathing is failing is a chest that does not rise or lips and fingertips that have turned blue.

Nerves conduct current better than any other tissue and are often injured without any external sign. The patient may be confused, agitated, or drowsy, and the level of consciousness is a more useful measurement than the wound because it registers the effect of the current on the brain. A seizure may occur at the moment of the shock, and the patient who has seized is protected from injuring the head and the limbs while the seizure runs its course, since nothing is placed in the mouth. Weakness, numbness, or an inability to move a limb may recover over hours or may persist, and the finding must be recorded and handed over rather than interpreted in the field, while a lightning strike may leave a temporary paralysis of the limbs with consciousness preserved that is mistakenly treated as harmless. Definitive hospital care examines the nerves and the spinal cord, and imaging such as computed tomography, or CT, or magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, may be used where the clinician judges it necessary, and none of that assessment can be performed at the roadside.

The electricity is only one of the mechanisms acting on the patient, and the fall or the blast that follows the shock may be more immediately lethal than the current itself. In a constructed illustration, a worker thrown from a ladder or a person blown from a transformer platform may have a fractured spine, a fractured pelvis, a broken thigh, a head injury, or bleeding inside the abdomen, and none of those injuries is visible in the burn mark. The spinal column is presumed to be injured in any patient who has fallen from a height, so the head and the neck are maintained in the position found and the patient is moved only with the technique the responder has been trained to use. A fractured pelvis may bleed into the space behind the peritoneum and kill without any external wound, and the responder must not press on the pelvis or spring it in order to test for pain, because pelvic pain, an inability to move a leg, or a difference in the length of the legs already moves the patient toward definitive care. Every figure in this chapter, whether a voltage, a distance, a time, or a temperature, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because such numbers differ between services, countries, and editions.

The burn at the point of contact is the mark that most responders see and the one that most misleads them. An entry wound appears where the current enters the body, and it is often small, round, and charred, with a pale rim and a depressed center, and it may be painless because the nerves in the skin have been destroyed. An exit wound appears where the current leaves the body, and it may be larger and more ragged than the entry because the current has spread before leaving, and the tissue around it may be cooked and dry. The current does not travel in a straight line, so the skin between the two marks may look entirely normal while the muscle, the nerve, and the vessel beneath are destroyed, and a patient may have more than one exit point because current can leave through both feet or through a hand and a foot. The burn is covered with a clean dry dressing, the patient is kept warm, and the wound is handed over as one fact among many rather than as the whole injury.

Muscle is injured in almost every electrical injury of consequence, and the damage may lie far from the burn. Muscle that has been heated by current breaks down and releases its contents into the bloodstream, and the pigment that carries oxygen within the muscle, myoglobin, travels to the kidneys and can damage them, a condition called rhabdomyolysis. The findings that suggest this deep destruction are muscle pain and tenderness out of proportion to the wound, a limb that is swollen and tight, weakness, and urine that has become dark, brown, or the color of tea. The trained responder watches for those findings, keeps the patient warm and still, and moves the patient toward a hospital that can measure the products of muscle breakdown in the blood and support the kidneys, because the poisoning of the body by its own injured muscle is a hospital problem rather than a field one. Fluid replacement belongs to the paramedic under a protocol and to definitive hospital care, and the substance, the amount, the route, and the timing are decisions made by the prescriber and the local guideline, so nothing in this chapter names them. The swelling of a limb can also raise the pressure within a closed compartment of muscle and produce compartment syndrome, and the finding that warns of it is pain that grows when the muscle is stretched, a limb that is tense, and numbness beyond the injury.

A low-voltage injury deserves attention even when the patient looks well, because household current can disturb the heart and can injure a small body out of proportion to its size. A child who has bitten or sucked on the end of an extension cord may have a burn at the corner of the mouth, and the danger is not only the burn but the delayed bleeding that can occur days later when the scab separates from a vessel in the lip, which is one reason every such child must be assessed in hospital rather than at home. A child has a smaller body and a lower resistance than an adult, so a current that would only startle a grown person can produce a serious injury in a child, and the same reasoning applies to a patient whose skin is wet. An older patient with an existing heart condition may develop a dangerous rhythm from a shock that leaves no mark at all, and the finding that makes that patient urgent is any racing or irregular heartbeat, any fainting, or any chest discomfort. The lay first aider does not decide who may stay at home and who must be seen, because that decision belongs to the clinician who can examine and monitor the patient, and every patient with an electrical contact, however minor the burn, is offered assessment on the basis of the mechanism rather than the appearance.

The most difficult patient in this chapter is the one who is awake, talking, and apparently unharmed. Electrical current can produce a delayed rhythm disturbance, a delayed loss of consciousness, a delayed swelling of a limb, or a delayed failure of the kidneys, and none of those can be excluded by a normal examination at the scene. The safe practice is to treat any patient with a documented electrical contact as a patient who requires monitoring, and the trained responder or paramedic applies a cardiac monitor and arranges transport to a facility that can continue that monitoring. The lay first aider keeps the patient still, warm, and observed, and prevents the patient from walking away or driving, since exertion can worsen a heart that has been disturbed, while a normal pulse at a single moment is never accepted as reassuring because the heart can change within minutes. The decision about how long the patient must be watched belongs to definitive hospital care and to the local protocol, and a patient who refuses assessment after a significant exposure is a patient for whom the receiving physician and that protocol decide what is safe.

Resuscitation of the electrical patient follows the same order as for any other cause of cardiac arrest, but two ideas belong especially to this chapter. The first is that the patient must be separated from the source and the scene made safe before any hand touches the body, because a rescuer who is electrocuted cannot help anyone and becomes a second patient. The second is that a patient struck by lightning may have a heart that can restart with prompt support while the breathing remains paralyzed, so effective CPR may be rewarded with survival even when the arrest appears prolonged, and the decision to continue belongs to the responder's protocol and to the clinician directing the resuscitation. The trained responder or paramedic follows the current resuscitation guideline of the service, and the lay first aider provides compressions when trained to do so and follows the dispatcher's instructions where the system provides them. When several patients are struck by the same lightning flash, the usual order of triage is reversed, and the patients who appear dead are treated first because they may be revived, while those who are awake and calling out are moved to safety and reassessed afterwards, since a brief loss of consciousness and the ability to speak do not exclude a later rhythm disturbance. The finding that ends resuscitation is set by the local protocol and by the clinician in charge rather than by the responder alone, and the reversal belongs to lightning incidents and must not be transferred to other multiple casualty scenes.

Cold is a complication of electrical injury rather than a detail of comfort, and it can be the factor that turns a disturbed heart into a stopped one. The patient may have wet clothing from rain or from immersion, may have had clothing burned or cut away, may be lying on cold ground, and may be unable to shiver because the current has injured the muscles or the nerves that produce shivering. Cold makes the heart more irritable, reduces the effectiveness of resuscitation, and worsens the tissue damage of any associated injury, so warmth is provided from the first moment of care. The responder removes wet clothing where that can be done without exposing the patient for longer than necessary, covers the patient with dry blankets, foil, or clothing, insulates the patient from the ground, and keeps the vehicle or the room warm during transport. A body temperature such as 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the line below which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that threshold must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted figure varies with the patient and with the way the temperature is measured.

The handover of an electrically injured patient carries facts that the receiving team cannot reconstruct from the wound. The responder reports what the source was, whether a household supply, an overhead line, a railway conductor, an arc, or lightning, and whether the patient was in contact with it or was thrown by it. The duration of the contact is reported where it is known, since a sustained grip on a live conductor produces a far greater injury than a brief brush, and the entry and exit points are described by their position on the body because the path between them predicts which organs were exposed. The time of any loss of consciousness, any seizure, any arrest, and the start of CPR are recorded, together with the rhythm seen on the monitor and the interventions performed, because the receiving team continues a story that the field began. Any fall from height is described with the height and the surface, even approximately, and the record is part of the treatment, because a mechanism that is not passed on will be investigated from the beginning by a team that has lost time.

Definitive hospital care owns everything that an electrical injury requires beyond support, and knowing where that line lies is part of competence for every responder. The hospital examines the path of the current with imaging, measures the products of muscle breakdown in the blood, watches the rhythm on a monitor, and supports the kidneys when they are threatened, and none of that can be done in the field. Surgical care removes dead muscle and dead skin, releases the pressure inside a swollen compartment, repairs or diverts the vessels that the current has destroyed, and sometimes amputates a limb that cannot be saved, and each of those is an operation rather than a dressing. The burn at the entry and exit points is cleaned, protected, and dressed, and the question of protection against tetanus, like the question of antibiotics, is answered by the provider authorized to make that decision under the local protocol, because the substance and the amount belong to the prescriber and not to this manual. A patient with a burn that is deep, contaminated, or extensive is assessed by a burns service, and the transfer to such a service is arranged by the hospital, while the responder's contribution is to protect the wound, to keep the patient warm, to monitor, and to deliver the patient to the right place with the mechanism clearly stated.

Two groups deserve a word of their own because their care differs from the usual. A pregnant patient who suffers an electrical injury is assessed as two patients, since the current can affect the fetus as well as the mother, and the decision about monitoring and about the well-being of the fetus belongs to definitive hospital care with the obstetric team involved. A patient with a pacemaker or an implanted cardiac defibrillator is at risk that a current passing through the chest will damage the device or the leads that connect it to the heart, and the finding that should be sought is any change in the patient's usual rhythm or a device that has begun to alarm, though the responder does not attempt to test the device. The responder's task in both cases is unchanged, which is to make the scene safe, to support the airway and the breathing, to monitor the heart, and to reach a hospital that can examine the patient properly. The device is described at handover, including what the patient says it is and where it was implanted, and where the patient cannot describe it, a relative or a medical alert item may carry the information.

The care of the electrical burn itself is similar to the care of any other burn, and the exception is the injury beneath it. The wound is covered with a clean, dry, non-adherent dressing where one is available, because a dressing that sticks tears the tissue when it is removed and opens a route for infection. Ice is not placed on the burn, oily preparations are not applied, and blisters are not opened, because each of those acts damages tissue that is already compromised. The limb is kept in the position found, the patient is kept warm, and the wound is not packed in a way that adds pressure, since the tissue within is already swollen, while the lay first aider covers the burn with whatever clean material is at hand and does not attempt to clean or inspect the deep wound. The trained responder follows the protocol of the local burns service for the covering, and the finding that should be reported is a limb that has become more swollen, more tense, or more painful during the journey, because that suggests the pressure inside the limb is rising and that the surgeon must be told before the limb is lost.

Reassessment after an electrical injury is not a single examination performed at the scene but a rhythm that continues to the handover. The responder returns to the airway, the breathing, and the circulation, and then to the level of consciousness, the pupils, and the movement of the limbs, because a patient who was alert at the scene and is drowsy in the ambulance has told the responder more than the burn can. The findings that mark deterioration are a falling level of consciousness, a breathing pattern that has become faster, slower, or noisy, a pulse that has become rapid and weak, skin that has become cold or clammy, and a limb that has become tense and painful, and these are compared with the previous set rather than judged alone. The monitor is watched continuously where it is attached, and any change in the rhythm is reported at once, while the patient is also watched for the signs of shock, which may come from the deep tissue injury, from an associated fracture, or from bleeding that the electricity concealed. The destination is chosen before the patient is moved, and for this injury it is the nearest facility that can monitor the heart and measure the products of muscle breakdown, because transport must be urgent and gentle when the patient may have a spinal injury, a fracture, or an unstable rhythm.

To summarize, electrical injury is a systemic event whose visible wound is a poor measure of its damage, and the first act is always to stop the current and to treat the source as live until an authorized person confirms that it is isolated. The current follows the tissues that conduct best, so the burn at the entry and the exit may be small while the muscle, the nerve, and the vessel between them are destroyed, and the pathway predicts the organs at risk. The heart is monitored because an arrhythmia may appear at once or hours later, the breathing is supported because the current can paralyze it, and the level of consciousness, the spine, and the pelvis are assessed because the fall that follows the shock may be the more lethal injury. Deep muscle destruction releases myoglobin that threatens the kidneys, and the findings of pain, swelling, weakness, and dark urine move the patient toward a hospital that can measure and treat it, while fluids, analgesia, and every substance remain the decisions of the prescriber and the protocol. The lay first aider keeps others from the source, covers the burn, keeps the patient warm and still, and calls for help, and the trained responder or paramedic monitors the heart, supports the airway and breathing, and transports, while definitive hospital care images, operates, and supports the organs that fail. Hypothermia travels with electrical injury, the mechanism and the times are recorded and handed over, the patient who looks well is still a patient who must be watched, and every figure in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 45 — Immediate Pain Management

A patient who is badly hurt will often speak about the pain before anything else, and the responder who hears only a complaint and moves past it has already missed a piece of clinical evidence. Pain is not a comfort that can wait until the bleeding has stopped and the journey is over, because pain itself quickens the heart, stiffens the breathing, and raises the demand for oxygen in a body that may already be short of it. This chapter treats pain relief as part of trauma care rather than as an addition to it, and it names the provider level that owns each act, from the lay first aider with bare hands to the trauma surgeon in the operating room. The lethal possibility to name early is pain out of proportion to the injury, because that finding can be the first sign of compartment syndrome, of an expanding collection of blood, or of bleeding inside a cavity. Every substance, amount, and interval mentioned here belongs to the local protocol and the prescriber, so nothing in this chapter can be taken as a prescription. This chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

No measure of comfort may precede the making safe of the scene, because a responder struck while kneeling beside a patient becomes a second casualty and takes the only pair of hands away from the first. The hazards that kill rescuers are moving traffic, fire and smoke, live electrical current, deep or fast water, an animal still loose, a person still violent, a structure that may collapse, and the contaminated material of the patient's blood, vomit, and tissue. The finding that a scene is unsafe often arrives before the injury does, as the smell of fuel, a wire lying in water, or a crowd that has not stopped shouting, and each such finding is a reason to wait at the edge. Personal protective equipment, or PPE, is worn before the first hand is laid on a patient, with gloves at the least and eye and mouth protection where they are available, and it is used for every patient rather than for the ones who look infectious. The lay first aider who cannot make the scene safe stays out and calls for those who can, while the trained responder and the emergency medical technician make it safe within their equipment and their authority. Only then does the work of easing pain begin, because the rescuer must survive the rescue to be of use to anyone.

Untreated pain is a burden on the body as real as the wound, which is why relief belongs to treatment and not to its aftermath. Severe pain quickens the pulse and narrows the vessels, increasing the work of a heart that may already be short of blood to pump. It stiffens the muscles of the chest and the abdomen, so a patient with a rib fracture or a belly injury breathes in small sips, and small sips lead to collapsed lung segments and infection. Pain also keeps the patient from cooperating with the acts that save life, such as lying still while a limb is splinted, keeping a dressing pressed, or turning onto a stretcher without tearing a clot. The finding that pain is doing harm is a patient who breathes in short gasps, refuses to lie flat, or grows restless while the pulse climbs without new bleeding, and that finding is treated as a complication rather than as a complaint.

Pain is also information, and it is collected before any attempt is made to remove it, because the description a patient gives is one of the few pieces of history that only the patient can supply. The site, the character, the moment it began, what makes it worse, and what makes it better are all part of the picture, and the change in that picture over time is more useful than any single answer. A spoken scale on which the patient says the pain is none, mild, moderate, or severe is enough for the field, while the numbers and the wording of any other scale differ between services and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol. The assessment is recorded before a medicine is given, because the level of consciousness is judged partly by the response to a painful stimulus. Some patients cannot describe pain at all, so a small child who cries, draws the limbs up, or goes quiet and still is assessed with the help of the parent or the familiar adult, and a patient who does not speak the language of the responder may under-report pain. Grimacing, guarding, and a limb held absolutely still are recorded in the same way as a spoken score, because the body speaks for the patient who cannot.

Pain relief never displaces the order of the primary survey, and it never delays the control of hemorrhage or the journey to definitive care. Airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure are attended to first, in that order, because a patient who is not breathing gains nothing from comfort, and a patient bleeding to death needs pressure and a surgeon before a medicine for pain. The principle that decides the order when two correct acts compete for the same hands is life before limb, and it applies here as life before comfort as well. Analgesia is given while the patient is kept warm, splinted, and moved, not as a reason to remain on scene and not as a substitute for the acts that stop the bleeding. The finding that tells the responder to defer relief is any patient whose airway, breathing, or circulation is still failing. The exception is the patient whose pain is so severe that it prevents the very acts that save life, such as lying still or tolerating a splint, and that balance is struck by the provider the protocol authorizes to make it.

The measure available to every provider, and to the bystander who has nothing at all, is reassurance, and it is not a small thing. A calm voice that explains what is happening, what is about to happen, and what the patient should expect removes the fear that sharpens pain, and a hand held, a face brought to the level of the patient, and a familiar person kept close are care the lay first aider can give while waiting. Silence, unexplained hurry, and a conversation held over the patient as if the patient were not there increase both fear and pain. Positioning is the next measure any provider may use, and its principle is that the body's own position of comfort is usually the safest position for pain. A patient with a chest injury who is struggling to breathe may need to sit up, one with an abdominal injury may draw the knees up, and a patient with a back injury is kept still in the position found. The responder must not force a limb toward the shape it is supposed to have, because movement of a deformed fracture can injure a vessel or a nerve that is still intact, and where the spine may be injured the position of comfort and the need to limit motion are balanced by the trained responder.

Immobilization is pain relief, because a broken bone held still stops tearing at the tissue around it and stops sending new pain with every movement. The rule of this manual is that a severely deformed fracture is splinted in the position found and is never straightened in the field to make it look normal, and the reason is the risk to the vessels and the nerves that lie close to the bone. The lay first aider may support the limb with the hands, a rolled blanket, a board, or anything that holds it against the body, and may bind it loosely enough that the fingers or toes beyond it stay warm and pink. The trained responder or paramedic adds padding over the bony points and a splint that reaches above and below the injury, and then checks what lies beyond it, because a splint that is too tight becomes a new source of pain and a new danger. The finding that a splint is too tight is a limb that has become pale or blue, a pulse that can no longer be felt below it, numbness, or pain that rises rather than falls, and the response is to loosen and reapply rather than to wait. A splint is not a treatment for the fracture, but a way of keeping the patient alive and as comfortable as possible until definitive hospital care.

Cold is a simple measure that belongs to everyone, and it works by narrowing the vessels and reducing the swelling that stretches the tissue around an injury. Cold is never placed directly on the skin, because it can freeze the skin and cause a burn of its own, and it is never placed on an open wound, on tissue that looks pale or dead, or on a limb whose circulation is already in doubt. A cloth, a bandage, or a plastic bag with a little water in it is laid between the cold source and the skin, and a short application is enough, with its length set by the local protocol and confirmed against the current guideline. A period such as 20 minutes is often described as a useful first application, and that number, like every other in this chapter, must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the safe time differs with the part of the body and the age of the patient. Cold is not a substitute for a splint, for a dressing, or for transport, and it must not delay any of them. The finding that cold should be stopped is skin that has become white, hard, or numb, or pain that is now worse than before.

An exposed wound is a painful wound, and much of the pain a responder can remove is removed by covering the injury once and leaving it alone, because air moving across a raw surface, a dressing that dries and sticks, and the repeated lifting of a dressing to check the bleeding all add pain and disturb the clot. An embedded object is stabilized in place and never removed in the field, because removal may release bleeding that cannot be controlled and may injure a structure the object is not yet touching. Cold is also a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort, and it makes pain worse at the same time as it makes bleeding worse. The lay first aider removes wet clothing, replaces it with dry covering, insulates the patient from the ground, and covers the head, because much of the heat is lost downward and from the scalp. The finding that warming has failed is a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold, because shivering is the body's attempt to make heat and its disappearance is a warning rather than an improvement. Every number used to describe dangerous cold, such as a body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius, is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted line differs between services and editions.

Medicines that relieve pain are a powerful part of trauma care, and they are also the part of this chapter that carries the greatest risk, which is why the decision to use them belongs to a named provider and to a protocol. This manual names no substance, no amount, and no interval, because those things differ between countries, between services, and between editions of the same guideline, and because a listener must not be able to take a prescription from a book. What the manual describes is the decision: who may make it, what finding makes it urgent, what finding makes it dangerous, and what must be watched while its effect is present. The finding that makes the decision urgent is pain that is severe, that prevents the patient from cooperating with care, or that is harming the breathing and the circulation. The finding that makes it dangerous is a patient whose airway is not protected, whose breathing is already depressed, whose circulation is failing, or whose level of consciousness cannot be followed reliably. Where those findings are present, the decision belongs to the physician or to the provider the protocol authorizes to weigh them, and never to the responder's own estimate of what the patient deserves.

The range of available medicines is wide, and the choice among them belongs to the provider authorized to make it rather than to whoever happens to be first. A simple medicine may be enough for mild pain in a patient who is fully awake and not vomiting, while a stronger medicine is reserved for severe pain, and which medicine is used, and how it is given, are settled by the prescriber and the protocol rather than by the responder. The stronger medicines that dull pain also dull the patient, which is why the choice is coupled to the ability to watch the patient rather than separated from it. A nerve block, which is the deliberate numbing of a nerve to remove pain from a region, is a procedure for a trained clinician and not for the field, and it belongs to definitive care or to a service that specifically authorizes it. Nothing in this paragraph is an instruction, and every substance, amount, and interval remains subject to the local protocol and the prescriber.

The patient who is bleeding is the one in whom pain relief must be weighed most carefully, because a medicine that dulls pain may also lower the blood pressure and hide the signs of worsening shock. A patient in shock may respond differently to a medicine than a patient with a normal circulation, and the amount belongs to the provider who can see the whole patient and knows the protocol. The patient with a head injury is the second such patient, because relief that sedates confuses the examination of the level of consciousness, and the Glasgow coma scale, which is the standard way of recording that level, loses its value when the patient has been made drowsy by a medicine. Relief may still be given, because pain itself raises the pressure inside the head and worsens the injury, and the balance is struck by the physician with the monitoring and the imaging that definitive care provides. The finding that must be passed to the receiving team is the time, the substance, and the effect of any medicine given, so that the next examination of the level of consciousness can be read against it. The rule is not that the injured brain is never given relief, but that relief is given by a provider who can continue to follow the brain afterward.

The patient whose pain is out of proportion to the injury is the most important patient in this chapter, because that disproportion is a diagnostic sign and not a complaint. A limb that is tense, that hurts far more than the wound suggests, that hurts when the fingers or toes are stretched, and that is becoming numb or weak is a limb whose pressure inside may be rising toward compartment syndrome, and the correct acts are to remove anything tight, to keep the limb at the level of the heart unless the protocol says otherwise, and to move the patient toward definitive care without delay. Pain that grows while the patient is watched, or that is not eased by a splint in the correct position, is a finding that demands escalation and a report to the receiving team in plain words. A small wound with pain far beyond its size may also mean a retained fragment, a deep track, or a collection of blood expanding beneath the skin, and the responder does not probe it to find out. The sudden disappearance of pain in a limb that was painful can be as serious as the pain itself, because it may mean that the nerve or the blood supply has been lost. A belly that is rigid and tender, a pain worse when the patient moves, and chest pain that worsens with a deep breath can all be signs of bleeding inside a cavity, and none of them is treated by binding the chest tightly, which this manual forbids because it prevents the breathing the patient needs.

A teaching that must be corrected is the belief that relief must be withheld so that the examination of the abdomen or the chest stays honest. The signs that guide the surgeon, such as a rigid belly, a growing distension, localized tenderness, and a change in the level of consciousness, are not removed by reasonable relief, and the trend of those signs remains readable while the patient is comfortable. Pain also harms the patient in its own right, because a patient in agony cannot cooperate with the examination, cannot breathe deeply, and cannot be moved safely. The decision to give or withhold relief belongs to the physician and the protocol, and the observations continue before and after it in the same order and at the same intervals. The finding that changes the plan is any new or worsening sign, because that finding is reported to the physician whether or not the patient still complains of pain.

Whenever a medicine for pain is given, the monitoring that must accompany it begins at the same moment and continues until the patient is handed over. The level of consciousness, the rate and depth of breathing, the oxygen saturation, the pulse, the blood pressure, the color and warmth of the skin, and the ability to speak and swallow tell the provider whether the medicine is helping or harming. The findings that should stop any further medicine and bring the protocol's reversal plan into action are a patient who is becoming drowsy, a breathing rate that is slowing or becoming shallow, a fall in the blood pressure, and a patient who can no longer be woken, and nausea, vomiting, itching, a rash, or a swollen face or throat are recorded and reported as well. The specific danger is sedation, which is the relief of pain carried one step further into loss of alertness and of the drive to breathe, and the line between comfortable and too drowsy moves fastest in the patient who has lost blood, the patient who is cold, the patient who is old, and the patient given more than one medicine. This is why a patient who has received such a medicine is never left alone, why the observations are repeated rather than assumed, and why the receiving team is told exactly what was given. The equipment and training this monitoring requires are the reason the decision is restricted to the providers a service authorizes, and a service that cannot monitor should not authorize the medicine.

The record of what was given is part of the treatment, because the next provider must be able to read the patient's course rather than guess it. The time, the substance, the effect on the pain, and any adverse effect are written where the receiving team will see them and spoken aloud at the handover, and the same care is taken with the measures that were not medicines. A patient moved with an embedded object or a tourniquet in place carries the times and details of those measures in the same record, because the receiving team must know what is in the wound and how long the limb has been without flow. The finding that the record is incomplete is any gap that forces the next provider to start the story again, and a gap of that kind is itself a harm.

The lay first aider may do far more for pain than most people expect, and may not do the one thing most people reach for. The lay first aider reassures, explains, stays present, positions and supports the injury, covers the wound, applies cold through a barrier, keeps the patient warm, and asks someone to call emergency medical services. The lay first aider does not give any medicine, does not take a medicine from the patient's own pocket without instruction, does not remove an embedded object, does not straighten a deformed limb, and does not loosen a tourniquet that has controlled bleeding. The reason for the last three rules is the same, which is that the act may release bleeding or injure tissue that is still intact, and pain is not a reason to break the rule. The trained first responder and the emergency medical technician work within a service, a kit, and a protocol, and their contribution is broader because they can measure and monitor: they assess and record the pain, splint and immobilize properly, apply cold, keep the patient warm, and repeat the observations that show whether the injury is worsening. Some services authorize them to give a simple pain-relieving medicine under a protocol or the direction of a clinician, while the finding that sends them higher is pain out of proportion, a limb that is swelling or becoming numb, a changing breathing pattern, or a falling level of consciousness.

The paramedic carries a wider set of authorizations and the monitoring equipment they require, and may make decisions about stronger relief within the local protocol. That authority carries the duty to watch the patient continuously, to record the response, and to withhold or stop a medicine when the findings call for it, and the protocol decides the substance, the amount, and the interval, none of which this manual states. The nurse meets the patient at the door of the emergency department, on the ward, or in the ambulance bay, and the nurse's part is assessment, administration, and surveillance: repeating the assessment the field began, giving the medicine the prescriber ordered, and watching for the response and the adverse effects listed here. The nurse is often the person who notices that the pain is out of proportion, that the dressing is soaked, that the limb has changed color, or that the breathing has become shallow, and that finding is reported to the physician at once. The physician decides, weighing the injury, the patient, the circulation, the breathing, and the diagnosis against one another, choosing whether a medicine is given and setting the monitoring that accompanies it, and keeping the diagnostic question open. The finding the physician treats as a surgical emergency rather than as a pain problem is a limb that is tense and painful on stretch with a failing pulse, because that finding may need an operation to release the pressure inside.

The trauma surgeon owns the definitive treatment of the injuries that cause the pain, and many acts that remove pain permanently are surgical acts. The surgeon explores the wound, removes a bullet or a fragment when it is clinically indicated and never because a responder decided it should come out, repairs a torn vessel or tendon or nerve, releases the pressure inside a limb when compartment syndrome is confirmed, and controls bleeding inside a cavity. A nerve block may be placed by a trained clinician as part of definitive care, in a setting where the patient can be monitored and the procedure and its complications can be managed, and nothing in this chapter authorizes any of those procedures in the field. There is also a group of patients for whom relief is not a step toward a cure but the whole of the care that can be offered, and this manual does not turn away from them. A patient who is dying, one beyond the reach of surgery, and one who must wait while others are treated first are still owed warmth, shelter, a position that eases breathing, and the presence of someone who stays. The decision about medicine for such a patient belongs to the physician and the protocol, and while nobody in this manual is authorized to end a life or hasten a death, comfort is part of care even when survival is not possible.

To summarize, pain in trauma is part of the illness rather than a complaint that follows it, and it is treated by every provider at the level that provider's training, equipment, and protocol allow. The scene is made safe and personal protective equipment is worn before any care begins, the lethal possibility of pain out of proportion to the injury is named early, and the primary survey in the order of ABCDE comes before any measure of comfort and is never delayed by it. The measures available to everyone are reassurance, positioning, immobilization, cold applied through a barrier, protection of the wound, warmth, and a calm presence, and each has a finding that shows whether it is working and a finding that shows it is not. Medicines that relieve pain belong to the provider whom the service authorizes, and this chapter names no substance, no amount, and no interval, because those are set by the local protocol and the prescriber; what is described is who makes the decision, what makes it urgent, what makes it dangerous, and what must be monitored. The monitoring that accompanies any such medicine watches the level of consciousness, the breathing, the pulse, the blood pressure, and the skin, and a patient who becomes drowsy, whose breathing slows, or whose pressure falls is one in whom the medicine must stop and help must be called. The patient whose pain is out of proportion, whose limb becomes tense or numb, or whose pain suddenly disappears is a diagnostic emergency and is moved toward definitive care. Every time, temperature, pressure, and number in this chapter is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 46 — Imaging

Imaging is a hospital act, and the first responder's part in it is restraint, because no picture taken at the roadside ever stopped bleeding that a hand could not stop. Traffic, fire, electricity, water, animals, violence, structural collapse, and the hazards of the patient's own body fluids are made safe before the first glove is put on. The lethal possibility of this chapter is a patient who bleeds while a team waits for a study. The imaging suite has dangers of its own, which are radiation, the magnetic field of the magnetic resonance scanner, contrast material, and contaminated blood and tissue that make personal protective equipment, or PPE, necessary in every room. This chapter describes what each kind of image answers, what it cannot answer, and who may ask for it, and it is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.
