No image is an answer in itself, because an image replies to a question and the question must exist before the patient is moved. An image ordered without a question produces a report nobody can use, and an image ordered only to reassure delays treatment the patient needs. The clinician who asks for the study owns the question, and the clinician who reads it must know what the patient looked like when it was made. The finding that makes an image useful is not its quality but its power to change what the team does next.

Who owns what in imaging is decided by training, authorization, and equipment rather than by urgency. The lay first aider never orders an image, never reads one, and never delays the journey for one, and the lay first aider's contribution is an account of the mechanism of injury, the time it happened, and every change since. The trained responder, the emergency medical technician, and the paramedic may use a bedside ultrasound device in services that carry one under a written protocol, and even then the finding is reported rather than treated. The nurse manages the patient during the study and recognizes the deterioration that must end it. The physician orders the study, the radiologist interprets it, and the trauma surgeon decides what the operating room must do about it.

Plain radiography is the oldest and most available image, and its strength is bone. A radiograph answers whether a bone is broken, whether a joint is displaced, whether a fracture is aligned, and whether a dense object lies inside the body, and it answers in seconds in almost every hospital. The examination is made in at least two views taken at right angles, because a fracture invisible in one direction is often obvious in the other, and the joints above and below the injury belong in the same study. A physician satisfied by a normal radiograph in a patient with continuing pain makes the mistake this chapter exists to prevent.

What a radiograph cannot do matters as much as what it can, and those limits are why a normal film never ends an assessment. Soft tissue, blood, and clot are shown poorly, so a fracture may be invisible at first, and an interval such as 10 to 14 days is a teaching illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because the timing differs with the bone and the patient. A rib fracture may be hidden, and a chest radiograph taken with the patient lying flat hides a pneumothorax and flattens the mediastinum that would warn of a torn aorta. The clinician treats the patient and the mechanism of injury and uses the radiograph as one piece of evidence among several.

The radiograph has a second and narrower use, which is the search for a foreign body dense enough to cast a shadow. Metal, most glass, gravel, and many fragments of a bullet are radio-opaque and appear as clear marks that can be located in relation to a fracture or a joint. Wood, plastic, thorns, and some glass are radiolucent and disappear against the tissue, so a clean radiograph never proves that nothing was left in a wound. The responder must not probe a wound in search of an object, because probing pushes contamination deeper and can injure a structure that is still intact. Every embedded object is stabilized in place while the patient is moved with it in place, removal is a surgical decision made when it is clinically indicated, and no first responder extracts a bullet.

The chest and the pelvis are the two places where a plain radiograph still earns its place in the first minutes, because each answers a question that changes the next action. A chest radiograph taken at the bedside answers whether a lung has collapsed, whether blood has collected in the pleural space, and whether the mediastinum has widened, and it does so in a patient too unstable to leave the resuscitation room. A pelvic radiograph answers whether the ring of the pelvis has broken, which predicts bleeding from vessels no hand or dressing can reach. A tension pneumothorax, however, is diagnosed with the eyes and the hands and not with a film, and no image may delay the release of air compressing the heart.

Ultrasound is the image that has moved closest to the bedside, and it answers one question with great power, which is whether fluid has collected where fluid does not belong. A trained clinician passes a probe over the abdomen, the flanks, the lower chest, and the region around the heart, and looks for blood in the peritoneal cavity, the pleural space, and the sac around the heart. The study takes minutes, can be repeated as the patient changes, uses no radiation, and does not require moving the patient out of the resuscitation room. The combination that matters most is free fluid together with an unstable circulation, because that combination sends the patient to the operating room rather than to the scanner. Ultrasound is performed by a physician or by a trained responder or paramedic under a protocol and never by a lay first aider.

Ultrasound has limits as real as its strengths, and a negative study never closes the question. Bowel gas, obesity, a distended stomach, and air that has leaked under the skin block the passage of sound and hide the fluid behind them, and a thin layer of blood can be missed by an experienced hand. The quality of the image depends on the skill of the operator, so a study performed in haste by an untrained hand is worse than no study. The examination is repeated rather than trusted, because fluid absent on arrival may be present an hour later, and the trend over time carries more meaning than a single view. The finding that overrides a negative ultrasound is a patient who keeps deteriorating without explanation, and that patient belongs in the operating room or the scanner according to the judgment of the trauma surgeon.

Beyond fluid, ultrasound answers several other questions at the bedside when the operator is trained and the protocol allows it. It can find a radiolucent foreign body that a radiograph cannot show and can display its depth and its relation to a vessel or a tendon. It can examine a vessel for flow and for a collection of blood around it, and it can guide a needle or a drain into a collection that must be emptied. In a pregnant patient it answers the obstetric question without radiation, which is why ultrasound is the first image in pregnancy whenever it can answer the question at hand. These uses belong to the physician and the trained clinician, and each is a report to the team rather than a treatment.

Prehospital ultrasound exists in some services and not in others, and where it exists it is a tool of the trained responder or paramedic under a written protocol. A service that carries the device uses it to answer a narrow question that changes a decision, which may be fluid in the abdomen, the absence of lung sliding over one chest, or the movement of the wall of the heart. What it never changes is the journey, because the patient is loaded and moving while the study is performed and no pause is taken for a better picture. The finding that ends field imaging is a patient whose airway, breathing, or circulation is failing, and that finding means the device is put away and the vehicle moves. The rule is therefore short and absolute, which is that transport is never delayed for an image.

Computed tomography is the reference image for the injured head and trunk, and its strength is that it shows bone, blood, air, and soft tissue together. The term is spelled out at its first mention in this chapter because computed tomography, or CT, is what a listener will hear named in every trauma room. A CT examination answers whether there is blood inside the skull, whether an organ in the chest or abdomen is torn, whether there is free fluid or free air in the belly, and whether the spine has broken, and it answers within minutes in a hospital that has the machine and the team. A whole-body study is performed in a patient stable enough to lie still, and it is the standard by which the injured trunk and head are assessed in a trauma center.

The CT examination of the head answers a few questions that decide between the operating room and the ward. It shows an epidural collection of blood, a subdural collection, bleeding beneath the arachnoid, bruising of the brain itself, a fracture of the skull, and air that has entered the skull. The finding that most often sends a patient to the operating room is a collection that compresses the brain and pushes the midline aside, and a shift beyond 5 millimeters is a figure quoted as an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the decision depends on the patient and not on the number alone. A patient who is awake and talking and then becomes drowsy may have a collection that is expanding, and that interval of apparent recovery is one of the traps of head injury. A patient whose medicine thins the blood may bleed after a blow that leaves no mark, so a normal CT in that patient does not end the observation.

The CT examination of the trunk answers where the injury is and whether it is still bleeding. It shows free fluid in the abdomen, an injury of the liver, spleen, kidney, or pancreas, a tear of the mesentery or bowel, a collection behind the peritoneum, a fracture of the pelvis, and blood or air in the chest. When contrast material is used according to the protocol, the study can show contrast escaping from a torn vessel, which is the image of active bleeding and the finding that makes the team move faster. The grade of an organ injury informs the decision between observation, an operation, and a radiological procedure, and it is one fact among several the surgeon weighs. The study is performed in a patient stable enough to tolerate the journey to the machine, and not in a patient bleeding faster than the team can replace.

The limits of CT are the limits of any study that requires a stable patient in a room far from the resuscitation area. A patient who is bleeding and unstable can die in the scanner, because the team that must stop the bleeding is separated from the patient by corridors and minutes. Movement to the machine removes hands from the patient and removes the patient from the place where an airway can be secured and a chest opened. The rule that follows is that the operating room is the first destination for a patient who remains unstable after the first measures, and the scan comes after bleeding is controlled when the question requires it. The trauma surgeon owns that decision, and no image is worth a life spent waiting for it.

CT is also the way a broken spine is found in a patient who cannot be examined reliably. A patient who is awake, sober, free of pain in the neck, and free of a distracting injury may have the neck cleared by examination in many protocols, and that decision belongs to the physician. A patient who is unconscious, intoxicated, or unable to answer has the whole spine imaged, because a missed injury of the neck can leave a patient paralyzed after a rescue that appeared successful. CT shows bone with great clarity and finds a fracture, a dislocation, or a misalignment of the spinal column. It does not show the cord, the discs, or the ligaments well, so a patient with a normal CT and an abnormal examination needs a different study. The finding that ends the use of CT for the spine is a neurological abnormality that requires the cord itself to be seen.

Magnetic resonance imaging is the study that shows the spinal cord, and its strength is the soft tissue that CT cannot resolve. The term is spelled out at its first mention in this chapter because magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, is what a listener will hear named when the cord and the ligaments are in question. MRI shows the cord, the discs between the vertebrae, the ligaments that hold the column together, a collection of blood around the cord, and swelling of the cord itself after a blow. It is the study that finds an injury of the cord when the radiograph and the CT are normal. MRI cannot be performed in a patient who is unstable, who cannot lie still, who has certain metal implants, or who has monitoring incompatible with the magnet, and it takes far longer than CT. A period such as 24 hours is sometimes named as the window in which the study is most useful, and that interval is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because the timing depends on the patient and the service.

The same study answers questions in the brain that CT answers only partly. MRI shows the fine structure of the brain, areas of bruising scattered through the white matter after a violent movement of the head, and changes that may explain a patient whose level of consciousness does not match the CT report. It is used when the injury is not explained by the earlier images and when recovery is not following the expected course. It is not a study for the acute resuscitation room, and it is never obtained at the cost of a delay in treating a patient who is bleeding or whose brain is compressed. The finding that makes the study urgent is a neurological deficit without an explanation on CT.

Computed tomographic angiography is the study that answers the question of the vessel, and it combines the speed of CT with the ability to show the channel of the blood. It shows the aorta, the vessels of the neck, the vessels of the arms and legs, and the great vessels of the abdomen and chest, and it can show contrast escaping from a torn vessel into the tissue around it. The study is performed with contrast material, and the choice of material, the decision to use it, and the preparation of the patient belong to the physician and the local protocol rather than to any rule taken from this book. It answers whether a vessel is torn, blocked, or bleeding, and it answers in a patient stable enough to lie still. The finding that changes the plan is an injury of a named vessel, because that decides whether the patient needs an operation, a procedure in the radiology suite, or close observation.

The limits of computed tomographic angiography are the limits of every study that depends on timing and on a stable patient. A small vessel may be missed when the contrast and the movement of the scanner do not meet at the right instant, and a vessel that has gone into spasm after injury may look normal while the tissue it supplies is dying. A patient who cannot lie still produces an image that cannot be read, and a patient whose kidneys are already damaged may be harmed by the contrast material, which is a decision the physician must weigh. The study also takes time, and a patient with hard signs of a vascular injury, which are bleeding that will not stop, a pulse that has disappeared, or a limb that is cold and pale, may need the operating room before any image is obtained. A normal study therefore does not exclude a vascular injury when the examination says otherwise.

Conventional angiography is the older study of the vessel, and it is the place where the image and the treatment are the same act. A thin tube is passed into a vessel and contrast is injected at the point where the question lies, so the physician sees the bleeding vessel and can then block it from the inside with material placed through the same tube. This is the procedure of choice for bleeding from the pelvis after a fracture, for bleeding from the liver or spleen in a patient stable enough to be moved, and for bleeding from the neck or from a vessel that an operation cannot reach. It is performed by an interventional radiologist, a physician trained in procedures guided by imaging, and it requires a circulation that can tolerate lying on the table for the time the procedure takes. The procedure is both diagnosis and treatment, and it is definitive hospital care in the fullest sense. The finding that makes it possible is a patient responding enough to the first measures to be moved, because a patient who is exsanguinating belongs in the operating room instead.

Conventional angiography has limits the team must respect, because it is a powerful tool in the wrong order. It is not a procedure for a patient bleeding faster than blood can be given, because the team would be away from the operating room while the patient empties. It is used after an operation when bleeding continues from a site the surgeon packed rather than repaired, and before an operation when the site of bleeding is known to be reachable only from inside a vessel. It requires a specialist, a suite, and equipment many hospitals do not have, so the local protocol decides who is sent where and by what route. The finding that tells the team to abandon the procedure is a patient who becomes unstable on the table, because the operation must then take priority.

For the prehospital provider the rule about imaging is the rule about transport, and it is written to be remembered under pressure. Transport is never delayed for an image, no image is a reason to wait, and the only images taken before arrival are those the service has trained the responder to obtain under a protocol that authorizes them. A study that changes the destination or the warning given to the receiving hospital is useful, and a study that merely satisfies curiosity is a delay that costs blood. When the patient has already been imaged at another hospital, the receiving team must be told what was done, what was found, and what has changed since, and the images and the report must travel with the patient rather than follow later. The finding that ends every field discussion of imaging is a patient whose condition is worsening, because at that moment the only useful action is to move.

The hospital uses imaging to decide between the operating room and the ward, but the decision is made by the patient's physiology and not by the picture alone. The patient who remains hypotensive after the first measures, whose abdomen is rigid and tender, whose chest is filling with blood, or who needs continuous replacement of blood belongs in the operating room whatever the image shows. The patient whose scan shows a contained injury of the liver or spleen, whose circulation is stable, and whose pain can be managed belongs on a ward or in a monitored bed where the examination can be repeated. The patient between those two belongs in an intensive care unit, or ICU, where the airway can be watched and the circulation supported while the team decides. The image informs the decision by showing where the injury is and whether it is still bleeding, and it never makes the decision by itself. The finding that moves a patient from the ward toward the operating room is any change for the worse, because observation is a treatment only while the patient is improving.

The limits of a normal image are the heart of this chapter, because the normal report is the one that most often misleads. An image records a single moment in an injury that continues to evolve, and a study performed in the first hour may be normal while a collection of blood is still forming. A small pneumothorax, a tear of the bowel, a bruise of the pancreas, and an injury behind the peritoneum may all be invisible at first and reveal themselves only on a repeated examination. The clinician therefore treats the patient and repeats the examination, and a normal image in a patient who is deteriorating is a reason to look again rather than to relax. A constructed illustration is the patient whose first scan is reported as normal, whose pulse rises through the night, and whose repeated scan the next morning shows the injury that was there all along.

Some patients need a different approach because their bodies or their circumstances change the risk. A pregnant patient is imaged only when the question cannot be answered by ultrasound, and the decision about which study to use and how to protect the unborn child belongs to the physician and the local protocol. A child is more sensitive to radiation than an adult, so the physician chooses the smallest study that answers the question rather than the most complete one. An older patient whose medicine thins the blood may bleed into the skull after a fall that seemed minor, so a normal scan in that patient is followed by observation and a repeated examination. Every threshold and interval in this chapter is an illustration to be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, because accepted practice differs between services and editions.

Imaging takes place in a cold room with an undressed patient on a hard table, and it is therefore a place where hypothermia begins if nobody prevents it. A patient who is bleeding, burned, exposed, or immobilized loses heat quickly, and the loss is increased by wet sheets, contrast material, a cold suite, and the time spent waiting for a report. The team keeps the patient covered between images, insulates the patient from the table where possible, keeps the room and blankets warm, and remembers that a cold patient clots poorly and tolerates blood loss badly. The monitor stays on the patient throughout the study, and the provider who owns the airway and the circulation stays in the room rather than watching from a window. A temperature such as 35 degrees Celsius is often quoted as the point at which cold becomes dangerous, and that figure, like every other in this manual, must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol because the threshold shifts with the patient and the way it is measured. The finding that stops the study is a patient becoming more unstable rather than less.

The image must be communicated as carefully as it is obtained, because a finding that never reaches the team was never made. Every study has a time, a name, and a report, and the clinician who ordered it is responsible for reading the report and acting on it rather than filing it. The handover between the emergency team and the ward, the operating room, or the intensive care unit includes what was imaged, what was found, and what the images do not explain, and it names the provider who will follow the result. The record of the imaging is part of the clinical record and is written with the same care as the record of an operation. The finding that demands a spoken conversation rather than a written note is a result that changes the plan before the next shift arrives.

To summarize, imaging answers questions and never treats patients, so the question comes before the study and the patient's condition comes before both. Plain radiography answers questions about bone, alignment, and a radio-opaque foreign body, and it cannot show soft tissue, a radiolucent object, or a fracture that has not yet become visible. Ultrasound answers at the bedside whether fluid has collected where it should not, and it depends on the operator, the body, and repetition rather than on a single view. Computed tomography is the reference for the injured head and trunk and shows bone, blood, and organ injury together, while it requires a patient stable enough to travel to the machine. Magnetic resonance imaging shows the spinal cord, the discs, and the ligaments, while computed tomographic angiography and conventional angiography show the vessel, the last of these being both the diagnosis and the treatment. The prehospital provider never delays transport for an image, the hospital decides between the operating room and the ward by the patient's physiology and not by the picture, and a normal image never overrides a patient who is deteriorating. Every time, depth, and figure in this chapter is an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, or the law of the country where you work.

# Chapter 47 — Wound Closure

Closing a wound is a decision taken in the middle of treatment rather than a finishing touch, and it can save a hand, a face, or a life while it can undo all three. The lay first aider never closes a wound; the lay first aider covers it with a clean dressing, presses on it if it bleeds, keeps the patient warm, and reaches emergency medical services, because a protected wound is a treated wound. The trained responder or paramedic dresses the wound and, where the local protocol authorizes it, may bring the edges of a small, clean, superficial wound together with an adhesive strip, but deliberate closure belongs to definitive hospital care. The lethal possibility named first here is infection rather than hemorrhage, and the finding that reveals it is a wound sealed over contamination, dead tissue, or a retained object, because such a wound can become an abscess, a spreading infection, or sepsis. Scene safety comes before the patient, so traffic, fire, electricity, water, animals, violence, collapsing structures, and the patient's own body fluids are dealt with before any hand is laid on a wound. This chapter does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

Closure is the final act of a sequence, and the sequence decides whether closure is safe. The first step is control of bleeding, because a wound that is still bleeding cannot be examined or cleaned. The next is examination of the wound and of the structures beneath it, including the tendon, the nerve, and the vessel, because a closure performed too early hides the injury that matters most. Cleaning follows, and it removes the bacteria, the grit, and the old clot that a closed wound would keep inside. Then dead tissue and reachable foreign material are removed, and only then does the question of closure arise. Closure restores the barrier of the skin and holds the edges of a clean wound in contact so that it heals by primary intention, while a wound left open heals by secondary intention, filling from its base with granulation tissue. Each path is a choice rather than a failure, made by the clinician who has examined the wound, the patient, and the injury.

Certain conditions must be met before any wound is closed, and checking them in order protects the patient from a decision that cannot be taken back. Bleeding must be controlled, the wound must be clean enough, and there must be no dead tissue, no foreign body, and no established infection, because closure over any of those seals the problem inside the body. The edges must meet without tension, since skin pulled together under tension dies, separates, and leaves a wider scar than an open wound would have. The tissue must be alive and the patient must be able to heal it, which brings the circulation and the patient's other illnesses into the decision. Before the skin is closed, the function beneath it is examined and written down, because a divided tendon, a divided nerve, and an injured vessel each change the operation the patient needs. The examination asks the patient to move the fingers or the toes, tests feeling at the wound and beyond it, and checks the pulse and the color of the skin downstream, and it is repeated after closure so that a change is noticed. A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient, is the hand wound over a knuckle that is closed as a simple laceration while the tendon beneath has been cut, so that a finger stops working.

Time is one of the conditions that decide whether a wound may be closed, because bacteria multiply as the hours pass and because the tissue at the edge of a wound loses resistance as it dries and swells. A clean wound seen soon after the injury is a candidate for closure, while the same wound seen much later is treated with more caution. The interval that separates those two situations is taught as a number that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because services, countries, and editions place the line differently and because the site changes the answer. The clinician uses the interval as one factor among the contamination, the site, the depth, and the patient rather than as an arithmetic rule. What the field responder contributes is the time of the injury, recorded and handed over, because a receiving team that does not know when the wound was made cannot decide well.

Sutures are the method most listeners picture when they hear the word closure, and they suit the wound that needs precise approximation and support. A suture holds the edges of a full-thickness skin wound together, and it can be placed in layers, so that a deep layer closes a dead space and a superficial layer brings the skin into a fine line. Sutures suit clean lacerations of the face, where the cosmetic and functional stakes are high, and they suit the scalp, the trunk, and the limbs, and they suit wounds whose edges will not stay together without a hold that adhesive strips cannot give. They harm the contaminated wound, because a suture line crosses a surface that already carries bacteria and gives those bacteria a closed space in which to multiply. They harm the wound with a cavity beneath it, because blood and serum collect there and become an abscess while the surface still looks tidy. They harm skin pulled together under tension, because tight sutures strangulate the tissue along the line so that the skin dies and the knots cut through. The finding that should make a clinician choose another method is skin that blanches and stays pale when the edges are brought together.

Staples are a closure method for wounds that are long, straight, and under little tension, and they are used most often on the scalp and the trunk, and sometimes on a limb where the cosmetic result matters less. Their advantages are speed and a strong hold, and speed is an advantage in a patient who must go to the operating room for another injury. Staples harm the face, where a fine scar matters, and they harm the hand and the fingers, where delicate structures lie beneath and the scar must not restrict movement. They harm a wound across a joint, because the pull of the joint opens the line between the staples. They are not a method for a contaminated wound, a bite, or a wound with a dead space beneath it, and they are placed by a physician or a nurse under a protocol rather than by a first aider. The finding that tells the clinician to choose fine sutures instead is a wound on the face or over a moving part.

Adhesive strips are a gentle method for small, superficial, low-tension wounds whose edges fall together on their own, and they suit a child or an anxious patient who will not tolerate a needle. They harm a wound under tension, because the strips lift and the wound gapes again, and they harm a wound across a joint, and they harm skin that is wet, hairy, or sweating, because they do not stick and therefore do not hold. Tissue adhesive is a liquid that bonds the dried edges of a wound, and it suits small, clean, superficial wounds that are not under tension, particularly in children and on the face when an experienced clinician applies it. Adhesive harms a wound under tension, a wound across a joint, and a wound that is still bleeding, and its worst harm is a wound in which the liquid runs into the depth instead of staying on the surface, because then the contaminant is sealed inside and an abscess forms beneath an intact surface. Neither strips nor adhesive is a method for a contaminated wound, a bite, a puncture, or a wound with a retained foreign body, and where a protocol authorizes a trained responder to use strips, deeper wounds still belong to definitive care.

The four methods are choices rather than rungs of a ladder, because no method is better than another in itself and each is better or worse for a particular wound. The clinician chooses by asking what the wound needs, whether that is a fine line on the face, a strong hold on the scalp, speed in a patient who is bleeding elsewhere, or the gentlest method for a frightened child. The site, the depth, the tension, the contamination, the time since the injury, the state of the tissue, and the patient's ability to heal all enter the decision. The experience of the operator enters it as well, because a method a clinician cannot perform well is not a method for that clinician to choose. The cosmetic and functional stakes decide the site, since a scar on the back and a scar across a knuckle are different problems. The wrong method placed in a dirty wound harms the patient far more than the right method placed in a clean one, so the question of whether to close at all comes before the question of how.

Some wounds must not be closed immediately, and the list is short enough to remember even though the reasoning behind it is long. The bite, the heavily contaminated wound, the puncture, and the wound with a retained foreign body are the four that this chapter names, and each is a wound in which closure would seal contamination inside the body. To those are added the wound with dead tissue, the wound that is already infected, and the patient whose circulation is too poor to heal a closed wound. A bite carries the bacteria of the mouth that made it deep into the tissue rather than across the surface, and an animal bite is often a laceration with a crush that leaves a rim of dead tissue which cannot resist those bacteria. A human bite is at least as dangerous, and the wound over a knuckle that follows a blow to a tooth is the classic example, because the joint and the tendon beneath may already be inoculated and because the patient often delays seeking care. Closing a bite primarily is a decision for the surgeon, usually made only after the wound has been cleaned, explored, and sometimes left open under a dressing for a planned interval. The finding that makes a bite urgent is a wound over a joint, a wound on the hand, a wound with loss of movement, or a patient who is unwell.

A heavily contaminated wound is one in which the bacterial load is high enough that the patient's defenses cannot clear it, and the common sources are the roadway, the soil, the farmyard, the manure heap, and stagnant water. The wound that follows a fall from a motorcycle onto a road is the example most responders recognize, because it carries grit and asphalt into tissue that is already bruised and deprived of blood. Contamination is not measured by the appearance of the wound, since a wound that looks shallow may hold a deep pocket of dirt, and the only reliable answer is proper inspection and cleaning. A wound of this kind is left open after cleaning, covered with a dressing, and reviewed, and any closure is done later when the wound has shown that it is clean and that its tissue is alive. The field responder shortens the journey by dressing the wound without probing it and by reporting the mechanism of injury, because that report tells the receiving team what contamination to expect.

A puncture wound has a small opening and a deep track, and its danger lies in the part that cannot be seen. A nail through a shoe, a splinter, a thorn, and a fine fragment of metal all produce a wound whose surface may seal over a track that still holds dirt, clothing, and bacteria, and the sealed surface creates the closed space in which infection can grow. A puncture of the foot through a shoe is a particular trap, since rubber and sock are carried into the depth of the wound and since the bones and joints of the foot lie close beneath the skin. A wound with a retained foreign body is never closed over that body, and the object is never removed in the field, because a knife, a fragment of glass, or a piece of metal may be plugging the vessel beneath it and removal may release hemorrhage that no available measure can control. Such an object is stabilized with padding built around it, the wound is covered, and the patient is moved with the object still in position, because removal is a decision for the operating room. The finding that requires imaging and a surgical plan is any wound whose depth is unknown or whose pain and swelling are out of proportion to the size of its opening.

Dead tissue and dead space are two conditions that a closure can create as easily as it can correct, and an established infection is a third reason to leave a wound open. Tissue dies when its blood supply is torn, when it is crushed, when it is burned, or when it is pulled together under tension, and dead tissue inside a closed wound is a culture medium that the patient's defenses cannot reach. Dead space is the cavity beneath a closed skin line, and it fills with blood and serum that become a place for bacteria to grow, so a wound with a cavity must be closed in layers or left open. An infected wound needs to drain rather than to be sealed, because closure would spread the infection along the tissue planes. Infection announces itself with pain disproportionate to the wound, with redness that spreads beyond its edge, with warmth, swelling, discharge, and a patient who feels unwell, and the most dangerous form is the necrotizing infection, which travels quickly along the deep tissue and can progress within hours. The finding of skin that is tense, discolored, or numb, with gas in the tissue, is a surgical emergency, and the clinician who suspects it does not close the wound and does not wait. The field responder's contribution is to recognize that a wound is not behaving as a simple wound should, to avoid pressing into its depths, and to move the patient to care without delay.

Delayed primary closure is the deliberate plan of cleaning a contaminated wound, leaving it open under a dressing, and closing it later when it has shown that it is not infected and that its tissue is alive. The philosophy behind it is that a contaminated wound should be given time to declare itself before it is sealed. The interval is measured in days rather than in hours, and a figure such as 3 to 5 days is often quoted and, like every interval in this chapter, must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the timing depends on the wound, the patient, and the service. A wound managed in this way is examined at the planned review, and it is closed only when the redness has settled, the discharge has stopped, and the base of the wound has become clean and pink. Healing by secondary intention is the related plan in which the wound is left open to fill with granulation tissue from its base, and it suits the wound whose edges cannot be brought together without tension, the drained abscess cavity, and the patient too ill for a long operation. The choice among delayed closure, secondary intention, and closure during the first operation belongs to the surgeon, who weighs the scar and the function against the risk of infection.

The patient decides as much as the wound does, because closure asks the body to heal a wound that has been brought together and some bodies can answer that request and some cannot. A patient in shock has diverted blood away from the skin and will not heal a closure well, and a patient who is cold has the same problem, so resuscitation and warmth come before the cosmetic decision. Diabetes, disease of the arteries of the limbs, immunosuppression, treatment with steroids, poor nutrition, and smoking each reduce the ability of tissue to resist infection and to knit. Tetanus and antibiotics are part of the wound decision, and neither is taken from this book as an amount, because the tetanus answer depends on the vaccination history and the nature of the wound and is given by the provider authorized under the local protocol. The substance, the amount, the route, and the timing of an antibiotic belong to the prescriber and the local guideline, and the field responder records what is known and states plainly what is not, because the receiving team cannot weigh what it has not been told.

Closure is done in conditions that allow it to be done well, and a wound closed in poor light with no assistance and no time is a wound closed badly. The clinician needs to see the whole wound, to feel its depth, to have the instruments and the material that the local protocol provides, and to have help if the patient is a child or is in pain. Cleaning comes before closure and makes closure possible, because a wound closed with grit, clot, and bacteria still inside it has been given a sealed environment in which to infect. The method of cleaning and the volume of fluid used are decisions of the clinician and the local protocol, and this chapter teaches only the order, which is that the wound is cleaned, inspected, and prepared before any method of closure is chosen. Closing a wound is painful, and the control of that pain is a clinical decision made by the authorized provider before the closure begins, because a comfortable patient holds still and allows a better closure than a struggling one. The substance, the amount, the route, and the timing of any medicine belong to the prescriber and the local protocol, and no reader should take any of them from this manual.

Two sites deserve their own words, and the first is the face, where closure is a functional and cosmetic decision that belongs in the hands of the most experienced clinician available. The face has a rich blood supply, which helps it heal, and it also has the eye, the ear, the nose, the lips, and the muscles of expression, whose function can be changed by a scar that crosses them, so a clinician who is not experienced in facial closure refers the patient rather than practicing on the face. The scalp is the opposite problem, because it bleeds heavily, it hides wounds in the hair, and the skull beneath it may be fractured, so a scalp wound is closed only after the head injury has been considered. The hand and the limbs carry a further set of considerations, because their wounds threaten movement, feeling, and the circulation beyond them, and a wound of the hand is examined for tendon, nerve, and vessel injury before it is closed. A wound over a joint is not closed with a method that cannot tolerate movement, and the limb is often immobilized after closure so that the repair is not pulled apart by motion. The finding that sends the patient to the operating room is any wound over a fracture, a joint, a tendon, or a vessel, or a scalp wound with a palpable fracture or an abnormal level of consciousness.

A patient who is dying from another injury does not have a wound closed, and this is the principle of life before limb applied one step further as life before skin. The primary survey comes first, so hemorrhage, airway, and breathing are controlled before anyone considers the appearance of a laceration, because a patient bleeding to death in the abdomen will not benefit from a neat closure of the scalp. The damage-control philosophy accepts that some wounds are dressed and left open while the patient is resuscitated and taken to the operating room, and that closure is performed later, when the patient is stable enough to heal it. The repair of a tendon, a nerve, or a vessel is not wound closure, and it is performed in the same operation while the skin may be left open or only loosely approximated, because a repaired tendon must glide, a repaired nerve must not be compressed, and a repaired vessel must not be kinked. A closure that is too tight can cause the same disaster as a bandage that is too tight, because skin pulled together over a swollen limb raises the pressure inside that limb, and the finding that warns the clinician is a limb that is tense and painful with pain that increases when the fingers or toes are stretched. The surgeon who expects severe swelling leaves the skin open on purpose, and a fasciotomy is a procedure of the operating room that no field responder performs.

A wound closed when it should have been left open produces a predictable set of complications, and the responder who recognizes them early shortens the patient's course. The first is the abscess, a collection under the closed skin that produces increasing pain, swelling, and fever and that must be opened and drained. The next is the spreading infection of the soft tissue, which moves beyond the wound, reddens and hardens the skin, and can become the necrotizing infection that threatens the limb and the life. The last is the infection of bone in the open fracture that was closed over, which takes weeks to declare itself and months to treat, and a common teaching places the first signs of wound infection within 24 to 48 hours of the injury, an interval that is only an illustration and must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the timing depends on the organism, the wound, and the patient. After a wound is closed, the patient is told what to watch for, where to return, and whom to call, because increasing pain, spreading redness, discharge, a bad smell, a fever, or a wound that opens all require review. The intervals at which any material is removed differ with the site, and a figure such as 5 days for the face and 10 to 14 days for a limb is taught only as an illustration that must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the site, the patient, and the technique all change the answer.

A patient waiting for closure is also a patient who is exposed, so the team keeps the patient covered, insulates the patient from the cold surface beneath, and keeps the room warm. Cold impairs clotting, deepens shock, and makes the heart more likely to develop a dangerous rhythm, and it is a complication of trauma rather than a detail of comfort. A body temperature below 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which cold itself becomes dangerous, and that figure must be checked against the current guideline and the local protocol, like every other figure in this chapter, because the accepted line differs between services and editions. The finding that warns the team is a patient who has stopped shivering while still cold, and the warming continues through the closure and after it.

Every act of closure belongs to a named provider, and the level is set by training, equipment, authorization, and protocol rather than by the urgency of the moment. The lay first aider covers a wound with a clean dressing, presses on it if it bleeds, keeps the patient warm, and sends for emergency medical services, and the lay first aider does not remove an embedded object and does not close the wound. The trained responder and the paramedic dress and protect the wound, report its position and the mechanism of injury, and, where the local protocol authorizes it, may approximate a small, clean, superficial wound with adhesive strips. The nurse and the physician close wounds within the scope that the local protocol and the law define, while the trauma surgeon owns the closure of the contaminated wound, the bite, the wound with dead tissue, and the wound that needs exploration, debridement, or repair beneath the skin. The techniques of this chapter are learned with a teacher, practiced under supervision, and certified by an authority that also defines who may close a wound and where.

To summarize, wound closure is a decision that comes at the end of a sequence and not at the beginning, and every step before it decides whether it is safe. Bleeding is controlled, the wound is examined for tendon, nerve, and vessel injury, the wound is cleaned, dead tissue and foreign material are removed, and only then is the method chosen. The methods are choices rather than a ladder, and sutures, staples, adhesive strips, and tissue adhesive each suit one wound and harm another, so the site, the tension, the depth, the contamination, the time, and the patient all enter the decision together with the experience of the operator. A bite, a heavily contaminated wound, a puncture, and a wound with a retained foreign body are not closed immediately, and a wound with dead tissue or established infection is never closed, so such wounds are cleaned and dressed open and are often closed later by delayed primary closure under the surgeon's plan. The wound that is closed when it should have stayed open becomes an abscess, a spreading infection, or a sepsis, which is why the conditions for closure are checked before the skin is brought together. Every interval, temperature, and figure in this chapter is an illustration whose exact value must be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, the provider level is named for every act, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country in which you work.

# Chapter 48 — Surgical Treatment

Definitive surgical treatment is the final stage of trauma care and the stage that decides what survival will mean for the patient, and it begins only after the work of the field has been done correctly or deliberately left undone. The operations described here are performed by surgeons in a hospital, and not one of them is a field procedure, even when the injury looks desperate and the hospital seems far away. They are described so that the first responder can understand what each operation is for, what it achieves, and what the prehospital provider must have done or refused to do to make it possible. That understanding shapes the first hour, because a dressing that is not lifted and a tourniquet whose time is written on the patient become part of the operation that follows. Every procedure in this chapter belongs to definitive hospital care, and the chapter is educational material that does not replace training, certification, supervision, local protocol, or the law of the country where you work.

The surgical chain begins before the operating room, in the decision not to become a second casualty, because no patient is saved by a rescuer who is injured at the scene. Traffic, fire, live electricity, fast water, an unstable structure, an animal, and violence are the hazards that kill rescuers, and the patient's own blood, vomit, and tissue carry infection through a break in the skin or a splash into the eye. Those hazards belong to the place where the injury happened, and the responder who cannot make that place safe does not enter it, while the trained responder and the paramedic work only within the authority and the equipment their service provides. Inside the hospital the hazards change shape rather than disappear, and the operating team protects itself with personal protective equipment, with safe handling of needles and blades, and with a plan for a patient who is agitated, intoxicated, or violent. The finding that must travel with the patient is any remaining hazard and any exposure that occurred, because the safety of the next person to touch the patient is part of the same treatment.

The first purpose of any trauma operation is hemostasis, which is the stopping of bleeding at its source under direct vision rather than through a dressing. Hemostasis exists because some bleeding cannot be reached by a hand, a bandage, or a tourniquet, and because a vessel that has retracted into a cavity will keep filling that cavity while the surface looks quiet. The surgeon opens the region, finds the torn vessel, and controls it by pressure at the bleeding point, by tying it off where it can be sacrificed, or by repairing it where the tissue beyond it depends on the flow. What this achieves is a circulation that can be sustained and a patient whose remaining injuries can then be treated, and no field measure replaces it. The prehospital acts that make it possible are all acts of restraint, which are pressure held without lifting the dressing, a tourniquet left in place with its time recorded, a foreign body left undisturbed, and a deformed limb left in the position found. The acts that make it harder are the probing finger, the blindly placed clamp, the loosened tourniquet, and the well-meant straightening of a limb that tears the clot.

An operation also depends on the story that arrives with the patient, and that story has a fixed shape the receiving team listens for. The mechanism of injury is given first, because it predicts which structures lie along the path of the energy and which cavity must be examined first. The time of the injury is given next, because every interval after it changes the urgency of imaging and the order of the operating list. What was done is then stated plainly, including direct pressure, a tourniquet and the exact time it was applied, splints, dressings, and any pain relief given before arrival by the provider authorized to give it. What was not done matters just as much, and the team must hear that an embedded object was left in place, that a bullet was not extracted, that a wound was not explored or closed, and that no attempt was made to straighten a severely deformed fracture. Any change observed on the way, such as a patient who became drowsy or a dressing that soaked through, belongs in the same report, because it is strong evidence that bleeding may still be going on.

Debridement is the surgical removal of tissue that is dead, dying, or so heavily contaminated that it cannot heal, and surgical exploration is the examination of the wound's depths that decides what must be removed and what can be repaired. Debridement exists because devitalized muscle, fat, and skin have no blood supply to carry defense or repair, and because such tissue feeds the bacteria that turn a survivable wound into a lethal infection. The surgeon examines the wound in good light, takes away what will not live, washes the remaining tissue, and repeats the process over the following days as the border between living and dead becomes clear. What this achieves is a wound with a blood supply and a clean surface, which is the only condition under which closure, skin grafting, or healing by itself can succeed. Exploration achieves a precise list of what has been divided and what is intact, and that list decides every repair that follows. A first responder must never probe a wound with a finger or an instrument, must never widen it, and must never test a structure by pulling on it, because each of those acts can complete a partial injury and restart bleeding that had stopped.

Vascular repair restores the flow of blood through a torn artery or vein, and its purpose is to save the limb while protecting the life of the patient who owns it. It exists because a limb whose main artery is divided will die within hours, and because the same injury can drain the circulation long before the limb is ever in question. The surgeon removes the damaged segment, rejoins the healthy ends, or replaces the gap with a length of the patient's own vein, and the repair is then protected by stable alignment of the limb and by close watching for bleeding and for swelling. What it achieves is a limb with a pulse and a patient whose circulation has stopped leaking, and the result depends heavily on how long the tissue was without blood. The field makes this operation possible by controlling hemorrhage without destroying the vessels, by splinting in the position found, by keeping the patient warm, and by reaching a surgical center without delay, and it makes the operation impossible by probing, by clamping blindly, or by loosening a tourniquet that has already controlled the bleeding. When flow returns to tissue that has been starved, that tissue may swell, release substances that harm the body, and provoke a dangerous rhythm of the heart, which is why the surgeon may release pressure inside the limb at the same operation. A period of 2 hours is often discussed as the point at which muscle and nerve begin to suffer lasting harm, and that interval, like every figure in this chapter, is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because tolerance differs with temperature, with age, and with the injury itself.

Tendon repair reconnects a muscle to the bone it moves, and nerve repair reconnects the pathway that carries command and feeling, and both are operations of function rather than of survival. A divided tendon leaves a hand or a foot without power, and a divided nerve leaves skin without feeling and muscle without command, and the loss of feeling is itself dangerous because a numb hand will be burned, cut, or crushed without warning. The surgeon brings the tendon ends together with fine sutures and protects the repair with a splint, and for a nerve the surgeon aligns the ends without tension and may need a length of nerve from elsewhere in the body to bridge a gap. The timing is a surgical judgment, because a clean wound may be repaired at once while a heavily contaminated or infected wound may have the repair delayed until the wound is safe. What these operations achieve is the possibility of recovery and never a promise, since a nerve regrows slowly and incompletely and the result is better in a young patient and in a clean wound. The field must not grasp at a tendon, must not pull on it, must not ask the patient to move against resistance, and must not close the wound over it, and instead it covers the wound, splints in the position found, and records the movement and feeling that were lost. Any new loss of feeling or movement after splinting must be passed on at handover, because that points to pressure that has to be relieved.

Fracture reduction is the manipulation or the operation that restores a broken bone to a position in which it can heal and in which the vessels and nerves beside it are not compressed. It exists because a displaced fracture can kink an artery, stretch a nerve, and lock a joint, and because alignment is the first step toward stability and toward the recovery of function. Reduction achieves a limb that can be held, a wound that can be examined, and a circulation that can be preserved, and it is performed where the patient can be monitored and where bleeding can be controlled if a clot is disturbed. That last point is the reason the first responder never straightens a severely deformed fracture to make it look normal, because moving the fragments can release a clot, complete a partly torn vessel, and turn a contained injury into a free hemorrhage. The field splints the limb in the position found, checks and records what lies beyond the injury, and moves the patient toward the place where reduction can be done safely. The finding that makes reduction urgent rather than elective is a limb that is pale, pulseless, or numb, and even then the reduction belongs to a clinician and not to the roadside.

External fixation holds a broken bone with pins that pass through the skin into the bone and are joined by a frame outside the limb, and it exists because some fractures must be stabilized before the soft tissue can accept a permanent implant. It achieves alignment, control of movement, and access to the wound, so that dressings can be changed and dead tissue removed without losing the position of the bone, and it is used for the open fracture with heavy contamination, where metal inside the wound would give bacteria a surface to grow on. Internal fixation holds the fracture with plates, screws, or rods placed on or inside the bone, and it is the definitive stabilization that allows early movement and reliable healing. Its existence rests on the fact that a bone held still heals in the position it is set, and the surgeon chooses the device according to the bone, the pattern of the break, and the condition of the skin and the muscle, which is a judgment no manual can make. Internal fixation is often deferred in a patient who is cold, still bleeding, or infected, and there is nothing wrong with that delay, because the surgeon is choosing the moment that gives the patient the best chance. The field must never remove, loosen, or adjust a frame, must not use it as a handle for lifting the limb, and must not let anything pull on it during transfer, and its task is to immobilize the limb as it lies and to report exactly how it was found.

Damage control is the philosophy that governs the care of a patient who is too ill to survive the definitive operation, and it reorders the surgeon's whole plan around that fact. It exists because a long and technically perfect operation can kill a patient who is cold, whose blood will not clot, and whose tissues are starved of oxygen, and because those three problems worsen one another in a circle that only resuscitation can break. The first operation is therefore short and focused, and it controls the bleeding, contains the contamination, packs the cavity, and closes the skin only enough to protect what lies beneath. What this achieves is a patient who reaches an intensive care unit, or ICU, alive, where warmth, blood, and time restore the conditions under which a longer operation becomes safe. The definitive repair is then performed in a second planned operation and the final closure in a third, and a wound left open or a fracture left in a temporary frame is a sign of correct judgment rather than of neglect. The listener should carry away the sequence that puts life before limb, in which hemorrhage comes first, contamination second, protection third, and only then the perfect restoration of a limb that can wait.

Fasciotomy is the operation that opens the tough covering around a group of muscles to release pressure that has risen inside a limb, and it is performed to prevent the death of muscle and nerve. It exists because bleeding and swelling inside a closed space can raise the pressure until the small vessels that feed the muscle are compressed, and because muscle starved in that way dies and releases substances that threaten the kidneys and the heart. The surgeon makes a long opening through the skin and the fascia so that the muscle can expand, and the wound is left open afterward because closing it would recreate the pressure that was just relieved. What fasciotomy achieves is a limb with living muscle and a patient protected from the consequences of muscle death, and the result depends on how early the pressure is released, since a late operation saves neither muscle nor function. The field must not create the condition in the first place, so it does not bind a limb tightly, it releases a bandage that has become constricting, it splints without compression, and it moves the patient quickly when pain is severe out of proportion to the wound. The finding that must be reported is pain that increases when the muscles are stretched, together with a limb that is tense and a region of skin that has lost feeling, because a pulse that can still be felt does not rule out the problem. A pressure measured inside the compartment may be quoted as the number that makes the diagnosis, and any such figure is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the accepted value changes with the patient and with the service.

Amputation is the removal of a limb or a part of a limb, and in trauma it appears in two forms that must not be confused. A traumatic amputation is an injury in which the part has already been torn away, and the surgeon's work is to complete the debridement, to shape the stump so that it can heal, and to decide whether the part can be rejoined. An elective amputation is a deliberate operation on a limb that cannot be saved or that threatens life, chosen when the vessels, the nerves, and the muscle are destroyed beyond repair, or when infection and muscle death are spreading faster than they can be controlled. What amputation achieves is survival and a stump that can later be fitted, which is a better outcome than a limb that kills its owner. Replantation, which is the reattachment of a severed part, is an operation of vessels, nerves, bone, tendon, and skin performed in a fixed order, and it succeeds best after a clean cut and worst after a crush or a tear. The field must never complete an amputation, must control the stump with pressure and packing and a tourniquet where the protocol permits, and must send the severed part wrapped in clean material, kept cool, and never placed directly on ice or in water. The decision about reattachment belongs to a trauma center, and the time the part has been without blood is one of the figures that guides it, to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol.

Removal of a foreign body is a surgical decision made when removal serves the patient, and it is never a field procedure. It exists because a retained object such as a bullet, a fragment of metal, a piece of glass, or a splinter of wood can lie in a joint and destroy it, can press on a nerve and cause pain, can sit in a vessel and travel, can enter the eye or the airway, or can slowly release a substance that harms the body. The surgeon removes what is indicated, leaves what is harmless, and searches with imaging and with the track of the wound rather than with a probing finger, and the operation is planned around the structures that lie along the way. What removal achieves is the relief of a specific problem, and the decision must weigh the damage of the search against the harm of leaving the object. A bullet that remains in the body follows a particular rule, and the first of those rules is that a first responder does not extract bullets, because removal is a surgical decision made when there is a clinical reason and because many bullets that cause no problem are left in place and watched. The wound track is not the same as the path of the bullet, since a bullet can be deflected by bone and can end far from where the track appears to point. The field stabilizes an embedded object in place, builds padding around it, moves the patient with it undisturbed, and describes the entry, the exit if there is one, and the object that was left, because removal may release hemorrhage that cannot be controlled and may damage structures that are still intact.

Anesthesia and pain relief are decisions made by the provider authorized to make them under a protocol, and this manual deliberately names no substance, no amount, no route, and no frequency. The surgical point is that an operation cannot proceed safely in a patient whose pain is uncontrolled, whose breathing is impaired, or whose stomach is full, so the anesthesia provider assesses the airway, the lungs, and the patient's recent intake before any procedure. What the field contributes is honesty about what was given, when it was given, and by whom, because the receiving team must not add a second decision on top of an unknown first one. Pain that is severe and out of proportion to the wound is also a clinical finding, because it may be the first sign of compartment syndrome, and it must be reported rather than simply relieved. The finding that makes pain control urgent is a patient whose pain is worsening despite splinting and positioning, and that finding belongs in the handover as a warning rather than as a complaint.

Antibiotics and protection against tetanus belong to the prescriber and to the local protocol, and the surgical decision that surrounds them is a decision about timing and about source control. The reason is that no antibiotic reaches dead tissue or a collection of pus, so the surgeon must open, drain, and remove before the substance can work, and the substance and the amount are chosen by the clinician rather than by this book. The finding that makes the decision urgent is a wound that is deep, heavily contaminated, caused by a bite, or already showing the signs of spreading infection, together with a patient whose vaccination history is unknown or incomplete. What the operation achieves in that setting is source control, in which the infected material is removed, the cavity is drained, and the wound is left open so that it can be watched and cleaned. The field's part is to raise the question early, to describe the wound and the patient accurately, and to refuse to make a prescription out of a manual.

The replacement of blood and the correction of clotting belong to definitive hospital care, and the reason is that they treat a patient whose bleeding has been controlled rather than substitute for controlling it. The surgeon and the resuscitation team decide what is given, in what proportion, and how the patient is warmed, and those decisions are made against the patient's response rather than against a formula printed anywhere. What the field contributes is a careful estimate of blood lost, the number of dressings soaked, the time a tourniquet was applied, and the trend of the patient's level of consciousness and pulse, because these allow the receiving team to judge how much has gone. A patient who is cold, whose blood will not clot, and whose tissues are acidic is a patient in whom surgery must be short, which is the damage-control principle seen from the resuscitation side. The listener should carry away one rule, which is that the operation that stops the bleeding is the treatment, and everything given into a vein supports the patient until that operation is done.

Imaging is the surgeon's map, and it is performed to answer specific questions rather than to look at everything. Computed tomography, or CT, shows the cavities of the chest, the abdomen, and the pelvis and can reveal bleeding, air, and injury to organs that no hand can feel, while ultrasound can be brought to the bedside and repeated, and a chest radiograph shows the lungs, the space around them, and the position of tubes and lines. What imaging achieves is a plan, because the operation that is chosen depends on which structure is injured, and a patient whose circulation is failing may go to the operating room without imaging at all, since the delay would cost more than the information gains. The field's report decides what is imaged and how urgently, because the mechanism of injury and the patient's condition point to the region that must be examined first. The limits of imaging must be understood as well, since a normal image does not exclude an injury, and a picture that does not fit the patient must never overrule the patient.

Closure of a wound is the last step of the surgical sequence and never the first, and the decision to close is made only when the conditions for healing are present. The surgeon closes a clean wound at once, delays closure of a contaminated wound until it has been cleaned and watched, and leaves a wound open when closing it would trap infection inside. What delayed closure achieves is a wound that can be inspected and cleaned each day, and it is the reason a patient may be told that a wound will be closed later rather than now. The field must never close a wound with sutures, staples, adhesive strips, or tissue adhesive, and must never seal a wound that is deep, contaminated, caused by a bite, or holding a foreign body, because closure over such a wound converts a surface problem into a deep infection. The finding that tells the team a wound is ready to close is a wound that is clean, living, and without spreading redness or discharge, and that judgment is made by the clinician who can see it.

Infection that follows trauma is often a surgical problem, because a collection of pus, a piece of dead bone, or a closed space full of contaminated fluid cannot be cured by any substance alone. The surgeon drains the collection, removes the dead tissue, and opens the spaces so that the wound can heal from within, and the operation may need to be repeated until the infection is controlled. What this achieves is the removal of the environment in which bacteria grow, which is the only way some infections are cured. Not every injury that once required an operation now does, and the trauma team may treat an injury to a solid organ such as the liver, the spleen, or a kidney by watching the patient closely instead of opening the abdomen, because an operation on a bleeding organ can itself cause harm. What non-operative management requires is the ability to examine the patient repeatedly, to measure the circulation, and to have imaging and an operating room available within minutes if the patient changes, and the finding that ends that plan is a patient who becomes unstable, whose abdomen becomes more tender and distended, or whose need for blood and fluid keeps rising. The field's part in prevention is surgical in spirit even when no operation is possible, because it removes visible dirt and debris by irrigation, covers the wound, keeps the patient warm, and delivers the patient to care without delay.

The operating room is a place where a team works in a fixed order, and the patient enters it only after the team has confirmed who the patient is, what is known, and what is planned. The surgeon, the anesthesia provider, the nurses, and the technicians each have a role, and the first minutes are spent on the same questions the field asked, which are the airway, the breathing, the circulation, the level of consciousness, and the exposure that reveals hidden injury. What this achieves is that no injury found in the field is lost between the door and the table, and that the operation matches the patient rather than the label on a chart. Documentation is part of the operation, because the tourniquet time, the medicines given before arrival, the wounds covered, and the changes observed are all things the team must have. After the operation the patient is watched as carefully as before it, because the complications of trauma do not end when the bleeding stops, and the patient may return to an intensive care unit, or ICU, for warming, for support of breathing, and for repeated examination. What the team watches for is bleeding that restarts, a limb that becomes tense and painful, a wound that becomes red and foul, a fever, a falling level of consciousness, and difficulty in breathing, since each of these points to a complication that can still be treated if it is found early. The chain from the first hand on the wound to the last dressing in the ward is one treatment, and every link reports to the next.

Hypothermia is a surgical problem and not a detail of comfort, because a cold patient bleeds more, clots poorly, and tolerates both anesthesia and operation worse than a warm one. The patient becomes cold from blood loss, from lying on a cold surface, from undressing for examination, and from fluids that are not warmed, and the operating room must continue the warming that the field began. What warming achieves is a patient in whom the clotting system can work and in whom the heart is less likely to develop a dangerous rhythm, and it is pursued from the scene to the ward without a pause. A body temperature of 35 degrees Celsius is often named as the point at which cold becomes dangerous, and that figure, like every temperature, time, pressure, and depth in this chapter, is an illustration to be confirmed against the current guideline and the local protocol, because the line differs with the patient and with the method of measurement. The field's part is to cover the patient before the journey, to insulate against the ground, to replace wet clothing, and to keep the vehicle warm, and it is done at the same moment as the bleeding is controlled.

A manual can explain what an operation is for, but it cannot teach the operation, and the difference matters at the moment a reader is tempted to act. Every skill described in this chapter is learned with a teacher, practiced under supervision, and certified by an authority that also defines what may be done without it, while local protocol decides which procedures are authorized, which equipment is carried, and which hospital receives the patient. Nothing here names a drug, an amount, a route, or a frequency, and nothing here should be read as permission to perform a surgical act outside the training and authorization that the reader holds. Where this chapter names a time, a temperature, a depth, or a pressure, it explains the reasoning and never sets a rule, because such figures differ between services, countries, and editions of the same guideline. The reader is asked to bring this understanding to training, to keep that training current, and to work within the system that supervises the care.

The prehospital contribution to a good operation is a set of acts and a set of refusals, and the refusals are as important as the acts. The acts are to control hemorrhage with pressure and, where the protocol allows, with packing or a tourniquet, to keep the airway open and the breathing working, to splint what is broken in the position found, to cover wounds with clean material, to keep the patient warm, to observe and record changes, and to move the patient to the right hospital without unnecessary delay. The refusals are to remove an embedded object, to extract a bullet, to probe or explore a wound, to close a wound, to straighten a severely deformed fracture, to loosen a tourniquet that has controlled bleeding, and to bind the chest tightly. Each refusal has a reason that can be spoken aloud, because an object may be plugging a vessel, a bullet belongs to a surgical decision, a wound closed over contamination becomes a deep infection, a straightened limb can tear a vessel, a released tourniquet can bleed again where no one can restore control, and a bound chest cannot expand. A constructed illustration, offered as a construction and never as a real patient or a real incident, shows how the order decides, when a patient arrives with a crushed leg, a tourniquet that has controlled the bleeding, a pale face, and a pulse that is fast and thin. The leg is the injury everyone can see and the temptation is to take the patient to the operating room for the limb at once, but the team treats the circulation first, warms the patient, replaces blood under its own protocol, and performs a short operation that controls bleeding and contamination, leaving the leg in a temporary frame with its wounds open. Only when the patient is warm and stable does the team return for the vascular repair, the debridement, and the fixation, and if the limb cannot be saved, the amputation is performed to save the patient, because life before limb is a sequence and not a slogan.

To summarize, surgical treatment is the definitive stage of trauma care, and every procedure in it exists for a reason that the first responder can understand and must respect. Hemostasis stops bleeding at its source under vision, and it is made possible by pressure held without lifting, by a tourniquet left in place with its time recorded, and by nothing embedded being disturbed. Debridement and exploration remove dead and contaminated tissue and reveal what is torn, vascular repair restores flow to a limb and a circulation to a patient, tendon and nerve repair restore movement and feeling once survival is secure, reduction and external and internal fixation restore and hold alignment, fasciotomy releases pressure that would kill muscle, amputation is chosen when a limb cannot be saved or threatens life, and removal of a foreign body is a surgical decision made only when it serves the patient. The damage-control philosophy governs the patient who is too ill for the definitive operation, and it puts the control of bleeding first, the containment of contamination second, and the complete repair later, because a cold patient whose blood will not clot cannot survive a long operation.
